Supreme Commander is an excellent RTS that still stands with the best of them even 10 years later.
The good:
- 4 factions which are well balanced
- Massive scale makes it good for macro players, but micro players can zoom right down and control individual units
- Unique resource scheme means that controlling your build is more crucial than ever.  Just two resources are available but the capability to over-subscribe and go into negatives makes it surprisingly nuanced.
- This isn't just a rush-fest.  Turtling is just as viable in this game.  A large variety of playstyles can be used each with their strengths and weaknesses.  Nothing quite beats the thrill of completing that massive artillery piece after 1.5 hours of real-time building it, then subsequently crushing your opponent fromacross the map.
The bad:
- Weak AI means that you have to use cheating AI, which is just unfair.  The Sorian AI helps but doesn't conpletely correct this.
- Online lobbies are a bit weak.  Thankfully Forged Alliance Forever largely fixes this:
The ugly:
- The un-modded AI tries to control dead units, which means that the game will slow down over time.  To make things worse, the original game hails from 2006 when multi-core CPUs were in their infancy.  As such it is single-threaded and your fancy 8-core CPU won't help.  All this means that the game will slow to a crawl during long player vs. AI games.  You really need the Sorian AI mod to fix this.  It is built into FaF:

Rating 7/10
Overview: Third Person Action
The Good:
+ Art style and presentation
+ In addition to the 12 main missions there are side missions and challenges, you can play every mission after you complete the game with different difficulties to try and get a higher ranking providing a lot of replay-ability.
+ The combat although simplistic for a Japanese action game, controls very well and feels very satisfying killing enemies. Combat revolves around slashing enemies and dodging at the right time. Hitting enemies also fills up a meter which allows you to pull off one hit kills.
+ Killing enemies rewards you with different types of gems that increase health, blood meter and skills
+ Cool looking bosses
The Average:
What happens when you do drugs and decided to write a story? You get a Suda51 game. This is one crazy game which is to be expected if you ever played any other Suda games before. Its not good or bad but it certainly is unique and creative. The dialogue can be pretty bad at times and the characters are one dimensional.
The camera can be problematic especially when you move against walls.
30 frames per second although this can be modified in .ini files which may cause some problems.
Easy achievements although many of them require some grinding
The Bad:
- A bizarre mini game has you ogling at women's private parts filling up a meter after which you can then give gifts in order to win her favor. Give enough gifts and watch a sex scene play out. Why is it in the game...who knows, like everything else in the game in doesn't make sense and it feels completely out of place.
- very poor graphical options
- The game froze on me and after rebooting my computer I lost my save file with no way of recovering it.
Conclusion:
I had a lot of fun with this even though it felt really strange at times. If you are a fan of Japanese action games this is a good game to check out.

Killer is Dead can be described as a weird and strange action hack and slash game.
The art style is unique in a way that sometimes you have the feeling that this is a sort of LSD-trip.
The story is very confusing and to this day I still not know what exactly I was doing. There are a lot of cut scenes that tell the story. It’s something complicated like some anime movies.
In short you play an assassin who’s called Mondo. Your weapons are a katana blade and a bionic arm – which can also transform I a gun that shoots blood. The fighting is rather simple and there are not a lot of combo’s – this is not a Devil May Cry style of game – the most important here is to learn to dodge and block enemy attacks. The game can be very violent and is not for children.
Graphic style: this can only be described as weird. It’s not something for everyone – check some YouTube videos
Sound: music and sound effects are OK
Gameplay: this sort of game plays best with a gamepad. I played it with an Xbox One wired controller and it works flawlessly.
Quality of the console port: this game is a console port and it has been ported with almost no graphic options. Resolutions are limited to 1920*1080. The only way to use other resolutions is via editing of an ini-file (check the forums) and via the program ‘Flawless Widescreen’. I tested it with a resolution of 2560*1080 and it works.
I took me 11 hours to finish. Replay value comes from playing higher difficulty, finding all the secrets, getting high high scores for every level and missions.

I played this title when it was given out to Xbox Live Gold members and even for free this game is a trainwreck. The art style in itself isn't bad, it's that the characters look so lazily designed, and feel so cheaply animated that it damages the actual appearance of the game. Another thing I noticed that damages the art style is that all the menu and ingame text uses some slim sans-serif font that doesn't fit the aesthetic of the game. Besides that though, it doesn't even feel like a proper puzzle game, as it feels more like a mobile cash grab than anything considering my next point.
The game itself is broken up in three ways, there's the typical free version with barely any elements that you can get by either owning their other game, or having a friend who owns tumblestone to give you a trial key they generate. Then there's a MP only version that you buy for $10, and then the full version with SP and MP. Guess how much the full version costs at full price? Yep. $24.99 is way too much for a puzzle game, especially one as lousy feeling as this. I'd suspect people who see appeal in puzzle games to be able to enjoy this, but personally it just feels cheap. The price is wrong, the marketing strategy about how they forced trials on some people that I am reading from other reviews is wrong. I'm not a developer, or a marketing expert, but pushing your games onto people is never a good idea.
Overall a TLDR;
• Personally I find the character design lazy and boring. Large head, little body. Half circle feet and floating Rayman hands.
• The fonts and character animations used contradict the overall theme of the game.
• The game was split into paid MP and SP+MP, and a free version that basically begs people to buy it. The price of the game is way too high.
• The developers supposedly forced a trial of this game unto previous customers of their other game, and managed to get it into their library through humble bundle to spread the games publicity.
• Don't even think about getting this without a heavy discount.

Aesthetically ugly, almost disturbingly so, this game sees fit to start you off with at least 10 levels of the most tedious, boring puzzle gameplay you may ever experience in your life. It's quite simple - you have a stack of colored blocks, and you can only remove blocks from the bottom of the stack. You must remove 3 of the same color in a row, or else you fail and have to start over. That's it. As far as I can tell this is literally the entire game. I was bored to tears in record time with this game because the concept is so simple and the developers give you nothing to change up the formula.
I only made it 10 levels in, but here's why: After maybe 15 minutes of this game, nothing new was added to the formula. Nothing changed. Every level felt as if it may as well have been randomly generated from the same algorithm. No progression, very little difficulty, absolutely nothing to latch onto. At level 10, the very first new mecahnic was introduced: basically, a glorified timer. Nothing new, just a time limit you need to complete the level under or else have to restart. And also, it comes with another neat trick: this level is three times as long as the previous ones, because you have to clear three separate fields, one after the other. Naturally, I got stuck at the very end of the third field with 6 blocks left on the board, failed, and it started me back at board one.
Immediately uninstalled, hid the game from my library and thanked God that this Humble Monthly came with one of the best puzzle games I've played (The Witness), because quite frankly this game is easily one of the worst. I can't even fathom how the developers can justify the $25 price point. I'm sure there's more to it than what I played, but purely judging on the basis of the disgusting visual design, how poorly they ease you into the difficulty of the puzzles, and how ridiculously long they stretch out the most basic gameplay elements and force you to do the same uninteresting thing over and over again without introducing new concepts, this is definitely a serious contender for the worst puzzle game I've ever played.
Also, couldn't help but notice that on the MAIN MENU of the game (keeping in mind, the OPTIONS menu is hidden underneath a sub-menu in EXTRAS) there's a giant option to send a Steam code for this game to a friend. Clearly, this developer is just throwing around every shady tactic they can think of to saturate everyone's Steam libraries with this game.
It's like taking a♥♥♥♥♥♥and saying it's the best puzzle game in years!

The game uses a "hub" system. Combat is instanced in small (and incredibly repetitive) areas. Content is recycled for about 20 levels all the way up to level cap, meaning for every twenty levels of play you're killing the same stuff, but recolored, in the same areas, either forward, or backward.
Classes are varied, but they are also gender-locked. Some classes have a lot of similarity, but they simply created a female version because thongs sell better than boxers (no joke, females are basically barbie dolls to dress up). Content is plentiful, but experiencing and unlocking this content is a nightmare. You are expected to run the same dungeons over and over, and when you're not doing that, you're reading (or skipping) long, tedious storylines that you are only able to skip one dialogue sentence at a time (how long can your index finger or thumb mash on those buttons before they're just sore?).
This means that even when they have Bonus EXP events, you will actually out-level the content that you're in. You are REQUIRED to play a lot of missions twice or more in order to fully "complete" the requirements to unlock the next mission. There are at least THREE LAYERS of restrictions on content, either "Completion" points, "storyline" completion or "character level". These three restrictions can be infuriating to deal with, since the majority of the content in the game (the normal story missions) can literally be completed in a matter of minutes.
I am not joking when I say you will spend more time talking (reading text) to NPCs than you will actually doing missions. You will have to talk to one, two, three, four or more NPCs to learn about a particular mission, and then it will only take you about two minutes SOLO to complete said mission. Only exception to this is Raid Bosses. They are the only fun element in Vindictus, but if you play in a full party (there is no level restrictions, you can get hard carried in these raids) then you can normally get away with dancing in a corner doing nothing while your allies whipe the boss in several minutes.
Another problem with this game is the business model. They've tried to be as fair as possible, but in the end what they've come up with is a system that heavily rewards paying users by giving them more exp, more loot, better loot, better consumables (potions you can drink while laying on the ground), more teamplay items (revive tokens etc) and just overall a better experience.
Being a free player in Vindictus is tedious, tiresome and not necessarily rewarding. To be a free player you need to spend dozens of hours preparing for the next section of the game either by crafting, buying/selling on the market or collecting mats from dungeons. This process is incredibly time-consuming, and does not feel rewarding. Finally acquiring that "next level" set of armor is only the first part of the puzzle. You will craft items in random (and disquesting) colors so if you care even a little bit what you look like then you'll be obligated to proceed to the next part of the process which is customizing the color.
If you do not buy things with real money you will literally be spending millions of gold (3.5mil approx for one color) to get the specific colors that you want. If you don't mind wasting time (and gold) you can roll for random colors for signifigantly less, but normally you will get hard clashing colors, desaturated colors, or poop brown. A lot of the time there is one item in the set that simply does NOT roll the same colors as the rest of the outfit, so you will have a clashing color no matter how much time and effort you spend rolling. Best bet is to farm gold to buy dyes directly from players. Unless you're fine with spending $3 to randomly get a color from six possibilities. Yeah, you read that right. $3 to gamble colors. That's Vindictus.
The other things you can buy through the real-money store is essentially wigs and underwear. There is a "depot" that contains pets, consumables etc. and if you plan to be a serious Vindictus player then you simply can't get away with NOT buying from the depot.
Casual players will want their characters to look decent, so they will likely want a wig and some underwear. $10 a piece. Why? Because breast physics and buttcracks. If you use the default, you'll have an ugly white cotton undershirt and shorts. Basically all the armor sets are designed WITHOUT these inner-armors in mind, so they will stick out like a sore thumb.
With all of these things listed above I simply will not recommend this game to anybody, ever. The business model is awful and punishes free players in almost every possible way. The pacing of the game is incredibly inconsistent and painful (literally, my finger & thumb go numb when I play for more than 30 minutes) and the story is your typical Eastern Anime-themed "Oh noes I'm a diety but because I'm a helpless girl I need every strong man to save me from stupid situations" and frankly it drove me nuts. You're a member of a mercenary group and the amount of petty squabbles, incompetent recruits (and generals) and whatnot is just appalling. It's hard to believe that these people even know which end of the sword to carry.
Don't bother with Vindictus. When it first came out it was basically the first Western MMO to play like this, but now we have different games that do the same thing in a much more fair and reasonable fashion (Tera, for example). This game will try your patience, hurt your fingers, frustrate you when it should be entertaining you. Unless you're a horny teenage boy or girl that likes looking up skirts, avoid like the plague.

Far Cry 2 is hard to reccomend these days. A few terrible ideas really kill this games mojo right from the start. Lets start with the bad.
- First off, the driving in this game is extremly boring, and you will be doing a lot of it. Not only is the driving about the worst driving ever experienced in a game in the 3D era, but if an enemy spots you while driving by, they immediately start shooting, no matter how close or far away from the action they may be. This wouldn't matter, but the more damage your vehicle takes, the slower it goes. So three or four pistol shots, and your already tortise slow car is slowed to a snails pace. Driving anywhere in the extremely limited environment of the game is not fun, and walking is preferred. Can't say I remember any other game where I would rather walk, that's impressivly bad.
- The "gun system" in this game is horribly flawed. If you pick up a gun off of an enemy, that gun will jam and lock up frequently. This can be alleviated by purchasing guns yourself, but in many instances you will be forced to drop that paid for gun because it is out of ammo. Thus, you always find yourself using the bunk guns way more often than you would like. It would be all fine and dandy, but your opponents don't feel the effects of their bunk guns. Thus, most fire fights become frusturating as Billy Bob empties thousands of rounds in your direction, without so much as a hiccup, but you sit there beating on the side of your shotgun every 10 to 15 shots (almost exactly). These inferioir guns also just break out of the blue, leaving you without said weapon. The resulting experience is not good, and really acts as a hinderance in the face of otherwise solid gunplay mechaincs. Nice idea, terrrible execution and it really downgrades the experience by a good bit. Eventually you get upgrades to hold more ammo, but that can't come quick enough and the jamming guns never quite seem to go away.
-The map is also one of the worst in game maps I can remeber. You must always glance down at your map, but you have to stop entirely if you want to see the bottom half of your map (which is usually most of the map). Also, there is GPS in every. Single. Car. No matter how crappy, even if it is a four wheeler. Not realistic at all, if that is what they were going for, and it does not work well. The end result is tediously following this map to make sure you are going in the right direction, which does not work well in the limited environment.
-The limited enviroment is awful. Narrow roads with enemy "guard posts" every so often, so there is no exploring or even trying to evade these enemies. The only way to move past these guard posts (without killing your vehicle of course) is to get out and take the enemies out one by one. Makes for a very slow pace to completing missions and such.
-Bugs break this game from time to time. Every time I start this game, I must hit Shift, Alt, Enter to make the screen fullscreen. There is no clickable option, you just have to remeber that little combo every time you open the game. Again, this is just another "small" inconvience that makes this game largely an annoyance more than an enjoyment.
Now for the good.
-This game looks incredible, even today. The graphics really are amazing for a game this old.
-The sound is spot on, weapons sound good. Fire is probably the best effect in the game, explosives are unimpressive and bland, though taking out vehicles is satisfying.
-My X360 controller plugs right in and is recongized immediately by the game, which is nice. This game was mainly made and sold for consoles unlike it's predeccessor; a controller is highly reccomended.
-It was $4 on Steam sale.
This game is a good game to grab for less than $5. Any more than that and I couldn't reccomend it. It is too dated, too buggy, too flawed in its execution to be worth any more than that. Having played and owned the first three games in the Far Cry series mutiple times, I can safely say this isn't the worst in the series (that would be you, Far Cry 1), but that doesn't mean it is anywhere close to far Cry 3.

I played Far Cry 2 after I played Far Cry 3.
It was neat seeing an unpolished version of what would lead to Far Cry 3. As a study in video game evolution, it might be worth it.
Pros
-You can see the map while driving vehicles (you don’t have to toggle between the map and playing)
-Weapon degradation. I actually liked this. You had to make sure your weapons were in good condition before jumping into a fight. If you didn’t, they could jam, or even break, and you would have to scrounge new weapons. Undone a little by having infinite free mint weapons at the weapon store.
-The bolt-action sniper rifle is very satisfying.
Cons
-No fast travel (not quite accurate, but close). Anywhere you want to go on the map, you have to move yourself. It makes you appreciate vehicles very much. There is a bus system, but the bus stops are few, and in remote areas. More than half the game will be spent in transit through the beautiful but repetitive African landscape.
-You cannot save outposts, so even if you destroy a checkpoint, on your return trip, it can still be dangerous. Nowhere is really ever safe.
-The challenge does not scale. Enemies do not become craftier, or carry better weapons, or a variety of weapons, or equip armour. The enemies you fight at the beginning are the same ones you fight at the end. From a narrative perspective, this makes sense, but as soon as you have your preferred weapon set, the game becomes a matter of rinse and repeat (again, most of which is spent driving).
-Story. The story barely exists, and does not really grab you. The main and side missions rarely seem to make sense, but you do them to progress the plot or unlock things. There is no variety (even in the dialogue) to the side missions for the gun shop or assassinations. You end up working for both sides in the conflict, but secretly, so out in the field, everyone is hostile. When you see someone, you don’t care to identify what faction they are (it doesn’t matter), or even if they’re hostile (everyone is), you just go ahead and shoot.
-Characters. The characters seem as if they were written intelligently, and then poorly executed. You never really learn what any of their motivations are, or even why they’re around. Your buddies just kind of show up, and then you’re magically friends out of nowhere. The dialogue is delivered fast, and without a pause for breath, making it sound very bizarre. Especially since the player character is silent.
-personal pet peeve: every single weapon is left-handed, but used as a right-handed weapon.
Conclusion:
This game is more like a driving simulator set in a war-torn nation than an action game.

I don't know about Hearthstone as I never played it, but I can't help but notice it's comparison with Magic the Gathering which I played for many years. Let me start off by saying I think this game is really good, if you've played MtG than you'll notice it's very similar yet with a slightly streamlined style which works very well. For a start you don't have to tap cards, and instead of declaring attackers and choosing defenders, this game has implemented a sytem where you directly choose who you want your creatures to attack. This makes the game play very smoothly and it's much quicker too. The drawback this game has in comparison however is that it does lack the same level of depth as MtG as there's less phases to the game, such as you can't case instant spells or react to enemy moves. However, what this game does so well is implement a few other mechanics which retain a level of depth which keeps the game challenging and engaging. One of these is the prophesy/rune system which allows you to draw a particular card in reaction to being attacked at certain stages of the game, this system actually allows for a bit of reaction play such as tapping down an attacker if they're making a critical attack in the last moment. Another great thing about the prophesy system is that it allows the losing player to draw extra cards which forces the later stages of the game to remain challenging for both players. Another interesting system is the lanes mechanic which means you have to plan ahead which side of the board you want to play cards, this works very well and adds yet more depth to the game.
As a MtG player I've found it very easy to translate my skills directly across to Elder Scrolls Legends, the colours mostly play the same rolls with a few aspects mixed around, there's also a lot of the same creature skills but with different names such as; breakthrough-trample, lethal-deathtouch, drain-lifelink, charge-haste, etc... although there's no flying. ESL although has it's own guard system which works well with the way it lets you choose attackers giving the defending player a sufficient way of protecting themselves.
I've played through the story mode which is really fun and the rewards are satisfying and allows for great fully customised decks. The soulstone system is great allowing you to gain extra cards of choice to further improve your decks strategy. The arena mode is also great allowing you to use tickets which can be bought with real money or earned in game coins and enter as sort tournament fighting against other real players where you draft a deck on the spot from card choices. The card art is wonderful, and although there's some aspect of pay to win I've found no problem with playing my decks against other players and not getting overpowered.

This is one of those games where perhaps you just had to be there to get it. I am a huge adventure fan and have been for almost 30 years, but somehow i missed this one first time around. Although Grim Fandango has all the ingredients for a great story - noir setup, swingin' jazz, Chicano swagger and a fabulously imaginative mythology - the actual mechanics and story structure don't hold up any more. You know an adventure game failed when trying to solve the puzzles is so tedious you resort to following a walkthrough all the way through, and it's still tedious.
There is lots of repetitive running back and forth to collect objects that form implausible solutions to opaque puzzles rarely even hinted at in dialog. There are also some frustrating timing puzzles that are made all the more painful by a truly awful user interface (most egregious example: to switch items you have to click one by one through your whole inventory). And for some puzzles there is an elaborate setup that if you miss one tiny piece you are stuck retracing your steps for the billionth time. But, most disappointingly, as cool as the character designs are i just didn't end up caring about any of them because the dialog lacks emotional weight. Perhaps i would not have noticed these things if i had played it in 1998, but in 2016 when adventure game interfaces have become so streamlined, when their characters are so much more deeply developed, when their stories are tackling poignant themes head-on, when their puzzles are intuitive and not a chore... This is really rough. I'm sure people who liked it back in the day will get a blast of nostalgia from this remaster, but if you're a modern adventure gamer into the sort of stuff that's come out in the last 5-10 years, this is going to be more of a history lesson than a tight and compelling story.

This is such a beautiful game... great characters, great story. It's absolutely hilarious but also has very touching and sad moments. The writing is brilliant. Puzzles can get quite difficult and confusing, but overall most are fair. Many say that this is one of the best adventure games ever made and you can't argue with that. It's a masterwork and hopefully they remaster more adventure games (ie. Lucasarts) from the 1990s.

DRAGON BALL XENOVERSE 2 is kind of a crap shoot in my opinion, if you like the genre you will probably enjoy the game well enough, if you don't I can't recommend the game. The current purchasing price(non-sale) is rather too much for the content in my opinion which feels extremely repetitive. As such my current recommendation comes with the tag of “only if it’s on sale.”
There is a series of things I enjoyed about XENOVERSE 2:
The fighting is fun and rather unique and doesn’t suffer as much from the repetitious nature that most fighting games seem to suffer from. This is primarily from the number of different special moves you can choose to equip your character with. Not to mention not fighting on a 2D plane really helps keep things interesting.
Most of the special moves have that anime epic attack feel to them making the special moves really fun to use.
Finally the voice acting in the game isn’t completely terrible as most games sent over from Japan seem to be. I know this might be a sentiment not echoed by all but to me the voice acting wasn’t a complete game breaker as it usually is.
There is a series of things I disliked about XENOVERSE 2:
The missions get really really really repetitive, go in stop world ending situation, beat up a bunch of baddies, repeat. This is pretty much the formula for the entire core game which takes away from you ever feeling like your character is a living person in a living universe(just a punching machine).
The online game play situation is really abysmal, the game totes you going in and playing with your friends but god forbid you ever just want to play with some random players to clear a difficult mission. Finding a online game to jump in on has been the bane of my existence since release.
Lastly the story, yes I know this is a Dragon Ball game so the story has been done many times before, and yes fans generally want to see or play their favorite characters. However, would it hurt to maybe diverge from this formula? Instead of being a character in someone else's story why can’t a story be your story, something that from start to finish has you as the main character instead of a character surrounded by main characters (I mean the writers set up a multiverse, why not use it).
I know I'm repeating myself, but buy this game when it is on sale.

Like oh so many early access titles, Grav looks like it ended up as abandonware...but it is so unfair to give negative reviews to a game, just because they stopped development (be it permanent or temporary).
Even as it is right now, the game is defintely worth a purchase, even at full price.
It has very good graphics and decent gameplay.
Yeah yeah, it has a lot more potential...that will never be fulfilled...story of our lives.
Yes its abandonware looks like, and yes it should have (and could have) been more of it, but as it is, you get your money's worth, that i can guarantee.
You wont get all the polish that this game could have got, but you get 100+ hours of good entertainment if you are into survival/crafting games.
After 200hrs of playing, i could say the game was very entertaining, and it left me wanting for more, wishing it would live up to its full potential...if you ever played a good early access you know exactly what im talking about.
This one looks like it wont get developed further, but even as it is, i can fully recommend it, even for the full price you will get more quality entertainment out of it than many a full-fledged release that cost more and offer less.
Highly recommended if you are into survival-building-crafting games.
Similar games i played would be Savage Lands, Fragmented, and 7 days to die, but Grav has its own personality, making it worth playing even after playing the above mentioned titles.
What im trying to say is that this game ofers quality entertainment for 100+ hrs, and i was very satisfied with what i got for my money (paid full price).
Personally i dont give a toss if it will be developed further or not, as it stands, its a good quality game. Yes it could be more, and we players would want more, but even without further development, what the developer offered is well worth the asking price....and thats the bottomline for me.

One of my favorite 2K's to day. I started playing 2K8 casually, got into 2K10 and continued from then on. The game seems more realistic and is smoother than past games, graphics are amazing even on lower settings, and the game modes are now more immersive and realistic.
Despite what people say, this game is not bad. There are microtransactions, yes, but I think it isn't an issue. I mainly play full games on MyLeague, and full games on MyCareer, so I get 1k+ VC per game. I think the fact that people are complaining that they can't make their MyPlayer or MyTeam to be 80+ overall in a few days is a result of being spoiled by doing so in the past. I think it's ludicrous that people are complaining that you can't do this. I think this makes the game more realistic and rewarding. Sure, people won't play more than 5 seasons on MyCareer max, but to start out as an All-Star rookie is stupid. This allows you to actually improve your player and become dedicated to that, otherwise if you want to take the cheap-not-so-cheap way to get to 80+ you need to pay, which helps fund 2K.
Actual gameplay wise, the game's only fault in my opinion is the ability to get steals. You get called for a reach more often than not, and if the ball runs into a player, the ball will either be glitched through the player or will be an immediate turnover. People complain that lay-ups are not realistic or you shoot a shot you never intended to, but that is all because they're inexperienced. If you actually paid attention to 2KTV or did some shoot around/tutorial you would know that the positioning of the shot sticks and movement sticks (if you use a controller, otherwise you're a looney for using the keyboard) matter a whole lot on influencing your shot.
TL;DR = Game is the best basketball game rn, cons are over exaggerated and produced by inexperienced players.

The Good:
+ Art style and presentation
+ In addition to the 12 main missions there are side missions and challenges, you can play every mission after you complete the game with different difficulties to try and get a higher ranking providing a lot of replay-ability.
+ The combat although simplistic for a Japanese action game, controls very well and feels very satisfying killing enemies. Combat revolves around slashing enemies and dodging at the right time. Hitting enemies also fills up a meter which allows you to pull off one hit kills.
+ Killing enemies rewards you with different types of gems that increase health, blood meter and skills
+ Cool looking bosses
The Average:
What happens when you do drugs and decided to write a story? You get a Suda51 game. This is one crazy game which is to be expected if you ever played any other Suda games before. Its not good or bad but it certainly is unique and creative. The dialogue can be pretty bad at times and the characters are one dimensional.
The camera can be problematic especially when you move against walls.
30 frames per second although this can be modified in .ini files which may cause some problems.
Easy achievements although many of them require some grinding
The Bad:
- A bizarre mini game has you ogling at women's private parts filling up a meter after which you can then give gifts in order to win her favor. Give enough gifts and watch a sex scene play out. Why is it in the game...who knows, like everything else in the game in doesn't make sense and it feels completely out of place.
- very poor graphical options
- The game froze on me and after rebooting my computer I lost my save file with no way of recovering it.
Conclusion:
I had a lot of fun with this even though it felt really strange at times. If you are a fan of Japanese action games this is a good game to check out.

Killer is Dead can be described as a weird and strange action hack and slash game.
The art style is unique in a way that sometimes you have the feeling that this is a sort of LSD-trip.
The story is very confusing and to this day I still not know what exactly I was doing. There are a lot of cut scenes that tell the story. It’s something complicated like some anime movies.
In short you play an assassin who’s called Mondo. Your weapons are a katana blade and a bionic arm – which can also transform I a gun that shoots blood. The fighting is rather simple and there are not a lot of combo’s – this is not a Devil May Cry style of game – the most important here is to learn to dodge and block enemy attacks. The game can be very violent and is not for children.
Graphic style: this can only be described as weird. It’s not something for everyone – check some YouTube videos
Sound: music and sound effects are OK
Gameplay: this sort of game plays best with a gamepad. I played it with an Xbox One wired controller and it works flawlessly.
Quality of the console port: this game is a console port and it has been ported with almost no graphic options. Resolutions are limited to 1920*1080. The only way to use other resolutions is via editing of an ini-file (check the forums) and via the program ‘Flawless Widescreen’. I tested it with a resolution of 2560*1080 and it works.
I took me 11 hours to finish. Replay value comes from playing higher difficulty, finding all the secrets, getting high high scores for every level and missions.

Some days, you want to release tension by head-shotting every single enemy in your sights. And some days, you are better off breathing deep and collecting your thoughts.
Viridi does not offer you the possibility to shoot anything, but it is one of the best methods I have found to take the time out of the day to pause and breathe for a little while.
The mechanics are very very simple, so even if you forget them you can easily relearn them. You see your plant, and if it is thirsty, you water it. You can sing to the plant if you want my scrolling till you are very close to it, and it's nice, but if you don't want to do it, you don't need to.
You can check in to see how your plants are growing every day, and you can even get achievements for growing your plants to full maturation and for being there when they flower, but if you only check in every once in a while, the plants are A-OK, they just need more watering.
It's a game that rewards patience, and requires very little actual input on your part to keep going, but that does reward you for continued playing, which I have found is the best way to make any habit stick.
Plus, learning that plants have a saturation point at which they die from being overly watered actually helped me not kill a plant IRL, so kudos to that.
tl;dr the game is calm and pretty and relaxing. if you are looking for that, awesome! if you are looking for literally anything else, it might disappoint
ps: the snail is immensely cute

An enjoyable game which can be played on practically any computer system. Far Cry 2 introduces some unique and interesting mechanics to the series which welcome an engrossing experience for all to participate in.
In Far Cry 2 (released 2008 by Ubisoft), the protagonist's goal is to eliminate the person distributing weapons to the factions on the island. In order to achieve this, you must do several jobs to gain trust and intel to where the antagonist can be found and over time you'll eventually get enough intel and you'll have the chance to meet the antagonist face to face. While this is a tense moment, it provides a welcome last minute twist to the politically driven story.
My first play-through was just completed with Dylan's Realism Mod and a HD model/texture mod, and the game looked respectable in quality and gameplay and so I began. It was also on the regular difficulty level as I tend to play on the medium difficulty on games I haven't already played, but I regret this decision as the game was seemingly too easy. This is likely because the only type of enemies are humans which only take a couple of bullets. Despite the virtually invincible protagonist who can take infinite bullets in comparrison, the ease of this game will be determined by your hand-eye co-ordination and this is a welcome change in a market flooded with games which operate on different values.
I was recommended that this game should be played initially with mods due to its "incompleteness", but aside from the "incompleteness" the game came in high regard as being one of the best FPS games of all time, the best in the Far Cry series and simply made like games used to be made. Is it the best of all time, definitely not - but it certainly is one of the best survival style first person shooters in that it makes you value your life and you want to plan for survival.
The game style took some getting used to in the beginning, and there was no clearly defined campaign path to follow. Such to this, I was able to explore a variety of side missions and features prior to getting into the campaign officially.
So you're in Africa and you have malaria, so you're in dire need for drugs to stay alive, while at the same time running for your life with jammed weapons which can sometimes completely explode on you, and then your head is wanted by everybody on the island for a steep price due to the damage you undertake since arriving on the island. This game really builds on the importance of survival, but there was a missed opportunity on top of the realism mod which I was using - but it could have been far more engrossing. I missed the animal attacks from Far Cry 3 as it is a survival and there was a massive opportunity for lions, tigers, bears, rhinos, elephants and the works. I've seen many zebras and I have heard there are lions which never attack, but it would have been really cool to include an animal mechanic such that of Far Cry 3. I would have also liked to have seen an optional eating/drinking mechanic where survival would really reign supreme, but I understand that would be asking too much.
In all this is a solid example of what a first person shooter should be. Shooters have always been about fun and graphics, but the survival style for me has always flopped with only one other namable exception to the rule - the Metro series.

When I first played this game, I underestimated on how addictive Far Cry 2 can be. I just cannot stop playing it and kept going on for hours.
What the game did right:
This game is similar to its predecessor but expands the limited open world that the first Far Cry game was trying to construct on.  The environment is now far more diverse, ranging from dry savannahs to humid jungles with thick vegetation.  There is also a dynamic weather system in which fog can overtake the land or a rainstorm can appear and change the way you play.
Adding to its wide ranges of landscapes, I can argue one of the more "tactical benefits" this game boasts is its fire.  A lot of games have a blaze kept at a constant size but FC 2 offers greater realism in that part. Throw a Molotov Cocktail at a dry patch of grass and see the fire consume the grass with its voracious appetite but in a humid climate, it will inflict little damage.
The A.I. of your enemies are no longer the same "dimwits" that got slaughtered in FC 1. If you're spotted out in the open or make too much noise near guard posts, they will come for you. They also converse with each other and try to protect themselves from the player which reflects real life. In one instance, a downed mercenary will be helped by another merc.
Stealth has been improved. If you're careful enough, your reward is being able to silently take down one enemy after another. For the most part, their awareness is fairly balanced, unlike FC 1 in which the mercs couldn't tell if someone else was firing a loud weapon but still could see the player behind tents and bushes. Also, your choices on when to use stealth makes a big difference. For example, you can go at night where potential assailants cannot easily see you but are alert.
A unique feature that FC 2 has is its buddies. They are in the game to help you with missions, increase your reputation by providing optional quests, or save you if your well-being has been thrashed to zero. I do enjoy interacting with them upon taking missions.
When combining the aforementioned aspects, you can do missions with almost any mentod you want.  You can either quitely sneak past foes or go in guns blazing. It's all up to you. Exploring doesn't easily get dull and the replay value is high.
While I do favor this game, some problems are existant.
What the game should have avoided doing wrong:
The voice acting for most of the characters is inauspicious. Most of the characters speak too fast and have a flat tone. One of your buddies' dialogue sounds like it was taken from Google translate and that makes it inauthentic.
Over time, the side missions get repetitive. The "convoy missions" are the most subjected to this.  It gets quickly mundane to find circling rival arms vendors and blow up their trucks. The worst part is if you want to have better weapons sooner, there's no other way around this other than to proceed through the main objectives most of the time.
The "weapon degradation system" is one that I have debated in choosing if it's interesting to keep in a game or conclude it's mostly annoying to have in a firefight. As of now, I have decided that it's a nuisance as some weapons degrade too quickly and jam at the worst times. Also, close to the end of the game, even with reliability upgrades, the game will punish you if your shots miss too much and you cannot obtain new weapons (unless you stored them).
Also, the malaria mechanism is very annoying, with no way to ever stop it, only delay it. When you're under attack by that damn disease, you can barely see well and cannot sprint away from danger. Although it doesn't last that long, it may cost some precious seconds for you to flee.
The diamond cases in this game may somewhat excite newcomers for a while but it's painful to endure when trying to reach for some diamonds on a cliff. Although not necessary to find, it's just a distraction from what the game can truly offer.
I did mention you can interact with your buddies, but that's very limited.  All you can do is accept 2 of their quests and after that, they will just say "hi" if you meet them regularly.
The (re)spawning of enemy mercenaries in certain locations is downright stupid. In one case, you can take down all enemies in a base but when you leave for a certain distance and look back with a scope, the place is then refilled with enemies as if nothing has happened. The developers should have put a time limit in how fast enemies can respawn when you're sufficiently far away.
The A.I. is good when confronting them but when they drive, it's a mess. The drivers tend to have problems in making a  U-turn and are horrible in judgement. One time, a patrol car tried to run me over but it missed and plunged into the water.
Finally, the storyline is woefully linear. Though understandable, your choices are very narrow and don't have much impact on the game. Trying to avoid providing spoilers, it's the same "bad" ending, if you decide to detonate some explosives or bribe some border guards to help out a fleeing country in need.
Other:
I haven't tried out multiplayer yet but I have heard that it's dead, which is sad. However, if you feel like allowing your imagination demanding to make a map with the African landscape, there is a map editor that is easy to use. Shamefully, it's quite limited and it's meant for multiplayer.
Customizing this game is almost impossible to do, unlike most games. For those who wish to mod, they will be sadden that this is almost unachievable. Still, there are a few mods that can enhance the game (and perhaps tweak balance), like Dylan's Realism Mod.
Conclusion:
This game is definitely worth a purchase. While it may have cons, the pros in this game will entertain you and not disappoint you for at least one playthrough. If you're bored of playing games that trap you in confined spaces, get this game and feel how open it is.

I absolutely love this game. Everything from Shadowrun Returns was made even better, and I really appreciated having a real crew and stories to become invested in, regarding my team - instead of (mostly) hiring strangers to go on runs with me.
All of the over the top cyberpunk flavored film noir meets fantasy meets futuristic dystopia you'd expect, is present. Even so, there are some parts of this game that really really got me this time around (especially Glory's backstory, damn!). And there are so many plot twists and levels of conspiracies throughout.
If there is one complaint you see a lot about these games, its that they are too linear and should be far more open world. I don't agree with this. I understand the idea and sentiment behind those types of comments, but that set up works far better in a tabletop game with a DM, than it would in a video game. If anything, I approve of the much deeper connections and invested interests you make from having a more detailed storyline, and you can't really have that both ways.
All in all its an improvement over Shadowrun Returns, which means I have nothing more to say about this game, other than clicking "recommended". Go ahead, jack into the matrix.

I did not play Shadowrun: Dragonfall which was supposed to be just an expansion of the original game. I'm really glad that I was able to nab this for free when I decided to buy it in its early state. I don't know what kind of additional content was put into the original release -- not that it matters now, as the only version that can be purchased is this one.
While hints of  Seattle can be found in the game, Dragonfall is a campaign of its own. While I haven't actually finished the campaign yet, I would probably say that it won't really be anything other titles have told countless of times before: Uncover an ancient evil's plot, obscured by side quests, but eventually lead into a final confrontation where all of the known world hangs in the balance.
Not to say that it isn't cleverly presented or written. The same care and wit remains in this installment of the game. More importantly, however, is that this German successor took its time to develop a cast of characters that you will get a stronger attachment to compared to the Seattle title. You will always be free to run with faceless runners (which you have to pay for... what the hell for, right?) but you will eventually grow to love the constant cast of broken and dark characters that the new campaign has thrown in your way. Their side quests give you pause in the main objective that is worthwhile -- something that I found lacking in the Seattle Campaign.
That aside, you more or less set out with the same streamlined system that we fell in love with during the first campaign. Don't ask me any level of improvements on skills and customization, as I only played the first title once with a Decker. I decided to roll out with a Physical Adept this time, and I have been having a neat time with it. Given that there no drastic changes or additions to the line-up of races or classes, I would probably say that the class customization still runs deep. One could easily just fall into the usual template of classes or mix Steel and Arcane to whip up something else altogether.
I would probably say that combat challenges are more difficult this time around but not to any serious degree.  But I do not intend to jack up the difficulty to prove otherwise either.
Again, I strongly recommend this to slow down from the usual fast-paced and glossy finished treats modernity has to offer. Reading through blocks of bent and twisted cyberpunk street talk made more twisted with German whatnot is a complete joy.

-Cannot Rewind to being in home town/base between missions: You can only rewind to autosaves during a mission, and also...

Keep in mind that a single extra click on the pre-selected map location will confirm the last action clicked, even if the action was updated sinceu the same map location was initially clicked.

Positive review because I love the story and the setting so far. I've been looking for a good cyberpunk movie or game and this hits the spot but man are there some bad game design decisions. The good UI is not noticeable because everything just works, but in Shadowrun (both the original and Dragonfall) the UI is annoying. For example, why aren't there hotkeys for Journal/Missions, Inventory, Character Sheets like every other normal RPG on PC? Why are there no hotkeys for actions? Clicking on items in the world sometimes requires multiple clicks. Text gets cut off of item descriptions when you use Hi-Res Text Mode and on and on. These are issues I expect from a poor PC port.
The world also seems lifeless--Don't get me wrong, the writing is fantastic and carries most of the world-building and the art is rather beautiful, but from a gameplay standpoint it all feels very static, like you're moving around a painting. There isn't a sense of depth, literally or figuratively to the environment. Not to mention that the 3D character models are frankly quite ugly for a modern game--it makes it harder to connect to the characters when they don't look like their portraits OR their text descriptions (Wasteland 2 has the same issue).
Combat while fun, also suffers from poor animations and poor sound effects. It's just not as tense or as satisfying to hit or kill an enemy as in other turn-based RPGs because the actions really lack any visual or auditory punch.
I recognize that this is an indie budgeted game and not a Triple A title like XCOM, but with a professional development studio behind the title I just wish more thought would have been put into the interface. This is the second standalone game, mind you, and although there are noticeable improvements over the first (namely in story and choice), there are still a lot of issues I wish they'd have ironed out when pushing this "sequel". It feels a lot more like a standalone expansion.
Overall, I still recommend it and I sincerely hope Harebrained Schemes will take the Shadowrun IP and give it a lot more spit and shine for the next iteration after Shadowrun: Hong Kong. Perhaps even move to rendering the world in true 3D (fingers crossed!).

Shadowrun: Dragonfall is a narrative-driven cyperpunk/fantasy RPG with turn-based combat, and it's one of the better gaming experiences I've had in recent years.
-----
PRO:
-The story is second to none with some of the best prose I've ever read in a game.
-A small but unique and memorable cast of major characters.
-Turn-based fights break no new ground, but the combat is diverse and manages to be mostly interesting.
-Graphics are simple, but the stylish art conveys a gritty mood that's true to the franchise. A clever character creation system matches a 2D portrait to the chosen 3D preset.
-GREAT soundtrack.
CON:
-Low-poly character models, and a lot of animations are very stiff. A fair number of blatantly recycled assets appear over and over throughout the game (and this applies to ambient audio as well).
-Certain fights are just too long, sometimes devolving into frustration, and get in the way of moving the story forward.
-The game is at times a bit too "retro" for its own good (e.g. describing a ventilation diagram in great detail instead of just showing it). Also, the video game-ified Shadowrun ruleset can make progression feel like a highly restricted crawl, and too few dialogues compensate for this by allowing team members to pick up the slack for the player character's weaknesses.
-Non-crew shadowrunners for hire need to bring a bit more to the table, or there needs to be more chances to earn disposable income. As it is, money is precious, and the hirelings just aren't worth it.
-Late in the game, a few moderately important NPCs are missing portraits. I don't know if the art budget ran out or what, but these omissions were very noticeable.
-----
All in all, despite a handful of minor issues, Dragonfall is a must-play for anybody interested in old-school-inspired role-playing with an A-grade story.

tl;dr: this is a Pay2Premium game, But pretty much pay2win when you break it down. 3.5/10.
Basically you can pay to get missions that unlock cards that aren't available to us normies. So us normies have decks full of filthy commons and we face against those who have obviously paid to play and have the best cards/decks. If you build the best POS deck out of your common and few random higher rarity cards and you make no mistakes at all, you might win 2/5 games, No joke.
I grinded to level 20 and I finally started to get decent cards. So now my chances of winning is about 3/7.. Actually, I was doing better than that and winning about 2 out of 3 games, but then I ranked up and now I'm playing in the middle of the night against the paylords who blew their allowance on this game. Idk why these 30+ year old unemployed NEETs are still getting money from their mothers, but hey, that's on them. So as a tip, play in the day time when the players have a smaller allowance, preferably around 2:30PM when the 12 year olds get out of school.
Joking aside, when it comes to matches, it really is easier to rank up in the day time. The matches themselves are more fair, probably because there are more of us normies on and our decks aren't super OP. So your chances of winning based on skill of play and deck building go up. It actually makes it almost worth playing this game if you regulate yourself to more normal hours. At any other time, considering the huge rise in premium decks at night, you might as well go to bed.
There is a fun story mode that is a casual feel of TES universe without having to boot up skyrim and log a couple dozen hours in a weekend. Obviously this card game is a dumbed down story line but it gives you choices in the story which can affect which cards you get. So think carefully when you make those choices as some are good and others are crap. I don't know how they expect you to know that, though, since your natural inclination is to make a deck suited to your play style. But you will soon realize that the game is severely unbalanced at the higher levels and you pretty much have to do one of only a handful of decks to try and compete with the pay2premium (read: pay2"win most of the time") players.
Once you are done with the 20 missions of story mode, there is nothing more. There is another set of missions but it is behind a substantial paywall for such little content (roughly $15 for what can't be more than 20 more missions). Or you can try and go around the paywall by trying to save up 1000 gold coins. However, gold is hard to come by.
Rewards for winning 3 matches is about 15 gold. So if you want to play story mode, you might as well get your wallet out for that content which should undoubtedly be built into the game. But if you don't want to spend real money, you will have to try to play against others to get that gold. With level ups and random bonuses you get a bit more gold, but I think I'm at 350 gold after 23 hours of play. Though I did buy a pack or two and an event ticket. Yeah, I'm not going to drop 60+ hours into this game to get the other 550 gold............... seriously....... but if you only play once per day and do a mission you get about 40 gold for completing the mission, So at 40 gold a day and 1000 to go, only 25 days and you'll be there!!! what a joke.
So I am definitely not recommending this game, even though I can see myself playing a bit more, to see if the devs rebalance the game. But, I'm so close to ragequitting. In fact this entire genre of pay2-COMPETE games is worthy of ragequitting. At some point, people are going to wake the frack up and stop paying for this garbage. OR, in the more likely event, someone's parents will start a lawsuit against game makers and say that they're akin to gambling and that the games are being solicited to minors. And then we'll probably get some legislation which will heavily regulate the industry. I am not a fan of over-regulation, my work is hell sometimes because of it. But this industry desperately needs a watchdog to ensure fair play for all.
So, in summary, I can't recommend this game. If you play in the day time, maybe. Outside of that, and when you go up against those paylords, this game is just another tired entry into the Freenium universe of pay2win games carrying a popular Intellectual Property. In TES's case, this IP definitely did not need a card game. In fact it cheapens the experience and makes me not want to play the real games. And no, I'm not talking about the MMO. That doesn't exist. NANANANANA I CAN'T HEAR YOU! The Elder Scrolls: Legends, you are the weakest link, goodbye. 3.5/10.

When one of the first perks you get in the game, just from overly-examining stuff, is a purely aesthetic perk called "Stupid Walking", chances are you're probably in for a good game.  When each one of those walk cycles has their own unique sounds associated with them, you KNOW you're in for a good game.
West of Loathing is a RPG from the people who made Kingdom of Loathing, and shares its artstyle, humor, and some gameplay mechanics.  Yes, the artstyle is just stickfigures and black & white graphics, but it works, surprisingly.  Everything's well animated and detailed, despite the simplicity, giving it a certain nice charm.  The simplicity also helps for the UI, as there's very little clutter.  This helps, because your inventory gets -really- cluttered (which is a good thing, stick with me).
Gameplay is the standard "loot and talk to people" out of combat then "turn-based combat" combat.  Combat's simplistic, you and your ally take a turn, then your enemies.  Combat's rather easy, not only because it's easy to just out-stat your enemies with the various food, booze, and potion buffs, but also because combat items don't cost an action, thus allowing you to use as many as you need to finish off enemies.  There is a hard-mode, but I've yet to try it and see how combat's on it there.
The true meat of the game lies in the out of combat stuff.  There is a lot of things out in the West, and thus, a lot of writing.  Every item out of the hundreds of items has a small quip of description that's worth looking at, every location seems to be handcrafted with a purpose, and the dialogue is superb.  Still, there is a -lot- of writing, as said.  Between exploring eldritch horrors and necromantic power you shouldn't be tackling with, to a heartwarming relationship between a lass and man-cactus hybrid, it's all smart, well-written, and humorous.  The sheer volume of writing can be a slight turn off if that's not what you're into, but if you've read this far into the review, chances are you'd be the audience this game is selling to.
It's also rather nice that there's very little filler in this game.  I finished it in 7 hours, but I always felt like I was doing something in those seven hours.  Not like Skyrim or Fallout 4's generic caves and dungeons, everything seems to have it's own unique story or twist, and chances are you'll bump into a quest or someone that will point you towards something new.
Not only that, but there's plenty of good puzzling to be had as well (most of it optional, if you're not the type, however), legit puzzles that get you Googling and searching about.  There's little grind as well, since there's plenty of just small flavor actions and text-encounters you have traveling about that grant you XP, though there are certain locations with infinite enemy spawners, in the off-chance you do want to grind.
It's also pretty decent to replay.  The three different classes seem to play fairly differently, and there's a fair amount of different followers you can bring with you, each having different quips and dialogue, alongside the aforementioned hard mode.  There may be no need to actually replay the game, however, simply due to the sheer density of content available.
While West of Loathing doesn't do much new in terms of gameplay, it makes up for it far more with it's superb writing and charm.  It avoids most of the pitfalls and downsides of most typical RPG games, with very little need to grind, and very little feeling of grinding.
And only for 11 bucks?  That's ridiculous, it's not even funny.

If you have never heard of Kingdom of Loathing, you may as well look that up and go play it for free first. The gameplay elements here are pretty much the same but presented differently. With that being said, they are presented very well and even had details that caught me by surprise. The minimalistic design was part of Kingdom of Loathing's charm, and that is not lost in West of Loathing. The addition of animation is done in a way that fits the style perfectly. It just looks right.
What really made Kingdom of Loathing special though was the humor. Simply put, it was different. That same style of humor is present in West of Loathing. The writing, the atmosphere, even the menus have this absurd humor. It is often "reference-based" humor, but done in a way that you don't realize that you are missing a reference. You know how sometimes you can "feel" that a joke was intended but you missed the reference so it just felt awkward? That doesn't happen much in KoL and WoL. If you miss the reference you just don't notice, because it's done in a way that fits well with the rest of the game.
My most concise description though would be: it's like an open world rpg had sex with ms paint and then went through a fax machine and was written by comedians with learning disabilites.

TL;DR: It has the same flaws as previous games in the series in terms of the CPUs 2nd and 4th quarter cheese, but the neighborhood is awesome, and the game is full of strategic touches and graphical improvements that make it much better than 2K17.

Long version:
Every release of NBA 2K is the hardest game to review.  It's so good, so close to NBA action that you want to give it a 9 and a ringing endorsement.  The character models in 2K18 are so realistic, the animations get better every year, and the strategy involved with the game is much deeper.   BUT....
Of course there's a 'but'.....this is the 19th iteration of the game, and the guys who program the A.I. STILL don't understand how to simulate the game of runs.  One of the programmers said "let's make it so that the CPU closes the gap no matter how large so the games are exciting..."  And they do this EVERY year.  You're executing on offense, using pick and rolls, getting green releases on your jumpers and attacking the basket.  You build a 16 point lead after the first.  By midway through the 2nd that lead is gone, and you feel powerless to hold it.  It doesn't bother me that the computer doesn't allow me to blow them out--that'd get boring--what bothers me is how obvious it is when the computer decides it's time to come back.  The CPU STILL makes your teammates play off of deadly outside shooters no matter what directions you give them.  Get a hand up, doesn't matter, role players are shooting over double teams in the second quarter.  On the other end, the CPUs on-ball defense becomes like a magnet as the same players you beat last quarter all become Kawhi Leonard.  It's obvious because you can see the switch flipped; you start to miss "good/wide open" releases  with 90+ outside scorers; you can see the algorithms turn against you and it ceases to be immersive, and you have to use cheap tactics to compete.
So why do I recommend the game still?  Simple.  If you're a die-hard NBA fan who games on PC, what else are you going to play?  The game still has epic basketball moments that make you feel awesome when you pull them off.  I love the Road to 99 in myPlayer that makes you earn milestones.  People complaining about microtransactions are the ones who used to just play the NBA cames on easy and keep doing the same moves until they unlock badges.  If you don't want to spend 500 bucks, you simply have to play A LOT of games.  Oh no! A game that forces you to play it!  Doesn't really matter though--you can still compete against guys who are 90+ even at level 75.  For me personally, the neighborhood and everything about it, including the voice acting of the side characters, is A++.

Quick Summary: third person hack/slash game similar to Devil May Cry, but with no platforming elements. Gameplay is mostly focused on sword combat and timing your dodge moves. The game’s art style is cel-shaded with mostly modern world environments, kind of looking like you’re in the Sin City world, but with color. A lot of the game seems like interactive anime and it’s kind of hard to understand what the hell is going on in the story, but the game is a lot of fun, and that’s what matters.
You play the character Mondo Zappa, an unassuming looking dude with a cybernetic arm and a big♥♥♥♥♥katana who works for the government as an “executioner.” The game’s world isn’t fully explained, but apparently there are demons called “wires” all over the globe causing trouble, along with ghosts, vampires, and aliens. Mondo works out of a small office with a few other people but his missions take him all over the world (and to the Moon), accompanied by his spunky sidekick Mika, who’s basically an anime little sister. Ultimately, it seems like most of the world’s evil comes from a bad guy on the dark side of the Moon, and it’s to Mondo deal with it.
The game is broken up into episodes, each one being a self-contained mission with a boss at the end. There are a few collectibles to find, such as life crystals (to increase your max life), blood (to upgrade your secondary weapon ammo limit) and moon crystals (to upgrade combat skills). The other thing to look out for are hidden Scarlett locations, which unlock “challenge levels.” Other than the Scarlett locations, most of what you get drops from defeated enemies, and as you play, your max life and max blood slowly increases a tiny bit at a time. Each mission also awards you cash, which you can use in the game’s store. The missions are almost all linear, and there’s really only one level that you might get lost in (because you’re searching for something). Since Mondo doesn’t jump in the game, there’s no platforming to do and the game is really all about combat.
If you’ve played third person hack / slash games like Devil May Cry or Darksiders, the fighting system in Killer is Dead should be pretty familiar to you. Your sword slashes come out in combos that cause enemies to flinch (unless they’re blocking) so most of the time you’re wiping the floor with the weaker wires. I played with Keyboard + Mouse but a controller might be a better choice. You have a “block” button that doubles as a “dodge” if you happen to be moving when you press it. Both the block and dodge have the potential to open up enemies to brutal counterattacks if you time them properly. However, unlike the Batman Arkham games, there’s much less warning that the enemies are about to strike so you can’t just mash the attack button or you’ll be in the middle of an attack animation when someone behind you whacks you with a mace. I mentioned Mondo’s cyber arm earlier, and the arm contains Mondo’s “guns” which are surprisingly strong. The Devil May Cry and Darksiders guns are infinite ammo peashooters that just give you something to tickle bosses with, but in Killer is Dead, the guns cause significant damage (including instant kill head shots on some weaker enemies).
Another major (but optional) part of the game is the “gigolo missions” where Mondo tries to romance girls between story missions. Some of the most common items that you’ll be buying in the game’s store are gifts for Mondo’s girls, and these gifts can get pretty expensive. In the gigolo missions, you basically need to stare at a woman with your x-ray glasses, trying to get a nice glimpse of their underwear while they aren’t looking. After you’ve gotten a good eyeful, you can give them gifts until you win them over. Completing gigolo missions unlocks guns for you (and lets you see half naked girls) so they’re worth doing. The gifts really drain your bank account though.
Pros:
+Interesting story, despite being hard to follow at times.
+Cool and stylish art design, including some giant bosses.
+After beating the game you can replay missions to your heart’s content and continue to upgrade. This means you can make yourself stronger in order to tackle the harder difficulty modes. Note that no matter how much you upgrade however, Nightmare mode will still kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you aren’t good at dodge timing.
Cons:
-The game seems to be rather demanding on my computer’s CPU and stutters despite being locked at 30 fps. This fps lock can be modified though.
-The game is obviously a console port, which normally isn’t a problem, but some things such as the menus were clearly not designed with pc users in mind. For example you use the mouse click and the space button to confirm/cancel rather than enter and esc.  Additionally, despite unlocking a bunch of “moves” through upgrading, the game doesn’t explain very well how to use these moves.
Overall the game is fun and worth playing if you enjoy psychedelic art style and a weird story. It’s all about the action, so work on timing your blocks/evasions and don’t worry too much about exploring every nook and cranny. Most of the hidden stuff in the game (nurse Scarett) isn’t hidden very well, and you can come back for them when replaying missions.

Let me be longwinded for a moment. You know that magical little title that everyone ranted and raved about once you got past the dificulty curve. Darksouls. Well this game is a lot like that. No seriously there is a surprising amount of storytelling in Vindictus. Really. Story. Chances are you'll play it for the gorgeous characters, fantastic armor, killer weapons, and ultra fast gameplay with spectacular skills. Look far enough into it and there is a rich untold story under the surface. Granted it's told a bit hamfistedly for most of it, there are some really killer moments and design choices that tell a story. The Mystery of Anile, the goddess, Ingkells, Tieve, Gwyn all memorable moments/characters. Each with there own stories.
Does this mean you should be looking for deep storyline? Until you get to around level 60 nothing really clicks. It's an unfortunate twist in the game, that requires time to get into the story aspect. While the rest of the game is really good, the story doesn't pick up to easily 20 or so hours in. It isn't, bad until then. It just isn't great. It's sort of there. Which again is the argument that was the end of games like ff13. Yet here the gameplay is good enough to keep me coming to the point where the story reaches a crecendo.
Season two is fast off the heels of S1 and tells another deep and rich storyline if you're willing to look. Yet the best is yet to come with s3 coming up fast. Tomorrow no less
As far as gameplay, assuming you maintain a stable framerate on a reasonable computer it's phenominal if a bit repetative. I recomend leveling two characters, one primary, and one durdle. It will keep you from getting bored of a given characters parameters before you start being able to seriously tweek the play style. Granted around level 40 the skills get VERY diverse and interesting.
Graphics: Well crank up the settings and be in for a pleasent surprise. It's quite pretty.
Story: While it starts rocky and somewhat confused, it gets really good!
Gameplay: Amazing, get a good computer and enjoy.
Character customization: pretty good, though could use some more options.
Replayability: I'm biased, I have 600 hours...

No game has ever ended for me quite the same way Far Cry 2 did. That is, I didn't see it through to the end at all, at least the indended end. What happened instead is that about halfway through, I accidentaly shot my sister-in-arms while she was bleeding into the dusty sub-Saharan soil, begging me for help. You see, when one of your "buddies" goes down in a firefight, a plume of blue smoke will direct you to their location. You then have the option to either heal them with a magic syrette, leave them to their fate or, it turns out, blow their brains out right there and then. That latter option is denoted with the prompt "Press 2 for handgun". Clear enough, you'd think. Except I had been under the impression that "handgun" in this context would mean hauling the buddy to their feet and dragging them to safety, while fending off remaining assailants with a sidearm in your free hand. Because that is precisely what the buddies themselves will do for you when you've eaten one too many helpings of cold lead. So when instead of lending a helping hand, I watched myself put a gun to my friend's head and pull the trigger, I was left agape. Literally agape. As in, my mouth was hanging open and I was staring at the screen, for a good minute or so. After that, I drove around aimlessly for an hour or so, picking random fights, absent-mindedly going through the motions to complete a side mission. After that, I hopped onto a boat, drove out to a rocky island in the middle of a lake, climbed to the highest point I could reach, dropped an IED at my own feet and blew myself to hell, And thus ended the short and miserable career of Andre the Haitian. Definitely recommended.

Far Cry 2 throws the player into the wild African savannah where you have to fend for yourself. No one is there to hold your hand, and the world offers limitless opportunities. Problem is, you have caught malaria and you are in the middle of a civil war. As a mercenary, you offer your services to the various warlords as you drift ever closer into the dangerous conflict.
If you enjoyed the first Far Cry, you will probably find Far Cry 2 quite enjoyable as well. While not related story-wise, the game offers a similar tone in gameplay. The game gives you the freedom to roam a massive world set in Africa. And there is no doubt in saying that the world is gorgeous, yet this is also where one of the most fundamental flaws lies. The world is sparsely populated; there are no massive cities, villages, or interesting locations to visit in the game. The world mainly consists of outposts with 100% goon density. This shallow attention to detail is what makes Far Cry 2 quite repetitive once you hit the 10 hour mark.
An impressive addition to Far Cry 2 is the durability of weapons. Unlike most FPS games, the weapons in Far Cry 2 can jam or completely break in the middle of a fight. This makes pre-mission planning much more fun as it promotes the idea of checking the weapon state. Yet this “realism” that Far Cry 2 so heavily promotes can be a pain at times. Your character contracts malaria early in the game, and forces you to do boring side-missions to acquire 1-4 pills. Depending on how long you play, you may have to do quite a few of those malaria quests. It is also bothersome as symptoms may show up in the middle of a firefight.
As for story, Far Cry 2 follows in the footsteps of the first Far Cry in that it doesn’t provide an interesting plot at all. The characters are poorly voiced and uninteresting, the plot never really develops, and you could care less what is happening around you. It becomes quite apparent after a few hours that the budget went straight into developing the world and not the story or its characters. At times, you may feel extremely lonely in this intimidating setting.
Overall, if you like a sandbox playstyle with goons who will make life hell for you as you try to traverse the African terrains, then this game should be plenty of fun. Even if you don’t plan to play the main mission, go raid some outposts. I found it quite entertaining.
