Honestly I have no idea how many hours I've logged in this game, but I truly cannot tell you if it's a good game. I've played since the beta using the
launcher, but with each update I would be locked out of this game for some time despite all efforts  (including uninstalling and reinstalling the software).
Now that my personal background with this game is out of the way, let me tell you about the Elder Scrolls: Legends. It's a card game (duh) featuring characters and monsters from across the Elder Scrolls series. Rememeber the Adorng Fan from Oblivion? He's in this game along with Cicero and Miraak from Skyrim. The Adoring Fan is just as annoying as he was in Oblivion so don't worry! See, he has special card attributes (known as keywords in ES:L) that make him a priority target. You have to kill the Adoring Fan before attacking anything else. In addition to this, he has another keyword that triggers when he is destroyed (called a Last Gasp) and his particular Last Gasp sends him right back into your deck to be played once you draw him again if you're lucky. Just like most card games, there is a hefty amount of luck involved.
The rune system, combined with this ingrained luck, drives me insane. Runes work like this; both players have 30 health, and when a player's health is reduced by 5 points a rune is broken, allowing the player who is being attacked to draw a card. In addition to this, there are cards with the keyword Prophecy, meaning that if they are pulled from a broken rune, they can be played immediately without any magic cost. I'm not sure if I love this mechanic or hate it. I love it, because if you are being demolished you could turn a match around with a lucky pull. I hate it, because if you are the attacking player you can wind up being punished for doing well.
In conclusion I love this game because I love The Elder Scrolls universe (I'm a lore freak), I love card games, and sometimes the rune mechanic works in my favor. Also, the deck building options are IMMENSE. I don't love this game when the rune mechanic DOESN'T work in my favor because I am a salty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and that's about it.
TL;DR: It's a fun and free card game with beautiful artwork, great deck building possibilites, and a good story (set during the Great War before Skyrim). However, the rune mechanic can punish you for doing well in a match.
PS: If I could have one thing added to the game it would be FLAVOR TEXT. Just a sentence or two on each card, something for a player to read in between matches.

I liked this game at the beginning.  It had a fun setting with a sense of humor that captured my interest.  Unfortunately that diminished not long into the game, as the puzzles are simply unintuitive and require endless running around and trying every object on everything until something finally works.  One puzzle requires the player to trick Glottis in a way that is entirely out of character for Manny.  The only reason I even got past it was by accident because it simply didn't cross my mind that an apparently good-natured character like Manny would do something like that.
I could overlook this because of the good writing the game has, but even that disappeared after a while.  Glottis very quickly turns into a typical, one-dimensional clown, which made me really dislike the character I'm probably supposed to enjoy the most.  His voice and stupidity are simply obnoxious and there's no excuse for a 2,000-year-old demon to be such a childish dunce.  The game attempts mechanics that are completely out of place and unsuited to the point-and-click genre, and it only results in frustration more than anything else.
The worst part is that once the first part of the game is over, the narrative skips ahead a year and alienates the player by introducing a whole cast of characters who the protagonist intimately knows while the player has no level of familiarity with them whatsoever.  This is a horrible decision on multiple levels.  Not only does this create a division between the player and the protagonist, but it also ruins all of my motivation to care about the story or the characters and makes it difficult to continue playing.  Even disregarding that, it makes no sense for so much to develop in a single year.  Manny goes from an employee at a diner to the owner of a successful casino that didn't even exist before, and Glottis abandons his entire reason for existence that he claimed to be unable to live without so that he could play piano instead.  In addition, I found it very hard to believe that it would take an entire year for Mercedes Colomar to make her way through an area that Manny passed through in the space of a few hours at most.
Because of all this, it's difficult for me to find any reason to continue the game.  There don't seem to be any redeeming qualities left and all engagement I had with the plot has been extinguished, leaving me with absolutely no motivation to continue.  The puzzles are poorly made and the pacing is atrocious.  I recommend looking elsewhere for an enjoyable experience.

Epigenesis is a kind of fast-paced arena shooter.
The rules are simple, take the ball, bring it to the ennemy base and score a goal to gain 1 point. But that won't be easy because a bunch of angry men are running at you firing lasers and trying to punch you, turrets are shooting huge projectiles right in your face and some tornados are here to bring pain and misery. Yep, it's not 2k14.
That game is pretty similar to quake or unreal. You can double jump, you can find bonus on the ground (blink, grab, pushback aoe etc), you are firing rockets and lasers. Jumping is the key of the game, the arenas are made of platforms and you to have to jump from one to another, there is no real ground. That means that you can fall and die really often if you fail your jumps.
Weapons are pretty original, the first one fires rocket that'll push your ennemys away or pull them to you, the second one is a laser that stops instantly the ennemy movement (really effective when shooting a men while he is in the air, he'll fall to death). You also get a construction laser.
Yes a construction laser! When a player scores, he gains a seed. This seed can be used on the biggest platforms to create a bonus. These bonus consist of turrets, mortars, ramps, shields, smokescreen and trench. Each of these bonus will help your team to win, choose them wisely because they can change the battlefield a lot. Each of these contructions also brings you a passiv bonus like an acceleration boost, a higher fire rate etc. But be carefull because the other team can destroy them and make you loose the bonus.
I really enjoyed it, it's not bug free but it's pretty solid at what it does. Give it a try!

After only about 20 minutes, I think you can probably tell if the game is for you or not.  It's hard to recommend, because it really depends on how patient you're feeling.  I would suggest giving it a try.
Here's an example of what I really dislike about this game:
There one puzzle where you have to cross a bridge, but it's covered in flaming beavers.  You have a fire extinguisher in your inventory.  Seems like an obvious solution, right?  Well, just spraying them with a fire extinguisher isn't enough, they'll jump in the water, then light back on fire when they get out.  How do you solve it?  You have to stand in a very specific spot, go into your inventory, take out a bone, throw the bone in the water, go into your inventory, take out the fire extinguisher, and spray it at just the right time, as the beaver as the jumps into the water.  Somehow, this chain of events kills the beaver permanently, and they never come out of the water.
How does this make any sense?  I found that too many of the puzzles in this game just made no sense, or were impossible to solve using logic, and I'm hesitant to recommend it.
Get a walkthrough, use it only when needed, and I think you'll enjoy the game for its story and characters, though.  The writing for the characters is witty, and I like the flirty dialogue. The game is fun when you're not banging your head against the wall.

I have to say that Grim Fandango is an awesome game, It brought new mechanics to the genre and it has its singular style and humor that marks it as a very memorable game. Still, it had some technical flaws back in the days, stuff like bugs and such. Back in the 90's there weren't DLCs, fixes and stuff like this, so those bugs remained there.
Now we have a thing called Grim Fandango REMASTERED, so you think that the game gets refreshing stuff like compatibility, new graphics, maybe new ways to approach the game and FIXES. We have some new 3D models, but the prerendered backgrounds are still the same (and look a little worse if you use the remastered version), the movements feel iffy and can be used only with tank commands, otherwise Manny will always get confused when moving to another area. But most of all, we don't have any fix for bugs, just a compatibility fix for new systems. Why do we need a Remaster then? I'm not even using the Remastered graphics because except the "new" 3D models everything looks worse. Even the dubbing didn't get an audio improvement (italian version, don't know for the others) and you can clearly hear the microphone noises of the 90's, some Audacity fixes could've help a lot, it's not asking too much I think, some basic stuff if you call your product REMASTER. But most of all, bugs didn't get a fix, I encountered some of them (crashed a couple of times) and now I'm stuck to Rubacava because everytime I try to give an object to Glottis to proceed, he starts running in circles and I can't command anything, so I'm stuck and the only thing I can do is close the game and start from the beginning and hope it doesn't happen again (reloading the savefile doesn't work).
Is the game worth playing? Grim Fandango is one of the most beautiful games ever made, so yes.
Is the REMASTERED worth buying? No, because it's just the same game with not much effort and not even basic fixes.

The first thing you notice about Far Cry 2 when you first set foot in (rather, sit down in) it is the absolutely gorgeous visuals and unique setting. For a game that came out all the way back in 2009, the visuals are outstanding, even when compared to new AAA titles that have come out just this year, especially if you are playing those new games on a console. This isn't only due to the setting of the game either. Most of the texture work is fantastic, with weapons and vehicles that show battle damage and rust (weapon rust is also part of a gameplay element in which your guns can jam), and excellent character models/textures. Every aesthetic element in this game screams polish. These visuals are made even more impressive when you realize the entire map is seamless. There are no loading times unless you fast travel or die, and the two parts of the map available (one unlocked later on in the game) are both absolutely massive. All of this is enhanced once you install one of the variety of different ENB mods available. Personally, I used the GES (Graphical Enhancement Suite) mod, although there are plenty more options to choose from. The only real complaint with the visuals I can think of is that the water looks good until you actually take a dive under it, at which point looks like the developers just went "Screw it, throw a greenish-blue tint over the screen and then let's go get lunch." This, however, is more of a nitpick than anything.
After choosing your character (none of which are female, which is a strange design decision), viewing the opening sequence and a few tutorial missions you are let loose to explore,♥♥♥♥♥♥ pillage, and murder as you see fit. Believe me when I say you will want to explore this gorgeous setting. I am unaware of any other game that puts you in a war torn Africa, let alone one that lets you explore war torn Africa. I was compelled to explore the landscape based on the locale alone, despite the problems present should you choose to roam around. It is explained to you within your first few minutes in Africa that the only currency accepted in this land is diamonds. Doing both main and side missions rewards the player with diamonds, however they can also be found in small cases while traveling the land, with the help of a detector you get which points you in the general direction of them. This presents the first problem with just going off and exploring. There are a ton of diamond cases scattered around the map. (over 600 if memory serves) On one hand it is nice because you often run into them while doing missions anyway, however it becomes problematic if you just wish to explore to find them. The vast number of them means that each one has very few diamonds in them, anywhere from 1-5 diamonds per case. This means that trying to earn money by treasure hunting is extremely time consuming, especially when you consider that figuring out how to get to some of these cases can take upwards of 20 minutes.  The second problem with exploration is that in the vanilla game (which I do not recommend playing, but we will get to that later) the checkpoints that are set up by the various mercenaries around the landscape respawn incredibly quickly. The way this works is that the map is divided into zones when viewed by the player. You can either view the entirety of the map, or view the zone you are currently in. (one zone normally constitutes an enemy checkpoint or facility) The problem occurs when you exit a zone, at which point everyone and everything that you just destroyed in the zone respawns. This can make back and forth commutes frustrating when you have to clear an area you were just in 5 seconds earlier again.
So with all that, how is the actual gameplay? The answer: pretty damn good. It is here that I will mention that I did not play the vanilla game. I played using the "RealMode" mod on the "Infamous" difficulty (which is the highest one), although there is another popular one called "Dylan's Realism Mod." The reason I did not and do not recommend playing the vanilla game is that a single enemy in the original game absorbs more bullets than goddamned Luffy in the entirety of One Piece. Other than making you and your enemies die like human beings should, the RealMode mod applies some balance changes to the various equipment upgrades as well. The gameplay aspect is what turns alot of people away from this game I believe. (it is a game after all) While the gunplay is solid and fun, it is the way in which the player interacts with the world that bring people to love/hate relationships with this game. The gameplay is heavily reliant on the chaos factor. What this means is that it loves putting the play in stressful situations that they have little control over. (although if you are good enough you can most definitely manipulate the environment to your favor) It is these "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥oh♥♥♥♥♥♥oh♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; moments that truly make the game shine in my opinion. You just charged a base in your vehicle, you get out in the middle of a grassy field. The enemy comes after you. You throw a molotov cocktail, hoping to catch fire to the grass, preventing your foes from easily accessing you. But oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ a guy you didn't see before has a rocket launcher, he fires, blows up your vehicle, now there is fire spreading to you from behind and in front, you see enemies attempting to flank you, you fire, but now your gun is jammed and the enemy closes in as you scream in your head "WHAT DO I DO NOW OMGWTFBBQ!!!!" These kinds of unscripted, player and AI driven epic moments were easily the best part of my experience with the game. The AI is also top notch, as they will flank, call out to each other, carry wounded, and spot you from far away if you aren't careful.  There is also an upgrade system for both weapons and vehicles, which you purchase from a shopkeep whom also provides you with side missions that  earn you new gear. It is unfortunate however that there are only two type of sidequests in the game. There are assassination missions (which are fun and allow you creative ways to down your target) or the shopkeep missions which only ever involve taking out a convoy of vehicles. These are still enjoyable mind you, the lack of variety is just a little bit disappointing. There are alot of different loadout combinations to play and have fun with, along with a true "do things your own way" feel. I should also mention that stealth in this game is difficult. Not impossible, just difficult due to the intelligent AI and the lack of a melee stealth takedown. Seriously developers, stealth without stealth takedowns (or at least a silent one shot melee weapon)= don't do.
Now the story, in my opinion, was not that compelling. Save for a few great moments, I honestly don't remember much about the story. It isn't bad per se, it is just sort of generic. What is good about it is the fact that later on in the game you get choices that affect the story. These choices are really just the ability to let certain people live or die. The other great part about the story is the buddy system. Some of the characters you get the option to play as before you start the game as well as some ones that you can't play as may show up in your game and offer their help. They help you in one of two ways. The first is that they will call you up during main missions and offer you an alternate way to complete the mission along with their help. This can lead to some really great moments. The second is that if you fall in battle, they will bring you back up to your feet. This is a game I love and will recommend to anyone, especially at the average sale price of $2.49. (Review shortened due to Steam character constraints)

What needs to be made clear here first, is that I'm entirely satisfied with the graphics and the world created in general, but the developers should've been more concerned about other things also. Like the actual gameplay. This game actually starts off pretty well: you get to some county, and get a simple mission to kill some weapons dealer who seems to be connected to every major paramilitary force there. You know nothing, you have nothing, thus you have to find your own way to achieve your goal. You need to collect some friends, explore the area, get some weapons, etc. The idea is pretty cool, as this is a scenario that could very well be in the real world too.
And here comes the bad part. Although the game is based on solid graphics and story idea, the realization of it is quite bad in my opinion. The game is just very highly repetitive, and in some cases also very annoying. First of all the basic story setting is the same everywhere. Two factions, you work for both of them, you always get a side quest from a buddy, you always go to the buddy prior to a mission and after the actual mission (always to save him from some bad guys).
Guard posts and patrols are the very worst of the game. They are always there, and even if you clean a guard post, people always respawn after ridiculously small amounts of time. And guard posts are everywhere. You can't go to a mission without the need to get through a number of guard posts. Also, if guard posts are alerted, patrols always seem to find you, no matter how you hide (even with the camo upgrade). They roam exactly to your location and try to go over you with their vehicle all the time.
Also, if you use silent weapons (e.g. silent smg) they find you in the grass too quickly no matter how dark it is, or how dense the vegetation is around you. But, if you use a very loud sniper rifle for instance, they try to hide instead. No running towards you, only in rare cases. Patrols try to overrun you nevertheless...
Missions are pretty much the same always: kill someone, blow up something, and in some rare cases free someone, so (s)he can turn to be your buddy. How you get there is through patrols and guard posts as always. No change here.
Side quests are equally boring: to unlock new weapons, just go to the other side of the current map, and blow up a truck. That's it. Or to get a higher history score with a buddy, kill someone for them (naturally). But before you can do that, go through some stupid guard posts.
So the game is pretty simple and repeats the same all the time: get a mission from a faction, get a phone call from a buddy, go to the buddy, get the side quest, go to the designated location, get something, go to the main location, do some damage there, get a phone call from the buddy, go rescue him from bad guys. Repeat again with another mission. And this simple queue of actions cycles throughout the entire game. Boring.
Far Cry 1 was more guided in story perhaps, but it was to its benefit, as that was actually enjoyable till the end. New locations, new objectives, and in the process get rid of guards on the islands that stand in your way. Or you could just sneak around them in many cases.
Also, who knows why, guards and patrols do not attack each other. But they attack you on site even if you try to get around them, try not to be threatening, and you just try to avoid them in general. No matter what you do you are attacked even from a distance, and even if you you just try to burst through (or nearby) their camp. It makes you feel like that whenever you sit in a vehicle, a sign appears over you which says: "shoot me, please", and the guards happily comply. Super annoying.
Also, in this game is advertised to be a sandbox style game, which is mostly true, but there are some areas that are simply not accessible by design. I mean in reality those many places could be accessed, but the game restricts you. You just suddenly hit an invisible wall at these places, and you don't understand why you can't go to these places, especially if you try to play the sneaky, sniping style. Getting to a good vantage point is a must if you play that style, but the game makes it impossible in most cases. This is the second biggest annoying thing of the game.
Also, weapons are somewhat weird. You immediately get this fancy crossbow which shoots bolts with explosive heads in a totally straight line. And after some time of flight it just explodes in midair if it doesn't hit anything. What is the point of the RPG then (which you can unlock only much later)? I didn't notice a real difference between rocket/bolt flight speed. To get the same amount of rockets as you have for the crossbow needs an extra upgrade. And pretty much you have two weapons with identical characteristics. What is the point of the RPG again? The other rocket launcher which is better than these (because it has a guided missile) always ignites the grass under you. You get burned before the rocket reaches target.
Also, weapons degrade too quickly. Even if you buy the manual (which slows degradation), your weapons start to jam after a not very long time, even if you avoid water. It would be fine for not having a manual, as a lot of dust can get into a weapon that could cause jamming, but why in the hell isn't there an option after you bought the weapon manual to clean the weapon? Could be somewhat similar to the "healing yourself after serious injuries" option. But no, it doesn't exist. If you didn't want to get through a number of guard posts to replace your weapon at the weapons shop, you're stuck with a defective weapon, which sometimes gets jammed and (quite oddly) you need to unjam the loading mechanism before you are able to fire it (even if the round is already loaded). You just hit the fire button (on a perfectly loaded weapon) and it doesn't shoot, but the protagonist starts to fiddle with the loading mechanism. Why?
All these oddities sum up and start to get on your nerves after some time, and you're just astonished that while a lot of details were took care of, these far more important ones that directly affect game play weren't. And that is why I don't recommend the game. Basic idea very good, implementing very bad.
Thanks for reading.
EDIT: The time I spent playing this game is actually more, than the showed, but for some reason steam doesn't record played hours if the steam client is used in offline mode. I actually did play the game all the way through, so this is not a review without being able to back up my claims with the necessary hours spent on it.

I still haven't beaten the game. I did all the sidequests I could before the main story missions, and then halfway through the (rather thin) storyline, the map suddenly and unexpectedly doubled in size. But before I went any further, I wanted to come in here and say just two things about why I'd recommend this game:
1) Yes, it's sometimes annoying when (a) your car gets shot to bits and (b) the enemies are rushing you with semi-automatic shotguns and (c) you need to take your malaria medication and (d) you can't find safe cover to rip the bullet out of your arm and (e) your weapon jams and (f) that fire you started is licking at your heels ... but when all of these things happen at once, it's some of the most exciting FPS-play I've ever had. Far Cry 2 is full of variability, randomness, and multiple approaches, and the game is at its most thrilling when things go wrong.
2) The world is just beautiful, and the developers work to immerse you in it. It fits together so well; it's explorable for its own sake; and the weather effects are lush. That heavy equatorial sun desaturates everything, and makes the air feel thick as you tromp through towns and jungles. The nights are cool and mysterious, particularly driving over sand dunes in the moonlit desert on the edges of the map. And when it rains, turning everything gray, it feels as refreshing as the end of an IRL drought. I'm playing on a laptop with an integrated chipset and the settings turned down to medium so the game stays smooth, but I still find myself smashing F12 to take a dozen screenshots every hour. That said, enjoying this takes the right frame of mind. If you can be patient and appreciative, you'll love it. But if you lament a lack of Elder Scrollsy fast-travel, maybe not.
The only caveat I'll give: if you insist on playing a hero, this isn't the game for you. Nearly everyone you interact with is a despicable, heartless human being. Bandits, mercenaries, murderers, drug peddlers, tyrants, human traffickers, corrupt officials. And you'll be the worst one of the bunch, like it or not.

AUDIO:
The voice acting in this game is iffy. The Jackal probably has the best voice actor in the game because he actually sounds interesting to listen to. Everyone else sounds bored out of their mind to be talking and they are speeding through their dialogue at maximum speed. The soundtrack is mostly just bongos and drums and the like, mostly for menus and fighting and stuff. Not bad.
VISUALS:
This game hits the extremes of good and bad graphics sometimes. For example, the graphics look freaking wicked when the sun rises or is in the sky. It's a beautiful sun, one of the best I've seen and it makes everything look spectacular. In contrast, the game is very brown and dark green without the sun rays. It can get pretty dull to look at sometimes, but maybe that's what they were going for.
PLAYABILITY:
Since the game is open world, it gives you freedom to tackle your objectives how you want. It also gives you more than one way to carry out your objective. The guns are all pretty nice and all of them work well, which lets you develop a favorite. The malaria isn't really a problem. I don't care what everyone else says, I never once had a problem with malaria. It gets repetitive having to travel sometimes though, and hunting for diamonds can get super boring, especially considering that they are currency in this game and you kind of need them.
DELIVERY:
My playtime was the amount of time needed to 100% this game. That being said, it's large. However, 100%'ing this is very dull. The missions are mostly the same thing over and over; assassinate a target, collect a briefcase, etc. The strongest point of this game would be the buddies. I found myself growing attached to the buddies I got and it made the game much more enjoyable.
SUMMARY:
Don't spend all your time collecting those damn diamonds unless you REALLY want to 100% this. Take the main missions, the buddy missions, and carry out your goals however you want. Make your own choices and don't think too much. It's not a bad game by any means.

If you love cyberpunk, you will love "Shadowrun: Dragonfall".

The quality of storytelling in this title is outstanding.
"Shadowrun: Dragonfall" touches on multiple classic topics of the cyberpunk genre and adds some metaphysical ones for good measure. Getting to know the characters in this story is a pleasure, as they have morality that is not black-or-white and just as humans are, these people have their flaws and virtues, they need help and somehow the story is done in such a way that they induce genuine compassion.
Tactical aspect is done well. Definitely an enjoyable experience.
Variety of available playstyles is satisfactory.
The only grudge I have against Shadowrun: Dragonfall is that it ends at some point and I'm afraid that replayability value isn't very high once you know the story.
Regardless, it's definitely worth the price for the 50hours of fun I had out of it.

The story may be good by game standards, but games live and die by gameplay being fun and fair.  Dragonfall fails at this; let us count the ways (mostly compared to XCOM EU/EW/2, which are much more polished):
- Almost nothing is explained.  Help menu is nearly useless.
- Lots of long-known, unfixed bugs, some game-breaking.  No dev action or community fixes.
- Teammates can't level.
- Can't melee from catercorner position, only cardinal.
- Controls are bad, not explained, and not remappable.  Left-click for move, attack, and choose team member, really?
- Can't rotate camera.  I don't care if it's because the backgrounds are painted.  Combined with the left-click-for-everything, this makes moving to a square one above a teammate an excercise in pixel-hunting.
- Nothing is voiced.  What is this, 1998?
- Animations janky and slow.  No apparent option to speed them up like in XCOM2.
- Can't autosave every round like XCOM.
- Graphics poor, load times still long.
- Character counted as flanked when she's not.
- Shot by enemy I cannot see.
- Can see an enemy, have line of sight, cannot target.  Move towards, teammate disappears.
- Displayed to-hit chances way off.  Just look at the threads on this.
- Enemy AI stupid, places little worth on self-preservation.
- Not enough things count as cover, e.g. doorway sides don't.

I liked this game at the beginning.  It had a fun setting with a sense of humor that captured my interest.  Unfortunately that diminished not long into the game, as the puzzles are simply unintuitive and require endless running around and trying every object on everything until something finally works.  One puzzle requires the player to trick Glottis in a way that is entirely out of character for Manny.  The only reason I even got past it was by accident because it simply didn't cross my mind that an apparently good-natured character like Manny would do something like that.
I could overlook this because of the good writing the game has, but even that disappeared after a while.  Glottis very quickly turns into a typical, one-dimensional clown, which made me really dislike the character I'm probably supposed to enjoy the most.  His voice and stupidity are simply obnoxious and there's no excuse for a 2,000-year-old demon to be such a childish dunce.  The game attempts mechanics that are completely out of place and unsuited to the point-and-click genre, and it only results in frustration more than anything else.
The worst part is that once the first part of the game is over, the narrative skips ahead a year and alienates the player by introducing a whole cast of characters who the protagonist intimately knows while the player has no level of familiarity with them whatsoever.  This is a horrible decision on multiple levels.  Not only does this create a division between the player and the protagonist, but it also ruins all of my motivation to care about the story or the characters and makes it difficult to continue playing.  Even disregarding that, it makes no sense for so much to develop in a single year.  Manny goes from an employee at a diner to the owner of a successful casino that didn't even exist before, and Glottis abandons his entire reason for existence that he claimed to be unable to live without so that he could play piano instead.  In addition, I found it very hard to believe that it would take an entire year for Mercedes Colomar to make her way through an area that Manny passed through in the space of a few hours at most.
Because of all this, it's difficult for me to find any reason to continue the game.  There don't seem to be any redeeming qualities left and all engagement I had with the plot has been extinguished, leaving me with absolutely no motivation to continue.  The puzzles are poorly made and the pacing is atrocious.  I recommend looking elsewhere for an enjoyable experience.

After only about 20 minutes, I think you can probably tell if the game is for you or not.  It's hard to recommend, because it really depends on how patient you're feeling.  I would suggest giving it a try.
Here's an example of what I really dislike about this game:
There one puzzle where you have to cross a bridge, but it's covered in flaming beavers.  You have a fire extinguisher in your inventory.  Seems like an obvious solution, right?  Well, just spraying them with a fire extinguisher isn't enough, they'll jump in the water, then light back on fire when they get out.  How do you solve it?  You have to stand in a very specific spot, go into your inventory, take out a bone, throw the bone in the water, go into your inventory, take out the fire extinguisher, and spray it at just the right time, as the beaver as the jumps into the water.  Somehow, this chain of events kills the beaver permanently, and they never come out of the water.
How does this make any sense?  I found that too many of the puzzles in this game just made no sense, or were impossible to solve using logic, and I'm hesitant to recommend it.
Get a walkthrough, use it only when needed, and I think you'll enjoy the game for its story and characters, though.  The writing for the characters is witty, and I like the flirty dialogue. The game is fun when you're not banging your head against the wall.

I have to say that Grim Fandango is an awesome game, It brought new mechanics to the genre and it has its singular style and humor that marks it as a very memorable game. Still, it had some technical flaws back in the days, stuff like bugs and such. Back in the 90's there weren't DLCs, fixes and stuff like this, so those bugs remained there.
Now we have a thing called Grim Fandango REMASTERED, so you think that the game gets refreshing stuff like compatibility, new graphics, maybe new ways to approach the game and FIXES. We have some new 3D models, but the prerendered backgrounds are still the same (and look a little worse if you use the remastered version), the movements feel iffy and can be used only with tank commands, otherwise Manny will always get confused when moving to another area. But most of all, we don't have any fix for bugs, just a compatibility fix for new systems. Why do we need a Remaster then? I'm not even using the Remastered graphics because except the "new" 3D models everything looks worse. Even the dubbing didn't get an audio improvement (italian version, don't know for the others) and you can clearly hear the microphone noises of the 90's, some Audacity fixes could've help a lot, it's not asking too much I think, some basic stuff if you call your product REMASTER. But most of all, bugs didn't get a fix, I encountered some of them (crashed a couple of times) and now I'm stuck to Rubacava because everytime I try to give an object to Glottis to proceed, he starts running in circles and I can't command anything, so I'm stuck and the only thing I can do is close the game and start from the beginning and hope it doesn't happen again (reloading the savefile doesn't work).
Is the game worth playing? Grim Fandango is one of the most beautiful games ever made, so yes.
Is the REMASTERED worth buying? No, because it's just the same game with not much effort and not even basic fixes.

I'll do this in bullet point format to keep things brief, while keeping the information relevant:

It doesn't "redefine the genre" like it claims, and several levels I've encountered are just downright frustrating and unenjoyable. In general I like the different mechanics for the worlds, the multiplayer is a blast, and the visuals are nice, it also runs fantastically on my laptop which can barely run bejeweled. I cannot stand the "solve 4 timed puzzles in a row without messing up because they'll randomize if you do" which cannot be skipped and are mandatory for story progression, I feel like it's needlessly frustrating and are the worst part of the game in my opinion. The story is also very cringeworthy, littered with pop culture references that are only barely relevant and will quickly wind up very dated. It's like when your dad tries to meme. The price tag is also a bit high for what it is, as I've encountered games with twice the depth, just as much if not more play time, and half the price. However it's a great thing to pick up on sale when it drops below 20$.
All in all despite the frustration I think it's a great game to grab on special and will keep you entertained for hours. The core mechanics are solid and entertaining, but be ready for the bit of frustration that comes with it.

Don't expect anything like the original Pac-Man except for the characters and the controls.
You don't ever have to think in this game. You don't move around trying to collect all orbs like in the original game - you follow spawning courses of orbs while waking up ghosts until you find a big orb so you can eat all the ghosts following you Snake-style. That's the whole gameplay - checkpoint races.
The game advertises 5 different game modes. Let me explain these modes to you:
1. Score Attack (5 Minutes): In 5 minutes, follow enough orb courses as you can.
2. Score Attack (10 Minutes): Same as 1, but with 5 minutes more.
3. Time Trial (Short): Follow all the orb courses as fast as you can. Divided into 10 seperate short courses.
4. Time Trial: All the 10 courses in 1.
5. Ghost Combo: Follow enough orb courses so you can eat a maximum number of ghosts in a single run.
I only see 3 different game modes with different lengths. Which one you want to play depends on how long the game takes you to bore you out.
With 7 stages, you might except that you need to develop different strategies. You don't because you simply follow the courses the game shows you.
When I first played the game, I thought: "Oh my God, I'm so full of adrenaline right now, I can't wait to try out the other game modes!"
Then I found out that there aren't really different game modes, and once I noticed how the game works and how I am supposed to play it to maximize my score, it became incredibly boring.
When I saw achievements such as "Gain 2 million points" I thought that the game would keep me playing for days or maybe even weeks until I'll earn all achievements. It took me 30 minutes.
I expected to be at least able to play the original game. You can't. The only original thing about this game is a visual style which you can unlock it earning every single in-game achievement. Which involves doing stuff such as uploading lots of scores to Facebook.
High speed, nice graphics, many stages and lots of customization just aren't sufficient if the gameplay lacks variety.

Shadowrun: Dragonfall does not quite match Baldur's Gates or Fallouts, but it is a rather good game.
Shortly:
- If you were disappointed in Shadowrun Returns, but you find the world of Shadowrun interesting, give it another chance with Dragonfall. For me Returns was a disappointment.
- If you haven't played any of the Shadowrun tittles yet but are interested then do "skip" Shadowrun Returns (the first tittle, although, the stories are completely separate) and go with Dragonfall.
I am familiar with the Shadowrun pen 'n' paper roleplay, but not really a fan of it. Still, the mood of the world behind the game is well captured and the storyline is solid. There are also additional companion missions, side missions and bonus objectives which are optional, although, some side missions (of your choice) have to be accepted in order to proceed in the main storyline.
If only there was voice acting in the game, it would be so much better.
Compared to the previous tittle - Shadowrun Returns - the Dragonfall fares a lot better. Several improvements to the gameplay have been made for a more enjoyable play. The NPCs in the team are more (meta)humane than previously, with more character to them. The game is less linear than Returns. There are some bigger choices and some smaller choices, some of which affect the game, but some are just immersion (which in itself is not necessarily a bad thing).
Still, a few mechanics in the game are annoying, although, some of them can be worked around.
The most annoying is perhaps that while out of combat (and able to move real time) you can only control the protagonist and the rest of the team follows. Firstly, This makes it impossible to pick up items with your team members. Inventory space is very limited so most items end up being send to your storage (no longer accessable during the mission). Secondly, the protagonist is always the one to open the door to an unexplored area. And thus ends up taking the first shots (and grenades and spells) from the enemies as the turn based combat begins. Not every protagonist is tough as nails. The second flaw can be worked around by spending points on Body (toughness) or getting heavier armor, but it's still bad game design, especially since the combat it advertised as tactical, but you can't arrange your team to a position in advance.

The shadowrun series remains my favourite turn-based strategy game. Everything is enjoyable, apart from the decking - which is bland and uninspired. SRHK tries to remedy this aspect but it still feels flat.

Before I begin, the steam version of Vindictus is the NA version of the game, which services to the NA region + Australia. There is an IP lock for a good reason. If you live elsewhere, look out for the European, Korean, Japanese or Chinese (<- no IP lock on this one!) version of the game depending on where you live. There are plenty of guides online that can help you get into any of the servers I mentioned, along with English patches.
So, I’m known as Penguin. If you use the forums, or play on the West server, you might know me +hello. I don’t usually write reviews, but after seeing negative reviews only exaggerate on the negative points, I decided to write this. For the record, I started playing Vindictus on and off since open beta in 2010. Yes,
Gameplay:
Simply amazing. This is the main reason anyone plays Vindictus. As far as I am aware, there is no f2p
on the western market that even comes close to how fluid and enjoyable the combat system Vindictus has to offer. The game runs around a normal/smash combo system where you use left/right clicks (or j/k keys or your gamepad buttons) to control your character. Unlike your traditional mmo, there is no tab-targeting, and your quickslots are mainly for potions and consumables. I fell in love with Vindictus’ combat system 5 years ago. 5 years later, I still love it. For comparison purposes, Vindictus is like Monster Hunter or Dark Souls.
Extremely skill-based:
As discussed in the above post, Vindictus is a non-targetting action mmorpg. Raiding involves learning how to use your character’s survival mechanic to survive the attack patterns each boss has. Unlike many other action mmos on the market, a fraction of a second is enough to determine whether you survive or die to a boss. Something I heard from Junyoop, a relatively famous player and streamer of Vindictus KR (Mabinogi Heroes):
. As someone who mains Fiona, it’s true. You can play shieldless Fiona and survive solely with your invincibility-frameless roll, granted you have the skill. There are a few instances of sandbag bosses (Lakoria, Kraken head, Pantheum), but for the most part, facetanking raid bosses will most likely end with you dead.
Extensive armor customization/Fashion simulator 2015:
Need I say more? Each equipment set has an extremely unique appearance, with most equipment having three dye slots that you can customize. You can even cosplay your favorite characters from whatever game/anime/TV/movie using the armor sets and dye system available in-game [and you can acquire the look you want using ONLY in-game gold!](click
for some examples). Seriously, Vindictus can may well be fashion simulator 2015 :D.
Amazing soundtrack
‘nuff said. Especially raids. Samples:

RNG, RNG, and did I mention RNG?
Probably the only real legitimate concern about the game. Loot is RNG, your damage has (slight) RNG, enhancing/enchanting your gear is RNG. Update: seal shop is here, you will be able to get your level 80 weapon within a week of raiding. In addition, Purple tier regina (Lv90) gear is dirt cheap.
Badly optimized
Vindictus was developed on the Source 1 engine. As a result, the game mostly runs on one core, resulting in your modern multicore processor taking performance hits (Intel runs better than AMD for this). As far as I am aware, there are no plans on moving to the newer Source 2 engine. DevCat has tried to remedy this issue by adding multicore support for raid hosts, and the function works amazingly when it does decide to work, but the multicore function is still in beta and can be buggy.
PVP is unbalanced
Because Vindictus was intended to be a PvE game. PvP was only added because of popular demand. Devcat has made some modifications to PvP in an attempt to balance the characters, but it isn’t quite enough. It’s still fun though.
Cash shop
Cosmetics, protection items, RNG boxes (don’t buy these, ever), pets, self-revives, temporary equipment, outfitters, consumables, VIP service. Nothing game-breaking here. Vindictus is F2P, how do you think it survives? I will discuss everyone’s favorite topic of “pay2win?”
.
Two ends of the community
Like every other game, there are nice people, elitists/scumbags and the silent people who just enjoy the game. As of late, I haven’t seen many elitists nor attack requirement boats, which is really nice. The silent people who just play the game take the majority though.
Grinding/Farming
“This is a Korean MMO, it’s OBVIOUSLY a grindfest” …. In terms of leveling: not really, especially with how the low level content has been streamlined. Back in 2010, it took me a solid 8-10 hours to get to level 12. Now, it takes me 2 hours. Exp is no longer split between party members, and story quests give ridonkulous amounts of exp. Of course, there still exists some form of grinding, as this is an MMO, but seriously, unless you have zero tolerance for any kind of grinding, Vindictus isn’t much of a grind as you think it to be.
So,

I've long lamented the lack of new quality battle puzzle games in the vein of Tetris Attack and Meteos.  Tumblestone's multiplayer mode is the first thing to scratch that itch for me since Planet Puzzle League came out on the DS all the way back in 2007.
The game overall involves several stacks of colored stones (tumblestones) at the top of the screen and you need to "shoot" (for lack of a better word) 3 of the same-colored tumblestone in a row to clear them.  You only have access to the first row of tumblestones so you need to avoid getting into a situation where you cannot get at three tumblestones of the same color.  In multiplayer you have three modes.  Puzzle Race involves up to four players trying to be the first to clear an identical board of tumblestones.  If you get into a state where you cannot continue clearing the board, you need to reset and start again.  In Battle the tumblestones slowly move downward.  If the tumblestones hit the bottom, you are eliminated.  If you find yourself in a state where you cannot get to three same-colored tumblestones in a row,  you have no choice byt to make a "bad move" (where you shoot a tumblestone followed by a different-colored tumblestone) which causes the tumblestones to shift downwards several rows instantly.  The goal is to be the last surviving player.  Tug of War seems pretty similar to Puzzle Race, but involves multiple sections of smaller puzzles.  There are also a variety of modifiers available for each mode that I haven't gotten the chance to play with yet.  All of the modes require the player to balance speed with trying to plan ahead.  Battle in particular is very compelling and evokes a similar feeling to other classic battle puzzle games while also providing a pretty refreshing take on a match-3 puzzle game.
I should point out that for $9.99 you get only the multiplayer component.  For an extra $14.99 you get a full single player campaign (you can upgrade at any time).  If you're interested in the game primarily as a battle puzzle game, you should know that the campaign is not a series matches against bots like it is in some puzzle games, but is instead a series of predetermined puzzle boards for you to solve.  I'm finding this pretty fun as well, but obviously it's a very different feel from the multiplayer mode.  If it doesn't sound like your cup of tea, then you should stick to the base $9.99 multiplayer package.

A really clever and unique puzzle game!
I'm really into puzzle games, and it's been a while since I've played something as new and fresh as Tumblestone.
The basic mechanic is very simple, and at first the game seems easy. As you progress, new twists in the rules are thrown in to the mix and you very quickly find yourself taking a few moments to contemplate each move. With a little thought, you can usually get past each puzzle board after a few tries... At least until the occasional timed or vs. AI level appears, and you have to switch gears and toss the tumblestones as quickly as you can.
The game has a quirky story that will make you squint and scratch your head at bit, but most of the time you'll be focusing mastering the new rules that are introduced with each new world you explore.
A great addition to the puzzle game genre, with a little more depth than your typical matching game, and hundreds of puzzles to keep you engaged for quite a while.
Definitely recommended for fans of Tetris, Bejeweled, and Candy Crush Saga looking for the next challenge.
And, it has multiplayer!
Disclaimer: I'm a huge fan of "The Bridge", and met the developer at GDC after playing his first game and was lucky enough to get an invitation to beta test Tumblestone.

What's there to say about
that hasn't already been said? I don’t think I need to recount how, despite a sterling critical reception, it sold so poorly that it signalled the - mercifully temporary - death of the P’n’C genre. This game about death, starring a bunch of skeletons on a mission to reclaim their rightful destiny. Now, in this remastered version, given a second chance at un-life, have they finally done it?
Aye, I suppose they have. Let me explain.
Okay, so
is a great game, we all know this. The sultry dialogue sizzles with attitude, the characters are desperate and devious, lovable and loathsome. The performances are top of the class, seriously.
It’s flawed, yeah. Oh yeah, it’s flawed as hell. After a strong start in the art deco masterpiece that is El Marrow, you’ve got a short, silly section in some brown woods with a bunch of trial and error puzzles. Then Rubacava, a massive area, with more interesting characters than I’ve space to list. A place you’ll really lose yourself, speaking both metaphorically and literally (it is a big area…)
And then more trial and error ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ a bit later on, and the denouement, which is just too small and brief to leave much of an impression. I don’t want to give too much away, so excuse me if I sound like I’m being flippant, or overly critical. There aren’t any truly terrible parts, but it’s inconsistent. There are signs that parts of the game have been rushed, and there are some puzzles that it might have been better off just leaving out entirely. But, I can’t think of any other adventure games which don’t have rough spots and dodgy puzzles. The highs of
are higher than most other games of this type. I don't mean to be fawning, but this game has a lot of soul.
So, what have they changed with this remastered version? The biggest thing is that now it’s entirely playable with the mouse! Nice! I’m not sure it was so terrible having to play with the keyboard, but hey, it’s good to have the option. Probably I’m a weird anomaly ‘cos I played with a controller anyway, but that worked fine, so yeah, thumbs up there.
Then there’s the textures. They’ve been redone, at much higher res than before. They look alright but it doesn’t make that much difference really, when most characters are just suit and skull, or boiler suit and fat orange arms. There’s also some shadowing thrown in, but literally the only place I noticed it was in Manny’s office, in front of the venetian blinds.
looked fine, it didn’t need to be prettied up, but it would be churlish to complain, really.
The big draw about this edition is dead simple. You can buy it. You can’t buy the old one, and haven’t been able to for some time. But, now you can, and that’s wonderful. Even better, there’s an option in most areas to listen to director’s commentary, enlightening chat from some of the finest minds in the industry. And Tim Schafer.
And, did I mention that the music has been entirely redone? It’s all orchestrated now, and that’s worth the asking price alone.

Words cannot describe how awesome this game is. Filled to the brim with bright, colorful graphics, energetic electronic music, and addicting, fun gameplay, Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ is hands down the best Pac-Man game ever created, and is very deserving of the nickname I have given it: Dubstep Rainbow Pac-Man.
The game differs greatly from most other games in the Pac-Man series in several ways. For one, the goal is no longer just to survive for as long as you can, but instead to create long rainbow trails consisting of hundreds of ghosts that follow you around the maze as you gobble up pellets. The ghosts randomly generate in patterns around the map, and moving past them will wake them up and they’ll join the chain. Power pellets return and function just as they did in the original game, and you can use them to eat the long trails of ghosts you create, but now Pac-Man can also use (a limited number of) bombs to temporarily send back the ghosts that are currently following him. Also, the game accelerates significantly (from speed 0 to speed 50) during the stages as ghosts and fruit are eaten. If you’re good, your score is very likely to go over at least a million points.
There are several different play courses to choose from, and they are unlocked as other modes on other courses are completed. In addition, multiple modes and different time trial settings are unlocked as things are completed. You may also change the graphical style to resemble the original game or almost any one of its sequels. The game also boasts an incredibly energetic soundtrack (Pac-Rainbow is my personal favorite) and there are a variety of songs to listen to while playing. Last but not least, there is optional paid DLC that adds several new courses, music tracks, and graphical styles.
A word to the wise, however: due to how many objects can be on the screen at once, the game can occasionally have some slow-down and lag. It doesn’t affect gameplay, but does put a slight strain on your computer. So if you think your computer might not be up to running such a game, check your specs before buying.
Overall, I very highly recommend Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ to anyone who has ever played a Pac-Man game, enjoys modern games with retro themes, or just likes arcade-style games in general. =)

I'm 2 hours in so this is a first impressions review.
In this game you wander around an expansive 2D black and white animated wild west full of snakes and skeletons, reading very funny and silly descriptions and interacting with quirky characters, some of whom want you dead. There is turn based combat (if you want it) and a whole host of adventure game style collect-and-cash-in mechanics. The menus and traversal are all quick and intuitive and the art style and animation are consistent, irreverent, and joyful. The music evokes spaghetti westerns.
The standout so far is that there is very little filler in the world - towns, caves and chasms you explore are short and sweet, densely packed with different things to click on, loot and/or kill. I don't know how long the game is but from the map it seems a bounty of riches for the seven quid it cost me.
Warning: if you don't like reading text, this game is not for you. Why did I write text there? Who knows.

Before I begin, the steam version of Vindictus is the NA version of the game, which services to the NA region + Australia. There is an IP lock for a good reason. If you live elsewhere, look out for the European, Korean, Japanese or Chinese (<- no IP lock on this one!) version of the game depending on where you live. There are plenty of guides online that can help you get into any of the servers I mentioned, along with English patches.
So, I’m known as Penguin. If you use the forums, or play on the West server, you might know me +hello. I don’t usually write reviews, but after seeing negative reviews only exaggerate on the negative points, I decided to write this. For the record, I started playing Vindictus on and off since open beta in 2010. Yes,
Gameplay:
Simply amazing. This is the main reason anyone plays Vindictus. As far as I am aware, there is no f2p
on the western market that even comes close to how fluid and enjoyable the combat system Vindictus has to offer. The game runs around a normal/smash combo system where you use left/right clicks (or j/k keys or your gamepad buttons) to control your character. Unlike your traditional mmo, there is no tab-targeting, and your quickslots are mainly for potions and consumables. I fell in love with Vindictus’ combat system 5 years ago. 5 years later, I still love it. For comparison purposes, Vindictus is like Monster Hunter or Dark Souls.
Extremely skill-based:
As discussed in the above post, Vindictus is a non-targetting action mmorpg. Raiding involves learning how to use your character’s survival mechanic to survive the attack patterns each boss has. Unlike many other action mmos on the market, a fraction of a second is enough to determine whether you survive or die to a boss. Something I heard from Junyoop, a relatively famous player and streamer of Vindictus KR (Mabinogi Heroes):
. As someone who mains Fiona, it’s true. You can play shieldless Fiona and survive solely with your invincibility-frameless roll, granted you have the skill. There are a few instances of sandbag bosses (Lakoria, Kraken head, Pantheum), but for the most part, facetanking raid bosses will most likely end with you dead.
Extensive armor customization/Fashion simulator 2015:
Need I say more? Each equipment set has an extremely unique appearance, with most equipment having three dye slots that you can customize. You can even cosplay your favorite characters from whatever game/anime/TV/movie using the armor sets and dye system available in-game [and you can acquire the look you want using ONLY in-game gold!](click
for some examples). Seriously, Vindictus can may well be fashion simulator 2015 :D.
Amazing soundtrack
‘nuff said. Especially raids. Samples:

RNG, RNG, and did I mention RNG?
Probably the only real legitimate concern about the game. Loot is RNG, your damage has (slight) RNG, enhancing/enchanting your gear is RNG. Update: seal shop is here, you will be able to get your level 80 weapon within a week of raiding. In addition, Purple tier regina (Lv90) gear is dirt cheap.
Badly optimized
Vindictus was developed on the Source 1 engine. As a result, the game mostly runs on one core, resulting in your modern multicore processor taking performance hits (Intel runs better than AMD for this). As far as I am aware, there are no plans on moving to the newer Source 2 engine. DevCat has tried to remedy this issue by adding multicore support for raid hosts, and the function works amazingly when it does decide to work, but the multicore function is still in beta and can be buggy.
PVP is unbalanced
Because Vindictus was intended to be a PvE game. PvP was only added because of popular demand. Devcat has made some modifications to PvP in an attempt to balance the characters, but it isn’t quite enough. It’s still fun though.
Cash shop
Cosmetics, protection items, RNG boxes (don’t buy these, ever), pets, self-revives, temporary equipment, outfitters, consumables, VIP service. Nothing game-breaking here. Vindictus is F2P, how do you think it survives? I will discuss everyone’s favorite topic of “pay2win?”
.
Two ends of the community
Like every other game, there are nice people, elitists/scumbags and the silent people who just enjoy the game. As of late, I haven’t seen many elitists nor attack requirement boats, which is really nice. The silent people who just play the game take the majority though.
Grinding/Farming
“This is a Korean MMO, it’s OBVIOUSLY a grindfest” …. In terms of leveling: not really, especially with how the low level content has been streamlined. Back in 2010, it took me a solid 8-10 hours to get to level 12. Now, it takes me 2 hours. Exp is no longer split between party members, and story quests give ridonkulous amounts of exp. Of course, there still exists some form of grinding, as this is an MMO, but seriously, unless you have zero tolerance for any kind of grinding, Vindictus isn’t much of a grind as you think it to be.

Tumblestone rocks! I don't normally play match three games but I love well designed puzzle games and also games to play with friends.
I bought this a while ago at PAX and I've really enjoyed it. My only reget was not buying more copies for friends. It really shines in multiplayer and especially in local multiplayer. It's a match three puzzle game with a variety of modes which are all fun.
It's good if you love puzzles but also enjoy them being fast paced (which is why I've described it as being like reverse tetris in the past). It's a match three game where you try to win before the other players. However, the trick is that it's a puzzle so if you do something in the wrong order you have to restart. You can be very close to being done then realize too late that you've messed up! The campaign is strong but expect some hard puzzles that will stump you right away; the difficulty gets high quickly. Rather than getting necessarily more difficult with each "world" it seems that it instead introduces another mechanic each world.
Buy this if you want a fun, easy to learn/teach local game for playing with friends or you enjoy fast paced puzzle games to play alone or with online friends/other players.

Tumblestone is deviously clever, especially as a multiplayer game.  Easy to pick up, difficult to master - a great party game addition, ranking up there with Towerfall and Nidhogg.  In no time, my friends and I were shrieking with triumph and disbelief.  Controllers recommended.
Essentially, you try to find 3 blocks of the same color, with 5 rows to choose from.  Choose wrong and you'll run out of options and have to start over (while your friends complete their puzzle)!  There are tons and tons of challenging mutators that add to the insanity.  There's also a surprisingly deep singleplayer campaign and some really competitive online multiplayer modes with a rotating challenge of the day. Much more content than your average puzzle game.
The visuals are simple, but easy to read.  The characters are cute and whimsical, which is infuriating if you've just lost to your friend for the third time!  The sound and music are well done - I liked how the background art and music change depending on who just won the round.  Overall, the game's style is cute, lightning quick and effective.
I recommended adding Tumblestone to your game night rotation, and also to people who like singleplayer puzzle games.

I've been playing puzzle games since I was young, but it's been quite a while since something has really grabbed my attention. I didn't think much of this when I first saw the store page, but I was so very wrong. Tumblestone is definitely the puzzle game I've been looking for.
Tumblestone is a Match-3 at heart, but it goes far deeper than you might think. The premise of the game is to match like-colored tumblestones in sets of three in order to clear the board. Your character shoots from the bottom of the screen to remove the lowest tumblestone of that column. This starts off as a rather simple task, but it quickly becomes a much more complex process; even the most straightfoward puzzles will require careful planning and execution to complete. As you progress through the campaign you will unlock modifiers, which mix up gameplay by changing the rules that are used when clearing blocks. Each of these modifiers will require you to think in a completely different manner than the others. You can also enable party mode in the options which will unlock every character and modifier to be used for local play only. In short, between its single-player and multiplayer modes, Tumblestone boasts a wide range of content.
The main focus of single-player is the story campaign. The store page isn't kidding around when it highlights this as a 40+ hour experience. There are 12 worlds in Tumblestone, each consisting of 30 stages. But even with 360 levels, everything feels like a unique challenge; otherwise, it wouldn't have taken me around 30 hours to reach the last world.  Each puzzle, with the exception of randomized milestone challenges, is hand-crafted in a way that really makes you think. To add to the depth, a new modifier is introduced in each world, becoming the main focus for that world. The first few stages of each world serve to get you acclimated with the new modifier. On the 10th and 20th stages, you are tested with a small gauntlet of randomized puzzles. The random puzzles being thrown in encourages you to figure out the puzzles yourself and improve your technique (rather than breezing through with a guide).  Although, if you are having some trouble, the game does reward you with a skip token from each world that is usable on any non-milestone stage. These tokens are cumulative and can be used at any point of the game. After passing your first gauntlet, modifiers from previous worlds are thrown in to stir up the gameplay even further. At the end of each world, you face off against the character of the next world in an action-packed puzzle race. Also, each milestone encounter is coupled with a story sequence that plays out with dialogue over gorgeous art stills. I was quite surprised as to how much I enjoyed the narrative; it even had me laughing out loud at times. Oh, and you can play as a sausage!
In addition to the campaign, there are 3 arcade modes: Marathon, Infinipuzzle, and Heartbeat. Marathon has no time limit for actions and is all about surviving as many moves as possible on a wider playing field than usual. Infinipuzzle, as suggested by the name, is an infinite string of randomized puzzles that keep coming until you fail. This mode also allows you to select a modifier, if you desire. And my favorite mode, Heartbeat, is a fast-paced survival challenge against a wall of steadily approaching tumblestones. Each of these modes, including each modifier in Infinipuzzle, has their own leaderboard. There are also leaderboards for your overall rank and the number of quests completed. Quests essentially act as a challenge list with objectives, such as: finish a level with the perfect amount of moves, complete a certain level, or win a match against a number of bots. And, just in case this wasn't enough content, there is plenty of variety to be found within the multiplayer as well.
Multiplayer can be played either online or locally with up to 4 players and/or bots across 3 match types. Battle is similar to your standard competitive puzzler where the more you clear, the more tumblestones appear on your opponents' boards. This mode is great for those who prefer traditional puzzle multiplayer. The other two modes, Puzzle Race and Tug of War, really break the mold when it comes to competitive action. Instead of fighting to knock your opponent out, you're trying to clear your board before they do. You gain a point in puzzle race by completing a full-sized puzzle before the others. Tug of war works a little differently, in that each player starts off with 2 small puzzles instead. Since they're smaller, they typically get cleared more quickly. However, to keep it interesting, another puzzle chunk is sent to your opponent once you clear yours. This mode is by far my favorite, as it has provided me some of the most intense and gripping back and forth matches I've ever had in a puzzle game. These two puzzle modes also allow you to activate any of the modifiers you've unlocked. Turning on all of the modifiers and randomizing them makes for some exciting matches as your mindset will have to change from round to round. It is also possible to customize other aspects of the multiplayer, such as how many rounds to win, or if you want everybody to have the same board or not. My favorite touch of the versus mode is that when a player wins a round, the background and music of the game change to their character's. The only downside to the multiplayer right now is there isn't a constant stream of players online. In these situations you can turn on bots--which range from pushovers to superhuman--or you can generate a friend key that allows them to play 5 matches with you per day. I'll admit that it is a bit cumbersome, but it's nice that your friends can try the online before they buy it.
Tumblestone is certainly a contender for my favorite puzzle game of all time, right next to Puyo Puyo and Tetris. However, keep in mind that this game can be quite challenging. There have been puzzles that I've reset hundreds of times on before figuring them out, but it's extremely satisfying to see that final shot slow down as your clear that last block. It is also quite addictive, as I often find myself returning to the game not even 10 minutes after exiting. All in all, Tumblestone is chock-full of content that will keep you occupied for countless hours; as mentioned before, I've spent over 30 hours on the story mode alone. Being a fantastic and challenging experience, I would absolutely recommend this game to any fan of the puzzle genre, without hesitation.

RuneScape Legends is an interesting game. You have multiple classes with different play styles. The concept is nice as I did have fun watching my 'hero' go about racing against the enemy as they slew monsters, bought items, and of course paid/killed someone to hurt my enemy.
The base value or 'interaction' with the game is great... but not so much when you try to advance.
Single player mode... that's to test decks. You can earn and win a couple of coins in the character unlock matches against the AI which also shows and unlocks the other heroes you can play as which can also net you two to three packs depending on your luck and your decks. The campagin will earn you a card, but VS is were it's mostly at.
To level up your character you need to fight someone else. To earn gold on your daily quests you need to fight other people. You earn money if you win, but you earn some experience if you lose... so get ready to lose a lot.
Card packs share Heartstone's formula which means extra cards are grinded into dust which are then used to craft the card you want. It isn't that bad considering a good hand , semi-descent deck and planning can do a lot but getting to the 'semi-descent' deck is the hard part.
To earn gold you need to win or loss a lot while hoping your quest doesn't require you to actually win a fight otherwise you already lost that gold. You can spend cash to buy packs, but a few packs won't cut it so your going to need to spend a bit or a lot more money if you want to win and earn gold.
Steam workshop seems to be a great idea as playing around with some of those ideas or making new single player quests to test your luck against or try to get a fair challange against is a wonderful idea... I just hope that the fix some of the issues as having to lose constantly just to 'level up' your hero enough to get some cards and see if you are luck in your dailys to earn some gold can be very frustrating.
If your willing to fork over some cash during this christmass sale than you'll be in luck. Otherwise... download the game and try getting your log in rewards until you get enough to make a semi-descent deck. I know magic the gather is loved for it's easier to collect all the cards method... but the fighting an AI and getting some gold and level up everytime you fight might be needed to be brought over here... even if it's only ten or twenty gold.
Packs cost 1,000 gold mind you.
So for right now... it's an interesting game, but what you can do is limited by your luck on packs and your wallet if you want to do PVP where a descent chunk of the gold comes in. So it's more of a 'Pay to Start' then take it from there.
Hopefully they'll fix the issue sooner rather than later.

First of all, you may notice that I have over 900 hours on this game, so when you see a negative review from myself it is not without a lot of thought.
I first discovered Chronicle back in March 2015 and was immediately hooked. The gameplay is like nothing else. Then I signed up and started playing from day 1 of the Closed Beta.
For those of you that don't know, my friend Ryan and myself ran a weekly Chronicle Podcast (Friends Of Al Kharid) where we discussed the latest goings on in the game as well as having devs on to chat about things. As well as this we ran the RS Chronicle League as well as other events.
In the short history of the game, I am the only person to have finished in the Top 10 of the monthly ladder five times and have also reached the final of every tournament which has been organised.
So now you know where I'm coming from, it's a place of total love for a unique game that I and many others could plainly see the potential for, I'll move onto why I'm posting a negative review.
In the past 6 months, Jagex have been proven to have broken promises regarding new features, balancing changes as well as a $10k Invitational Tournament. The development team has been shrunk from an already small number as people move onto other projects and key future features like a Spectator mode and Mobile release have been shelved.
All of this has been without any official announcement from Jagex. This is seemingly to give the impression that development on the game is still ongoing, in the hope that they can still milk in as much money as they can from unsuspecting players.
This is completely dishonest in my opinion and a seriously ♥♥♥♥♥♥ way to treat their loyal player base. I've defended them a ton over the past year but even I have had enough.
The game was released too early, missing key features and thus failed to keep new players.

Hard to say; have you got OCD, but not ADD? Then this is for you!
OK, the game starts in 2001, and is an accurate representation of the world at that time.
What I like:
Detail, I love detail. This game can be played as a poor, corrupt nation that you need to build up, or as an established super power that can wipe out others with a flick of the hand (I prefer playing as the former). It is open ended; you can chose what goals you want, like actually attempting to recover a piece of territory historically stolen by a neighbor of your chosen country, or you can set a series of specific goals in a time limit for your challenge, like "conquer the world", or "develop your nation".
Once playing the game, you do need to pay attention, very closely, to international causes and effects of actions (these include actions that are not only yours). They all do something, sometimes mysteriously (until you know what to look for), other times very obviously. The resource, budget and trade roles are extremely entertaining, as is figuring out what treaties are most beneficial with which countries, to your ends.
And yes, you can go to conventional or nuclear war, or do some espionage and sabotage and frame other countries for it.
What I don't like;
It is a hard one, for me, as this is decidedly my type of game, but with all the screens of information there are already, I still want a couple more. Like, it would be nice to know a breakdown of your diplomacy costs, I don't seem to find that. Also, with diplomacy and trade, it would be nice, for example, to have some indication (other than guesswork) as to why a common market you've established is not receiving favored trade, and such. I feel the effect of diplomacy is a tiny bit under-represented. That it is not completely transparent is realistic, but sometimes you could push a treaty a little more to measure its effect.
In all; not a game if you are into furious action. You need patience and broad, ponderous awareness of what's going on, and any tendency to tunnel vision onto one single aspect of your policy or goal will lead to failure of your government, market or military, and thereby the game.

Superpower 2 is a fantastic geopolitical simulator which still holds its own 12 years after its launch.
The game is a sandbox geo simulator in which you control the economy, politics and military of any country in the world.
Don't expect here deep story driven scenarios because, in line with its sanbox design, Superpower 2 gives the tools and allows the player to craft his own narrative of world domination, economic revolution or diplomatic path to world peace (which is almost impossible).
The military aspect is pretty barebones, with no real tactical or even strategic depth, albeit that was a deliberate choice by the developers, who wanted a more hands-free aproach to war. Therefore it is pointless to campare this game to Hearts of Iron or any other franchises which focus specifically on the combat, because that is only one aspect of what constitutes the Superpower 2 experience.
On a side note I have to mention that the Strategic screen from where you command nuclear strikes all around the globe is very cool (it nevers grows old to watch a barrage of hundreds of nuclear missiles falling on your enemies - if nuclear war is your thing this game is definately for you).
Finally, one of the most important aspects of this game that has to be mentioned is the modding community which has been diligently updating the game's database and including awesome features for the past 12 years (Strongly recommend Mr. Mondays mod).
Superpower 2 is far from perfect, with simplistic combat, cumbersome espionage and diplomatic mechanics, but it is also a simple yet deep experience and loads of fun.
In short, definately worth the price!
