Far Cry 2 has nothing to do with Far Cry 1 and you can not compare them to each other because of that. Which is great. Because Far Cry 1 was a mess. It wasn't inherently bad of course. Hell, it was cutting-edge at its time! But I didn't like it too much.
Nontheless, Far Cry 2 is just as hard as its predecessor. You're in Africa. You got malaria. Everyone wants to kill you. Ammo is scarce. Weapons jam frequently. Cars do, too. And I'm sure there's one bad person the dev team didn't like for every god damn guard post in this game. Oh the guard posts. Also, the AI is pretty good, especially on higher difficulties, making some fights seemingly impossible to win. Perfect for the masochistic player.
One could argue that the main objective of a video game is to be fun. And you would be right. Seeing all these elements in Far Cry 2 and playing it for myself I can't say the game is always "fun". The game can be a frustrating, challenging and enraging piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥that slaps you for wanting to play with it. At times, Far Cry 2 doesn't like you nor does it want to play with you. Essentially, this game has a lot of conflict between casual video game fun and stress. But that's what makes this game a good game.
It's not outstandingly great, by any means. But it's pretty solid. Although a lot of the missions come down to "Kill this guy", "Blow up this thing", "Steal that thing" or "Collect 1000 of these, pretty please". Also, you drive around. A LOT. Seriously. If there would be an african driving simulator, this would be it, I can tell you that for a fact.
You could argue that Far Cry 2 can get boring at times. And it does, it certainly does. But then again, I've played MMOs so I'm up for the challenge. I don't get bored that easily. And if you don't get bored that easily like me, Far Cry 2 might just be the right game for you.
You like shooting guys in the face with a variety of weapons? You like burning down vehicles, small, destructible buildings, people and gas stations? You like blowing stuff up? You like a gorgeous looking open world FPS? You don't have anything against repetitive quests and objectives? Having a constant, life-threatening condition that could strike you down at any moment doesn't bother you too much? Driving around in a car that breaks down all the time due to tons of guys shooting at it is no problem for you? If you said "Yes!" numerous times in the last 20 seconds, I advise you to get this game and have fun (or frustration - who cares, both words start with f so that's fair enough) with it!
I like Far Cry 2 so far and if you think like me, you will like it, too. If you don't, it can't be helped. Not everyone can have a decent taste in video games. But you'll learn, I'm sure of it.

FOR THE MORE REFINED GAMING PALETTE; THE THINKING MANS SHOOTER.
Easily the best in the series, and a deeply underrated experience that just gets better with age.  I'm on my dozenth play-through, and have owned this on PC, Xbox and PS3, and the game still feels fresh, and unrivalled.
It's not your run of the mill shooter; it's adult, grown up gaming, set in the real world, with strong moral content that stays with you long after the credits have rolled, without going over the top into cheesy emo edgyness.  Less is definitely more; you'll never quite work out the perfect the weapon loadout, or have as much ammo or as you'd like, and the game is all the better for it.  The game feels like an uphill struggle from the start, but the satisfaction that comes from using the game mechanics (e.g. night) instead of ignoring them is unrivalled in gaming.  There's also one of the strangest endings in gaming, full stop...

Poor balance kinda ruined it for me. A level 1 spider hits you for 4 damage, a level 3 mob might hit you for 30 damage, but your level 4 warrior hits for 17. You end up with weird battles. One hex you just mindlessly click buttons to win a battle and the next hex over has enemies that one-shot kill your party that you just spent the last 70 turns role-playing.
Most turns are slow paced and directionless, clearing low level mobs that have no chance of hurting you, then you get attacked by a party that one hits you and forces you to re-start. End up being boring, knowing that your choices dont matter.
*Edit 1 Another thing that grinds my gears the battle system. I generally hate card based games, because it seems like you are wasting so much computing power trying to copy something that you do in real life (handle cards with little pictures drawn on them) only BECAUSE YOU DONT HAVE THE COMPUTING POWER TO DO IT BETTER. So you are using a computer to simulate handling cards when in real life you dont want to handle cards. You only use cards because you dont have a computer. It makes no sense... I digress.
Thea's card based system does work for fighting battles. You just have to think, "ok these are my support classes", "this is really a dodge", "this is really a block", "ok, card order is initiative", and so on. Basically re-inventing the wheel, but it works.
What seems down right wrong is that the game copies it's battle card system and uses it for everything else. Want to pull a sword from a stone ("physical challenge") it runs that exact same "battle" system with cards but changes your stats based on physical stats and not on your combat stats. Instead of the cards showing the enemies attacking you, it shows a generic card (chess piece) and you still use the same sorts of moves you would in a real battle. It represents you over coming the physical challenge, in battle form. Same goes for "intelligence challenges". YOU FIGHT A BATTLE WITH CARDS. Very un-creative and feels like they rushed the game and didnt bother to think up anything better.
The worst part of all, and the part that really makes it seem like a wrong decision to use card battles for everything, is that glancing at your characters it is hard to tell how good they will be a certain task. The UI and game in general gives you a good idea about the combat strength of your characters. You have a damage value on your character screen - one guy has a 32 another guy has a 11. Ok the guy with 11 is going to be worse in combat. Ui is clear on that. When you go into an "intelligence challenge" the card battle is based on other stats but it is not clear. If you look at the damage value for those same two guys in this new intellegence challenge the first guy might have a damage value of 5 and the other guy, who is smarter but worse in combat, will have a damage value of 14. Before I knew that the game just copies the battle system for all of the challenges, I though I had clicked on the wrong button...
*Edit 2 Another thing that bother me about this game is how tacked on the village and camp portions of the game seems. Leading an expedition and having an adventure is 99.9999% of the game, the village and camp part shouldnt have been added. You village is only allowed ten buildings (which you can tear down to build others), but once you build your ten buildings, your resources just start piling up and there is no use for the resources. Maybe is it just bad game balance.
For example, I "gather" mushrooms near my village, I get 14 mushrooms per turn. If you build a field (as one of my ten building limit), the field allows you to harvest 1 mushroom. Thats right, just 1. A sinlge guy wandering in the woods can harvest 14x TIMES AS MANY MUSHROOMS. The only reason I could see to send out a harvesting party ("expedition") was to gather rarer food items so I could cook other dishes. By turn 80 or so I was playing it as a cooking mini-game, because there is nother else to do. By turn 90 or so, I had 150 turns worth of food and 200 turns of fuel (or some thing like that). This game really should have been made as a mobile game.

Thea is a never ending bedtime story.  Mechanically, it's a really interesting mixture of a lighter version of Gwent and a strategy RPG.  A lot of the game is randomized, and with that, there are a lot of curve balls that come at you and force you to change how you're playing the game.  That means that on top of the well written and pleasantly voice acted stories that are scripted into the game, the more potent drama often comes from emergent content.
For example, you might find yourself in a situation where your food stores have been wiped out in an event, so you have to send some people into exile from your village to die so that the rest have a chance at surviving long enough to forage.  So you death march them off to fight an impossible boss, and against all odds they win, and can come back to the village with enough meat, berries and rare loot to save everyone.
It's also a very unobtrusive game.  You can keep it in windowed mode, and it uses very few resources, so it's easy to take a break between turns, get some work done, and then pick up where you left off a few hours later.  The music serves as very pleasant background, and I've actually let it run overnight on accident a couple times because of how soothing it is.
I've completed the main campaign twice and failed it three times.  A full playthrough takes about 10 hours, but each time you unlock a new character, which changes the story slightly and presents different content and playstyle options.  Highly recommend this lovely, fun, relaxing game.

Played the game on Bethesda Launcher before it was released on Steam. Finished the free single player campaign but never player PvP.
It felt like a mixture of Magic and Hearthstone. The deck construction is like magic where you can mix up to two classes of cards, while the battle system is like Hearthstone where magicka (like mana crystal in HS) grows up by 1 each turn and how attack works. There are also supports and items which are pretty much similar to the artifacts and equipment in Magic. Creature abilities are basically a sum of both games: summon (battle cry), guard (taunt), breakthrough(trample), last grasp (deathrattle), lethal(poison), drain(lifelink), pilfer, regenerate, etc.
It does introduces something new in this game: Mainly the two lane system where each lane is its own battle ground, so you'll have to be more tactic about distributing your creature cards on the field. Also the special rules of each lane (stealth-like right lane and level-specific left lane) makes it worthwhile to consider which lane you want to lay down your card (In a way, it's a reinvention of Magic's flying creature mechanism). There's also the rune sytem which acts like secret from HS that let you draw 1 card when losing certain amount of health. There are cards that interact specifically with such mechanism. Second-go player are quite compensated with jewel rings that are like the extra coin in HS but you can use it three times.
I have to agree with what others said about the balancing. I feel that the three uses of jewel for second-go is a bit too much, but at least it's not completely unplayable for first-go player. Also I'm not a hug fan of 50-card minimum requirement for deck construction. This makes it extremely hard for beginners to build decent decks that don't contain "filler" cards (which essentially lower your chance of draw combo cards).
Overall, I still think this is definitely a game worth playing. You can play through a quite lengthy campaign for free and unlock others with in-game currency that you earn. There's even a solo Arena mode (like in HS) but you play against AI, great for PvE players like me. I think it finds a balance between the casual side of HS (simpler rules and faster pace) and the hardcore side of Magic (creature abilities, deck construction). It's a game you don't have to heavily invest your time in. You can simply pick up and leave any time when you have around 15min to spare, good for killing time. It would, however, be even better if it's brought to mobile device (which I think it's going to happen) for even better access to game.
It's very light on hardware and friendly to touch-screen. I would simply keep the game installed so that you can play it while waiting for a class to begin or having a coffee at Starbucks.

In a half-hour, I played through the game twice. It quietly horrified me both times. There is one decision to make in the game that you ought to try both ways to see everything the static speaks my name offers. It's a very much worthwhile experience if it's one you can handle--the game openly (but not exploitatively or luridly) handles suicide, abduction, torture, and severe mental illness. Prepare to be haunted by it afterwards.
Sad and fun and weird. All of those things

It could have been a compelling tale about mental illness, or some philosophical observation about suicide. It COULD have been. It needed something a little more than it gave to make any sort of profound statement. Instead, what you end up with is a slightly disturbing existentialist time waster.

First off, this is one of my favorite RTS games to date. It's very different and unique from other games and has it's own learning curve. Just because some units are higher tech does not make them better. Experiemental units don't win games and can be stopped with overwhelming force and numbers. Forged Alliance is oodles of fun, but has some issues.
The campaign is solid. Nothing all that different aside from characters yelling at you to help their worthless asses and different maps. I admittedly stopped after 4-5 missions. Do not care for campaign but it gets the job done. Skirmish and multiplayer are where this game shine. Oh, and if you don't like micro managing this might not be the game for you. Don't worry about hotkeys and actions per minute, but if you want your forces to fight intelligently and without too much human intervention then this might not be a fun game. The same goes for setting up a base. You need to layer air and ground defences properly, spread them in such a way that no side is weaker than the other or is supported by troops, blah, blah, blah. Lots of micro and strategy. Anyway.
Games start with your ACU (armored command unit) spawning in alone, and you have to build up from that. Depending on any in-game mods (it comes with a few) the game progresses quickly or slowly. You have to balance resource expenditure with resource gain, expand in a way that does not spread you out too much, and keep an eye out for enemy attacks from land, air, and sea. Early game is tense and nerve-wracking, depending on how quickly and efficiently you can amass a fighting force and defend your home base or ACU. Mid and end game are either quick steamrolls, (either you or the AI get smashed by others) or an hour or more war of attrition. Generally AI in this game is ok, but misses as much as it hits. They'll leave hundreds of land units stuck on an island, or drive them up and down the map without attacking a base.
However, I cannot express to you the terror of seeing a hundred+ enemy bombers flying towards your base. Same with experimental weapons. They can be countered, but god help you if they catch you off guard and unprepared. There are also nukes in this game. They're able to be defended aginst with missile defence silos, and  don't wipe out entire sections of the map, but they do enough damage that, should they land, it is very difficult to recover and can end your game.
There are plenty of units in each faction to construct unique and versatile fighting forces, and different tiers have different types of units. Tier 1 generally has the mass-produced and numbers over quality units. Tier 2 is the best of both worlds, decent fighting strength and affordability. Tier 3 is specialized and extremely expensive. The unit is good at one thing and nothing else. Tier 3 Interceptors command the skies but have nothing to attack the ground. Tier 3 bombers annihilate ground targets with MOABs and blinding speed but fall easily to well-placed Tier 3 and 2 AA defences as well as some patrolling Tier 3 Interceptors.
One major problem I have with this game though is that, the larger the battle, the slower the in-game time goes. In an 8v8 battle with AI it got to a point where the passage of a single in-game second took five real-world seconds. And it wasn't because my computer couldn't handle it, but the game itself slowed down because it assumed I needed it since I was micro managing hundreds of units. At first this is a cool aspect, so you don't fall behind AI who can react instantly and manage thousands of units and productions at once, but it is unadjustable. Therefore once I've created the perfect base which supports and defends itself perfectly and I can just focus on fighting the game gets boring fast. It is the most frustrating thing to watch Tier 3 planes (the fastest units in the game) crawl across the screen like a snail. But if you have the patience for that, which I usually do but only for one to two hours, then this'll hardly be a detriment. To be frank though I'd rather have the slow-down than not, it has admittedly saved me from missing an experimental unit steaking through my lines more than once.
I could go on and on about this game, but in the end it's only $15 and if you like RTS games and have a few hours to dedicate to figuring out a whole new way of war, give this game a chance. It is not THE best strategy game (there isn't one) but it is certainly one of the best. It stands out from all others with it's scale, depth, strategy, and attention to detail. Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance is definately one of the benchmarks in strategy games and well worth a measly $15.

TL;DR It's a fun card game with a twist. Instead of using minions to fight eachother you use a hero that you power up in weapons, attack, armour and money.
Core gameplay
It's not like other cardgames like hearthstone since you don't use minions to fight the other player but you use minions to power up and get money to your hero. You can use money to buy stuff like healing, armour, weapons, attack increase and more. You place out minions and buy stuff until the other hero dies or you go to stage 5. Where you get to power up your hero one last time and then duke it out in a duel.
Graphics
You might think that since it's a card game the graphics are not that important. However since this is more like a walk though diffrent enviroments than a card game it's more important to showcase the enviroments and this is done well. The graphics have a nice "runescape" feel to them and in my opinion the graphics look good. It's not crysis 5000 and hyper realistic but it's also not a boring 2d card game.
Learning curve
The game does have a tutorial but I wish it was more in-depth on how the game works. It doesn't really teach you about how the stuff in the bottom of the card is what you will get and the top is what damage it will inflict, cost and what health it has.
Conclusion: I like this game. I don't see myself playing this all the tim but you gotta check it out. 7/10

So... I've played this game for a measly 6 hours, yet here I am, writing a negative review.
First of all, I'm not hardcore into TCGs. I kinda like them but they're not my main gaming focus. I've tried dozens of TCGs, including classics like Magic. But the one I mainly got stuck on was Infinity Wars, at least for some time. I dropped IW due to a massive lack of polish and then the occasional luckstomps. Sure you can't avoid luckstomps entirely in games like this, but not losing a game due to gamebreaking bugs would be nice.
In general I liked the gaming concept of IW however, and thus I came here thanks to steams recommendations.
So what is my beef with ES:L, so much so I feel I have to give the thumbs down and move on after a measly 5 hours?
Let's talk lanes and targeting first. Similar to IW, ES:L has 2 lanes (some very rare rounds have 1). Very unlike IW lanes here only roughly restrict your targeting. There is no pre-set attack order and turns are not simultaneous, so you can hit everything in your lane, but also the enemy if he/she doesn't have a unit with guard.
Some lanes also have RNG effects which are nice at first, and simply annoying and pesky later.
Now the purpose of this is putting depth into card placements. Basically the question is put your cards in the way of enemy team A or B? Exploit effect A or B?
Effectively though this brings tons of problems with it, combined with the other factors. The balance between defending and rushing is extremely fragile, a bit of drawing luck from your enemy, a bit of misfortune from you, and a superior force will be gone in a single turn. And we're seriously not talking about skill here, just to be clear.
Not really fun to me.
Theres even one card that injures all of your units in one lane, then there's another that kills every injured unit in one lane, exacerbating this kind of problem. No caveat either, and not difficult to play. Stuff like this seems to be rather common, and if you don't have a counter... tough. It's a key-lock situation. If you have the lock deck, get familiar with the location of the concede button. Or prepare different decks for... well, anything and everything.
Next we have Magicka, basically your summon resource.
You use it to summon cards. That's it. No spending Magicka to draw cards, no shuffling, nothing. So you have to keep up an adequate stream of cards by having other cards that allow you to draw more. Obviously RNGeezus is gonna have a couple words with you here.
If you miss your curve, draw too many high cost cards early, or not enough later on, or even better both, have fun wasting half your Magicka each turn. Have an enemy with a bit of luck and watch him spam the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you.
Even midway through the campaign it was common to have fights that were entirely based on RNG, with the stampede swinging both ways. Same deck, same strategy, some times I win with 20 HP left easily, some times I lose with enemy having 20 HP left and no chance from the beginning.
Oh, also the player that moves second gets a mana ring to make up for being late. I feel that's not quite balanced either and I've seen many people have the same problem.
And really, at this point I don't even care about further pros or cons in the game since the main mechanics are not my definition of TCG fun.
If you're prepared to dig through a seemingly unpleasant meta, and if you're prepared to face RNGeezus himself. Go for it.
Otherwise... pass this one up or be careful. Or try Infinity Wars, it's not perfect but has the whole 2-lanes/summoning resources business down a whole hell of a lot better in my opinion.

They took like 5 different genres and managed to squish em together into a really well done masterpiece! I give Thea: The Awakening a solid 5 outta 5!
Full Version
If you like dark fantasy, turn base games, tactics, cRPG style gear management and immersive mini choose your own adventure then chances are you will enjoy this.
The pace is slow. You manage a single village and send expeditions out to gather resources and do encounters around the map. Each game is unique because its randomly generated and the quest events you may or may not see are picked based on what tile they occur in and time of day and distance from map and many other factors... also there are many hundreds!
When you play a game you pick which deity your village is aligned to. All the xp you get in that game goes toward a passive tree for the god you played: play more with 1 god and your worshipers will be a bit better! Think of it like how FTL is a rouge-like but there's goals to work toward for unlocking new ships. Its a very enjoyable system! Rouge-likes and most 4x style games that don't have a point other then 'win or loose' don't intrest me so much. This one does it right!
Every combat encounter or skill check, such as tying to search an ancient library for any tomes you might have use of, is based on a card game. It was confusing to me at first but after some time I have it mostly figured out. The card game itself is fun and your cards are all based on various stats. Its very very well done.
But what I enjoy best is the random events and quests. The free DLC makes most of them narrated. They are written and voiced quite well. The graphics are just fine. Hand drawn art is good. Music is fantatsic. Crazy replay value. Non-liniar sandbox style game in that you can largely play the way you like within the game's ruleset: stay in your village and build up slow and safe or be a gathering/ crafting settlement... there's quite a few ways to mix and match playstyles.
Note: my friend owed me some money and when I saw this on sale for $9.99 USD I asked them to gift it to me (after I did some research on it). HIGHLY worth $10... heck its worth $20 easily. Three free DLC and there's even some player mods to add more events!
Now for the imperfections: Parts of the UI is clunky at times, such as adding resources to an expedition. I wish there were keyboard shortcuts for some common elements in the card game screen. While the in-game help menu is extensive its not explained very well in a few places so I felt newbish and had to bumble through some things till they clicked in my noodle. Some of the events do not offer many choices, just 'tell me more' and a 'okay' and 'goodbye.' I feel they should have made more dialouge paths for the smaller events. Fixable, but I should mention that I had to dramatically lower the music to make the narration intelligable. I am a bit over critical when it omes to gaming, though. Far Cry 2 is a open world first person shooter with some small RPG elements set in the African savannah.
You have a aim, killing the Jackal, the person who supply the African war groups with weapons and causes the whole country to suffer even more.
When arriving in Africa you get driven by a taxi driver to the main city Pala.
While driving through the magnificent looking landscape you see several things and also notice your Malaria.
You get a Malaria attack and get unconscious.
You wake up in a house in Pala and see your enemy, the jackal.
He decides who lifes and dies and he lets you alive.
After this you have to get out and get unconscious again after a while.
You get saved by a group called UFLL. There are 2 groups who have war against each other.
UFLL and APR. Who is the good and the bad have you to decide even though both are not perfect.
I personally prefer the UFLL. Only my opinion though.
On your way through the story you visit a lot of places and meet your buddies who help you.
I wont say more to dont spoiler too much.
The gameplay is actually very nice. I love the first person weapon handling.
It feels realistic and there is a big range of weapons to choose from.
All being buyable in the Weapon Store for diamonds.
Thats the currency of the game.
You can also buy upgrades for you and your weapon.
Your weapons degrade! Maybe too fast for some but for me its fine, especially with upgrades.
You can change them for free in your Weapon room and "repair" them like that.
I wouldnt recommend using weapons of the enemies, they are weak and in bad quality.
You often get quests to finish certain aims. The mission variety is fine even though not big.
But its fine for my taste. You mostly get diamonds or medicine for completing quests.
You can also find collectables in the game. Diamond suitcases with 1-3 diamonds in each and Jackal tapes.
There is a incredible amount of this stuff. Also there are 8 gold AKs in the whole world.
The difficulty is higher than normal. Dont try rushing over the enemy, this mostly wont work. You always have to watch out. And the health doesnt regenerate, at least not completely. You need some sort of medics to heal yourself and you cant carry unlimited of those.
The open world is extremely big and you have your feet, cars, boats or the bus to reach several places.
Busses are helpful for those who prefer fast traveling even though the busses just have 5 stations per map.
Enough for me though. The fact that you have to travel actually I like about the game.
Its nice visiting the landscape and I like this sort of oldschool traveling.
Some may dont like this sort of system but I love it.
While travelling you will often pass some sort of checkpoints of the enemy who will shoot you on sight.
Each of those checkpoints have some special ammo or medicine. Mostly with around 5 enemies at each point.
A little bit annoying about this game is the way how the Enemies respawn and hunt you with their cars after they saw you. You mostly have to kill the car until you can continue passing. Also the enemy is often faster than you. After you erased a point, the enemies will respawn fast after going away and come back and that is the most negative point about the game. I got used to it, even though I agree its not perfect. Beside of those checkpoints there are also other places which are often specially named. Places like bases of the enemy. Trainyards, camps, whatever. There are often 10+ enemies and you should watch out, most of those places you see automatically while doing missions.
There are also animals in the nature, around 5 sorts of animals in the whole game. Realistic behaviour and they shun humans. I often think they could add more animals and also hunting animals but on the other hand its not as unrealistic as in Far Cry 3. The animals there are to much if you ask me.
The graphics and engine in general are amazing.
I rarely saw so much realism. The whole engine simulates real world nature. Wind, rain, sun and day cycle.
The graphics in general look amazing. Especially fire effects. Definitely 10/10 in terms of graphics especially for 2008.
Some say Crysis or CryEngine 2 is better but I think they are equivalent. The Dunia Engine just has its aim on realistic day/night cylcle and weather cycle. A little part of the CryEngine is in the Dunia Engine btw!
The Music is also amazing and fits perfectly into the whole setting.
The African setting like that is pretty unique and thats great.
The Multiplayer is ok.
Some sort of CoD sort of Multiplayer which is just more realistic in general.
Not many people play it online anymore though.
Fortunes Edition DLC:
This is a small DLC which adds 3 new weapons, some new cars and some new Multiplayer maps.
Nothing special but not bad either.
And now our favorite part.
Can it compete against Far Cry 3?
I say yes.
Its maybe not everyones taste but Far Cry 2 counts to my favorite games and can compete against Far Cry 3.
It maybe doesnt have so many gameplay tweaks as Far Cry 3 but I like this rustical way how Far Cry 2 handles everything. Reminds me a little bit of oldschool games. Not a lot of gimmicks but everything thats neccessary to have a nice game. I love the atmosphere of the game. The whole nature is amazing and the music fits perfectly into the game. Maybe its even better than Far Cry 3 in this part.
Some of you are maybe spoilered of Far Cry 3.
Try ignoring the things that Far Cry 3 does better.
I already played the game 2009 and I loved it back then.
Far Cry 2 maybe isnt perfect but it does a lot of things right and it has a great experience.
You should definitely try it especially because of the price. I think the game will get 9/10 from me, maybe overrated but I think this score fits good for me. Make yourself an own picture of the game and dont listen to people who say its bad.

This is possibly the best RTS game I have ever played, rivalling even my long-time favorite AoE2 and AoM.
Lets start with the premise for this game. If you ever played an RTS and felt like it was a bit small, Supreme Commander is the answer to your unasked question.
The game plays out on absolutely giant maps, with distances that take average units ages to walk across, requiring you to build transports to move them at an even slightly acceptable speed. It allows for actual artillery to be laid down and strike your enemies from afar, sending a hailstorm of screeching shells into your enemy's frontline or even their home base. It allows for nuclear strikes that can wipe out entire fields of units if you're not prepared for it. There is so much feeling packed into Supreme Commander of being an almighty God that you cannot help but go a bit mad playing the game.
That's not to say Supreme Commander isn't balanced; quite the contrary. There are four factions, each with definite strengths and weaknesses, none of them so great that they cannot fight the others, but require different tactics and approaches. You can play the UEF, the remnants of a federation of humanity, trying desperately to restore order in a galaxy of chaos, brought about largely by themselves. Signing on with them nets you a straightforward fight, with classic artillery, tanks and choppers. Or you can play as the guerilla cybernetic freedom fighters, the Cybran, who seek to bring justice to all those melded with machinery from the tyranny of UEF. The Cybran are decidely more versatile, often equipped with cloaking devices, EMP strikes and amphibious vehicles, which give them an easier time doing many different things, as the situations change, but not quite the same headstrong charge of the UEF. If you play the long game, you can take your chances with the Aeon, an almost religious group, using long-dead alien technology to bring their fanaticism to the rest of the galaxy. Your units tend to be more maneuverable, hit harder and have slightly longer range, but with slow firing rates and a general inflexibility; each unit does one job only. As the story mode unfolds, you can play with any faction, advancing their campaign to an eventual endgame to decide the fate of the galaxy, whether it be in the hands of a shattered UEF, the fledgling Cybran or the mysterious Aeon.
In Forged Alliance, a whole new faction is brought to bear; the Seraphim. An alien race, believed extinct and vanished, returns in the aftermath of the first game, bringing with them a hellfire that fractures what's left of all three factions of the first game. Only by uniting together will they be able to defeat this threat. But the strain of these alliegences threatens their goal and the game opens with the entirity of the humanity on its last legs, trying to stem the tide of the Seraphim. Playing as the Seraphim offers a unique sensation. They combine many elements from each of the three factions, while remaining very distinct from the others, not merely in aesthetics, but also in their unit options.
And still, I need to speak more about playing the game itself. Every game begins with a Supreme Commander; a builder, elite soldier, gatherer of resources and military overlord all in one. These commanders represent your player and if they are eliminated, traditionally, you are too and the game is over for you. Even if you allow for the deaths of commanders without ending the game, it can often lead to it indirectly; the explosion left behind is massive.
There are two resources, energy and mass. Mass is only found in specific locations, while energy can be harvested from anywhere, but the buildings for doing so represent huge targets for your opponent and a loss of energy, even temporarily, can often knock out many of your elite units' special abilities, costing you more than you might realize. The struggle for more mass extractors promotes territorial conflicts as players scramble to collect as many as they can, build defenses and station soldiers there.
Once the resources pour in, you lay down a few factories, either to make air units, land units or sea units; each with distinct features and systems, but none of them isolated: land units are quite capable of downing aircraft, aircraft can bomb land and sea and a vessel close enough to the land will often obliterate nearly any land unit that gets too close. And when you've got enough units around you and a few engineers out from them, you upgrade your factories and start producing newer and often better units.
An interesting facet of Supreme Commander is that even late in the game, older units never become completely obsolete; they are always generated faster, cost less and often 50 tier 1 units can outmatch the equivalent cost of tier 3 units. In this way, keeping tier 1 factories around is rewarded, rather than punished and it promotes a genuine question as to when to upgrade, rather than just as soon as possible.
But when it comes time to end the game, Supreme Commander is a spectacular show of so-called "Experimental Units" which can only be built by engineers from tier 3 factories and often at absurdly high costs. But if you can afford it, you will not regret it; experimental units are designed to end games that would otherwise continue indefinitely and they are often highly succesful.
And that's not even getting into all the complex features of radar, cloaking, stealth systems, reclaiming, neutral camps, terrain, air fighters, submarines, tactical strikes, ground defenses, shields, mass generators, upgrades for your Commander, support commanders and so much more. In terms of features, Supreme Commander cannot possibly be said to disappoint. They never become overwhelming; so many of them simply make the game a joy to play. Queing actions has never been easier and more visual than in Supreme Commander, nor has transporting large swathes of units across the map or setting patrol routes.
Besides this, the game is highly innovative in its ideas, forgoing a minimap in favor of simply being able to zoom out so far that the main screen becomes a minimap, letting aerial units actually go off the map if required to by their maneuvors, aircraft carriers, submersible aircraft carriers. And if you were to zoom in, you will find that despite the game's age, it is quite a detailed and carefully crafted game, visually speaking (though it does tend to cost your performance some when too many units begin to gather onscreen, which, given the absurdly high limits for how many units can be on the field, is quite often possible). Not to mention a very good, if not always very memorable, soundtrack and sounds that instantly convey their meaning.
If you like RTS games at all, this is one you simply have to try.

The Good:
+ Similar mechanics as previous Shadowrun Returns. Allows you to just jump in and play if you have played that game.
+ Interesting story that develops as the game goes and keeps you engaged.
+ Forces you to make some tough decisions. I appreciate that in an RPG because it allows you to evolve and play your character. Give your play though and character depth.
+ Game does not waste your time. No real unnecessary grinding. Play though took ~19 hours.
+ Lots of interesting missions.
+ Good characters.
+ Play the kind of character you want.
+ Replay-ability. Missions have multiple ways to complete them. Also being forced to make some decisions it would be interesting to see how the game would possibly turn out if you played a different route.
+ A better combat interface than Shadowrun Returns.
The Bad:
- I feel like even scaled up the text is generally smaller than I would like.
- Still some wonky interface stuff. For example healing other team members in between combat.
TLDR;
It is a well crafted RPG that will not waste your time, and tell you a decent story. It is an improvement of previous games in the series. I would highly recommend it.

Xenoverse 2 released with multiple flaws (connection issues, hit detection, cheaters, and many more) but I still defended it and would still play it. So when it came out that a anti cheat would finally be in place to get rid of cheaters and boosters I was pretty excited. Sadly the anti cheat update put the last nail in the coffin that is this game. The update caused a connection loop that caused players (cheaters or not) to be stuck connecting before the main menu (so I guess it stopped cheaters by just killing the online). This also affected one of the biggest saving graces of this game which is the mods no longer working.
There is two work arounds, neither are good/acceptable fixes but for now its the best we have.
1. Inside the Xenoverse 2 Folder, find EasyAntiCheat. Delete EasyAntiCheat_x64.dll  (WARNING this method can be considered a way to bypass their anti cheat and you can be banned for it)
2. Switch steam to offline mode(or disconnect from the internet) this will skip the connection loop and you can play offline.
(I can't confirm if either method allows mods to work because I personally haven't modded the game)
IN SHORT
It took a passable game that had issues and made it basically a unplayable mess that I can't recommend. DO NOT buy this game until the new anti cheat issues are fixed, if they ever are. If you already bought the game hopefully the work arounds allow you to play at least offline or try and refund it.

After around 10 hours of play, through every section of play, I'm still on the fence about this game.
The Good:
Firstly, I would recommend this to anyone who loves the Elder Scrolls universe and even remotely likes card games. The cool factor of having familiarity with the universe is the same for me when I first started playing Hearthstone. If you don't, no worries, as that universe uses many of the ideas from D&D, (like most other RPG's), so there's a lot of consistancy here where the card types/interactions are concerned.
The early game and tutorial parts are amazing! You begin by selecting from TES races and begin. This choice will dictate what kinds of cards you get when you level up so make sure that's the type of game you'd like to play! The story mode takes you through 2-4 hours of gameplay, introducing the core concepts of the game and helping you to build multiple decks to use once you've finished this part. I really like that you occaisionally get choices, (in the story mode), that allow you to choose what type of card you want to add to your deck. It felt challenging but never overwhelming.
Each card type/color, (INT, STR, END, etc), seem to be very well thought out and decks built around these attributes really seem to create a unique experience compared to the other colors. Its much closer to Magic the Gathering than Hearthstone where this is concerned and was probably my favorite thing about the game so far. There are so many different combinations of cards you can put together that every match has felt different up to this point.
The Bad:
And here's where I had to give the game an overall thumbs down.
Immediately after the starter content the game falls apart completely. There doesn't seem to be much skill required in this game's matches. You either hit your curve and win or you lose in spectacular fashion. This game rewards the player that goes second with a bauble that grants 1 extra mana and you can use this item in three different turns. Since hitting your curve perfectly determines whether or not you win, this item breaks the game in my opinion. Maybe others are having a different experience but I am currently at 100% wins when I go second and 100% losses when I go first.
Something that compounds this is what I originally thought was a good thing: the uniqueness of the decks. Some color combinations have little to no ability to deal certain things so that means some decks will have natual counters. This wouldn't be so bad except nearly all of the games in my first two solo arena runs were blowouts in the AI's favor because of this. Vastly different decks on my end with the same outcome. My one run through PVP arena was better but only because my opponents nearly all missed their curve. The rewards were still decent, but who cares when your losses are total and your wins just feel pathetic? So far, only one match that I've played felt in any way competitive from both sides.
I'm a direhard fan of TES mythology so I'm going to give it another few hours to see if anything changes, but can't honestly recommend this to anyone who isn't also a fan of this universe. And even then, only because its free to play.

This game is good. It is not like most CCGs. Many card games try to be like Magic: The Gathering (Hearthstone is guilty of this). Chronicle: RuneScape Legends does not. It is about anticipating what your opponent is going to do. It is about setting up a story for yourself that will land you in a better position than the story your opponent creates for themselves.
Don't be misled by how badly this game wishes it were Hearthstone. It has the upper hand on Blizzard's card game in many ways, and is certainly worhy of your time.

Despite not being a lucky fellow, I generally like card games. In my opinion Chronicle has a really nice and fresh approach and I enjoyed my first hours in the game. Having done a tutorial match against all classes, I had my first moment of disillusion. If you want to create your first deck, there is very little to work with. You will have to put almost every card available in your first deck. Ok, booster packs are a little easier to achieve, in comparisson to hearthstone, but the heroes show little difference at that stage (only few different class cards available in the beginning).
That by itself would be quite alright for me to work with, but as far as I have played the game seems to have some major balancing issues. There are 3 AI tiers, that allow you to battle every hero on each tier. I had no problem obliterating the AI on tier 2 until I faced the smith. She uses some few cards to build absurdly strong weapons, that won't just smash you in the final showdown, but can be used to deal critical damage to you during the journey. It is quite possible, that this may change in the later stages of the game, but if that frustration is what I have to endure going far enough to develope counter strategies, I'll rather quit right now.

4X, PVE, RPG, turn based, Roguelight, Survival, startegy.
Let me break this down.
You explore, explote, ect ect. PVE since you don't fight other players or npcs. Then what is the point? With ever growing odds that you can change yourself you fight off ever spawning monsters that come to raid your village. On top of having to manage food grathering rates along with other items -for the most part using them to make weapons, armor, shields and buildings. Each /peon/ is a scaled down RPG char that you build up to be a beefy monster, or depending on their class since a gather should not be doing 9999 damage in most cases. When vary complex and fun. The issues is to figure it out with out failing at lest a few runs. This game have you covered though. With every game you get XP based on how well you did. You use this Xp to level up your god.
What is your god? Your god gives you special actions in the random events with quite a few making challanges either easier or flat out ignoring bad random effects with no skill check but this is vary rare. For the most part where you will see the most use is the mission for your god which is the same challanges for every god but gives a fat chunk of XP when done. When you level up you get buffs like +1 to this stat for every villager you have ect ect. After 5 levels you max them out and get really nice buffs with them that make future games with that god much, much easier.  Which is where the roguelight comes into play.
I personally don't enjoy every 4X that I own but this one is quite frankly one of the funner ones even if I personally class this as a Surival game that you build up to being able to do well regardless of the bad things that will be thrown your way.

Ok so, After 100 hours of game time i have to say... This is one of my most favourite games of all time! And I strongly feel that it is FAR better than the second game.
How did i put 100 hours in and why am I still playing?
Well, lets see why.
First of all, the gameplay is so well streamlined, that you never forget what button does what, and when to use certian items. Literally everything you do becomes muscle memory after your first two to three hours of playing.
The graphics are absolutely stunning, although I will say the optimization can be a wee bit spotty at times, mainly on the freeways leading into Chicago's heart.
The characters are all memorable, and their voice acting is absolutely fantastic.
The story is extremely well written and executed.
And being a Vigilante is jsut plain out badass.
You can do either an evil or nuetral or angelic playthrough. And your "Karma" actually matters.
The weapons and firearms all feel real. Firearms and explosives have an "oomf" to them that most video games don't have. A .50 Desert Eagle feels like a .50 pistol should, although Aiden somehow has the ability to one hand it, i jsut chose to ignore that.
The game is challenging and in some parts really bloody hard, but it is never unfair.
And the side missions give you reasons to play them. Hunting down the serial killer was my favourite of all the side missions.
I highly reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys Third Person Shooters, and i give it a much higher reccomendation than the second game.
Please do yourself a favor and buy this game, you wont regret it. (So long as your computer can run it.)
PS. The Vehicle handling could have been a wee bit better, but it is more than tolerable, and some of the faster cars jsut take a bit of getting used to.

Despite being confined to a video game, Dragonfall is almost the quintessential Shadowrun experience. While it still has an unhealthy emphasis on combat, the story finally lets the players loose in this wonderful fantasy/cyberpunk world to let them do what they want.
Shadowrun Returns was an enjoyable tactical game, but in the end, it wasn’t much more than that. It lacked the role-playing, the vast freedom this strange fantasy/cyberpunk setting has to offer. And this is where Dragonfall comes in to not only remedy most of the mistakes but to become something larger.
For starters, Dragonfall can finally be called a real cRPG. We have freedom to choose missions, to make choices with actual consequences, and an entire team of individual characters with their own (somewhat clichéd) backstories. Even the main plot lets us experience most of the things Shadowrun quests can offer, from clean-up jobs to corporate espionage or assassination; and a huge campaign against a clandestine organisation and their sinister plans (which is quite cleverly written, even by cRPG standards).
Game mechanics feel more polished. Almost all skills can be useful now, including previously underutilised ones (like throwing weapons). There are no mandatory items to use, so all builds can be as viable as any other, from sword-wielding street samurais to summoners constantly hiding in a corner.
If there is still a weak spot, it is probably the decking (hacking). Most NPC deckers have pretty mediocre builds, but many missions offer nice additional rewards in cyberspace. It forces the player either to run a decker, sacrifice a spot on the team, or skip rewards; certainly great for role-playing, but feels restrictive.
Still, in the end, Dragonfall is clearly a better game than Returns was. Better enough to advice newcomers to start with it? Frankly… I am almost inclined to say yes.
Cyberpunk + epic fantasy? It actually works. Very well-made game for whoever likes coherence between the different storylines and the main plot.
Just like Shadowrun Returns, this was outstanding. I really love the gameplay, and the storytelling is fantastic!

Holy hot damn, finally got around to finishing this and I'm glad I did.
Gameplay for the Director's Cut has been fixed dramatically. Where Returns had issues of all kinds, including but not limited to the complete irrelevance of Deckers, some Etiquettes never being used, a clunky as hell interface, and general balance issues, Dragonfall has smoothed most of that over. To my knowledge, every etiquette was used more than once, Having a Decker in the party is useful for pretty much every mission, and just about every class and build has a place. Granted, the balance isn't perfect; while playing a Steet-Sam, I was damn near invincible by the end of the game, and that was after dumping a ton of points into charisma.
Thats not to say everything is perfect. Clicking can still be a bit wonky, which makes me wish we had a macro to click through enemies to move to spaces their model is blocking, or a macro to undo your last move. The difficulty here is great and nicely challenging for the most part, but there are some missions where RNGesus will forsake you and some where RNGesus doesn't leave your side. This kind of statistical play is common to all RPGs, but at low levels it can be extremely frustrating to miss two point blank hits in a row, only for an enemy from across the map to crit you twice in a row. It isn't just possible but common for a mission to have entirely different outcomes based on your dice-rolls, which turns the pulse-pounding tension of the game's combat into a head-throbbing annoyance.
Plot is great. I don't want to spoil it, but just know that its great. In your head, you're expecting things to twist in about one of thirty different ways, which is fantastic, and I love that it keeps you guessing. In addition, it drops enough hints that the twists doesn't come entirely out of left field; It ain't no Shamaylan flick.
Includes the mod-kit, and tons of fan-made campaigns, but even ignoring that, this game has plenty of hours of content and a lot of replayability.

Shadowrun Returns Dragonfall - Directors Cut is a science fantasy turn based tactical role-playing game developed and self-published by Harebrained Schemes. It has a game editor for making new missions that the community been using to improve it with and to extend the life of the game. Go through the Workshop and subscribe to the large selection of community made campaigns. It comes with the HBS campaign called Dragonfall.
You play a character that can hire others to his team and do a mission.  You control the actions of each member of the team. While gameplay is mostly linear, some small amount of exploration is possible while completing objectives. The player can enter into dialogue with various characters, with different statistics and skills giving new dialogue options.
It comes with the new campaign called Dragonfall which is based in Berlin, Germany.  The Dragonfall campaign starts out pretty hard.  Check the Workshop for other user created mod campaigns, try some of them if you are stuck on Dragonfall compaign. They have worked the bugs out and added more Shadowrun items to this newer version.

Some ninjas prefer the path of stealth, fading into the shadows like Kevin Spacey's career. Other ninjas prefer the path of violence, their destruction of their noodles striking fear into the waiter's eyes.
You are Strider Hiryu. Your path is to pelt pigeons at people's faces.
Strider is the fifth entry in the Strider franchise, that began with Strider and whose latest entry is Strider. Now I know that can get confusing, so for clarity's sake I'm going to call this one Strider.
It's a Metroidvania, which boils down to "there's a couple of colour coded doors, come back when you're rocking their fashion sense". Touted as a retelling of the classic Strider story (the other Strider) I'm still not entirely sure what the story is. The wikia says that Earth got sucker punched by a dictator and Hiryu here is the youngest agent sent to go sort it out, who drew the short straw as it was the only one left.
Most I can say about the story is that Hiryu speaks with a comically thick Japanese accent, which is novel to hear.
For the gameplay, it's well defined; about half of it can be defined as good. For the good half, Hiryu can icepick his way along any surface; overhangs and small hills are no match for his mighty tools. For the rest of your amazing platforming moves, you get a double-jump and a dash. Don't let your jaw hit the floor too hard. It's solid and the platforming challenges are the highlight of the game. After you're done, there's these "Beacon Run" time trials that I absolutely suggest going for.
Once you've passed the highlight, you come to the combat. Which is not the highlight. See, Hiryu swings his immasculated toothpick as fast as you can hit the button, which has the effect of it feeling like an itty bitty tooth-cleaning device. Weak, ineffectual, unsatisfying, and roughly half the game.
Course, said toothpick is spiced up a little by the elements - Cold, Reflect, Gravity and Explosions, the classical Greek ones you're used to - and the introduction of "options" that involve throwing pigeons at people's faces for significant damage or cats for paltry damage, but it never ascends beyond combat that's just a chore.
A launcher and a slide are there if you really feel the need to make your chip damage slightly less useful.
That's on Hard, mind. On Normal - I didn't even touch Easy - enemies dies almost instantly, going too far in the other direction to braindeadville. I mentally clocked out either way.
Now, apart from that core combat, the world is nicely contextualized with platforms that double as rooftops, balconies, prison meeting areas, your mother's secret fetish dungeon, et cetera. Combined with a nicely paced OST that's fairly experimental, and it's a 2.5D game that looks great - like finding a unicorn in hen's teeth.
Just a shame it's boring to play.
Going back over fully completing Strider, it's just not a game I'd recommend. For every decent aspect, and there are a few, I just keep circling back to how empty and listless the combat fundamentally is.
I'd advise you go check out some other Metroidvanias. I don't recommend Strider, but it is totally playable if you're here for that.

I'm a huge Megaman X fan so this game is right up my alley. It's overall a fun game but I feel like it could have used some more polish in terms of presentatioin.
Here are some of my frustrations while playing the game.
---No Intro---
Some people would see this as a plus because they'd wanna' drop into the game and just start playing. I count this as a negative as I want some context before I play. A minute worth of intro would have been nice.
---Soundtrack is lacking---
I'm not asking for an epic score but it would be nice to have some Capcom-like soundbites from the 90's.I mentioned before that I'm a huge Megaman X fan and this is one thing that would have made Strider's fun experience into a memorable one.
---Some Glitches---
Sometimes the door animations won't play as they're already open when i enter the room. This would be fine if I could walk through it but no. The game still reads it as a closed door thus rendering it inaccessible. This has happened only 3 times in my 9 hour run of the game.
It often suffers from slow down and I've read that it's happened to everyone so I have no idea if it's cuz of bad optimization or my laptop is just crap. haha
Steam version may not be the version to pick up.
---Enemy variation---
This is can be taken as either positive or negative. Most of the enemies are soldiers with guns and robots. Sometimes they use different guns. I say that this can be taken as positive as it does feel like you're fighting against a military force instead of a wacky funhouse.
Now, I'm moving onto the positives.
+++Fluid Play Style+++
Any of Strider's abilities will work on almost every enemy. At first, your options are limited, but in time you'll find abilities that you can stick with throughout the entire game. You can play aggressive like I did and use the fire upgrade the most or you can use the ice upgrade to incapacitate enemies. Etc.
+++Awesome Visuals+++
Character models might look like late PS2 era but the environments look beautiful.
+++Huge Map+++
The 2D map here is done almost perfectly. It annoys me because it's so close... Megaman ZX and ZXA could take notes from this 'cuz, man, I can actually understand the map here. A game whose tedium makes tooth extraction without pain killers look like the best time you'll ever have. You start with a ship that is as tough as wet tissue paper, and every ship after the fact is just a slightly higher grade of wet paper that costs more in time and effort than they really should.
Combat lacks any degree of finesse or preciseness; you click on a vague area of space and your ship just putters along without giving you any means of making sudden course corrections to avoid fire. Combat is something to be avoided... if you can manage it. Be sure to always pack an EMP, because there's no other way to outrun your enemies. Of course, if you don't have one, expect to have your ship destroyed, lose whatever secondary weapons you do have, all of your missiles and get stuck back in the starter ship, losing whatever modules it can't equip.
My only regret is that it took me too long to finally get around to playing this, because I cannot get a refund. Don't make the same mistake I did; avoid at all costs and find a better, much more fun space sim that doesn't go out of its way to punish you for daring to try and play it as anything more than a trading/mining sim where combat is something you should never try, because all your ships and options suck.

There ought to be something wrong with a game if you don't feel bad resorting to infinite money cheats after just a couple of hours.
Why? Because this game can, by and large, be characterized as Farmville in space. You need money to buy expensive ships and weapons to do story missions, but the only way to get it reliably is by mining asteroids and trading, which have about the same degree of complexity and player's involvement as Cookie Clicker. Now, do it again, again, and again for several hours. You can also grind the same 5 mercenary missions over, and over, and over again, or just fly around and shoot other ships, but that will be just as much of an underwhelming and repetitive chore. Also, if your ship does get taken down (usually by a group of pirates suddenly appearing out of nowhere and catching you unawares, sleepy or AFK after several minutes of flying through empty Space with nothing happening), you'll lose some of your precious equipment.
Star Nomad is not atrocious, and could be an OK distraction if you're listening to music, or thinking about something, but that's about it it.
It is also true that the game harkens back to other space sims like Elite and Star Control, but it has so little variety, and the combat system is so simplistic that it fails to keep one's attention for any significant period of time. (the realisation that you've got nothing else to do in the game happened in Elite as well, mind you, but it came much, much later than here). Bland writing, lame, sometimes sexual, jokes and no memorable characters does not help the case, either.
Sexy (if not sexist) art tho.

Let me start by saying that I really like this game. It's a card game that is significantly different from the two main themes I've seen in card games: battle each other with creatures and spells until opponents life is depleted, and row allocation of cards to win hands (and gain points or deal damage). This one differs in that each player tries to 'level up' some RPG class hero through 5 sets of playing cards.
In Chronicle, you define the adventure your character is having by playing monsters to defeat for gold or upgrades (like weapons, armor, health or raw attack power) or supportive items like weapons and armor and allies or locations. Cards can trigger special effects, such as duelling with the oponent's hero (having them attack each other once) or perhaps casting a spell on the opponents hero, monster or (upcoming) equipment. If both heros survive the trek across these 5 'chapters', they face each other in a final confrontation where the strongest will survive. But if someone happens to die before the other, the surviving hero is victorious.
This game also have the traditional tempo-based strategies. Do you intend to cause as much trouble for the opponents hero on their journey, sabotaging their weapons and stealing there gold to make sure they get in a bad shape at the final confrontation? Do you lay traps and prepare ambushes and cast spells at you opponent, causing them to misstep and perhaps die before reaching the end of the last chapter? Or will you in weather the storm with protective gear and helpfull allies and beat your enemy into a red pulp with a big weapon? All are valid strategies to create your deck around.
I've found the free to play model implemented in this game fair. You can get a decent set of cards to start with as you gain experience with each hero and doing daily quests, which only a few require you to win games and most just require you  to play the game. The cardset is not too big that starting at the time of writing puts you at a huge options-deficit.
Matchmaking is decent enough. In ranked play, I'm often paired against people of similar strength and similar card-pools. And after having created some decent decks myself, I'm at a point where I can beat people with very rare cards without having access to them myself. (Some statistics: you needed around 500 card packs before the release of Movran to complete a cardcollection. This number is higher now after Movrans release. I hope that this statistic gives you some feeling for the size of the cardpool)
There is a drafting mode, which I haven't played that much. So I cannot comment on that one. Besides that there is a practice against bots (yields you cards for beating them for the first time!), non-ranked online play, ranked online play and dueling amonst friends.
Grapics are okey (looks nice, but I personally suffer from some bugs related to the depth of field rendering), the play-history ingame is realy nice, and gameplay feedback is suffiecient to get the information you needs during play.
Personally, this game completely replaced Heathstone for me. I didn't like the pressure I felt in the game to keep up with the sheer volume of new cards they kept cranking out and I didn't play the game frequently enough to make buying packs worth the investment in my regard. I do not feel that pressure with Chronicle. And I'm happy with that. :)

I'm about 12 hours into this game, and I felt I had to comment about it.  It's very unique in that it blends together a number of gameplay elements from different games, and pushes forward some new ones of its own.  I would have to describe this as a "4X Survival" game.  The closest comparison I can think of is playing a game of Civilization (or, more appropriately, Endless Legend) with only 1 city element to deal with, while also mixing in a top-down RPG feel.
Oh, I don't know if the game is based on "Slavic mythology" exactly, but the names and themes feel very Slavic in presentation.  I consider this a big plus because it's a mythos that I haven't been exposed to much, and it's a twist on your standard elves and dwarves fantasy trope.  The art style is fresh to me, and no part of the game feels like a rehash of something else (aside from, you know, they have swords and stuff :D )
Games that I think inspired this game:  Master of Magic (ancient Microprose game), Age of Wonder, Endless Legend, Civilization, XCOM
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys 4X games (Xplore, Xpand, Xploit, Xterminate), top-down RPGs, big picture strategy games, and turn-based games in general.
Thank you MuHa games, and I hope to buy future games from you.
Update after 120 hours in:  I've really enjoyed this game much more than your typical 4X game.  There is a lot of replayability because everything in the game is random, and each "god" you choose has traits that will shape the way you run your village.  This is the first 4X I've played that has an element of developing your meta-avatar between games, so each game you play "means" something besides just your score.  It's not a major element, though, so the full game is accessible with only one or two plays, but anyone, like me, who gets really into it will find some meat to chew on here.

In 2012, magic returned to our world, awakening powerful creatures of myth and legend. Among them was the Great Dragon Feuerschwinge, who emerged without warning from the mountains of Germany, unleashing fire, death, and untold destruction across the countryside. It took German forces nearly four months to finally shoot her down - and when they did, their victory became known as The Dragonfall.
It’s 42 years later - 2054 - and the world has changed. Unchecked advances in technology have blurred the line between man and machine. Elves and trolls walk among us, ruthless corporations bleed the world dry, and Feuerschwinge’s reign of terror is just a distant memory. Germany is splintered - a stable anarchy known as the “Flux State” controls the city of Berlin. It’s a place where power is ephemeral, almost anything goes, and the right connections can be the difference between success and starvation. For you and your team of battle-scarred shadowrunners, there’s no better place to earn a quick payday.
Now, a new threat is rising, one that could mean untold chaos and devastation. One that soon has you and your team caught on the wrong side of a deadly conspiracy. The only clue: whispers of the Dragonfall. Rumors that the Great Dragon Feuerschwinge may still be alive, waiting for the right moment to return…
Shadowrun: Dragonfall is a cyberpunk turn-based tactical RPG developed by Harebrained Schemes and set in the Shadowrun universe. It was originally released as DLC for Shadowrun Returns in 2014, and has been enhanced and expanded into a separate release (the Director's Cut). This version comes with improvements made to the original combat engine and interface, as well as the addition of several bonus missions and new music tracks.
Dragonfall takes place in magical cyberpunk Berlin, home of countless free-states, gangs, and corporate interests. In the main campaign you'll assume the role of a Shadowrunner who has recently arrived to join old partner Monika Schäfer, Dietrich - a former punk rocker turned shaman, Glory - a distant woman who has become heavily augmented with cybernetics and Eiger - a troll weapons expert and former member of German KSK.
The inital run is a rabbit hole into something far more complex. In this case, a simple raid to a data vault explodes into a conspiracy full of mistery, scientific hubris and the worst kind of cyber-stalker. On a more personal level Dragonfall revolves around the Kreuzbasar, an autonomous neighborhood in the midst of Berlin's urban chaos. The Kreuzbasar is more than a hideout and a resting place for the crew of shadowrunners. It's a community to build, to protect, to exploit. Visiting its inhabitants and getting involved in its dramas are welcome contrasts to excursions to the outside world. The residents of the Kreuz are a resilient group. Checking in on their lives deepens the world, develops a strong sense of place, and provides many side quests.
Shadowrun: Dragonfall - Director's Cut burst from Shadowrun Returns like a blood-titanium phoenix. It's hard-wired with enough features to run like a top-of-the-line pleasure rig, a great game packed with atmosphere, heists, and intrigue. Dragonfall is worth any RPG fan's time and money unless they don't like cyberpunk, dragons, or quality tactical combat.

I tend to hate turn-based tactical games. Some games that thrill most fans of the genre feature horrible miss chances on normal difficulty, squad members who have no personalities with weapons that are more interesting than the people wielding them, no personal investment, and a boring "story" make up that game (X-COM Enemy Unknown is an example of these things I detest). Also, though I played Shadowrun Returns, I thought it was okay, but a glitch made the game freeze at the start of a mission quite late into the game, and I wasn't having enough fun with the game to even bother restarting the mission to continue.
Then came Shadowrun: Dragonfall. I lean toward detesting this genre, but holy crap, this game is great! All the drawbacks of X-COM Enemy Unknown that I mentioned above are nowhere to be found in this game. The miss/hit chances on normal are satisfying, you have characters who can boost those chances for the whole team or its individual members from the very start of the game, the characters are some of the very best I have ever seen in a video game, and the story is quite nice with twists and turns throughout. I will say, however, that the ending is a bit of a whimper, but it wasn't offensively bad (Mass Effect 3) or anything.
Both in and out of combat, the characters are great. Each has things you don't know about them, and after every mission or two, you go back to a sort of home base and the city block that it's in, and you get to learn more about your team members. They have some really interesting stories...especially Glory.  Wow. All of the squad members and minor characters will generally have something new to say, and there is so much atmosphere. The NPCs look like crap in this game, but with the isometric view above, it's easy to just not care. the art of the areas is great, and the game's setting is so perfect. The game has this cyberpunk setting with an intriguing tone of simultaneous melancholy and hope.
Not only did the backgrounds and the well-written characters draw me in, but the music is so atmospheric for the locations you visit and the events going on in-game, and the narration writing is superb...by that, I mean the word artistry  the game charms you with time and again. There is oodles of reading in this game, as there is no voice acting at all, but I honestly prefer it this way despite normally not having the patience to read fiction...like ever. The game's writing is seductive, I tell you!!! You just have to read the narration and dialog when you go to new places and talk to new characters. It's incredible.
My biggest gripe about the game is probably the tight-waddedness of its "Karma," which are the points you spend to make your character more powerful. The game is -really- tight on there points. I received 198, and that's with me doing every mission and side mission, and trying to milk every Karma gain I could find in the game by starting off with 6 Charisma and looking up beforehand on forums what the best 3 Etiquettes (speech specializations) were. If anyone is reading this who isn't going to play a Shaman, do NOT take Charisma above 4. You can buy armor in the northeast corner on a "trial" side mission for a group that wants to hire you in-game, and it gives you +2 Charisma while you wear it. I believe 6 was as high as I ever needed, and Security and Corporate are the best Etiquettes. The Gang Etiquette would let me spend a bunch of money to skip one fight that wasn't all that tough. Whoop-dee-doo. =/  I wish so much that someone could have convinced me to take Charisma 4 instead of 6. I BEG you, do not take Charisma 6.
Back on topic, in closing, yeah, I typically hate this genre. However, Shadowrun: Dragonfall is magnificently atmospheric through its background, its music, all of the story except the -very- ending, the characters, and the gameplay was enjoyable even for someone such as myself who doesn't tend to like this sort of game.
I do not give many games this high of a recommendation, and I generally dislike the genre this game belongs to. Therefore you, dear reader, can assuredly realize just how amazing this game was to drag this much adulation out of a hater of the genre such as myself.

text:
Best Pac-Man game EVER!
But long loading times.

Gameplay's mostly basic Pac-Man style regarding dot eating, power pellet acquiring to eat ghosts for score, etc. What makes this much more unique are the cool game modes & features and how fast it can get along with the ravey music and style of the flashing lights.
How this game goes is that if you eat all the pellets on one half of the maze an item will appear on the other half. If you eat said item then the maze opposite from where the item resides will change with the addition of more dots and ghosts and so the cycle continues. The game never truly ends until you run out of lives, the timer runs out, or you complete whatever objective you chose to do.
Most ghosts now stay stationary and when approached will become aggressive and follow you endlessly until they are eaten. The more that follow the higher your score oughta be when you get a power pellet and eat them in a combo chain. To add to the challenge, as the current game goes on additional ghosts will spawn in the ghost house and will thus follow basic Pac-Man ghost rules. If you've got an army of ghosts on your tail however the said ghosts will add itself to the large addition of followers.
If you are approaching an instance where you're about to touch a ghost the game slows down for you so as to give you slightly more time to react until you they catch you or you've managed to get far enough away from said ghost that caused the slowing in time. Makes the game easier and I hoped for the option to turn it off however these moments can give off really tense feelings especially when the game speed has reached its high. The game speeds up as you play until it reaches its limit.
Another item that makes the game easier are the "bombs"that are available to you. How these work is that if you get a chain of ghosts following you then you can send them right back to the ghost house where they'll come right back out immediately. Using them decreases the game speed which, for those who want high scores, in turn lowers the score you'll receive.
My personal gripe with this is that there isn't a CLASSIC MODE in this though there is the classic Pac-Man skin available after you've obtained the achievements and in-game achievements (medals).

I wish i could recommend. I wish i could like this game. I racked up over 24 hours of play time in 4 days of trying the game.
This game is hand's down the most frustrating and tear provoking game that invokes levels of nerd rage i did not know possible.
Why is that?
I'm glad you asked.
This game has the depth, and pontential to be great. However as it stands the mechanics are god awfully skewed in a way i did not forsee.
ESL has less RNG spam as Hearthstone, which should make it a better game right? Wrong. The impact RNG has on this game in a single play can decide an entire match based off 1 lucky RNG roll.
The RNG mechanics of this game impact very high value moves. The rune system means if you get all 5 of your runes poped and no prophecy, and your opponet pops 2 of his, and both are prophecies you are done. You will likely not over come 2 free (often powerful) card plays.
In the most critical of needs RNG will fail you. Absolutely, and unapologetically. Leaving you to go 10-15 game losing streaks. Intellect, stragey, tactics, and brillant deck building means nothing. In the end all that matters is luck. The only silver lining is that the P2Win fest that is Hearthstone is less applicable as even a dekc of 30 legendaries can, and will still get screwed by bad RNG rolls.
** One pro was the story mode, it was fun, and interesting. However over all this game falls flat on it's competitive play being decided for you. You don't decide anything, the draw decides everything.
*** I once went 8 games in a row where i would get stuck with a 9 cost legendary in my first draw or intial hand in some way. I had 70 cards in that deck, and yet 1 out of 70 chances out of 8 games i got stuck with a useless card that caused me to lose vs opponents who always have the right cost cards for opening play. There is nothing more infuriating then knowing you are losing to people not because of skill, or tactics - simply because the game decided it didn't want you to win. That is not a fun game.
