I used to play Hearthstone very casually and mostly f2p.  I started in the beta and was able to obtain a decent collection through very minimal cost to my own wallet (many of the must have legendary and I could build any meta deck basically).  At least that was how it was until the last two expansions; blizzards choice to push anti-consumer practices to their breaking point because they have such a large player base is completely ridiculous.
Now, what does that have to do with TES legends?  Quiet a bit I would say.  I've tried a few other CCG/TCGs since the release of hearthstone.  Most of them were fun, but they didn't have that kinetic and polished feel that hearthstone has (gwent might be an exception).  Despite it's extremely ridiculous payment model, Hearthstone is extremely well made and the cards feel powerful when you play them.  TES legends is the same in this regard.  When you play a powerful card or attack with a powerful creature, you feel it, hear it and see it very clearly in the animations and sounds.
TES legends feels like what would happen if a company took hearthstone and merged it with the MTG duels series of games.  For the most part, the cards are fair and there are quite a few archetypes in the game that just don’t exist in HS.  There is an extensive single player experience and it seems that many of the expansions will be released in this manner as well. This means you can pay a single price (either in gold or money) to gain access to the expanded set of cards and not have to worry about the potential RNG of opening an endless amount of packs.  The way that packs and rewards are given to the player is quite a bit better then many other games as well.  For instance, as you level your character class, you gain access to card upgrades as well as other rewards.  Thus far in my play experience, I have obtained at least 20-30 card packs simply from playing the game (and not spending money or gold).
Also, the RNG of the packs in this game seems to be much more balanced then a game like hearthstone.  There is no 40 pack rule in TES legends though this makes more sense because you are allowed to 3 copies of all rarities in your PvP deck.  There are a few cards that only allow you to have one of them in a deck, but they are very few and far between as far as I can tell.
The game play is solid.  It is very reminiscent of MTG and it uses some of the mechanics from Hearthstone as well.  There is a very nice come-back mechanic where you gain a free card draw for every 5 hp you lose and this adds yet another dimension to the game.  Unlike MTG, the game feels less ”turn based” and more reactionary.  If the card you draw upon loosing your 5 hp is a prophecy card, you can play it immediately at no cost (in my opinion this is a much more elegant solution then secrets).  This can make for some interesting situations as it is not always the best choice to just keep slamming your opponent in the face due to the potential for reprisals.  While this does add an element of RNG into the game, it isn’t out of control like some of the RNG elements from HS.
The game is far from perfect of course.  While the payment model and the polish is great, there are some features that are lacking.  For instance, the android support seems to be very spotty at the moment.  Hopefully this will change in the future.  Also, it can be hard to figure out the lane mechanics when you first start playing, though I feel that it adds another dimension to the game.  Some of the card mechanics also feel slightly more “safe” then with other CCGs.  The board clears seem fairly weak compared to other games for sure and the direct damage spells tend to be a bit slower as well. I also feel as though the player who goes 2nd actually has an advantage over the player who goes first.  They gain an item which lets them boost their magicka for 3 turns.  While this is certainly an improvement over the coin from HS which only lets you boost one turn, it feels slightly too extreme in some cases though I would like to see win rates before really jumping to a conclusion on that one.
Overall, this game is fun and it is worth playing.  Even if you don't intend to invest money into the game, you will get the chance to play through all of the features of the game just by playing through the story mode and getting the rewards.

Chronicle: RuneScape Legends is a weird, but different taste/twist on the collection card game genre. It's more of a placing your cards in strategic positions in which so can out smart your opponent. Instead of just battling your opponent hand after hand. They added chapters to the game (game consist of 5 chapters), after the 5th chapter if both heroes are left standing, they battle it out 1v1 style. The one with the most armor and weapon damage will most likely win.
Things to know; straight off the bat, the game had server issues once I opened the game. Bad start there. It seemed after I waited a few hours I could actually complete the tutorial. There isn't a campaign, just multiplayer. You can battle against AI's in which you can get practice at the game more. I noticed that the game uses the 24-hour format instead of the 12 hour format. Sadly in settings, there isn't an option to change this. V-sync is turned on automatically once you open the game, be sure to turn that off. The UI does look like something out of 'Hearthstone: Heroes of Warcraft'... kinda weird. Since it is a free to play game, the game does have micro-transactions to buy new cases to unlock more playing cards.
Note: When I was 'practicing' against an AI, the game did a hard crash to the desktop. Game is still buggy.
Me personally, I haven't played RuneScape since I was like 13 years old. And now in 2016, I know nothing about the game. Some backstory or even some info to shed some light on why you are fighting... this info would have been useful.
What would be added to this game (If I had the power), I would add more animations to the characters on the battlefield. The animations are kinda iffy and lack luster. And lastly, a storyline... maybe?
Just because of the different taste/twist on the collection card game genre, I would recommend this game. I came off not liking it since it's "another" card game, but this game seemed kinda fun once you get used to it.

I quite enjoyed playing the game for a while, there's a lot of charm to it and the way that the card system works is fairly interesting.
However, the way the card system works is very much based on luck unless you make a very safe deck or a very meta deck.
Which brings me to why I just couldn't continue the game: metagaming.
The problem with how the way that the game works as opposed to something like Hearthstone is the amount of faceblasting cards there are and just how ridiculously overpowered they can be.  There's a lot of ways you can 1-turn-kill by going face which are completely and totally unblockable unless MAYBE you were lucky enough to have, drawn, and played at the right time something with a specifc counter which is probably too expensive for you to use anyway.
Rarer cards are straight up better, and even as one of the first people to play the game I was still coming up against people with ridiculous amounts of rares smashing me apart with simply better cards that do more for less, which is obviously frustrating because no matter how much time or thought I put into my deckbuilding I'm still going to get destroyed by some guy who has better cards than me because he forked over more cash for card packs to get rares.
I gave the game 20 hours to impress me and I was considering buying some card packs, but then suddenly in a matter of days I was running into every single game being a metadeck that goes face and makes anything I try to do worthless because they can 1-turn-kill me by the second turn.
Go find some friends and play Pathfinder, because you're not going to find much fun here unless you like losing constantly.  (and if you DO like losing, then go play Dwarf Fortress, it's worth the investment of time to learn it)

So far i'm really enjoying this game. It's a card game that also has a bit of luck and at times a bit of skill. With most card games you are dealing with one form of currency, and this one uses multiple forms of currency. In a way, you are also playing against yourself. You can do damage to the other player, but if you pick the wrong cards, the cards you picked may kill you first. When you start a chapter (there are 5, and each chapter allows a maximum of 4 cards), you can place as many creatures as you or put down some kind of support card. Most support cards use gold, but some use armor or health as a currency. Your base attack is 2 at the start, but you can get a support card that gives you a piece of equipment and now you can attack something and kill it faster. While i'm not the best writer, i'm mentioning the basics of the game.
Now imagine that you line up your first 4 cards very nicely, you kill a goblin, he gives you 4 gold, now you have support card ready that costs 4 gold. Your next steps were to kill 2 other creatures, you were counting on the fact that it would take 1 hit each to kill each creature as long as you have the weapon, and as long as you have the gold, and by the time you get to the last creature, as long as you still have durability on the weapon by the last creature. Every one of the 4 spots gets handle one after the other alternating between both players.... meaning that if you go first, you reach your first card first, then the other player reaches their card, and it alternates back and forth until you get to each of your 4th cards. Now a player that goes up against another may choose to steal gold, remove armor, or weapon durability, and any of these factors can throw a real wrench in your whole plan. As time goes on you learn how to counter some people, and like  any card game someone will continue to counter you at times.
I've really been enjoying the game, and I love playing hearthstone, i've played a bunch of the other card games in the past, but this game has been keeping my focus lately.
As of late, there have been some issues with disconnections and the servers but i'm sure those will be taken care of soon like in other games.

Game is fun, innovative and presents a really interesting spin on the CCG genre. There's a surprising amount of cards and deck combinations you can do, considering the game came out a while ago. The team also seems to be very engaged with making it balanced and fun, wtihout nerfing cards to the point they are no longer usable (looking at you Hearthstone, devs).
My only complaint up to this point is that after the newest patch (1.4.0) the servers are ridiculously unstable, not even in peal hours too. They should really do something about fixing that.

The Good
-For a space trader it is fairly easy top throw a half hour at here and there.
-upgrading is easy once you get the hang of it.
-lots of little details are pretty cool. Like people talking about the Iowa vs. The Yamato kind of clevar.
The Bad
-you tend to have to grind a lot at the beginning. Early on you basically need to find a safe route to either mine or trade until you can get some decent gear.
-no real faction choice to my understanding. I had a chance to join the pirates for a moment there but no real choice.
-the police in this game are insane: I am smuggling drugs and there are 6 ships right behind me destroying ships (potentially murdering people) for money and suddenly I am public enemy number 1? what this hell is in these drugs!?!
-almost no customization: you have almost no choice to upgrade your ship in specialized ways. You can chose to make your missiles hit harder or your beams hit harder and that’s about it.
-there is no choice to stand down your weapons or surrender. I am playing a smuggler not a murderer. I don't want to have a shootout with the cops until I can leave the system. I would rather stand down my own weapons and divert power to shields or speed to get away.
-space stations don't care about pirates or smugglers? Here I am being shot at by pirates I dock at a station and they just let them blow me up? By the same token I am running from the police because they spot me with drugs but the station just lets me dock? I can't fathom a universe where the ships have weapons but the space stations don't who is asleep at the switch?
Things I Would Change
-Give the ships 2 to 5 modification modals and add more than just missile power and beam power to it. It could have the weapon boosts but also extra storage adding an extra 4 slots, a temporary cloak costing power (preferably called a Fader :) ), extra shields, shield mods that increase effectiveness against beams or ballistic respectively, crew pods for extra crew (see below)
-more detailed mining add a scanner to increase the chances of getting certain resources over others.
-more weapon types please. We have an EMP that jams weapons can we have one that stalls engines? Maybe mine layers, how about a machine gun stile gun that fires smaller weaker beads of energy fires faster but hurts less maybe a tractor beam that slows and eventually stops ships to force a boarding rather than destroying ships.
-crew customization. Give each ship a crew capacity 2 to 6 each crew man can do different jobs on the ship such as work the engines, weapons, and shield to make the work better, the ability to navigate and increase maneuverability, or simply board/ repel boarders.
-random mission offers. Passing ships give me all sorts of messages (including quite often the cops telling me how to break the law and expunge my criminal record lol) I think it would be cool if ships randomly offered me a job to protect them or deliver something or even kill someone.
-gear/ships you can't buy. I would love to have experimental gear you have to find and earn rather than buy.
-buy hanger space. I have built up my bad♥♥♥♥♥ship just the way I like it. Now what? Story missions? Personally I would like to buy a hanger slot and start building up another ship. It would also be more realistic to me than them just handing me a new ship every time I blow one up.
-radar mini map. Down in the corner a tiny map that shows what ships are in the area upgrades and or crewmen could tag patrol ships or pirates or both.
All and all
all and all this game is fun! It could be more fun but it is fun, but at the end of the day I am happy with what I spent on it. I know the developer is working on a sequel so I hope they read this and take these suggestions to heart, but right now the game is fun and worth more than I spent on it.

Being an older game, it is more limited by its engine in many regards, such as enemies' strange ability to see the player from incredible distances and snipe with improbable accuracy, but forgiving it the wrinkles of it's age, it's still a great experience and one I would recommend to anyone interested in a realistically-influenced shooter without the complications of "hyper-realism".

The game is very different from others games I have played. You have a village with some people starting in it, and a group of people who you can use to explore, hunt, fight and gather. All "challenges" (which are not just fights, but also other things like diplomacy or sickness, which use other attributes) are turn-based combat regulated simply by the order of characters you and your enemy engage.
There is also a research component that can be advanced via crafting, for which you need to claim or gather resources. Researching helps you get better resources, buildings and crafting possibilities. In the end, you want one (or maybe even more) large group of well equipped humans/orcs/elves or whatever you managed to get on your side, to finish either the regulary story quest or the giant's quest, both leading to victory. There is also an "advancement" victory but it requires grinding to unlock, if you play on the highest difficulty.
The game is mostly fun due to the mix of characters you can get, due to the crafting, the village improvement, the randomness of the world and most of all the great amount of events and options during these.
I greatly enjoyed the game for the following reason:
+ True grimdark
+ Great setting
+ Lots of random events that keep things alternating, the choices in the events depend on your party member's skills and the writing and flavour is great in them
+ Crafting is fun
+ Love the characters and that you can get orcs, goblins, dwarves, even rats on your side
+ Awesome beginning of the game and awesome mid-game.
+ Good story, although I feel like it was not as captivating as it could have been. A lot of yadda yadda.
- End game becomes very repetitive, a bit imbalanced (too easy & too hard) and a bit lacking
- Victory is too quick and easy once you know the game, it feels like there are greater challenges in the game than the victory itself
- Gaining experience seems to do very little, in the end you replace your beginning characters, which you kept alive with so much energy, by better ones you attract through buildings or events.

I actually like polygod, and I was very close to giving this game a positive review, but I can't in good concious reccomend this game to other buyers unless you are willing to play a rough, unbalanced, and IMO unfair game. Polygod's core gameplay is relatively fun, upgrading your bullets is satisfying and fun and there are a couple good combos/builds to play around with. The main problem with Polygod is that enemy hp is balanced horribly. As the game progresses enemies get stronger, they move and shoot faster, and move in more complex patterns making them harder to hit, but their hp also scales up drastically. If you dont increase your dps enemies take forever to kill. This means that going for non dps upgrades is a waste of time in most cases, because you already move relatively fast and hp isn't very valuable as you will eventually get to a level that is almost unbeatable due to the tankiness of the enemies. This means that even if you get an op damage build you cant really see its effects very well because enemies still take too long to kill. Also the game does not punish camping, you can shoot most enemies from very far away with little to no drawbacks, especially on the second level. I've played the game for a decently long time, and only ever got to the fourth level, and unlocked one achievement. I have played many other rogulite games and been able to progress in them relatively well, but this game just seems too unbalanced. You have to get an op build to realistically beat it, otherwise you will just be kiting the bullet sponge enemies for unfun amounts of time. My advice to the devs would be to reduce the hp of enemies while making their attacks more damaging. This poor balancing is pretty unfortunate as the level generation and enemy design and attack patterns are actually very well done. This could be a pretty great game if is was just better balanced.

Checked the demo out at EGE2017 and had a great chat with one of the lead devs. Amazing team with passion for their project and truly want to make it as good as they possibly can in anyway they can, including taking suggestions from us, the fans.
In the small amount of time I played the game at the expo, as well as in my own time, I can say their hard work has paid off.
Polygod isn't particularly unique within the fast-paced, Quake-style FPS genre, BUT it does offer some really interesting tweaks to the formula, as well as extremely polished and well balanced gameplay for an early access title, and, while I haven't gotten too far into the game because I suck hardcore at it, I can say it's definitely worth the current asking price on concept and execution alone, and depending on how much is added in the full release, it'll definitely still be worth a bit more.
What I find really refreshing about the game is it's difficulty. It never feels like the game is cheating me, but rather I'm just really bad at it and I need to improve myself to make it easier. It doesn't hold your hand through anything. You're just dropped into one of the randomly generated worlds, given your gun and set off to go shoot things. There is a story going on from what I can tell, but as I haven't even gotten past the first boss, I have not seen much of it.
Overall though, I purchased this  game, not only because it's well made, well balanced and fun as all balls, but because talent like this from the South African game dev scene need all the support they can get.
I'll definitely reccommend Polygod to all my mates, as well as stay active within the community because I see great potential in this titles future as both a LAN favourite and even eSports title.

This is quite possibly one of the worst games I have ever played in my life. As a huge fan of Dragonball franchise myself, all I can say about this game is just one word, "Lazy".
I thought Xenoverse 1 was pretty enjoyable overall. But this game...
First of all, I can see the fact that the graphics look "slightly" better than the Xenoverse 1. But the story of Xenoverse 2 is literally the same frigging thing you did in Xenoverse 1. Same cut scenes (And just a few new cut scenes that no one would really care about) and everything (Maybe the major difference between Xenoverse 1 and 2 in terms of story would be that, 2 has Masked Saiyan). I guess this is because the Xenoverse series is all about protecting the timeline that has been altered by bad guys and basically the purpose is to revisit Dragonball Z story. And also the difference between Xenoverse 1 and 2 is that, 1 went into the story of Dragonball GT, but 2 goes in to the Dragonball Super story instead, after you are done with Dragonball Z story. But yes, how many times did we repeat the same story over and over in the previous Dragonball games honestly? Is it impossible for them to make some kind of an original story, when they have Dragonball Heroes? Could they not have come up with some sort of more major plot twists within the Dragonball Z story at least, when Xenoverse series itself can take advantage of that time-altering concept? I wanted to see more of Masked Saiyan stuff, but there really is not much, honestly. Xenoverse 2 is just simply lazy in that area. But at least the final battle and the Zamasu saga were interesting.
And secondly, this whole new anti-cheat program that has been implemented within the game recently has been quite controversial, this game ended up getting tons and tons of negative reviews because of it. The problem is that it does not let you mod the game at all. I never use mods, so I am not sure about it myself, but apparently you can not use mod even if you play the game offline and everything.
But the real major problem with this game, is that it does not even CONNECT to the server. Meaning, completely unplayable at this moment. Apparently you can still play the game if you turn off the internet but I do not see why that is my responsibility. I have no reason to do anything just to be able to play the game that I could play without an issue before. And if this whole thing is being caused by the EasyAntiCheat program, then that just completely defeats the purpose now, doesn't it? Why not just remove the multiplayer mode and allow only singleplayer mode if you are going to handle the online stuff this horribly?
And really, there really is not much difference between Xenoverse 1 and 2 in many ways. For example, most maps (If not all) in Xenoverse 2 are pretty much the same maps from Xenoverse 1, so if you played Xenoverse 1 a lot like I did, then you will feel like you are playing the exact same frigging game when you play Xenoverse 2. And the skill motions. Kamehameha and everything, they are all pretty much the same from Xenoverse 1. In Xenoverse 1, when Goku uses Kamehameha, it zooms in onto his face and shoots Kamehameha and literally it just goes same like that in Xenoverse 2. There is literally ZERO effort in all of those. And not to mention, this game is way overpriced for no reason. Charging full price for a game that feels more like a cheap DLC of Xenoverse 1 is pretty dishonest.
And the new DLC is coming out and apparently the season pass that we have right now will not cover it. But oh hey, don't even expect any PC version players to buy the DLC, since we can't even play it right now anyway. Not to mention, the new DLC (Or are they the free ones?) only includes Dabura and Gohan-absorbed Majin Buu? Are they serious? Exactly who the heck is going to pay money just to be able to play Dabura and that optional Majin Buu?? Why were they not even included in the game to begin with? Do they not even have the courtesy to just include those characters in the game?? Who the heck would honestly care about Dabura and Gohan-absorbed Majin Buu when the Universal Survival Saga is on Dragonball Super right now?? Does Bandai Namco even know how to do business seriously?
And I highly doubt I would buy Xenoverse 3 if it ever comes out, because I can already see Xenoverse 3 having the exact same frigging maps I saw from 1 and 2, exact same graphics, exact same skill motions, exact same Dragonball Z story and everything with just a small difference.
All I can say about this game is that, do not buy, as the game is not even worth the full price. But get it if it is at 50% off or more. And I mean, get the game, if the game ACTUALLY WORKS. Or just simply get Xenoverse 1 during sale.

Many moons ago, I came into possession of a new game for my Sega Genesis. After rushing home, popping it into my console and turning on the power, it was then I was almost immediately treated to one hell of a show. There I was, gliding into an enemy base, sirens blazing, only then to start flipping majestically through the air while making short work of the enemies that were foolish enough to cross my path. This was my first encounter with the Strider series, and safe to say it was a pretty lasting one.
Fast forward to this latest addition to the series, then, and it’s a delight to see that everything that made Strider cool back when I was a kid has made the jump to today.  That feeling of being a legendary ninja is re-ignited at the very beginning of the game, as you fly in yet again with the instantly recognisable theme song blaring away in the background, and easily manages to sustain itself from there.
You see, this is action thrown at you at an almost frantic pace. There’s a seemingly endless swarm of enemies always attacking you, and it’s up to you to flip and dash around them... Or, better still, simply go to town and cut them all to ribbons, with the thrill of murdering everything in a room without even stopping for breath being an oh-so-satisfying one. Start sinking your teeth deeper into the Metroid-vania style gameplay, and it only gets better. You’ll unlock items that can deflect bullets back at your foes, set them on fire, or (if all else fails) simply obliterates them via a spirit eagle that you can summon to do your dirty work. Whatever your choice, such systematic destruction never gets old.
It’s not just endless foot soldiers that end up falling to your blade, however.  Things truly come to a head when it comes to fighting the game’s numerous bosses, which challenge you to take your skills and apply them to battles that are (for the most part) challenging yet fair. Learning the attack patterns of each boss, deftly dodging them and then unloading your own assault to come out on top is a process that is very pleasantly rewarding... Yet no matter the combat situation, there’s many a moment that just feels cool, and you’ll want to keep going just to try and generate that next cool moment for yourself.
It’s annoying, then, that some of the game’s design seems to primarily exist to slap you cruelly back down to Earth. For instance, far too many enemies have attacks that can stun you momentarily or knock you down for a second or two.  Not only does this break the flow of the action far too often, but you’re so vulnerable once you’re in a stunned state that it’s not uncommon to end up trapped in a cycle where you’re knocked down again the second you stand back up. The same holds even more true with the traps mounted on the many walls you have to climb, with a single brush against a spinning saw blade or similar obstacle sending you tumbling off the wall like an ungraceful idiot. You will encounter many a moment where you’ve nearly reached the peak of a grand ascent, only for a tiny miscalculation to send you crashing into an obstacle and plummeting down to right where you started. It’s something that will hinder your progress so much, you’ll start to wonder why the enemy hasn’t just plastered such obstacles on every flat surface possible.
There’s also some weird level design in play that doesn’t really fit the aesthetic of you being an unstoppable ninja. The most glaring of these comes about halfway through the game, where three large water valves block the path you wish to proceed down. Two open up easily enough, but opening the third sees you travelling halfway across the world to obtain an item that only then removes this barrier. It’s a minor criticism, I concede - the game has to hinder your progress via some method - but the contrast between being a screaming whirlwind of death one second and then some sort of weird errand boy the next is still a tiny bit jarring.
It doesn’t help that the map you’re travelling around also feels a tiny bit uninspired, with only two or three little areas sticking in my memory when I try and cast my mind back to where the adventure took me. The rest of the world remains distinctly forgettable, a bland mix of grey buildings and unremarkable landscapes that do little to spark the imagination. If you’re hoping there’s an exciting storyline in place that can perhaps compensate for this, then you’re sadly mistaken – while the characters themselves look cool, the smattering of cut scenes they play a role in never really explain anything in regards to what’s going on. Put simply – you’re a good guy, you’re trying to kill the bad guy, and things don’t really go anywhere beyond that. If you’re looking for a compelling tale to captivate you, you’ve come to the wrong place.
Still, even though I’ve spent as long critiquing the game's faults as I have done pointing out its strengths, none of them even come close to destroying the sense of joyous carnage the game manages to capture. You might be frustrated in one moment, but give it a few more moments and you’ll most likely be back on the adrenaline rush where it feels like nothing can stand in your path. We’ve come on great strides (Ha ha) since my first encounter with the series, then, but this version of Strider is still one that is well worth checking out.

UPDATE: I have to change my review... the game is broken when you reach a certain point. Constant bugs with changes to inventory not being managed and, worst of all, game 'freezes' where characters don't respond to commands causing you to lose all your progress. This is really bad and happens on end-game missions that are the longest and most difficult ones. I just lost 2h of gameplay on one of the last missions due to this bug. This has been reported by other players since 2014. I can't recommend the game until this is fixed.
The game has great visuals and good (but not stellar) storyline. Character customization is not very deep, but good enough (although customizing your crew uses a different system which takes a bit to get used to).
Weakest point, IMO, is the combat system with awkward cover and line of sight mechanics (there's no cover where you would expect and line of sight sometimes makes no sense).
If you enjoy XCOM combat mechanics and/or want a decent cyberpunk story, I would recommend.

You're probably wondering why you should buy this, why not just boot up MAME or something, well, this isn't classic pac-man. This is a new take on the classic formula, and I think it works quite well. It feels like what would happen if pac-man was made nowadays (wihout all the dubstep, drm, screaming 10 year olds and dlc) and overall it just feels much more frantic and fast paced. what's that? 4 ghosts who wander around aimlessly? how about 10-20 ghosts who relentlessly pursue our poor cheese wheel with bitter determination. There is a multitude of modes as well, including a time trial and a "eat everything before time runs out" mode as well as some others i havent tried yet. There is a multitude of maps and courses, and numerous skins and music choices including some that pay homage to other classic arcade games, as well as one that mimics that stupid cartoon my brother made me sit through an episode of (the villain is called "Lord Betrayus" and they were actually surprised he betrayed them), one thing I love is how Pac-Man is essentially now a genocidal terrorist, you can throw bombs at the ghosts to knock them back to the center and when they go blue and you do get them, they don't go to the center, THEY'RE DEAD, and there is about 10-20 on the screen at any one-time. Get it, it's fun, enjoyable and it's not just a reskin of pac-man, it is it's own thing and it does it quite well.

: Truly exceptional world-building! It's a fun mix of Dan Brown, Assassin's Creed, and Tintin. There's a nice balance of occult history, Venice travelogue, Judeo-Christian mysticism, and political thriller elements. The narrative hits all the right notes for me.
I don't even mind that the present-day sequences don't use the art style from the original comics, because I wasn't very familiar with Corto Maltese before playing this game (other than a few tangential references in League of Extraordinary Gentlemen).
Many of the puzzles are genuinely fun, even if they seem a bit ridiculous in the context of the story. In fact, I wish I had thought of the explorer/Age of Discovery puzzle myself. (I run a brainteaser-oriented game night in Manila.)
I like how the Compass mechanic works, in general. It's a neat way to bridge the story and gameplay elements.
Bonus points for the puzzles that make use of real-world outside resources: Google Maps, Wikipedia, even TripAdivsor
It's quite a bold risk because it involves user-generated content that might end up getting deleted, later on. But for now, it feels inspired.
: The over-reliance on AGS-style connect-the-squares mini-games. Gets hella repetetive, especially in the late game. There's some occassional wooden voice acting, which I can forgive.
The stuff that makes this game unplayable at times comes from sloppy QA, rather than poor creative decisions by the devs. So it falls under...
: At least four of the expert-level/hard-mode puzzles are basically unsolvable because of poor implementation. I can't go into detail without spoiling it, but have a look at the discussion for this game, if you want to get an idea.
The most obvious example are the hints for a mid-game puzzle involving book titles. The in-game tips make reference to books that aren't even mentioned in the puzzle!
Also, the Achievements seem to be completely bugged. NOBODY has been able to get them, so far.
Based on other people's feedback, I get the impression that the original Italian version may have better quality control.
It's a shame -- I *really* wanted to like this game. The premise and gameplay have SO MUCH appeal to me. But the actual execution is unacceptably sloppy.

This is a fair warning to all Corto Maltese and point-and-click genre fans rather than a review of this game.
Why? The game simply won't work. What you get for a full game price is a Corto Maltese screensaver because it gets stuck on a loading screen and refuses to go any further than that. It's been at least one full week since the issue has been known and except for two humble "we're aware and working on it" replies on Steam forums there is no clarification on what could possibly be the problem. There is no official warning (in a form of a stickied discussion or a news post) and the Steam store page won't let you know of this unless you go into game's Community hub to investigate on your own.
I feel bad for everyone who bought this for a full price since the Steam Winter sale is right around the corner and there are chances of this game being discounted at least for the sake of selling more copies of this unreasonably priced Corto Maltese screensaver.
Some might say "have some patience for god's sake, don't be a crybaby, they will fix it!", well, I am patient but I feel it's also my duty to let other people know that they will be buying a game that most likely won't run. I like Corto Maltese and I like crime solving games so I had high hopes when I got this, but now I know for sure that I will enjoy this game way less than I could because of this unpleasant experience. Wasn't the game tested before it's release? I couldn't come up with a single excuse or an argument in developer's defense even if I really wanted to.
In addition, I wouldn't be writing this for everyone to see if there was an official statement from developer/publisher. Again, a stickied discussion or a news post saying something like "yes, we screwed up, we are sorry, have a pretty concept art picture to look at while we fix it" because that's what I saw other developers do when they are delaying game's release or working on patches. It's called common courtesy in my book. I suppose with all these ways to communicate directly with your audience we have nowadays, a simple seller-consumer communication is too much to ask for.

Far Cry 2’s greatest enemy is invisible and highly lethal. It is known as Plasmodium and it is the parasite responsible for malaria. Malaria is the most constant threat in Far Cry 2, yet, it feels to me that the disease is utilized half-heartedly as something that only annoys the player, rather than truly limiting them.
Randomizing malaria attacks is designed to remove control from the player and provide a boundary to exploring the vastness of Far Cry 2’s carefully crafted countryside. The rapid onset of a malaria attack is coupled with blurred, swirling vision and reductions in stamina, but symptoms can be quickly relieved through the use of an immediate-action miracle pill. Of course, the pill box eventually empties and the malaria attacks keep coming, which sees the player faint and return to one of two locations where they can acquire more pills. There is no harsh punishment for death, because there is no death. The parasite does not kill you, it simply stops you.
The quick-fix pill box renders the gameplay mechanic meaningless. It no longer becomes something that has to be micro-managed but something that becomes a frustrating distraction to the core gameplay. The mechanic itself is parasitic, damaging its host every time it randomly blurs the screen with a yellow tinge. If it was designed purely as a plot point, it should have been used as such. If it was designed to be micro-managed, then it should have been implemented with less abandon.
Overall, I do not recommend Far Cry 2. It's a really bad Malaria simulator.

This game is fantastic.
The economy in this game is one of the best in the genre, one which SupCom2 fails to uphold. The continuous economy system is great in practice and intelligent in design. Instead of a staggered income like in Starcraft where your resources are tied to workers physically traveling back and forth with an infinite storage, you have resources being aquired per game tick and finte storage. This facilitates building as much as possible when possible.
What is especially unique about SupCom1 is that when spending resources (mass and energy, the only two resources other than time) you don't pay the entire cost the moment you click build. Like the income, your spending is also on a per tick system. This is not only intuitive, it bypasses a lot of the tedium of macroing in other rts games. Instead of being charged upfront for queing 10 units, paying the entire cost of each unit before a single unit rolls out, you que units as you please and get charged the build cost per tick (something like every 1 or 2 seconds, i dunno).
You may think this is inconsequential, but when combined with spare resources in storage, you can build expensive structures or units extremely quickly for as long as you have the resources for it. In that same thought, if you have insufficent storage, you can use your engineers (all purpose builders, repairers, recyclers) to reclaim mass from destroyed  friendly and enemy units. After a large battle near your base, it's entirely possible to greatly increase your production per tick if you have engineers get the mass, allowing you to build some costly things for a short time.
The scale for this game is amazing. Unlike in other games where the camera is only ever at a fixed distance, requiring you to pan, click on the minimap, and use hotkeys to snap to places constantly, you can simply zoom out to see the entire map in SupCom. This gives you a better picture of your own army and buildings. Depending on your units' line of sight and sensors or dedicated radar/sonar structures, it's possible to locate every enemy unit and building on the map (barring some gameplay features).
There are several core ideas to fight the enemy SC in the game. All of which involve building a main army, probably consisting of many tier 1 units and a smattering of Tier 2 and Tier 3 units when possible. T1 units are the most cost-effective, after all.
One way to fight the enemy SC is to deny their mass income by destroying Mass Extractors as often as possible. Build a few units and send them out to deny as much mass as possible. This should slow down their production and development slightly. Of course, if they are also destorying your MEs as well, it gets more complicated.
Another idea is to use air transport units to attack structures that are important to the enemy. If your scouts see an undefended Shield Generator, for example, it might be worth dropping some T1 units into it to both deny the enemy SC protection and waste their resources and time by forcing them to rebuild it. It may also be a good idea to prevent large strategic buildings and Experimental units from being completed in the first place. No one wants a constant rain of artillery in their base or a giant death robot massacring their army.
The concepts in this game are inspiring and the execution of it is just so fun. It's clever and avoids some pitfalls or annoyances of other games of a similar genre. I suggest you at least try SC:FA.

While I strongly recommend this game, its only down side (and it is not that much of a downside) is replayability. The game encourages you to replay again and again, to unlock bonus feats that allow you to play at higher difficulty levels which in turn make the card game part of the game more strategic, however by the time you have replayed it three times (approx. 70 hours ish), very similar to when you have replayed FTL a few times (although they do mix them up a bit) you know the best choices for almost all the random stories and the best card/group combos, so it all gets a bit repetitive.
Even then, similar to  FTL, I can see myself brushing off this game in 3 to 6 month time, and playing it through again. It's that good.

Shortly:
The game is fast paced hack&slash styled action game, where you play as Mondo Zappa, who works for as an assassin in a certain mercenary corporation where he takes on contracts to kill specific targets.
The gameplay mechanics are pretty basic. If you've even played the Devil May Cry series or anything that resembles it, you'll pretty much see no difference in this game either. The only real difference in combat is that as you hit enemies with your sword, you'll gain Blood, a resource that you can then use for your special kills, such as range weapons or even executions that will one shot most of the enemies once their guard is down.
As you kill enemies and complete missions, you'll get both experience points and money, which you can then use later on between missions. With experience points you can buy new skills and upgrade them, and with money you can buy items from the shop. The items that you can buy includes health/recourse upgrades, resurrection cards in case you die during missions and don't want to restart from the last checkpoin, and Gifts for Beauties that you can "date" (I'll tell more about that feature later on).
As for the content in this game, the main story contains 12 different missions plus one extra DLC mission (episode 51). There here are 12 submissions and 20 challenges, which mainly gives you only money and little bit experience, but they'll also give costumes if you achieve the highest rank in them (achieving them is guite hard if you ask me).
Graphics takes some time to get used to, sounds are doreable and voice acting could be better.
As for the Story, I'm still trying to grasp it, because it doesn't really make any sense. Nothing is really explained, as the game presumes that you know all the background stories already, and because of that you'll get even more confused as you make progress through missions.
As I mentioned earlier, this game also has these Gigolo missions, where you can flirt with the game's Beauties and offer them gifts that you can buy from the Shop. The way you flirt with them is by looking them through these X-ray classes while they're not noticing, which then increases the progress bar. Once the bar is full, you can offer the beauty a gift, and if the gift is their likings, the beauties will reward you with items such as sub-weapons and stuff (and perhaps some night activity). I'm a guy in my late 20's, so this feature didn't really attract me at all. If you ask me, this whole Gigolo feature was implemented to the game only to attract more buyers such as boys in their teens.
Pros:
+ Pretty simple battle mechanics, easy to learn
+ Money's worth of content
+ Works well with Keyboard and Mouse
+ Hard boss battles
+ 2 language options for the voices, English and Japanese (better immersion with japanese voices, because its japanese styled game)
Cons:
- The art style, my eyes started to hurt after playing more than 30 minutes or so, but that's only for me
- Story is really...really...really hard to grasp of what's going on
- The game assumes that you know all the background stories
- Camera angles are sometimes irritating
- Gigolo feature is out of place and it was probably only added to the game to attrach young customers
- English voice acting could be better (especially Mika's voice acting is irritating for most of the time)
Do I recommend?
Not really. Not only I felt naucious because of the art style, but the biggest problem with it was the story. Each time I started to grasp of what's going, the game gave another new information bomb (so to speak) that confused me even more. But if you really wan't buy the game for it's hack&slash style, I would recommend you to go KiD's wiki sites and read all the background stories from there before you start to play it.
Verdict: 3 / 10 - Bad game
( 1 = do-not-bother game
5 = Average game
10 = Must own game )

Well balanced gameplay and slick visuals define Strider. Its Metroidvania design, scan lines reminiscent of CRT TV and the silly, run-of-the-mill good vs. evil story evoke nostalgia of the '80s and '90s.
The dystopian setting offers a variety of areas influenced by science fiction, cyberpunk and the Iron Curtain. In general, the graphics are beautiful and polished with an atmosphere fitting its respective area. Only a few scenes that shine a spotlight on the characters reveal static, comic-like faces. Clearly though, Strider is not a game with important character interaction, dialogue or even the slightest need to engage in the story. The music and sound effects are light, with less bass and more treble, yet crisp and generally underline the swiftness of Strider Hiryu.
Although fiddly in the beginning, the controls are precise and responsive to the point that even changing direction in mid-air is not only animated well but also happens instantly with just the right feeling of control. The enemies and bosses have balanced attack patterns that later on grow in complexity and need to be faced with consideration rather than full offence button mashing.
Strider hits the nail on the head and offers a solid, highly polished platformer.

I usually try to avoid card games, since most of them use some kind of pay to win system, despite them being free to play. The only other similar card game I have played is Hearthstone, which is an okay game for what it is. For me, it did get boring pretty quickly and most classes don't really bring anything interesting to the table, especially if you're not familiar with Blizzard's universe. Elder Scrolls: Legends, however, is similar to Hearthstone, a card game with the same core mechanics, but Bethesda's execution is better than Blizzard's.
Graphics/Artwork : The game should be a breeze to run in modern hardware, considering it plays very smoothly on my toaster. The artwork is really good, everything is pleasant to look at, even in Very Low graphics settings. The overall feel created by the game is perfect, the colors are not too vibrant but not too dim either. Card artworks are great and definitely do justice to characters from the Elder Scrolls franchise.
Sound/Music : Come on, it's a Bethesda game, you know what to expect. Bethesda is known for their great, atmospheric soundtracks that take the feel of their games on a whole new level. In Elder Scrolls Legends, it's business as usual for Bethesda. Music is great to listen to, and I really found the tutorial guy's voice really soothing (no homo).
Gameplay : The core gameplay is essentially the same as other similar games, you play cards using Magicka (instead of Mana), you fight your opponents' cards and you reduce his Health Points to 0 to win the game. There are, of course, card abilities like the familiar Guard (Taunt), Charge etc. although Legends also adds more abilities like Lethal. The addition of lanes and runes also help increase the skill cap of this game compared to Hearthstone. One very interesting aspect is card evolution. Certain cards evolve while playing Story Mode and you get to choose which one of two possibilities your card evolves into.
Although the game did freeze on me a couple of times on the loading screen (I am however playing on a toaster), looks bug free considering it released a few days ago. The only thing that did kind of throw me off a bit is that there's already DLC available. It seems, however, that it's just Story Mode content involving the Dark Brotherhood (unless I'm mistaken) and, at least, Bethesda is not so much in your face about it. Other than that, looks like all the cards can be obtained through packs, without spending any of your money, since you earn gold for completing quests.
In essence, this is a really fun game to play, even when on the side, while waiting for a different game to load or your friends to get online. Even though I haven't had the chance to play as much as I wanted, I can definitely see myself spending lots of time playing Legends.
Conclusion : should you play this game? Yes. Even if you're heavily invested in Hearthstone, this game's biggest rival, it's definitely worth a shot.

I used to play this game years ago, back when the only characters were Evie, Lann and... uhh... that other one. The sword and board chick.
I quit it around the time they first introduced Karak (pillar guy), because the game became this huge, insane, confusing grind once you get past the first few starting areas.
I signed on for killing a bunch of mooks, dodging traps, and then fighting a big ol' boss at the end. I didn't want to go look up strategy guides to figure out whether I wanted spears or swords on my Lann, or the ins and outs of this game's really weird crafting system (though I don't even know if that's in the game anymore).
I came back today, and immediately I notice that all of my characters are GONE. My only remaining character is Lann, who now looks like a prepubescent boy, is missing all of his armor/items and has been reverted to level one. I decide "fine, I'll make a new character" and start as the hunter. He's pretty cool, I had a good time shooting arrows and kicking kobolds in the face.
Immediately after finishing the tutorial, I was absolutely bombarded with popups and items and all sorts of nonsense. One of the first things I received was a box that contained a full set of late-game armor and weapons, equippable at level one. They were a bit ridiculous-looking, but the stats were at least 10 times higher than the default gear. Jumping into the first mission, I found that I could one-shot every single enemy without them ever getting close enough to touch me. I couldn't figure out how to turn off all the screen-filling clutter, so I just let it sit there flashing and moving around. Partway through the mission, someone dropped in and helped me instakill everything, despite setting my party to "private". It's not a big deal, they didn't bother me, I was just under the impression that I'd be instakilling things solo. I guess even that doesn't work the way I thought it did.
So maybe the game's better than the last time I played it. Maybe the skill trees are reworked, the boss battles are bigger and better than ever, and everything's streamlined once someone sits you down and walks you through it. Maybe this "road to 85" thing they have going on at the time of this writing is some kind of fast-track to the level cap so you can see all the content back-to-back with less grind.
I wouldn't know.
I'm probably not going to find out.

Viridi is simply a relaxing and nice game, not that much to name in my opinion.
I recommend Viridi, just one word: Patience
A virtual succulent. Overall, a very happy plant that's easy to take care of.

Do you ever stop and think about how bizarre the concept of a plant is? Its a living thing that is completely stationary, and generates its own food from the light of the sun. They are bizarre aberrations covered in organic solar panels.  This should terrify you. It should scare you to know that you share 35% of your DNA with these grotesque mockeries of life.  There is part of that plant inside you. You are part plant, and no matter how hard you may try to clean yourself, you will always be part plant. That soulless monster will always be inside you, begging you for sunlight so that your nonexistent chlorophyll may feed you.
There is a part of you that is always starving, and thirsty, and you can feel it, but there is no physical way to sate it.
Viridi is a very relaxing game about taking care of succulent plants. The succulents are very beautiful, and come in a wide variety of colors, which are also relaxing. The seeds have a random color plant for most of the species, which I am a fan of. The game is relaxed and chill, because the game is a simulation of plants. This game loves to exist. It wants you to relax and be happy and tend to virtual succulent plants.  Or so it may seem...
Is there anyone who hasn't tried raising a succulent plant in real life? How many people can truly raise their hands and say they have never killed a cactus or aloe plant because of their poor knowledge of botany? I know that I cannot, I know what I did to those succulents.  Not exactly, I mean. I either overwatered or underwatered them. It's one of those, and that's the important part. The life of a succulent was so simple before humanity. Now, well, now they can't do anything.  They have lost control of their own fates. They have no recourse when someone impulsively purchases them at a supermarket, fake flower glued to them. Because they are succulents, they are doomed. Succulents are at the mercy of the whims of humanity, their own cousins. Humans can take care of babies better than they can succulent plants.
Viridi has a wide variety of succulents, and even though it is a free game, they are generous enough to give you one free succulent seed per week. This has been a major boon to myself as it has largely prevented me from having to actually pay real money for these virtual succulent seeds. I even got the one that hangs off the pot and looks the coolest, totally for free one week. ♥♥♥♥in rad, man. There is a way to get some more pots, like spending real money or owning some game called Eidolon. Buying a key for Eidolon was cheaper than paying whatever they charge for the Cat House room.
This game is free and gives you free virtual succulent seeds on a weekly basis. There is no reason you should not be playing this game, if you care at all about our poor, freakish cousins, the plants, and especially if you care for succulents.  These virtual succulents even have the courtesy to tell you if they need water.  While real succulents can also do this, human beings are currently unable to understand their language. Viridi also gives the option of having the player sing to a particular succulent. Singing in this manner causes the succulent to grow to gigantic proportions, again, exactly like real life succulents. I'm sure everyone remembers learning about the Irish all singing at once to the same succulent, causing it to grow to almost half the size of the moon, ending the great famine while also permanently altering the orbit of our planet, the initial cause of global warming.
Speaking of global warming, have you ever thought about snails? Do most people think about animals at all?  I feel like nobody really understands how strange a snail is. Can you imagine the selective pressures exerted over millions of years that would result in such a creature? A snail should be awe-inspiring to people, as impressive as a dragon. But no, nobody really thinks about snails very much. Why would anyone think about snails? Why, indeed...
There is a species of hermit crab that has become specialized to only use the shells of one certain snail species. That snail species is now extinct, and the hermit crabs are running out of shells.
This game has a snail for each room that makes a circuit around the rim of your succulent pot, and the snails look different in every succulent plant pot biome, which leads me to conclude that they are four different species of snail in spite of them sharing identical shell shapes and body sizes. The snails in this game show no interest in eating the succulents you may be growing.  They will not harm your succulents by eating parts of them. This is despite the game denying the player the option of feeding the snail. There is no option in this game to feed the snails.
Who is feeding the snails? How did the entity that feeds your snails get into your succulent rooms?
Viridi takes a turn for the sinister and forces you to question reality itself.  Are these really your succulents? This game is free, how do you know you haven't just stolen another person's succulents? Can you own something that is virtual?  Do you have the right to privacy in a virtual space? Can a virtual entity invade your privacy? Did someone own these succulents before me? Me? You? Is there really a difference in the end? There is someone or something else coming when we aren't around and feeding those snails. If we don't water the succulents, they will die, and I don't see how the snail could be exempt from eating, as per the rules which the universe of Viridi has established. Viridi wants you to know that there is another being in the game, who, at any time, can come into your succulent rooms. Your privacy and sanctuary are illusory. The pleasantry of caring for your succulent plants becomes overshadowed by the ever-present threat of the Snail Feeder. You know he may come at any moment, you water your plants as fast as you can and close out the game. Your heart is racing and you haven't exhaled since you started the game up.  Viridi is now causing instinctive reactions in your plant DNA and your frightened, tiny, protomammal DNA.  You are now the plant, but you have also become the prey. And like most prey animals, you won't have any warning.  One day, the Snail Feeder will be there.  One day everyone has to meet the Snail Feeder.  And, I don't think it's going to be possible for me to explain to the Snail Feeder that I couldn't feed the snails, I wanted to, but I couldn't. I can only pray to whatever god will listen that when the time comes, Snail Feeder takes pity upon me.
The player does have the option of misting the snail with a spray bottle, this does not harm the snail or have any effect on his circuitous trek around the rim of the succulent pot. The player does also have the option of considering the snail to be some sort of clockwork automaton, and that none of the snails are actually real. Maybe there is no Snail Feeder.  There is no way in the game to investigate this, which adds to the player's feeling of the loss of reality. You are never sure if your life is truly in danger, or if you are actually being spied upon. The more the game is played, the more real the succulents and suspicious the snails become, the more it is played, the less real you become. You begin to wonder which song is a particular succulent's favorite, you begin to think the virtual snail is spying on you. Sending messages about you, what you've been doing, to people who hold power over you. Every time you play you know you are putting your life at risk, but, you have come to love your succulents. Of course you would put your life on the line for your succulent plants!  You begin looking over your shoulder, you start taking different routes to your house, because no matter what anyone says, everyone is scared of the Snail Feeder, whether they say they believe in him or not.
Are the snails real? Is the Snail Feeder real? Are the succulents real?
Are you real?

Positives:
- Unique feeling 4x game.
- High early enjoyability.
- Easy to learn.
- There is a nice juicy plot and backstory if you enjoy that. If you don't they are easy to skip. Well done.
- No game impacting bugs for single player (there are definately a few exploits, but this isn't a multiplayer game, so you'd only be cheating youself out of fun).
- I enjoyed the Slavic pantheon, a nice change from seeing Zues, Thor, or Ra in every freaking game under the sun.
Negatives:
- Replayability is limited as each god doesn't feel unique enough. Also you are punished for trying all the gods and play styles because the level up mechanism on Gods requires you to only play that god or you don't get enough exp to have it hit level 5. I found the god level up system to be very poorly designed. I feel like if they released a good patch to the God mechanics I'd easily call this a $40 game, as it stands though the price is reasonable because it turns into a grinding game after about the first 50 hours of game play. That said, $20 for 40-50 hours of enjoyment is a fair cost.
- The different challenges (social, physical, hex, etc.) all have the same combat system. This makes it so that if you go for a different team composition, it still feels like the same play style. I'd recommend they shoot for fewer challenge types with more uniqueness to each type of combat.
- The game is definately more fun with less villagers as you don't have to manage as much equiptment juggling and you don't end up with surplus workers and crafters that you end up assigning busy work to. The default 10 villager start style should probably not be an option as it is a superior game with 9 or 7 villager starts.

Thea: The Awakening is a hard game to define. It has elements of survival, card based combats, crafting, a deep narrative like an RPG, it uses procedural generation and has permanenth death, like a roguelike game. If you summarize all this, it would be correct to say that Thea is a "4X Roguelike" game, as these are the most apparent characteristics. Just like a 4X game, you'll need to explore, expand, search for exploits and exterminate to win.
This is a cautious recommendation though. Thea is not a game for anyone, and even the most persistent will need to be patient while learning some tricks. Despite the simple mechanics and the robust tutorial, this game has a rather high learning curve. There are several times when the player finds himself in a seemingly impossible situation, even in the easiest difficulty setting, and it will take a good deal of strategy. If you're willing to be patient and experiment enough to know how to deal with each situation, Thea will become more and more enthralling.
Based on Slavic mythology, Thea tells a tale of a cursed world, and it's up to you to rebuild it before it collapses. Even using random elements, such as more than 100 missions and differentiated quests, there are some passages that are always the same and must be completed with each game to achieve victory. These passages are special missions that give continuity to the narrative, and there are several different endings for the player to discover, which increases the replayability.
The gameplay basically has three pillars: collect, craft/ build and battle; Everything is done in your village and also during expeditions that you send to clear dungeons and complete objectives. There are several classes available, and you can choose the focus of your village when you start the game. Would you rather have more gatherers than warriors? Or it's better to focus on medics? Either way, whatever your focus is, the game distributes the classes well, and soon your village can have all of them; The focus you have chosen will increase the chances of a child growing up to become a chosen class when it reaches adulthood. Well, these three pillars are equally important, although it's possible to create a slightly more inclined strategy for some of them. Food and wood must be collected to support the population, and it's necessary to craft armor, items and weapons to equip your people, so they will be able to perform well in battles.
Speaking of battles, there are nine types of battles in the game. It's not necessary to resolve conflicts only in fights, but also in discussions (social challenges), challenges of strength, cure of diseases, among others. Each character class has the most accented skills in some aspect that will be useful for each different conflict. For instance, warriors are exceptional in fights and strength challenges, but on the other hand they can't cure sickness like medics, who are also good at social challenges. All these types of battles are resolved in a very strategic card game that was developed by people (from MuHa Games) who created Gwent, the card game of The Witcher 3, which recently became a game on its own. This system is easy to learn, but I'll tell you a detail that is not mentioned in the tutorial: Determining which card will be attacked (left or right) is done randomly, with a 50% chance of being left and 50% of being right. If there's a card between two cards, it can attack any of them, but if the card is the first card on the table, it will always attack the front card, just as the last card at the table will always attack the back card. With that in mind it is much easier to plan your strategy, since we have to take into account the two closest cards instead of just leaving a card with more health points always ahead, for example.
Although it can be considered a 4X game, the expansion aspect is not taken here in the traditional approach of this genre. This means it's not possible to settle or conquer new villages, and you will fight only against monsters, not other civilizations. The expansion in Thea is done at the population level. Gradually new children will born in your village, and every turn there's a chance to this child become an adult. It's not possible to interfere in this, but it's possible to build constructions that can attract more (already adult) people to your village, in addition to being able to attract some creatures to join you too. There's also no way to know when your character will level up. Extreme randomness, incidentally, is a watershed in Thea. It significantly increases the replay value, making each match unique, but on the other hand it can generate impossible situations, such as the fact that your village (which always starts at a fixed place that you can't choose) is located in a place that doesn't have food available, requiring restarting.
Thea seems to take the concept of roguelike to the extreme; More than Conquest of Elysium took. The game also adopts the roguelike save system, in which it's not possible to "save scum", all actions are permanent. I understand that this is a game design choice, because it was developed with this challenge in mind, but this makes some mistakes lead a match to its end, because the player will hardly be able to recover from a whole dead expedition by a dragon, for instance. This makes the game extremely brutal for people who are not familiar to games that feature permanent death, which unfortunately can take away a portion of the community that is passionate about RPGs and 4X, which are other strong genres in Thea, and can discourage some people to continue playing. In fact, Thea was made not to be beaten in the first match, even in the easiest difficulty. Each god chosen at the beginning of the game has five levels with buffs, which are unlocked as you accumulate points at the end of each match, even in a game you were defeated. In addition to premade options, you can customize the difficulty the way you want, but notice that even though it will not guarantee victory for a long time, it's a great tool for when you get more experienced and want to add extra challenges.
Thea has received several content patches and free expansions, so you don't have to spend extra money to experience the full game.
* Addictive and fun to play
* Great card battle system
* Excellent tutorial
* Remarkable soundtrack
* High replayability
* Narrative very well developed
* UI is a bit confusing and unintuitive

POLYGOD is a great game. It is a rogue-like first person shooter. Unlike othere games in this genre POLYGOD is really really good. The developers listen to the community and regular updates the game. They frequently make changes to the game balancing when enough players requests it.
The game itself has an old school feel to it. The gun is in the middle bottom of the screen (like the original doom). Each enemy a specific attack pattern. The levels are randomly generated. Usually this means poor level design but with POLYGOD this is really well done. The levels has a seed that can be adjusted by the player. The games blessings (will come to that shortly) is attached to the seed so each run will be the same with the same seed. There is also a daily dungeons for competing against other players. The blessings is basically a power ups. They are bought using souls, that s acquired from killing enemies. The power ups are great, varied and the more powerfull power ups usually have a down side, for balancing purposes. A great touch is that each power up affected the look of the gun. The graphics are simple low poly style graphics with no textures. This style works really well. POLYGOD is definitely worth the asking price at the moment. Great gameplay and a responsive developer make this game one of the few Early Access games thats worth the risk.
P.S. Bonus points for splitscreen co-op on pc.

Polygod is a first-person-shooter rogue-lite with a strong focus on upgrading the crap out of your gun and fighting a ton of enemies who shoot bullets everywhere.
While I do think that Polygod is quite enjoyable to play and has a lot of potential to be a great game on launch, it has its fair-share of issues that seem to come with most rogue-likes.
First of all, your enjoyment and success in Polygod seems entirely hinged around getting lucky and finding the best upgrades. There is a bit of skill and game-knowlege involved but for the most part the game becomes a boring slog if you don't have the right gear to take on enemies and bosses, especially during the later levels.
The game's difficulty curve also seems to be a bit wonky at the moment. The first boss is a run-killer while the later ones don't seem to be quite as difficult in comparison and can be easily cheesed.
Of course Polygod is in early access, so pretty much everything about the game is bound to be changed or improved. The developers seem to be very respondant towards community suggestions and complaints so I believe that the game is in good hands.
PROS:
- Fun and fast-paced gameplay.
- A clean and pleasing visual-style.
- Good soundtrack.
- Interesting and varied weapon-upgrades.
- Lots of potential.
- Great for listening to podcasts while playing.
CONS:
- Enjoyability is hinged on luck.
- Level-generation is currently a bit limited.
- Difficulty curve is very uneven and takes a sudden spike.
SCORE: 7/10

Easily the worst hack and slash game I've played in my life.  Beyond the fact that its PC port is disastrous, the actual gameplay is a shambled abortion of bad concepts.  The player character controls clunkily, awkwardly, his combos have little actual 'oomf' and don't interupt the most basic of grunts.  Each swing of his sword is slow, awkward, and just terribly unimpressive.
The bizzare thing is that this awkwardness actually makes the game 'harder'.  A large portion of the game is blocking and dodging just in time.  Now, not a big deal typically- long term ninja gaiden and DMC player here.  The problem is that enemy attacks lack any sort of rhythm or pacing.  They swing like old men, not hardened combatants, so if you block/dodge when you feel you should be hit- it'll be too soon.  You cannot start the dodge at the beginning of the swing, you have to wait, and it just feels terrible.
Perhaps the most egregious part however is the boss fights.  The first one is perhaps one of the worst I have ever seen in a game.  The boss is 'deadly' because her attacks do ludicrous amounts of damage, not that they're interesting or hard to dodge.  While they have a better pace than the common mooks, the real issue is the overall combination of phases. After emptying her life-bar, nothing happens. You can't damage her anymore.  The game gives no indication that the only way to continue on to the next phase is to wait until you knock her down, then perform a finisher. You'll spend a minute swinging away at someone who should be dead without any progress.  Then you repeat this three times until you reach her 'final form'.  All she does is cling to the ceiling and shoot down lttiel insects- these insects, beyond having a terrible block timing, are not stumbled when you attack them. If you attack them directly, you'll get hit and have over a tenth of your health taken out.
It's not hard, it's just not fun.  The whole thing is repetitive and down to repeating the same thing endlessly.  Worse, the actual combo options for his sole main weapon are more limited than Nero from DMC or any Ninja Gaiden weapon.  It's terrible.
Please do not buy this game. Even when it's on sale for 80% off, it wasn't worth it.

I've put in more than 40 hours into this game on the Xbox 360 version, as well as the non-Steam version, so don't mind the lowly 9 hours I've put into the game here on Steam.
This is a fantastic game, and I personally prefer it over Far Cry 3. I was a huge fan of the original Far Cry (no, not the one on Xbox called Instincts, but the very first one on PC!). It was a flawed but fun game, with glitchy AI but beautiful levels and an open world design, where you could do a mission multiple different ways. I was worried when Far Cry 2 was announced to be in Africa and not a tropical island like the first, and that Jack Carver wouldn't be returning. I bought Far Cry 2 anyway when it released on PC, back when games didn't always come with Steam keys.
I was immediately addicted. The game is very gritty, with just about everything out to kill you. It's definitely not for casual gamers.
Weapons start rusting and breaking after long uses, eventually exploding in your hand, damaging you and forcing you to scavenge for a weapon off the ground while enemies are shooting at you from all directions. Cars can start to break down, requiring you to quickly get out, pop the hood, and use your magical wrench to fix it all while enemies are driving down the road trying to find you.
Bones will break. Shrapnel will stab into your thigh. Bullets will require pulling out of your arm. You'll need to heal yourself, which uniquely has your character fix himself through multiple animations of ripping out large chunks of metal from his legs, bandaging himself, etc. It all looks fantastic and gives the game, as I said earlier, a very gritty feel.
The game is flawed, just like Far Cry 1. The AI is iffy. It's hard to stealth. The story isn't delivered very well. Everyone talks like they've got to get to the last rocket off Earth. There's respawning guard outposts (though you can easily go around them, to be honest). But even with all of that said, I still think the game is much more unique and fun to play compared to Far Cry 3. I love exploring Africa, it looks gorgeous. If you ask me, I think the engine they used for FC2 (Dunia Engine) looks much better than the slightly cartoon-y style FC3 had with the Dunia Engine 2.
I'd recommend the game if you're looking for a different, less casual type of FPS. It's got an incredible amount of detail, the weapons are fun to use, there's some very cool features like weapons breaking down, the healing system, and the way AI interact with each other (enemies will try to drag their friends away after they've been hurt, for example).
It's a very underrated game, and I hope one day we'll get another Far Cry like this. One that isn't afraid to be different and try new things.
EDIT:
I recently started playing Far Cry 4 on my Playstation 4, and I just wanted to say that if you were a fan of Far Cry 2, but sad that FC3 removed a lot of the neat ideas 2 brought with it, you should definitely check out FC4.
It feels like a mix of all the things I loved about FC3 and brought back a few things I missed that FC2 had, like fire realistically spreading (FC3 sorta had it still, but it didn't work well), being able to go to sleep to change to a specific time of day, and hell, even a certain character returns from FC2! I won't spoil who it is, but it took me by surprise, since he wasn't a particularly big character in FC2. He's also the first recurring character in a Far Cry game, other than one other character who returns from FC3. Seems like Ubisoft is starting to make the games connect a bit!
