This is an excellent game that I was initialy unsure of due to the turn-based isometric style approach. That said, I really enjoyed the original XCOM and UFO games when they first came out (a very long time ago now) and soon took to this game. It can be fairly unforgiving if you charge in FPS style and expect to get away with it, often resulting in your team being crippled and no way to recover other than to forfeit the mission on harder levels.
The dice rolling can be a little odd at times, with your top shooter missing frequently at point blank range yet making long range shots more often than not. It almost seems as if once they start to miss they keep missing? This does add to the tension though, and there is a genuine fear that you might not make it through, unlike most FPS/RPGs where you can simply take cover and wait for the auto heal to fix you. There is no auto heal when you drop out of combat and the next wave are just around the corner.
However, the game is very enjoyable, particularly as you start to notice the small details and get more into the story. The old cliche of 'you get out what you put in' definitely applies to this game. Stick at it, grind out a few weapons and upgrades and you will be up and running in no time.
One tip - when decking, take as many offensive programs as possible, plus APs. This will massively speed up your progress and forget the shields once you have an AP helping you. Am not finished the game yet but will be playing it again soon to race through another few missions.

If you haven't played any of the HBS Shadowrun games, to me they seem like something of a cross between the "interactive novel" style of a jrpg and the combat of a turn-based squad tactics/strategy game. The combat is fun, though not always challenging in a strategic sense (sometimes not in any sense).
My two biggest complaints are the same as from the first game:
1) The game feels a little too short. Not to say I didn't feel like I got my money's worth (especially since I've gotten them all on sale), it just felt like it was over pretty quickly in both cases once the story really took off.
2) I didn't enjoy the Matrix bits at all. I appreciate what I think they were trying to do (keep it somewhat true to the source material, and make it more than a skill check), but I didn't personally enjoy it.
That said, I still like them quite a bit. Without giving spoilers, this second one made me consider my actions a bit more in a couple of places, which I liked. I also enjoyed the wider variety of cyberware & weapons. One of the key points to an rpg for me is the character options and progression, and this game definitely scratches that itch. I will probably go back and play through again at some point with a different character type.
So yeah, not perfect, but still quite good.

I like many things about this game but there are things that really hold this game back for me. I love a good open world/survival game, and the original vision of this game had me very excited to try it out.  I am however slightly dissapointed that this game has been in early access for two years and it still is suffering from many of the same issues.  The optimization of this game is lacking and it can and most likely will cause stuttering and lag issues, you will probably also suffer from the occasional crash.  This is something I do understand comes with the early access territory, but it has been two years.
Besides optimization problems, I also disagree with some gameplay decisions taken by the devs.  First, I feel needing to find blueprints for a good chunk of the buildable items in this game is kind of annoying.  I will let it slide as you kill a very large number of mobs as is so you don't really need to go out of the way to get more blueprints.  However, I do feel the costs of building the blueprints is pretty steep.  This is more of a problem with building your base than anything else, you need to grind for a fair amount of time to acquire the resources to build even a modest base.  I don't have anything against resource gathering but I do feel the material costs for some of the items should be decreased or resource nodes should give more materials.
Resource problems aside there is only so much you can do in this game before you have seen all, done all, and crafted all.  This is in my opinion a serious problem, while there might be a lot of blueprints most items are just reskins of other things which play the same way as everything else.  I really do not want to build and use exactly the same things over and over again, more variety would alleviate this issue in my opinion.
To end this I will reiterate my first statement: hold off on this for now.  Wait to see if the devs return to fix the optimization problems, tweak building costs, and generally add more content.

I've been hunting for a game similar to Heroes of Might and Magic.  I'm not happy with where the franchise is going, so I've been looking for something similar to play.  I've found a few that were pretty cool...  But then I found this.
Thea: The Awakening might be my new favorite in the genre.  It adds a lot of depth, but it is also more manageable.
You have one city to manage.  There are a variety of building upgrades to research/build.  Certain upgrades unlock new classes.  Some provide skill/stat bonuses.  Other upgrades produce resources.  You can build one of each, or you can build multiples, though some effects do not stack.  You are limited to 10 total upgrades, however.
By default, you start with 10 characters.  Each character has a set of skills.  Any character can have any skill, but specific classes develop certain skills faster.  There are three base classes (warrior, craftsman, gatherer), but many additional ones which can be unlocked through building upgrades.  Some characters/classes can be acquired through events/quests, including classes from different races, animals, and monsters.  Your units progress individually, so each one is important.  Losing units hurts.  Spread yourself too thin, and you'll be in serious trouble.
You can assign your characters to groups.  The groups can walk around Thea, gathering resources, killing monsters, or just exploring.  You have to manage each group's food and fuel.  (each character eats 1 food per turn)  You will encounter random events along the way.    More on that soon.
There's a complex crafting & research system.  Crafting gives you research points which you can spend on unlocking new resources, crafting recipes, or building designs for the town.  There are about 3 dozen resources that you can collect. The crafting recipes allow you to arrange the resources in different ways to produce items with stats that you desire.  There are hundreds of combinations for each type of item.  (1h/2h sword, 1h/2h axe, light/medium/heavy armor, rings, etc)
The game's event system relies heavily on RNG, but it's not like FTL, where you're just waiting for the random event that's going to kill you.  Instead, the random events introduce new quests.  Sometimes they hurt you, but they give you the opportunity to recover.  There's almost always more than one way to approach a situation.  It might be the best event system I've seen to date, which is made all the better by...
The fantastic event editor.  You can craft your own events, or download them from the Thea forums.  You can use the event editor to craft your own quests with a variety of paths/outcomes.  It would be nice if they had workshop support.  They are making a sequel...  Perhaps the sequel will have workshop support.
(*There's only one significant problem with the event editor;  You have to exit the game in order for changes to take effect.  I didn't see this documented anywhere.  I found it on a forum.  But I pass it on to you here.)
If you're looking for a game with some similarities to Heroes of Might and Magic, but that puts much more emphasis on unit development (rather than developing one, or a handful of characters) give this game a go.  I highly recommend it.

I want to like this game. I really, REALLY do. It has potential to be a fairly decent addition to anyone's library. But at the moment (2/10/2017) I just can't recommend Polygod. Let's talk about why.
The good
-Interesting "blessing" system where you purchase buffs to change your weapon in unique ways.
-The buffs can interact with each other, similar to The Binding of Isaac.
-Rewards high skilled players.
-Decent amount of content for a game at it's stage.
-Multiple characters to unlock and play.
The bad
-Certain buffs have massive problems with each other.
-Buffs are not explained well at times, making you expect one thing and end up with something much worse.
-While levels are randomly generated, everything in each level looks and feels exactly the same.
-Enemy variety is very poor.
-Why can we get on the top of the walls in the Garden of Gaia? Seriously, it feels unintentional but it's so easy there's no way it's an accident.
-The bosses are difficult beyond the point where they should be, and in a way that can be easily exploited with one or two buffs. And no, before you say it, I'm not just being a little ♥♥♥♥♥. Bullet sponges are not fun. Running around a sphere hoping you can run fast enough for 5 minutes trying to avoid infinite rockets is not fun. Trying to hit the first boss, which can fly incredibly quickly (and there can be more than one) with bullets that have a really, really slow travel time IS NOT FUN.
-Specific buffs take away any form of challenge to the point where if I don't have one or two of around 7 buffs by the first boss (OUT OF 75) I just start over, while the rest of the buffs are either weak, useless, way too expensive, or detrimental.
-Those ♥♥♥♥ing blue shrooms. Just....just no. That explosion radius is not okay.
-While some of the characters are interesting, it feels like the developer just thought up some random♥♥♥♥♥♥without thinking of deeper lore and slapped it in. There's just no depth.
-Some enemies have extremely annoying attacks.
-Lots of glitches, which is a weaker point as the game is in early acces.
-Enemy pathfinding is awful.
-Never found a multiplayer server.
-I'm not even going to say it has a tough difficulty curve because everything depends on your buffs. Sometimes you just get screwed.
-Every time you die you have to go back to the title screen (unless you want to play the same map over and over again which kind of ruins the point of a randomly generated game) and walk through a small hallway to actually get to the gameplay. Which sounds like I'm just nit picking, but when death is fairly common it should be a very quick wait to get back into the action.
-Some enemies are far too difficult for how soon you can encounter them.
-Sound effects are somewhat poor, but not awful.
-Going through the later levels just evolves to you standing on a high point and sniping everything you can see until you reach the boss.
-Boss fights are one of 3 things. You destroying them in 20 seconds, a long and painful fight that lasts 15 minutes, or them ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on you because you didn't get anything good.
If someone asked me if I could recommend a game where the pro-to-con ratio was roughly 1:4, it would be absolutely not. So here we are. Ultimately, this game needs a major balance fix, more enemies, and a better UI before it should even be considered by anyone, even those who can appreciate a tough learning curve. However, should these issues be fixed Polygod will be a good game, perhaps even a great one. Keep an eye on this game, and be patient for the day when it is improved.
Final note, if I am incorrect or you have a differing opinion (or just want to ♥♥♥♥♥ at me) please comment so I can edit this post.

In Polygod, you challenge the evil Gods in a special trial (Trial of Gods). The twist is that every level is randomly generated. As you kill enemies, you gather “souls” which you can use to improve your character. And while it all sounds great, I have mixed feelings about the game.
Pros:
-	Fast paced gameplay
-	Beautiful low-poly graphics, distinct style, colorful levels and effects
-	Lots of different upgrades
-	Challenging
Cons:
-	Only one weapon. (Yes, you can get various modifiers, but at the current point it just feels very repetitive to start every game with it).
-	Menu issues with gamepad, some UX/UI trouble
-	The shooting sound of player’s weapon does not feel enjoyable
-	Pathfinding is not that great, monsters get stuck behind walls
I can see that a lot of work went into the game, but my main issue is with the gameplay right now: pace-wise it’s good, but there’s actually a big game design challenge. In “linear” shooters, you are often given weapons to solve some kind of an “issue.” I.e. you are given rocket launcher before tank appears or shotgun for close-quarters or sniper-rifle before long-range combat starts. If the process is randomly generated, it’s just is not there. Therefore it becomes somewhat repetitive, because you have a gun and specific enemies that you can defeat using pretty much anything.
Overall, I’d say the game has its own style and the gameplay principles are there, but it feels that the game went into early access a bit too early. At the time of writing the review, not all enemies have shooting/movement sounds, so you can’t hear where they are nearby. I’d say skip this one for now and check it out when it’s done. Looking forward to when it's done and I'll be glad to take another look.

I left my initial positive review below to illustrate how my perception changed over time from a straight-up positive to a mediocre overally negative one.
It isn't that it feels P2W, but it certainly does feel purposely imbalanced.
Bethesda has designed the game to not only favor luck, but also to foster what Roger Dickey of Zygna fame terms "fun pain".
Take a 50-card deck to start, which compared to 30 card minimum decks dilutes out the probability of scoring multi-card synergies.
But the biggest luck generating factor in Legends is the overtly unbalanced 3-point crystal advantage given to the "second" player, who more often than not will actually go first only with a 3-point advantage that they can carry throughout the game if they wish.
These 2 factors result in:
- increased luck factor
- imbalance advantage for the "second" player
Why would Bethesda want to have an imbalanced game?
By fostering imbalance and a greater luck factor, inferior players stand a greater chance of winning 50% of the time, and as such keeping them in the player base.
Also, superior players are more likely to lose matches that they believe would have been won had they not been put at a 3-point disadvantage, fostering fun pain and theoretically leading to spending money to get that additional edge to overcome the overtly unfair disadvantage.
Another unfortunate result for those of us who favor more complex deck design, is the simpleminded low-cost rush deck are disproportionately favored, once by the 50-card minimum threshold, and twice by the 3-crystal scheme.
In this way a rush deck is more likely to actually get to something out right from the first turn and minimize the 3 point disadvantage, and of course a 3-point advantage for rush deck design is a veritable cornucopia of aggressive options.
…so little units out with charge > little guard > play both lanes > item stacks, KABOOM!
Rinse and repeat mindless gameplay, which is also why the AI practice matches rely on this strategy in most cases, as mindless is easy to code.
In additional to undermining intelligent gameplay, I believe the “fun pain” frustration approach to game design that Bethesda has adopted lends itself to a toxic community as people get increasingly piXsed off at unfair matches.
It illustrates that the definition of a well-designed game for skilled players is not the same as one for the devs, as fun gameplay through balance is not necessarily the most profitable route as "fun pain" = $$$$.
...also don't be surprised to find more players start to concede matches right from the start to fulfill their dailies in casual matches, especially concerning quests for decks they don't particularly favor. Bottom line, why play a deck you don't have a strong affinity for against a 3-point disadvantage when trying to knock out unfavorable dailies, as opposed to just forfeiting as rank doesn't matter?
TL;DR:
The 3-point advantage is what is most likely going to drive skilled players from the game, which isn't necessarily a bad thing for the devs, so long as there is a net increase in players over time (mediocre or otherwise).

Date of review: 10.24.2014
Platform: PC
Released in 2008, Far Cry 2 took a sharp turn from the first Far Cry, and threw the player into a much more realistic, grim, fictional African country. Forget the super mutants and crazy scientists, and get prepared for arguably the most authentic game representation of an African civil war.
Story:
In Far Cry 2 you can choose to be one of 9 pre-created characters, and while the choice itself will not have any real impact on the outcome of the story, the characters have interesting backgrounds and the ability to choose definitely improves the immersion.
However, no matter who you choose, you will be a mercenary, sent to assassinate the Jackal, a notorious arms dealer who is arming both warring African factions, the UFLL and the APR… (the remaining characters will also show up in the game, as “buddies”, and they will help you throughout your progress). Of course things will go wrong, very wrong, and you will find yourself in the middle of a bloody war, AND sick with malaria.

The story is exciting, and unique. Forget the good guy(s) who fight(s) the honorable war against the evil enemy kind of stuff... In Far Cry 2 everyone is a corrupt, backstabbing son of a b****,  and as you progress through the main plot you will realize that there is no good or bad choice, there is only bad and bad, and there is nothing you can do about it. Definitely not your average approach, but you know you are dealing with something unique when you get a Nietzsche quote right at the beginning of the game…
10/10
Visuals:
Far Cry 2 could obviously not  keep up with today's AAA games in terms of graphics, but maxed out it still looks very good. The African wilderness is very well depicted and diverse, with deserts, vast savannas, and jungles, and lively with several forms of wildlife running all around the place. The towns are filthy and dilapidated, with signs of poverty and war visible everywhere. On top of that, Far Cry 2 also has a live day-night cycle which is not only visually pleasing, but also adds a lot to the immersion.
While I was more than satisfied with the visuals of the Dunia Engine, I did have some problems when enabling DirectX 10, which was causing seemingly random crashes on Windows 7 64 Bit Ultimate. On Windows 8.1 64 Bit Pro the problem disappeared…
All in all, nice visuals, with some technical hiccups here and there. Today's computers should run it without any problems even on maximum details (for reference, you can check test system specifications at the bottom of the review).
8/10
Gameplay:
Far Cry 2 follows the path created by the first Far Cry in terms of gameplay, but it also polishes and adds a number of new features to it. The world is truly open and huge (50 square kilometers) and provides a ton of things to do.
You get a decently long main story with varied and interesting missions, and plenty of side quest from weapon dealers (who will reward you with new weapons), from buddies (who will reward you with safe house upgrades) and from the locals (who will reward you with malaria medicine). And on top of that, you have a lot of miscellaneous “quests” as well, like diamond searching and outpost scouting.
You can probably rush through the game in 15 hours or so, but you can easily spend 50+ hours and still have things to do.
But this is an FPS, so what about the weapons? No need to worry, the weapons are also varied (from pistols and sub machine guns to assault rifles, sniper rifles, light machine guns and even exotics such as the flame thrower and the mortar) and provide several ways of combat. It’s up to you to decide whether you will try to dispatch your foes from far or in a bloody close combat. Stealth however didn’t really work for me, and as far as I can tell, the developers didn’t want to make it a really viable option… something I can understand in a way, this is a civil war after all. Still, it’s fun to shoot, the weapons are quite realistic (don’t expect an ArmA type of game though) and the flame thrower is really awesome, even if not very effective actually.
Still, this wouldn’t be a Far Cry without vehicles, right? Right! You also have vehicles in Far Cry 2, from small cars and modified assault trucks to boats and gliders… and while they feel completely arcadish, trust me, you will be thankful for them as the distances can be really huge.
Unfortunately however, Far Cry 2 has its problems as well. Some of the side missions become repetitive after a while, the weapons have a degradation system which is interesting, but way too fast, the AI is simply painfully stupid sometimes (although when it works, it will surprise you…) and… well you have the “outpost system” which is one of the most frustrating features I have ever seen in a game. There are dozens of outposts scattered throughout the map, manned by the soldiers of the warring factions who will shoot you on sight. While the concept does make sense, and clearing the outposts is fun at first, they will soon become frustrating because of their insane re-spawn rate… it’s really not fun to clear out an outpost, walk away a couple hundred meters and come back to find it fully manned again. Ubisoft, this was really stupid!
8.5/10
Sound:
In terms of music and sound effects Far Cry 2 is above average. While the soundtrack isn’t really memorable, the African tribal theme is pleasant and adds to the immersion, and the environmental and combat sounds are actually quite good. Unfortunately the dialogs are a bit soulless which sometimes kills the characters.
8/10
Replay value:
While the plot is linear and there aren't any choices which would significantly change the outcome (which was done on purpose as far as I can tell, because in the end Far Cry 2 is story oriented and has a very strong message to communicate), the game provides countless possibilities, and can easily suck you in, making the game worth returning to.
9/10
Conclusion:
Far Cry 2 is a very good game, with a unique setting, a unique plot, and a strong message which raises some very interesting moral questions. And while it might be a bit outdated by today’s standards, it’s definitely one of those games which you have to play at least once.
I really recommend it if you are willing to invest some time into it, and if you are interested in something different, something special. If you are looking for a simple “tunnel shooter” however, you might get somewhat disappointed.
8.5/10
Test system specifications:
AMD FX-8350 (OC @ 4.6 GHz); 8 GB DDR3 RAM @ 1866 MHz; AMD Radeon R9 280X (AMD Catalyst 14.4), Windows 7 64 Bit Ultimate / Windows 8.1 64 Bit Pro.

Killer is Dead is a stylish 3rd person beat 'em up game from Grasshopper Manufacture. While not perfect, I really found this to be a beautiful game that left me highly impressed. The game stars Mondo Zappa, a hired executioner and certified lady killer, who battles "wires" (metal monsters) while seeking assassination targets. The gameplay is all hack and slash with a little bit of fps mixed in via Mondo's gun, which serves as a secondary weapon.
+Absolutely beautiful and unique art. Everything about the game is stylish, from the menus, to the unique cell-shaded graphics, to the overall flashy look. The game is worth playing just to admire how amazing it looks.
+Great soundtrack that fits the game.
+A totally unique, multi-stage boss battle at the end of every single mission.
+Good hack and slash gameplay. I don't play many games in this genre, but I found the gameplay to be quite entertaining. The combat layout is an attack button, a block, a dodge, and a guard break, and some other things mixed in. As a secondary weapon you have Mondo's gun, which is fired in first person. Using the gun, or special attacks, consumes a secondary meter. There is a large handful of upgrades available to be bought throughout the game.
+The player can choose between the English and Japanese dubs.
+/-Fanservice.
+/-The game actually has a great story, but it's a little hard to understand as shown in the game. You have to put the pieces together or it just looks like a totally random mess. I had to read a plot summary after finishing to fully understand, although I don't think this should be necessary if you stay sharp and pay attention.
-Too short. The main story only took me around 11 hours, although there is an abundance of side missions aside from the main story.
-The level design is fairly linear. It didn't really bother me because the combat was good enough to keep me entertained, but it's worth noting.
-The English dubs were a little overacted in my opinion, particularly Mondo. I tried to play English and ended up switching to the Japanese, which was much better.
-The character models look fantastic, but they are not animated well. You can tell watching the cutscenes that their faces have very little joints, which causes their range of expressions to be overly limited.
I am pretty surprised at the hate for this game. Yes it has its flaws, but it's such a unique and worthwhile game in so many ways. The art is beautiful and the kind of thing you won't see in any other game. The story is on one hand an interesting, somewhat light hearted sci-fi story, and on the other hand a clever satire on classic lady killing male heroes like James Bond. The gameplay is not revolutionary but it was definitely entertaining. All in all I found this to be a simply fantastic and totally worthwhile game. It comes with my highest recommendation.
Stunningly gorgeous art. Good hack and slash gameplay. Level design is linear. Game is short (~11 hours). The game's high artistic value lends it my highest recommendation.

Chronicle: RuneScape Legends, is a card game that almost plays like a euro-boardgame.
A lot of cards revolve around multiple resources, and depending how you build your deck there can be a lot or close to no interaction with your opponent. (Although the first rather than the latter is usually more effective)
Balance wise the game does not offer a lot for the new player. If you aren't gonna dish out for 30-ish packs (150 cards). You will find yourself struggling to compete with just about anyone. Apart from a few exceptions most of the basic "free" cards are complete rubbish compared to their more rare equivelants.
Currency for packs can be earned through a daily/weekly system as well as a draft mode (price: 1.5x pack prize, guaranteed 1 pack).
The gameplay feels to me like a euro-boardgame almost. Rather than battling each other with a field of minions you are setting up plays to collect certain resources to aid you in your win-condition. That being said, at the time of writing, the best win-condition is sabotaging your opponent's wincondition rather than creating your own and beating them to it.
The biggest gripe I have with the game is that the gameplay although able to have a lot of dept, basically boils down to a 5 turn game. Which requires you to do a lot more prediction and "luck"-based guessing rather than allowing you to plan as you go. After the turn is set up there is no more user interaction and everything is just played out. No countering counters etc.
I'm also not a fan of the variable turn length. Once one player has set their cards a timer 'll start that indicates the end of the turn. If you are a slow thinker vs a fast player (or a simple deck). You will find yourself short on time.
Pros:
- Haven't seen this style of collectible card game yet
- If you like RS lore, you will enjoy a lot of RS references going from ingame items to important quest figures.
- Graphics look good, fun art
- Addictive
Cons:
- It's a collectible card game, so if you want to be competitive (without first grinding for 6 or so months), you'll dish out a big wad of cash.
- Balance wise some cards seem very iffy
Gripes:
- Not a fan of how easily plays are countered in this game.
- Boils down to a game with 5 elaborate turns. (playing a max of 20 cards out of your 30 card deck)
- Variable turn timer is horrendous
The game of course promisses expansions, new cards and the like. Overal it's worth a shot if you want to try something new. But as I play for free after a few days of playing everything already feels fairly stale to me, most decks I face (baddy gold rank), are filled with cards I do not have the ingame currency to craft or obtain otherwise.

Dungeoneering is a great way for players to not only earn their card packs and the all important gem shards but allows them access to all cards in the game and experiment with decks first hand, helping them to develop strategies to be used later on when adding cards to their own collection.
It's still in its early stages and others have posted some fair points such as the repetetive/unecersary animations but overall I would say regardless of whether you are a fan of Runescape and it's lore this is definitely a game anyone can come into and enjoy from the get go. Looking forward to more cards, heroes and game modes in the future. Also hoping to see it come to mobile soon!

The joys of having a developer and director as auteur driven as Suda 51 are varied. Some games he'll make are pure gold and something that is fun for everyone. Most of the time, he makes weird games that you, very slowly, realize is someone's masturbation aid.
Killer is Dead falls into that second category.
The gameplay focuses on the protagonist Mondo Zappa, an immortal cyborg samurai assassin from the moon who can use ancient spirit magic through his sword and robot arm that can shoot blood bullets. The action of the game is based around a brawler style system; you wander around and go slash/shoot things that are not you, using a system of combos and special abilities to weave around enemies and strike at their vulnerable sides.
For the most part, the game has the problem of giving you too many tools to kill an enemy. You can attack them with your sword, you can shoot them with your gun, pierce them with a drill the size of a suitcase, use moon-based charge magic attacks to slash at them, use a weird slow-time like sword attack at random on them, use guard counters or guard breaks on them to either do the slow-time sword attack or a single powerful slash, you can use dodge combos... or you can just mash X and dodge occasionally and accomplish the exact same job.
Artistically, the game's fine. Has a cel-shaded art style and presents itself like an average anime. Which is where the game falls apart, it's trying to make EVERYTHING dramatic and EVERYTHING a twist, so you're some weird man from the moon who uses magic but isn't magical even though he has a drillgunhand thing, and you're friends with a space unicorn... I was bored from the first thirty minutes, and the game has done nothing to endear itself.
You know how you get extra weapons and new skills and combos? You do Gigilo Missions. You go out and find a pretty lady, stare at her♥♥♥♥♥♥with x-ray glasses until a bar fills up, then you give her a present. Repeat for sex, whereupon you get guns. Combined with the awful voice acting and acceptable gameplay style and a poor story, it's just... bland. It's like a 90s pastor trying to get kids "RADICALLY HYPED ABOUT JESUS!", but at best succeeds at making them flip out their phones and see how their farm's doing.

You know what, I thought of writing a complete and full rewiew with complex details, but to hell with it. I'll just give an honest opinion. Is KiD is a fun game? For me it is! It does contain a good balance between coocoo crazy humor and action packed adventure. Is it worth full price? Nah, but I bought it on discount price, and not regreting it.
So final thoughts. If you like slashers then Killer is Dead won't dissapoint you. But you should probably buy it when price dropes.

If you've played any open-world game released in the last couple of years, there's not too much about Watch Dogs that differentiates it from the others.  As far as Ubisoft open world games go, this was probably my least favorite game out of the bunch.  It's not bad, but rather unspectacular.  I remember hearing a lot of people around launch day saying this game was very shallow in comparison to what was advertised, and after finishing the campaign and DLC, I'm inclined to agree.
The story does a decent enough job to see you through to the end, though I found virtually no likeable characters out of the entire bunch.  So many of the central characters in this game feel like hollow, stereotypical "hackers" that some out-of-touch design committee put together because they assumed that's how they look, act, etc.  The game tries so hard to come off as cool, hip, and trendy to its audience, but doesn't really succeed in doing so.
I liked the gameplay, but again, there's really no USP that makes the game feel unique or special.  The hacking ability is fun to use on people in the game the first couple of times, and then loses most of its interest afterwards.  Perhaps the game's best feature is being able to take advantage of hacking cameras and using them to your advantage by scouting enemies in front of you, sabotaging/boobytrapping certain guards to assist with stealth, and doing a few hacking minigames to progress through the story.  Money is practically useless to obtain since you will never usually have a problem looting ammo, supplies, guns, etc. from enemies after you emerge from gunfights.
This game seems decently optimized and I never encountered any major framerate drops or glitches, although I did have one problem a few times where there was no sound at all when launching the game.  I have no idea what was causing this, but restarting the game or my computer usually did the trick.
Overall, if you're really interested in playing this, wait for a pretty heavy sale and don't expect anything too revolutionary.  There are much better open world games to play before needing to check out this one.

Its kind of odd that I am recommending this.
Watch Dogs 1 is another one of those games that showed everyone the kind of lies companies will tell the consumer just to make their product look better than it truly is.  Even though graphics don't make or break a game, I was still greatly dissapointed that the E3 presentation wasn't the true representation of (at least) the PC version.  2014 was one of the lesser years for gaming, and I'm certain Watch Dogs was on a lot of peoples'♥♥♥♥♥♥list.
That being said, I admit (to my greatest shame) that I actually enjoyed my time with this game.  I had already heard many reviews claiming the game to be mediocre at best, before actually playing it.  So I set my expectations to the lowest point possible....
STORY:
This game's story is not very compelling.  It tries to tell this gritty revenge narrative about a broken man, but it just isn't well done.  Aiden Pearce isn't a very interesting dude, so its very hard to sympathize with his motives and goals.  There's no real tension or actual stakes for the player to truly give a damn.  It isn't all bad though.  There are some parts I particularly enjoyed.  Even though Aiden is boring, some of his dialogue with the other members of the cast is quite entertaining.  Jordi Chin is a perfect example.  He's a fun character who throws Aiden♥♥♥♥♥♥ and is used properly for comedy relief.
VOICE ACTING:
I thought the voice acting in this game was pretty solid.  Even though I wasn't affected by some of the more "emotional" scenes, I could tell the actors were doing their best to protray the characters they were playing.  Jordi, T-Bone, Clara, Lucky Quinn, Iraq, and Damien all had convincing performances.  Even though I didn't get attached to Aiden, I thought Noam Jenkins did a great job with the gruffer tone Ubisoft was looking for.  Shame that the story's direction couldn't highlight this good voice acting.
GAMEPLAY:
Combat in this game is like any other third person cover shooter with SOME added layers of depth.  There are different ways the player can approach certain scenarios and its all thanks to the hacking elements.  If you successfully clear out a room of enemies with hacking and stealth, it can feel really rewarding.  I remember I once threw explosives onto a car, hacked it so it ran into a group of gangsters, made a blackout, and stealth killed the remaining enemies.  It was good fun.  The side activities were surpisingly entertaining.  Criminal Convoys were my personal favorite because I loved setting up ambushes and going guns-blazing in the middle of the street.  DRIVING IN THIS GAME IS VERY POOR, IT FEELS LIKE THE ROAD HAS SOAP ON IT OR SOME♥♥♥♥♥♥  ALSO SOME OF THE PHYSICS ARE TERRIBLE.
GRAPHICS/ART DESIGN:
As stated above, I was disspointed that the game didn't look like its E3 presentation.  The graphics are ok but they are certainly not the best.  Nothing truly impressed me and it was just meh.  I do appreciate the fact that Ubisoft tried to give an accurate depiction of Chicago.  It shows that there is a good amount of dedication in the level design/development.
SOUND DESIGN/OST:
The sound design in this game was good.  Not fantastic, but acceptable.  The soundtrack wasn't all that memorable but it did serve it's purpose and changed the mood appropriately.  The techno stealth music is a great example.  But the in-game radio...well, I wasn't a fan of it.  There were no songs I really enjoyed other than one or two.  I was able to give this a pass because I know its difficult implementing outside music into a game.  Legal trouble and what not.
BAD BLOOD/DLC:
This was an alright expansion.  I'm glad I got the complete edition for 12 bucks on sale cause I wouldn't do a stand-alone buy for this DLC.  It was cool to play as T-Bone, and I thought some of his new gadgets were fun.  However, the gameplay was practically the same and the story was again, not very compelling.  T-Bone only has a few animation differences than Aiden.  The only other notable DLC was the new digital trip, and I didn't think those were all that fun to begin with.
VERDICT:
It's a medicore game.  I guess the reason I am recommending it is because despite all the negatives, I enjoyed myself.  I had some fun and I don't regret playing the game.

This is a reimagining for the strider series where you play as a deadly sword wielding ninja. It does a good job at capturing the feel of the classic arcade game. It has responsive controls, maintains the unique wall climbing and offers a good mix of platforming and combat. While the arcade game had linear stages this uses the ever popular Metroid formula, with different themed areas, where progress is gated with weapon coded doors. However the game doesn’t focus on exploration. Your objective is signposted and you can follow a linear path with a minimum of backtracking if you do not want to collect hidden upgrades and secrets.
The presentation is faithful to the original with many remixed music tracks, sound effects and familiar enemy designs. Part of the greatness of the original was the art and world design and the nostalgia is a double edged sword here. This game simply doesn’t offer the same kind of surprises and global adventure. The areas of the game that aren’t direct copies of the original are rather drab with a few good set pieces such as boss battles thrown in. The city you explore is made of military and industrial districts which aren’t that thrilling.
The visuals can be very cluttered at times, especially later in the game, with lots of effects and bullets on screen. There are also too many upgrades for the run time. There are 4 types of sword, 3 active abilities, air dash and kunai. For a fast paced action platform game it can feel a little contrived to only switch weapon to activate switches or destroy shields.
The story lasts around 6 hours (more if you want to hunt down secrets) as well as offering unlockable challenge levels. Overall it’s solid, there are better 2D action or platform games out there, I would recommend it when it’s on sale.

My guess, you are reading reviews because you haven't played this game. You've either come here because of it's own merits, or you probably saw the more popularized and recent Planetary Ahnnilation and probably saw reviews talking about it there. So let me tell you why I would buy and play this game over PA, even ignoring price differences.
**Disclaimer** I don't pretend reviews can be unbiased. Giving it a rating in areas like graphics, sound, controls, story or even as a whole devalues what makes games (and all media) amazing; our own expierences.
1. In Supreme Commander, I love that you can zoom out and see the whole map on a single clean interface, and see all your units and enjoy playing the game as needed from that view. PA tries to offer that, but the 3 dimensional, 4-layer multi-planet battles make it abosultely impossible to achieve the same clean result. Don't be fooled in thinking that using Picture-in-picture provides the same result. It changes how the game feels, and just plain makes it more difficult to keep track of units and bases and you are constantly rotating your camera around mutiple orbs. I'm NOT saying OTHERS can't enjoy that expierence; but all it does is for me is add little-to-no immersion at the cost of LOTS of additional mental processing required to manage units and bases. A strategy game should be about making strategic choices, not scrolling around a ball because you're trying to remember with of the 6 planets you are currently on, which way was North (because now your facing SW), where your base was, where their base is relative to yours etc. etc.
2. Supreme Commander offers multiple unique feeling factions. While you can find many similar units between them, there are many faction specific units AND structures that can change how you might play, or what strategies you choose to use. PA offers no factions, which guarentees balance I suppose but really hinders what I like call the "spice" of the game. It just feels a little blah to only be killing robots that look EXACTLY like your robots, all the time, every game.
10 years ago I was working at EB Games (Canadian GameStop) when Supreme commander was released. And including the copy I bought, for the 2 years I was there I don't think we sold more than 3 copies, and I can't remember seeing a single piece of advertising for it the entire lifetime of that game. As of writing, I can see ~400 ACTIVE players on Steam alone.
By comparison, PA released 3 years ago, stormed the internet through kickstarter, and powered it's way on to the front page of Steam when released. And, at time of writing, has less active users.
I believe there is more to enjoy in Supreme Commander. PA can offer some cool stuff, smashing moons into planets is pretty neat. But even 10 years old I'd still rather load up SC. It just has that special spice I like.

This game will test your mettle in a way that will make old fans tingle with a sense of unforgiving nostalgia, and will make clear to newcomers just exactly what Pac-Man is all about.
Unexpected good PAC-MAN version.

I'll tell you now, if you're looking for the dear old Pac-Man, based on how strategically avoid being caught by ghosts while eating all the pills, avoid this game: you're going to be disappointed.
HOWEVER
If you're looking for a flashy, colorful and fast paced Pac-Man experience that will make your blood boil, take it now.
This game is pure competition. Get the best performance (highest score, best ghost combo, best time) and become the number 1 among players.
Many people say that this game is too easy.
Yes, you're absolutely right: lives are extremely easy to score, there's a slow motion that helps you to change direction at the very last moment, the AI of the ghosts is most of times pretty lacking, and there are bombs to save you in the most tight situation.
But remember: this game's objective is NOT survival, it's about getting the best score and surpass the other players.
Losing a life, abusing bombs or moving aimlessly means wasting time, and more time you waste less points you are going to score.
The challenge is not the game itself: the other players are the real challenge. Do you think you can do better than that person right above you? Prove it.

More or less same result) or just me because I'm not well accustomed to the very high speed this game can reach. Excluding this, it's okay most times.

The randomly generated level design isnt bad at all and the "binding of isaac"-like upgrades are extremely fun. The variety given by the various stackable upgrades gives it a good amount of replay value and kept me playing until I finally beat the final boss. The controls are pretty good but it could be abit tighter with the movement. One thing that I really like about the game is the ultra accurate hitboxes on enemies and objects. The enemies are alright, but AI is somewhat wonky and the enemy dificulty scales very oddly from level to level. Level one is fun and easy, two is somewhat harder, three tends to be easy, and four is ridiculously difficult. Personally I ended up having to just run pass enemies and get to the final boss both times I fought him. The bosses are unique and interesting, each one has a different playstyle that I found fun yet challenging. One complaint though is that the first boss is signifigantly harder than all the other bosses because it actually requires you to aim very well.
Hopefully in the future I'll come back and write a better review but I really do like it despite it's flaws.
Maybe wait and buy it during a 50% off sale, it's at least worth that much.

Game needs a new title, and I encourage the game Developers and Publisher to consider what I have written here.
I say that up front, but in fact this game is a hidden gem in the gaming world.  Many may be turned off by the game's name, which is obscure, and/or the female wearing a warrior bra as part of the title page of the Steam Store page that offers Thea for sale.  Publisher - you are losing tons of customers by advertising this game as if you're trying to attract a "dumb" crowd that cares about scantily clad women, when your game is exactly the opposite - this game has as much depth and breadth as the Civilization series or other complex strategy games.  While you don't get to control the individual character growth, you do see randomized level-up across all the characters that you control, to include children that grow into adults (or grow into something else magically), and you can obtain additional characters through events or randomly attracted to your town, that also end up leveling up along the way.  This "mass RPG" aspect is one of the winning points for me, that you have such a diverse crowd you can develop to try and move your civilization ahead.
So, what other names could/should this game have been called?
Well, howabout just "Thea" as a one-word game title, because the colon followed by "The Awakening" makes one wonder if this is a game add-on, or part 2 to a series, or such.  Can't stress this enough to both this game company and other would-be game developers and publishers - you need to simplify your game titles!  And - don't use women as objects to try and sell your product any more!  There are many moms and dads out there - bypassing this game for that reason alone, if they review a game for potential purchase by their kid (for those that actually play their real life role as a parent).
Ok, enough critique, as to the game itself, this game is more addicting and fun to play than the Sid Meier Civ series, to me personally.  That says something - I've put in far too much time in the Civ series in the past.  The mix of exploration, mass RPG of a player-controlled crowd, card-based tactical play, randomized events, and progressive accomplishments of varying starting gods makes for an engrossing experience.  You can end up trying out numerous combinations in the crafting menus also, and the repeat play potential is huge here - some gameplay may only last a short time, whereas you may go for days on another attempt, but all the while you can opt to end your game at that point, which contributes points to your current "god" in play to progress to a better starting point or other stats boost for the next startup - and that's across up to 8+ gods in 5 tiers each.
I bought this at 50% off full price for just under $10, a steal at that price considering the amount of game-life and time available here.

After finishing the game once and instantly starting a new game, I figured I might as well give this game a review.
So, what is Thea: The Awakening? In short, it's a turn-based strategy game with a light card game mini-game mechanic  to spice things up. The game itself is set in very flavorful fantasy world full with all kinds of mythological creatures. Instead of the typical greek or Christian mythos though, the game seems to mostly use what I figure are slavic / russian mythos. For example, the game uses the term "Demon" to describe many creatures you meet, but they really have nothing to do with the Christian understanding of the term, but rather the term encompasses anything from nature spirits to vampires, hostile to neutral and beneficial things, including servants of the deities.
The background plot in nutshell is that some event severed the bond of mankind with your pantheon and it was only recently, with sun re-merging that you have re-established some small connection with them. The player takes the role of this awakening god, seeing the world through their follower's eyes and subtly guiding the survivors in efforts to uncover what has happened and possibly fixing the world.
Gameplay-wise, the game works a bit like Civilization games on the surface. You have a randomly generated world map, a village and a handful of survivors. Your villagers need food and fuel to survive. These needs can be satisfied by assigning your villagers to work whatever resource nodes happened to spawn within your village's gathering range. For any resources outside your range, you need to send expedition's to gather. This is actually where nearly half of the game happens: controlling your expeditions around the map, searching for points of interest, questing and clashing with hostile forces.
The other half of the game is resolving these Challenges, as the game calls them. Rather than rolling a dice, you play a card mini-game. And this is where the juicy bit of the entire game lies: every time you fight a challenge, your deck of cards is formed from the members of the expedition. Having a Fight challenge? The weapons, armor, trinkets with Fight-related bonuses? All that directly translates to the power of the card that represents that particular member.
To make matters more interesting, Fight is not the only challenge type that exists. Rather, you have a variety of challenge types, from Physical challenges to Intellectual and Social ones. Usually when you're initiating an event you get to choose which type of challenge best suits your party.
The mechanics of the card mini-game are always the same regardless of the Challenge type you choose, but the numbers and abilities on your cards depend on the type of challenge. While in basic Fight challenge your attack damage would depend on your character's innate Damage-skill, weapon and item bonuses, you would instead use Intelligence-skill in Intelligence challenge. In Breaking a Curse challenge that Intelligence would instead grant you Counter Offence-support ability instead. As such the members of your party determine what the best approach to each situation would be. The game encourages you to build diverse groups, to better handle variety of Challenges.
Another reason to spread out your skills from just pure beatdown is that Fight challenges are exception to the norm in that all damage your cards take ALWAYS translate into damage and potential character deaths after the Challenge. The game VERY rarely deals instant removal of party members via challenges, but any character whose card was defeated or heavily damaged in a Fight has their health reduced to critical levels. Each turn there is a chance for every critically wounded character to die, rolled separately. The chances of this happening can be lowered by having a character with Medic-skill in the party, but it is still no guarantee of their survival. While this means that even losing a Fight challenge doesn't automatically mean you lose everyone in the expedition, their chances of survival are that much lower - well, not taking save-scumming into account.
Which actually leads to one very odd design decision that the developers did with this game: you can only ever have a single regular save + auto-save. Outside force-quitting you only have the option of Save and Quit to close the game. When you finish one of the main objectives of the game, you get to choose between finishing the game or continuing. If you choose to finish the game, that's it - the save file is finished and you can't continue anymore, as the game warns you.
The other somewhat questionable design decision is that while the game features 8 gods to play as with their varying bonuses, the game randomly(?) unlocks 2 of them for you at start. Each time you play through the game you unlock more. Considering my first playthrough took me 16 hours or so, this means you need to be somewhat dedicated player to even have the chance to see what all the gods have to offer. Oh, and in those 16 hours I apparently only unlocked 3/5 bonuses for the first god I first finished the game as.
To sum things up:
Pros:
- Rich fantasy world based upon less commonly used real-world mythos
- Variety of quests and random events to discover and react to, from funny to absurd.
- The skill sets of your characters in your expeditions actually matter. Bringing a bunch of pea-brained warriors to Intelligence challenge is not a good idea, for one.
- At the same time a very simple and very complex card mini-game instead of your typical random dice roll system.
- Narrator who narrates ALL events as they happen, including lines of the NPC characters. Great for atmosphere of the game.
The in-between:
- I'd imagine the card game can be a total hit-or-miss. It makes or breaks your experience with the game, since it's constant part of playing the game.
- Only a single save-slot. A bit roguelike-ish decision without going all the way thanks to being able to save/load.
- Losing Challenges is rarely a big deal. At worst your team gets critically wounded and you have the chance to lose people.
Cons:
- A single playthrough of the game is a bit long-ish for requiring you to unlock the gods to play them.
- Controls on the map can be unresponsive. Often you need to hold and drag mouse cursor on an enemy next to you on a map since simply right-clicking them doesn't always seem to work.
- It is hard to figure out just how well-suited your team is to a challenge. While the game does show you what skills give what benefit before starting the challenge, you don't get to preview your deck for a given challenge. With the amount of skills out there, it becomes really cumbersome to figure out your strengths and weaknesses in any exact manner.
- After a while you start getting repetitive random events. The problem is compounded by the fact that each entity (village and each expedition) gets a random event rolled separately for them, so you will end up seeing a lot of the same common events.
- The auto-playing of Challenges seems very random at times: it has both lost easy challenges and won challenges I felt were nigh-impossible to win manually.
- Related to the above, the challenge rating of encounters is occasionally off by a mile. I've faced 2-skull challenges that were harder than 4-skull challenges. This is most evident when rating non-Fight challenges: a big scary orc army with 4 skull-rating can destroy your team in a Fight challenge. The same orc army's Social challenge may also be rated at 4 skulls but they barely scratch your team that isn't even built for social challenges in the first place.
Overall verdict: Heartily recommended, with the cave-at that if you DO NOT like card games I would recommend you to avoid this title. While I've listed more cons than pros, the cons are mostly annoyances rather than real problems. The game could definitely use some polish and quality-of-life improvements, but it is very enjoyable package as-is.

I struggle to decide what I really think of Far Cry2. On the one hand, it's a really good pick-up-&-play with a great weapon load-out, decent application of the sandbox model & an interesting premise. On the other hand, the AI seems to have xray vision, you can't really pick a side & the game feels a bit incomplete on some of the details.
The premise is simple; you are a mercenary sent to a war-torn African country with the simple task of killing an arms-dealer who is selling to both sides & prolonging the conflict. At the time you arrive, there is a shakey peace, but you contract Malaria & fall ill in the local town. You are found by the arms-dealer, named the Jackal, who decides not to execute you, presumably expecting you die a rather miserable & painful death on your own.
You awake some time later with the ceasefire broken & that's where you start; escape the town & get put to work by a member of one of the two factions. The problem is, the game starts to break down even here as you can't choose one side or the other, or neither. On top of that, everyone shoots at you, no matter who you're working for. The excuse is none of the soldiers know which side you're on so shoot first & just forget to ask questions. In reality, the programming for random friend/foe AI was too hard, too expensive or would've taken too long. Or all three. Either way, it can really annoy. The other thing that really annoys me is the fact the AI seems to be able to perfectly spot you in dense jungle, even if you are stood still & behind bushes & trees. The fact you can't see them thanks to the same foliage makes it even more of a fight weighed against you on purpose. These flaws feel like the design team ran out of time to put these mecahnics in, but for me, the making or breaking of a game is the details that really pull you in, & Far Cry 2 feels like is misses that trick.
The game does have some upsides; the weapon load-out is well thought out both in what you can carry & what guns you have access too. There are plenty of weapons for stealth & a night attack where no-one hears or sees you until you kill them is very satisfying. The 1-man army load out will also work great if you're careful with timing & smashing a heavily defended check point without taking any hits is good fun. Vehicles handle ok & there is enough variety in the missions, even if it does usually end up requiring you to simply shoot everything. There is a 'buddy' system, where you can befriend other mercenary characters who assist you or give you missions, even rescue you when you're health runs out. The graphics make it a very pretty game & some of the effects are excellent. My favotire thing are the tape reordings of interviews with the Jackal, some are rather disturbing in how cold the guy is, the little details that help you invest in the world.
The story is basically two parts. In the first, you do missions for the two sides in no particular order, plus a 'resistance' group smuggling civilians out, you're then asked to kill one of the leaders. In the second part, the exact same thing happens again. Needlessly. It does make the world massive, with a huge area to explore, but it feels a little thrown together.
Far Cry 2 is so nearly there; allow you to work for one side or another, allow that to effect how you're seen by each side, make some checkpoints on the roads friend, some foe, some abandonned & make one half of the story cover the whole game & it's potentially a fabulous game.
It sounds like I don't like Far Cry 2, but in actual fact, I do. As a pick-up-&-play, for no more than a few hours, it's great. There's little thought required other than how you want to go about your mission & what weapon load-out to go with, it's a lovely game to spend time in visually, the number of guns you can pick from is wonderfully varied & there are loads of missions to keep you busy. But it's no more than that. If you can accept Far Cry 2 for those flaws, then you'll probably enjoy it as a kind of 'library title'; a game to play between the games you get heavily invested into. Because I am able to see & accept Far Cry 2 for what it is, I feel I CAN recommend it, but with the previso to not expect any real depth from it.

So, I don't feel like suggesting this game (if not with a discount). I see that the dev tried to simulate a realistically hostile environment but I believe that the result is way too "serious". A game is supposed to be fun at the very end and to me, FC2, wasn't for a big chunk of it. I keep playing hoping for something new to happen, something interesting, unexpected (no, I wasn't hoping for monsters, mutants or aliens) but no, life is tough in FC2: you are in Africa, sick with Malaria and surrounded by people who wants to kill each other; not a pretty picture but sadly, a realistic one.

I have never had the need to write a bad review for any other game, no matter how bad I thought it was.
But that isn't what you want to know. Why is this game so incredibly bad that I actually took the time to give a bad review? It has nothing to do with gameplay, or what this game is all about. The thing is I have no idea what this game is all about because the text is always blurry no matter what resolution I set it to. There is no way to zoom on any cards or text...but I digress. This is getting ahead of myself. First things first.
First start up:
I use dual monitors. It starts on the wrong monitor. I change the settings to use monitor 2 (my main is monitor 1, which it is actually set to...but yea anyway). While this is happening, apparently things regarding choosing main characters and such are happening without me being able to see what is going on or choose anything because currently in process of setup. The game tells me to restart. I restart. Bear in mind that the text options in the settings menu are pretty blurry to begin with.
Second start:
It starts on the same monitor. Check the settings. It is set to monitor 2 (wrong monitor) so I think OK, if I change it to monitor 1 now (correct monitor) maybe it will work. Change to monitor 1. Have to restart. Restart.
Third restart:
Lo and behold it is still on the wrong monitor. Change it to windowed mode and drag it over to the correct monitor. Even with the resolution being correct it is too big for my screen and the settings and some other stuff I haven't even looked at are out of the screen. I can't even maximise...who knows why but you can't click it. In the mean time the game has jumped into the tutorial, so I've missed a bit of the game already. They are losing my business fast.
Many restarts later:
I've tried many things, and combinations of things to get it working on the correct monitor to no avail. Changing resolution, windowed/full etc. I check online. It is a known problem and I have to use Windows+shift+arrow left/right to switch between monitors. Great. Except the problem has been know for over half a year and nothing done to fix it. And guess what? Using that method glitches your mouse so that you have to click a space away from the actual button to trigger. Check online. Also a known problem and also been more than half a year and nothing done to fix it.
I finally (by sheer luck), figure out a way to have it fullscreen on my main monitor and with no mouse issues. Cool. Onward to the game which has started the tutorial and I have apparently chosen a knight or something as my char. Not that I did any of the choosing although I saw an option to do so while I was trying to get the screen issues resolved.
I face a sprite, elf or wizard or something. across what looks like a board of some kind...is she my buddy? One of my chars? And a card being explained to me in the form of:
"This is a card (click to continue). This is damage (click to continue). This is health (click to continue). Now place that on the board along with 3 other cards, which aren't explained to you and now you have to battle...(click to continue)"
So my knight (at this point I realise the knight is supposed to be me and the wizard is my "rival") goes along and does stuff which isn't explained and I magically win the battle. I say magically because I have no idea what just happened.
Anyway. I win the battle and now I get told there are 4 more of these unexplained magical battles I need to do before the map is won. Nothing gets said about what are my cards, my deck, or how to utilise them. Which I find strange because isn't this a CCG?
Round two and now my "rival" is in on the game. I have to get her health down to 0 but you aren't told how to do that although i grant at the end of the 5 battles you may have some idea. So I putter along with nary any information and win the last battle. Yay. Now I can do what I want.
I have a look at deck building. The text is so small and blurry, even on my 42in screen at any resolution, so that everthing is practically illegible. There is no way to zoom in on any of the cards. Which may be a blessing so that I don't have to look at the atrocious "art" but at the same time I can't read anything on the cards at all.
And this, ladies and gentlemen, is where I decide this game has absolutly no place in my future except to warn off others.
I'm not sure how long this game has been out, frankly I don't care, but there is no excuse to release such a poorly put together piece of crap that I had to spend an hour to get it working, just to find out I can't even read any of the cards.
Well done devs. You've succeeded in taking a huge dump on the CCG community. I recommend Card Hunter instead. That game will not dissapoint on any level for a f2p CCG. Just some proof for you guys: Even people who "Highly" recommend this have so few hours in it that it should be enough to indicate how bad this game really is.

I am biased towards most free to play games.  Mainly because most are scams to trick customers into paying more money for less content.  This game is no exception.  It's clearly designed to be free to grind and pay for a huge advantage.  The ratio of grind advantage verses pay advantage is skewed so heavily for the fat whales that I don't think any normal person could keep up with a paying customer.  Hence, why I think the "free to play" business model is a scam.

First of all, don't be put off by the fact this game has "Runescape" in the title. It's quite an innovative little game.
Each game takes place on a set of boards with four nodes each that each player has a hero walk over. As the player, your job is to populate these nodes with creatures for your hero to battle or items for your hero to buy. As you go you accumulate power for your hero or try to debilitate the enemy hero, leading up to a final battle between the two heroes that determines the winner. It's a great idea!
Aside from increasing the power of your own hero you can deal direct damage to the enemy or perhaps sneakily buff the creatures they put on the board to do more damage to them. There's a lot of different ways to approach winning the game.
The game has an Arena style buy-in draft mode for the competitive players amongst you, though the entry price is a little high for my liking.
Overall, it's worth at least a look because it's free and it's something new. These games do demand a long term commitment from you, and I wasn't prepared to make that, but I still enjoyed the couple hours I spent exploring the mechanics.

Strider was quite the popular arcade game from 1989 (with a sequel in 1999) that had you in the role of the titular ninja Strider. You moved fast, could double jump and cling to nearly every surface available. The game was punishingly difficult but rewarded memorization and fast reflexes.
This Strider isn't a remake or remaster of those games, but a sort of reboot. Since our PC and consoles no longer have a quarter slot, the game is designed to stretch out your twitch skills more than your wallet. Still taking the role of Strider (well,
Strider now named Hiryu), now you'll start pathetically weak and require various upgrades to progress.
Set in a future time, in a pseudo-soviet communist dictatorship, you're trying to topple the shadowy leader behind the government: Grandmaster Meio. To do so, you'll need to infiltrate their headquarters. But with their advanced technology, well equipped troopers and numerous powerful allies, you need to find help in the form of allies and power-ups. Other than that, the story is pretty straightforward.
However, given how uncomplicated the story is, the game drags it on and on. The pacing of the game feels like it should have been a much much shorter game. When I felt I was at a boss that had to be near the end, I looked it up and that boss was the 1/3rd mark. Not that lots of content is bad, but the story telling doesn't match the pace of the game.
Before discussing the tech behind the game, we have to set our expectations. The game was 15 dollars on launch. The graphics are well done, but do not expect an AAA experience. Models are well done across the board but the textures are a little on the blurry side during cut scenes.
The music in the game is totally awesome and makes me wish they sold it separately. The audio is clean and informative, with hits being clearly registered. Enemy sound is less telling, but you're so much faster than your foes it isn't really a component of gameplay.
Sadly, the music is almost inaudible during the game. I only noticed how awesome it was once I paused the game.
Each boss you come across generally protects a small golden console that gives you a new power. Plasma blades that cut through shields, dashing mechanics or flaming spirit dragons. Foes will start relatively easy to defeat, but over time each mini-boss you defeat becomes a normal troop that you'll fight. This will put your upgrades to good use, as without them those fights are what qualifies them as mini-bosses.
So you'll start being able to jump, slide and attack. Over time your attacks will get better, cutting through shields or gaining new abilities like using shuriken. Your jump becomes a double jump and the spirit animals that help you in combat will give you new ways to go through old maps. It's not quite a metroidvania but it has many elements that remind me of that genre.
Something I really enjoyed was the bosses. They all feel very very unfair at first, requiring multiple deaths to learn their patterns but each time you die, you end up a little further than before. That sense of 100% skill based progression was very very satisfying.
One sore point for me was the foes getting better as you do. They'll replace weaker foes with more difficult ones you come across and while that keeps the game challenging, I never felt a sense of progression against the common enemies, only bosses.
At 15 dollars, for around 10-20 hours of gameplay, yes. Economically, the game is worth it. However if you're not a fan of difficult games then you might want to avoid it. The game isn't famously difficult but it doesn't hold your hand. If you die, it's because you messed up and you'll be starting from the last checkpoint you visited. Those are far apart, so you could be backtracking far and often. If that all sounds like an incentive to get better at the game and not die, then it's probably right up your alley.

POLYGOD is a rogue like First Person Shooter which looks to brighten up the world by flinging a flurry of small bob shaped objects. Does it succeed in its ambition, or falls flat on its various made up playgrounds, let’s find out:

POLYGOD reminds me of Lovely Planet and Rogue Legacy. It is a rogue like where each death sends you back to the start of the journey. Where Lovely Planet was a game where you had to remember each enemy placements and all the paths, POLYGOD mixes it up with a hint of randomness. You start out in a garden like place with a gun and some entities around you. From there, you travel to the world of Gaia where you kill various enemies and bosses to progress to the next world and then repeat till you beat the game. Now, why I mentioned that it was similar to rogue legacy was the fact that its randomisation of worlds feel exactly like how castle rooms were randomised in Rogue Legacy.
While initially it feels that there is a lot of variation every time around, slowly it starts to grow on you. You sense the levels were exactly same before with a random enemy placed or removed. It is not helped by the fact that it is quite linear in nature. Again, like Rogue Legacy, at times you might be given two paths at a point, but both of them will result in going at the same place. There is a false sense of direction and at times it feels as if some parts were far too empty than they should’ve been.
POLYGOD features an upgrade system which is fairly basic. You get souls from enemies every time you kill them, which in turn can give you favours at altars present at various paths. These upgrades enhance you in a way that there is no best choice. One upgrade might give you a very easy breeze through the normal enemies but will make it insanely more difficult against bosses and some will make it go vice versa. The shooting is pretty solid with the hitboxes being pretty consistent. There is an average variety of enemies which may pop out of anywhere and some seem to have a very good way of flanking you. They spin around, move towards you or randomly pop out to surprise you.
They do a good job of making the game difficult. POLYGOD has a brutal difficulty and given that there are no benefits whatsoever of making progress and getting killed, aside from getting more skilled, it makes it a lot difficult for newcomers to the genre. As POLYGOD is in early access, it is very much prone to bugs and has a serious lack of content.
There is a lack in variety of enemies as you pretty much get used to each one before long, same goes for bosses. Aside from a new world, there is nothing that pushes you to actually explore. Even the upgrade system feels a bit lacking with an very apparent lack in variety is shown right away. But what makes you keep coming back in a rogue like for one more session is its basic gameplay loop.
And POLYGOD does it really well, where you don’t leave the game because you know you can do better the next time around (even when you get killed by the first swarm of enemies.) It does have that feel that you can just play it for a few rounds and then leave, casually which makes it quite replyabale.
Aesthetically POLYGOD seems very similar to Lovely planet. With colours popping out from every corner, though POLYGOD sports shinier and brighter visuals than the latter. While enemies are difficult to distinguish sometimes, it has a very soothing feel to it, which makes it lighter on the eyes.
POLYGOD’s worlds are the ones that attract the most. With a pretty colour background which makes it liven up to its otherworldly enemies. Enemy designs are fairly basic and don’t surprise at all. Overall, it is light on eyes and features a colourful world.
POLYGOD’s soundtrack is a mixed bag. While its peaceful music is really good to hear and goes with the art design, the sound loop that pops up when an enemy is nearby is very annoying. You kill enemies, just to make the sounds go away and it could have been far better than it is right now.
Everything else again is average. From the gun sounds to the sound of jumping. Everything is done neatly and well. If that annoying aggressive music was excluded, it would’ve been a very good music choice for the game.
Polygon is still in early access, which gives it a pass for having a lack of content but its gameplay loop is interesting enough to make you keep coming back. It does have its fair share of bugs and other issues, but it has a lot of potential. I will keep coming back to this game for the time being.

If you're a fan of Far Cry 3 and are interested in trying this one out, be warned that it might not be what you're expecting.  It's more closely related to games like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. than any of the other games in the Far Cry series.  It's brutally unforgiving and slanted more towards realism and immersion than action-adventure.  The world is large, but exploration isn't necessarily a large part of the gameplay, as the only real purpose for doing so is finding diamonds, hidden tapes, and golden guns -- none of which are particularly essential to the experience of the game.
At its core, the game is about tense gunfights and missions, and the different tactics you can use to ensure your survival.  The game has a robust array of different systems that organically create compelling moments -- last second escapes into the jungle while bullets whiz past you, guns jamming at the least opportune moment and forcing you to flee for the nearest sign of cover, buddies arriving just in the nic of time to save you from an otherwise unwinnable firefight, enemies whom you thought you had killed crawling to their knees and shooting you in the back for revenge -- the list goes on and on, and I'm still discovering new possibilities after hours of play.  Playing with the music turned off increases the tension in the game IMMENSELY, as you never know if there's an enemy around you just waiting for the perfect time to blast you apart and ruin the last ten minutes of progress you'd made.  You'll find yourself checking every corner, listening intently for footsteps or enemy chatter, and cursing yourself when you inevitably miss that lone gunman who finishes you off as soon as you step into the open.
The narrative of the game is also smart and very sensible and aware of the topics which it brings up, which is a helluva lot more than you can say for most modern military shooters.  Don't expect to leave this one feeling like the hero.
tldr;
It's absolutely brilliant, especially if you're into S.T.A.L.K.E.R.-like games and emergent gameplay.
