This game is unique to the genre because it has an Evolutionary Human Emulator (EHE). This is the name given to the game's AI. Each country in the game has it's own unique AI system, which evolves the more you play the game. Each country has certain priorities and takes actions according to the perceived outcome of its actions. As you play, the EHE "learns" new behaviors, drawing connections between actions it didn't know existed and updates previous connections. This EHE makes for very thrilling and unique situations the more you play.
There is a dedicated community that has been keeping the game up to date for the last 12 years. Taking into account the community mods available: the game is set in 2015, practically every nation in the world has updated GDP, population, military values, treaties and diplomatic relations. Also with mods, you can now fight Hezbollah, Taliban, Daesh/Islamic State, etc. There's also mods that set the world in WW2 or the Cold War, all these are also turned into multiplayer sessions.
Play in multiplayer matches with your friends and conquer the world together. Or play peacefully and manipulate the world through proxy-wars, espionage, subterfuge, black market funding, economic exploitation and diplomatic cunning.
Play in multiplayer matches with 20+ other world leaders and roleplay an international community as you wage cold wars, forge alliances and strive to develop into superpowers. In multiplayer matches, it is common for the host to set "rules" for the lobby to abide by, which keeps order and stability to the game world. When you have a good server with a good host, this game rivals that of any strategy multiplayer experience. If you're into geography, history, politics or current events, you'll love this game.
Play in singleplayer sandbox mode: design your own military units, transform the economy of Malawi to have the largest share of fruits and vegetables in the world, become a monarchy and ally with the royal families of the Arab world, start a pan-African/Middle-East Alliance to counter the global North, create covert ops cells to steal military secrets from China, research nuclear weapons, deploy and launch your ballistic missile subs off the coast of India, declare war and conquer your neighbors, then trade conquered territory to your allies, give money to the poorest nations of the world and watch them develop into regional powers, build attack helicopters and put them up for sale, force Israel to annex the West Bank and then watch WW3 unfold.
In terms of gameplay, you can set your own game speed. The pace really depends on you. The game technically never ends. So you can choose to get to year 2100 in two hours, or you can play for hours and only get to year 2030.
The learning curve is not as hard as you might think. It's way easier to learn than Europa Universalis or Dominions, if you ask me. It's not nearly as buggy as it is made out to be. Judging by its low-scores on IGN and Gamespot, you'd think this game would be unplayable; it's a complete exaggeration. The game is very much alive through its Steam and Gog communities. It also has fantastic modular support that allows many new features, such as changing your country's name in-game.
This game is actually one of the most powerful pieces of educational software available. If you're an educator, I highly recommend this game to you. Supposedly, this game has been used by governmental agencies worldwide. If you're a parent, buy this game for your children. I know of countless people who grew up with Civilization I & II or approached the game later in life and learned so much about history from it. This game has a very similar effect on people. Don't know the population of Bangladesh? Not for long. When you play this game, you'll learn quickly where all of the most populous countries are, who produces all of the world's tobacco, as well as the difference between Bahrain and Brunei. It's worth more than its price on Steam for just the reference/educational value alone. It's like a digital encyclopedia.
The depth of this game is a bit difficult to explain:
There's 193 default countries,
each with up to ~30 territories/provinces,
each territory/province has a production value for 24 different resources,
each territory/province has a population that is divided into under 15, 15-65 and 65+,
each of these population categories contributes to the territories consumption of resources,
each of the resources is listed in the world market and traded with all of the other territories from all of the other countries in the world,
each of the resources have a tax rate that is adjusted by the player,
each of the countries have a dynamic economic ranking that id based upon them meeting their production/consumption ratio, political stability, human development level, etc. that determines their priority in the world trading list,
each territory/province also has its own infrastructure and telecommunications level that is influencable by the player, each country in the world has it's own budget sliders for ~12 different spending options (health care, military research, education, tourism, etc.)
each country has its own expenses based on debt, political corruption, imports, budget sliders, etc.
each country has its own inflation rating, interest level, GDP/per capita, personal income tax
....that's just economic
When it comes to politics:
Each of the 193 countries has its own approval, stability and corruption rating
Internal laws (illegal/legal freedom of speech, child labour, polygamy, abortion, etc.)
Government type (democracy, communist, theocracy, dictatorship, monarchy, etc.)
Capitol city (can be relocated)
Languages
Religions
Immigration and Emigration
Political parties
Treaties which are divided into ~15 types
Diplomatic relations with every other nation in the game (from -99 =biggest enemy, 99=best ally)
These diplomatic relations are influenced by the similarity between their religions, languages, government type and treaties.
These diplomatic relations determine everything from who the AI chooses to trade with, goes to war with, builds military units from, etc.
The military side of things are equally compelling...
~12 unit designs (infantry, bombers, tanks, fighter jets, artillery, etc.)
~12 stats for each unit (speed, stealth, missile damage, gun precision, armor, etc.)
~10 levels of military technology (i.e. stealth 1, stealth 2, stealth 3, stealth 4, etc.)
Each country has an infrastructure level that determines how many units it can build concurrently (infrastructure is determined on a territory/province basis and influencable by player decisions)
Each country is automatically ranked for its worldwide competitive compared to every other country in the world
Each type of unit can be named by the player
Each unit can be sold to the world market
Each unit can be trained up to three times
Each unit can be build domestically or outsourced (built by an ally)
Each unit can be merged into army stacks and moved anywhere on earth that you have military access to (regions you control or that of military allies)
Each army stack can be sent into a battle
I disagree that this game has a bad community, as other reviewers have said. I also disagree that the political, military and economic spheres lack depth.

1 – GENERAL
Grav it's still an early access survival, multiplayer game. In this game you can explore a multitude of procedural generated planets with similarish aliens and dungeons. You can craft a multitude of stuff like weapons, bases, vehicles, whatever...
The visuals are impressive. For me the best thing of this game. Top notch.
Ambience sounds are interesting, with relaxing soundtrack. It all seems to come together to make a great game. But then we start playing.
2 – GAMEPLAY
I have to start by saying that all servers are dead, and in about 4h of gameplay I've failed to met any other player. I've seen some bases, but no player at all.
Well, are you asking if I just play 4h of this game? And my answer will be yes. Despite the visuals, the game failed to deliver, at least to me. I had 4h of boredom where I've forced myself to keep going, expecting that with leveling up the game could feel better, but in fact the general experience remained the same. We grind, or harvest if you prefer, we kill aliens, we built and we dance around the campfire. Yes, we dance, you have heard right.
You can say that I have to wait longer to see the magic, but that's not right. How much longer? I admit that I can spend a couple of hours trying to get into a game, but then we have to have something that makes us come back, and Grav doesn't have nothing of it.
Sometimes people are talking in the chat, but the community seems quite small so, even being polite, they simply ignore your questions and keep talking with their friends.
3 – CONCLUSION
Survival is a saturated game genre. This may appeal to a certain type of player, but to me it has no charm or interest. It's just boring. It's easy to find this game in a sale, but even so, I think you can try other games.

WARNING: This game is NOT for casual players. You WILL die and become frustrated often. Proceed with caution.
Firstly, the developer himself was kind enough to provide keys to anyone who had specific achievements on a game that heavily inspired him, and also happens to be one of my favourite videogame franchises, The Binding of Isaac. Thank you very much!
As for the game itself? Keep in mind that the game is still in Early Access, and that everything I'm about to state is all from personal opinion, so don't get your grains of salt in a twist. Also, I'm terrible at FPSs.
PROS:
+Very clean and simplistic visual display
+Perma-death and bullet-hell mechanics make this a very difficult game to play at times, excellent for challenge lovers
+Appears to have a morality system regarding who or what you shoot (I think)
+Randomly generated maps, no two levels are ever the same
+Enemy and upgrade placement is also randomly generated
+The roguelike elements stated above grant this game a near infinite level of replayability
CONS:
-Soundtrack seems a bit repetitive and annoying
-Character movement is a bit too quick (I later discovered that there's an upgrade that decreases speed, whch is a good thing for me)
-Mouse sensitivity is very high and currently there's no way to change it
-Walking and jumping about, I discovered that you can pretty much skip an entire level by just walking on top of the boundary walls, and you can also fall into oblivion while doing this, I'm not certain if this is intentional or not (although it does make for a very interesting challenge, trying to beat a boss without collecting any upgrades)
There appears to also be some plot, but I'm not exactly gifted in story interpreting, so I can't really judge whether it's a good plot or not.
Final thoughts? This game has a LOT of promise, and I'm honored and glad I got to be one of the first to mess about with it (and for free, by that matter, thanks a bunch!). I'm looking forward to seeing more features being added. Until then, I'm going to keep on playing it, I'm addicted to it already!
P.S.: Screw those "floating mine" looking enemies.

3) "Prophecy" cards, one of the new things I haven't seen in other card games. basically for every 5 health you lose(starts is 30) you get to draw a card, if you draw a prophecy card you can play it for free....it's a nice littel catch up mechanic that can sometimes prevent your opponent from steam-rolling you.
4) lane mechanics(singleplayer...due to technical difficulties I never got around to play vs. so don't know how it works there) the game board is split into two lanes creatures can only attack each other in those lane....in some cases lanes have special rules....fx. hidden for the first round they're in play.
5) upgradeable basic cards. when you you level up your account, some of your basic cards gets upgraded and at times you can even chose an upgrade path...it's a nice touch it does mean though that match making can be a problem if you get matched with a higher level opponent, since he can have upgraded versions of your base cards. but at least for the singleplayer prtion it gives a nice sense of progression.
cons:
1) boring presentation.
2) boring card mechnics...basically not much that haven't been done before.(outside of the pophecy mechanic)
3) Technical problems. the game constantly crashes for no apparent reason...considering it's a basic card game having the game constantly crash is simply unforgiveable and it's the primary reason I won't recommend this game and the reason I'm uninstalling it.

Part Card Game, part text adventure, part resource/loot management, part strategy game.
Card Game Combat:
The card combat is a little confusing and I've engaged in a few fights where I had zero chance of winning. But it never felt frustrating or unfair. Once you learn the game mechanics you can make sure to avoid fights you can't win.
Text Adventure:
Strong story elements. The random encounters are fun and creative. The story is intriguing enough to push you to play for the objectives, yet not demanding enough if you just want to run around and explore. I never minded reading the story but they give you the option to skip the sections involving a lot of text.
Resource Management:
You'll usually never be in danger of starving or running out of fuel for fires, but the really fun part is managing your loot. Do you give the two handed spear with piercing to your warrior or craftsman. Does this character need to be a tank or damage dealer? Do I need to spec this person for sneak attacks or tactics? After a certain point you will have too much equipment and the game would benefit from a rarity system (so you can easily see what to trash) but I really enjoyed getting a new character and then trying to figure out the how to outfit them
Strategy:
It was fun exploring and making expeditions. Encounters were random and very rewarding when you found you had the proper team members present to provide hidden text options. Diversity is key and I enjoyed trying to stack my expedition so that it was ready for anything it encountered
Conclusion:
Absolute steal if it is on sale but totally worth it at full price. Play throughs can be short or long, depends on how motivated you are to complete the story objectives. I beat my first play through in under 20 hours but will definitely be going back for more. Its a very rewarding game. Overcoming a certain text/card challenge or bringing in a big haul with an expedition is very satisfying
An interesting and original mix of a game that takes inspiration from a dozen sources and yet somehow manages to make it click. Definitely worth your time.

Far Cry 2’s story isn’t great. you are sent into an African country in order to assassinate an arms dealer who is supplying both sides of a civil war. Over the course of the game you work for each side trying to get ever closer to your target blah blah blah basic stuff.
If it sounds like I’m irritated, that’s because I am. This is due to Far Cry 2 having the gaming equivalent of the Plagues of Egypt. Respawning guard checkpoints, guns with no durability, constantly being followed around by jeeps with gun turrets and an actual plague itself in the form of your character having malaria.
Each of these require careful management to keep you on top. It’s frustrating, but damn is it good. If you can get the hang of keeping your guns in order, sneaking through guard checkpoints and topping yourself up on malaria pills then what remains is a great single player experience.

Personally, I found Far Cry 2 to be a bit of a mixed bag. I enjoyed the story; it felt pretty "Heart of Darkness" towards a certain point of the game, and it felt cool roaming the desert areas in a buggy.
On the other hand, there were a lot of bits I didn't enjoy. You constantly have to drive around from place to place because the fast travel system(Bus depots) were few and far between each other, and moving from one area to another ends up playing musical jeeps because there will almost always be an enemy jeep on your keister. Also, the gunplay felt very stiff, with the pistols being the worst guns in the game, you were better off spraying hoping you hit your target.
With the missions, you have the option of either playing it hard and fast, or a tad longer but slightly easier, with an enemy encounter occuring where your Buddy with almost always take a bullet.
I guess I can only recommend this if you are a VERY VERY patient gamer, but if not, I'd go with Far Cry 3 for a more overall better experience or Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon for raw action Fun.

You might pass Dolphin Up over for it being on mobile devices and that’s fine. I completely understand. For those of you who didn’t stop reading instantly Dolphin Up is a simple game about doing tricks as a dolphin. A simple game, a very simple game. The more tricks you do, the higher you go, the larger your score.
The fun and skill comes in when you try and land your tricks. Landing takes a little finesse, you want to enter the water at the correct angle. This allows you to keep building your trick combo. The bigger combo, the faster you go, the harder it is to make the landing and pull out of it to keep the trick going. It also gets interesting as your porpoise flies into space. Yeah the game doesn’t take itself too serious.
And you do want to land the tricks and build that combo, it’s a score attack game. You’ll be competing to get on global, local, and friend leaderboards all tied into steam. It seems that the leaderboards are for the whole game and not per level. Each level is a little different so I’m not sure how it’s fair all the scores are on one list. It would be better for each level to have it’s own leaderboard. At least the dev should consider adding the level to the high score list.
It’s one of those games you’ll pick up and play for a few min at a time. After all the game timer is 2 minutes. There are few tricks to perform in the air and a few more closer to the water. With practice I’m sure you could chain reverses, tailslides, and air jumps into quite the combo. I do wish there was more, but I can see how being a dolphin can be limiting.
Since the landings need aiming you’ll want to have a controller. I can see the mobile nature of this game with the limited controls and time limit but I still think it works on desktop.
My Peppinion of Dolphin Up is that it’s a very simple game not for everyone. It might be something you’re looking for to kill time at the right price point. It’s $1.50 on mobile, there is a limited free browser based version you might want to check out first.

As a start, while this game looks similarly to Hearthstone in the card/card stats, it plays very diferrently. Chronicle plays where you have five stages (rounds) while being able to play up to four cards a stage. While this is a fun and new way to play these sort of card games, it breaks the mold of almost every other card game by, essentially having each player play up to four turns behind the other player. With this set up, it becomes much harder than normal to predict what the other player is planning on doing this. Playing this far behind what the other playing is doing makes it feel like your moves mean nothing, and your standing at the beginning of the round has no indication on how the next rounds will play out. Some may argue that this is put in place to set a much higher skill ceiling for the game, which is true. However,  it feels awkward and almost like adding in artificial difficulty to make gameplay seem more nuanced and strategic to watchers.
In all, this game is good at what it sets out to be; however, it is built on a faulty base game. The four-move system feels awkward and turns the game from a strategic card game into a meta that almost favours buffing yourself with hopes that the other player will buff themselves up less. So, in my mind, I would not reccomend this game to anyone looking for an online card game. Just play Hearthstone if you really something like that.

Strange game.
Each game consists of 5 rounds. In each round you and your opponent play all or most of your hand simultaneously. You do not respond to his cards, nor he to yours. Most of the time you don't even know what cards he played, since the animation is too quick for you to notice what he is playing.
The battle in all 5 rounds before the final 6th is not between him and you, it's between your legend or avatar and your own cards! When you attack or gain support from your cards, damage can be done to the opponent, but that need not happen and is not in fact the normal strategy.
Once the cards in a round are played, the "battle" is automatic and advances to the next round. The only strategy available in a round seems to be to take a look at the opponent's legend's stats and maybe do something based on that info.
For the main 5 rounds, you barely notice you have an opponent! The point is, for the most part, simply to buff your hero, in attack, health, and armor, in preparation for the final showdown. (You may need to weave damage to him, healing, and self-buffing, but it's a single-player experience.)
The final round is completely automatic and just alternates between your legend damaging the opponent with basic attack and vice versa until one is dead. So, I don't get it.
It's F2P and pretty to look at, so check it out anyway.

This is certainly a great game, and let's face it, the Elder Scrolls universe is one of the better fantasy-verses out there. The game is polished, visually very nice, and pretty much reminds of "Eternal" in terms of style and overall presentation. Other than Hearthstone and Magic, these are the only other two card games I've played, and as far as that goes, Legends is definitely in the top three.
That being said, for me personally, none of these reach Hearthstone. Why? For one, none of these games have such an easy, well organized and easy to manage deck building system. Card overview, sorting what you have, and organizing it, is the most important thing in a card game. Most digital card game interfaces are clunky, cluttered and you can easily feel overwhelmed. Legends is no different sadly. Plus, choosing and then building  your entire game around one character (as I understand it now), seems quite restricting. I haven't quite figured out if you can change that, but for now it doesn't seem like it.
It's a great game, it's fun, has some unique tactical features, but will it draw me away from Hearthstone? Definitely not. Legends does have potential though, and for die-hard Elder Scrolls purists who always wanted a card game to accompany their universe, this is definitely going to be the absolute go to game!
If you're not sure whether to try it out, it's F2P. Try it. At least you can say you tried it.

Its a great card game, they put a suprisingly large amount of effort into polishing and balancing this. Suprising because I figured this was just an attempt to capitalize off of the growing CCG fanbase, while also expanding the Elder Scrolls universe. Bethesda has been diversifying the Elder Scrolls series as of late, in what seems like attempts to monopolize the series in the video game world. Elder Scrolls Online treaded into the MMO world, and now this treading into the more casual game world. Im not really sure how I feel about it yet, but one thing I do know, they cant seem to make a great Elder Scroll game that ISNT an open world RPG.
Just like ESO, this game misses its mark, and falls short of being noteable in any way. That doesnt mean it isnt fun, and its definitely a way to kill half an hour or so. Sadly this game only makes me want to play Skyrim again, and quite simply, it does NOT scratch that itch.
The game plays similar to Magic: The Gathering, but its card graphics are nowhere near as cool looking. The cards are generally lackluster and unimpressive, I was hoping they would utilize some visually appealing art style, but instead its just a generic western fantasy style. Magic has a more gothic and visceral style, where ES Legends has a hokey cartoon style. There are sound effects when cards are used, which is cool until about 3 minutes into the game, when the cards spout out the same lines repeatedly. A Daedric Cultist card will say a korny line like, "for the queen of darkness," every time it attacks. Now imagine there are four Daedric Cultist cards on the table, and a dozen turns left in the game, you will hear "for the queen of darkness" literally 48 times, over and over, until you just mute the game altogether. That was my experience, and sadly I now play the game on mute, which should never have to be done.
Overall the game is just ok, but since its free its almost impossible for me to NOT recommend the game. Because of this I imagine the steam rating will stay really high, you should note that its NOT indicative of the quality of the game, because in my opinion the game is really not great, its just ok. Not even the subject matter of ES can save this one, and to be honest this game has nothing on hearthstone or other more well established card games. Despite that there is literally no reason not to give it a try, considering its free.

So I've put a few hours into POLYGOD and it has been tremendously fun... its far harder than any rougelike I've played which is saying alot.
The pros of the game are that it offers fast paced, open, and unique combat while remaining random and rougelike in nature. In addition everything synergizes the way you think it should... nothing just overwrites or doesnt work.
There are currently 3 main cons: lack of i-frames means you can die before you can react if you get hit by multishots which happens frequently past floor 3. Lack of bullet "thickness" means moving while shooting is almost impossible, and items like explosive concotion are almost worthless due to never hitting. Those are both easy enough to fix, but the third con is slightly less so which is lack of items for how frequently you get them. On averge I get around 3-4 items a floor, and with only about 50 items in game this means currently many runs feel very similar to past runs. This removes the rougelike feel and turns it into a bullet hell/fps which isn't great for what its trying to be. Either work on adding more variety of items, or reducing the number of items you get per floor and making them more impactful.
Overall I'd give the game a 7/10 in its current state with 5 being dead average.

TL;DR: A good JRPG fighter mix that is pretty solid, however it is pretty much like Xenoverse 1 with a few expansion packs and patches. It doesn't really add anything new that makes it significantly better or different as the story and everything else is almost the same. If you have Xenoverse 1 then don't really bother unless it's on sale, if you don't have Xenoverse 1 then this would be the one to get instead.
Let me start off by making two things clear:
-
No.
-
Yeah, probably. Unless you like sequels that are almost the exact same games as the previous ones.
Xenoverse 2 is a direct sequel (I think passage of time isn't a thing in Toki-Toki City which is now Conton City, IDK, was never explained.. So I guess direct sequel?) of Xenoverse 1; a JRPG with a 3D fighting battle system. As pretty much 95% of the Dragon Ball games, the story has something to do with the events of DBZ but also a bit of Dragon Ball Super but with a twist.
It is unique in that you actually don't directly follow the events of DBZ. Instead, you create your own character that is a Time Patroller. Basically you punish those that mess with time and try to alter history; Towa and Mira and their allies.
The battle system is a 3D fighter with skill sets like in action JRPGs. You don't use special inputs to use skills like in most fighters, but you just press a key combination to execute them. That doesn't mean there's no depth in the combat system; you can do many different combos and there's things like super armor and stamina to take into consideration. It's very simple, but with depth to it... But you can just spam, that works, too, against PC-controlled enemies.
Character customization is pretty straighforward and MMORPG-ish: Choose your race and gender, choose your fighting style and level up and distribute your stats points accordingly (Or not at all if you have no idea what you're doing). You can learn pretty much every move in the game either through the master system or quests which, means you can make the DBZ OC of your dreams!
The game offers a lot of side quests and missions. A lot are pretty much the same (It's a fighting game, what did you expect?) but they all have unique dialogues in them so that you don't get too bored. You can do these Parallel-Quests alone or with others, but online mode isn't unlocked right away, which imo is a bummer.

Well... You can't really do a "Yes and No" review. However:
It's really hard to call this game a sequel... A
sequel, IMO. In every way this feels like Xenoverse 1 with an update that added a few more things, but down to the core it's pretty much Xenoverse 1, still. That wouldn't necessarily be a bad thing, but...
The story is pretty much the same with a few alterations here and there and the addition of 3 new baddies that you forget about pretty fast once Mira has the main focus again. They try to make your old character matter (If you played Xenoverse 1, otherwise you can choose a standard model), but they're mute (Of course they are) so they get a total screen time of around 10 minutes unless you count a certain battle.
The "few more things" that have been added are the bigger hub city, some side-quests that are pretty much the same and a minor overhaul to the master system with a few more masters if you have the DLCs.

I get that you can't do much about the standard DBZ stuff and battles, but it would have been super interesting to see things happening to Conton City and other time patrollers; instead they decided to do the whole time rift thing that just recycles the same old DBZ stories and quests over and over again in another perspective. The only use out of them is getting extra moves that you wouldn't otherwise get, but their usefulness is... Meh, depending on race. (Human being the worst by far. Neat, but terrible.)
They modeled in a class room that you can access, but there's absolutely no significance to it and it's unimportant. I believe that at some point in the development they would have made you go through a school setting a la Naruto or My Hero Academia style which would have solved the story problem mentioned above, however the "school tests" (actually called advancement tests, I think) are now just a bunch of side quests with the same old DBZ characters... A result of time constraints or just budget issues since they'd have to do a lot more voice acting?
The only two changes that really mattered was how Ultimate Finishes were handeled and the master system. In Xenoverse 1 meeting the requirements didn't mean you wouold automatically get an Ultimate Finish which was essential for getting certain outfits and moves, in Xenoverse 2 you always get an Ultimate Finish which helps a lot. The master system was also changed so that you could learn moves from all masters at the same time, in Xenoverse 1 you had to commit to one master at a time.
Overall I cannot recommend this game at full price for people that already own Xenoverse 1 and for those that don't own it I'll say just ignore Xenoverse 1 and grab this game instead.

I am really hoping that the developers make a sequel and build off of feedback from this game to make an even better version, because I think it is really ambitious and interesting in its own right, but has enormous potential be even better. I think with some work and polish, it could be come its own franchise to rival Civ or the Endless series.
It is probably more useful, though, to say a little about the game. The best way I can describe the thoroughly unique experience of Thea is an unlikely meeting of worlds between a game like Civ, Endless Legend and / or Age of Wonders, and a game like FTL: Faster Than Light or Convoy. It’s a rogue-like 4X exploration game, with loads of replay value both in terms of single-session variety and meta-game progress.
(Long review below: thanks for reading)
You act from the mixed (and admittedly somewhat confusing) perspective of what I can only assume to be some kind of avatar of a given deity. Each deity has their own specialties, and benefits they grant to those that are dedicated to them. As this sort of Avatar, you function as the leader of a band of survivors eking out a living in the aftermath of a sort of global calamity. The worst seems to be passing, though, and your small village is able to bravely venture out into the renewed world. This experience is put into action through a few mechanics.
Firstly, you have to manage your settlement. This involves striking a balance between leaving adequate (and appropriate) characters in your village to gather resources there (they give you a couple of basics available to get recurrently in your starting local, usually wood and some kind of food) while also having a strong enough adventuring party to brave the wilds in such of other resources (the VAST majority of resources you will need to progress have to be gathered outside of your home). Managing your settlement involves assigning the people who you choose to leave behind to gather, craft or construct. Every character has a wide array of skills (all of which may be levelled up each time your community gains a level) but only a couple of these apply to these efforts. There are different classes that your villagers will be members of that will determine where they are best suited. Gathering obviously gives you resources, crafting produces (based on what blueprints you have unlocked) the huge assortment of types of equipment that can benefit you, and constructing allows you to add structures to your settlement, which grant a variety of boons ranging from chances to get new villagers, children, and / or resources; bonuses for skills and stats of new children who have grown up there; different class options for children who grow up in town; or boons for your community of other forms. Crafting and constructing are the two main ways to generate research points which allow you to unlock new gathering, crafting and constructing options. That’s it in a nutshell, but obviously there is nuance. You can spend a LOT of time just fiddling with your settlement as time goes on.
Secondly, you explore the world and attempt to overcome various tasks, events, challenges and quests. The world can be of various sizes depending on how you set up your game initially, but personally playing on default settings I didn’t even come CLOSE to fully exploring it. It is rewarding, challenging and has that same feel of the first 200 turns of Civ or Age of Wonders. This is also where a lot of the FTL / Convoy piece comes in, with different choices available in the many, MANY scenarios you can encounter. Encounters may simply random, happening as you travel, or they could be guided by quests. Each god / goddess has their own unique quest chain, then there is a main storyline that sort of parallels it that is similar for all playthroughs, and there is the free DLC for the game, Rise of Giants, that spices things up (and sometimes makes it really, really hard) around the 150 – 200 turn mark. Sometimes these quests and events resolve simply by making certain choices, but largely this is where we encounter another really unique but (in my opinion) very well done mechanic of the game: the card system.
This is the third mechanic of managing the game and it’s a big part to be sure. Rather than dice rolls, pure RNG or an active-time combat system of some form, skill challenges and combat alike are resolved using Thea’s unique card-based system. Without getting into the nitty-gritty, each character has lots of skills and those various skills contribute to their attack, shielding, health and utility options that they have as cards. You and your opponent (which is sometimes represented by abstract cards representing the challenge at hand, while other times directly personifies an enemy or adversary in front of you) take turns playing your cards hoping to best the other. Again, I don’t want to go into the details because there is nuance, but I find it really refreshing and solid overall. I would recommend trying it or at least watching gameplay videos before you go “ugh, card-based system – PASS.” I almost did that but I’m glad I gave it a chance.
The last mechanic to mention is the meta-game. When you beat the game (or lose I think?) you get given a score based on how long you lived and what you accomplished (big bonuses for achieving one of the victory conditions, and big bonuses for completing the giant quest content) and that gives your god or goddess experience. With that experience, they gain levels, adding new cool benefits that they offer if you play under that god in future playthroughs. They can earn up to five special traits this way, potentially allowing you to turn up the difficulty and endure even more challenge! To this end, as well, increasing the difficulty gives you a multiplier on this final exp, while lowering it makes you receive less exp (though not in a hugely punishing way). Hooray for replay value!
Okay, wow, that’s already a long review so I’m going to try and wrap up. Thea is really solid and has tons of replay value. But it is not perfect (what is?). Many of the events that happen most commonly lack variety (one particular even involving boars comes to mind for me) where it could have been so easy to simply code in a few more varied outcomes to keep you on your toes. I feel like they lost a bit of this because they insisted on having voice acting for a lot of the script. Personally, I feel they could easily forgo that part and focus on writing, since I realize it is burdensome creating that type of variety while also having a voice actor. I’d way prefer they prioritize the former than the latter.
(My review, perhaps unsurprisingly, is too long for Steam. For the rest of the review, if interested, please see the comments)

Grasshopper Manufacture is one of the more interesting developers on the market. Spearheaded by a japanese auteur Goichi Suda51 their games could be characterized by a very strong and unique style that more than made up for, at times, lackluster gameplay and outdated technology.
Grasshopper's latest intallment - Killer is Dead is a Hack'n'Slash game in the vain of their previous work such as No More Heroes and Lollipop Chainsaw. If you are a PC gamer, you probably haven't played those titles, so allow me to elaborate. Imagine a combat system that sits somewhere in-between Platinum's games/DMC and the Batman games. That is, parrying at the right moment is key and even though you are ubable to jump and your juggling abilities are limited, there is a heavy emphasis on combos.
In Layman's terms - it's a button masher.
Overall, the combat is functional, yet shallow compared to other games of its genre. Considering that you will be in combat for 80% of the game, that isn't a good sign.
Let's discuss the story, shall we.
The story centers around the tittular government assassin Mondo Zappa. He seems to be a Moon Cyborg Vampire Nymphomaniac brought to Earth on a magical unicorn. Quite unfortunate that even with all of those characteristics, the man has the personality of plain bread.
It seems that the game is attempting to stylize itself as an anime/manga series, where every chapter starts out as an episode of a television show. First, showing a crime being commited, then showing the victim sending a commission to the execution office, then a brief dialog between the main cast, followed by the level itself. After completing the level itself, you are given a short epilogue. Though after a few hours of playing they do begin to grind on one's nerves, the strong cast of characters carried me though.
A burly cyborg in an ugly hawaii shirt, a blonde sidekick with 8 arms and a high pitched anime girl who violently punches you in the chest if you fall in battle in an attempt to revive you. As typical as they are, they begin to grow on you after a while.
Just like any episode of a long running anime, every story centered episode is followed by a few filler ones. Some of the more interesting filler segments have to be the "Gigolo missions" in which the player has to seduce one of Mondo's many girlfriends in order to get a bonus item. As much as I dislike to bring up identity politics in a game review, that segment really rubbed me the wrong way. I don't mind looking at a woman's breasts to get enough points to aqquire a new weapon, yet the whole think felt like cheap tittlation, which could've been handled way more tastefully.
Out of place fanservice, one more thing the game has with mainstream japanese animation.
Now is a good time to talk about performance. No use in beating around the bush - the port if♥♥♥♥♥♥ It took me a while to fix the infinite loading screens and even then I would get frame dips from time to time. It's odd, since the game performs adequadely in crowded areas, but freezes in empty rooms.
Speaking of irrational decisions, the style is a bit of a pain. Basically, the game takes certain values and replaces them with a thick gradient, which gives an ink shaded feel. Think of Sin City for reference, if you are unfamiliar with eastern comics. Which is fine and dandy in earlier missions and during cutscenes. However, your view gets frequently abstructed by flashy visual effects and even other enemies, which can be a pretty big problem on higher difficulties.
After a while the game gets grindy with tedious minigames, such as turret sections and territory control. Thankfully, those are skippable.
Remember when I said that Mondo has the personality of a wet napkin? Well that is one of the reasons why this game begins to fall appart after a while. Grasshopper games ride the post-punk aestetic and since the lead lacks any emotion and is unable to react to what's going on around him, the colourful shell crumbles. Playing the game further feels like staying in the circus after the roof cought fire. Yes, there are colourful clowns running for their lives is fun to look that, though it is becoming progressively difficult to observe past the thick layer of smoke.
In the end, you feel a tad burned out. Like a standup comedian who told all of his best material in his first 20 minutes and is trying to fill time before he can leave.
All in all, enjoyable romp while it lasts. A good sale pickup. Go in with low expectations and leave with lower ones.

A number of players, including myself, have experienced issues with stuttering (if this happens during gameplay, I recommend pausing a moment until it clears up) and an infinite loading glitch in chapter 3 (check the forums for a fix).
That said, those problems didn't ruin my experience with what is otherwise a great game. Killer is Dead is surreal, stylish, and a whole lot of fun. The gameplay is challenging without being overwhelming, and definitely rewards skill; when you're doing well, you'll feel it. The story, while not the most sensical thing out there, was consistently entertaining; it didn't take long for me to grow attached to these characters, even if I didn't always understand what was going on, and it went a whole lot of places I didn't expect. The game doesn't always take itself seriously, and I loved it for that. It looks and runs pretty good too (stuttering aside), even on my old-timey Frankenstein of a computer.
It's a bit short (though there's plenty of challenges for completionists) and I'm not sure I ever got used to the controls, but honestly, aside from the problems with this port, any complaints I have are relatively minor. Definitely worth a try.

It may be a little late to write a review for Dragonfall - especially when you own this game already for quite a while (like me). But I'm playing it again right now, so it may be still a good idea. Well, Dragonfall is not perfect. For instance it is quite difficult (perhaps even impossible?) to give objects from your inventory to one of your party members. Or the story, especially the Dragonfall story, is at times really cheesy when it's adoring and worshipping Monika and the romantic criminal life in anarchist Berlin. Don't get me wrong - Shadowrun IS a scenario which romanticises a criminal Robin Hood life. But neither in Dead Man's Switch nor in Hong Kong is it as obtrusive and embarassing as here.  I'm very much with Lucky Strike, a NPC runner which you can hire for missions, who is expressing just these thoughts.
But - doesn't matter at all. Dragonfall has an unbelievable atmosphere, and as soon as you start the game you surrender to it. Having said that it HAS a lot of advantages. The story, though cheesy, is more detailed and more epic than the story of Dead Man's Switch. And even though the story of Hong Kong is probably even better, Dragonfall has by far the superior matrix system. And that, although the matrix of Hong Kong was supposed to be an improvement. Typical case of making things worse by trying to improve them. Worse to an amount that I stopped playing at some point and never bothered to start again. Also Dragonfall has a lot of excellent user campaigns in the Workshop. "Antumbra" for instance or "Mercurial" are real classics, and you don't see a difference to a professional campaign designed by the developers. Hong Kong has only one campaign, I believe. Don't know anything about it's quality. But six or seven or even more high class scenarios for Dragonfall compared to just one - that speaks out loud enough, don't you think?
So, without any doubt Dragonfall is the best Shadowrun game for PC up to now. And having said that, I don't believe there are many games to follow. Shadowrun is a game system which definitely hasn't aged well. In a peculiar way it seems to have fallen out of time, and so probably Dragonfall will be it's ultimate legacy. At least as long as we talk about PC games ...

Updates are frequent, and new cards have already been added to the base set with more on the way. Good stuff!
Pretty fun so far. There are elements similar to Hearthstone, but overall, the main mechanic of the game is different and feels that way. Worth checking out if you're looking to try another CCG.

i have played this game as a nice little time filler for a few weeks now.
i looked at this because it was free and knew nothin going in.
it's unlike anything i think exists before and it's completely different to hearthstone as people keep pointing out.
the solo campaign is short but is a good way to get a first few decks.
there are currently about 340 cards and you get 5 cards a pack. i have opened about 54 ish packs of cards and have about 260/outa the 340 cards.
i do not think this game is pay to win at all as while some cards are definitely strong cards there is enough copper given per day to do an arena run a day or if your a bit casual at least do the epic quest every 4 days for 1000 copper thats a pack every 4 days even if you played 10 games once every 4 days.
the issue i am finding is people are failing to realise not to straight up buy decks from the shop as that gets expensive.
what you actually want to do on this game is buy arena runs with plat.
for 100 plat which is about $1.99 you get 1 arena run which works similar to heathstone.
not only do you get 15 rounds of drafting 2 cards out of any card in the game allowingg you to test cards and see what you may want in a premade deck easier. but for every win in arena you can get copper.
if you get 7 wins in arena period you get enough copper to buy another free arena run. both arena runs give a pack each by default so you can buy decks for a dollar and potentially win enough to buy another arena run so it can be a dollar for two packs plus about 2 hours of entertainment learning the game and cards.
if you get fairly far you also get given shards which are like dust so arena runs can even grind the dust needed for specific cards on top giving you 2 5 card decks and possibly one card of your choice for a dollar each time.
i have spent about 10-20 usd on this game and got over 50 packs from chain winning arena.
♥♥♥♥♥ all over the 300 odd usd your paying for one set of hearthstone.
gameplay is solid the feelings of pulling off a killing tactic are incredible and its worthy of time even if you have no love or knowledge of the runescape world cause i sure as hell never played runescape.
to make this non bias and more worthy i will list some cons.
the price for a few of the legend cards ae a little too high for a dust grind and while you don't need them to win this game will require a lot of time to grind all the cards unless you bought a bunch of packs but you never need to and i've been happy with most of the games cards getting to gold rank and trying to reach plat.
classes have varied playstyles and its nice to see the choice but it's also too easy to see the choice. it's far too easy to notice the other players tactic because his whole deck is given away in a card or two.
theres no room for creative decks there are playstyles which have a much higher win rate and i would argue the mage class is way too easy to break and is sorta overpowered.
each class does have a counter to the strong tactics but you have to learn fast exactly what your doing and how to block them and that might be a stressful learning curve.
once the mage gets 16 gold and there are cards which can give 4 gold then be doubled and doubled again so you could get in theory 16 gold in 1 chapter. then turn 2 you can be hit for 32 damage which is 2 more than lethal. you would need to play smart to take away a mages gold before that combo hits or it's a very quick game.

Overall: 3/5, not terrible but better off playing a different card game
Pros:
-Great Elder Scrolls Taste
-Various Modes to play (story, arena, vs), you still have plenty to do against AI
-Not too difficult to get into
-You can choose to play it completely free
-Story mode offers many rewards
-Has two lanes
-Neat Prophecy system that allows you to draw a free card when your health passes certain intervals. You can draw certain prophecy cards giving you a competitive edge or turning around a trade
Cons:
-Story isn't "fantastic" (about average) so isn't really worth playing for story, just gameplay
-Has same card effects as other card games just with different labels, ex: Divine Shield (HS) -> Ward (ES:L), Life Link (MTG) -> Drain (ES:L)
-A lot of content is locked behind levels (will explain later)
-Feels like a lack of cards, the starting card decks are majority of all the cards
-Less to offer compared to other leading card games such as Hearthstone and Magic (when a competing card game should attempt to equal or surpass in other ways)
Just overall this game just starts to feel a bit bland after a while, due to lack of wide diversity of cards, material too similar to other card games, and "level barriers". Yes, I am aware that as a card game it should feel similar to other pre-existing types, but it just matches too much. The main difference in this is image, the two lanes (which sounds neat but doesn't add a whole lot of change) and the prophecy system.
Rant: One of my major complaints is what I am calling "level barriers". A decent chunk of content is locked behind certain levels you need to reach to unlock it. This is understandable to a certain point, you should have enough experience with this to play more advanced stuff but is just overused. Certain starting decks (helpful to new people) are locked behind needed levels or progress in the story. Arena modes also require even more progress and levels (although it does make sense in respect to the story). There are also cards that start off fairly bland (no modifiers) that require you to reach a certain level in order to upgrade them. This sounds cool but think of it like this: you get a new rare card that has limited abilities since you aren't a high enough level. Polygod is a game with a ton of promise, that also requires a ton of work. As with all early acess games be advised that you should only pick it up in this state if you wish to support the development and provide feedback to make it a better product on launch. Anyway on to the review.
Even in it's current state Polygod has a ton of content, there are a ton of upgrades you can get and all of them feel unique and meaningfull.
The game's art style is also pleasing, it looks very sharp and well done, honestly playing with anti-aliasing I think this is the sharpest game I've seen, every single shape looked perfect with no pixelation or tearing.
The gameplay takes a while to get the hold of since it isn't quite what is expected, movement feels a bit clunky and jumping feels like it has a bit of visual delay, but after you get used to this it's almost like playing quake 2.
The best part without question is the gunplay and the crazy variety of it.
As with all rogue-likes expect the game to either have the highest skillcap possible or the lowest.
You can get an upgrade set that makes it like you're playing with the quake railgun, precise and deadly although with a pretty huge break inbetween attacks, so you have to make every shot count.
Then on the other hand you can just get a completly easy hold m1 set like proximity mines, spreadshot and splitshot. And then it all just becomes a chaos of explosions as you just hold m1 and breeze through the levels.
You might think this is a bad thing but every playstyle has it's advantages and disadvantages, going the easy route will get you through the levels easely but you'll get destroyed on the bosses and the oposite for the other build. So there's a nice balance.
In this current state the game has some problems and downsides that need to be worked on.These aren't "bad points" they're something that will improve during the game's development cycle but I think I should let consumers know of what they're getting into.
The game currently lacks enemy and level variety. It's ok for your first couple runs since you'll be learning enemy patterns and all but you'll get sick of fighting the same enemies and the same bosses on the same arenas over and over and over again with little to no difference except the shape of the level.
The game needs some mechanical polish, movement overall requires a bit more to feel good and some more complex game mechanics would be nice. Currently there aren't really any complex things you can do it's pretty basic fps run and gun. Maybe with the increase in upgrade and weapon variety we'll see some complex and interesting interactions that make the game more mechanical skillfull and appealing.
The hitboxes for the enemies are fine, they're excellent even, it's the player that doesn't seem to have a very clear hitbox, I've had times when I got completly barraged by bullets and took no damage and others where it felt like the attacks missed me but they still dealt damage. This isn't that much a bad point but consistency is really welcome.
Polygod is an amazing game with a ton of promise that based on developer and community commitment could be an incredible game with huge following. Honestly after playing almost every fps rogue-like on steam I though Ziggurat was as good as it was gonna get, but we have a serious contender here for the best fps rogue-like on the market. If you liked Ziggurat, Tower of guns or the classic doom and quake era fps' and would really love to see them mixed with a rogue-like then this game is a must.

Some classic games age better than others.
Pac-Man is one of those titles that still plays well today despite the fact it originally came out in 1980. That doesn't mean that it's perfect, however, nor does it mean that people have been happy to leave it alone since that time. Indeed, the Wikipedia entry listing all the Pac-Man games throughout history includes no fewer than 51 games (not including compilations) that either focus on or feature Pac-Man and/or his family at one point or another -- though many of these games radically deviated from the original formula of eating all the dots in a maze while avoiding the unwanted attentions of four ghosts.
Of all the adaptations that remain at least reasonably true to the original game, two of the finest are surely 2007's Pac-Man Championship Edition, which made the game a timed score-attack affair, and its 2010 follow-up Pac-Man Championship Edition DX.
Om nom nom. Or something.
Pac-Man Championship Edition DX (hereafter Pac-Man CE DX) was a masterclass in how to modernize an arcade classic: it kept the original gameplay intact while simultaneously incorporating features that simply wouldn't have been possible on the hardware of 1980. Its biggest change to the formula was the addition of "sleeping" ghosts scattered around the ever-changing maze layouts; passing close by them would cause them to wake up and start following Pac-Man in an ever-lengthening rainbow-colored trail. Scoring highly in Pac-Man CE DX was a matter of deliberately building up this trail to be as long as possible, then unleashing a Power Pellet to gobble up as many as you could in rapid succession, the screen exploding in a shower of disembodied ghost eyes flying off the screen as Pac-Man chomped his way to victory.
The simple addition of the sleeping ghosts had a huge impact on the way you had to play Pac-Man CE DX. Because they were always in the same, predictable locations, it became possible to calculate an "optimum" route through the game's maze layouts, though actually successfully executing that optimum route became more and more difficult as the game accelerated to speeds '80s arcade game makers could only dream of. Fortunately, the game provides a number of "time attack" modes which prioritize quickly completing mazes over scoring as many points as possible, and these provide a helpful means of learning the layouts a little at a time before applying them to the 5- or 10-minute score attack modes that provide the game's main, insanely addictive draw. Alternatively, you can use the "Ghost Combo" mode to test how many ghosts you can successfully chomp in one go before a Power Pellet's effects wear off.
If you played Pac-Man CE DX back in 2010, you already know all this, of course, and you're probably wondering what that little plus sign at the end of the title indicates.
Well, it's not a completely new game, though the "Plus" edition does mark its first appearance on PC platforms via Steam. Rather, the new version -- available as a free update for those who already own it on console -- adds a few extra bits and pieces while keeping the core game experience just as it's always been. Specifically, it adds some social and comparison features to make it a little easier to check out how you're doing compared to your friends, and a new set of "medals" to complement the existing bank of achievements and trophies. The game also now has support for add-on content which can either be purchased separately or acquired via the "All You Can Eat" bundle. Currently available DLC includes four new mazes, three new visual themes (based on Dig-Dug, Rally-X and the upcoming Pac-Man and the Ghostly Adventures) and two new background music tracks, one of which is the finest piece of Japanese jazz funk/drum and bass I've heard from Namco since Ridge Racer Type-4. Have a listen for yourself.
The new mazes are interesting and worth a look for veterans. The Championship III course is a particular highlight, offering a significantly tougher challenge than any of the other courses in the new content -- I found it hard to even break a million on this one, while I'm comfortably well over 1.5 million on most others. Big Eater offers an entertainingly ghost-heavy (and consequently potentially high-scoring) romp that will probably take a few attempts to get your head around, while Mountain offers a highly technical, asymmetrical course that will likewise require a bit of practice to work out the best route through. The weak link in the new courses is probably Highway II, which is just a little too similar to its predecessor for comfort, though nonetheless features some interesting "wrap-around" layouts that require a keen awareness of how both sides of the maze relate to one another as you gobble your way off one side and chomp back on the other.
One of the more annoying new features about the update is the ability to share achievements and medals on Facebook. Indeed, three of the available medals are tied directly to how many other things you've shared on Facebook, and in order to unlock the classic Pac-Man skin for the game, you need to share all of your achievements and five medals, making for a total of 17 separate posts cluttering up your Facebook page all in the name of making the game look like its 1980 original self.
There are three main problems with this: firstly, the medals and achievements are all extremely easy to acquire with the exception of one, meaning they're not really worthy of bragging about; secondly, there's no means of posting the one thing you might genuinely want to share on social media, i.e. your actual score and leaderboard position; thirdly, try as I might, on both the Xbox 360 and PC versions I could not make the Facebook functionality work at all anyway, making the whole thing somewhat redundant. It feels like a half-hearted, unnecessary and badly implemented attempt to add social gaming features into a game that was already pretty good at encouraging competition between friends and among the community as a whole without shoehorning Facebook into the equation. It doesn't need to be there, and the fact that it doesn't work properly and thus actually locks people out of game content just adds insult to injury.
The "Classic" skin is locked behind Facebook sharing. Boo!
I can't stay mad, though. Despite the Facebook-related idiocy, Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ remains as ludicrously addictive as it was the day it came out back in 2010 -- and the addition of a new Steam version means that a whole new audience can now discover it for the first time. Good integration with Steam's network on the PC version means that you can quickly and easily compare your performance to your Steam friends list right from the game's main menu, though it might have perhaps been nice to see a more direct means of challenging one another. Steam Cloud support also means that you can transfer your progress from one computer to another without having to unlock everything all over again, though the reliability of this was occasionally a little flaky while I was trying it out. I lost progress on one occasion, though it's possible this was more due to the dodgy Internet connection I had at the time than a problem with Steam Cloud or the game itself.
Regardless of a few flaws here and there, Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ remains the perfect coffee-break game -- you can sit down and play for just five minutes and feel like you've had a rewarding experience, but at the same time if you want to spend several hours perfecting your cornering on the game's wide variety of mazes, you can do that too. It's an enjoyably intense experience by yourself, but if you can recruit a few friends to set up an impromptu league of your own, it becomes one of the most addictive games in the known universe. You have been warned!

I put about 12 hours into Thea, mostly playing in co-op with a friend. This game does not make a great first impression. There are quite a few systems in play that do not feel well explained even after reading all of the tutorial tool tips available. In fact, my co-op partner ended up watching a 1.5 hour video on the game on youtube to learn the ins and outs and explained them to me.
Once we got into it, we found some of the story events interesting, reminding me of the random events in the Banner Saga series. However, often we found ourselves in extremely punishing situations. The "skull" difficulty system for fights is not that reliable. I lost many many villagers, irrespective of whether I camped after the fight to maximize their recovery. You don't even have to leave your initial village to get into trouble however, as some of the catastrophic world events (fires and plagues) come to you. "You have lost 5 children." Ouch. In a town of maybe 15 humans total, that's a doozy.
The gathering/crafting/building system was somewhat unique and warrants some praise, but the research tree is quite slow. You soon find that you'll need to constantly be crafting with the rarest materials you have available to obtain research points at any reasonable speed. However, the research tree itself is not particularly exciting, and I couldn't really get excited about any of the options available.
In the end, I think this is what soured me on the title. Interacting with the gathering, crafting, and building system made up a lot of our play time, and it just wasn't very exciting. I can put a research point into some type of metal, another point in a type of sword - then I need to send out some villagers to get some of the metal to put the sword together, but I just didn't find this engaging or particularly rewarding.
I wanted to get out into the map to experience the random story events, but any missteps were so incredibly punishing that I spent the majority of the game sitting around waiting for wounds to heal or for additional villagers to arrive that might allow me to maintain my village and still send out an expedition. Additionally, the fog of war and day/night cycle leave you feeling as though you haven't explored anything, even if you have travelled many hexes in either direction. There is no permanence to the map. I can see how some players might find this "emergent," but it just made me feel ineffective.
Thea has some good ideas, with some reviewers calling it "an entire game about the first few turns in a Civilization game." However, this game never got me to say "just one more turn!"

In Thea you play the people of a little Slavic village trying to survive and prosper amongst the mounting threat of the mythological monsters around you.  Your village becomes your home base, while you send foraging parties out to brave the wilderness and see what resources they can discover.  It often ends in tears, until you find your footing.  The combat system is unusual and takes a little getting used to before you get good at it, but persevere and it can get quite rewarding.  The crafting system allows you to build up your village's assets, harvest better ingredients, or make better equipment.  There are loads of options and choices, and you rapidly become involved in strange happenings at the instigation of your patron deity.  Your choices matter.  It has tactics, strategy, you name it.  Thea is a game that builds complexity on simple ideas and does it well.

Thea is, if nothing else, an interesting and worthwhile experience. I'll do my uttermost to break down why that is in the following paragraphs. Essentially, there is no specific aspect of Thea: the Awakening that is totally good or totally bad; each aspect has its own high and low points.
Lore: The lore in this game is rich, rich like red velvet cake with mousse baked inside somehow. It's based on Slavic mythology, and having done some cursory research, I can say that the game does take significant inspiration from Slavic and Eastern European mythology. Elements such as Striga and Zmey, as well as gods such as Perun and Veles, are taken more or less straight from the original stories and myths. Creatures such as Vily and Hohlicks, however, I couldn't find an origin for, but those who are better versed in the mythology might know where their inspirations come from. Certain other elements, such as Kostey, seem to be modified from an original story; in Kostey's case, it seems to come from the story of Koschei, an Eastern European sorceror who was unable to be killed except by finding a needle that contains his soul. The lore of the game itself, regardless of how closely it follows actual Slavic mythology, is incredibly engaging, and one of the highest notes of the game. The voice-overs also deliver the narration passing fair, but I'm 99% certain that the British-accented narrator is mispronouncing some things. Regardless, the lore is really compelling and the stories worth following. The main plot concerns the end of the world, and your peoples' attempt to rebound from it. This actually does a lot to set up the main rogue-lite mechanics of the game, as it means that survival will be deathly important.
Marriage of Mechanics: This one's gonna be complicated, mostly because this game is very unique. Basically, the game is an attempt to marry rogue-lite persistent elements with 4x gameplay. Bascially, when you first boot up the game, you choose from one of two randomly unlocked god characters each of which give you bonuses in game. Then, once you win, lose, or quit your run, your god gains experience points, and levelling them up grants them additional bonuses which they confer on you in later runs with them. You unlock other gods upon hitting certain thresholds, usually hitting a certain level with your currently unlocked gods. The actually gameplay consists of managing a single village in a 4x world, trying to gather resources, explore the map, and complete quests, chief among them being the "Cosmic Tree" and "Return of the Giants" quests. The best analogy for the game I've found is that it's the opening exploration phases of a game of Civ, but it's the whole game. While some of the mechanics can be a bit obtuse, the game does a great job with its tutorial, and by the end of it, you'll have found your footing. These mechanics do indeed grant the game additional, tangible replay value. After all, when you complete a game of Civ, nothing presists beyond, save perhaps for a vague sense of accomplishment and a desire for another round. Having persistent, efficacious avatars to level up and play as grants this game actual, physical reason to keep playing. When someone asks you, "Why have you spent 67 hours on Thea?" you can say, "I was trying to level up Horos to his final form." But when someone asks the same about Civ V or VI, all you can say is "Sid Meier owns my soul." However, there are problems that arise on repeated playthroughs. Because the game doesn't provide infinite story or quests, it can take only a game or three to exhaust most of the side quests and lore. This can make one feel as though after a few games, one has seen all that there is to see, learnt all that there is to learn. In a way, the wealth of in-game content works against the meta-game's avatar persistence, as after seeing all the game has to offer in terms of quests and encounters, playing subsequent games can feel like you're only trying to level your god. In other words, the rogue-lite and 4x mechanics experience the seven-year itch after a few games. My suggestion to the devs would be to have more god-specific quests, or additional quests relevant to your god's experience level, or additional quests that only unlock at certain difficulty levels. Now, this seven-year itch is mitigated somewhat by the inclusion of an "Event Editor", which allows users to create their own quest-lines, allowing for theoretically infinite content. However, the interface for the editor isn't exactly user-friendly, and without apparent workshop support, it may be difficult to find user-made content.
Combat and Challenges: Combat in this game resolved via a neat little card-based minigame. Whenever you encounter an opponent on the overworld map, your party and the enemies engage in card-based combat, with your party members and the opponents represented as cards with abilities based on their stats. You have an offensive hand and a tactical hand. The cards from your offensive hand you may play directly on the field, where they engage in combat with the opponents' cards. Cards in your tactical hand can use tactical abilities, such as delaying an opponent's attack, or discarding a card from an opponent's hand. It's actually a fun little mini-game! Other challeneges, such as Stealth challenges, Hunting challenges, and Intellect challenges, are resolved exactly the same, except against the challenge itself rather than an opponent. However, the mini-game can get rather repetitive and wrote, and sometimes doens't actually work as an abstraction. For example, how does having additional people help with a Stealth challenge? Well, in this game it does help! Somehow. These situations can be seen as less a flaw of the minigame and the result of fridge-logic instead, but it can still be jarring to some players. Regardless, the mini-game does its job well enough.
Ease of Play: The game's interface is pretty easy to wrap one's head around, and as mentioned before, the tutorial is pretty good. As for the actual game... Well, there's a reason I've referred to it as "rogue-lite", as opposed to "roguelike". I personally found the game a smidge too easy on Normal mode, but it might provide a meatier challenge to someone who is unfamiliar to 4x games or survival-based mechanics. As for me, even when I messed up in a major way, it was never enough to stop my run. Someone looking for a greater deal of challenge should either look elsewhere or play on a higher difficulty level.
To sum up, Thea: the Awakening is altogether an interesting idea competently executed. It's a fun game, and the lore and mechanics are rich and deep enough to warrant repeated playthroughs. It does suffer somewhat from having limited quests and content, and the endgame can be a bit of a slog, but a few tweaks in future endavours from the devs could mitigate that somewhat. I would definitely reccomend this game, if only because few, if any, games have attempted what this game has.

Grasshopper Manufacture is one of the more interesting developers on the market. Spearheaded by a japanese auteur Goichi Suda51 their games could be characterized by a very strong and unique style that more than made up for, at times, lackluster gameplay and outdated technology.
Grasshopper's latest intallment - Killer is Dead is a Hack'n'Slash game in the vain of their previous work such as No More Heroes and Lollipop Chainsaw. If you are a PC gamer, you probably haven't played those titles, so allow me to elaborate. Imagine a combat system that sits somewhere in-between Platinum's games/DMC and the Batman games. That is, parrying at the right moment is key and even though you are ubable to jump and your juggling abilities are limited, there is a heavy emphasis on combos.
In Layman's terms - it's a button masher.
Overall, the combat is functional, yet shallow compared to other games of its genre. Considering that you will be in combat for 80% of the game, that isn't a good sign.
Let's discuss the story, shall we.
The story centers around the tittular government assassin Mondo Zappa. He seems to be a Moon Cyborg Vampire Nymphomaniac brought to Earth on a magical unicorn. Quite unfortunate that even with all of those characteristics, the man has the personality of plain bread.
It seems that the game is attempting to stylize itself as an anime/manga series, where every chapter starts out as an episode of a television show. First, showing a crime being commited, then showing the victim sending a commission to the execution office, then a brief dialog between the main cast, followed by the level itself. After completing the level itself, you are given a short epilogue. Though after a few hours of playing they do begin to grind on one's nerves, the strong cast of characters carried me though.
A burly cyborg in an ugly hawaii shirt, a blonde sidekick with 8 arms and a high pitched anime girl who violently punches you in the chest if you fall in battle in an attempt to revive you. As typical as they are, they begin to grow on you after a while.
Just like any episode of a long running anime, every story centered episode is followed by a few filler ones. Some of the more interesting filler segments have to be the "Gigolo missions" in which the player has to seduce one of Mondo's many girlfriends in order to get a bonus item. As much as I dislike to bring up identity politics in a game review, that segment really rubbed me the wrong way. I don't mind looking at a woman's breasts to get enough points to aqquire a new weapon, yet the whole think felt like cheap tittlation, which could've been handled way more tastefully.
Out of place fanservice, one more thing the game has with mainstream japanese animation.
Now is a good time to talk about performance. No use in beating around the bush - the port if♥♥♥♥♥♥ It took me a while to fix the infinite loading screens and even then I would get frame dips from time to time. It's odd, since the game performs adequadely in crowded areas, but freezes in empty rooms.
Speaking of irrational decisions, the style is a bit of a pain. Basically, the game takes certain values and replaces them with a thick gradient, which gives an ink shaded feel. Think of Sin City for reference, if you are unfamiliar with eastern comics. Which is fine and dandy in earlier missions and during cutscenes. However, your view gets frequently abstructed by flashy visual effects and even other enemies, which can be a pretty big problem on higher difficulties.
After a while the game gets grindy with tedious minigames, such as turret sections and territory control. Thankfully, those are skippable.
Remember when I said that Mondo has the personality of a wet napkin? Well that is one of the reasons why this game begins to fall appart after a while. Grasshopper games ride the post-punk aestetic and since the lead lacks any emotion and is unable to react to what's going on around him, the colourful shell crumbles. Playing the game further feels like staying in the circus after the roof cought fire. Yes, there are colourful clowns running for their lives is fun to look that, though it is becoming progressively difficult to observe past the thick layer of smoke.
In the end, you feel a tad burned out. Like a standup comedian who told all of his best material in his first 20 minutes and is trying to fill time before he can leave.
All in all, enjoyable romp while it lasts. A good sale pickup. Go in with low expectations and leave with lower ones.
