First off: this is not a good port. I'd recommend getting the console version over this if that's a reasonable option. A number of players, including myself, have experienced issues with stuttering (if this happens during gameplay, I recommend pausing a moment until it clears up) and an infinite loading glitch in chapter 3 (check the forums for a fix).
That said, those problems didn't ruin my experience with what is otherwise a great game. Killer is Dead is surreal, stylish, and a whole lot of fun. The gameplay is challenging without being overwhelming, and definitely rewards skill; when you're doing well, you'll feel it. The story, while not the most sensical thing out there, was consistently entertaining; it didn't take long for me to grow attached to these characters, even if I didn't always understand what was going on, and it went a whole lot of places I didn't expect. The game doesn't always take itself seriously, and I loved it for that. It looks and runs pretty good too (stuttering aside), even on my old-timey Frankenstein of a computer.
It's a bit short (though there's plenty of challenges for completionists) and I'm not sure I ever got used to the controls, but honestly, aside from the problems with this port, any complaints I have are relatively minor. Definitely worth a try.

Overall: 3/5, not terrible but better off playing a different card game
Pros:
-Great Elder Scrolls Taste
-Various Modes to play (story, arena, vs), you still have plenty to do against AI
-Not too difficult to get into
-You can choose to play it completely free
-Story mode offers many rewards
-Has two lanes
-Neat Prophecy system that allows you to draw a free card when your health passes certain intervals. You can draw certain prophecy cards giving you a competitive edge or turning around a trade
Cons:
-Story isn't "fantastic" (about average) so isn't really worth playing for story, just gameplay
-Has same card effects as other card games just with different labels, ex: Divine Shield (HS) -> Ward (ES:L), Life Link (MTG) -> Drain (ES:L)
-A lot of content is locked behind levels (will explain later)
-Feels like a lack of cards, the starting card decks are majority of all the cards
-Less to offer compared to other leading card games such as Hearthstone and Magic (when a competing card game should attempt to equal or surpass in other ways)
Just overall this game just starts to feel a bit bland after a while, due to lack of wide diversity of cards, material too similar to other card games, and "level barriers". Yes, I am aware that as a card game it should feel similar to other pre-existing types, but it just matches too much. The main difference in this is image, the two lanes (which sounds neat but doesn't add a whole lot of change) and the prophecy system.
Rant: One of my major complaints is what I am calling "level barriers". A decent chunk of content is locked behind certain levels you need to reach to unlock it. This is understandable to a certain point, you should have enough experience with this to play more advanced stuff but is just overused. Certain starting decks (helpful to new people) are locked behind needed levels or progress in the story. Arena modes also require even more progress and levels (although it does make sense in respect to the story). There are also cards that start off fairly bland (no modifiers) that require you to reach a certain level in order to upgrade them. This sounds cool but think of it like this: you get a new rare card that has limited abilities since you aren't a high enough level. The game makes these upgrade cards worse with their crafting system (soul trapping, just like dust in HS) by making it so you cannot soul trap them until they are upgraded. To explain, if you do not want a card, you can soul trap it for material to make cards you want. Since you cannot soul trap these cards (many are legendaries, worth more material) you will hold on to them until you reach a high enough level to finally disenchant. When I first saw the screenshots, I thought I was dealing with yet another Hearthstone clone (trying to piggyback on the new-found popularity of CCGs with casual gamers), but boy was I wrong :D
Turns out the game is not only very different, but very inventive.
It plays pretty much like a boardgame and I like that each turn feels like a mini-puzzle, trying to figure out the best course of action but also, depending on your deck and your opponent's, what they might try to do and possibly counter them (or play around what they will do to impede you in your progress).
Although they don't give that many shards for trashing the lower card rarities, they are pretty generous with gold so you can acquire a fair amount of packs for free (in fact, a lot of players in the top leaderboards did so the F2P way). If you do opt to spend money, it doesn't feel too expensive compared to other CCGs.
The devs appear to be fairly active on the forums and reddit, and they also put out content regularly on youtube.
All in all, very recommended and very fun : )

I wasn't sure what to think when I initially saw this, but I gotta say, I'm impressed.  The TL;DR version of this would be something along the lines of it's a combination of Shadow Complex and Strider for the NES.  Still not sure what I mean?  Okay, so basically it's a metroidvania, meaning there are very light RPG elements a la finding perma-powerups and such throughout the levels as well as some fast travel elements and backtracking.
It's also 2.5D, which I know doesn't appeal to everyone, but it looks pretty fantastic to me.  Finally, I say Strider for the NES, because that version of Strider WAS actually a metroidvania.  If you're looking for a more arcadey version of Strider, there are plenty of other titles, but this one is full on metroidvania.  It's fun, frantic, over the top, and has a lot of references to characters in past versions of Strider.  A must for any oldschool Strider Hiryu fan!

It's a decent adaptation of the tabletop setting, and good for getting your SRPG fix. The story is solid, the characters interesting, the art mostly great ... I have few problems with it overall. There are also some minor quibbles about the game mechanics (like how there's no loot at all from taking down foes) and some design issues that could have been amped up (any time you are in the Matrix it's a complete slog, which is sad given the potential for minigames in that setting), but nothing that's a dealbreaker. It's also definitely not going to scratch your free-roaming sandbox RPG fix, and replayability is limited. Still, it's a very, very good game for what it is.

Also worth noting that even at this stage the game does have number of minor bugs which have not been fully resolved. Nothing game breaking.
Easily recommended - great example of old TB RPG done right.

much meatier offering than the first shadowrun returns. good turn-based combat gameplay remains intact, decent integration of skill choices into various dialogue box interactions thoughout the story. well-designed missions and dungeons. well-written characters with an abundance of interactions. a little bit stingy on the karma, but ultimately that's a balance and difficulty issue. completed on normal mode with only a few points in various missions presenting high risk. suffers a little bit from presenting various dialogue choices that have the same ultimate effect, but that's a minor quibble. significant weakness was leaving me wanting more, teasing various bits of lore and possibilities, telling you about places you never get to visit, but every adventure ends sometime. if youre new to the peculiar shadowrun setting this adventure might be jumping into the deep end, you may have a bit of reading to do to understand what certain characters are talking about. If you like the first Shadowrun game(Shadowrun Returns) by Harebrained Schemes, you'll like this one.  The game is almost a perfect second effort by this developer, with a few exceptions that I could find:
1. In Shadowrun Returns, you had the ability to click on your character and go into "combat mode"(turn-by-turn mode for each of the characters under your control) even if no enemies had seen you yet(or there were no enemies even on the level).  That way it would allow other characters under your control to pickup items.  It also allowed you position all your characters optimally(behind as much cover as possible) before opening a door.  I wish that they had kept that feature in this game.  For example, if my character is a decker or street samurai with no conjuring skill, a spirit talisman is useless to my character on that level.  I have to wait until the level is over and play the next mission with a shaman in my group in order to use that spirit.
2. I wish I could have seen Eiger, Glory, Dietrich, Blitz, and Dante(if he "joins" your team") stats at any time, especially while shopping around in the Kruezbasar.  It was frustrating to buy a spell and not be sure(and worse, wrong) whether or not Dietrich has a high enough spellcasting/conjuring number to be able to use that spell.  Same goes for weapons for Eiger/Glory.
3. I wish I could have had the ability to move items between characters under my control while on a mission/level.  For example, if I want to move a grenade or medkit from my character's possesion to another character's possesion.
4. There were times that I successfully cast a Mind Wipe spell on an enemy and although the status of that enemy would read "Mind Wiped", it would still attack my characters.  I only noticed this happen with Firedrakes and the enemy mages in the final level.  If the developers intended that Mind Wipe would have no effect on certain enemies(and it wasn't just a bug), they should have had those enemies say "Immune" when the spell hits them, rather than "Mind Wiped".

Thea is, if nothing else, an interesting and worthwhile experience. I'll do my uttermost to break down why that is in the following paragraphs. Essentially, there is no specific aspect of Thea: the Awakening that is totally good or totally bad; each aspect has its own high and low points.
Lore: The lore in this game is rich, rich like red velvet cake with mousse baked inside somehow. It's based on Slavic mythology, and having done some cursory research, I can say that the game does take significant inspiration from Slavic and Eastern European mythology. Elements such as Striga and Zmey, as well as gods such as Perun and Veles, are taken more or less straight from the original stories and myths. Creatures such as Vily and Hohlicks, however, I couldn't find an origin for, but those who are better versed in the mythology might know where their inspirations come from. Certain other elements, such as Kostey, seem to be modified from an original story; in Kostey's case, it seems to come from the story of Koschei, an Eastern European sorceror who was unable to be killed except by finding a needle that contains his soul. The lore of the game itself, regardless of how closely it follows actual Slavic mythology, is incredibly engaging, and one of the highest notes of the game. The voice-overs also deliver the narration passing fair, but I'm 99% certain that the British-accented narrator is mispronouncing some things. Regardless, the lore is really compelling and the stories worth following. The main plot concerns the end of the world, and your peoples' attempt to rebound from it. This actually does a lot to set up the main rogue-lite mechanics of the game, as it means that survival will be deathly important.
Marriage of Mechanics: This one's gonna be complicated, mostly because this game is very unique. Basically, the game is an attempt to marry rogue-lite persistent elements with 4x gameplay. Bascially, when you first boot up the game, you choose from one of two randomly unlocked god characters each of which give you bonuses in game. Then, once you win, lose, or quit your run, your god gains experience points, and levelling them up grants them additional bonuses which they confer on you in later runs with them. You unlock other gods upon hitting certain thresholds, usually hitting a certain level with your currently unlocked gods. The actually gameplay consists of managing a single village in a 4x world, trying to gather resources, explore the map, and complete quests, chief among them being the "Cosmic Tree" and "Return of the Giants" quests. The best analogy for the game I've found is that it's the opening exploration phases of a game of Civ, but it's the whole game. While some of the mechanics can be a bit obtuse, the game does a great job with its tutorial, and by the end of it, you'll have found your footing. These mechanics do indeed grant the game additional, tangible replay value. After all, when you complete a game of Civ, nothing presists beyond, save perhaps for a vague sense of accomplishment and a desire for another round. Having persistent, efficacious avatars to level up and play as grants this game actual, physical reason to keep playing. When someone asks you, "Why have you spent 67 hours on Thea?" you can say, "I was trying to level up Horos to his final form." But when someone asks the same about Civ V or VI, all you can say is "Sid Meier owns my soul." However, there are problems that arise on repeated playthroughs. Because the game doesn't provide infinite story or quests, it can take only a game or three to exhaust most of the side quests and lore. This can make one feel as though after a few games, one has seen all that there is to see, learnt all that there is to learn. In a way, the wealth of in-game content works against the meta-game's avatar persistence, as after seeing all the game has to offer in terms of quests and encounters, playing subsequent games can feel like you're only trying to level your god. In other words, the rogue-lite and 4x mechanics experience the seven-year itch after a few games. My suggestion to the devs would be to have more god-specific quests, or additional quests relevant to your god's experience level, or additional quests that only unlock at certain difficulty levels. Now, this seven-year itch is mitigated somewhat by the inclusion of an "Event Editor", which allows users to create their own quest-lines, allowing for theoretically infinite content. However, the interface for the editor isn't exactly user-friendly, and without apparent workshop support, it may be difficult to find user-made content.
Combat and Challenges: Combat in this game resolved via a neat little card-based minigame. Whenever you encounter an opponent on the overworld map, your party and the enemies engage in card-based combat, with your party members and the opponents represented as cards with abilities based on their stats. You have an offensive hand and a tactical hand. The cards from your offensive hand you may play directly on the field, where they engage in combat with the opponents' cards. Cards in your tactical hand can use tactical abilities, such as delaying an opponent's attack, or discarding a card from an opponent's hand. It's actually a fun little mini-game! Other challeneges, such as Stealth challenges, Hunting challenges, and Intellect challenges, are resolved exactly the same, except against the challenge itself rather than an opponent. However, the mini-game can get rather repetitive and wrote, and sometimes doens't actually work as an abstraction. For example, how does having additional people help with a Stealth challenge? Well, in this game it does help! Somehow. These situations can be seen as less a flaw of the minigame and the result of fridge-logic instead, but it can still be jarring to some players. Regardless, the mini-game does its job well enough.
Ease of Play: The game's interface is pretty easy to wrap one's head around, and as mentioned before, the tutorial is pretty good. As for the actual game... Well, there's a reason I've referred to it as "rogue-lite", as opposed to "roguelike". I personally found the game a smidge too easy on Normal mode, but it might provide a meatier challenge to someone who is unfamiliar to 4x games or survival-based mechanics. As for me, even when I messed up in a major way, it was never enough to stop my run. Someone looking for a greater deal of challenge should either look elsewhere or play on a higher difficulty level.
To sum up, Thea: the Awakening is altogether an interesting idea competently executed. It's a fun game, and the lore and mechanics are rich and deep enough to warrant repeated playthroughs. It does suffer somewhat from having limited quests and content, and the endgame can be a bit of a slog, but a few tweaks in future endavours from the devs could mitigate that somewhat. I would definitely reccomend this game, if only because few, if any, games have attempted what this game has.

Do you know the first turn in Civilization games? Where you have one settler and one warrior, and you have the choice to either build your first city on the spot or start exploring and hope for a river? Thea is an entire game built around that concept. And if that doesn't convince you this is an amazing game, then you, sir, are a filistine.
On the whole, Thea is in the same street as 4x strategy. You build a civilization by gathering resources and advancing through a tech tree. Most events and encounters offer combat and non-combat resolutions, which are both resolved by playing a card game. The difference between combat and non-combat lies mainly in the skills involved and the fact that characters don't risk getting wounded if you choose non-combat.
A big difference between Thea and ordinary 4x is that Thea is strictly PVE single player. There's no AI opponent to outsmart. There's also a much greater emphasis on story and roleplay elements. You could probably piece together all of the narrator's dialogue to create a good 5 hour audiobook. There's multiple options to solve 95% of all challenges and diversification is strongly encouraged.
The system for crafting items and managing food is deep and immersive. allowing you as many options as there are different resources. And there are a lot of different resources. I don't know how much number crunching was required to reliably create situations where you have to choose between matching X or Y with N or P, where people choosing XP can still scrounge up some N or Y from other sources to meet their basic needs. It's an incredibly refined experience and I respect the amount of work required to create it.
There is still a fairly easy 'complete' strategy that'll win you the game regardless, but I won't spoil it and it's not a big hindrance to the overall fun.
While the majority of the storytelling is great, the finale left me a little befuddled. Without going into specific spoilers, I'll say that the various options to complete the main questlines all seem to lack definite impact. The score screen says I've done the thing I was supposed to do, but it doesn't really feel that way. There's no gameplay feedback and ultimately the whole thing leaves me a little unsatisfied, at least until I start another game.
Summary: Excellent game, recommended to those that like 4x strategy and rpg's.

TES: Legends falls into the same trap so many other CCGs have - it's not a game anyone actually wanted to make, so they just took some mechanics from existing games, slapped some differnt pictures on the cards and called it a day. Mechanically, it's perfectly functional; the interface is clean and works nicely, while games flow pretty quickly and will usually take no more than 5-10 minutes. The single-player campaign serves as a tutorial that introcudes the mechanics for those who haven't played similar games, but if you've seem almost any CCG before you'll quickly get bored as you're forced to play an hour or so of easy games just to unlock the rest of the game.
As for the mechanics themselves, it really is almost all just a copy and paste of Hearthstone. You gain mana each turn with no need for lands or similar, you play mainly creatures which can choose to attack either each other or the hero, you also get spells which are the usual damage, debuffs, and so on, and you have extremely minimal interaction during your opponents turn. Pretty much all creature abilities are taken directly from Hearthstone (charge, deathrattle, etc.), with the exception of trample taken from MtG (MtG itself has far more abilities, so it's clear which game was being copied here). You even start with 30 health and have decks with a default of 30 cards.
There are precisely two things in the game that aren't identical to Hearthstone. Firstly, the board is (usually, although not always in single player) split into two lanes, with creatures in a lane only able to attack other creatures in that lane. In single player sometimes the lanes will offer different effects, but in most games it's simply one normal and one that gies creatures stealth for a turn. In theory this is supposed to open up more tactical choices, but in practice it really just brings the game more similar to MtG by opening up a bit more freedom in attack and defence. It at least makes things a little different from Hearthstone, but it still doesn't bring anything actually new to the table. The second part, which might actually be original, is that each time you take 5 damage (relative to your starting health, so healing will delay it), you draw a card. This makes rush decks slightly less powerful and opens a a bit more possibility for comebacks - a player who falls behind early can end up with a 5 card advantage which is quite a lot in games like this - but it doesn't really change the game in any significant manner. Related to this is the equivalent of Hearthstone secrets which give the sole interactivity during an opponent's turn. When drawing a card due to damage, if it has the "prophecy" ability you can play it immediately at no cost. Unlike Hearthstone and MtG, neither you nor your opponent have any idea if or when this will happen, so while this can be quite powerful, it's extremely unpredictable and impossible to plan around. It's at least the one thing not ripped directly from another game, but it's really not an improvement.
There are no heroes as in Hearthstone, but rather classes that combine two card colours. Each colour focusses on certain things, such as big creatures for red or spells for blue, but other than restricting which cards you can put in a deck that's the only effect classes have. If this sounds similar to MtG, that's because once again it's essentially identical, other than restricting you more than MtG does in exactly the same way that many recent CCGs have done. The influence of Hearthstone can really be seen with some of the colours, such as yellow focussing on summoning lots of small creatures and then buffing them, to the point it couldn't have been any more obvious what they were copying if they'd actually name the tokens "Silver Hand Recruit".
As for the game types and free-to-play model, again, see Hearthstone. You have single player tutorial/practice mode, adventures (one available so far), online ranked matches and arena. Packs and arena even cost exactly the same as in Hearthstone, and you can disenchant and craft cards in exactly the same way. As a new game, it's not really possible to comment on how fair progression is; there are nowhere near as many cards available as older games so the ability to get a decent number of cards early on doesn't mean much. This question can only be answered over the next few months and years as it becomes clear if (and how much) money is needed to have a decent chance of competing, or at least having fun as a new player.
Finally, where the game really falls down is its utter lack of character. The strength of the TES games has always been in the writing and the interaction of the player with the world. The world itself is just a rather generic fantasy setting with your standard elves and cat people and so on, and since each game has been set in a different time and covered different events, there aren't really any established characters, places, famous weapons, and so on. This means that unlike Hearthstone, where many cards are recognisable and themed arpound their lore, and legendaries are well known bosses and important characters, cards in TES:L range from "generic elf" to the legendary "slightly different generic elf". The lack of animations (plenty of particle effects but no actual movement) just makes it worse - instead of dropping Ragnaros with a big thump and burst of fire, you just place a card with a picture of an elf on it. If you care about TES lore, this game won't offer you anything recognisable or anything new. If you don't already care about TES lore, this game is certainly not going to get you interested in it. It's a functional, generic fantasy CCG with mechanics copied directly from other CCGs, mainly Hearthstone with a bit of MtG, and a total lack of any character or anything of interest to recommend it over the many other similar games currently on offer. It doesn't offer new and interesting gameplay, it doesn't offer interesting characters or gripping story, it doesn't connect in any way to previous TES games, it just exists for the sake of having a CCG with the TES name attached to it.

This is my most favourite game so far. Recommended ( but keep reading befor making decision ) if you love open world stealth, good challenge, first person shooting and do not mind backtracking through hostiles and breathtaking vistas.
The game has shortcomings. It must be played in a specific way to be enjoyable (which is true for most games anyway). I usually do not like limitations in gameplay that force you to play in some specific style, but in this case the style was exactly my style, so the shortcomings worked for me.
The gameplay is....different. If that is not your thing, you will hate the game. Lets see. Enemies in the world are bullet sponges and respawn as soon as the area is reloaded in RAM. So there is no value in engaging them before you reach objective. Hardest difficulty will force you to find alternate routes and practice stealth movement and long range combat to thin out enemies around the objective. CQB stealth is broken but shooting is not. You can definitely run and gun if you have godly reflex and aim.
Yes, guns are worth discussing. The loadout is too complex in this game. Ammo is not abundant. There is no good medium range gun (something that was fixed in FC3). I used to switch between Dragunov and MAC 10 for everything. The condition of silenced guns is even worse. The dart gun has very limited ammo and it is long range. The DLC silenced shotgun is very short range and will leave you vulnerable in open fields. The silenced MP5 is trash. The weapon slots are restricted, so you cannot carry the shotgun alongside a medium range weapon. You can carry the dart gun alongside a real sniper gun though, but that will disallow you from carrying rocket laucher or IED. That is no big loss outside specific missions, becaus there is no good rocket launcher. RPG is too inaccurate, but still better than others, the GL and MGL take slots of secondary and primary, so not worth carrying outside certain missions, the Carl G puts your♥♥♥♥♥on fire, and the viewfinder of the explosive bolts reflects sunlight so you must find proper angle which is not always possible.
That leaves you very vulnerable in case your stealth fails and a vehicle with mounted guns attacks you. MAC 10 helps, but not against GMG mounted vehicles. I enjoyed the suspense, you might not. I spent more time staring at the map (I got a PDF from web and printed it) and in stealth travel than running and gunning.
Has high replay value. I was not a completionist, so did not go collectible hunting, amd more than 40% of the areas were new to me during second play where I found new ways to approach missions.
In my opinion Africa is the most beautiful location in the World, yet it is never explored in videogames. This game might have outdated graphics, but the quality of ambiance can only be compared to legends like HL, Morrowind, Minecraft etc. There is one fault in graphics though, it is graphically too demanding compared to its graphics quality. It does not run smoothly even in rigs that are just enough to handle Crisis unmodded.

I've been playing this game since closed beta, so the hours listed at the time of posting this review are not accurate. Where to begin? This game is a Collectible Card Game, and it features an incrementing resource (Magicka), and creature combat in which the attacker chooses targets. If that sounds familiar, it's because that is the same core concepts behind Hearthstone. If you think this is a "Hearthstone clone" or a "re-skin," you are sadly mistaken. This game offers several different mechanics that cause the games to play much differently.
First, this game features two separate lanes for combat. There is a Field Lane and a Shadow Lane, with different rules for each. Creatures can only attack other creatures within the same lane, which means lane positioning is very important. Second, each player has five "runes" associated with their health. When a player takes enough damage to break a rune, they get to draw a card. This gives the defending player more resources to try and recover. Taking this "come back" mechanic one step further is the presence of cards with "Prophecy" that can be played for free,
, if they are drawn from a rune breaking. This drastically impacts the strategies for this game.
Deck building is wildly different from Hearthstone as well. There are five attributes that contains certain themes, and decks can be made from any two attributes. This makes deck building more about mixing cards with synergy, and less about whatever template that a "class" has. There are also no hero powers, and decks are fifty cards in size. This adds some extra variance, making each game feel similar but different. Don't confuse variance with straight RNG, however, as there is much less of that in this game. (It's not non-existent, but it has certainly been toned down).
The free-to-play model is pretty excellent for this game, and numerous people have proven that you can hit Legend rank in competitive play on budget decks. There are also some solo game modes that many enjoy, including a solo arena. The story modes are fun if you like the feel of The Elder Scrolls universe.
Overall, this game is wildly enjoyable. I play a large number of card games, but I've been coming back to this one over and over for the last ten months. I think that says a lot.

I know it's not fair to compare a game made in 2008 to one made four years later. But I started by playing Far Cry 3 and enjoyed it so much I thought I might as well try it's predecessor. Not a good idea. Number two stinks.
It lacks almost everything that makes FC3 a great game. FC2 has a dull story line, and most missions are exact copies of earlier ones, especially the side missions. Example: to unlock weapons you have to blow up a convoy coming from the east. And then one from the west. And south. And yes, dealing with the convoy coming from the north is exactly the same; they drive around in circles, you blow the lorry to smithereens and you're done; you can proceed to the next mission. Public transport is the best choice to get there, as driving a car or boat takes about 10 times longer. That's because every 100 meters you have to deal with two homicidal maniacs in a car or ten of them at yet another road block.
You have a choice of nine to pick your main character from. It doesn't matter much which one you pick. Every character in the game has a personality as flat as roadkill at a monstertruck show.
The feeble attempt at a story line is hard to follow for someone who's not a native speaker, like me. Everyone speaks as if they've just done an ounce of speed, and even the subtitles have a hard time keeping up. From what I picked up, the story basically goes like this: first you work for this person, then you work for that person, then you work for another person, then you kill one of them and another person appears. You work for that person too, and then for another person and then you kill one of them and another person appears. Repeat until everyone dies. Game over.
So, no. I do not recommend buying this game, even though the graphics are pretty awesome for a game made in 2008.
I
recommend Far Cry 3 though, which was fun, entertaining and trippy.

Hoh boy, where do I even begin with this?
Well for a start this game had alot and I mean ALOT of problems at launch and still does have a few problems, loadtimes were just horrible, the servers had alot of issues and wouldn't allow me to connect for a solid 2 weeks after launch and after that it was a 50/50 chance of connecting (which thankfully has been fixed by now) the game was some how deoptimised from Xeno 1 and it runs like crap in comparrision to it (Even though my pc should be more than capable at running it perfectly) this has been improved slightly however I'd say the best experience of this game would be on the consoles (PS4, Xbox One and Switch though I've heard the switch isn't much better)
While I'm at it a current problem with the game which I'm going to flat out say it's just killed the game for me,
but it's the new anti cheat they've implemented thing is it flat out doesn't work, all it has done is killed the one thing keeping the game alive. Modding. the one thing to get the PC version over any other version of the game, as for the anti cheat not working stuff like the max stat QQ bangs (which I'll explain what they are when I get to character customisation) still exist. It's honestly a joke.
The fighting system was improved massively over Xeno 1. (No more super saiyan spam <3 Bandai)
Stamina breaks are a great way to change the outcome of a fight if you know what you're doing however depending on the character and their combos quite a few of them can be extremely unrelieable and allow opponents to just dash away because they either just flatout miss or due to lag. (This can also apply to some moves, like the old Dragon Fist)
I feel like some moves are still way too OP even after patches and such (looking at Justice Combination and Hit Awoken moves)
And grab spam is still far too easy.
The new characters are a nice addition, however I'm not a fan of the "Super Villain" characters having seperate slots this also applies to characters with different forms e.g (SSGSS Goku & Vegeta, Rose Goku, etc) these could easily be costume slots. This is just done to make it feel like there's more characters although to be fair some are fairly different like Rose Goku Black who has a different combo set than base Goku Black.
Speaking of the characters though, some just plain didn't need to be included (Like Saibamen, Frieza Soldiers, etc) I mean c'mon they got in but characters like Buuhan and Dabura are coming as DLC? they should've been in from the start and by that I mean Xenoverse 1. (also gibe pikkon pls, pls? ;w;)
Now for my favourite thing to talk about interms of characters, Balance!
All I'm going to say is: SSGSS, Hit (Awoken), Golden Frieza and Gogeta. Nuff Said
Custom Character customisation is great, much more options over Xenoverse 1 and is still getting more content
however I'm still not a fan of some of the hair/head styles if they added some existing character hair/head styles in that'd be great (Like Raditz hair for Saiyans, Third eye for humans, Super Buu style antena for Majins. that kinda stuff)
Alot of the clothing options are great and few are limited to specific races and genders which is nice however I feel some clothing options were pretty lazy like the colourable Gi which there was like 5 varations that changed nothing but the symbol on it (Speaking of which it'd be better if there was a version that didn't have a symbol on it kthx bandai!)
Also new to Xeno 2 is the QQ Bang system (mentioned above) with this you don't need to worry about clothing changing your stats so you can go crazy with your looks these will replace those clothing stats.
Equipable moves for custom characters, hoh boy this will be fun. this area is sort of a mixed bag as there's alot of moves that are just plain useless, don't work as intended, fun, spammy and ridiculously over powered (looking at Justice Combination again)
Not all moves can be unlocked although a massive amount is so it's really nothing to complain about when it comes to choice or picking your favourite characters moves, buuuuttt... a few moves are locked behind DLC pay walls which I think shouldn't be the case as some of these moves are just plain broken and give those with said DLC a massive advantage (Oh look the third time Hit awoken has appeared) another example of this would be "Rocket tackle" from ol No. 16 which doesn't do alot of damage to be fair but the invincibillty frames can be abused so much as an out of jail free card (I use it to dash away most of the time)
Due to the nature of being able to combine almost any move into one moveset people have made quite over powered death combos which is really unfair to people who don't use custom created characters for PVP.
My favourite move combo though is: Light stamina break, Whirlwind Blade followed by Emperor's Edge and a finish with Giant Storm.
However I won't lie Whirlwind Blade is far too easy to abuse and Giant storm is pretty unrelieable.
The story was eh, not much over Xeno 1 (Mainly because a fair chunk of it was a copy paste job from Xeno 1 with few changed) though the original stuff like the new Namek, Android, Battle of God saga stuff was pretty nice.
The story was best from the DLC campaigns as these are totally original and the CGI cutscenes DLC or not were brilliant.
Needless to say,

I must admit, I was going into this fully expecting it to flop hard. And I'm pleasently surprised!
Review is semi-long, so TLDR is: Overally, great game. Has the same pitfalls as Hearthstone, but generally plays a lot nicer, and I'd happily recommend it! (Even if you've never played Runescape before!)
Pros:
+ The art style and visuals are very reminiscent of Runescape, and I absolutely adore it! (Especially when they've encorporated items and characters from both games!)
+ Most of the classes seem balanced, and feel enjoyable to play.
+ The way it's played feels much more skill-focused than Hearthstone; although it still suffers from a heavy RNG focus, it's no where near as bad as HS.
+ It's definately worth about £5-10, in my personal opinion, perhaps more.
Overall, a good looking, fairly enjoyable little card game. Jagex have really impressed me.
Cons:
- F2P = P2W. Sadly, like all HS clones, money = power, and Chronicles is no exception. Thankfully, in my 4-ish hours of game time, I've only come across 1 P2W player, so I'm hoping it's no where near as rampant as HS; judging by some of the reviews however, I may be (sadly) wrong.
- RNG. It's a CCG, RNG is expected; although it does seem a little more reliant on skill, with the ability to plan ahead, and combo a tonne of "seemingly useless" cards.
[Slight ranty paragraph incoming. TLDR: Pricing is too steep, in my opinion.]
- Pricing. And this is where I start to find myself worrying about the game's future. 1,000 coins for a single starter pack is steep. Far too steep in my opinion. (4 hours of playtime, and I've only managed to gather around 1,500 coins. Yet, nothing is stopping someone with "Mommy's credit card" from buying 5-10 packs for £5 immediately.) I understand this is a F2P game, and thus, needs a method of funding it, but allow your players to gain cards at a semi-fast rate. Chronicles has the makings of a FANTASTIC CCG, and the one glaring flaw is it's business model. This is a massive shame, because it feels like Jagex have almost everything else right. They've managed to do what Hearthstone failed to do, in my opinion, but have kept Hearthstone's "give us all your money, or fall behind" approach.
[These are more suggestions, than "cons".]
- Lacks a chat option. This might be for the better, but it's a pain having fought a really fun, close fight against someone, and not actually be able to congratulate them! Even just a PM system would be fantastic!
- The inability to see what the last 5-10 cards both of you played really urks me sometimes. Some of the opponents cards pop up too fast to read their effects, and it would be a nice addition to see what just comboed me for half my health! (Lol)
Overall, the positives outweight the negatives, for now. Even with the P2W model, chucking £10-15 into the game (The normal price of a typical indie game) is plenty enough to get a good 20-30+ hours of enjoyment out of it, and if you're happy with grinding quests (Which are quite abundant, simple, and fairly easy to complete at a reasonable pace; unlike HS) it's a much more enjoyable alternative to HS, and other clones.

A good number of people have said bad things about Watchdogs, but I enjoy this game very much, despite that. With the Worse Mod, which restores the lighting and high resolution textures of the E3 demos, this game looks very good. It also maintains a steady framerate at ultra settings.
The gameplay is similar to the newer Deus Ex games, albeit dumbed down. The game encourages a player to tackle each scenario from many angles and with many options. I found myself playing one of the gang hideout side missions for 40 minutes, because the parking garage it was located in had three different means of entry and so many differing ways to accomplish my goal. The side missions, albeit quite similar to the checklist type ones seen in Assassins Creed and Far Cry, are fun if you enjoyed them in those series. Driving is definitely the worst aspect of this game, it has some of the worst vehicle handling and physics I've ever seen in a game.
This game has a good story, in my opinion. It is very dark and gritty, the characters are fleshed out (especially if you take the time to collect audio logs) and interesting, and the missions are fun. The game, similarly to Deus Ex, also has a very fleshed out setting. Through world building dialogue and events, the player really gets a sense of the hyper-surveiled Chicago setting.
Overall, I would reccomend this game, but make sure to install the worse mod for graphical fixes.

I grabbed this game for two reasons:
1. Elder Scrolls Obssession
2. It Was Free
I was very pleased to find a game that, so far, I haven't had to spend money on to be able to play. You can purchase booster packs with in-game currency.  The game itself is simple and elegant. Pick two colors to base your deck on and go to town. The single player tutorial/story mode is pretty good and so far the people I've come up against have been good sports, win or lose.
The Prophecy mechanics are really wha separate this game from other TCGs.  you have 30 life.  For every 5 life you lose, you draw one of your rune cards.  These are random cards from your deck.  If a rune card has the keyword prophecy, it plays for free.  I haven won (and lost) several games that seemed certain to be about over based on someone's drawing of a prophecy card.
Overall, I'd say 9/10.

I wanna start off by saying this is a great game. Everything I like about Elder Scrolls is here. Story line is somewhat challenging but very engaging and the ability to choose your own cards at times and choose how they evolve is awesome. It really allows players to customize and play to their individual strengths instead of trying to understand something that is just not something you are comfortable with.
Personally I have read a bunch of the negative reviews and I just laugh. Most of them boil down to basically "its too hard." Beyond the initial tutorial there is no hand holding here. You are given free reign to do whatever you want and play whatever you want. Are there abilities to buy cards with real money? Sure. But do you need to to be able to play? No. Alls you have to do is play the campaign, figure out what card type suits you best, and play from there. Once I created my first deck I've managed to beat probably 60-70% of my matches in PVP.
Rewards are given out generously (especially compared to some other more higher profile card games), and creating cards is not nearly as grueling as those others as well. All and all it is a very fun game and I only hope they continue with it.

Ive spent about 50 hours with this game-
The first half with Steam, the second with the client version.
Ive also spent 50 Euro for cards, played endless PVP matches and watched a lot of Twitch.
I am in the position to review this game honestly, objective and as a whole.
In the following review, i will try to cover all important aspects in two variations:
A short version, that brings my oppinion to the point, and a long version, that is a full review:
The short version:
Dont start playing this game, if you are not willing to spend much money.
The basic cards are boring and useless, rewards are worse than in Hearthstone, card packs are small, drop rates are bad, crafting-rates are awful, PVP punishes players badly for losing, the balance is out of control and everybody you will face in ranked has very strong decks already.
The review:
CRL is surprisingly unique, with a very different attempt to combine tactics and CCG, where players do their parallel quests on two separate lanes, and use their cards to determine their next four actions per round.
Which, with a complex card-pool, leads to deep games, where the order of actions, the choice of actions themselves, and the interaction with the opponent requires careful planning and thinking-ahead.
As a beginner or free player, though, matches will often feel boring, flat and/or unfair, as the free cards leave little room for strategy, and have little value and influence.
Cards are acquired through doing solo-missions (though thats a very minor part of the game), through buying packs, or mainly, buy playing online, which is the obvious focus on this game:
Unlike most other games, theres not only one daily missions, but many small ones. Which is basically a good idea. But, since all dailys reward only little, and some require much time to complete, the feeling of getting rewarded for playing is soon replaced by a feeling of having to work for progressing- at least in my personal case.
There is one Epic quest per week that unlocks at level 15, that grants 1 free booster, but which is really tough to beat, especially, for new and free players (for example: win 10 PVP games with a certain hero).
Brawl in Hearthstone rewards the same, while being MUCH more user-friendly!
Additionaly, non-premium-packs are expensive, card-packs are small (5 cards) and the drop-rate of card-packs is bad.
Which, again, can feel frustrating for new and free players, as the progress without paying is really slow, and opening single packs is often disappointing.
Which also means, that having strong cards or nor snowballs pretty fast, as fast wins grant good progress, while losing alot will lead to stalement.
The presentation itself is top-notch, without negatives:
From the comfortable interface, to the charming graphics, the great presentation and the relaxing music: Chronicles always feels like a professional product!
But, then again, the game and server are not stable atm.
I just had a game, where the server disconnected in my last round, and just before i had won.
By the time im writing this, the game is still offline. And, of course, i didnt receive any rewards.
And another time, the game crashed while i was overworking my deck-
very annoying, really!
Concerning the balancing. Its broken. That simple.
High-end-decks, will easily win using half the amoung of cards than normal decks.
And finally, the matchmaking...
Let me make it simple by advicing not to play ranked for a long time, or until you have bought a good amount of packs.

Since it is a free game I really recommend trying it out!

A good number of people have said bad things about Watchdogs, but I enjoy this game very much, despite that. With the Worse Mod, which restores the lighting and high resolution textures of the E3 demos, this game looks very good. It also maintains a steady framerate at ultra settings.
The gameplay is similar to the newer Deus Ex games, albeit dumbed down. The game encourages a player to tackle each scenario from many angles and with many options. I found myself playing one of the gang hideout side missions for 40 minutes, because the parking garage it was located in had three different means of entry and so many differing ways to accomplish my goal. The side missions, albeit quite similar to the checklist type ones seen in Assassins Creed and Far Cry, are fun if you enjoyed them in those series. Driving is definitely the worst aspect of this game, it has some of the worst vehicle handling and physics I've ever seen in a game.
This game has a good story, in my opinion. It is very dark and gritty, the characters are fleshed out (especially if you take the time to collect audio logs) and interesting, and the missions are fun. The game, similarly to Deus Ex, also has a very fleshed out setting. Through world building dialogue and events, the player really gets a sense of the hyper-surveiled Chicago setting.
Overall, I would reccomend this game, but make sure to install the worse mod for graphical fixes.

At first glance, this looks like a very good game. It has the same aesthetic that makes you think of Papers, Please, and a very gripping concept for those of you who like a relatively laid back game that you can play at your own pace and watch unfold.

The most variety you'll get is having a worker fired or maybe a letter sent to you for talking about someone a little too harsh.
Even the ending is unfulfilling; It's simply the credits explaining what happened after you finished, with the results feeling less connected to your actions than those you get from one minute "personality test" quizes. At least personality tests don't take an hour of your time and seven pounds to complete.
A good concept and design has been wasted by poor presentation. In conclusion: Don't waste your money nor time on this when you can get the same satisfaction, if not more, from a BuzzFeed quiz. Seriously.

I've played through Thea a couple times now on two different computers, and  while it runs a bit slower on my (admittedly older) laptop, I can still play the game fairly well even if the hardware isn't up to today's standards. Granted, I'm not running it at any of the higest settings. :)
As far as gameplay is concerned, I've enjoyed the struggle to keep my village alive and expand my benevolent survival to as many stragglers as I can pull in. Granted, for some reason, Fat Rats keep showing up to populate my village... But that may just be due to all the food that I have. (And the fact that I've got Attract Beasts+ on at least one of my buildings)
The skills are interesting and varied and although level up is random for each member of your village and exploration party, it does seem to be good as far as building on whatever skills your people have, whether naturally gained or from various stat boost via your crafted equipment. Some of the harder skills to find are the ones that make the game easier to deal with in the long run, so learning all facets of the crafting trees are essential to the game. But with low speed that you earn skill points to unlock crafting options and the multitude of items to spend on (buildings, crafting recipes, gathering materials) it does force you to pick and choose between all the options; will you use it to gain the ability to harvest better materials or learn recipes for buildings or equipment? The order that you choose can sometimes sink your game before you even get very far and although it can be frustrating, I've had fun learning how to make do with what I have and to compensate through encounters.
Encounters are sometimes a major point of pain and rage, and sometimes edge towards over simplification due to the various methods the developers have given us to utilize. Skills come into play here and rewards and hazards vary depending on how well developed your party is in any given skillset. As a rule, higher level parties with more members tend to do much better at surviving, though with the expansion of the giants, even high level parties don't have the luxury of just sitting on their laurels if they want to survive.
The save feature is a godsend.
The only thing that I haven't like about the expansion so far is that the earthquake events seem to happen way too quickly during gameplay.
Aside from that minor inconvenience, I've definitely enjoyed my time spent in this dark world and would recommend that anyone with interest pick it up. It's worth it!

I love this game for its setting, its quirky humor, and its uniqueness. Turn-based survival is not a common genre, and the fact that this game is hard to describe is one of the things I like about it the most. It is more of a roleplaying game than a 4x strategy game, and has more in common with Don’t Starve and Darkest Dungeon than Civilization.
In this fantasy themed (though not even remotely stereotyped) world, you are tasked with rebuilding from a nearly world ending calamity. Most of the game revolves around resource and people management, as you send your villagers out to gather the materials you need to both stay alive and rebuild your village. The further out you go, the more dangerous it gets, but the better materials you can find. As you progress, many different stories emerge, and you learn all about the calamity that befell Thea, and what you can do to help (or hinder) its rebirth.
You get attached to your villagers very quickly (they are by far your most valuable resource), and even though they never speak or interact with the story directly, they develop personalities nonetheless. The world of Thea can be very unforgiving, and playing through adversity is a major theme of this game (people die, and that is just part of life). While the main storyline is the same each time, there are different ways to approach it. The side quests and God quests are quite varied, and, based on how your characters develop, may change dramatically from play through to play through.
Combat is a fascinating card game, that is initially a bit hard to understand. Once you grasp the basics, it becomes an interesting puzzle each time. Then, just when you think you have it figured out, it throws a curve-ball at you (often resulting in the deaths of beloved villagers). I also love that it is the same basic interface regardless of what kind of combat you are engaged in (fighting, negotiating, sneaking, etc.) but your characters strengths and weaknesses change based on what what you are trying to do. This means that a character with low HP and damage might be worthless in a regular fight, but could carry the team in an intellect challenge, and is thus just as important to the overall party.
My only real complaint about the game is that sometimes, especially in the late game, there becomes more to manage than the interface can really handle. You will spend a lot of time scrolling through an overflowing inventory, trying to keep track of an ever growing number of unique villagers with a somewhat staggering list of different skills. There are tools and filters to try to assist with this, but even so, it is a challenge (and hardly unique to this title).
Regardless of that, I have spent many wonderful hours wandering the wilderness of Thea, and I look forward to many more to come.

This game has become an obsession. Where's the 12-step program? Seriously, who's the Betty Ford of gaming? I need her.
Thea has that addictive, just-one-more-turn quality that keeps me clicking way past my bedtime. It's by no means perfect, but I'm enjoying it so much that I just chucked some of my hard-earned cash into the developer's "coffee for coders" electronic tip jar.
The premise is unique--not quite an RPG, not quite a 4X title, but an utterly appealing middle path. You can build up your one village, your people, and their gear after the manner of a 4X title, but not establish an empire. The quests are varied, interesting, and lead to meaningful (and sometimes agonizing) decisions. There's more lore and backstory than I wanted to read, but it's reasonbly well written (for the most part) and has a fascinating flair borrowed from Slavic mythology.
A few complaints: the interface is utterly clunky. It often takes six clicks to do what should have been easily accomplished in two. I really hope they will either re-open development on this game and give it another round of polish, or work to streamline things substantially in their next game (which I will definitely buy). One example: say you want to rip up a particular character's outdated shield for its components. You can't do it from the equipment screen. You have to close that screen, flip over to inventory, find the shield, drag it to a box, and click on a dialog box. This could have been done so much more elegantly with a "scrap" button in the right click information dialog for the item. There are dozens of examples of this sort of poorly-thought-out UI choice--that's simply one of the most egregious ones.
The look of the game is gorgeous, but it's not very deep. There are lovely line drawings of all your characters, for example, but when you swap a fighter's starting sword for the big honking new axe you just found, you're still left staring at her sword-wielding drawing.
The voice narration, similarly, is very well done but shallow. There's only one narrator, and while he's outstanding, the game really could have used a full cast production.
The quests, card-based battle system, and crafting system are deep, complex, and completely satisfying. I get the feeling I could play another thousand hours and still be learning the intricacies of the crafting and battle parts of the game.
The actual characters you control, however, feel shallow. They only rarely feature as individuals in any of the quests. You learn little of their backstories. They needed to be fleshed out and developed, so that when one of them dies (which is inevitable), it means something more than just losing a generic warrior or gatherer.
Oh, and a note on DLC. They released it for free! Take note, Stardock and Paradox! If you do enjoy the DLC as much as I did, be sure to leave a tip. (Buy the "coffee for coders" DLC.) Let's reward them for being pro-gamer!
Overall, an outstanding effort. I'll be watching eagerly for this developer's next effort. And, while I realize it's unlikely, I wish they'd revisit Thea and give it another round of polish. Then it would easily be better than a lot of major studio games I've paid $60 for.

Typical ubisoft game. Bad design decisions spoil the game. There is much to show during a gameplay session for marketing purposes, but the overall game just does not meet the expectations. Most of the elements are bare-bones, designed for "casual gamers", console limitations. So much potential, wasted in the end.
The graphics are ok, however they are not on a far cry/crysis level. Performance is not the best, there are issues with fps. The world design is pretty boring, however it has some memorable places, but nothing special. Of course it is hard to create something more interesting when you work with a theme like this. Or, is it possible? With less linear paths and more really open places? I have seen better that is for sure.
The story has a lot in common with Far Cry 3's plot. You are saved from a fatal situation, then you are starting to work for the locals, earning you mighty respect among people, and of course wealth, guns and power. But the everydays of a mercenary are not that shiny. There are various missions. You can do work for factions, your guys, and others too, but these missions are tedious and repetitive.
My experience with gameplay mechanics are mixed. The gunplay and combat in overall is a dull mess. Fortunately Dylan's realism mod made it more digestible with proper weapon damage, so an enemy does not need half a magazine to die now. Unlockables are good, there are options in gamestyle with the different weapons at hand. All the needed upgrades are there, like accuracy, reliability, ammo, repair, etc. The setting makes it difficult to actually find an enemy soldier who is shooting at you. The direction indicator is useless. That is because of the many bushes and other vegetation that caused many problems in previous games too. So when there is nothing to see, sometimes the ai finds you anyway. It is hard to code an ai that reacts to the environment properly in every case, but this is pathetic. The fights this way are chaotic and hard to enjoy. The way the vehicles work is okay, it is fun to have one under your control. However, there are bugs. For example sometimes when I attacked while I am on a boat I have a hard time to switch to mg. In cars there is a key for switch, but that cannot be used on boats. You need to stand up and then mount the gun, but mostly you are just sitting back into the boat's chair while you are shoot to death. There is not any indicator that tells you what you are doing, only a hand. That is a big help, thanks.
Other disturbing thing to mention is the spawn system. You need to walk, drive or sail long distances on the map to reach the actual place where the mission is. That is a very good way to increase gameplay time, but my main problem are those guard posts. Once you get near one of these, people in the camp will attack you relentlessly, often making you or your vehicle broken in mere seconds. So, you do not really have a choice when you meet these people, you need to kill them. You can clear the post, that is a collectible feature, but that does not stop the militia to spawn back at the place. When you come back 5 minutes later, they are there again, constantly harassing you with their aggressive behaviours. With this addition you will have a hard time traveling from one point to another, while doing the same thing over and over again. Also it seems that there are limitations in because of the consoles' memory limit which may affected the way spawns and ai work.
Another feature are the safe houses. They have weapon crates, a bed to sleep and pass time and save option. I am not sure, but I think that these are the only options in the console versions of the game to save the game. So, these are important spots on the map, and like that there are many of them placed. But, in the PC version you can save your game whenever you want with a keypress, instantly. That way the save function is pretty useless. Besides that there is not much use of the safe houses. This is another interesting design idea I need to say.
Overall, I cannot recommend a game like this on a release steam price (about 50-60 dollars). For the current price which is 10 bucks it may worth a buy, but sometimes I feel I could not play this game anymore even if they would pay for me to do. It can be so disappointing and frustrating at times.

If you've played the original Sup Com, play Forged Alliance on HARD
As a Sup Com veteran having completed all three campaigns on Hard a couple of years ago in my CD, I must say, Forged Alliance starts off with a bang, literally.
I found Forged Alliance both harder and stupidly a hella lot easier compared to Sup Com in some missions. In the original, you start off with the basics, T1s and slowly progressing to T3s until you finally get to play with Experimentals. Forged Alliance starts you with everything (with an exception of 3-5 new toys per faction) available at your disposal in the very beginning. This makes sense given the context and situation of the events in the game. Yes, this means you can build Fatboys at the very first mission, and that's exactly what I did. You have more freedom in tackling with your mission objectives with the wider options you have.
Starting my first play through as UEF on Hard, I found it relatively easy after getting used to the controls. I ended up turtling until I had a couple Fatboys and an godly number of Percivals, the UEF's new T3 Bot to pretty much cake walk the mission.
The second and the fourth missions I found the hardest in all six missions (yes, there are only six missions). Reason being, for the majority of the missions, you start with your ACU only, that's it. The enemy will be constantly harassing and sending waves after waves of units at you. Grabbing a foothold at the start of the missions IS the hardest part of the missions themselves.
This is basically what I did for the entirety of my UEF playthrough on Hard. You can live off with only 2-3 Mass Extractors, create a defensive perimeter, tech up to T3 using only a single Factory and start spamming T3 Gens and Fabricators until you have enough to start massing Fatboys (15 is a good number, but there's no stopping you to go for more). From here, you can start tackling your first objective and pretty much steamroll the enemy until the mission ends.
The problem I found in Sup Com in general compared to other RTS, say Starcraft is that you have all the time in the world to tech up and spam high tier units before proceeding to your FIRST main objective. It really breaks the illusion of urgency. Another problem I found in FA is it's short! Six missions shared between all 3 factions compared to Sup Com's 18, with six "unique" missions for each faction. However, with the introduction of the Seraphim means a 4th faction with a whole new box of toys to play with, but unfortunately, there is no campaign for the Seraphim.
Although Sup Com in general is a slower paced game with battles that could last for hours, the ability to change the game speed is an AMAZING addition. Because why wait for half an hour to create a nuke silo when you can speed the game up to +10 and wait for only like 30 seconds? Players with slower reaction times can perhaps play the game on lower game speed whereas players who find the game pretty slow can speed it up or you can do both to mix things up.
All in all, I had a blast playing Forged Alliance and it was certainly a great addition to the game.  At $18 NZD, the price is a little too high IMHO. If you're gonna buy FA, buy the Sup Com Gold Edition instead, or better yet, buy it when it's on sale

First off, this is a gorgeous game of which I have enjoyed every minute spent on it. It is at flawed space in its timeline, like so many pre-release games, but I have been playing it for nearly its entire arc here on Steam, and it has come a long way.
I do want to note that if you have even a moderately old or underpowered machine, at this point in development you will see a lot of lag. My previous machine was a 3ghz quad core with plenty of RAM and a 970GTX, and GRAV would stutter like a nervous crying child. New generation i7, SSD, and a GTX1070 STRIX? Buttery goodness with naught a missed frame in over a solid day of gaming.
I have come to the realization that while the mechanics for better things are in place, many of the elements of this game are hollow at the moment, waiting to be filled in with better content. Too many repeated creatures, a dungeon system that feels like .HACK 1.0 with some normal maps draped on the walls, and a very linear tech progression system.
Again, an as-yet unfinished game, what one would expect from early access.
But there is inspiration here, and just the smallest tweaks in various areas would elevate it higher. There is a definite sense of accomplishment when you progress along the tech line. The Monocycle instantly expands your reach in the homeworld. The glider makes it more interesting to scale the heights of the landscape. The Jetpack lets you reach what before just looked like pretty environment decorations, often with prizes letting you know the devs wanted you to get here all along.
There has been a definite attention to balancing what you get when, as some of the later game content has been made accessible much earlier, like the buggy, and all that may change again and again before we get to the end deal.
My primary complaints lie in a lack of content that the game seems to be leaning toward but just isn't in place yet, a void with haphazzard placeholder. The many clones of Wei Wei the Weary Wanderer speak indicate some idea at a narrative to keep driving you forward, but no actual semblance of it except a tutorial goal window exist at this time. We don't know why our character is where they are, we just are. The only goal you have from the outset is basically 'Don't die' and 'Don't starve'; only the basics of a openworld survival game are yet here.
At this point, I can recommend this game if you enjoy the aspects of resource gathering, base building (which comes with its own odd frustrations at this stage of implementation), and watching your character grow as you ford through the various available class options.

Kind of obvious, but the better your cards the better you will do. The more packs you open, a higher chance of better cards, so there is a pay to win model in there. However for free to play, the drafting mode is a leveler and when playing with your own collection in ranked you progress through 5 leagues, bronze, silver, gold, platinum, diamond; once you get promoted you cannot go down a league until the next season. This brilliantly puts you with people at around your level in terms of skill/deck. Currently with 80 hours or so played, I am in the top third of the gold league.
The more I play the game the more I am impressed by the nuances in strategy in both building a deck and using it during gameplay.
I cant recommend enough trying this out one evening, put a few hours into it for free just playing with the preset decks to see how it works and I'm confident that I will come across you in one of the leagues in couple of weeks!

I’ll recommend the game for those that think a strategy-card game, that incorporates roleplay elements in a Slavic fantasy world could be interesting for them. This game really has the “Just five more minutes…” kind of feel for me. Where I end up playing far longer than I probably should have into the night.
Let’s get the negatives out of the way first. And they are just negatives for me, they might be positives for you. I feel there is a bit too much randomness in combat at times. Since if the enemy or your unit attacks the card to the right or left can often end up being the main deciding factor in combat, or the enemy getting a type of bonus damage can be devastating, it feels like you have less control at times. I have tried reloading after a battle that ended in crashing defeat, because I thought, I might be able to win, if I tried a slightly different tactic. Only to see the enemy’s strongest monster having a different type of damage, which turned the fight overall into a cakewalk.
Then there are the skulls, which is the way the game shows a challenge’s difficulty. They feel wildly inconsistent at times. One group at a certain level might wipe the floor with my party, while another won’t even be able to injure a single person, despite having the same skull-level.
But while playing the game those problems don’t really feel that big.
On to the more positive side of things. I like the pantheon, where you pick your main deity. Each with different personalities, and they even open special approaches to some events out in the world.
I also find the world, and especially the demons interesting. Much like with the witcher series, it introduces me to some creatures from folklore and mythology, that I am just not familiar with along with some of the more common fantasy species. I do wish you could start off as something else than human. You can get other types of creatures in your party, either through events or the type of building materials, but you will still be a human village. But I think it could be fun to just start out as an orc or elf village. Maybe in a sequel or DLC.
Last a little side note. This might be due to my own stupidity, but the inventory menu wasn’t so logical for me at first. Moving many stacks of materials from one group to the other was very slow, until I, mostly by accident, discovered I could do it by just holding shift as I clicked. :P

This game is fantastic.  It's like Oregon Trail meets Age of Wonders.  The beginning of any game is very fraught with worry and peril, but you're rewarded for carefully choosing encounters.  This game's for thoughtful players looking for a 4X game with a heavy story focus.

It's a rogue-like turn based strategy game with a focus on crafting.  There is a huge variety of materials, weapons/armor, and underlying stats for all of your characters.  Some unique stats include things like Traps, Attractiveness, Stealth, Perception and a ton others, and they each have their own roles to play in different battle types.  In some encounters you can choose to outright Fight (favoring stats like armor, strength etc) or do a Social challenge, where your individual stats with Speech and Attractiveness play a large roll.  If you see the card based battle system and are hesitant about buying this due to the complexity, don't be.  The tutorial is really helpful and the in game links to YouTube are clutch.
The lore is also well written and very interesting.  I have completed a few runs now (although none with completing all 3 main quests) and I think on average I have completed about 15% of the events, which means there are a ton of events I haven't even seen yet.  If you have played Eador before (highly recommended, see my review) you'll appreciate the wider range of random events to help keep the game fresh.
The only thing I would have liked to see is a small amount of individual character customization beyond just what to equip. The ninja-quick review: A rollercoaster in both thrills and its odd pacing, Strider is a very fast paced Metroidvania that remembers mechanically a lot of what makes the original good while adding some new features and not getting -too- carried away with  it.
For a review more the length of the titular character's ridiculous scarf, I'll start with the negatives.  First off, the game is awkwardly paced and short.  I beat it in four hours and change, and four hours is the speedrun time- I certainly spent a fair amount of time dicking around as well.  There's a couple sections where you need to open specific doors or activate objects and the game takes you on a tangential objective.  One such situation actually has you go on no fewer than four tangential objectives at the same time, a cascading necessary sidequest involving multiple boss fights.  If anything feels like being given the runaround, it's this part of the game, but there's also some other points that feel like backtracking.  The difficulty is also a bit all over the place; if two enemies surround strider the game you can do almost nothing, but otherwise you're all but invulnerable.  Some of the special abilities are easy to forget about and a bit awkward, and the elemental switching is almost always a very black-and-white choice (since only one weapon type breaks the majority of shields and does like double damage).
There's also some things that are more middling.  Metroidvania format has its ups and downs.  There's a lot of secrets to collect, but almost none of them are even that helpful, and although it's kind of cool that the special kunai and dash elemental abilities are hidden, keeping them hidden means they can't be all that fantastic and sure enough they're pretty middling.  Another hit-and-miss thing is the art design.  It's as flashy as it should be, but the models sometimes make it difficult to determine what's a plaform or what's going on at all at times.  Finally, the music didn't really do anything for me, and the story/dialogue is straight out of console generation 4.
The good bits of Strider are the speed, breadth of movement and attack directions, the controls are awesome besides the fairly uneeded specials, there's exactly the right number of enemy types and bosses for the game's length and they're matched well to your abilities, bigass levels that are enjoyable to explore and some ridiculous setpieces to blow up.  If you want to play a fast platformer where you cut half the level and slide through robots by the dozen to get to crazy bossfights- I mean, it does it.  It does it really well.  I didn't find a single bug or stutter, nothing.  Fifteen bux is an okay price even with the length but it's gonna go on sale, and if this interests you at all you should get it then.
