A difficult recommendation.
The Westport Incident tries to hit the same trigger "Papers, Please" did and show how difficult it is to operate within a repressive dictatorship. You are taking the role of a newspaper editor who has to basically choose between being a government mouthpiece, and keeping the paper running while being complicit in the government repression; or reporting the news in a more truthful manner, but by doing so putting not just the paper, but also your employees at risk.
Gameplay consists of choosing which articles to put in the paper, how to present them, and who to write the article. For example you may get an article about a bombing. Articles can be roughly separated in two categories: politics and fluff.
Fluff is without risk, but doesn't do much for your paper's popularity.
Politics is where the risk is.
If you are fully loyal throughout it's easy to complete the game, although you do end up supporting a totalitarian regime.
If you decide to be disloyal (and report the truth), you will run into several problems. The most clear one is that if you become too disloyal to the government before time runs out, the paper is closed and the game ends. But even if you try to balance this somewhat by occasionally reporting something with a government slant or publishing fluff instead, you may still risk your employees as they all have their own suspicion meter. Allow this to go too high and they are arrested and you will have one fewer article you can print each week.
Increasing the difficulty further is that your employees have different political leanings, a Loyalist supporter will not be happy to write against his government, for example.
The various loyalties and suspicion rates make the game pretty difficult to balance. There are several possible endings, and it will require multiple playthroughs to unlock them all.
While I like the concept a lot, I have a few issues with this game and they hold it back from being a new classic like its obvious inspiration Papers, Please.
First off, the various mechanics are not really explained. Unless you read this or other reviews, your first playthrough you will likely have no idea about the different employees' suspicion meters, and their arrest will come at a complete surprise. The game has a too brief tutorial and it doesn't tell you about this at all. It is also not clear exactly how the advertisement works, and if this even matters. Each district has two subjects it cares about, but does that mean you are wasting advertisement points by still placing adverts in a district if your paper doesn't include a subject they like? The game doesn't tell you this.
Second, the presentation. There is no voice acting outside of the intro, there is very little animation, and the game simply does not look that impressive. You will be spending most of your time on the same screen just sliding things around with no variation.
For $/€ 10 as it currently priced on Steam I expect more from a game, but at a discount price I can recommend it.
Pick it up if you like Papers, Please, or the idea of working as a newspaper censor in a totalitarion society.

It's an interesting concept, but not much of a game. A single playthrough should not take more than an hour, and I can't see much reason to replay it because it's a bit tedious and empty, with no real sense of control over outcomes, no outside system to affect, no personal life to manage, and no plot. My point isn't that games need to have these things, but it helps to have something of substance, doesn't it? This is a bit like solitaire without the replay value.
You alternate between choosing which stories to run, and viewing little cutscenes. This happens about 12 times.
In the cutscenes, the employees gossip lightly about their realistically depressing personal lives in a way that has no clear connection to anything you've done. These cutscenes are ignorable and don't really carry a lot of plot or character.
Editing has a few wrinkles which don't really do anything. Mostly, it is just choosing stories. Occasionally you might strike out a paragraph to avoid making the government or whoever angry. This has no obvious cost, there is no particular information to consider; it's just an arbitrary choice. If the person you give a story to refuses to write it, then you just choose another. Makes you want to hire an understudy who you can just hand the stories to, and they will shop the stories around until each one has a writer. Then there are the letters you receive, but can't read unless you drag them to exactly the right part of the screen.
After each cycle, you get a little feedback about how the papers sold and how they shifted public opinion, for all the difference it seems to make.
After the last cycle, you get different ending texts which might reflect your choices. Or maybe not, it's not very clear.  I think I'll skip replaying this for achievements which just meant that I sat in the chair a few more hours like this one.

While $9.99 USD is a tad steep for a game that can be played through in under an hour, it is a good introduction to the world of Westport and an experimentation in games that focus on censorship, writing, and the power of the press. There just needs to be

The Westport Independent has an interesting concept but it isn't backed up by its gameplay.
You are the editor of an independent paper and in 12 weeks the loyalist government will shut you down and enstate their own propaganda newspapers. What you must do is choose which articles are printed each week and which of your writers will write them. You can choose the headline of each article and delete any paragraphs in the articles. After a few in game weeks you also get to choose which articles get the front page and how much of your marketing budget to put into the four areas of the country. This is very simple and it basically tells you where to put your money. Moreover, there are only 2 headlines to pick for each article and a maximum of 4 paragraphs to censor.
Each member of your group has a name and a sliver of a backstory, with information about whether they support the rebels of the loyalists. They also each have a comfort meter which will decrease if you force them to write articles they disagree with.
You really have to make your own goals in this game. You choose whether to publish articles about celebrities, industry or articles that praise or disparage the government. Each article you chose will affect your paper's popularity, the government's suspicion of you and the public's opinion on the rebels and the loyalists.
My problem with the game stems from the fact that there is no objective, no goals to reach for. You have to set your own. Do you want the public to support the rebels or the government, or will you focus on celeb gossip to sell papers. Normally I enjoy games where you make your own fun but there was little motivation to do anything in The Westport Independent. Personally I found it easy to sell papers as long as you put a bit of everything in and by the end my government suspision was ridiculously high with no negative effects apart from a few letters warning me not to badmouth the loyalists.
Your staff members can also be taken out by government officials if they write too much rebel propaganda but I found it hard to care as they have only barebones backstories and barely any personality. On top of that they're literally faceless, only being presented in silouhette. They do chat amongst each other in between levels but nothing really separated the characters other than two liked the loyalists and two liked the rebels. On that note, I found it hard to care for the paper as well. Sure I wanted it to do well but only because then there'd be no more levels to play. As for the rebels and the government I think the game needs to be less black and white and have a few more gray areas. In all the articles the government is clearly shown as evil and despotic or the paragon of kindness, should you choose the other headline. There's no middle ground and it makes it hard to want to support them in any way.
I gather that the point of the game is to make you endure the struggles of censorship in a world where your government is truly evil but the game fails to make this difficult and therefore it lacks impact. I managed to come up with a paper that was popular all over the country with litle government interference while disparaging them every chance I got.
The game ends very anticlimactically. You get a written description of what's now happening in each district of the country but it doesn't feel like anything has been achieved. This is a consequence of the lack of any objectives.
The game isn't all bad though. It's short and has a decent bit of music in.

Yes, the game is short, but I don't think that's necessarily a point against it. That being said, for a game that is short, it's incredibly repetitive. I only played through it once, and even though I only got 1/5 of the achievements, I didn't feel like going back for more, or to attempt to get other ones. Even in one playthrough I found myself getting the same article over and over again, which really killed the realness of the world when, after dropping one article in my rejected bin, it just came back again in the next "phase".
Additionally, it felt like most of the time nothing was happening. I got letters from the government once or twice, and a letter from the rebels once near the end, but it never felt engaging, or like I was making any meaningful choices. the level of Loyalty vs. Rebellion, Trust vs. Suspicion, and Popularity in the various sectors never seem to really mean anything, since you're not managing finances of your paper, and those levels dont seem to affect what kind of articles you get.
It would have been much more interesting if, once you reached a certain level of popularity, The Rebels and Loyalists gave you slanderous or false articles to put in your paper, or popularity in one sector meant that you got insider news from your fans. Personally I ended up pandering to the Southern districts, but that choice never meant anything. No doubt your actions affect the ending you get, but it would have been more rewarding if those choices were actually reflected while you played.
Westport Independent is not a bad game. It's an interesting premise mixed with a tried and true Papers Please artstyle, although the choice to emulate that might not have been in the game's favor. I was suddenly aware of how low the stakes felt when compared with Papers Please--the anxiety of not being able to keep my family alive was much more intense than seeing my suspicion bar rise a little. The insinuation that "your editors will follow you but don't expect them to die for you" is also odd, since aside from them sometimes resisting writing an article they never seem to care one way or the other about what you're printing.
The most disappointing thing about Westport is that it really doesn't offer many moral choices, and it doesn't have anything to say. It's a commentary on censorship in the media that doesn't seem to say much other than "this is a thing that happens, and media is important". Unfortunately, can't reccomend.

Unfortunately, I can not recommend this game, even though I was hoping it'd be good.
As many others have mentioned, it seems quite similar to "Papers,please" (a game I really liked a lot), and I think that's due to
- the old school graphics which look pretty much like a C64 game. However, it doesn't matter much, as Papers, Please proved (even though I think it should be obvious) that a game doesn't need triple A graphics and can be fun even when it looks very outdated, as long as the GAME is good!
- The theme... the story is set in a region/country with a quite oppressive government, and you have to play along with the rules or suffer harsh consequences
- The fact that you have to decide a lot whether you DO play by the rules, or try to be rebellious.
And I think the game COULD have been fun. However... please take a look at the amount of time I played. That's one and  a quarter playthrough...
Yes.
Uh huh, I am serious. I finished the game in what, 33 or 38 minutes? I can't for the life of me understand why there are only 12 "rounds". 12 weeks where you put together a newspaper with 4 articles once per week.
You have different authors, some more in line with the regime, others rather rebellious. You decide whether you print news about politics and spin them to make the government look nice and caring, or try to tell people the truth.
For my first playthrough, I tried to satisfy the government just to see how that'd go. And I finished the game after less than 40 minutes. SO I figured, "Ok", maybe this is supposed to be played several times with different decisions.
However, the replayability suffers because everything stays pretty much the same...your editors, their cutscenes in between weeks (even though they do refer sometimes to decisions you made, many of them stayed the same the second time I played), the headlines/stories.
If they at least had put in randomly generated editors, so you'd have SOME variety when starting over. If they had put a pool of possible stories. I saw the exact same ones in my second game, so even though the game is short, I totally lost interest in replaying during, I think, week 4 of game 2. I had tried to "rebel" against the government this time, but with THAT much repetition, it felt dull.
I think this game COULD have been cool had they put in more randomly generated stuff. More variety. An increasing difficulty (like Papers please, where each day, a new thing to watch out for would be added or changed). More "time". Why only 12 rounds? This feels like a demo for a much bigger game, but sadly, that's all there is.
Even on sale, I don't think the game offers enough for about 5 EUR, not when there are games with more content and depth for like 99 cents. This had the potential to be good or at least decent, but now its a demo-sized game that feels as if the devs started with a great idea and then either lost interest, ran out of ideas or had to meet a deadline and finished the game in a rather basic shape.
Too bad, I would have enjoyed a Papers,please type game with different story and mechanics (newspapers instead of a customs officer), but this is just too little content, gameplay and mechanics. Try it if it's on sale for a buck or two, but I don't think this is worth 5-10 EUR.

Pretty good 2d hack'n'slash metroidvania.
You run around several different locations hacking down enemies with your sword, killing bosses, and gaining upgrades that allow you to access previously inaccessible locations.  You'll start off weak and grow more powerful with every upgrade including more health, more energy, long range attacks, etc.  Enemies and bosses have tactics and weaknesses that you learn and exploit.  There's not really much of a story to the game, you're there to assassinate the baddie, that's pretty much it.  Characters aren't really explored and are cliche for the most part.  Expect the dialogue to be not so good.  Game is pretty much constant action/exploration which makes it enjoyable.
The game does have several issues.  The biggest is probably the wall grapple controls.  You can attach to almost every wall/ceiling in the game and move around.  Getting off of these can be problematic at times.  You'll press the jump button to detach and instead he'll keep on hanging there.  The game automatically moves you up platforms if you get to the edge of them instead of waiting for a prompt from you to do so.  This can get annoying at times if you're trying to get close to the edge of a platform without wanting to go up on it.
The second problem is that the difficulty is inconsistent.  I played on hard and while I found the very beginning to be sufficiently difficult, it got easier from there, especially once you get the first 2-3 health upgrades pretty quickly.  Some areas are overabundant in health pickups & killing enemies gives you a little health back as well.  Save points recover all missing health.  There's occasionally an area or two where the difficulty spikes for a little, but not too often.  Once you learn the basics of enemies, they'll usually give you little problems.   Later on, you can usually just run by enemies and mostly ignore them.  Bosses also suffer from the same problem.  There're 2-3 that are pretty tough and will probably kill you a time or two until you learn from your mistakes and win, but others are incomprehensibly easy.  The Pooh Sisters will barely put up a struggle and will probably only take down a fraction of your health before you slaughter them.  I beat both the final boss and his alternate form without dying once, and I arrived at the final boss with only about 40% of my total health.
The game can get a touch repetitive as you'll be fighting most of the same enemies throughout with occasional palette swaps which grant them different health/damage/special abilities/weaknesses/etc.  Would've been nice to have more enemy variety, though enemies do use different weaponry (Rifles, Snipers, Shotguns, Rockets, Machine guns, etc) which do make fights feel different.
You don't unlock the quick travel points until about 60-70% of the way through the game and the most that any one area will have is 1.  Some areas don't have any.  This can make backtracking for upgrades/pickups a little annoying later on when you've got all the special abilities.  Especially since some areas are relatively sizable and could take 5+ minutes to run through.  Most 'essential' stuff is usually somewhere close by where you find a new special ability.  It's usually only the unlockable art/intel/character info that are far off somewhere, so it'll only be really annoying for people trying to 100% the game.
Graphics are fine, music is hit and miss but is decent enough for the most part.  Didn't run into any bugs/crashes at any point.  Most of the games problems are minor points, though I would have really liked the game to be much more challenging, especially the bosses.  It's a solid entertaining game.

I gave this a good try, but i just can't like it.
The gameplay is mediocre, if you're expecting a Devil May Cry or a God of War - the combat just doesn't deliver. It's a button masher, and I couldn't make it into anything more, no matter how much I tried to use special abilities and attacks, (and I have plenty of experience with action games.) Controls were fine with a controller, (I can't speak for M&B - i didn't try), but it was just boring.
As far as art assets and story go... Someone compared this to Lynch.. This is NOT Lynch. Lynch has a soul, and a certain depth... This just felt like someone found an equation for surreal art and simply followed it without actually believing in it. Random stories, obscure humor, characters that have no explanation of why they are there and who are they really, just a ton of disconnected strings all over that don't make up a cohesive whole. I mean, maybe some people are into that, but I'm not, so I can't recommend this. I love Magritte, and Lynch, and in their surreal there is at least something that ties everything together. This game is more like someone just colored a canvas black, added a big red circle, then decided to add a robot arm, and then thought let's throw a unicorn in there for the hell of it, because why not.
I guess I'll give this game some points, but only because it's at least something I haven't seen before. And there were some decent comic-book-style cutscene shots that were visually well delivered, I guess. But overall - it was a pretty mediocre ride on most accounts.

From the Pacific islands to the African savannah, Far Cry 2 is a big departure from the Crytek-developed original. 2004’s Far Cry showcased Crytek’s CryEngine, which helped create the excellent Crysis. CRY. But Far Cry 1 was a first-person shooter that felt more like a tech demo than a game and was later remade into the much more enjoyable, but less pretty, Far Cry Instincts for the Xbox. This game was developed by Ubisoft Montréal, a development powerhouse under the umbrella of Ubisoft who owned the publishing rights to Far Cry and have now taken it upon themselves to develop the sequel.
Shifting the setting has brought about a new style of shooter. Gone are the feral monsters and Hawaiian shirts and added are realistic conflicts with grounded characters and a host of protagonists to choose from although playing as them takes away their voice. Far Cry 2 is a far cry from Far Cry and it probably could’ve become a new franchise.
Story
The story begins with a choice of mercenaries to play as, all with interesting backgrounds but without their own voice, or even seeing their face, means their personality is never explored. It’s an odd thing for the game to include this option as is it doesn’t change the experience and it could’ve been just one voiceless, faceless protagonist, ala Half-Life. Although, depending on your character, the other characters can become your buddies, which is the game’s ally system. Your buddies can save your life when you health runs out by dragging you to safety and giving you a gun to fend off attackers. But they can also get injured themselves giving you the choice to save them by giving them syrettes or by ending their life with a bullet, an overdose or just leaving them to die. But when they die, they die, preventing you from completing certain side missions or being able to rely on them when you fall in battle.
The setting is an unnamed, central African country whose government and civilians have all but left leaving two opposing factions and you as a mercenary, brought in to kill The Jackal, an arms dealer supplying both sides. Most of the time, the dialogue isn’t very dramatic and the voice actors tend to mumble through their lines so the narrative didn’t leave much impact, despite being based on Joseph Conrad’s ‘Heart of Darkness’.
Gameplay
Exploring the open world of the African setting offers you gorgeous vistas of the savannah, lush tropical forests, harsh heats of the desert and extensive rivers through valleys and lakes. Far Cry 2 also uses its first-person perspective to the fullest in the best use of the viewpoint since Breakdown. Every single action from getting into a vehicle to switching to the gunner position is smoothly animated with realistic motions. When health is low, an animation shows the character healing themselves in a variety of ways from twisting dislocated thumbs back into place, removing bullets and shrapnel or patting out fire followed by injecting a syrette. All of this takes place in front of your eyes and immerses you deep into the game. Far Cry 2 never wants to break this immersion with navigation handled by an in-game map and GPS that can be brought up whilst on the move and the HUD only fades into visibility during firefights similar to The Chronicles of Riddick.
The guns are varied, beautifully designed and animated and can be purchased, along with upgrades, using diamonds found throughout the game. More guns can also be unlocked by preventing convoys of trucks that transport the goods from reaching their destination. The enemy AI can be unpredictable and possess a strange habit of chasing and attacking you even if you’re not provoking any of them. They also respawn at checkpoints even if you turn back only after a few minutes. But the unpredictability of the AI coupled with the variety of attack means the narrative can be created in game based on your actions. The loneliness of the setting made this internal narrative feel very personal and created some of the most intense stalk and pounce gameplay I’ve ever played in a shooter. It was this emergent style of narrative gameplay that overcame the poorly scripted story.
The fire-spreading mechanic also created a risk/reward strategy that could slowly move enemies into tight groups either to engulf them in flames or to kill them with one well-aimed grenade. The risks involved included being trapped with your buddies in the inferno or losing the escape vehicle. Vehicles cover ground, sea and air and control quite responsively. Thankfully, as distances between objectives can be extensive. In certain truce zones, you will be amongst enemies, who will not attack, unless provoked, with your weapon held close to your chest. It’s seems like a small detail but it’s the small details that really added to the immersion. Guns picked up from enemies will also degrade a lot faster than purchased weapons as they rust from the humidity and collect dust from the deserts. This was an interesting mechanic to add and it really made me think about how to manage my armoury including storing additional weapons in my safe houses. Malaria didn’t add much to the experience as all it catered for was to occasionally push a button when prompted. This feature could’ve included more nuance or in my opinion just gutted completely.
Technical
The graphics are fantastic with great lighting from the day/night cycle. The sounds are greatly detailed with impactful weapons and eerie ambient sounds punctuate the loneliness. The soundtrack offers African-inspired music that helps immerse you in the setting and dynamically changes depending on the action taking place on screen.
Verdict
This is one of my most treasured games. The flaws such as respawning enemy checkpoints, unprovoked attacks by factions when travelling, malaria and a sub-par story seem irrelevant compared to the pros. Far Cry 2 is so immersive that it takes on a very strong, personal, emergent narrative whilst playing and inspires scenarios and backstories in your imagination.

My review of GRIND Reborn:
The game has a job system, different jobs gives you some passive and active skills after you level them enough.

The sound is also a nuisance, music is not really good (when you can hear it) and sound effects are really annoying, every weapon has the same reload sound.
Mobs spawn is also a problem, in a planet you will see a lot of areas with none of them around and some areas where they are all clustered and fighting each others.
Basically it will take hundreds of hours just to level all jobs that's why I called this game GRIND Reborn.
I'm not against grind in some games but if I have to do it I want to sense a great feeling of accomplishment in the end, wich I doubt you'll feel in this game.
If you're interested in this game I suggest you wait until goes out of EA to see if it has changed for the better.

"Thea" is definitely good for several play-throughs, and worth the money at full price. The quest writing, the music and the voice talent are all really, really excellent. I give it 4 out of 5 stars. The game has the potential of becoming a classic, 5 stars, a really great game, if they add more quests and if they balance the early, mid- and end-game better. By the end-game, I am winning all fights/quests easily on auto-resolve, however this may be due to the AI fighting my side using the best card combos? Also, it would be great if you could start play as the other races, e.g., Orcs, Goblins, Elves and Dwarves and not always have to start as humans (this would requiring play balancing as the other races are typically stronger and end-game characters). Try it, you will like it if you like games like Civ, and especially if you like card combat games.
I have played "Thea" all the way through three times now. It took me about a day each time, but I was progressively making it harder each time.  I haven't really figured out the card combat that well, but there is a good tutorial on their wiki site. If you like card combat it looks quite interesting to try and figure out (I just have never gotten into it). Your RP characters are your "cards" and at the beginning of a engagement they are split into two decks, offense and tactical.  Playing the offense cards is obvious but playing the tactical abilities of your characters/cards takes some learning.  There is one round of laying out cards, and then two rounds or combat, and if there are still characters left, you start over again.  However, you don't have to do the card combat, as you can auto-resolve all engagements.  Once I have built up a reasonably tough "expedition" team, I mostly just auto-resolve engagements. This also makes the game go much faster, if that is your desire. 
 Below are a few things I learned on each play-through. You can start the game as many times as you want for the first turn, so try to start with at least three materials to gather within your town's zone of 7 hexes, i.e., vegetables and wood and another building material besides wood, like sandstone, clay, or granite (in that order), and herbs, leathers and/or metals are also very good. Don't leave your town undefended as you only get one town. Keep gathering and producing things as much as possible every turn. More production leads directly to more research points. Use your earned research points allocation smartly between resources you can gather (look at resource map first), crafting new items (don't pick swords if you don't have metals, etc.), and building your ten buildings. I tend to build several gardens first to attract human children and adults and destroy them later to build different buildings or better gardens (using better materials). Do craft better gathering and crafting tools as soon as possible, the better materials you use the more effective the tool/weapon/armor/shield/charm is. 
Try to construct buildings as quickly as possible (but the better materials you use the more benefits they give so try gathering those first, which means you may have to select them first with your research points, so plan ahead).  Trying the different construction materials for buildings is also fun, as some might give you access to children, Humans, Elves, Goblins, Beasts, etc., depending on the type of material you have available and use.  Or you might get a much better sword or armor by changing up the materials (three types per item).  You have an unlimited party size, so outfitting your RPG characters is lots of fun assigning weapons, armor, charms, tools, etc. There are weight constrictions (strength) on how much each character can carry, so pay attention to that when assigning armor, etc.  You have to take wood (<10) and food (as much as you can spare while leaving carrying capacity, in other words, your expedition, between its outfit, wood and food should equal about half you carry weight, so that you have capacity to carry back stuff you have gathered or gained in fights/quests). 
While building a party of mostly warriors with stats in damage, armor and shielding will work, you should also bring along other characters in your expedition(s) that have other stats (herbalism, divination, dexterity, sneak, magic, etc.), because you can solve quests not just by fighting, but also in other ways. In other words, a fight against a dragon might be 5 skulls versus 2 skulls to sneak past him if you have that skill improved on a couple of characters. I like to take a mix of fighters, hunters, a medic (so you can camp and heal while out of town), and any other beings you collect along the way through quests (e.g., Witches, Humans, Elves, Goblins, Beasts, Demons, Giants, Trolls, Orcs, Dwarves, etc.). Camp immediately after an engagement during which your party members were seriously wounded, or they may die. 
There are two primary quests, one for your god and the other to quell the giants, do those carefully as they are both worth extra victory points. If you play on the lowest two difficulty settings you can save before most every quest, fight, etc., that you initiate, so you can replay if you screw it up.  However engagements can be initiated during the AI's turn, and they frequently are, sometimes several in a row, so save often. If you play on the last two settings, you do not get to save then you permanently suffer the consequences of the quest results if you lose (cursed, killed, wounded, sick, etc.). On the other hand, since many of the quests repeat, most of the fun is in the first play-through when you don't know which paths work best to choose when answering the quest's questions.  There are different consequences (I.e., better rewards or more painful results if you choose A, B, C, or D). It is worth continuing to keep playing after you have "won" to build up the victory points for the total for that god (there are 8 in all that give you different starting benefits).
When crafting items, there are typically two types of ingredients and one catalyst.  You have different choices of materials for the first ingredient and then again for the second ingredient (and sometimes they overlap, e.g., you could use wood and sandstone, or wood and wood). The catalyst only affects the quality (but only after you have built the smithy, so only use wood until you do). Coal and gold make good catalyst. Never destroy items, instead break them down into their components to reuse, preferably in town so you don't have to carry them around, but you will have to do this at times while on an expedition to keep below your carrying capacity. Your party eats one food per turn and burns one wood per camping turn (to stay warm and cook food). They don't burn wood while moving but they do eat food while moving. You have to camp to gather materials and to heal (very important as new characters are slow to be attracted to your town in the early game). You can move 5 hexes per turn, but there are terrain affects (though apparently just for movement and not for combat).  You can barely move or cannot move at all, if one of your party is carrying too much weight. Inventory control for the expedition party is important, compare items and disassembly the poor quality ones. Keep an eye on the weight of an item as well as its other stats, as a level 20 axe may look great, but not if it weights 200 pounds and none of your low level characters can carry it. Warriors can carry a two-handed sword in one hand and a shield in the other, while Dwarves can carry a two-handed hammer in one hand and a shield in the other (and you would think that Orcs could then carry a two-handed axe, but they can't, go figure). Anyway, you can tell I enjoyed the game. Have fun!

Disclosure: Key provided by publisher for review at
The Westport Independent started life as a gamejam entry that the developers thought was promising enough to expand upon. Players are tasked with managing a newspaper under a dictatorship and are forced to choose between the truth and censorship.
CONTROLS (3.5/5)
Controlling a newspaper is surprisingly easy if The Westport Independent is to be believed. Players will receive articles and letters and simply need to drag an article to the center of the screen, click to remove lines or change a headline, and then toss it into a writer’s folder.
Everything is simple and functional and clearly designed around mobile controls first. Some elements of the UI could use work, as establishing if a story will count as coverage in certain topics can be a little hard to tell until you’re in later steps.
GRAPHICS/SOUND (3.5/5)
The game is clearly meant to evoke some of the movies of the ‘40s and ‘50s, and it mostly succeeds doing so. Everything is black and white, and what little is seen outside of the newspaper office appears to be a blend of noir and art-deco. Things are kept relatively clean and simple, and I enjoyed the ever shifting newspaper cover you can get depending on how you handle advertising.
Audio is similarly simple and drenched in film noir. A handful of what appear to be public domain tracks that have made their way into a dozen noirs in the past, or ones attempting to mimic them, are present. There’s not much else to speak of beyond that light soundtrack, though the production values for the intro propaganda reel are great.
GAMEPLAY (2.5/5)
In the fictional city of Westport set in a vaguely American country, the government has effectively decided to end freedom of the press. In 12 weeks, a bill will be going into effect turning the titular newspaper into a government-owned propaganda factory. Fortunately in 12 weeks you can affect a lot to change the world around you.
Players are tasked each week with writing a few stories, but even with the law yet to take effect, the government won’t sit idly by if you libel them by printing the truth. And so it is suggested perhaps to edit out embarrassing details, such as the cost of a statue honoring the President.
While you can comply with their requests, you can also spin the narrative against them by leaving that information in or tweaking a headline. Westport is struggling between two factions, the Loyalists and the Rebels, and the paper can help sway the population to one side or the other.
After deciding what stories to print, you’ll need to assign them to your writers. Each writer has their own personality and opinions, so a hardcore rebel might not like printing pro-government drivel. However, there’s also suspicion mechanics at play, so if you’ve been letting him write a bunch of Rebel stories, forcing a puff piece into his hands might save his hide.
Lastly, players will get to decide how to layout the paper. Each story has one of four attributes, and the placement of stories closer to the front page will strengthen them. In turn, each attribute appeals to certain sections of the city, and you’ll need to decide who to market the paper to depending on your content. The district that likes society and crime news might not buy your paper if it’s a bunch of celebrity gossip, after all.
A lot of this may sound good on paper, but the execution is a bit lacking. First off, the game is extremely short, and so it can be hard to really get a feel for the world of The Westport Independent. Everything is also a bit too vague.
Your reporters, for instance, have little actual character, and so caring about their fate or comfort is hard. Half of the ending goes into what happened to them, but I couldn’t tell you anything about most of them other than if they were Loyalists or Rebels. They felt like resources more than characters.
Similarly, there are often few interesting choices to make in the articles. Often the headline is the big thing, offering one that’s clearly offensive to one side or the other. The body of the articles is typically three or four sentences long, and a lot of the time articles didn’t feel like they had content worth removing or keeping in that would affect much. More in-depth articles that allow players to clearly shape the narrative were desperately needed.
In the end, the bill is coming, and you’ll get endings depending on the status of each of the four districts in town. Rebels will riot, Loyalists will party. There are a decent amount of alternate endings to achieve, and some meta-game goals like attempting to get all districts to be Loyalists or Rebels at once.
In these scenarios, managing your writers’ comfort, sales and government suspicion are quite a challenge, but first-time players aren’t likely to know the mechanics enough early on to seek these out, and the relatively bland first run isn’t going to intrigue many to return.
OVERALL (2.5 /5)
The Westport Independent is a great concept, but there’s not enough follow through. Those looking to manage life in a dictatorship are more likely to find enjoyment in the game’s clear inspiration, Papers, Please.

First off, Far Cry 2 still looks absolutely gorgeous. Africa has never looked better in a game. You will find zebras and gazelles roaming the grasses. You will enjoy mountains, waterfalls, and canyons, travel across the small lakes, visit Pala, Sefapane, and Mosate Selao, and speed across the dirt roads to hunt for enemies.
The gunplay in Far Cry 2 is undoubtedly realistic. This is no Call of Duty; your guns behave like real ones and there is not much "running and gunning" unless you are playing on easy.  There is gun jamming and degradation, so you will need to take care of them. There are weapons for everyone. There are multiple rocket launchers, grenade launchers, pistols, machine pistols, snipers, and explosives. There is even a dart rifle and a explosive crossbow!
The missions are fun but may get boring. I would advise playing on Hardcore or Infamous difficulties because when you play on them, the game becomes much more challenging and even more realistic. There are respawning outposts with enemies, and these provide good fun since you never run out of people that are trying to kill you. Many people are not used to such a harsh game; expect everybody outside of the Ceasefire zones to try to kill you. Is that good? Your call.
There are tons of weapon upgrades and some vehicle upgrades, plus upgrades that will allow you to carry more ammunition or molotovs. The second half of the world unlocks when you complete half the missions in the game, and this second world adds new Jeeps, boats, and guns, plus new locations to explore.
Fire is my favorite part of the game because it is so well-done. The fire is better than Far Cry 3 because it was not designed to play a large role in Far Cry 3. Far Cry 2 has seasons and rain, so expect fire to work less effectively when the grass is green or there is a downpour. When the grass is dry and there is no rain, fire becomes the game changer. If I feel overwhelmed during gameplay, I may throw a molotov cocktail into some dry grass to start a (potentially massive) fire. This fire scatters enemies, forcing them to change their attack plan; if you are lucky, you may even get one to burn to death.
The audio in this game also never ceases to impress me. You can hear birds and monkeys in the trees, the wind rustling the leaves, the whine of the mounted gun as it swivels. When you are around enemies, you will hear their conversations (they sound believable). The music in this game is a nice change as it is what you would expect and African band to play.
You have malaria during the game, and it puts an interesting spin on your gameplay. You may have to wait out a malaria occurence, and this can kill you. The best tactic to do is throw a molotov and hurry to cover.
Note that it took me 30 hours to complete my first playthrough. After that, you can do a new one on a harder difficulty (feel free to change difficulty anytime you want). The ending of the game is unexpectedly deep.
All in all, this is a game like no other. Everything I said above amount to an amazing experience. This is an experience like no other that can be had, during a sale, for just $2.50.

If you love fantasy, you might like this game. If you hate fantasy, then you still might like this game.
The Book of Unwritten Tales is a point-and-click adventure very heavily inspired by fantasy works like The Lord of the Rings and Dungeons and Dragons, with a very tongue-in-cheek, self-referential sense of humor about itself. Nearly every single fantasy trope under the sun is referenced, discussed, or blatantly mocked. But rather than undermine one's enjoyment of the story or its beautifully rendered setting, this sense of humor actually helps propel the story forward.
There are a few technical hiccups which may detract from the player's immersion, but the interface is intuitive, easy to use, and the game itself doesn't require moon logic to solve any puzzles. If you enjoy traditional adventure games, epic tales of fantasy, or gut-busting comedy, then I recommend giving this one a go.

A fantastic PnC adventure for adventurers! I love the humor in the game. The references and jokes weave their way through (and sometimes are) the story, much like a Pratchett book. The characters other than the gnome have virtually no backstory, which I actually didn't miss.
The puzzles are overall very straightforward and quick, with a fairly good range of puzzle types. Walking everywhere is done well (double click on doors/roads to skip walking across a room, and a quick-travel map system is employed in a few sections) and the developers did put in holding spacebar to show clickable objects.
It was interesting to me to solve puzzles by swapping the playable characters and using their individual characteristics. The gnome is short, the human is strong, etc. Having to employ two or three characters to solve certain puzzles adds a level of complexity that I really enjoyed.
It's a pretty short game (I clocked in at just over 12 hours for a full playthrough, some of which was idling) which is on par with most other PnC adventures I've played.
Very much recommend this game for anyone who likes the genre, Pratchett-esque references and has a sense of humor.

is a sandbox gardening simulator with a great soundtrack and a diverse selection of gorgeous plants to nurture. Caring for the plants is unrealistically easy (just water until sated, and if you want to, sing to them!) and my enjoyment has been primarily derived from watching all the plants mature and come together to make a beautiful potted garden. Every bite-sized session is a calming, mindful experience. It gets a
from me!
The player starts off with a free starter pack of various plants. A random free plant is given to the player once a week, and a store that sells every plant for at most $0.40-ish (and at the cheapest, <$0.10) is always available to visit. A cool thing about storing unplanted seeds is that they're actually kept in your Steam inventory, and can be traded with other
players for trading cards, CS:GO gear, other plants, or anything else Steam allows for trading. The community is also very generous and has been known to give free plants to those who ask.
Plants live for as long as you can keep them watered (but not
watered!). Since the plants grow in real-time, they die after a real-world week of neglect, give or take. If you anticipate being away from your computer for a long period of time, a free "vacation mode" is available in the nursery that freezes the plants' growth and thirst until the next time you turn the game on.
Any unwanted plant, dead or alive, can be discarded by double-clicking its "lift/move" button (it actually turns into a "discard" button once first clicked, and turns back into a "lift/move" button once the plant has been placed back into the pot, but lots of folks don't notice because the button doesn't draw much attention to this change). Living plants are placed in an unseen vast garden distinct from the garden the player is responsible for. Dead plants are used as compost. The game has three achievements for discarding enough mature living plants, and to me, it incentivizes trying out new garden layouts with all the nursery plants. This keeps the game fresh and dynamic.
The only complaint I have with the game is that there's a persistent bug in the game's code that wilts my plants' flowers immediately after the flowers mature. I can only admire the flowers while they're still sprouting and aren't yet mature. This problem was ostensibly fixed for most players months ago, but I'm personally still seeing this bug and I'm not aware of any fixes for it. Also, there is a cute snail slithering around the pot that you can interact with as if it were a plant. I personally love the snail, but some nitpicky players don't, because they know that in real life, snails are bad for gardens. I ask those players to suspend disbelief. This is a nice snail! It won't hurt your plants. It is your friend.
In all, this is a delightfully exaggerated gardening simulator that'll probably lower your blood pressure. It's free, and I definitely recommend trying it out to anyone who's looking for a zen/detox game!

Since GRAV is in Early Access, I can't really review it. I can assess, based on its current state, whether or not the game is priced fairly given the amount of content provided.
As a single player adventure, I’d say GRAV is worth a look as long as you catch it on a sale of 50% or more. The developers update frequently, but the game still has a long way to go in terms of content. If you’re the type who likes to explore every nook and cranny of a game without any real objectives, then GRAV may be for you.
If the RPG tag on the store caught your eye, be advised that there’s no real RPG elements beyond changing your job class. In it’s current state, GRAV is a pretty sci-fi survival title that is purely sandbox.
If you’re looking for something to play with your buds, but don’t have the patience to hunt each other down, I’d wait until the game develops further. There is no friend’s list, no icon on a map that will show you where a friend is relative to your current location whether or not you’re in a party, and no sort of intuitive way to tell where in the game world you are or are headed. If you and your friend(s) are patient and willing to stumble around blindly until you run into each other, go for it.
Either way, seeing as the price won’t increase upon full release, waiting for further development may be your best bet.

I never got into MyTEAM last year simply because I just flat did not like 2k17's default gameplay and had to use my custom sliders whenever I played. This year, the default gameplay is the best it's been since 2k14. (More on that later.) Team building, however, is a pain. Pack odds are terrible and are obviously designed to make you spend more money on VC to buy more packs. Any additions you may notice to the mode are simply not enough over last years offerings to keep things interesting. I'll pass on this mode, thank you.
- MyGM (6/10 - What's Old is New Again)
So 2k apparently decided that the cringe worthy dialogue of the MyCAREER mode was so great that they needed to fill another mode with this nonsense. In "The Next Chapter" you take control of a former NBA player who blew out his knee after scoring 36 points in the 2011 Western Conference Finals on the Dallas Mavericks. Now having moved past your playing career, you take control of a team of your choosing and decide how to run them from the present to the future.
The concept sounds promising, but talking to the original story characters in this mode is downright painful. The owner that you talk to at the start of the mode is incredibly awkward and it's something that you'll never get used to. (Especially since he's gone after about 10 games and a new owner buys the team.)
The flip side is that the actual NBA players and coaches in this mode are extremely bland and generic so that their lines can fit for any team that you pick.
If you don't care about the story, then you don't have to worry, as it's not nearly as intrusive as the MyCAREER mode. Also, there's no terrible voice acting in this mode, only text that can be skipped if you so please.
All in all, not too bad, but definitely not as great as 2k was hyping it up to be.
- MyLEAGUE (9/10 - An Untouched Masterpiece)
Given the fact that 2k is adament that story is the wave of the future, I'm thankful that my personal favorite mode in 2k is untouched.
OK, so it's not completely untouched. It keeps all the same things as last year like team relocation and rule changes. However, it also has a handy analytics tool that will help you to see which players will help your team the most.
There are also more teams to choose from if you want to use the classic or all-time teams.
If you want to play some kind of season mode, this is the place for you to go.
- PlayNow (9/10 - From Worst to First)
Let's not mince words, 2k17's gameplay with default sliders was simply terrible.
2k18 however, fixes a lot of the problems that 2k17 had.
^Dribble moves have impact, but now drain more stamina, meaning that you can still feel like a legend by mixing up defenders as Allen Iverson without just spamming moves left and right for 23 out of 24 seconds.
^Shooting again feels nice, and threes go in about as often as they should, though non-stretch big men still hit a few too many.
^Players actually MOVE when on offense or defense, though it's still not quite what it should be.
^Defenders miss less assignments than before but get confused on when to help or double team.
^Players who are fast can actually beat slower players up the court due to the new animation system.
^Garbage timeout adjustments menu from 2k17 with the whole "Right Stick Geometry Class" is replaced with a much easier system to use.
^Tons of new classic teams and the brand new All-Time teams add alot to the vanilla roster without the need for downloading custom ones. (Major players like Charles Barkley, Reggie Miller, Moses Malone, and others are notably absent however)
=Losing the ball in traffic occurs less often than in 2k17, but still happens far too frequently.
=It is now rather difficult to hit green releases, this makes shooting actually feel better.
=Commentary is as good as it has been in previous 2k's. This is no longer the best commentary in the industry though, that belongs to Madden.
=Presentation is now snappier, but there's still quite a bit of downtime between quarters.
vLayups are STILL TIMED, despite what 2k said. You will still likely make a wide open layup regardless of timing, but timing it well will lead to much greater success.
- Customization (6/10 - One Step Forward, Two Steps Back)
2k is the most customizable major sports game for the last 3 years now. Specifically in the MyLEAGUE mode, which allows you to rebrand the entire league if you want.
The quick edit tool which allows you to edit stats right from the roster screen is now able to access things like badges and vitals. Meaning you can now tweak the league to your liking without going into each player individually.
The major thing that 2k does that actually makes it worse from last year's offerings on the customization front is the butchered CAP (Create-A-Player) system that you will also use if you create custom draft classes.
Shaping each player's head is a thing of the past as we return to the 2k14 next-gen way of doing it: Pick a head, pick some hair, done. While making it easier to create multiple players quickly, they are less likely to be similar to whomever you are re-creating. With the proper knowledge of the system, it still works fine. But it's far from perfect.
There are still some things absent from the Customization tools as well.
vNo Create-A-Team still, even with the MyLEAGUE tools we have!
vCreated players are forced into a cheesy nickname.
vNo option for showing all players portraits, which is a downside if you use a roster with moved players.
vHair options are still pathetic and many hairstyles look terrible.
vNo tatoos for Create-A-Player system, although MyCAREER has a setup for it.
Bottom Line: 2k is great again, as long as you don't mind ignoring the biggest mode in the game and ignore 2k's pleas for more money.

Above all else, this is a game for anyone who gets a kick out of precise controls - assuming you have a decent controller to hand. Strider's signature katana arc is in full evidence here, allowing you to let loose a pleasing flurry of attacks or charge up for a longer-range strike. Movement includes an array of somersault jumps and combine with a wall-climbing mechanic that is never too clingy (as such mechanics can sometimes be). Basically, every room of enemies can be a fun, adrenaline-filled dance - and this is just with the basic toolset the game starts with.
There's some interesting depth here - you not only get ranged kunai attacks, a short teleporter hop and three extra modes for your sword, but each of these get different effects in combination, giving you plenty of high-energy options to take down even bigger foes with finesse. There's also a chain-based higher damage mode you can get to if you score a high succession of hits - I never popped the achievement for doing this 25 times, but I managed to quickly take down the one boss I had any real trouble by trigging a succession of these, and like everything else in this game's combat, it has the capacity to make you feel like the ultra-badass you probably aren't.
Elsewhere, the game can be unexceptional, though not in any significantly detrimental way. This Strider goes full Metroidvania, and while the aforementioned puzzles are great to track down, it lacks the clever item placement of something like Super Metroid (and for better or worse, there's nothing like that game's shine sparking to test your skills/patience). The environments are thoughtfully if visually unspectacular in their construction - though gameplay is on a 2D plane they've done a great job of layering things in the background and foreground, but it can all look a little samey and the series' distinctive cyber-soviet environments seem a little low-key this time round.
Enemy design is a similar story - in terms of function they've nailed it (on sight you have a good idea how an encounter is going to go down, and attacks are appropriately telegraphed so you can get on with the business of dodging and obliterating) but the designs don't really stick in your memory. Bosses are a little better on this front, though they're ultimately lifted from earlier games (and they have some over-used chatter before you encounter them).
Still, unless you've recently burned yourself out on Metroidvania-esque titles, there's more than enough style and substance in this game. I've owed this one a review for three years now - taken me around this time to actually have a machine that can run it (oddly) - Chris covered for me on thereticule
, but I couldn't resist singing it's praises myself, especially as three years on, it seems to have largely been forgotten. A shame.

Strider is a reboot of... well, the Strider franchise. Strider was a dose of intense arcadey goodness, and when I heard it was rebooted as a Metroidvania, I was pretty surprised, but ready to give it a chance.
On the side of action, the game succeeds. Unfortunately, there's not a lot I can say that speaks to this. It feels as flashy and wild as it should. Bosses are frantic, enemies are dynamic, and the abilities you acquire are fun and empowering, kunais, dashes, new blade types, etc. My only real complaints here are that at the occasional gravity warping sections within the game, you never feel quite as in control as you should, and that switiching blade types on the fly can feel stressful. Oh, and turning around is kind of weird? But anyway. Graphically, it's exactly what it should be, throwbacks to the old games show up in proper spaces, but also aren't carbon copies. The soundtrack is actually really sick, unfortunately it is turned down too low to appreciate, like a lot of soundtracks nowadays. I recommend cranking it up a little! But otherwise, the combat is nice, the presentation works. Playtime is around five hours, and that's just about the right length. It all checks out.
But then we get to the fact that, again, this game is a Metroidvania. That means backtracking to get collectibles with new found power ups. But the issue with Strider's layout is that backtracking is genuinely annoying to go through. There are only a few warp points in the game, and they are far out of the way from the "Plaza" (the place you consistently return to over the game). The collectibles, too, are almost never worth going to get, with the exception of a few upgrades to your health and mechanical upgrades. Furthermore, rather than in a, well, GOOD Metroidvania, you aren't led silently to where you need to go to next by map design and the designer's invisible hand. You're given a waypoint on the map to head to. What was the point of making this a Metroidvania, then? If the areas were stacked in order, the game would have felt relatively the same, though a bit funky to backtrack through small parts of areas. I often feel compelled to collect everything I can in games like this, but in Strider, I just didn't bother. They're not hard to get, usually, theyre just not worth it. I didn't want to waste my time.
That being said, Strider is still a fun game. The action is frenetic and fun, but I'm honestly hesitant to recommend it. I actually felt like it wasted my time often when playing it. This is one of those many times I wish I could give a middling review score rather than the binary of "Yes" or "No". It's a good action game, but whenever it tries to be like a Metroid game, it just becomes boring. Buy at your own discretion.

Media censorship and corruption is certainly an intriguing topic, especially in this day and age when we are bombarded by the media from all sides. When a game tries to tackle this topic, it should definitely be applauded for its valiant effort. Video games are broadening their horizons on an almost daily basis and it’s the independent scene that is usually able to provide a razor-sharp focus on a certain theme because the design is usually smaller in scope compared to big budget games. This approach has brought us games like Papers, Please, which provided poignant insight into a life of an ordinary person trying to make a living under a totalitarian regime. I usually don’t like to directly compare games to one another in my reviews, but in this case that is impossible. The Westport Independent was obviously influenced by Lucas Pope’s seminal title, and perhaps even more so by his prior game, The Republia Times.
In The Westport Independent, the player takes on the role of an editor-in-chief of a local newspaper of the same name. Unfortunately for the media, the oppressive government of the nameless country is introducing a new bill in 12 weeks that will make freedom of speech a thing of the past. In those 12 weeks, you can try to shape public opinion through the presentation of the articles you decide to run. You can’t lie, but you can alter article titles or delete paragraphs. In doing so, you will either comply with the Loyalist Party or show support for the rebel movement that is trying to overthrow the government. After you’re done editing the articles, you assign them to the writers. You have four writers at your disposal, all of whom have a slightly different take on the situation in the country. They will also react differently to the articles you submit to them. For example, if you give a pro-rebel article to a Loyalist Party supporter, he or she will say that they can’t write it. You can either give in and assign them another article (or change the article in question) or force them to write it.
Depending on your choices, you will be contacted both by the rebels and the government. The latter will either threaten or commend you. If one or more of your writers publish too many anti-government articles, you run the risk of having them arrested and removed from the newspaper. That will leave you with one less writer and one less article per week as you can only assign a single article to a writer each week. Between each week, you will be treated with a short cutscene which will depict a brief conversation of your staff in a local bar. They will make various comments on the articles, newspaper, government, rebels, and personal issues.
Apart from making choices, the game also has a management component to it. When you’re done choosing and editing the articles, you have to decide on the most appropriate marketing. The city contains of four districts and each has an interest in different topics. For example, the wealthy district is most interested in celebrity and industrial articles, whereas the poorest district wants to read about societal issues and crime. You can choose how much copies to send to each district. Your articles will influence the views of the population and the popularity of the newspaper.
Unfortunately, while all of this sounds extremely interesting, the execution is severely lacking. The thing that made Papers, Please so fascinating was that it successfully wrapped mundane gameplay of pushing papers into a compelling whole. There were many subtleties that made you care about everything you were doing. The Westport Independent simply fails at that. It just feels hollow, I never really felt immersed into it, I didn’t care about the events or the characters. It all felt soulless and empty, devoid of any poignancy and meaning. I also have to point out that the game is extremely short, I managed to complete two playthroughs in two hours. The worst thing is that boredom set in even before the end of the first playthrough. The game is meant to be played multiple times, but the articles are always the same and the game world is simply not nearly compelling enough to make me want to see all the different endings. I saw two and neither gave me any sense of accomplishment in regards to the choices I made.
The graphics are in the same retro style as Papers, Please, but with a more monochrome color palette, which I found suits it very well. My only complaint is that the text is sometimes hard to read. The soundtracks consists of a single derivative 1940’s jazz track. A lot more effort could have went into the entirety of the sound design.
As I’ve said at the beginning, The Westport Independent is a valiant effort, but there’s simply no escaping the fact that the execution just isn’t there. The game world and the characters aren’t compelling, the gameplay is too simple, the game is far too short and it doesn’t provide much incentive for repeated playthroughs.

Card design overall is focused much less on RNG and instead lets you use cards in creative ways and in varied combos, facilitated further by dual-class deckbuilding. Frequent small tweaks to individual cards helps keep metas fresh and permissive, and you'll find wildly different decklists in ranked play even near the top of the ladder. Individual games can suffer from pacing problems when both players are afraid to make a move, but overall it's a refreshingly strategic experience that achieves a fair amount of depth without unnecessary complexity.

On the one hand I've played this so far for 17 hours. On the other hand about half of that has felt like a grind, and it's really hard to go on.
The problem with the game comes from it's generic and very repetative setup. You go find a mission, it's to go to x and kill y, and so you drive there and kill them. Along the way there are check points you must fight through. That's the entire game, repeating, so far for 17 hours. Aspects of the game do not change, ever. It's always the same enemies, with the same weapons, that you take on in the same way, half the time in the same areas (since it's an open world and a lot of territory is reused).
There are some minor parts that help with the story, such as tapes you find that help fill in background info. That 5 minutes of novelty does not make up for the rest.
What has helped to keep me going for all that time is how well polished the game is. It looks good, weapons and vehicles feel nice, and there are some cool aspects like easily being able to set off forest fires (since there is long dry grass everywhere). It's also nice sneaking through the bush hunting people down. The result is that you can easily play the first few hours and think this game is amazing. The issue is that 'amazing' ness never changes, and just repeats, forever ...
If you have *nothing* to play, and this is cheap, sure pick it up. However I'd skip it to be honest. There are a lot of better alternatives out there, such as Far Cry 1.

Puzzles: entry level, meaning it is easy. In comparison to the Deponia series, there are less steps of mucking about with your items to reach solution imo.
Graphics: when resolution is maxed the graphic is crisp. There are little glitches throughout the game but since this is point+click, it shouldn't bother you.
Bugs: I encountered only 1 bug in which I couldn't select anything or open menu so I had to restart the game but luckily I saved not so long before. If I haven't, I would have been very annoyed.
Parody: this game is full of little parodies and homage to movies, literature and games. Such are Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, Terry Pratchett, World of Warcraft, etc.
Characters: as this is a 3rd person point and click game, you get to play number of different characters. Different characters such as a gnome, elf, human and a strange pink creature called Critter becomes a protagonist that can be played. Sometimes you get to switch between 2-3 characters at once to solve puzzles that involve teamwork or interaction.
NPCs: Great amount of time will be spent on interacting with other characters and they are all very funny. Compared to The Book of Unwritten Tales 2, the interaction needed between you and NPCs are somewhat shallow and too easy.
Length: It took me 13 hours to finish and approx. 2-3 hours of that has been just leaving it running while I was doing something else. I wanted it to last a little longer.
I have played The Book of Unwritten Tales 2 before the first game and believe me, the second one is waaaaay better in length and puzzle complexity but in order to play the second one, I highly recommend that you play this one first.
You'll see that almost all the NPCs reappear in the 2nd game and you'll get to know more about them better as a character.
My recommendation is to put this on the wishlist until it goes on sale and spend that extra money on The Book of Unwritten Tales 2.

I want to like this game, and it's so close to being good, but it just has too big of an issue.  If you forget to play for a week all of your plants die.  You can avoid this by entering vacation mode but then your plants never grow.  There's no way to bring them back, so you lose literally all of your progress.  All the plants you earned over so many weeks and all the plants you bought are just gone.  And, you can't just take out any dead ones, if one is dead you have to start over because there appears to be no way of deleting a plant, or at least not one I could find.  But not only can you not take them out, but restarting the game requires you to go into the files and delete specific things and rename things.  It shouldn't punish you so much for being too busy to remember to play.
The cutest way to watch grass grow. And moisten snails.

I like the concept of a virtual succulent pot -- but one of the advantages of virtual plants over real ones is that they don't necessarily have to die.  These do.  And it's based in real time, not "while the game is running" time, so if you forget to play for a few days, bam, things are dead and unrevivable.  Sure, you can purchase replacements, but if you're an intermittent player, those will just die again.  (There is a vacation mode that suspends time, but that can't be applied retroactively.)
I started out loving this, but it only really works if you are able to (and remember to) play daily, and/or if you have a lot of spare cash.

As a huge fan of base building survival games - ranging from Ark to Rimworld - this game was
good.
My only experience with it involves a 4 player LAN (and alcohol) for about 10 hours straight. The included dedicated server was easy to set up with easy customization options. However the game settings are not as user friendly. Some settings, like FOV and mouse sensitivity, had to be set either through the console or a text file in the games directory, and even for EA not having at least basic settings like that in-game isn't okay.
The gameplay was fun and the game pretty bug-free, but around ~5 hours in the gunplay started to get a little repetative, most of us used the assult rifle from hour 1 - 9. It was genuinely fun finding dungeons, establishing a base, defending it from attacks, and leveling up your skills/research. The heat/cold mechanic works pretty well, as did the air mechanics on the moon. The food mechanic didn't really seem to have much complexity, it generally just boils down to press J when it flashes hungry -  I literally never thought about where food came from either I just had it on me and kept getting it or its just unlimited who knows.
Around hour 9 we were about rank 30 - 45, some of us focusing on one job more and others focusing on getting all the jobs to a minimum level to maximize diversity. We didn't get super far into vehicles, the highest being the Dune Buggy. But the tanks looked really fun and the mob size was getting larger in the fields so I could see that turning into something pretty fun. As well as some sort of space area would be cool, even if it was just above the planet map and had some asteroids or something.
We got a moon stargate around hour 4, and that was a really cool experience. We got the low-planet stargate around hour 7, and that was even cooler. None of these really change the gameplay that much, as far as I can tell. The best part about this game are the vistas, the terrain generation just seems really on point. That was really the main draw of these other planets, as well as the higher level content but that could have just been on the same planet.
The loot was alright, a little underwhelming when it came to weapons. There seemed to be enough choices of armor, with some to protect against heat/cold/no air/etc. The building system was what I would call above average but not amazing. It was sometimes unclear what you had to do to get a piece at the height you wanted. I could not for the life of me figure out how to place stairs going up towards something that has been placed already, such as transitioning from the ground into a deck.
Overall I think this game has great potential, but needs some more love to get it in a really coherent and compelling state.

Shadowrun: DragonFall is a cyberpunk themed turn based strategy game/R.P.G. developed by Harebrained Schemes and published by Harebrained Holdings. In 2012, magic returned to our world, awakening powerful creatures of myth and legend. Among them was the Great Dragon Feuerschwinge, who emerged without warning from the mountains of Germany, unleashing fire, death, and untold destruction across the countryside. It took German forces nearly four months to finally shoot her down and when they did, their victory became known as The Dragonfall. 42 years later in 2054 a new threat is rising, one that soon has you and your team on the wrong side of a deadly conspiracy just as whispers of the Dragonfall hint that the great dragon Feuerschwinge may still be alive and waiting for the right moment to return. Dragonfall is the next chapter in the Shadowrun series featuring a new story, a new location and a revamped combat system as well as a host of other significant changes. Harebrained Schemes has taken everything that made the first game, Shadowrun Returns, so great and improved on it in every way which should be the goal of a worthwhile sequel. Featuring a unique cast of playable characters and highly memorable NPC's, I really enjoyed Dragonfall's intriguing storyline even more so than Shadowrun Returns.
Like any terrific R.P.G., there are a number of available classes, attributes and skill sets to choose from which allow you to build the type of character that you want to have. For example, the Street Samurai uses combat skills to dominate the battlefield while Shamans and Mages summon powerful allies and cast deadly spells. If hacking is your bailiwick then a Rigger or Decker would be your character of choice. As your player levels up, you earn experience points that you can then use to upgrade a number of abilities for not only you but your team as well. When it comes to the customization of your character Shadowrun: Dragonfall does not dissapoint and this deep level of customization also immensely adds to the replayability of the game.
Graphically, this title is very pleasing to the eye as it's filled with beautiful colors and smooth animation. I've always been a big fan of the isometric turn based role playing games. I like to pick apart the backgrounds and see how many details the developers can squeeze into them and this game has some superb environments and set pieces. For example, with this being a cyberpunk themed game, I can almost guarantee that I spotted an homage to Kaneda's bike from "Akira" and that's just one of the many awesome items to keep an eye out for.
My favorite thing about Shadowrun has always been the strategic turn based combat and Dragonfall definitely takes what made the previous title Shadowrun Returns combat so great and polishes it to a beautiful shine. The battles are just as fun and even more challenging while the user interface is now much more refined and easier to use.
While not quite as cinematic as XCOM: Enemy Unknown, another fantastic title in this same genre, Shadowrun: Dragonfall does rank among the top tier of turn based strategy games in my opinion. If you're looking for a title with a compelling story, thrilling combat, high replayability and who doesn't love cyberpunk then you can't miss with this game...highly recommended!
