Shadowrun: Dragonfall - a game that has been on my radar for a while, but due to circumstances I never really got around to that. I've recently decided to give it a try, and it only took half an hour for me to get hooked. After a short but intense tutorial, you find yourself in a beautifully designed, atmosphere and futuristic Berlin. At times it can feel overwhelming, especially if it's your first cRPG experience. Which is what it was for me. The world is absolutely packed with lore, and the best thing about it is they don't force feed it to you. It's only there for people who want to know about it, it's completely optional. A lot of those little pieces of information can be put together and it really helps make Berlin feel alive. It all contributes to the amazing experience of the main story. An excellent story filled with mystery and plot twists. I'm also very positive about the characters. Each one of them has different stories to them, and they're fully fleshed out that make all of them very memorable.
Another thing I really liked - or even liked the most - was the insane amount of player freedom. There are many situations that can be solved in more than one way, in a handful of ways, and frequently even more than that. You can be smooth and talk your way through (or into) trouble, or you can be as subtle as a brick to the teeth and let the bullets do the talking. Or, I don't know, smash a wall and make yourself an entrance if you're into that. Or are you the type of guy that likes to bribe people? Intimate them? Or use different skills to pass through? There's a lot you can do to solve encounters, and that amount of player freedom gets even better if you factor that most of the stuff you choose to reach your objectives have their own set of consequences.
Are there any flaws? Well, actually there aren't. At least not in a way that really bothered me. However, there are two things I'd consider unfortunate, but not actually flaws themselves. But still. The biggest one (and probably even the only one) is that you can access your team mates' inventory during missions. It's only available at the start. After that it's not possible any more to change their inventory, only yours. Also, some fights can take a little while. Especially the ones with time pressure ("in X rounds Y will happen") felt like they could have ended sooner.
And that's all she wrote. This is the first "traditional" cRPG I have played, and it has set the bar extremely high. Even for newcomers, it can maybe feel a little overwhelming at times, but stick with it like I do, and if you like narrative-heavy cyberpunk experiences, this will be right up your alley.

I read a bunch of reviews since I've owned the game from day 1 and have been thinking about writing one myself for a while now. As you can see from my playtime, I've never played the game much, and when I considered why that was, I didn't find much overlap between my view of the game's shortcomings, and the negative reviews.
The main complaint I see in negative reviews is that this game is too easy and the non-boss enemies are way too easy (some say the bosses are too easy as well, personally I don't mind a game where I can kill the boss after figuring out his tricks over 3-6 attempts). I think this complaint mostly stems from imo misunderstanding what this game is and isn't supposed to be.
As I see it, this game is not supposed to be "I Wanna Be The Guy" with a Strider skin, and the open world enemies aren't supposed to privide much, if any, challenge (though to be fair, the Heavy Trooper Mechs come in different variations that can be fun/interesting to handle). They're there to provide scenery and something to slash with your increasingly powerful skills as you fly by, and that's it.
The main thing that put me off playing the game for longer was the open-world approach they have taken with map-design. If I need to spend time looking at the map, frankly, I'd prefer a minimap. It just kind of makes me wonder "who asked for this", but I guess it was probably cheaper to do it this way and stuff some collectibles in there. I for one find the idea of exploring to find my way and traveling between zones via phoenix in this kind of game off-putting. Ori and the Blind Forest did a similar thing and I didn't like it there either, just give me a linear level path imo.
That said, if you want to play a metroidvania style game that makes you feel fast, agile and powerful, which isn't very hard but a quick blast of fun, I can definitely recommend the game (as long as the map thing doesn't turn you off). I'll finish it one day, surely...

===UPDATE===
Thanks to the Community Discussions tab, I've been made aware of just how unconscionable adding EAC actually is.

What it does:
1. Block modding completely, even on pirated copy you can't use it due to massive 256bit encryption on files
2. Scan your HDD, not just the game folder, including C:\Windows and My Documents and record whatever data it sees fit
3. Stays open even AFTER you quit the game and stays like this until next reboot

There are three kinds of enemies that can kill you in this game: malaria (doesn't really kill you, but will knock you out cold if a symptom attack catches you without the much needed pills), blood-thirsty mercenaries just like yourself (who duke it out supporting dubious causes for a hefty payment in blood diamonds), and the CoD-ey, impatient, quicktime-event-trained, short-attention-span mentality you WILL have when you first boot up Far Cry 2. All the past years, games in the likes of Call of Duty, Medal of Honor et al. have all created a FPS playerbase with a tremendously short focus of attention, a shocking lack of thinking and planning tactics, and a complete disregard of taking your mind off the shootybanging going on in the foreground, in order to soak in the atmosphere in the background. Far Cry 2 is, apart from a solid shooter, a magnificent atmospheric game, full of engrossing ambience and breathtaking vistas that will provide with a cheap vacation alternative to sub-Saharan Africa, albeit in a much more hostile environment than you would ever wish for. The nature that surrounds you can be both an ally and an enemy if you don't treat it properly, as a vantage point you used meticulously to pick off guards in a distant outpost can become a death trap at any moment, should a raging wildfire cut off any escape routes. Propagating bushfire mechanics can be harnessed to cause chaos and mayhem to enemy positions, but can also uncontrollably harm your character as well. Getting from point A to point B in this game can seem tedious at first, as you will have to walk or drive to wherever you need to be, but as you get more and more used to the feel of the adventure, you will discover alternate routes, shortcuts and safe zones to better facilitate your travelling needs.
Don't expect fauna to be a threat, or to have any intelligence. Grazing herbivores are all you are ever going to see, and zebras tend to one-bump-one-kill themselves on your car, even if you are fully stopped. A full time-of-day cycle and dynamic weather effects will paint a much more convincing picture of your surroundings as you comb through the map length- and widthwise.
TL;DR- An incredible experience worth the price of admission, it is a must that you should not overlook, especially since it goes dirt-cheap on sales more often than you would change underwear.

I had high hopes for this game but sadly it fell short. I started with a full Loyalist playthrough and it was dead easy. I had my more rebel leaning journalist write about celebrity gossip and my loyalist leaning journalists write about the glorious actions of our beloved government (Heavily censored of course) so that they would always feel safe and be happy. I quickly gained big favour with the Loyalists, turned all four districts to full loyalist support and won the game. On my second playthrough I decided to, no matter what, go full rebel!
...The Loyalists arrested Frank on turn four. I think he was the one that was a rebel, here you see how much the game had me care about the employees. I don't know who is who...). The Loyalists then shut me down at turn six.
I can see that the challenge of the game is to run a rebellious newspaper without getting shut down and hopefully see the Rebels overthrow the Loyalists in the end of the game but frankly I can't be bothered to try, not now anyway. When playing as a loyalist there is really nothing that counts against you since there is no risk that rebels attack your offices.
Many people have compared this game to Papers Please, and I can see why as they are set I very similar environments, and with similar gameplay elements, like the big bad government and resistance movements. But in Papers Please, going for either one brought different challenges and different rewards. I would like to point to my previous paragraph and once again point out that the rebels are no threat to you in this game.
Is this game worth its price? Absolutely not! The game is maximum twelve turns and i've seen people finish it in around 40 minutes. For me it took an hour. If you want to test it out I suggest that you buy it on the appstore instead where the price is around half of Steams price. Some things change, such as which articles appear on which turn but on my second playthrough I didn't really see any new articles that I didn't get in my previous playtrough. Between turns there is a cutscene where your journalists discuss the current state of the country somewhat based on the articles you decide to print but how the discuss them don't really change depending on what you censor and to which side you lean.
It's a good concept but it doesn't feel finished or fleshed out and for that I can't recommend it as of now.
If you want to drop a lot of free time into a game, this game will surely deliver with fun dungeons and great graphics. Be willing to spend A LOT of time to make it to the end game.

The inevitable comparisons between
and
are kind of unavoidable. With its lo-fi visual style, themes of an oppressive totalitarian government and it's simple drag-and-drop mechanics it shares a lot of similarities with Lucas Pope's 2013 indie hit. (And is almost a carbon copy of Pope's earlier gamejam game -
.)
But where it differs is in its ability (or lack there of) to engage with the player and create feelings of empathy for the game's characters through its mundane, paper pushing actions.
At it's heart
is a management sim. You are the editor-in-chief of one of the last remaining independent newspapers in Westport and its your job to get the truth out to the public. Unfortunately the new Loyalist government has other ideas and its new Public Culture Bill is crushing free speech and freedom of the press throughout the country. You must tread that fine line between reporting the news accurately and not raising the suspicions of government too much.
You do this by picking out which stories you think you can get past the unblinking eye of Big Brother, changing the headlines and censoring certain sections of the story as necessary. You assign these articles to your reporters who all have their own political allegiancies and levels of suspicion from the government. And all this whilst trying to maintain the papers popularity.
But whereas
had you really caring for your little immigration inspector, his family and even the people passing through his booth in
I felt nothing for the editor, the reporters or even if the paper [inevitably] got shutdown.
What's more there is no urgency to the game. In
you had that ticking clock adding to the stress of processing people quickly & accurately but also the need to fill your quota for the day so you could actually feed your family. In
you do have a countdown to when the Culture Bill passes in 12 weeks time but whilst you are sat at you desk no time passes what so ever.
It's a real shame as I had high hopes for the game, as I thought the idea of trying to maintain an honest news organisation under the heel of an oppressive government is a fantastic concept. Unfortunately the execution just feels a little lacklustre.

The best digital CCG out there, a perfect balance between the simple, pick-up-and-play nature of Hearthstone and the tactical complexity of Magic. The game's weakness is that it's very similar to Hearthstone, but that's also it's strength in that it's pretty unambiguously better designed from a gameplay standpoint. The two-lane system adds a lot of depth, ensuring that total board control is much more difficult to achieve and making the "optimal" play less obvious. In Hearthstone I usually felt like I was basically auto-piloting my deck once I had constructed it and drawn my cards. The rune-breaking (draw a card every 5 damage) and prophecy mechanics help players stabilize, adding a lot more back-and-forth, and also makes aggression much more tactical. Rewards are generous. And lastly, there are many fewer (though not zero) playable RNG-based cards. As a sweet bonus, the single-player story modes and different special game rules in Chaos Arena are a lot of fun and help keep the gameplay fresh and varied.

if you like pac man, but has considered trying a faster and more challenging version (and as a bonus also more dynamic), this is it.
the game is simple but pretty amusing. the overall new rules are to grab all the pellets offered on either side so it'll unlock a "fruit" (like the original fruits but there are some other items with the same purpose) on the opposite side and the fruit will reset this side of the maze, with more pellets and more sleeping ghosts. any ghost gets to hyper-rainbow-mode when you get near them, which mean the sleeping ones awake, and that's how you end up with the massive agile line seen in the trailer.
there are some facilitators in the game which may frustrate the most hardcore players but it made it more bearable for casuals like me: slo-mo when you go towards a ghost, the bombs (which sends all awake ghosts back to the spawn area, only to briefly get out in the same quantity and in formation tho), and the ready-made ghost-eating combos.
and trust me, it's far less confusing than it looks from the trailer over there. I mostly got lost when crossing sides and confusing exits - i mean it does gets way faster than the original...

Don't let my time on here fool you, I've been playing for quite a long time in the open beta.
I've been playing card games for about twenty years and ES;L is easily my favorite F2P CCG.
Right off the bat as you start the story and begin to level up they dump tons of free cards, soulstones and gold on you, even letting you choose between which ones you want from time to time. Then you can start leveling solo arena and if you do decently enough the rewards from that will be enough to get you enough runs to become grand champion. After that's done you should have a decent enough grasp on arena to start leveling in VS arena and so on.
The deck size and x3 card limit as well as non-unique legendaries may seem daunting to build a competitive deck but if you settle on an archtype you wanna play and then soultrap aggressively you can build a competitive deck well before you're even finished leveling.
This game has the most generous prize support of any free to play game and even then the main incentive to buy packs is the bundles that include awesome alternate art versions of select cards. Other perks include the fact that the game adds at least one new card every month that you can get up to a complete set of as ranked rewards, the ability to grind easy soul gems by playing practice mode and the well balanced and diverse meta.

- Game isn't exactly terrible but it's pretty much like many others CCGs under a different name which makes it a subpar experience. Their PvP pairing system not being good also doesn't help.
that almost nobody cares - If you've been playing CCGs like I did over the last 10+ years, you will find Elder Scrolls Legends familiar. It really looks a bit like a 2000 made in flash CCG (even if with better graphics) and that doesn't look great.
- The idea of two boards is actually great and welcomed to any CCG since it offers a bit of strategy and force you to think a bit about the game but that's the only positive thing about it (and even that isn't new since I remember playing some CCGs in Kongregate years ago with that...).
- Initial Story mode is the same as a long tutorial with clips that you will mostly skip besides the ones that give you free cards (no, you can't skip those besides one that seems bugged because it goes fullscreen? Well, it's Bethesda, bugs are a thing in their games no matter what). You will get almost half of the core cards (positive aspect) of the game but the options to make different strategies with each faction are limited (negative) which ruins the experience (specially with multicoloured cards...) but at least they offer you a bit more than other CCGs (which doesn't help much when they're so limited and you know what to expect from each deck being played). I didn't tried the second campaing since it ask you to buy it and I'm not going to grind gold nor pay for it but I noticed that they show you the cards of it in the album and well, that's a bit bad. While in the sense of marketing it's clever, it sucks seeing those cards there and you can't use souls to make them. And it doesn't even warns you that they locked them behind a story expansion, it just has the name to which collection it belongs and nothing more.
- Arena is more of the same: you pay a fee to play, get less gold than what you paid unless you achieve a perfect max/almost max number of victories but with a few extra cards. It's not exactly bad or good, it's just a copy of any other CCG adapted to their model.
- The only thing that could save this was Play Mode (PvP) but even for that it fails.
Initially it looked great (was enjoying it a lot and looked very balanced), I was being paired to people of the same rank I was and I was winning a decent amount of them (close to 50/50). But after a dozens of wins I was dropped into duels with people 4 ranks above me and tons of founders who seemed to have all the cards of the game.
And later, as if this wasn't enough, I started noticing that playing second actually beneficts you a lot so ends being a race to who plays last instead of who plays first and we end in the same crap that a lot CCGs nowadays don't know how to balance.
One extra usable mana for three turns that can be activated whenever you want? Talk about a broken compensation...
In the end I had a very bad experience (at least their Legendary cards aren't exactly broken and decide games like in some CCGs) and I don't recomend this game to anyone in the PC. In the mobile it may be okay to pass time once in a while against the AI Arena and some random players, in the PC there are better ways to have fun with a CCG.

Is this game only based in slavic mythology with taking enough creative license to deviate from the myth, or does it actually present the mythos in a manner that could be used in discussion without a theologist punching me out?

I don't regret purchasing this, because this is innovative in a good way, but I don't particularly care for it and can't recommend it.
The game is split between the two meta phases of the roguelike "learning" (when you play blind) and "knowledge" (where you make concious and deliberate decisions), which will find you going from a sense of wonder to not having anything major to do.  It uses a 4x/Civ style map to navigate and locate resources, but the layout of the map can entirely invalidate the collection of said resources, because they have to be retrieved, turning large portions of the game into waiting games.
The resolution of combats/challenges also seems heavily random.  Combat itself will commonly feel tedious, despite its interesting play.  It lacks UX features which would allow it to go faster, and you might then find yourself using auto resolve, despite the risk, to just get through it.... and then you'll eventually find out that auto resolve scales faster than your ability to perform.  (Example: worst case chance of manual combat early game is some damage, but it'll be major damage in auto.  Late game it'll be risking people dying as a best outcome for manual, but auto can result in unscathed)
While the game gives many paths through it, they're all shadows of eachother, so while there is Fighting, Hunting, Stealth, and other challenges, they use the same mechanics but are derived from different skills, which gives a lot to keep track of when you're not actually doing different things.
At the end of the day, this is not much more than a Survival game crossed with 4x, but that doesn't mean it's all that bad, I just find the "playability" elements to be very tiresome.  A lot of information isn't conveyed, a lot of what you do is waiting for animations, a not a lot of the time really feels different from the rest.  Numbers change, "new things" become available, but it doesn't fundamentally change all that much from turn 1 to turn 200, aside from world scaling with you.
The game has a lot to offer for people that like micromanaging, because proper management, and a little luck, can lead to drastically accelerated progression, but the overall experience is just way too slow for me to get much out of the learning loop.
I have no real technical complaints outside of the game not having a very refined UX element, making clicking confusingly ineffective and easy to click on the wrong thing, and difficult to investigate the things you want to look at, wiht too much reliance on those hard to access tooltips to get anywhere.
If you're into the methodical nature of survival games, I can imagine you'd like this, but I can't swing it.

It looks like a Hearthstone ripoff. It sounds like a Hearthstone ripoff. It even UIs (yes thats a verb now) like a Hearthstone ripoff. And ontop of it all it's got the Runescape branding. It's gotta be nothing but a cheap Hearthclone right?
By god do not mistake it for that.
Chronicle:Runescape Legends (an unweildly name if there ever was one) is, far from another in a long line of Hearthstone copycats, it instead perhaps one of the most innovative CCGs, on par with the equally interesting tabletop RPG CCG "Card Hunter", which by the way, I also reccomend you check out. While most card games are a simple draw a card, play mosnters and traps and spells against you opponent affair, CRL instead completely flips the formula.
See, you aren't playing cards against your opponent. You are playing cards against YOURSELF. Yes, yourself. In 5 rounds of up to 4 sequenced cards (Drawing 3 per turn, and starting with 7), you are instead attempting to build up yourself to take on your opponent in a final showdown, and balancing five stats in order to do so. Your Weapon, Attack, Gold, Health, and Armor.
Every turn of 4 cards, you play down cards in a sequential order, as your opponent does the same simultaniously. These cards can be mosnters to fight, items to buy, allies to recruit, and so on and so on. All of these will modify your own stats (and sometimes your opponenets) in a variety of ways in order to build yourself up. Monsters, for instance, must be killed in one blow by having an equal or higher attack than their health, or else they will strike you back, which may be a worthwhile tradeoff if the rewards for fighting them are high enough. Weapons and Armor work like in most other card games, where a weapon has a power it adds to your attack and a number of attacks its good for, and armor stops damage from reaching your health.
Your attack meanwhile, is perhaps your most important stat, as, with very few exceptions, it can only increase, never decrease, and can be the difference between life and death as it allows you to face stronger monsters, and if need be, face off agaisnt your opponent in the end.
While this menas many matches will have little in the way of player interaction besides the final showdown, there also exists possibility to screw with your opponent, cards whcih chip away at their health, or destroy their weapon. Some can slightly tilt the odds in your favor, some, if timed right, can absolutly obliterate an opponent, such as removing their +7 sword as they go to fight a 16hp monster.
All in all, it's one of the few CCGs that actually do something refreshing with the genre, and you would be doing yourself a disservice by passing it by based on either "It looks like a hearthclone" or "Oh god it's Runescape".
PS: I note some reviews are mentioning an advantage of CRL is it doesnt have crappy F2P expansions like Hearthstone. But that's not really valid, as this hasn't been out long enough for anyone to have a true feel as to the long term dev cycle.
PPS: Also check out Card Hunter if you're in the market for really unique CCGs, that's ace too.

Chronicle: Runescape Legends is a solid 9/10
NOTE: I've been playing Chronicle since the Closed Beta, so my time played on steam is deceptive.
TL;DR
- Refreshing and very very different style TCG compared to MTG and Hearthstone
- Not P2W, can grind Dungeoneering for Card Packs
- Runescape themed!
NTL;WR (Not too long, wanna read)
I'll start this off by saying that Chronicle is a genuinely unique TCG.
Before Chronicle, I played many many hours and spent many many dollars on card packs on Hearthstone. The sheer imbalance of the game (1 or 2 decks in the current version to get high in the ladder easily) deterred me from Arena mode, as everyone used the same thing. I didn't spam those decks because I don't believe in games that are 1 strategy to win, such as the Brood Wars where it came down to whoever had the higher APM would win. Maybe a mind game here or there.
I also have AT LEAST 1,500 hours across all of my Runescape and Runescape Classic accounts since 2004. So, naturally, when I heard about a Runescape card game, I was really excited. Soon after, signups for the Closed Beta opened, and I was lucky enough to get picked in the first wave of players. I used my beta key, and gave my other 3 keys to some friends so they could try it out. Unfortunately, 2 of them were biased for Hearthstone, as that's what they have invested so much into, so they never played for more than a few hours. My girlfriend loved it for a while, but then finals came around and she slowly forgot about it. I, however played on.
In the beginning there were completely broken things, such as armor stacking on Blacksmith (now Linza the Blacksmith). From the state of Chronicle's Closed Beta (More Hearthstone-y where there were 1 or 2 clearly overpowered decks) to the full release of Chronicle, the balance team have done an absolutely AMAZING job at balancing the game. With each patch, the tuning of strong\weak strategies were more finely made, and the game became much more diverse. I firmly believe that ALL classes are capable of beating any of the other classes. I firmly believe that Chronicle is an environment where there is no 1 or 2 overpowered strategies to win. I FIRMLY BELIEVE that given enough of a playerbase, some more  cards and a few more classes, Chronicle can easily replace Hearthstone.
Hearthstone and Chronicle are similar only in 2 or 3 facets.
- You have cards
- You play versus the other player and one of you wins
- You can buy extra card packs from the store
That is it. The gameplay of the 2 games are COMPLETELY DIFFERENT. In Hearthstone, you are directly attacking your enemy and their cards with your cards. In Chronicle, you are essentially attacking your selected Hero to make them stronger, so they can face off against the opponent's hero. In Hearthstone, your only resource is Mana, with which you can obtain weapons, armor, and place cards on the field. In Chronicle, your resource can be anything. There are cards that will take your weapon as payment (which you can also use even if you don't have a weapon for some free stats) or even health or armor but the main resource is gold (to buy things such as health restore, armor, temp\perm attack, weapons, even more gold), and when your hero defeats\purchases a certain card it can inflict potentially massive damage to the enemy hero, hindering them in their quest to defeat you. Overall, Chronicle is a more immersive card game.
Even when you lose, there is hardly any salt, as the characters will say something positive upon defeat, when in Hearthstone, all you will hear is "WELLPLAYEDWELLPLAYEDWELLPLAYED" any time you make a mistake or lose.
The Card Crafting System that is really neat. After a match, you will get coins and you will also get some gem fragments if you won. Each of the gem fragments correspond to a tier of cards, and you can either combine or disassemble\disenchant gems into higher or lower tiers. You can also dissassemble\disenchant cards into gem fragments if you want to get rid of any extras. There are also plants to implement the upgrading of cards (presumably for gem fragments as a currency).

Without a doubt one of my favorite games of all time. Having 100%ed it (Still missing dlc, so I unfortunately will not be able to 100% those for a while) I can definitely say that i've had a LOT of fun with it. The story is without a doubt highly underrated. This game, to me, feels like the story of a mentally fudged vigilante who believes he's doing good but is only hurting those around him, and his attempts to escape the world of crime he's involved himself in. The gunplay in this game is very, very satisfying, as the guns have a real-feeling recoil system attatched to it. The stealth mechanics are wonderful together with the AI. For example, I've had times where I've thrown around a noise maker to distract some guards, shot one in the back of the head with a pistol, and threw another noisemaker around. The guards realisticly prioritize gunshots, they don't see you unless they ACTUALLY CAN, and unless they get time to scream, if they see you, noone else will know you've been seen. The side-missions, collectibles and locations are all incredibly fun hacking puzzles in which you try to align qr codes to cameras, attempt to find a way inside a garage, for example, hack into people's homes, find the story of Maurice, Deadsec, and blume employees. This entire game, whilst downgraded from e3, looks beautiful, and hangs together perfectly to give a well-rounded explanation of the story of Aiden, the people around him, deadsec, and blume, and chicago's crime syndicate. Every side-mission feels as rewarding to complete as the next, and it truly feels wonderful to play.
Now, for the downsides.
Although this game has a beautiful options menu with a plethora of options, some have to be changed in inis and such, and the port of this game to pc is rather bad. My rig (a gtx 970, i5 4460, 16gb of ddr3 ram) could only run this game on a reasonably smooth 60 at medium settings. Some of the menus feel bad when using mouse and keyboard as they were designed without them in mind, and the game is prone to 1 or 2 crashes every 10 hours or so.
All in all, if you've got the PC to run this awful port of a wonderful game, it's definitely worth it.

Pros:
-Beautiful graphics, good music, decent sound design.
-Large and varied worlds to explore.
-Solid, meaningful progression.
-Deep crafting system.
-Wide range of armors to craft.
-Very wide range of weapons to craft, including various rarities/qualities.
-Decent building mechanics allow pretty deep creative expression.
-Basic tower defense capabilities can be built on your base.
-Very fun to play with friends.
Cons:
-Pretty buggy still. It's early access so that's not unexpected.
-Although the different biomes have decent variation, there's not a ton of different mob types.
-Although I did not have regular lag problems, occasionally things would slow down if there was a lot of activity.
-Dungeons get pretty repetitious. And the crazy fast spawn rates make them sometimes frustrating.
-Inventory management gets pretty overwhelming and it could definitely use some love.
Pro or con depending on the person:
-It gets pretty grindy as you start to craft higher end items. It's no worse than any MMO though. I personally found collecting resources relaxing.
-PVP seems to attract griefer types. I played on a private server with IRL friends, so this had zero impact on us.
So, yeah, overall I love the game. It's got an MMO-like scale to it. There's lots to do and it's a fun challenge to try to survive on hostile worlds (until you get the proper armor sets to mitigate the various planets' environment). Most of the negative reviews I see seem to stem from people encountering cheating griefers on public servers. It's understandable that that would impact their perception of the overall game. But I run a private dedicated server for friends, and of course everyone worked together and we built some pretty amazing stuff. So if you do buy the game I strongly suggest running your own world.
There aren't a lot of games that allow you to run your own massive and customizable MMO-scale world. Grav is one of them. And I enjoy the game immensely.

Finished in about 20 hours, so I will talk very consciously about it.
Game started quite bad for my taste, but then things got slightly better... and stabilized on average. I didn't know it was an indie kickstarted project developed for smartphones and tablets in mind and this explains a lot of cons.
First, I would like to talk about the gameplay. Having experience with a lot of RPGs and turn-based games I have been disappointed: percentages to hit seem to be flawed, covering system is ridiculous, inventory is caotic, some combo are overpowered (you'll instakill with rifles and relative stats at 8+), experience points are given randomly and not by killing enemies, the stats of your party members are scripted, AI always attacks first (resolved in S:HK) and it' also dumb (you can wait for them at corners or take them from the shoulders), some mobs can't suffer critical hits, you are not given so many possibilities of attacking, you can't use your items outside of combat, often you are not given the option of using your teamates abilities in the quests, etc.
Then, the story: I spent 20+ hours in the game clicking furiously and skipping 2/3 of the useless dialogues. Why "useless"? 1) They are scripted, the choices you'll make DO NOT alter the game (if not a couple of occasions) 2) Skills are useless for dialogues: even when you are given the choice to use them, they just provide a couple of more rows of text to read 3) *someone die, so we have to find the culprit* bla bla *turns out all the city is in danger* bla bla *random excuse for making side missions* bla bla *gear up and go final attack*.
Graphics: from the screenshots it seems to be very powerful... it's not. Just colourful. Game has big optimizations problems even if it's just a 2D world with 3D characters (welcome back '90).
I got more than a couple of freezings but game always managed to stay alive (one way or another). Quicksaves often "saved" the day, but no crashes as told in some other reviews.
Shadowrun Return has the same graphics but don't suffer from these problems: even level loading are quicker! If we compare the two games (with the same latest engine), Dragonfall has a more polished UI, a more intriguing story, nicer matrix puzzles, more turning points, but feels like a revised expansion (which is, in fact).
The matrix puzzles, the door keyboard puzzles, the stealth mission and some side quests to dig into the past of your teammates are nice additions, but in the end they are just another *clicking*. I would have preferred more attention to the gameplay.
I enjoyed it? Yes and no. Yes because I like these type of games, no because X-Com, Civilizations, Fallout still stand on a higher level. I would call it a nice time waster. If you are looking for a solid game, you should look elsewhere. I hope they'll get better in the next chapters.

After taking the 22 minute trip down memory lane that was Far Cry (It was awful), I was immediately impressed with how much better the sequel's visuals were, and the ability to choose from multiple characters (I assume this has no other effect aside from the way your hands look).  I was a little off-put in the first minute of the game, when I saw a group of village youths walking along the side of the road, and they were bouncing high into the air, like they had Moon Shoes on.  A little later, I started to notice that a lot of people are apparently suffering from severe Parkinson's disease.
Despite these strange (and strangely common) graphical bugs, I could feel myself warming to the game more and more as I cleared out a safehouse and then set everything on fire with a flamethrower.  This game was such an improvement over the first one, I felt as though I had leaped 10 years into the future!  A future where Moon Shoes have made a comeback, and 3 out of 5 people has the Fox Fever.
But then it all went to sh**.
After breaking my new best buddy out of a fortified camp by just walking around the outer perimeter of the place to the back (it was that easy), I shot the place up for the hell of it and ditched my yellow Datsun for a jeep with a .50 cal on it.  I roared out of the now silent camp, and back to the slaughterhouse where my handler was waiting to give me something else to do.  He told me to go into town, to a bar called Mike's Bar, and meet up with my buddy.
Pulling into town, I entered the gun shop, as my current objective bid.  The owner wasn't in, so I used the 1980's computer sitting in the corner to order some new guns, which I was then to go next door and pick up.  Done and done.
Time to check out Mike's Bar.  Goody.  So I step inside, and there are three people.  My best buddy is leaning against the bar.  I know he's my best buddy because the game says so.  He tells me to talk to the guy sitting at the booth to get some medicine (I've got the Black Sh*ts).  "Ask nicely" he says.  Okie doke.  So I approached the guy at the booth, and he indignantly shoves a tape recorder at me and says, "You're just a jackboot, you are".
He then continues to say that over and over and over again, and the tape recorder flashes mockingly at the edge of the table, unable to be picked up.  The woman leaning against the wall to my left introduces herself after I walk into her for several seconds mashing the interaction button, and then goes back to leaning against the wall.  The guy at the table continues his chant, "You're just a jackboot, you are".  My buddy stands at the bar and bids me ask the man at the booth for medicine.  "Ask nicely" he says.  I go to leave the bar, on the off chance I can un-snag whatever is snagged, but I'm prompted to speak with all three people in the room before I can leave.
And that's it.  My game is over, just like that.
I didn't even get to fire my sweet new crossbow or silenced shotgun.
0/10

Let me start off by saying that Far Cry 2 is already LEAGUES better than Far Cry 1, mostly because Far Cry 2's AI doesn't ♥♥♥♥ing spot you from half an island away and you can actually DO STUFF in this game without getting cheated by Far Cry 1's type of AI.
I also just adore this games type of "open-ended do whatever you want but wait there's also a story" kind of gameplay. Basically, you're sent into Africa to deal with some dealer only known as "The Jackel" who has been supplying both sides of the war raging on in Africa. You're just plopped right into the middle of it all, and you'll definitely feel so as both sides try to gun you down.
With both sides trying to nip at you, you have a large assortment of guns to help with the gun fighting such as small pistols, small repeaters (IE Uzi's) Rifles, etc etc. THAT, and you'll mostly find yourself driving around the map using the jeeps with the turrets and using that turret to gun down attackers as well.
One last thing I can say is that the immersion is TOP NOTCH! There's no real interface, besides ammo count and health. If you want to see where you have to go, you instead pull out a map to really see where you are going in game, it's no pause menu! Plus, with the type of environment you are in, you'll find yourself using trees or rocks for cover, or maybe a car. LASTLY, you'll find yourself scavaging for ammo, even maybe picking up guns from dead bodies, WHICH, I might add, are usually rusted from its extended use and may jam from time to time.
I was blessed to get this game from the summer sale for 2.49, and thanks for me scraping up the money due to the steam market, I'm able to enjoy this game for such a cheap price and I am having SUCH a blast!

When I bought a game, I didn't know much about it and didn't have high (any) expectations. The main reason why I bought it was that it is an adventure which as the genre I enjoy playing. The quick scope on reviews both personal and professional (ie gaming magazines) was indicating highly quality game.
After finishing it, shortest description of it would be like trying a most trendy, hip cocktail in town which everybody is drinking and telling you that it's amazing, but you just have a sour taste in your mouth after tasting it.
Now, the game is not bad, it's just.... in the middle.
The game is dancing on the line between comedy/parody of fantasy RPG genre with the story of heroes who are saving a world. Comedy/parody part really didn't work for me. Jokes are way too cliche and outdated to be interesting or fun. Majority of jokes are directed to mocking WoW which I see as plain laziness of authors. Few jokes would fit better (maybe) but when the majority of it is in that direction, it just doesn't cut it. Most fun part for me was the sarcastic personality of Captain Nate which is present in his conversations. Ivo has her moments too in that light. Since parody goes deeply into the game, it's hard to take story anyhow seriously which by itself looks unfinished or full of holes (if it's intended to be done in the way how it was). Shortest summary of the story would be: heroes are on the mission to hide already hidden artifact even from themselves. Yes, I know how it sounds and that's how it feels when you finish the game. In the end, it doesn't feel like there is any big or inspiring story, just a bunch of lined side quests.
Puzzles are pretty simplistic and not presenting any significant challenge.
In the end, the game is not bad and for players who didn't play much or at all adventure games, it is a very decent introduction to a genre. For veterans, it is an easy, relaxing piece.
I don't regret buying and playing it but I don't think that I would miss much if I didn't.

I don't regret purchasing this, because this is innovative in a good way, but I don't particularly care for it and can't recommend it.
The game is split between the two meta phases of the roguelike "learning" (when you play blind) and "knowledge" (where you make concious and deliberate decisions), which will find you going from a sense of wonder to not having anything major to do.  It uses a 4x/Civ style map to navigate and locate resources, but the layout of the map can entirely invalidate the collection of said resources, because they have to be retrieved, turning large portions of the game into waiting games.
The resolution of combats/challenges also seems heavily random.  Combat itself will commonly feel tedious, despite its interesting play.  It lacks UX features which would allow it to go faster, and you might then find yourself using auto resolve, despite the risk, to just get through it.... and then you'll eventually find out that auto resolve scales faster than your ability to perform.  (Example: worst case chance of manual combat early game is some damage, but it'll be major damage in auto.  Late game it'll be risking people dying as a best outcome for manual, but auto can result in unscathed)
While the game gives many paths through it, they're all shadows of eachother, so while there is Fighting, Hunting, Stealth, and other challenges, they use the same mechanics but are derived from different skills, which gives a lot to keep track of when you're not actually doing different things.
At the end of the day, this is not much more than a Survival game crossed with 4x, but that doesn't mean it's all that bad, I just find the "playability" elements to be very tiresome.  A lot of information isn't conveyed, a lot of what you do is waiting for animations, a not a lot of the time really feels different from the rest.  Numbers change, "new things" become available, but it doesn't fundamentally change all that much from turn 1 to turn 200, aside from world scaling with you.
The game has a lot to offer for people that like micromanaging, because proper management, and a little luck, can lead to drastically accelerated progression, but the overall experience is just way too slow for me to get much out of the learning loop.
I have no real technical complaints outside of the game not having a very refined UX element, making clicking confusingly ineffective and easy to click on the wrong thing, and difficult to investigate the things you want to look at, wiht too much reliance on those hard to access tooltips to get anywhere.
If you're into the methodical nature of survival games, I can imagine you'd like this, but I can't swing it.

I've only recently started this game - played a few drafts, played a few days of quests... But here is what I've got from it so far.
Pros:
The game is very finely balanced. Almost every game I play is a close match. Very rarely have I said "oh, I've lost" or "Yep I've definately got this" at any stage but the last. There's nothing more satisfying than winning by predicting your opponent and ordering your cards in a precice way. Or just building a deck that is strong enough to consistantly grind most others out.
Its innovative - different from any card game I've seen. As you can see in the video I'm sure. But it really works - the new mechanics are just fun.
Has a nostalgic runescape feel without being too much like runescape which I'm honestly bored as heck with.
Cons:
Yeah, it is freemium. It that standard virtual card game business model - free players grind daily quests to get packs or draft, paid players buy packs and drafts. Other than that it seems reasonably fair so far and from what I can see it doesn't get worse over time.
Pro inside the con: It is possible to get way more for your money as either free or paid by being good at drafting. There is card crafting mostly for people who win at drafts, meaning free to play and pay to play are on pretty equal footing here.

I'll admit, when I began playing, I had expected something of a Hearthstone type TCG. But what I got was something nicely refreshing in comparison. Chronicle: RuneScape Legends, is both unique, and most definitly inspired by Hearthstone, but despite this I feel it has enough to offer that there is a clear distinction.
The game itself is still in that awkward, "I'm a new born game." kinda phase, so it's hard not to feel frustrated during the intial time you spend playing the game... although once you get the hang of it (which only took me about half an hour), you quickly start bubbling up with ideas for decks, and premises that you want to look into.
But the big thing for me, was the fact that RNG seemed ... "fair". During the game, I felt like not only me but both sides had the potential to screw eachother up. Normally you play your cards in response to eachothers actions, or somthing along those lines... but from what I've played thus far, it's more like you are setting up "potential" responses to what "could" happen. So it's always fun to see what hilarity ensues, and who knows, perhaps you'll both try to kill each other indirectly, or spend an entire turn buffing up. There's always an air of mystery, and a sense of strategy, thats quite enjoyable.
I probably won't stop playing Hearthstone anytime soon for this, but for those times when I take a break, I think this would be the perfect change of pace.

Gorgeous, a bit addictive... and before going to steam, the company actually refused to make their launcher work at all for rural bandwidth. They made it worse than HTML for transferring data.
Prior to steam, in order to use this at all, I had to download the files from another source. It was, in the community, a known issue, and over the last year, the company has actively refused to acknowledge it or fix it in the slightest. I tell you this because customer service has to be a VERY high priority for a game/service of this type, and Bethesda and Dire Wolf have made it absolutely clear that if you do not have high bandwidth, they do not want you as a customer and they will not acknowledge that they have made an objectively worthless launcher that cannot ever finish downloading... despite this being under a gigabyte. I should be able to do that inside of two hours. On steam, I can.
So I absolutely do not recommend this game. If they break something, they'll pretend it works fine and refuse to test it for as long as possible. They will train their community managers to lie and give the same unhelpful advice that cannot fix the problem. That launcher is *still* broken.
I do know that they have fixed some minor problems *within* the game. The game itself, if you can get into it, is pretty, and pretty easy to use... but when my mouse clicker was dying, I dragged a lightning towards the enemy and it got dropped on my own face, because that's possible, and has no "Uh, you sure you want to nuke yourself?" But that's not on them. The patch notes are a treat, covering a ton of the usual weird interactions you want fixed.
Now, for the game itself. Actually quite nice. Two lanes gives you enough of a tactical choice to keep deployment interesting without the slowdown from moving a ton of units like in some games of Duelyst. Decks are built from any two factions of choice... I'll often build my deck around an interesting cross-faction card. Only one casting resource, so you don't have the tempo weirdness of games that require a separate resource for each. So the only reason to stick to a single faction deck would be for the cards that synergize with their own color only.
Card keywords seem to involve a bit of rock-paper-scissors. Lethal is blunted by ward... once. Regeneration can blunt regular damage and works great on a blocker. Lethal can take that out regardless of health. Silence can take all the keywords and weapons off of a target...
The card draw from player damage, and the prophecy system (if the card you draw says "prophecy", you play it instantly, free.) can be a reversal... but more often, it will just make the inevitable take a little longer.
I'd have played it more but... A) prior to coming to steam, the excremental launcher meant the game broke every patch... B) The usual problem with trying to draft for arena. I had a run where I got multiple legendaries and even with an unreasonably good deck, had an embarassing run. It clicked in my head that no matter how carefully I play, and how ideal the deck, *I* am not the important element in determining if I win. And neither is my opponent. So how does this differ from a very colorful coin flip?
Eh, maybe I need to look into some kind of miniatures wargame. But they just don't have cool card effects. ^^;
Also, at this time, the game is still not playable, and I'm really hoping it's just the login servers not being able to handle the influx of players... but... well. You already know my opinion on these guys and their powers of repair for anything outside the game client itself.
If it seems unfair of me to rag on this game for something that largely cannot be present in the steam client... you're wrong. I'm sharing my experience with the product and the company behind it and history is a thing that exists and persists.
Edit: Minor update... It's not the login server. They didn't make the steam screen for logging in properly hand off to the game. So you log in correctly, and you get an error message. And you force-quit the game because, if you haven't gotten past that screen? There is no quit. They don't let you quit from there. After you force-quit, somehow, your credentials are now saved and it'll start properly.
That's a bit garbage.
And now I can see the new cards... that you can't craft. You must buy them either with in-game currency or real money. The only way to gain currency is to win games, or with daily quests that range from 30-50 gold. You're aiming for 1,000 - 1,500... to get more power over your opponents... and win more consistently. Some of these are actually not overpowered cards, but I'd want them to flesh out a few deck types. A 2-cost pilferer that gives me 2 cards and then dies... sweet. I rarely get more than 1-2 cards out of the core pilfer:draw 1 card guy. Useful, not overpowered.
Then there's Ring of Imaginary Strength... +2 health, and set minion's attack equal to health. Picture throwing that on the 0/5 blocker that regenerates. 7/7 regenerating blocker. There's less powerful legendaries.
So as these get into the system and give people an edge... that's an advantage to earning in-game currency for people who buy these. They're technically buyable with in-game gold... you can win gold every 3 *wins*, 15-50 gold. And you can do that 10x daily. So, 150-500... plus 30-60 for the daily. If you lose a game, you get nothing. It was a waste of time unless it aided your daily quest. So, if you spend a few hours a day, you could get 200-550 gold... IF your win % is not awful. Getting these cards will... eh, it'll take a week of grinding in which you can't spend any getting new cards.
And as I've established, I don't condone giving these guys a lot of money when they won't fix things.

We've started playing GRAV with my friend like in summer 2015, which is more than a year ago before this review. And this game became one of the games I will never forget in my life. Space life experience, these BitMonster guys made it earlier than NMS devs or any other Early Access games about wandering on other planets. And the atmosphere in game is very different from anything you find alike. I really started to enjoy farming for our base, my friend got inspired by designing the place and crafting weapons and armor, and together we made a good combo of players exploring this endless (actually endful but nevermind, this sounds cool) space... And this is not something about the game process or the value of rewards or something, it's just the game that makes you love it.
GRAV really brought me true joy and happiness. Planets are pretty bright, the sky is absolutely incredible, and the soundtrack is very deep and inspiring.
Yes, some things have changed since 2015 including "Reborn" update, and new lags and the fact that all the new updates are not as massive as before, and the game is still very "early accessed". But I do believe in its future, I think it has a big potential of making a great game in future with better optimization, impressive graphics and deep plot. I am waiting for the devs to make a next step. I would seriously recommend GRAV to all space lovers and people who enjoy exploring, farming and creating in good atmosphere. Those who enjoyed NMS should like it as well, I'm sure. This game is something I will never forget. I tell you.

I highly reccomend this! I love RTS strategy games and this one is quite interesting. I like the game for It's economic system and how the AI Doesn't completely fail in the economic side, unlike Supreme Ruler where the AI builds nothing but Tanks, jets, naval stuff, ect ect, this is quite fun. I have already put 44 hours into the game and in that amount of time, i managed to turn county's like the Congo and Israel into superpowers. It's not all about agression in this game, it's about getting on everyones good side. You can't just simply take a random country and just build tons of units and destroy the world. It takes time and i love the way it does it. You have to sometimes depend on other country's for aid and you have to work your way up bit by bit untill you can actually annex something.
I love how the resources work, I mean, you don't have to manage resources all the time. You can get that all privitised and let your people expand it. That doesn't work all the time, you need to put some money into it so you can help your resources grow and the people will carry that duty on. Let's say Canada was the leader in Dairy production and you take that place, Canada will start to hate you and I love how it works.
Nukes, oh how I love them. They are not too over-powered, but yes they do pack a punch in this game. Nukes are quite cheap, depending on what nation you play as,but they take a long time to build and are quite exspensive to maintain them. In packs, nukes can destroy populations and dammage your enemy's resources heavily and turn military's to dust. Think before you use nukes, cause using nukes will devistate your relations with other country's and if you use nukes in very small packs... Well, you will be better off throwing toothpicks at your enemy.
Here's where it gets bad. This game wasn't really made for Windows 7 or 8 and so it tends to crash a little bit. There are bugs in the game where some country's are nothing but luck to try and set up for becoming a superpower. Like the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rebles and some others. There's also a bug where you can't take certain land and so on. The game really does have some downfalls, sometimes to relations tend to mess up. I got nuked by Russia and instead of people hating Russia, they started to hate me more. I don't understand this much, but it doesn't matter aslong as you have a much more powerful military then your enemy's.
Is it worth the price considering the bugs? YES! You might get annoyed from the bugs, but indeed it's a fun game. Very easy to get used to and you will always find new ways to beoming powers. If it's from economic domination to just pure agression.

I have really mixed feelings about this game, and wish Steam had a 'maybe' or 'neutral' option for the recommendation.  Without that, I have to err on the side of not recommending it.
The Good
The actual combat is fun enough.  It's turn-based strategy style.  There are a good number of decisions to make without being overwhelming.  The biggest of these are which of two guns to use, which special skills to use and in what order, and where to position yourself (mostly about accuracy vs defense).  Whether using guns or magic or fighting through a summoned creature or drone, skills include: wide range or spread shot, stun, damage over time, armor breaking, and various buffs.  Choosing which to use in which order (they have cool-down times so you can't just spam 'the best skill') is probably the most fun aspect.
The stories are complex and multilayered.  The plots are amazing.  And the political and philosophical aspects are deep (though easily ignored if you're just into it for the steam-punk-ish fantasy).
The Bad
The stories are almost entirely told through walls of text.  There's no animation, no voice acting, minimal cut scenes, etc, to tell the story for you.  And even when story could be told through gameplay itself, it's done through more pop-ups to read.  (For an idea of what I mean, think of games like Dragon Age or Skyrim, where you find books that explore the lore and history of the worlds.  In this game, the whole story is kind of presented that way, not just the lore and history).
The cash and shop system is pretty lame.  You only purchase things for your main character, so the vast majority of shops and goods just get in the way (eg. if you're a spell-caster you have no interest in the summoning totems, guns, drones, spirit magic, implants, hacking tools, etc).  It'd be great if you could purchase gear for your team as well.  On top of that, it mostly feels like you're just buying upgrades, rather than choosing different gear for different strategies.  There's a little bit of the strategy thing (like stun grenades vs direct damage grenades), but it's really minimal, and the upgrades are too essential to waste what tight money you have on optional things anyway.
The decking/hacking/matrix aspect seems like it should be the most unique aspect to the game... but it's just simplified version of the usual combat.  Same effects, same strategies, but only one character, fewer abilities, and simple graphics.  It really should be some unique kind of minigame; or at least involve a very different style of combat.
There is little or no point to exploring.  All that happens if you explore is: you wait a minute for your character to run to where you want; you see a white magnifying glass icon; you click on it and get a useless amount of money or low level healing pack.  That is, you don't uncover interesting enemies, side plots, unique items, secret areas, mini-games, etc.
All in all, I enjoyed the game while I was playing it, but when I wasn't playing it I had no drive to hurry up and start again.

Shadowrun: Dragonfall is a solid sequel and I recommend it for anyone who enjoyed Dead Man's Switch.  The story is better this time, and with far more dialogue immersion.  There is a great deal more combat in this game, but you can still avoid most of it with clever decisions.  All of the classes are useful, and the NPC team is highly competent.
The director's cut edition fixes many of the problems from SR:R.  There are a few times when enemies will take a long time with their turns, but it's rarely more than a few seconds delay if they do get stuck.  During two playthroughts, I've only once had to reload a save due to a glitch.

A good sequal to the original Xenoverse title. There's many reviews here that explain why. But as many are aware, a new anti-cheat was installed into the game's bin files today. Normally i'd be happy with this, (cheating is bad kids) but that isn't the case sadly, as now you cannot use cosmetic or other 3rd-party mods OFFLINE.
The game is pretty fun to play, but eventually there's a extremely noticable point where the end game (we're talking end of story / doing DLC story and late game PQ's) is very grindy and becomes boringly stale. That's where modding came in.
Online anti-cheat is a very logical, and honestly, acceptable answer. 100% recommend for online anti-cheat.
But i cannot approve of this whilst offline. For example, normally Sayian CaC could only go to SSJ3, but there were a variety of mods that added new transformations (SSJB, SSJR, for example) that worked wonderfully. This was the major key point for me, (following DBS, if Goku could become SSJB, why couldn't my CaC?) and now they've targeted a very dedicated and hardworking community.
Recommend if you are a die-hard fan. Can't recommend if you wish to enjoy the game in the long run. Never thought i'd ever not recomment this, but here we are.

Can't enjoy the modding community even if you only play offline, sound fair, doesn't it?
EDIT: There is a workaround, BUT all this drama from other players couldve been avoided in a variety of ways. I begrudgingly changed my recomendation ONLY out of respect to the modding community & because I want people to know it isn't dead, and you CAN mod this again.

I'll start out by saying i love Goichi Suda aka Suda 51. I first got introduced to his game with killer 7 on the Nintendo Gamecube. With that being said i truly enjoyed the romp-through of this game, the randomness, the comedy that is normally expected from Suda 51.
This game i will admit is the reason why i upgrade my PC. Killer is Dead had an error that would cause a event in the game to lock and prevent the player from progressing the story. This error pretty much effected those with dual core processors. Because of the devs reluctance to patch this game i was forced to upgrade since their were no patch in sight.
When i finally got back into the game their were put offs about it that prevent me from playing. Bumping into blockage that are boss fights also prevent me from progressing further. I then realize that their were key elements to mastering this game and its enemies. The key element being "Dodging", the main fundamental of this game, the key to your victories. You master this, you master the game.
Anyway this game is pretty much a thrill ride. The lack of complex moves and skill will prevent the most die hard of beat em up fans from enjoying their play-through, but the satisfying feel of taking down enemies will keep your average player hooked.
The story; though not great, is your semi-cliche anime type of twist, but who is playing for the story? Not me! The game is separated in episodes so you'll feel like you're watching a season of a particular anime series. The presentation is all there for the player to love and enjoy while enemy bashing your way through the end.
I found this game very enjoyable once i mastered dodging into countering and boy is that satisfying. This game is a definite buy for the beat em up crowd and definitely a game one should have in their Steam library. My dream one day is to have even more Japanese beat em ups to choose from in the future but having this game among others on steam is a great start.

I have to be honest. My initial thoughts of this game were pretty negative.  There are some things that I do not like about the game, but the positives far outway the negatives.  I'll start with the negatives. I'm not a fan of the way the story progression is set up. It's like a flashback to an old school RPG before character animations and voice acting was implemented.  I don't like having to read the dialogue from a tiny box next to a portrait of an anime character.  It can be pretty boring... which is why I have almost no idea what the storyline is about. It just doesn't keep my attention, so I end up skipping a lot of the dialogue.  Also, the character customization is extremely basic.  I expected quite a bit more, but was disappointed. It is possible to get better hair cuts, costumes, dyes, and armor, but it will cost you quite a bit of real life money. Needless to say, I'm not interested in paying money for in game underwear.  Lastly, I don't much care for the way the quests are set up.  It's not open world, which is kind of lame, so questing is different in this game. Each battle (this is what the quests/missions are called in game) is like a mini-dungeon that is replayable. It's replayable because each battle has a list of achievement-like side quests.  These reward you with gold and experience when you complete them.  So this is a completionists worst nightmare, or wet dream... I could see an argument for both.  None of the battles are too tough, even on hard mode, to finish alone, but the raids require a little more muscle.  So the positives.  The game looks decent enough. The graphics aren't spectacular, but they did a good job on the characters' looks. Especially the female characters. They look pretty damn great. The female characters' costumes would fit perfectly into every nerdy teenage boy's hentai fantasy.  The combat is pretty cool.  It took a little getting used to initially, but once I got it down, I liked it. It's a little big buggy at times when it comes to the dodging and parrying against enemies, but still a lot of fun. It sort of reminds me of Dynasty Warriors back in the day.  You know, before they made 57 remakes.  Overall, it is a pretty fun game. Definitely worth trying if you're even a little bit interested. Plus, its free. How the hell can you pass up trying a free game?  GET THIS GAME.

It's hard to say that this game doesn't take an interesting twist on the card-based games that have become popular in the last few years.
The game seems to be very good, and the community is rather active already, even when it's the dead of night in some places. Combining an active community with a fun gameplay mechanic is really nice, and leads to a game that has more longevity.
In brief, you are given a few 'legends' to play as, who each have their own specific cards at their disposal, which offer different playing styles. The game is played on a 3D plane, in which your 'legend' goes around attacking the battle cards, or paying (or doing whatver is needed for) adventure cards. The games are generally pretty short, and have five 'chapters', which is basically just five times in which you draw and play cards. If neither player is dead by the end of the fifth chapter, the two legends engage in a fight, during which your current attack rating, armor rating, and HP all come into play.
Sadly, there are some issues with it. The most glaring one is the horrid matchmaking. The casual and competitve matchmaking both seem to (for whatever reason) either put you against people far below your level, or much higher than you. While it could just simply be an issue of the game not being able to find a game for you against somebody of your same skill level, I believe putting you against people who aren't close to your skill range is either unfair for yourself, or the other player.
That said, this raises the second issue. As I mentioned, you may get matched with a much higher, or much lower ranked player, but the odds may be in the underdog's favor. The reasoning for this, is because the game seems to rely very heavily on RNG, and luck. While you can say all card-games have a degree of luck involved, this game seems to have it moreso due to the lack of actually needs gems or crystals to play cards. I've been on both ends (in two hours) of people getting a lucky string of +4 or +5 armor cards. While you can build your deck in such a way that it promotes these cards to pop up more, it seems that deck building isn't as neccessary as other games. That said, I have seen people prompt people looking up deck builders on the forums or Youtube channels, but for the casual player of the game, this may be a tad annoying.
Lastly, this is neither an issue nor a good thing. There seems to be no chat function (at least from what I've seen). While this does keep people from mocking other players, or hurling insults, it makes the game feel a little bit more empty, due to the lack of communication between the two players. While a chat system didn't need to be in, it would have been nice to see.
While the game isn't amazing, it has a fun new twist on the card-based game series, and due to the fact that it's free means that there is more incentive to actually try it out.

It's not a "pay to win" game, but it is a bit less new player friendly than say, Hearthstone. There are things that can only be countered by cards that are not included by the basic set. Now this game is very different from Hearthstone except tha they're both virtual card games, but there the similarity ends!... Ok, they're similiar in that you're trying to win both too.
That said, it's still tons of fun. And how you catch up is you do dungeoneering. Do not spend any copper on packs, only do dungeoneering, if you want to spend real money on it (I will admit I dropped the starter pack $8 on it) don't spend it on packs, spend it on dungeoneering. Three wins will make you break even, more will get you far better rewards, crystals (dust to Hearthstone players.) I will also say that it is a lot easier to make a decent dungeon deck than a decent arena deck.
Though that said, the game is not quite as well balanced as say Hearthstone, as the rarer cards are simply better than non-rare ones in about 90% of the situations.

This game flew so low under my radar, it's a miracle I ever took notice. But thank Perun I did! Explaining Thea is tricky, let me try some ways:
- it's a "CCG", in that any interaction that would require dice rolling or stat checking in other games is presented in the form of a turn-based card game. Learning it's mechanics takes mere minutes, but trust me, mastering it will take a while.
- it's a strategy game, in that you manage your village, build structures, hunt and gather, and most of all, think "just one more turn"
- it's an RPG, in that every villager or creature you have is a unique character. It might be only represented as a card illustration, but you'll quickly be able to tell it from everyone else. Units differ by classes, are able to carry equipment (that you can gather or build), and have an insane amount of stats.
- it's a "Rogue-lite", in that you aren't expected to win first time around. You aren't expected to stop playing after the first walkthrough. You will keep finding new quests, unlocking new ways to play, setting your own difficulty, and it all can spiral out of control as a result of a single event turned sour (well, you can always turn on saving ;) )
The best thing is, the developers from MuHa Games managed not only to flesh out all of these aspects, but do it in a surprisingly coherent fashion. And the story, set in a slavic fantasy world, makes it both mysterious and slightly unsettling, so you keep exploring, but do so very cautiously :)
And hey, if you're not completely convinced, try out the "Demo" version, which is the full version of the game at the state it was in Early Access! However, since then the devs relentlessly updated and tweaked the game, including a bunch of completely free DLCs, you know, just because they're THAT great!

Thea has a blend of turn based management and combat.  The combat system is an unique use of card combat -- placing troops and using abilities at the right time to get the edge over an enemy or to make sure your team doesn't take a loss (especially one of your better characters).  It is something new -- though I still prefer some tactical turn based games over this system, it is nice to switch things up with this innovative and challenging style of play.

Beautiful visuals but horrible controls.  Most people will probably love this game but I'm very picky about controls.  I prefer direct responsive controls, not scripted animations. This game isn't as bad as fly-by-wire games such as the Arkham series, but it was still annoying.
If I'm running left and I press right, I prefer the character to start running right, not to do a nifty slide animation that causes you to lose control of your character for a half second.  I also hate wall clinging, especially when it is very difficult to get your character off the wall.  The only wall clinging I'm ok with is when you have to hold a key to cling to the wall and you let go of the wall when you release the key.  This is one of those games were the walls seem to be made of fly paper. Getting off of them requires pressing jump and the thumbstick away from the wall at the same time.  And by "away" I mean exactly 180 degrees on the thumbstick.  190 degree or 170 degress causes you to flip upward on the wall rather than letting go of it.  Similarly, when you jump and try to press up to attack an enemy above you, if your thumbstick goes SLIGHTLY left or SLIGHTLY right your character flys left or right very quickly instead of aiming up. An example of scripted movement is that when you get close enough to a waste high platform in front of you, your character automatically hops up onto it and takes a few animated steps forward, often running into a damaging obstacle.  This kind of scripted behavior makes for a very cool looking demo video but a very frustrating game.  Like many games, the most challenging boss was the controller boss.
If you are not as anal as I am about controls, you will probably like this game. I love how it rewards exploration with lots of little hidden secrets.  And the boss fights would be really fun if the controls weren't so mushy.

I picked up Strider at some point in one of the many bundles I've bought on sale over the years and went in blind. I expected some sort of platformy hack and slash, I ended up with a fairly engaging ninja-themed metroidvania game.
As with most metroidvania games, you start out with fairly minimal abilities. Minimal to the point where I was not very impressed at first since I was just spamming the slash attack. Once you get a few power ups though, your combat options open up immensely and it becomes way more engaging. This isn't to say that it's perfect, I found the combat actually got annoying at several points in the game as some enemies were bullet (slash?) sponges no matter which powers you used, to the point where I found myself skipping over a lot of enemies. I also found some enemy types incredibly annoying to fight against due to the fact that they can stunlock you to death in large packs. Sure you could dodge the bullets, but if you mess up even once, a sufficiently large pack will refreeze/stun you as soon as you break out. Aside from those fights though, I found the boss fights to be very fun with varied mechanics.
Movement in this game was great, especially as you unlock powers to increase your movement options and unlock new areas. I always felt like I was in control when moving, which is great for combat. My only complaint is that some maps are fairly large and I found myself wishing for a quick way to traverse large flat areas, such as with some sort of charge/sprint power seen in some other games in the genre. I also found it annoying that the dash skill you eventually unlock completely kills your momentum. It's great for giving you more fine control, but it makes traversing through old areas to look for unlocks annoying.

Wonderful point-and-click game with lovable characters and interesting puzzles and one of my favorite games in the genre from the last five years.
I often feel that games that try to be funny often end up being cringeworthy instead, but the characters in this game are actually amusing. Even when they fall short of funny, they still achieve lovable and whimsical rather than awkward. The voice actors must take quite a bit of the credit for this as they are brilliant. The puzzles should be solveable as long as you make sure you click on everything and try all combinations, and the game does not contain any puzzles of the type that requires lots of calculations or trying to guess what the developers thought a certain symbol looked like etc.
Although I generally really, really like this game, its weak points might be the traditional storyline (an ordinary person must save the world), as well as the villain being a bit too cartoonish for my taste. However, this might be a positive aspect for a younger player as this means the villain is not scary. The difficulty level of the puzzles might also be an issue for those who want more challenging games - although the puzzles are not super easy, they are not extremely difficult either. This game is also more on the light-hearted side, so if you are looking for something darker and more serious, this might not be the game for you.
That being said, I strongly recommend this game for someone looking for a casual, delightful and charming point-and-click game with entertaining and logical puzzles that do not stop the flow of the game.
