9/10 - Tremendously entertaining game with elements of Grand Theft Auto but a more compelling story and a unique hacking mechanism that makes it far more interesting to play than GTA. The plot is linear, but there's enough to do between campaign missions that the Chicago setting feels like a genuine open world and though the graphics may not be state of the art, the city looks great even without volumetric lighting effects. The Person-of-Interest-style infoboxes that pop up as you walk past NPCs and the telephone conversations/messages that you can hack into make the city feel alive, at least until they start becoming repetitive and random. Some of the mini-games, especially ones involving car chases, aren't to my taste. (I hate third-person driving sequences; it doesn't feel like a natural way to drive.) The psychedlic game "trips" are cute 3D arcade games, but won't be to everyone's taste.
Yes, Ubisoft has borrowed the basic formula of the recent Far Cry games, but there's enough variation on it to make the gameplay seem fresh. The sequel, Watch Dogs 2, has a less linear narrative, but I actually preferred the fixed narrative in this one. The characters are interesting, the voice acting and motion capture in the cut scenes are top notch, and the story never gets boring, which is more than I can say for Far Cry 4. There's only one genuine story decision that the player gets to make and it comes at the very end, but it's the most important decision in the story and determines whether you've had a moral epiphany at some point during the earlier scenes.
The collectibles are well done and, with one exception, aren't completely meaningless. The serial-killer collectibles, for instance, lead to a small but genuine reckoning. The only truly meaningless collectibles are the visits to Chicago Hot Spots. (Visit often enough and you can become...the mayor of the spot! Uh, yeah.) But they also provide snarky commentary on Chicago history that's interesting in its own right. Yes, I visited all 150 and got pretty much nothing for the effort except fun.
The game allows you to keep playing after the story is over, so you can choose to finish the collectibles and side missions at your own pace, as long as you have your saved game intact. (I'm not sure if it's on your disk or in the Ubisoft cloud.) I'll probably never play the game again from the beginning because I know the story, but I'll continue visiting the world to see if it has any surprises left.

To kick off proceedings I will begin with a simple observation, I purchased this game when it came out (2 or 3 years ago?) and only now have I finished the campaign. No this game does not win the prize for longest campaign in RPG history, instead for least engaging storyline.
Watchdogs was to be this amazing experience in a technologically advanced city where virtually anything was hackable, granted this wasn't really the case but that's not why it deserves its thumbs down. The truth is the make or break of any RPG with such a developed character cast is its storyline. Now watchdogs could have gotten along just fine without having a campaign, however, this would probably have relegated it to the unnewsworthy leagues of Need for Speed Online.
No the truth is, the storyline was cliche, an uncle seeking revenge for his niece, basically similar to a dad seeking revenge for his daughter, you have the typical crazy brute in Jordi, a shadowy string pulling figure in Lucky Quinn and a young and naive hacker. Really, it didn't have an emotional grip to it, which is weird because ultimately Mass Effect was of much less relevance to the player (what with being set in the future outer space) and yet still made more of a connection.
It's hard to put a finger on what exactly could have gone better here, but suffice it to say, that this story lines linear, unchangeable nature probably played a factor

If you've played any type of RPG or adventure game in the past, there are some great sequences poking fun at the genres, players and developers, lovely stuff. The humour doesn't always hit, there are some off screen sequences that don't quite come off, but its good to see a game try something a bit different.
The artwork and style is lovely, although there are occasional glitches and not all animations fully reflect the actions that are taking place. But these are minor fiobles that don't detract from the main experience. The voice acting is generally top notch too, great to hear a Welsh accent from one of the main actors.
The game is quite easy however. Items are easy to come by, sometimes just given to you when talking to other characters and experienced adventure game players will find themselves solving puzzles before knowing why they need to. This can lead to a bit of awkwardness, but that will be the player messing with the natural flow the developers had in mind.
That said, at 17 hours playtime, the difficulty level is not too far off the mark and the Book of Unwritten Tales does not out stay its welcome at any point. A thumbs up from me and roll on the next adventure in the series..

This was a great adventure game. Sadly, the developers abandoned it. There are many graphics and audio incompatibilities across all platforms. The game needs significant development to reintegrate with the latest versions of these dependencies in order to recreate a working build system. They said this is simply not going to happen, and that the bugs will not be fixed.
As there is no way to tell if the game will be completable for you, I can't recommend you buy it.

I must confess it was rather surprising to go back to a proper point and click adventure after a streak of somewhat half-baked ones light on puzzles and perfectly content to hand hold you throughout the entire experience in favor of delivering their narrative. Make no mistake, The Book of Unwritten Tales makes couple of modern concessions but it is, at heart, a traditional genre representative.
Starting off, I have to say this is one helluva charming game even if it does have a few things stacked against itself, as I'll explain later down the road in this write-up. Visuals succeed almost entirely in blending various 3D and 2D assets, with few exceptions here-and-there marring the presentation primarily because age creeps into everything eventually, as well as appropriate use of soft colors and lighting goes a long way in selling you on the locales you visit. Pleasant artwork certainly helps, as well. Standout element I REALLY have to give props to is the soundtrack – it's brilliant. Fantasy fare and nothing you haven't heard before, but packs a punch and I'd bet no expense was spared in putting it together. Polygonal characters are most of the time lovingly animated with, well, character and it comes through especially when they emote.
Speaking of characters you'll be contending with more than just Wilbur the Gnome, who is portrayed as the game's central figure on most of promotional material, but as far as I'm concerned he is this game's genuine protagonist forsooth. Somewhat of a black sheep in his family comprised of a biologist, roboticist and engineers in general he instead aspires to become a mage one day. Sudden turn of events thrusts a great destiny on his shoulders and sets him down on a long road to potentially save the day and maybe, just maybe achieve his lifelong dream. Second character is a she-elf named Ivo who ends up enrolled in this adventure thanks to random chance rivaling that of Wilbur himself. There is a third person involved, but I'd rather not spoil who that is. Well, there's also a fourth. Sort of. Kinda. It's a whimsical game, what do you want?
Now that I've gushed about the positives let's get down to gritty negatives... of which there aren't that many, surprisingly. I'd only list two real negatives, because if you're into point and click adventures you already knows you're signing up for with few nonsensical puzzles and such, even though The Book of Unwritten Tales dispenses with those for [mostly] perfectly logical puzzles, and they are as follows; entire playable cast does not get equal amount of character development and that game ends rather abruptly, following what is possibly the most arduous and tedious section of the game. Which you have to retread twice. I don't know if they simply ran out of time or money, but the ending itself felt rather automated and resolved much too quickly for all the buildup that lead to it. One point that's going to be divisive for most is game's heavy use of references, both playing them straight or ridiculing while portraying how genre savvy developers are. It doesn't get into obnoxious territory and ranges from your classical Discworld to Star Wars and World of Warcraft mentions, but there was one section that served as commentary of MMORPGs and TCGs as a whole which made me bolt a smile on my face for five minutes straight.
So, closing words. Should you get it? If you want a modern game from a genre past it's prime, but one that's long overdue for proper revival I would say yes. It's not a masterpiece but for me game's charm carried it from beginning to end.

The book of Unwritten Tales is very funny classic point and click adventure.
This means that you'll often be tearing your hair out trying to solve puzzles that seem illogical until you realise what some of the stuff in your inventory does and what to use it on.
Just like the good old days then.
But where it absolutely shines is in the humor:
The dialogues you have with the other characters is really funny,especially if you have likeb fantasy novels, movies and games as there are plenty of nods, winks and satire to be found featuring most of the well known fantasy worlds and their tropes.
It's world  has a kind of Diskworld vibe to it, meaning that nothing is as you would expect it to be in the average fantasy kingdom and that the story isn't simply just about "Go you hero, get the legendary jewelled sword to slay the evil one" but that it is more about the protagonists and the sticky but strange situations they find themselves in often without any real fault of their own.
If you like old school adventures (with all their faults) you'll like this one, and the best bit is that the sequels are just as funny as this one.

Eh. It's alright. While it's not really like Hearthstone in terms of gameplay, it apes Hearthstone in most other ways. Grind 1000b(100g) for a booster packs, or spend 1500b(150g) on an dungeoneering(arena) run. There's no tavern brawl, instead replaced by a weekly "epic quest" that awards you a booster for winning X number of games in a week with certain legends(heroes).
The gameplay is a neat twist from the standard TCG fare, the visuals are beautiful, but in terms of how content is portioned out, its like a more stingy Hearthstone; there are no adventures to pick up so you're stuck either buying price-inefficient booster packs or getting slaughtered in the dungeon (because the gameplay systems are completely different alien to new players so you're going in with almost no notion of the worth of cards you draft unless you use a tier list).
With Hearthstone, the cards are characters, weapons, spells, and memes you know and love. For Chronicle... I don't think there's that same mainstream appeal. Why is a penguin called a KGP Agent and why is he taking my card to give me attack power? The cards, as far as I've seen, don't have in-game lore descriptions to mouse over. It makes it difficult to connect with the cards.
Just my opinion. I would probably keep playing the game if the pricing model was different, but it's hard to justify fitting this game into your budget when there are alternatives with more content that can be acquired more quickly.

The building placing can be rather wonky sometimes in how it works and doesn't explain itself well (like how placing buildings next to each other actually expands the room, what preserving walls means, ect., maybe I just didn't read the tutorial correctly though, so possibly all my fault), not a big deal once you do figure it out, though. The fighting is simple, it works how it's supposed to, nothing complex is going on, which is completely fine in this game's case. Provided your computer can run this game; it looks beautiful with all graphics settings on, the animations are nice, too. And the lack of a legitimate hunger bar is very refreshing in a pool of survival games where hunger becomes annoying. I hope they make hunger optional via server options or something if they ever choose to implement it.
In it's current state; I recommend this game.
EDIT: I also bought this game when it was 10 dollars, which I think is completely worth it if you ever see it on sale. But, I wouldn't have minded playing 20, as it's still clocking hours for me.

TL;DR: Good strategy game based on eastern European mythology. High amount of RPG elements through villager skills and quests. Lots of crafting with different ingredients and recipes. Relatively short games, but with high replay value. Most negative point is the way battles/challenges are resolved, a bit repetitive after a while.
----
The world has fallen into darkness, and you're a god, trying to lead a last enclave of your followers through the dark times and towards morning. Your task is to figure out what happened in the world, and how to go forwards in it.
You start out with a village (and will never have more than the one) with a small population. Each of your people is unique, with its own combination of skills that make them suited to different tasks. In the village, you gather, craft and build. You can send out scouting parties across the hex-field-filled world to explore, fulfill quests, fight enemies and fetch rare resources. Dangers are posed by roaming bands of monsters and random events; and a dangerous world it is indeed. Death of a beloved villager is always a possibility, and each and every one will be missed.
There's two things here that I really like about the game that I should stress: The crafting system and the events/quests. The latter are well written, especially for a primary strategy game, with different creatures than you'd see in your standard fantasy genre. The former consists of recipes unlocked by research (research points are generated through practially any event and through crafting). The wonderful thing is that you get a recipe that allows many, many different combinations of resources that not only impact the stats, but also the name and appearance of the result. Experimenting is fun! Without good equipment, the most experienced warrior is but a bloodstain in a giant's path.
Then there's one thing I've grown to dislike about Thea: The card-based challenge system and the multitude of challenges. I won't go into detail about the card system, but it does get tiresome after the umpeenth time you play the same basic idea. Fortunately, there's an auto-resolve. Unfortunately, it occasionally screws up badly and you're in danger of losing people you really can't lose. Me, I use the configurable difficulty scale to allow manual saves and reload if necessary. Cheating? Maybe. But I'm playing to have fun. There are also many kinds of challenges; not everything is combat. That is good. It is, however, quite difficult to keep all the stats and the way they interlink in mind. A little less may have been more. That's a minor squabble, though.
The good absolutely trumps the bad in Thea. I very much recommend that you check it out for yourselves!

Absolutely and utterly the best RTS game you can get. The hours recorded in steam does not reflect the time i have spent in this game. I mostly played on GPGnet, but since its demise all players now use FAF - forged alliance forever, a community of dedicated players reaching at times up to 1000 players on at any given moment. FAF has player rating for balanced games, 1v1 ladder, and custom games. The game within FAF has been modified to rebalance the game further, whilst this is work in progress, major alterations have taken place to improve gameplay for the better.
The game features what i consider a must for any large scale RTS which is called Zoom. This means you can seamlessly zoom in and out of areas of the map that need your attention. Fixed view with minimap is no use at all for this scale of game where you control 100's of units.
The game is difficult i wont lie. Its made harder by the fact that dedicated players like myself have played the game for a long time and know it inside out, but we are here to help new players learn, and this is where FAF plays a great role in introducing and helping new players by offering video tutorials and a community lobby where people can chat in public and private messages.
The game features a flux economy system. This in my opinion is fantastic, you accumulate resources per second, and spend resources per second. Each structure or unit costs resources per second, and the time in which it takes for something to complete can be decreased if you have enough resources by channeling more build power into the particular unit or structure. This adds a dimension of strategy to the already obundant strategies available in game.
You have 2 resources, mass and energy. Mass is mostly made from building an extractor on fixed locations throughout the map forcing the player to expand, energy is made by making structures that produce it. You can enhance your mass production by upgrading the mass exctractors that you have built. Doing so will cost you mass and energy but you will be rewarded on completion with more mass per second. Finding the balance between spending resources and increasing them either makes you win or lose the game. It is extremely hard to find that balance especially when you play different maps.
Each game is its own, it feels different, because there are so many variables within a game, choices that you make or decisions that your oponents make. Playing the same map over and over will not bring you boredom, instead you will retain the interest and hunger for the win, cahnge your style, adapt your choices.
Like any RTS you are encouraged to expand, and rewarded with resources for doing so but what makes FAF so diverse is the map selection. Gameplay can vary extensively based on the type of map you are playing, so for those of you who are new to the game or prefer not to move to much, there are maps that cater for that play style. We call them turtle maps, where resources are located near to your start location minimizing any early raids so you can focus entirely on a smaller number of tasks.
Actions per minute do matter in this game, there are many things to do, early on you have less units and less things to monitor, its nice and relaxed, but as the game lengthens you are forced to do more as your units multiply, it becomes more challenging and it begins to become much more intense. A replay feature which can be watched at any point will show you your mistakes or how you won, its a great way to learn.
There are 4 tech tiers
Tech 1 - basic units that you can build right away, low heatlth and damage but low cost.
Tech 2 - higher health more versatile, better selection, costs a little more
Tech 3 - high health and damage, costs alot
Experimantal - Collosal units with very high health and damage, game changers, slow to build, cost a lot
Certain maps enable games as big as 8v8, games can last as little as 7 minutes or as long as 2 hours depending on how balanced or aggressive the teams are. The rating system is based on trueskill, new player ratings will fluctuate greatly to begin with until it works out how well you play.
As you might already know the game features base building, engineers are a unit you have to build to make structures, you can have 1 engineer make a building in 3 minutes or 10 engineers make it 10 times faster, but it will cost ten times more per second. Structures you can make are land factories, naval factories, air factories. Point defense building to defend with, tactical long range missile launchers, tactical missile defense, nukes and anti nukes, stationary shields, or even giant artillary that can reach the entire map.
There are 4 factions at the moment, each faction is diverse, it feels different and has different buildings and units with different stats. You start the game with one unit, the Commander, which can be upgraded, it can build structures and fight against units. Your commander is on of your most formible units which can be useful both passively and aggressively. If he dies, you die so you need to keep him alive at all costs.
I have probly played this game more than 10000 hours in the 7 years i have owned it, i still play it most days even now. Please if you are an RTS fan give this a try, dont be put off by its difficulty, it can be frustrating at 1st but it is so rewarding when you start winning.

Chronicle: Runescape Legends is by no means a "Hearthstone" killer, but instead brings something new to the table.
CCGs were thought to be strictly competitive, but the storybook chapters and PvE elements you make for yourself are truly refreshing. Due to the mechanics of the chapters, games are fairly concise whereas in Heartstone, there are decks built around fatigue and can last up to 15 minutes a match.
I adore that with each chapter the pages turn and your characters are on a new setting, but I wish there was something interactive to them that add another layer of strategy, planning and general reward for knowing the terrain.
The 5 playable heroes and their playstyles are immediately recognizable to any meta-conscious Hearthstone player, and will fit nicely to their expectations.
I was never into Runescape, never played it, but C:RL does not discriminate or alienate players for being ignorant of the lore and world.
It's free to play and well worth your time if you're feeling ennui with HS and looking for an alternative or want to get into a really fun, different CCG.

The classes are horribly unbalanced, mages have the highest damage and the most "sabotage" cards.  The vampire and to a lesser extent the tank, are outmatched as their mechanics rely on sacrificing health, when the mage can already deal 30+ damage with just 2 cards.
If an opponent disconnects it says you win but it does not count towards your wins, in dungneering(arena) it actually takes a life from you just like a loss.  DO NOT spend real money on arena until this is patched!
Base attack should not be allowed to drop below 2, in ranked people are using this mechanic to grief, in arena mode if you draft a card that reduces your opponent's base attack it is an instant win.
They really should've stepped out from Hearthstone's shadow, the gameplay of Chronicle: RL is much different than Hearthstone, yet they've borrwed so much from the latter.  The gamemodes, art style, pack opening, turn timers, etc. all make it look like a cheap knockoff of Hearthstone.  That, combined with numerous bugs and flawed concepts makes me question if the people behind this are actually commited to the title.
EDIT: Permanently altering your oponent's base attack is horribly unbalanced, paticularly in arena-clone where the availability of base attack increasing cards is much more scarce.  Once your attack reaches 1 you are combat ineffective, even weak creatures can take off a good portion of your health, you can really only hope that you draw an affordable weapon before the final fight.
The draw mechanic is pointless in the final chapter (aside from a class-specific ability involving hand size), so if you pick draw cards with no additional effect you run the risk of it being a dead card.
The concede button doesn't skip animations, the final battle really drags on when you already know you've lost.  Additionally there are 3 post-game continue buttons (just to show your progress in level, rewards & acheivments) that add uneeded click-through time to the process.
Going first is a major advantage, Besides getting in the first hit of the final battle, going first is the only way you can guarantee the outcome from any card, and it happens up to 5 times per game (once per chapter).  Meanwhile the player going second has to gamble on whether you've sabatoged what they earned in the last chapter (gold, weapons, and/or armor) or otherwise altered the state of their board (by adding health and/or attack to enemies for instance).
"Dungeonering" (AKA HS Arena) drafts are incredibly awkward, the game is biased toward big, expensive cards that A) you won't have the gold for OR B) will deal massive damage to you.  The easy, cheap cards rarely appear, so you will most likely wind up resource starved, smashing your unarmed character into overpowered monsters iust to keep pace with your opponent.
TLDR: If you are intending to spend real money on packs, I'd recomend waiting a few months to make sure the community and developers are still active.

On the positive end: they fixed the intro mission (for the most part). The combat controls are nice, simple, and responsive and the system of combat is viseral, imidiate, and fun. The graphics aren't anything to really write home about these days, almost Dreamcast ish with the way they design somethings (like the spider beast in the tutorial), but in other spots (such as faces and over all design of character models) it does hold up still. Yes, I'm underselling it a bit, but this is really how I feel about the graphics. I could say 'they look incredible', but compared to the games I've been playing over the years, it's really midcore at best, especially given...
On the negative end: First foot stepped out into the game world proper, all I got was lag. I'm running a fairly monster system. Not top of the line, but more then you should need for games outside of Crytek's latest. And this thing was chugging. I haven't tried it on lowest settings yet, but given this game doesn't -look- top of the line, it should be an issue.
Mind, it is far from bad looking, but I've played games with far more detailed graphics at higher settings and got zero issues. What I'm saying is that the optimization, though fixed from how it was when it first hit steam, is still crapping the bed.
That issue aside, another problem that I have is the places where you progress the story or buy items or the like. Sure, there is are deciently animated cut scenes in the intro (and I assume sprinkled through out the rest of the game), but then right after you finish that, you are treated to an empty room, camera softly swaying back and forth as if you are on a sort of boat (you aren't), with the woman you just saved as a pic to the side with a small dialog box that only allows a single short line (well, two if you count the few actions it barely discribes her doing) to tick along slowly. The scene (aside from the camera sway) is more in line with a dating sim then a damned action rpg.
They could have at least put the characters in the room, statically. But no, empty bed, empty room, empty world it feels like when you are in these scenes.
When I had finally stepped out into the game proper and had the frame rate pitch a fit, I tried to at least bring up a menu or some such, but after teaching me how to fight, the fracking tutorial level forgot to teach me how do use the damn UI. I have played Wildstar,DCUO, WoW, Guild Wars 2, City of Heroes, and Chamions, amoung other games through out the years. It took me a good 10 minutes pressing buttons, trial and error, and a ton of waiting to get anything to actually work. There were sometimes where a button would do one thing one moment and feel like it did something different the next. Espeically true of how my camera control changed on the mouse.
And the main reason I had this issue? No 'esc' menu. The most basic method of -every- game I've played. Didn't work.
I'm sure a lot of other folks got the hang of this, but there is something wrong when a company feels so much like a special fracking butterfly that it has to break things that are basic to any game. It's like when games love to move the jump button to somewhere besides the bottom of the four main face buttons of a controler. If there is a reason for it, maybe, sure. But the 'esc' menu is gaming ui/controls 101 for gaming, espeically mmos like this one.
If it were just a bad game, I could just walk away and I wouldn't care, but the trouble is that I greatly enjoy the combat system and character styles. It's a nice mix and shows that there are some really keen and great folks working on this mess. It makes me so sad that under the issues I've already complained about as well as Nexons infamous business model, there is no way I can recogmend this to anyone. I don't even understand how it got such a high rating.
If you are patient enough to deal with the crashes due to it's poor interaction with the steam overlay (at least I'm guessing that is the issue), frame rate drops in cities, and the rediculous 'dating sim' style events that are even crappy by dating sim standards, by all means, I'm not going to stop you from enjoying this game. Like I siad, there is a good game in here.
But I definately say this -doesn't- deserve the metascore it's got. A deightful combat game wrapped in a crap mmo model driven by a money grubing crap publisher. If it weren't f2p, I'd say skip entirely.

Far Cry 2 is the only main series entry worthy of being a successor to the original in my opinion, as well as the most realistic game in the series. It was sort of a "love it or hate it" thing for a lot of people and that's probably why they went back to the saturated island, somewhat stylized thing for the next game in the series.
In a large sense, it's very different, but if you really get into the game then it's far better than it seems at first glance. Far Cry 2's greatest quality is its ability to capture the essence of a setting on a large scale. People would often complain about driving and whatnot but for me, that only enhanced what it was they were going for. Disregarding bullet ballistics and weapon degredation/jamming and looking only at the format, this is a serious candidate for one of the most realistic shooters of all time - and by that I mean truly realistic in regards to the events that occur. There's no huge chain of scripted events. There's no heavy story, it's very minimal. It plays out how a confrontation like this might actually play out in real life, as opposed to being over the top or reliant on fantasy. Yet you still blow things up and rain chaos on your enemies, just in a way that you don't generally see in shooters.
You may or may not like Far Cry 2. Personally, the weapons, grenades, vehicles and atmosphere are fantastic to me, and disregarding Blood Dragon as a "main entry" to the series, this is my favorite Far Cry game. It does what it's supposed to do so well that suspension of disbelief isn't even really necessary.
So, immerse yourself in the grasslands and the jungles (on max graphical settings, with good headphones for the audio) and see what you think of it.

Very fun digital card game set in the Elder Scrolls theme. The game is very good so far and is a nice alternative to hearthstone.
You start off in a story mode that also features a how to play introduction. You choose your class and charcter type, each having different strengths and weaknesses. In the begining you play through the story mode to unlock more cards but what makes this card game different is you just dont get new card the base cards can be upgraded to better cards with a variety on different attacks than the base card had to start with. For example lets say you had a base card with 1 defense and 1 attack and was soldier. This card could upgrade to a 3 attack 3 defense knight or it might upgrade to a Gaurd ( same thing as a Taunt card in Hearthstone )( If you dont know what a Gaurd or Taunt card does its a card that must be removed from the board first before you are allowed to hit other cards or the main character )
Something unique about this game compared to lets say Hearthstone is that the playing board is split in half. You may lay your cards on either half but can only attack opponents cards that are on the same half of the board unless you play a card that can attack across the board.
Also when you play the story it gives you a choice on how the story will go. If you kill this person you get this card if you spare them you get this card and the story adjusts to your choice.
Everytime you or your opponent loses 5 health they draw a card in addition to the card they get t draw at the begining of each turn.
Yes there is a store to buy card packs this is a free to play game they have to make money some where, but like hearthstone you can earn coins from playing matches to buy packs without actually using real money.
I reccomend this game if you like trading card games. The Elder Scrolls theme is a bonus but you dont have to be a fan of the games to enjoy it

Peggle Extreme is a simplified introduction to the Peggle games and can be picked up any time for some casual puzzling. How the game is played, either by trial and error or more strategically, is entirely subject to whim.
Within ten levels, five challenges and the help of one playable character, namely the Peggle Master Björn the unicorn, Peggle Extreme teaches the most basic mechanics that are needed to understand the Peggle ruleset. By and large, the game is very much akin to many arcade games that involve a ball to hit specific targets in a 2D environment. It's a twisted mix of pinball and Breakout with the exception that the player has more than enough time to potentially plan the next shot.
The otherwise colourful, child-friendly graphics and sounds are interspersed with images based on Valve's games and a few of their respective voice lines. Its difficulty is rather easy with a little bump when tackling the Master Challenges. The winning shot slow motion, glittering fireworks and the playing of the Ode to Joy feel a little over the top rewarding but that's part of the game's appeal.
Peggle Extreme is a charming bite-sized puzzler perfect as an in-between snack.

Thea: The Awakening is a base building game in which the storyline is railroaded from start to finish and in which you are limited to a single base to build for the duration of the whole game. If this don't tell you my point right here then I'm uncertain of how to put it.
The idea and the concept of the game is great. The graphics are excellent for a game of this nature and the story in itself is very well done. There unfortunately stops the congratulations on the game since there is actually nothing more to the game itself. It is like playing a Civilization game without any enemy short of barbarians and being limited to a single town all game. I enjoyed reading the story on my first playthru but then the voice over, while not that bad, is done
. Try to imagine how many pages of text such a game would require for the entirety of one single game and multiply that by the amount of different persons portrayed thru the game and imagine what it would be to sit down for 4 to 6 hours listening to the same person dull and apparently uninterested voice. Then imagine that you have to restart the game at least 20 times to
the only appeal the game provide. Ugh.
As I mentioned, the concept of the game is great. What is truely and stupidly lacking is the execution of said concept. You have many buildings to unlock and build and of course not only you are limited to a single town but you are also limited in the number of buildings your settlement can have... So you have to choose wisely.
, depending of the materials you choose and sometimes the order in which you place such materials then you get "bonuses" which are extremely important since the vast majority of the buildings and the items you build youself are extremely plain. Those bonuses end up being what make a building or item good or useful but
; you have to either know it all already or remember it by heart. Item production suffer the same fate and problem and I ended up clicking on the "infinite" option for food even tho I wasn't producing it 90% of the time simply to keep the templates up and going for when I needed it.
Thankfully when you build something you get to preview the result. If it wasn't of this single feature then this would have been one of the worst game of all time considering how important crafting is in this game...
Akin to the same problem,
aspect of the UI and the game itself require you to click pointlessly a stupidly high amount of time and no time saver function whatsoever exist. For example, when creating an expedition (which is
to do anything in the game by the way) you will need to "equip" your team with food and fuel so they don't starve and have something to make a campfire. So far so good but wait, when I select something then the game prompt me for my team to take it all from the town stockpile... What? Oh wait, there is 2 buttons right underneath: one for +1/-1 and another one for +10/-10. Uh, why? . The same problem happen when you return from a long expedition and want to send your best men out there to continue fighting for the storyline. I ended up several times utterly frustrated from equipping items from other members and realizing on the way that they had left without a weapon because I took it from them without realizing to equip it to somebody else. Really interesting twist on Boss Monster that is something you can play when you don't have 2-3 friends at your house to play.
As to the fairness of the microtransactions it's hard to tell, I know when I was playing a silver ranked AI it managed to get a stupidly powerfull four card combo that killed me on turn two so definitly some things that could use some balance tweaks. But otherwise it is very much like Hearthstones F2P model where its fairly quick to get a couple free decks but then slows down after that when most your currency comes from doing dailies or winning against other players (since you only get gold the first time you beat the AI at its current rank). Like Hearthstone you also unlock class cards as you play with a class more to level it up.
But with that said other then the F2P model, that its a TCG/CCG, and that the main menu is a book, it is nothing like Hearthstone. Like I said its closer to Boss Monster with light Hearthstone in mechanics then it is to Hearthstone or Magic the Gathering. You play up to four cards per turn  to try to build up your hero by fighting monsters to gain attack and gold to buy weapons or spells for five turns and then if neither hero has died in the prossess you battle each other to the death, which gives the person who goes first a slight advantage at that stage but the person who goes second starts with one more card so a slight advantage while building up the hero.
All in all, I would say I rather enjoy it and it didn't feel like a waist of time trying it since it is actually fairly interesting and fells like the devs went "Hey we want to make a Boss Monster like, but with a bit of Hearthstone feel, and the Runescape characters" I never got big into Runescape, played it a bit but not much, and having no clue about Runescape didn't take away from the game at all, I am sure that if I was bigger into it I would get more of the character and enemy references, but you don't need to like Runescape lore to enjoy this game. Its definitly worth trying since its free while not being a waist of time like some of the badly made "F2P' are.

GRAV is a good game. I open with that statement as, unfortunately, the game is hanging around the 60% positive review mark, which, in Steam terms, is terrible.
Does the game deserve negative reviews? Yes, of course, every game will have people who dislike it, and that's fine.
But does the game deserve THIS MANY negative reviews? No, I wouldn't say so. GRAV isn't a bad game, and you will notice from most of the negative reviews that people who dislike this game are people who have only played the game for a few hours, or people who complain about how the servers aren't fully alive and active all the time. That is because these people do not fit into the target audience.
I will adress all of these subjective "flaws", but first I will point out to you that GRAV has a LOT of grinding. This is not necessarily a bad thing, even though the general public would assume so. The game is absolutely FULL of things to work for, and many of these things take a very long time to achieve. In my opinion, this is a great thing. You always have something on the horizon to strive for, you'll always be able to try out that new equipment you just earned, and you'll always,
feel satisfied with the results of a long grind. That is why you should take another perspective on any review with under 10 hours played.
As for server activity, PvP, etcetera, I don't recommend this game if you're looking for a purely player-versus-player experience against random people. GRAV isn't built for that. A few experience levels make a huge imbalance in damage and total health, and so the game doesn't hit the mark as far as public PvP environments go.
If PvE isn't your thing, though, don't be strayed away! I think GRAV is great as a team game, where everyone starts at the same time and has a race to the top, in some sort of red vs blue scenario.
But, where this game really shines for me, is with or against friends. Progression is made much sweeter when you have a partner or two by your side, so I recommend this game the most to those who favour PvE or team environments. GRAV has so much to offer in terms of fun player interaction, and memorable moments are a plenty. I've had many epic experiences gliding through the air alongside my small group, riding a futuristic vehicle over plains, or simply dancing around a fire with friends.
So, in conclusion, I can easily recommend GRAV. It is fun and it is good. However, you should take some more time to consider if you are wanting to play the game alone. That can be said for a lot of multiplayer-compatible games, but GRAV in particular shines with friends.

Vindictus is an enjoyable hack-and-slash mmo. I feel like I'm playing a "slower paced Dynasty Warriors", and note that "slower" doesn't mean anything bad. It just means there is less chaos involved. I highly recommend this game to be played with friends.
It is clearly designed with party play in mind. As you level up the missions require a little more teamwork.
It has a fantastic "new player introduction" system, and this will ease your learning experience so you can get right into killing things! Even the pre-game lobby is instanced, where you and your party can run around practising combos on various objects before you set sail to new lands.
Recap the goods: easy to pick up, fantastic party game.
Now, some less happy things: it is still a f2p mmo. It will have a cash shop. And this cash shop is for various convenience and cosmetic items. No the cash shop is not necessary to play the game, and you get many free passes into it at times. Secondly, like many Asia mmos, there is a grind element to it. This is not always a bad thing however, and the grind begins rather late in the game naturally.
Final thought: I really enjoy playing this game with friends. The boss battles are epic, the controls easy, and graphics are nice and pleasing.

A pretty fun- but uneven- gameplay experience and mediocre story hamper some great ideas. When it works, the game is brilliant; giving intuitive control over your environment so you can steal information from an area without even having set foot in it. It's these moments that successfully make you really think about the game's message on the disadvantages of an "ever-connected" world.
Where it doesn't work are usually to do with the controls... a cover buttom that has a tendancy to send you directly in the firing line rather than where you want to go; an awkward system for selecting different types of weapons.
Personally, I quite like Aiden Pearce- he was a great contrast to the Nathan Drake's of the world. I think it was the story that didn't help people get to like him. Despite a disappointing ending, the twist itself was actually quite brilliant- again highlighting the themes of today's society, and how a tiny thing for one person can change the entire life of another. I think Aiden- just about- manages to act within his moral compass in a realistic way. He questions his actions and feels remorse... Before deciding he's so deep in the game he may as well embrace it entirely.
Overall, I'd recommend it if it's on sale. It's not as bad as the press seems to claim- it just wasn't a masterpiece when it needed to be. Oh, and install the e3 pre-release mod for the best experience.

Far Cry 2 is a game that simulates what it's like to be a gun-for-hire in some war-torn African country.  And it is very good at that, for better or for worse.
And from what I've experienced of it, it's for worse.  The constantly-jamming weapons, the fact that everyone's trying to kill you no matter who you align yourself with, a map interface that's clunky at best, and the malaria...oh, god, the malaria.  You have to take malaria pills every half-hour in-game, or you die.  And you only get four doses at a time - you replenish your pills at one specific in-game location.  It's all very frustrating, and all in the name of "a realistic experience."
Let Far Cry 2 remain as an example of how realism doesn't always make a game better.

Strider is a great, fast-paced Metroidvania game that is fun to play.  It's a bit on the shorter side (you can complete the game in under 4 hours), and the collectable/"Metroidvania" aspect of the game isn't focused on too deeply.  Most of the collectables are within the grasp of where you're supposed to be story-wise, so you never have to veer too far off-path.  I don't think there are any puzzles or any really tricky collectables, so it is missing out on some of the complexity that other games of the same genre have.  The combat and how smooth the game plays makes up for it though, in my opinion.
Strider, however, has one major problem.  It tends to crash.  A lot.  My first bits of gameplay were enjoyable, with the game running perfectly fine without any issues whatsoever.  As I progressed further into the game, Strider crashed more and more often.  I'm not exactly sure why, but it is an issue that other users are havnig as well (there's enough proof of it in the forums).  While I've had no problem trying to play through this game constantly crashing (enemies aren't hard to face and it doesn't take too long to progress so it's somewhat manageable), it is definitely annoying (and even impossible if you can't get to the next checkpoint without it crashing).
Although it's an enjoyable game, the constant crashing makes it nearly unplayable.  You can still progress, but just hope that you reach the next checkpoint before your game decides to give out on you.  I can't recommend it in its current state, and who knows if the devs will ever look into this problem and fix it.
Don't buy unless you either get it in a bundle, or the devs fix it.
Looking for a nice metroidvania to kill your time with? Strider will do just that.

I played this game a lot during the beta on the standalone client and if you want to compare it to Hearthstone, then it's better by a long long shot.  I highly recommend TESL to fans of card games in general, especially fans of Hearthstone and even recommend checking it out for fans of the elder scrolls games/lore, quite some interesting stuff to find out about.
This game still has many of the core mechanics that HS does, such as: mana gain per turn, no blocking (except for taunts), mulligan initial hand, one phase per turn and some minor things. It however has two features that lift it way over the simplicity of Hearthstone's gameplay: Prophecy and Split dual lanes.
--- Short description ---
Prophecy: Every 5 hp you lose, you lose a rune (you start with 30hp and 5 runes). Once a rune is destroyed, it won't trigger again (incase you heal above). Cards drawn by destroyed runes will trigger if they have the keyword Prophecy (which means they can be played as soon as the rune is destroyed), which allows you to interact with the opponent's turn/play.
Split Dual lanes: You have 2 lanes on the board, meaning you can place creatures (up to 4 per lane) on either lane and those can't be attacked by creatures from the other lane (unless specified in card text). One lane is normal, the other lane is a shadow lane. The shadow lane stealths every creature (except for taunts) the turn they get dropped there. This means your opponent can't target them until the next turn. Certain cards interact with lane behaviour (turning the other lane into a stealthlane aswell for example).
The Prophecy feature endangers your opponent from stupidly go for face every turn with every creature he has on board. Going face at the wrong time might actually end up losing him the game as you can draw lethal on the spot. TESL also has a dual lane board (shadowlane and normal lane), which makes placement of a certain strategy or specific minions ever so important. Depending on how the opponent plays, you'll need to deploy creatures to each lane in order to prevent him from executing his tactic as intended. So smart damage distritbution is a required skill in both face damage and board placement, unlike Hearthstone where you just drag and drop anywhere then hit face or trade.
If I rated Hearthstone with a Difficulty of 1/5 stars and Magic the Gathering 4/5 stars, then I'd certainly rate TESL somewhere in the middle at 3/5 stars. It's still casual friendly while also delivering a bunch of complexity in higher up ranks.

THIS GAME is amazing! SOoo addicting! Peggle Extreme is free to play! That's a big plus! It's different from the other Peggle games because it has it's own Portal / Half-Life / Team Fortress theme. Also it's more of a shortened version in comparison to the original Peggle game. If you like puzzle games and pinball games you're good to go with this one!
What do you have to do in this game?
You have to shoot your ball from the top of the srceen downwards and clear the orange squares in order to complete a level.
Your ball can fall in the pitt below when it's done bouncing around, but there is a ballbucket that moves constantly from side to side. That's where the ball you shot can fall into. When that happens your ball get's spared. When you begin a level you start of with 10 balls. You can earn extra balls if your ballscore is high enough which you can achieve by planning and timing your shots just right. Most of the time there is luck involved in this game.
There are different types of squares that you can hit with your ball. Blue, orange, purple and green.
They all have a different purpose and give you power ups or extra points.
Blue squares (They are called Pegs) are normal point.
Orange Pegs are the ones you need to clear in a level to complete it and they give you more points then the blue ones.
Purple Pegs randomly appear on different spots and are always alone. This is some sort of multiplyer Peg that gives you a great deal of points, because every other Peg you hit gets multiplied!
Green pegs come in pairs in a level and are actually a Power Up for your character named 'Bjorn'. A weird Unicorn creature.
They give you guidelines that make it easier to see which Pegs you are going to hit with your ball.
There are Different modes in this game. An Adventure mode, Quick Play, Duel and Challenges.
These different modes give you enough fun to play this game for hours! Believe me. You want to buy the other Peggle games after this, it's that fun!

I don't usually write reviews, but Im willing to make an exception in this case. There simply aren't too many reasons not to like supcom fa. In other legendary RTS games, battles are made in rock paper scissors-style. Spears defeat cavalry, cavalry archers and archers spears. And of course, upgraded units defeat weaker ones. In the background economy plays a big role. Thats ok, but it lacks deep multidimensional strategy that supcom offers.
Battles are fought in underwater, groundlevel and air simultaneusly. Instead of dealing less damage to sub-optimal enemies, units have limited capability where they can operate. For example, cannons cant kill submarines and AA-guns are required to kill aircraft. This itself requires more thinking than just normal RTS. Most of the guns can shoot longer than they can see, so radar and scouting is required to utilize units full capasity. Game offers excellent radar and intel system, which ads even more to the strategy aspect. And when you you think this cant get any more complicated, game introduces intelligent missiles and missile defenses, energy shields, nuclear weaponry, EMP weapons and much, much more. In the background, your economy produces units instead of just buying them unlike any other RTS.

Levelling up could be vastly improved by adding more depth (not to the Underrail / Fallout degree) and allowing more flexibility. E.G., if you're interested in becoming a professional smoothtalker, but are not interested in casting spells and the like, a lot of the benefit of having a high charisma is wasted.

Overall; Recommended.

As someone who’s not normally a fan of point-and-click adventure games I wasn’t particularly excited when I sat down to play The Book of Unwritten Tales - but I got it on sale so I thought “what the heck.” I have to say I was pleasantly surprised. While the game follows the general rules of point-and-click adventures - you go from room to room picking up various objects and figuring out how they interact with each other and the enviroment -  what really sells the game is the humor.
I find that it’s really hard to make games funny, but The Book of Unwritten Tales succeeds. The key is that the game just doesn’t take itself overly seriously. and the writers feel free to poke fun at it, and wider gaming topics, at will. In addition, the game makes you the think, but none of the puzzles feel unfair. You just have to be willing to spend some time poking around a bit and trying out different things. The whole game only takes about twenty hours to complete.
There are certain points where I found particularly small items a little bit harder to find that I felt was fair - and the game doesn’t explain that you can right-click your items to find out more about them - but those are really my only complaints. The game might not be worth the full twenty bucks Steam is currently asking for, but it’s certainly worth picking up on sale!

I'm really enjoying this game. It's different from Hearthstone in that you're essentially placing cards down a linear path of 4 nodes, and your hero or avatar moves 1 space per turn and battles or loots whatever is in that spot. So you decide the order you want your guy to encounter the cards. Your opponent does the same thing and things resolve based on who started first. This goes on for 5 "chapters", so you basically are dropping up to 20 cards (you can drop less). If at the end no one has died, you then take turns smacking each other automatically until a winner results.
The production value is high. The art and animations are very nice. I like the background music too. The single player modes are a fun way to learn the game with some nice unlocks. The Book of Unwritten Tales is a classic Point & Click Adventure. It follows the paths of the gnome Wilbur, the human Nate, the elf Ivo and the Critter on their journey to save the world after the archaeologist Mortimer McGuffin finds a powerful artifact, that can decide the war between the Army of Shadows and the Alliance.
The story sounds very clichee, but that is wanted, because the Book of Unwritten Tales is just one big parody of everything that has to do with fantasy, science fiction or adventure movies and is filled with many references to them. Even the music sometimes sound suspiciously close to some of Hollywood´s classics.
The design of the game is very good for a Point & Click Adventure and fits the mood of the game very well. The 60 locations all have their own feel to them so that the game does not get boring. The Book of Unwritten Tales also did not fall for the trap, that many Point´n Clicks cannot avoid to step in. There are no annoying and unlogical puzzles. After some thinking everything makes sense, so that you do not have to randomly combine items without a certain goal. All in all the Book of Unwritten Tales was a really nice experience, that took me about thirteen hours to complete.

I love this game. The puzzles aren't as crazily difficult like the Deponia series but are solvable by using simple intuition and the Spacebar. I enjoy solving the puzzles but they are more of a "If you can't do this, keep clicking on any other available spot"
PROS
1. Good Graphics
The 3D is a step up from the cartoonish drawings of the Deponia Series.
2. Interesting World
Transport Dragons, Mummies, Elves, Gnomes, Orcs, Mages and Death himself.
3. Good Title
Book of Unwritten Tales. Very catchy.
4. Weird Ideas
Using a Telephone Booth (aka Tardis concept) to teleport? Interesting.
CONS
1. Linearity
There is really only 1 way to solve a puzzle and your choices don't really matter at all. You are just solving one puzzle to get to the next.
2. Dead World
You can't interact with anything except what the developers want you to interact with. There is nothing that you can interact with for fun.
3. Colour Issues
When you make a potion, purple is not pink.
4. Number of Stirs
How do you count 3 stirs clockwise? Why is not stirring considered a foul?
5. Abrupt Ending
The ending was so easy and abrupt.
SUGGESTIONS
1. Removing the Linearity
I would suggest referring to the Witcher series for examples on how to use multiple ways to solve one issue. Or the Osbourne kids' books.
2. The Mighty Card Game
It would have been great to have a real Mighty card game within this game.
Lovly game,

I great new take on the 4x genre. Instead of sprawling empire you are a god and have 1 small town and small group of men and women who worship you and that need to scavenge off the land and fight evil monsters.
Combat, dialogue, sneaking and more is done using a card game mechanic which means that with clever moves you could win an unwinnable challenge or lose an easy fight.
Death will come, your town will fade but your god will grow, unlocking new gods and new bonuses to your village.

You play a God with followers, your village is for harvesting resources, and you can send our parties to quest, harvest more resources, or explore. There are multiple ways to "win" the game, The combat system is card/stat based, and each encountered can be resolved in a variety of manners (flat out combat, stealth, social, magic, etc.) So, depending your character layout, you can choose how to approach every encounter. Permadeath exists in the game, but like most roguelikes, the reward for playing is that every playthrough adds overall XP to whichever God you're playing as. Overall worth playing.

Checkpoints are way too far from your objective, but is the only way to advance from point to point.
About the graphics, i must add that they are nice, some old vibe (robot anime series) here.
The sound is quite simple but satisfying, not intrusive.
Menus are classic, you can feel as you were playing some Super NES game, which made "nostalgia" grows.
You can beat the game in 10 hours. (my real gametime isnt showed, cuz i lost internet connectivity all weekend, so i had to play offline)
All in all, is a good game. I recommend to fans of the genre and alike.

My family had a few classic arcade cabinets in our basement, but the original pacman was always our favorite. This reinvention of the original classic is perfect in nearly every imaginable way. Design, sound, controls, variety, nearly everything a veteran of the original will enjoy. The game shifts away from pure survival (which can be taken advantage of with patterns) to a more fast-paced score attack where speed and score become more important. This makes the gameplay far more satisfying as you make split second decisions at extremely high speed to a kickass retro-inspired soundtrack to score as high as possible. Namco elaborates on this by incorporating a vast leaderboard system to compete with friends, reinvigorating the love of getting the high score on that arcade machine to a friend list or global level. I honestly can't think of anything bad to say about the game, other than the menus being a bit tedious at times, but this is irrelevant compared to the rest of the game design. This is an absolute must-by whether you are a long lover of the original games or have never tried it before.

An extremely fun card game to play. I have played this game for hundreds of hours before it was released on Steam. I highly recommend it to anyone who wants to play a game that is a lot fairer and cheaper to get into than Hearthstone or most other online card games.
PROS:
- Prophecy mechanic to allow there to be a comeback potential in matches.
- Very generous arena rewards, especially if you are good at it.
- Solo Arena, which exists to help introduce you to the game mechanics against the AI.
- Single player story content with good voice acting.
- Receive anywhere between 15-30+ gold and a random card (even a legendary!) every 3 matches you win.
- Crafting costs for legendary cards are cheaper.
- Good starter decks for new players. A skilled player will have a good chance to beat another player with a bigger card collection.
- Controlled low RNG cards or very few cards with extremely crazy RNG effects.
CONS:
- Some may not enjoy the game art style.
- Below average premium/golden versions for most of the cards.

A game that far eclipses Hearthstone, in terms of story, of gameplay, and of f2p progression.
The story is of a decent length, fairly well written and engaging, and gives a plethora of in-game rewards along the way.
The gameplay is intuitive, and the dual-lane setup and prophecy system promotes player skill, rather than SMOrc-ing your way up the ladder and hoping for insane RNG every game. (I say this as someone who played Hearthstone since Season 2, and watched the game deteriorate into more and more RNG. There is a reason the old pros don't top events anymore.) 50-70 card deck limits really increase the diversity of decks, and make the matches themselves much more diverse. The prophecy mechanic in particular was a great choice, because it punishes reckless aggression. Sure, sometimes you just die to a Lightning Bolt when you're at 3, and that's unavoidable, and it sucks. But Prophecy allows for comebacks, and for tempo swings, and as such teaches the player to play around them, giving another dimension to gameplay.
The game also gives so much more value for time invested than Hearthstone, in the sense that every 3 wins (up to 30 a day) you receive 15-50 gold (instead of exactly 10) and a random card, which can be literally anything. You occasionally even get a pack instead of a card. (It's very very rare, but it is still possible.) Legendaries also cost 1200 dust insterad of 1600, yet still disenchant for 400. This may not sound like much, but the numbers add up over time. This comes at the cost of commons costing 50 instead of 40, and foils commanding a 4x multiplier instead of 2x, but those are crafted a lot less often anyway. The end of every season gives you 1, 2 ,or 3 copies of an unrealeased epic based on reaching rank 9, 5, or 1 of 12 respectively. These cards are usually very good, and sometimes can define the meta in the month following their release. (See Hist Grove.)  This is much more desirable than say, a cardback that has no functional use. (and can also never be crafted in the event you miss it. You can craft Monthly Rewards upon their release. You can also disenchant them if you don't want them.)  Your rewards for leveling up are quite liberal, with 2 guaranteed legendaries, thousands of gold and dust, and many other cards along the way. All of which you can disenchant. (In my opinion, soulbound cards that weren't even good being given as milestone rewards was insulting.) In one week of playing the Beta, I amassed 67% of the total collection. And that was playing entirely f2p. I would guess that I earned around 1500 gold cumulatively from completing the story. I currently have over 5000 gold, and that's been saved over the course of only about a month, with  only around 15 or so wins a day. I wasn't terribly active in May.
The rewards of Arena are particularly interesting, given that each of them have you start at rank 9, and work your way down to 1. I really enjoy Solo Arena, because the 9-wins-and-then-boss-battle setup is intriguing. There are many custom board rules which come into play, and all of them are fun. Each win presents you with a choice of three more cards to draft from. The boss battle is challenging, but usually not oppressively so. Upon defeating the boss, you rank up. You then get rewards (on top of your regular arena finish rewards) and the AI becoomes a little more challenging. At Rank 1, the AI basically plays an actual Constructed-tier deck, and is very skilled. It is ultra-challenging, and punishes even the most minute of mistakes, but it is not impossible. (I've 9-0'd solo arena rank 1 twice. It was a nightmare, and it was nerve-wracking, and sometimes you do lose to their perfect topdeck, but it is possible if you draft right and play right. And have just a little bit of luck lol.)
Upon finishing your Solo Arena run, you get a lot of bang for your buck. From what I can remember (haven't played Arena in about a month) you only need 4 of 9 wins to get 2 packs. 9 gets you 2-3 packs. The trade off is that whilke you get more packs, you get less gold. In this sense, you can't actually "go infinite", but you can certainly assemble a complete collection with many less Arena runs than in Hearthstone.
The developers listen to the community, and while sometimes quiet on the home front, they have never yet failed to deliver. I have received several surveys asking detailed questions for improvement. DireWolf Digital has proven to employ developers who actively engage with their audience. The only thing I currently dislike about the game is the chat UI. (I have to manually open and close a chat window to talk/play (no hotkey) and cannot chat while in queue.
In summation, I feel that my time and my play are much more rewarded playing this game, and I optimistically look forward to the future of ESL. I look forward to streaming this game soon, and to playing in their leagues when they launch. 95/100

Obsidian, take note. This is what people mean when they want an "old-school RPG" - an RPG with a *really strong story* and *memorable characters*, not the awkward gameplay of Baldur's Gate combined with a 60-hour mediocre campaign. Why yes, I'm bitter about Pillars of Eternity, why do you ask?
I mean, sure. Dragonfall has its low points, mostly related to the AI. Why does every enemy shoot for my main character when they're having their face eviscerated by my melee team members? SImple, they want you to lose rather than to stay alive. Here's the deal, though: while that really got on my nerves, the sheer strength of the story and characters easily carry the game.
Basically, it's a fantasy/cyberpunk setting that takes the dark aspects of those and builds a great world. Even the sidequests are interesting, even if there aren't too many of them - there's no boring fetchquests, everything is jam-packed with action, characters and stories. There's moral choices done right, as in, you simply get to choose between being pragmatic and earning a bit extra, or not committing horrible deeds for a little less. Your team members all have distinct personalities (who needs voiceacting?) and you'll really be looking forward to their comments about the runs you take.
That's the thing with RPGs. If you focus on a great story and great characters, somewhat clunky gameplay is easily overlooked.

Growing up as a tabletop roleplaying gamer in the nineties, one of the game I played a lot (a LOT) of was Shadowrun. Flash forward a couple of decades, it wasn't a game I thought too much about in a while. But the first Harebrained Schemes game (Shadowrun Returns) managed to intrigue me. I played it, and it amused me for a while, but it was fairly linear, and while the story was good, none of the characters were very memorable. Shadowrun Dragonfall is very different though, miles better in my opinion. The non-linear nature of the middle part of the game was great, the central area (the Kreuzbasar) was really fun to walk around and talk to people, if a trifle big. But the best thing about the game were the characters. All memorable, all flawed in their own way, but still realistic as people (even if not all of them were 'people'). If you like turn-based video RPGs with good plots and well written characters, and have a soft spot for fantasy/cyberpunk crossover games from the nineties, I would heartily recommend this game.

This is a game I have bought very recently and it has not been found wanting.
I was introduced to the SupCom franchise via Youtube after incidentally coming across Supcom 2 fanmade epic gameplay vids. A month later I bought Supcom 2.
It has been many years since then and I have always heard or read reviews of how Supcom 2 (which in my mind was a decent RTS) had failed to meet the high expectations of loyal fans from Supcom and Supcom FA. My curiosity urged me to discover a little more about this antique and not too long ago, I happened across a steam sale where the bundle pack was sold for 5 SGD (3.45 USD).
In a short timeframe, I have spent many hours into this game and it has left me astounded that such a relic has not been properly glorified. In other words, this game had happened upon us too early for its time. Rarely do we ever come across such a priceless bundle of packaged joy (at such a steal too!).
It had been frustrating but incredibly worth it when I first started this game. My base was constantly getting wrecked by early T1 units simply because I made the noob mistake of jumping to T2 at the start. Eco management in this game is incredibly different from SupCom 2 and when handled improperly, would cost you the game. I only learned about 'ghetto gunships' a week ago and had so much fun pounding enemy bases with 28 mech marines per T3 transports.
There are really very little restrictions when playing this game and it forces players to abuse as much of the unit abilities as possible. Hell Starcraft 2 did not have this type of complexity when it comes to eco. (or unit management)
To my fellow RTS gamers out there that are still deciding to buy this antique, give this a shot and you might be pleasently surprised at how complex this game can be.

I can agree with what most other are saying about the title. Overall, It's very fun and engaging. It allows you to have a sense of acomplishment and excitement about your character throughout the initial stages of the game. The content is very interesting if you read the dialogue, and I believe it can appleal to fast pace action fans and rpg fans alike. However, in my opinion, from lvl 30 and on is where you begin to realise your character is starting to buckle.
I myself, as a non paying player, followed several online guides related to my class in order to obtain the "optimal" skill levels and gear necessary for comfortable to advanced gameplay. Getting as close to these recommendations as possible, I continued to progress my character. After breezing through the first couple of chapters being able to solo all of the content on "hard" difficulty, I found it more and more necessary to have others in your party to be able to make any progress through higher tiers of content. This is completely understandable for "Raid" and other missions requiring exceptional damage output. However, the fact that I am not able to gear my character appropriately with that stats on the gear that I can OPENLY obtain, makes it extremely difficult to be of any significant value to other players who have donated personal funds to advance their character as such. Therefore, I feel it's going to take more than an average "casually serious" player, to be able to have any inforcing role in true end-game content. My positive recommendation would be for any player not wanting to progress seriously, or any willing to pay for a more serious, exciting end game experience. Simple as that. It's true, there are elitist jerks in the community who want to demoralize you and make you feel like less of a person through a video game. This can be said with any MMO ever released, but it's your game that this company released for free for YOU. You should be able to play it the way YOU want to. However, unless you are able to pay a premium, you will never live up to the expectation of your fellow gamer. It's very sad that a gaming community has come to this, but what can we do as players?
That being said, I will continue to play the game FOR FREE and document my experiences and how I am able to proess as a casual, non-paying player.
Cheers!

Strider is a remake of a 1980s era action platformer.  By every measurable criteria, the modern Strider far surpasses its predecessor.  I was not a fan of the original and though it looked great, the action was clunky and overly challenging in spots, which were hallmarks of the time.
The modern Strider, released in 2014 by Double Helix Games is a graphical delight and a blast to play.
The combat is fast paced and represents gaming at its best.  Lower tier enemies are quickly dispatched and it is quite enjoyable to utilize your speed, mobility and ninja moves to savagely respond to a group of rifle toting cyborgs putting you under fire.  Bossess and larger enemies take some pattern recognition, which is reminiscent of the finest old-school gaming.
Strider simply has the best platforming mechanics in gaming as well.  Double jumping, wall climbing and ceiling climbing have never been done better than this.  Jumps are fast, controllable and tight and climbing a wall is not a chore to accomplish.
The game has leaderboards and is littered with hidden collectibles and unlockable options adding quite a bit of content and replayability.
This remake was refreshing to see and Double Helix did a fantastic job here.  Though the game has top-notch graphics, they did not try to force 3D and perspective change to modernize the game as the Castlevania series regrettably did.  This is how you remake a game, by taking what was good about the original, do it better, focus on fun gameplay, improve and modernize the graphics and add in a ton of extra content.

Runescape Legends is a surprise to me as I dislike CCGs. The rules are generally obtuse and the reasoning behind card-placement and synergies usually contrived. I especially grow annoyed by cards that are awesome but only reach potential when you successfully play other cards first while hoping that the opponent doesn't draw cards that dispel your assist-cards and blah, blah, blah. Annoying times two.
Runscape Legends is different. Your opponent and you resolve your own cards and the effect of that may or not may damage your opponent and may or not may help you, or indeed the cards may hurt you and help your opponent. If that sounds weird, well that's because it is. However, it makes sense in game as you learn that the cards that you should play depend heavily on the situation of the moment. Sometimes, personally taking damage to strip your opponent of their armor is the right move to take.
I suggest to download the game and at least work through the tutorial. The tutorial does a better job of explaining the concept than I do.
The game is F2P and the model is not entirely benign. Your startingcards are weak and while the game rewards singular cards and even basic boosterpacks, they come too few and far between to stay competitive. Someone who buys the 50 boosterpacks bundle will blindfoldedly blow you away, because the truly devastating cards are in the basic boosterpacks.
What are truly devastating cards? Those are the cards aimed at a specific hero, which play on the strenghts of your given hero. Usually, these cards can only be played when a condition is met but with some smart deckbuilding it is possible to field 20DMG+ cards in the second round and in so doing taking away more than 60% of your opponents health in the early game!
Yes, in the game's defense it is possible to grind your way to greatness but the schism between a buyer and a rube is most notably there, which makes this F2P game decidedly P2W.
Positively in the game's advantage are it's colorful graphics, fun gameplay idea, nailbiting battles when you're lucky to battle another rube and the joy of gaining cards and boosterpacks without spending a dime. Since the game is overly stacked against rubes, this is where the challenge lies. A buyer will be insta-pwnage, winning because they dropped money, not because they came up through the school of hard knocks.
It's not their fault, it's because the developers thought that this model works best for them. You can't fault a buyer for using the options available to them, even though a rube must be lucky to have won exceptional cards to be able to stand up to a buyer. Smart deckbuilding only takes you so far, afterall.
I think that this a fun game I will play for some time to come. At least until the buyers have chased all the rubes off. Jump in now before playing the F2P becomes pointless and milk some free hours of fun out of it before it is too late.
