This is a strategic card game in the theme of RuneScape. You may think "wow, another Hearthstone clone??" Well, let me be the first to tell you that's where you're wrong. Chronicles has an unique playstyle, something i haven't seen in other card games.
The focus in this game is building you own character - getting higher attack stat, get armor, and all the while you're doing this, your end goal is to beat your opponent in a glorious duel at the end of five turns. You are not directly battling against your opponent until the end, the exception being the odd card here and there. This makes the game stand out from other strategic card games.
The game has great visuals that fits it's overall theme, and satisfying sound design. The game includes soundtracks from RuneScape, and they are all very nice. For people familiar with RuneScape or not, the game is just as easy to pick up for both. I would say the game is easy to learn, but hard to master.
My only pet peeve about this game is the amount of time it takes to progress and get new cards/items. I know it's supposed to be slow so people are encouraged to buy packs, but it would be reasonable to speed it up a little. I have no problems with microtransactions in this game, they are all reasonable.
I would highly recommend you have a little try. I've never liked the strategic card game type games, but this game is a great exception to that. Try it even if you don't like these kinds of games, you  might be positively surprised!
Have fun :)

I came across Chronicle almost by accident. If I hadn't had the day off and poked my head into TotalBiscuit's stream, I'd have never known this game even existed. As a longtime player of Hearthstone, and of CCGs in general (Yu-Gi-Oh!, Magic, heck even Marvel Overpower back in the day), Chronicle scratched an itch I honestly didn't even know I had.

Yes, it borrowed some concepts from Hearthstone but the execution is so fundamentally different as to be wildly refreshing. Being burned down in three Chapters is the kind of thing that would have me throwing my monitor out the window in Hearthstone, but a combination of the presentation and the heroes being optimistic even in defeat ("Losing is the way in which we learn." for example)...the game's really low stress.
Give it a whirl. You may be as surprised as I was.

As someone who never played Runescape, I don't know much about the universe this card game is set in. What I will say is that this a very intresting take on a TCG. Unlike most TCG's, you don't play your deck directly against your opponent. Instead, you play your cards against yourself. You defeat monsters to earn gold or attack, or use allies you power up. So deck building is based around trying to do damage to the opponent as well as power up your hero.
The game consits of up to 5 rounds (called chapters). If you get your opponent down to 0 before round 5, you win, but the 5 turn limit stops games from dragging on to long.
Theres a single player mode vs the AI at 3 ranks (bronze, silver, gold) as well as online 'casual' and ranked play. Theres an additional 'dungeon' mode once you level up to rank 15, which works a lot like Heartstones Arena mode (you build a deck  by picking 2 cards from 5, up to a 30 card deck). It's quite a lot of fun.
The only real problem at the moment is the rate of unlock. You unlock cards for each hero by ranking up that hero by winning games. It costs 1000 bronze for a booster pack, although you can buy platinum to unlock faster. The price is quite steep though, so if you want a lot of cards quickly, it will cost you a lot. When you first visit the store, you get a 'special offer' of £5.99 (about $7) for 12 booster packs. This should be enough to build a custom deck good enough for casual, but you will get stomped on ranked mode unless you can build a good deck.
It runs well, even on my crappy laptop, and the art style is colourful and dynamic. Sadly there is not option to speed up the ingame animations, which can grate on occasions.
It's a fun game if your looking for a casual experiance, but if you really want to play on ranked mode, be prepared to spend a lot to get a good enough deck.

Oh did I mention achivements? Why Yes there are 12 of them and they are preety easy to get form my experience. There are also 12 medals to get by completing tougher challenges. No cards though.
Do I reccomend it. preety much. Though this game puts a wrench on the type of people who like to play by tusing the ghosts as there are now a lot more of them cluttering up the maze

PAC-MAN Championship Edition shows just how good of a concept the original game was (is) as it is still a fun game that is easy to pick up and play for anyone while still holding the attention of the more serious gamer. It's really hard to explain what it is about Pac-man that works so well. It's such a simple game: eat pellets, eat fruit, eat power up, eat ghosts, but it's this same simplicity that makes it so easy to get into. I find this game to be a really good game for when you're not really in the mood for most other types of games, yet despite it's easy going nature, you will find yourself playing it for hours without noticing. It's impressive to see just how little they could change about the game while still adding some fresh new elements, making Pac-man feel more timeless than ever. Pac-man is worth owning for the historic value alone (this was the last game designed by the series creator before retiring), but it helps that it's also a fun, simple and addictive good time.

Far Cry 2 gives you a set of tools (guns, explosives, stealth, vehicles, the environment, etc...) and puts you in scenarios (getting through checkpoints, avoiding/destroying patrols, assaulting shanty towns, villas, or hunting lodges, blowing up convoys, etc...) wherein you are free to use those tools in any way you wish. If this sounds appealing, give the game a shot.
Keep in mind though, that the game is hard: Encounters quickly spiral out of control. Enemies can kill you in a single shot. The A.I. tries to pin you down and flank you. When things go right, you'll want to jump up and down and spike a football into the nearest endzone. When things go wrong (and they often go wrong), you'll have 5-10 minutes of the tensest gameplay imaginable as you try to regain the upper hand. Expect to ragequit a few times.
Unlike Dark Souls, however, the difficulty doesn't make the game a tedious process of trial and error. When you fail, you will know why you failed. If you take some time and think through your options, you'll come up with something that will work. The game is cool like that.
The story is nothing to write home about, but it does have a few interesting things to say about the arms trade in post-colonial Africa where war is often a product manufactured for export.
One more thing; a small thing. The voice overs are good. I hate games with American/Canadian actors doing bad, inconsistent, European accents (I'm looking at you Skyrim). All the voice overs were recorded in South Africa, so the accents at least sound... African.

Some kind of paradox, that game is. It takes name from very famous FPS Far Cry - and giving a very diverse experience. So, basically, like heritor of Far Cry - it sucks really. First Far Cry was in its core quite oldschool shooter (like Doom or Half Life) - just with so many fixes as one could imagine 10 years back (like outstanding physics, witty and challenging level design, clever AI behavior).
There, in Far Cry 2 - we have a nice engine, yes. AI may not be very smart... but it has some explanation by overall agenda. We're talking about setting of that game. It rests in the middle of some civil war in Africa, in one of many so called "countries" where state wasn't existed at all and people continuosly swallowing by warmonger tribes habits. That quite realistic setting lies so far from "just a tropical island afar from anywhere, where some mad doctor making a war mutants from mercs" - base of first Far Cry. But not a sip of realism made diversion between first and second games. Far Cry 2 is a sandbox. That's her bless and curse.
Let's start with bad side:
I quote there since I cannot say better: "Driving across beautiful but lifeless world while fighting infinitely respawning enemies to complete unimaginative missions for people who all try to kill you" (yougamers)
Where first Far Cry gameplot offers dramatic episodes "like in the movies", sandbox game just leaves you to entertain yourself by continuous driving through the countryside, killing almost everyone on sight. Gameplot is awful, storyline doesn't have any cultural value. Just a reference to a movie "Lord of War". Protagonist (any of them) its just a brief bio like "Tall, strong, divorced, reserved, alcohol habits". No personality besides that. Mandatory "twist" in the midst of game just slightly changing decorations, nothing more. Ok, there are some little "twists" around every story mission, but it's just a choice between two shootouts, with big blood or with much-more-than-big blood spilled. Oh, and story motivation - running from one dose of drug to another - kinda frustrating, I guess.
Now, question - is it worth playing at all?
Well, yeah, there is a good part.
This particular FPS game still a way more wiser than any flat but overrated shooters like whole bunch of Call of Duty series. While it's not as complex and addictive as Stalker games, for some points it's easily beats Ukranian games. For a start, it's size feature. Big vastes can be depressing, but, when you are planning to hit a conwoy or clear up a fortress full of soldiers all by yourself, you surely need some room for elbows (Bewegungsfreiheit, as Germans might said). And, all of sudden, moving in these vastes could be quite relaxing. Natural. Really, I've just played Far Cry for 7 hours not completing any missions. Just wandering around and collecting hidden diamonds. Game setting fits just right to simple wandering around. Almost like you're on vacation, on safari, of kind.
Sadly, we have a very few FPS games in one-player modus, that allows player choose it's destination, planning your moves before rushing forward in battle, and using long-range rifles from distance more than 100 meters. Project IGI comes in mind now, for some missions (not completely). Xenus (another Ukranian game) - an ambitious sandbox, but poorly executed. Op.Flashpoint/ARMA are too simulating to be fun. What else?
Overall: While many might find Far Cry 2 too boring, it has its own place. Like it was with Assassin's Creed 1, which too was a pretty boring openworld experience. If you can look behind its bad sides, game's good one, with some originality, charisma and clever details.
Fair 7.5/10 in my collection.

The only reason you don't have to press Y to eat or 'use the facilities' is because you've mainlined so much morphine you're still digesting the meal you ate before the first cutscene. Ruined my life; five stars. :P
Seriously, though, this is a game you either love or hate, and as far as I can tell how you feel about it depends on what you were expecting.
What it's not:
A scripted, linear power fantasy with clear objectives, frequent checkpoints, lots of hand-holding, and jingoistic moral certainty backed up by a cinematic orchestral score (I'm looking at you, COD).
What it is:
An open-world survival game that gives you shooting, driving, and stealth mechanics so you can go from point A to point Z using whatever combination of the other letters you see fit. It has all the hallmarks of a shooter, but I hesitate to call it one because shooting is only the means to an end; in many cases, your interests (and the interests of your employer) are best served by minimizing or avoiding enemy contact. It's best described as a survival/horror title disguised as a cross between GTA and COD.
The game is set in an unnamed African country, a pastiche of every African civil war of the last few decades. Everyone you meet is either an enemy or a potential enemy, and there are far more of the former than the latter. You're not such a great guy yourself; you're a mercenary hired through unofficial channels to find and kill the Jackal, an internationally notorious arms dealer who has been supplying all sides of a conflict that has killed thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands.
At the very beginning of the game you find the Jackal (or rather, he finds you) after you're incapacitated by a bout of malaria. Since you've failed in your mission and are no longer being paid to kill him, the Jackal taunts you and leaves you to die. You're rescued by one of the factions in the war, and, since you're now trapped in-country, you start doing missions and sidequests for the various factions and individuals you come across.
You will be very glad to come across some of them. One of the game's most interesting mechanics is the Buddy system. Buddies offer alternative solutions to faction missions. These solutions are more convoluted than the original mission, but are sometimes easier and always result in an upgrade to the player's safehouses. Buddies also save your life. The first time you're killed in a firefight, you're only wounded. Your buddy drives up, drags you to safety, and helps you finish off nearby enemies.
This is good, because the penalty for dying is severe. Save points are located only in safe areas, which are few and far between. This really ratchets up the tension; you're a lot less likely to try something stupid if you know it will cost you half an hour of progress. For me, at least, that's a good thing: the crazy moments are exhiliarating /because/ they're not spoon-fed to you.
Edit: just discovered the quick-save function. I wish they hadn't included it. This game is all about punishment; if you want something easier, you're playing the wrong game. I'm not saying this as a snob. There are plenty of games where this function would be welcome, but it doesn't belong here. :(
The shooting mechanics are decent. Aim, shoot, repeat. Enemies take way too many shots to put down on the highest difficulty, but if you're running and gunning you're playing it wrong. The whole point of an open world is that it doesn't funnel you through a series of checkpoints; if you hit each checkpoint just because it's there, you might as well be playing Halo. Guns in this game degrade, jam, and eventually break. This increases tension, especially because of how often it happens, but once I learned to stop by the armory between missions, I never had another jam.
The stealth in this game works well, but it doesn't hold your hand. There are no on-screen detection indicators or mini-radar to show you who's spotted you; you just have to listen for footsteps, engines, and enemy chatter. Enemies react to gunfire, near misses (even from silenced weapons), engine noise, and of course, direct visual contact. If you want to be stealthy you're going to have to stay low, still, and in the dark. Even then you're not perfectly invisible, and the enemy will search your last known location if they lose sight of you. They're not actually cheating; on multiple occasions I've fooled the AI by firing an unsuppressed weapon and relocating. The AI is just very good, especially on the higher difficulty levels.
The driving mechanics are "meh". You point the car, hit the gas, let off the gas when you get there. Hit the brakes if you're going faster than you meant to. Not complicated. Vehicles take damage but can be repaired, which is good since you will be doing a LOT of driving. Fast travel is limited to some bus stops spaced roughly equally around the map. You're going to do some walking and some driving even if you take the bus, which is probably for the best since the game rewards exploration with conflict diamonds (the only in-game currency) hidden all over the map.
Player progression is indirect; there are no experience points. You earn diamonds, buy better equipment, become more effective. Enemies become more effective as their factions also gain access to better equipment. You never permanently depopulate an area, but you can unlock safehouses all over the map and upgrades for those safehouses. I personally prefer it this way, but your mileage may vary.
Plot-wise, you really have to pay attention to what's going on, or all the different factions and missions blur together. I think this was intentional. One of the game's central themes is that in wars like this there aren't any good guys. The pointless violence and constant danger wear you down because they're /supposed/ to. It's a survival game, not an action movie. Or rather, it's an action game about all the things that action games usually glamorize, ignore, or gloss over. It's Game of Thrones with AK47s and IEDs.
TL;DR:
This game is a little rough around the edges because the developers were trying to do something new and unique instead of publishing new missions for an old game with minor tweaks to the gameplay. This turns a lot of people off, not because it's bad, but just because it was a different kind of awesome than they were expecting. (In case you can't tell, I despise the COD/Halo crowd for what they've done to gaming. >:( ) FC2 is only $10, including the DLC/preorder bonus, so give it a go. The setting is imaginary, but the PTSD is only too real. :)

I played this game when it came out and I must say that although I was very impressed with the game at first, it soon became boring and repetitive.The mission structure is very similar-basically go and blow something up or free somebody etc.Characters are shallow and not interesting.The world seems kind of empty with nothing much to do than destroying camps and dealing with very annoying armored jeeps that follow you when you pass by.
Now 5 years later I bought a new powerful graphic card,found some great mods and decided to give it another go.
I must say that I'm very pleased with the game.What this game gives you is very unique experience and that is enough to cover all it's flaws.This game made me realise what I've long forgotten.It's that not everything has to be action packed,flashy story,indepth customization of everything,points,cover system....It's just simple and beautiful.It makes you appreciate the time spent just roaming the wilderness with nothing on your screen to destract you from beautiful world around you.Total immersion.We need to stop with consuming games like an always hungry fat kid and appreciate the atmosphere and experience.
You will often feel alone and kind of lost in this great world,which coupled with an amazing weather system,beautiful graphics and fitting background music makes the experience very unique.Sometimes it feels like a dream to me.Like you never really know what is going on but you just exist,just to watch that beautiful sunset.It gives you time for thinking between action parts.
And action is great and the whole weapon system is designed very well.From buying,upgrading to the shooting mechanics and wearing out including great jamming system and animations.The arsenal is also pretty big with plenty to choose from.
The other thing that shines is AI.Although they can act like idiots at times mostly they are smart and they will very often surprise you and flank you.They will also detect you quickly even if you just peak out behind cover to take a quick look.Just like IRL,they are not blind like in other games (Hitman:Absolution for eg) and there is no "detection meter".If they see you, they see you.Your best bet for sneaking is to attack by night wearing stealth suit and even then it will not be easy,because if you are too close they will hear louder sounds such as bumping in objects or reloading etc. and come to investigate.GREAT STEALTH GAME right there.Using quick save and quick load is much recommended.
As I don't want to write a book here I will conclude and tell you to try it if you are looking for a trully open world game with a great action,juicy explosions and shooting,GREAT STEALTH possibilities and an amazing atmosphere.You will love Africa after this,or hate it.Whatever.What you will not find is many RPG elements and a great story.But lack of those gives the game its charm and keeps the focus on other things.
WHAT I HIGHLY RECOMMEND is getting this mods from moddb:sproyds_FC2_SweetFX_config and VERY important DylansFC2Mod1.4 as it will basically fix the game.Just check it out even if you don't like mods(like me)Play on highest difficulty and enjoy!

Thea is a wonderful blend of genres. You lead your adventuring party and explore the vicinity of your village, gather better equipment and bring back new resources. At the same time you micromanage production and resources in the village itself, construct buldings, research now crafting recipes and raise children to become new heroes.
The turn based system also has a day / night cycle (with night being much more dangerous), so you have to carefully plan your exploration trips (mostly on higher difficulties). Be warned, characters die quite often as Thea is still infested by creatures of Darkness. Mourn the loss of your heroes, but don't let it frustrate you.

Any game that uses "In The Hall of The Mountain King" (from Peer Gynt/composed by Edvard Grieg) as backgound music in a dwarf bar is already right up my alley (so to speak) humor wise.  Of course all the parody lines from classic movies like Platoon, Stars Wars, and Lord of the Rings, plus the whole MMORPG and RPG buffing parodies, a bit of 4th wall breaking and a few omages like Discworld's Death (Terry Pratchett), Raiders of the Lost Ark and Planet of the Apes (the original Charleston Heston version) make this game's blatant to subtle parody humor all that much better.  The game, itself, is even better then its humor.
Storyline: Wilbur Weathervane, gnome, wannabe wizard, adventure day-dreamer, sometimes tinkerer, and full time employee at a dwarf bar gets the chance of his lifetime when Mortimer MacGuffin's (gremlim, archaeologist and chronicler) prison cage literally nearly drops on his head and hands him the ONE RING, before "quest" tasking him with delivering the ONE RING to the Arch-Mage Allister in Seastone before the Arch-Witch can get it.  Mortimer, the gremlin, who had been "freed" by the wood elf, Ivo (incognito Princess and wannabe adventurer) is recaptured and taken to the Arch-Witch, who of course is the cause of the endless war since she wants to rule the world.  Meanwhile, Ivo has also been given a "quest" task by Mortimer while she was freeing his cage from the cargo dragon.  Ivo is to find and retrieve a book, which has directions to the amulet of ultimate power, from the gremlin's secret cellar and take it to the Arch-Mage Allister in Seastone.  While all this is happening Munkus, the Arch-Witch's son is hot on the trail of finding the amulet of ultimate power so he can over-throw his mother and be in control of the world instead.
Gameplay: Point and Click adventure with a build and use inventory of items.  The gameplay is easy to follow and the tasks/obstacles are very logical given the circumstances (and people involved).  There are a few objects that are "well hidden" but if the gamer thinks for a bit, the object needed is easy to locate. (Careful searching will also accomplish the same task.)  Any encountered character gives clues about the task at hand and the main character will basically tell the the gamer what needs to be done and often times what is needed to accomplish the task.
The gamer will eventually play as four different characters, all with their own perspective, personality and knowledge that each character would possess due to their background.  In one area the gamer even has a choice of one of three characters to play, and each character solves the task at hand differently using their natural abilities.
There are 5 chapters total.  During any chapter the gamer might play as a completely different character doing a completely separate task, once another character has finished their objective. There are also places when two (in one place three) characters are available to play at the same time by switching between them.  In these areas one character is capable of performing certain tasks the other character is not.  Also the knowledge each character possesses is clearly seen/heard.  The characters must work as a team to complete the task, and often times need to talk with each other to share knowledge and to trade inventory items.
Overall, wonderful game, superb witty humor and an excellent story of unlikely heroes.  Well worth full price.
Note: This is the first of two games and there are DLCs available.

Dragonfall is infinitely better than Shadowrun Returns to the point of making the original worthless. Anyone who remotely enjoys turn based RPGs or has an interest in Shadowrun's cyberpunk/fantasy hybrid should strongly consider this game as their entry point for the series. Shadowrun: Dragonfall was already one of the best things to come out of Kickstarter and the Director's Cut somehow manages to blow it out of the water. Smart writing, one of the coolest settings in RPG history and a cast of some of the best characters I've seen in a LONG time. If you can't love a game where you can play a cybernetically enchanced Ork packing automatic weapons and a bad attitude, I'm convinced there's no hope for you.
The art style is great. The story is great. The combat can be damn difficult at times, but it's great. Overall, what sets this game apart from the pack are some of the best designed quests I've come across.  Pick this one up, it's a throwback to what made CRPG's king in their heyday.

An excellent little gem of an RPG with a tight contemporary story, engaging characters, snappy dialogue and more roleplay options than most AAA RPG's. The player dialogue options are a particular highlight, with plenty of flavour and skill options to make me feel like my character was truly mine. Combat is fun and tactical (if occasionally a little drawn out) and there are often ways to avoid combat altogether, should you choose. Companion characters are all fun and narratively relevant (Glory, in particular, who's story you get to explore in depth with the directors cut content). None of the side content felt arbitrary; everything added something to the narrative experience with no filler just for the sake of bloating the play length. The atmosphere and visuals are cohesive and it's beyond refreshing to play an RPG that isn't in another medieval inspired fantasy world.  Fully recommended.

I was not sure about this when I first tried it, so much so that I left it alone for about a year after my initial experience. Rarely have I been more thankful that I went back to a game, it is now one of my favourite RPG's!
The game has some design quirks that can initially frustrate, you will get over these and may even like the simplistic streamlining of your team members level progression by it's end. Combat is mostly solid but I did find it was at it's best when I played as a mage/shaman, though it was probably easier in the early sections as a samurai with the opposite being true in the game's latter stages.
Some will tell of the APEX quest crash which thankfully did not happen in either of my two play throughs. I did what the devs said, no quick saves in this quest, regular save as little as possible, and make a back up before you embark as an extra precaution.
The story is good with many well thought out moral dilemmas that give your character a fully fledged selection of well fitting choices for the situation that they are in. One of the places where Fallout 4(which on the whole I enjoyed a great deal!) seemed to get things a little bit wrong.
It has several endings, one of which stands out as possibly my favourite of any RPG ever. I really can't think of another that finishes your adventure in such a perfectly executed and unexpected way.
On the whole I can't recommend this enough, a game I could have easily dismissed turns out to be an absolute gem!
...also, for any fans of the old SNES Shadowrun like me, you may wish to know that a remake of that game is being developed as a mod for this and it looks like it will be completed in the next few months.

Played this after playing Far Cry 3 and Blood Dragon.
Things I like:
- "Buddy system" where people you meet come help you when you're in trouble
- Cool healing mechanics (digging out bullets, syringes, etc.)
- Enemies are non-descript and combat is difficult
- Open world feel with one objective, "do what you want" atmosphere
- Pulling up map and GPS is very inventive and immersive
Things I dislike:
- Voice acting is very fast paced and sounds unnatural
- Takes a LOT of bullets to down an enemy
- No melee, only if you pull out your knife and whack 'em, which is pretty useless in a fight
- Map is bothersome if you're trying to walk around with it, pops up and down while you're walking
- Blur effects on aim and sprint. OMG the sprint. It made me sick every time I tried to move faster. It focuses in and out while you sprint and it's nauseating.
- No direction as to what I'm supposed to do
- "Scouting" outposts is confusing as even after eliminating all enemies I have to walk around the whole place several times to get it to trigger
- Currency is in Diamonds - you have to find diamonds using your GPS, which is annoying and distracting - no other way to get diamonds (?) besides missions maybe? I didn't really have any motivation to do anything
Mostly I just couldn't play long enough because the blurring effects were hurting my eyes. This was with bloom and "post" (which I'm assuming is post processing) off/low. Also, I didn't really have any motivation to do anything, the rewards weren't tangible.
At this point in time you'd be better off playing Far Cry 3 and/or Blood Dragon, I honestly think they're more fun.

Finally got around to playing this game. The only reason i never finished it before is because I was annoyed with the malaria aspect but it turns out only to be a minor annoyance in the game. I finished Far Cry 3 before finishing Far Cry 2, although I started playing it years ago. I always knew I would come back to it and I am glad I finally did. I won't do any comparison to the original FarCry because that is entirely a different game, in my opinion.
I found FC3 far too easy, being able to track your opponents, even through trees and rocks nerfed the difficulty enough, and getting special superpowers as you level up only made it worse.
In FC2, you have malaria, which is like, the opposite of a superpower and became a hazard if you started having an "attack" in the middle of battle. And also, you have weapon jams which happen randomly as your weapon wears down. A weapon jam might sound annoying but it is a little detail in the game that adds a little realism and extra challenge to the game which I can appreciate.
Your "buddys" are randomly chosen from your character choices from the beginning of the game, each with their own look and dialog.  You also have the chance to get incapacitated instead of dying, getting revived by a buddy for a second chance to finish the fight. if you go down too soon after though, it is game over. When you are low on health and apply first aid, the animations go from wrapping up a wound on your arm to pulling a bullet out of your flesh with a knife and plyers.
Another way it differs from FC3 is your character is not the focus of the game story whatsoever. The story is really about the Jackal, the factions and Africa, and you are just someone who is in the right place at the wrong time. You do get to choose a character, which only effects how your hands and arms look in the game
All these little details make a very unique first person shooter experience, and I think really smart game devs can learn from playing this one
In the end, the only real problem I had with FC2 was not the malaria, but the fact that I couldnt use a custom loadout. Every weapon falled under primary, secondary or special and you could only carry one of each. Meaning I could not use a sniper rifle and an SMG at the same time as they were both considered primary weapons.
The good far outweighs the bad though, and if you are jaded with your regular FPS experience, give this one a try.
-edit- 2 years after this review
I'm convinced this was one of Ubisoft's last good games. Also, it doesnt require uplay.

I used to play SuperPower 1 and 2 back in the day, and had fun with both. Having lost both games over time for one reason or another, I decided to purchase Superpower 2 for Steam for nostalgic purposes. What I encountered was a little underwhelming.
As other reviewers have pointed out, realism pretty much flies out the door with this one. One time I played as Croatia and, after an hour of play, had China randomly invade and annex me. In another game I watched online, Italy invaded and annexed China, then started eating up African countries, with no one in the world seemingly caring. I know there are realism mods out there, but as is, the game leaves much to be desired in this regard.
Related to this is how the game's mechanics react to your decisions. Example: I started with a multi-party democracy nation with basic political freedoms, and then - practically overnight - outlawed every religion and language except one, removed freedom of contraception, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, then transformed the government into a military dictatorship. You know what the drop in popular support was? MAYBE like 5%. I'm not kidding. It went back to normal after a while. Government stability didn't take a hit either. I had done this to see just how insane my nation would go, but discovered that it didn't do anything even negative in the short-term. For a supposed geopolitical simulator, that's a bit lacking.
One of the most aggravating aspects of this game is the economic model. At first glance, it can seem like a wonderful simulation of the world trade, but after trying to figure the thing out...I just can't make a surplus. Well, to be fair, I did once, but I don't even remember how I did it. I've tried various methods, and I've read tutorials online on how to set up your economy, but nothing seems to work. I've dealt with the economic models in other games from a variety of developers, and even if they were at first difficult, I managed to figure them out after a while. SP2, however, has a model that will aggravate the casual gamer and give them headaches, trying to figure out how to keep those numbers from getting red again.
One of the few things I appreciate about this game is the way wars and armies are done. Unlike SP1, which were a bit more clustered and limited to various cities, you can move armies around the map like you could in real life, and let them engage across a wider front. It's fun to see the symbols flying around on the spec-ops-style map, and watch the battles between two sides unfold.
Is SP2 worth purchasing? I honestly don't think it's worth even $10. It can be that one game you take out every year and play for a while, before you remember why you uninstalled it in the first place, but it probably won't be something you play on a regular basis.

My reason: Watch_Dogs has the same amount of story, is more easy to pick up as a new gamer, costs half as much and has a lot of "bonus missions"
These bonus missions are: Fixer Contracts, where you get money for making a decoy by racing through checkpoints, driving a guy through the city without being spotted by the police, and more.
Gang hideouts, where you get Skillpoints. Skillpoints are used to improve your hacking, combat, driving and crafting skills. You scout out an area, find the target and knocks him down, not killing him.
Criminal Convoy, where you get XP for killing a guy in a car. IT can be easier later in the game when you buy more weapons, but it is always fun to blow up a car with a grenade launcher.
Cash run: run through a small area against time to get money while avoiding the skulls lying on the ground.
It contains hours of fun gameplay and has a lot of freedom to support your playstyle. It doesn't matter if you rush in, sneak in or stays out of the area and uses the cameras. Every gamestyle is supported.
However, this game does not come without glitches and bugs. I haven't found any, but they do exist.
In this game you also get reputation. If you do bad (Killing civilians and killing police) Your reputation goes down, but if you stop criminals that can pop up anywhere at any time.

First let me say that GRAV still has the potential to be one of the best survival games available.  The crafting and combat system, as others have said, is quite possibly the best, though I'd like the ability to create/demolish single walls.
Endgame is making a drill platform in the best spot on the highest level High Planet before anyone else.  There was good population in every server before the update which included the Drill platform.  Also, on wipes, this isn't like other survival games, it's more like having your character in an MMO wiped.  If they can't wipe the worlds without wiping characters then they shouldn't expect to keep their players, and they'll keep getting bad feedback which will continue to kill the sales.  When the population was good, nobody was quitting due to vehicles falling through the map or invisible rocks, they laughed at it and learned where not to go.
Some suggestions would be; completely remove drill platforms and add the blueprints to mob drop tables, then make DG PvE based omni-elemental.  The PvP was much, much, much better before DG.  Also maybe add a sniper style weapon, similar to assault rifle but with better zoom and lower rate of fire; it could be a special Player Soul blueprint.  Or add a function to increase zoom with mouse wheel.  Could also add/change some weapons to be tuned more towards PvE or PvP, like a longer but slower and harder hitting melee weapon etc.
GRAV could be fairly labeled as a "grind-fest" the way it stands today, mostly due to endgame blueprints.  Leveling happens at a fair rate.  Also with this merge coming, the gap between new players and established players will never be filled because all of the experienced players will create their drill platforms in the best regions before anyone else, discouraging newer players, and people will quit because of it.
Also consider having new players start out with more equipment, such as a few more tier 1 pieces of equipment and a few stimpacks or something, just to make their first hour easier.  I see new players leaving after a short time too frequently, usually it seems due to frustration.
The reason other survival games maintain population is because it doesn't take much for a new player to get on equal grounds as the established players.  With the leveling and loot system in GRAV that gap is obviously and enjoyably larger, though the current system will eventually bring the majority of players to a frustrating wall where many don't have the time or conviction to overcome.  I can't recommend this game until they remove drill platforms or create a better system for getting the DG blueprints from them like having all regions on all high planets give the best blueprints.

Strider is the sort of man who flies a hang glider into a warzone. He doesn’t get bogged down in the details, preferring instead to slice first and ask questions later. His latest hack-and-slash action game is the same way. Without preamble or pretext, you’re dropped straight into the action, cleaving through one hapless guard after another. Strider’s capacity for carnage is boundless, and the acrobatic precision with which he dispatches his foes makes him a delight to control. Right away, you have everything at your disposal to feel like a one man army, and as your arsenal grows, so too will your enjoyment of this well-crafted game.
Simply being Strider feels great. The way he moves from running to sliding to climbing a wall to bisecting a robot is so seamless that you feel like a tempest on the battlefield. From the arc of his jump to the range of his slide, all of Strider’s movements are perfectly measured to give you complete command of the action. In the beginning you can do little more than jump and slash, but by exploring the world and defeating powerful bosses, Strider unlocks new techniques for his arsenal. Reflecting bullets, throwing knives, and summoning a eagle made of pure energy are just some of the powers you earn, and those powers expand your fighting repertoire in new and interesting ways. Instead of mindlessly cutting down the competition, you could send your eagle to intercept airborne foes while you take out those on the ground. Alternatively, you could employ a long-range strategy using the throwing knives and reflection cypher to dispatch foes from afar.
Whichever you choose, juggling these powers together is a real delight, and cartwheeling through the air while dispensing death at 360 degrees is extremely empowering. There are plenty of locked doors to be found early in your quest with no means of entry--this is the game’s way of teasing you with the promise of new powers--and they grant you no choice but to pass them by. As you unlock new powers, referred to as cyphers, you are able to return to these spots and open the doors associated with your new cypher. This can help you advance along the main storyline or reward you with hidden unlockables such as concept art and new costumes.
As you acquire new cyphers, Strider's scarf color will change to indicate which cypher you currently have active.
While Strider’s world is filled with surprises, the backdrop itself is disappointingly drab. The game looks slick and clean, with a subtle scanline effect that harkens back to the ninja’s arcade roots. However, the moment you touch down you’re greeted with a futuristic, industrial aesthetic that rarely relents as you progress. Gloomy pipes and heavy machinery follow you wherever you go, splashed with all the browns, greys, and whites you can handle. Admittedly, this style has the benefit of making Strider--in all his crimson-scarfed glory--pop against the background, but even so, more variety in the different arenas would have been welcome.
Certain enemies also sport a splash of color to indicate a weakness to a particular cypher. Against such a foe, Strider must switch to the appropriate cypher and use it to disable the enemy’s defenses--most often a color-coded shield--before dispatching him. These enemies help keep fights feeling dynamic as they force you to mix up your tactics and utilize Strider to his fullest. One cypher, the cold cypher, does rise above the rest with its incredibly powerful ability to quickly freeze enemies. Frozen enemies can take no action, and are locked in place for several seconds. Other cyphers add to the enjoyable chaos of Strider's combat, but the cold cypher does the opposite. It simplifies encounters and feels more like a crutch than a compliment to your other abilities.
Unlike most rank-and-file grunts, Strider's bosses maneuver around the arena making them very different--and enjoyable--encounters.
Once you finish Strider’s main adventure, you can try your hand at the game’s challenge modes. These challenges come in two varieties: survival and beacon run. Survival challenges are all about testing your combat prowess. You’re granted a pre-selected loadout of cyphers and turned loose against wave after wave of enemies. Beacon runs, on the other hand, are all about speed and agility. Your goal is to pass through each of the beacons on your way to the goal, all the while navigating a trap-and-enemy-infested environment. This mode is especially welcome since Strider is so fun to control and the main game rarely tests your platforming capabilities. When a challenge is completed, you are graded on your performance and can compare your stats against others on challenge-specific leaderboards.
From the moment you embark on your journey right up until the final deathblow, Strider is a blast to play. Controlling this agile ninja feels empowering right out of the gate, and each new upgrade brings with it an enjoyable new way to engage your foes. While his world is a little drab there’s still plenty to explore even after the job is done. Strider is fun, pure and simple, and serves as a fitting revival of a classic video game hero.
Strider / PlayStation 4 & Xbox One / PC

Dragonball Xenoverse 2 is a hybrid between an MMORPG and a 3D fighting game in the vein of previous DBZ titles and while it incorperates elements of both, it also compounds some of the flaws of each.
Let's begin with what's good about the game. Character creation is back from the original and even better than ever. With the ability to transfer your character, their moves, and their equipment (with a very few exceptions) you can start the game with a decent and familiar moveset for your custom character. The races all return from Xenoverse 1 with slightly altered stats. If you check out the Steam Guides you can find the Big Numbes Guide for this game by the same person who made the one for the first DBXV, and the first thing you notice is that the racial multipliers are drastically reduced. This means that you can pick basically any race you'd like and play basically any playstyle and at least in the story and co-op modes succeed (mostly, I will touch on this again when I get to the cons).
There are new customization options, including new hair, voices, accessories, clothing, and a new addition in QQ Bangs, which are accessable very early on in your playthrough and are made from other pieces of clothing, miscellaneous items, and a small fee of the in-game currency, Zenni. This means you can wear whatever you want and the QQ Bang will overwrite the stats, meaning you can give your custom character a look that is all their own without sacrificing stat bonuses.
Speaking of stat bonuses, every race now has its own unique transformation which you get by doing side quests in various areas within the hub world. Each race gets a unique benifit, as well as the universal Kaioken and Unlock Potential transformations. Not only this, but they have their own slot on the move wheel, allowing you to have a transformation AND two Ultimate Techniques.
As for the Skills themselves, Super Skills are mostly returning from DBXV1 with a handful of new ones added. Some of them have been altered slightly or rebalanced, but most are the same. Ultimate Skills are similar, with some balance changes made.
Combat is basically the same as the first game, except each race gets its own unique combo chains which is nice. This lets you pick your playstyle (again I will touch on this later).
Story is very similar to the first game with some twists and new bosses and story segments, this time drawing from Dragonball Super's first two arcs instead of movie plots for the last few story missions. It takes between 3-4 hours to finish completely, sans DLC of course (I will not be talking about the DLC content in this review other than here to reccomend getting it for the additional content and additional moves).
Parallel Quests are also largely the same, with some basically being copied straight from DBXV1. This is both a strength and a weakness, because the only changes made are win conditions generally, and they were in the first game.
There is a new type of mission added for this game: Expert Missions. These missions consist of fights of varying difficulty where you and 4 other people team up to fight either a superpowered normal enemy with new abilities, a large enemy with those same powers, or a normal enemy with tons of HP. These vary wildly from cakewalks to brutal marathons that will require teamwork and skill and your most powerful moves.
The shops in-game have been left largely alone, aside from the addition of TP medals and the TP medal shop (open Friday-Sunday every week). While you can use TP medals (which you earn from Expert Missions, doing new Parallel Quests for the first time, or get as gifts from the devs from time to time) to purchase regular items, moves, and equipment, you're much better off saving them up in the literal hundreds to purchase moves from the TP Medal Shop. Moves here cannot be acquired any other way except maybe from your DBXV 1 create-a-character's import process. These include powerful moves like Goku Black's Black KameHameHa Ultimate and Final Shine from GT. You can also get exclusive gear here, which may or may not be to your taste but the option is there.
Now for the bad stuff.
First of all, Combat has become a mirror of what it was in DBXV1. In the first game, beamspam was dominant in PVP and PVE and a female saiyan with Super Vegeta and beam spam was basically unstoppable. This game outright will punish you for using energy attacks in 1v1 scenarios. There is a new mechanic added called Stamina Break, which immediately depletes all stamina your opponent has and leaves them wide open to attack. They can't block, they can't dodge, they can't boost dash, they can only float around helplessly as you pummel them in a combo or knock them to the ground before dropping a huge ultimate on their head. This means that Stamina management and melee combat are the two most important things, especially for PVP. If you go into a PVP match with a Ki-based character, expect to be chewed up and spit out, unless you're doing 2v2 or 3v3 and your teammates can for sure keep the enemy off of you while you wind up that flashy super or ultimate move. Not only that, but many energy ball Ultimates have had their tracking nerfed and all attacks can be blocked so long as you have stamina save for a select few like Destructo Disk and Special Beam Cannon. Basically, if your'e going to do PVP, avoid making an energy-based character at all costs because you will be destroyed. This isn't even to mention the pathetic anti-cheat in place; it is rare, but i have encounted the same players using trainers or some other cheat tool in PVP more than once.
Finally, the issue of connectivity with the servers is also there. You need to set your Steam download region to the one you want to play in. This is how the game determines your location.
So, remember that Stamina break thing? Yeah guess what, the bots abuse the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it. With their perfect reaction times it is incredibly difficult to land any sort of attack with a windup as they'll simply dash behind you and break your stamina, leaving you open to an AI-perfect beating. The bots are brutally hard.
Also, every time you make a new character you have to unlock all the PQ's again and beat the story... again.
Overall I'd reccomend this game most if you plan on getting the DLC/Season pass but it's still fun without those things, so give it a chance if you have the money and the time.

The gameplay can be divided into two modes roughly. One mode is going moving your character around on screen from an isometric perspective and looking for things to click on.
The other big part of gameplay is "X-Com" like combat. The problem is that the system is "miss heavy" especially in the first few hours of the game.

Well this is a series I'm just never going to get into.

I don't know why; I like SRPGs, I'm okay with cyberpunk, I think the writing is good. But, well, I just found this too long and, by the mid-point, pretty boring. I wasn't a big fan of the first game and, were it not for the fact that I'd bought both games at the same time (for pennies) then I wouldn't have bought this.

Problems from the first game persist in this: the matrix is still painfully dull, being just a palette swap which does nothing interesting (though there is much less of it this time around at least); there's a very definite core team you'll likely use for every run (likely only switching Blitz and Dietrich depending on situation) and the plot just meanders along with no urgency or a great deal happening. I found the ending very disappointing, too, and whilst the game gives you some choices to make there's never any consequence - I think it's poor design to have any character choices have no impact until a sentence or two on the 'End' screen - even Telltale games provide more in this respect.

There are definite improvements from the first game - your core team now have some rudimentary level-up mechanics in place which at a stroke makes them both viable throughout the whole game and conversely discourages you from ever needing to hire any of the other runners; you can actually have a bit of a say as to what weapons and items/spells characters can take on mission (though it's annoying you have to reselect for each run) and melee characters have more joy.

But overall I was left feeling mightily relieved it was all over. Like I say, I was disappointed with the plot in general - it starts building up to something but never delivers, I never really found combat too exciting (I was a mage, as per the first game, and at least felt more powerful) and little things started to grate (like the ponderous movement speed.)
Shadowrun: Hong Kong was long taken off my wishlist as I was discouraged from reading that it suffers from a fair bit of padding in the hub world and doesn't is more of an expansion than a sequel, but having now finished Dragonfall it's crystallised that I definitely won't get Hong Kong now no matter the price.

Shadowrun-Dragonfall is a turn-based science-fantasy RPG which improves on its predecessor in every aspect of the game.
If you are not averse to a lot of reading, as this game is heavily packed in narrative presented in a read-it-yourself format and like fantasy settings mixed with a bit of cyberpunk, then do yourself a favor and get this game ASAP, as it is a 10/10 title.
Multiple endings, multitude of options to direct your self-created character via a desired development path, choices with consequences, all accompanied by a sweet and beautiful graphics reminiscent of the classics.
Now, to go a bit more into details.
Really good and immersive, even though the ending mixes up needlessly cryptic dialogues for the sake of it.
Definitely the strongest feature of this game, the story, although not a direct continuation of the previous storyline, puts you again in the shoes of a shadowrunner, who ends up being involved in something bigger than bargained for.
Some elements tie into the overall plot better than the others, with the spotlight given more tangibly to the famed Dragons from the previous game, but, with the exception of couple of dialogues cryptic for the sake of it, make up a coherent and plausible world (at least to this universe).
The choices you make starting from the class you choose open up various options in dialogues, with some choices opening up different ending possibilities, but the game does a great job of not bombing you with ramifications of your choices straight away.
Almost every choice matters in the end, allowing for the creation of a solid main character of your own choosing.
Companions are well crafted, some sideline characters are nicely intertwined into the main story which does make feel the world even more coherent and the presence and actions of your character that much more impactful.
It is definitely longer than Shadowrun Returns, but it does not feel like it is needlessly dragging out, because what your character does in the game, is given enough purpose and ties into the main plot that it keeps you occupied and engaged.
Turn-based at its finest, with custom-made main character of chosen race and class which furthers the immersion in the story.
It is a turn-based game where each actions take a designated amount of points from the total your character has each round. Even though, the fights rarely feel like they drag too long.
The system itself rewards you for a thought-through actions and punishes you if you don't take a second to actually learn it. It is not the most convoluted system, though, so it does not take that long to get it.
There are multiple races to choose from, which do not limit your choice of classes you can pick, but have an impact on how far you will be able to push a certain class—some are better suited for ones than the others (Elves can push Summoning/Conjuring the farthest, but end up with the least amount of health in the end).
There are a couple of classes to choose from, but you can mix and match those as you play.
The options to choose from all seem valid and offer enough incentive to get immersed in them. And there is a little twist with cybernetics and how it affects magic which must be taken into account while playing, which, alongside the possibility of multiple endings, adds to the game's re-playability potential.
A modern take on classics with beautifully crafted environments and attention to detail that is impossible not to appreciate, once you're hooked.
The graphics take some getting used to, as they are heavily inspired by the games of old. At a first glance it might feel not detailed or high-quality, but, once you get over the initial "dated" feeling, you will notice that the environments and characters have a lot of details to them, the settings make sense story-wise and, overall, it breathes a lot of fresh air to the otherwise nostalgia.
It looks good and, in the end, you love it like the AAA titles which forgets that amazeballs graphics are not everything.
Of course, nowadays, amazing storyline is no excuse to s ♥♥♥♥♥♥ y graphics as well, thankfully, the developers had a vision for this picture-esque esthetics and it shows.
My only beef with this game is that spells, at least the projectile ones, feel too similar to one another and blend in with standard firearms, in the end.
The higher tier spells are barely different than their low tier equivalents and not that different from normal bullets.
Of course, to each their own, but I like some splendor and flare with my mages, thank you. Mind you, I still loved every single bit of my Sorcerer Elf, I just wish his magic showed a bit more, at least during the fighting bits.
Haven't played Hong Kong yet, but I hope that has been addressed, to some extent.
All in all, I invite you all to give this game a try – I loved it and will definitely replay it a couple of times.

I'm only pressing recommend due to the fact that I don't think that this game is unplayable; rather, I think it will strike some audiences very well. But I'm seeing a pattern with Jagex, trying to suck on the teats of more successful ideas. Of course, it does make a twist on the regular card game mechanic, but just because it doesn't play like Hearthstone doesn't mean it's not a Hearthstone clone (down to the aesthetics, even). Anyway, that personal gripe out of the way.
The game is streamlined with rudimentary learning curve that allows you to jump in and understand the mechanics immediately. You could probably spend an hour or so playing and start in on ranked mode and do relatively well. But the ease of it is what turned me off in the end... I didn't mind so much sitting there and watching the animations occur, but it's rather easy to win should you just keep in mind rather simplistic and common sense strategies (card order). People may disagree, but I feel as if other games like MTG or Hearthstone have a nuance of play, but admittedly, most cardgames are 30% strategy, 70% luck. Sometimes RNG will screw you out of a sure-fire win.
I wouldn't say this game is pay to win, but I was disheartened to see the amount you needed to grind in order to afford a basic booster pack (1000 copper here vs Hearthstone's 100 gold, which can easily be gathered with doing daily quests). It feels as if Jagex is sort of twisting your arm and pressuring you to spend real cash in order to speed up the process, and that doesn't sit well with me.
Not for me, but it definitely has an audience. Might be a game I return to when I'm bored and have nothing better to play. It's a worth a try, and the idea they attempted to execute was novel.

Far Cry 2 has nothing in common with its predecessor other than the huge open world that characterised the first game, as well. In fact, the first episode was rather linear (practically, each level was a different island) whereas here you can go wherever you want. There are two maps with an enormous amount of territory to be covered. Just look at the pictures posted on the store page to see how beautiful and varied these areas are.
As already stated, the game is beautiful. The jungles, the rain, the burning grass and trees (pyromaniacs will love it) once you obtain a flamethrower. It is just gorgeous! Too bad the story does not hold anything special in it. You complete missions for two competing factions that try to rule the area. If I'm mistaken this is all fictional and there's not even a mention as to which African country you are in.
The game is very difficult. Even on a normal difficulty enemies you pass by in a vehicle can shoot you from a distance - I'm amazed how precise shots they have each time. If you go through a single outpost it is almost impossible to do that without being hit by the enemies. Another issue is how the enemies in these outposts throughout the game get respawned for no apparent reason. Mission destination points are usually deliberately placed to the farthest place on the map making sure you need to go through at least a couple of outposts along the way. This is bad as the game is prolonged due to some unnecessary, repetitive actions.
Still, overall, this is a good game. It is entertaining and you can have some really funny moments during the combat with enemies. If you are not familiar with the franchise, however, I think the best is to choose the 3rd episode which is a more refined version of the Far Cry experience.

Disclaimer: I have put hundreds of hours into this game in Open Beta before it was on steam.
I can honestly say this is the best card game I have ever played. In my background I was an avid player of yugioh and chronicle: runescape legends. I also have played shadowverse and duelyst.
Where this game stands out the most is its extreme attention to balance. I have never played any other card game so percisely balanced as elder scrolls legends, nothing is cheap, everything feels fair and deliberate. Too many card games are overly reliant on RNG such as Hearthstone but if you win in elder scrolls legends it will be because of your skill.
The meta is vastly diverse and has consistently been. Dire Wolf the developers have done a great job slowly rolling out content to make sure that the meta is perfectly balanced.
This game uses a similiar mana system to Hearthstone. The biggest differences are its two lanes: the board is divided in half and monsters played in one half cannot interact with those in the other.
And the rune system. An absolutely genius mechanic. Each player starts with 30 health and when you lose 5 health a rune breaks and you draw a card. There are certain cards designed that if you draw them on a rune break you can play them for no mana cost immediately.
At first the rune system may appear as RNG, however it is a brilliant system to keep aggro under control which runs rampant in many similiar games such as Shadowverse. The instant play cards are very balanced and how likely you are to benefit off of this effect is very directly related to how you build your deck, it is a very controlled RNG.
Elder scrolls legends shares many similiarities to Hearthstone and Shadowverse.
Overall
Pros:
+ extremely well balanced
+ generous free to play
+ diverse meta
+ rune system
+ minimal RNG
+ very few useless cards
Cons:
- artstyle may be offputting to some
- small cardpool
- updates aren't very frequent

So..
this is my opinion about this game after playing it for over 6 months with over one thousand hours played.
Short form: Extremely fun game with nice balancing that has some minor flaws here and there.
Long form:
This game combines alot of interesting aspects making every game played to something realy cool.
Im talking about a dual colour system, prophecies, 2 lane mechanic and much more.
A dual colour system allows alot of deck creativity and at the same time viability. Currently there is only one colour combination that i dont see as viable, even though people still have success with it.
This alone also speaks for great balancing. Bethesda is constantly balancing cards. Not only nerfing the op ones but also buffing underplayed ones. Thats simply amazing.
Prophecies make the game exciting and frustrating at the same time. It just prevents this game from getting boring and you learn to play around it as much as possible.
The 2 lanes make this game also more skillbased than for example hearthstone. You always have  a decision to do even if its obvious which card you have to play. This is one of the reasons i like this game so much.
Another point that is probably very important for most people is the f2p model.
Bethesda is being very generous with their rewards. So dont be discouraged by the expansions we already have. It will take you maybe 2 months to get all the content unlocked and have most of the cards. Without any investment besides playing the game for 3 hours a day.
So compared to other games the f2p model is realy rewarding. Since you get 15-50 gold every 3 wins and a random card or pack. It can even be a legendary (even though rare) Epics on the other hand are not so rare. You usualy get atleast 1 epic card.
The only thing that i dislike about this game is the compatibility for either my hardware or windows 10 as it sometimes lags ingame.
Overall a great game!

Finished the story in 3 hours. Arena is quite cool, but overall? It's not worth spending money on. The second story is about as long as the first and they want GBP19.99 to unlock? I think not.
Pros:
Free to play
The one story you get is pretty good
The mechanics are probably better than hearthstone, which is it's closes rival.
The deck types are quite cleverly laid out and have good internal Synergy: Willpower is generally about helping your creatures out, whilst intelligence is all about direct damage and synergising off of action cards for example.
Arena is fun, microtransactions will get you back in, though I'm not sure you get the cards you pick which is a let-down.
Cons:
Cost. It's microtransaction based, fine, but don't then charge me most of the cost of a full title for one < 3 hour story expansion. You've got to be kidding.
Complexity: For all that it's probably better than hearthstone, it's not a patch on Magic: The Gathering, the mechanics just aren't deep enough.
Very pay 2 win: Didn't pay out for the booster packs? Sucks to be you then.
All in all it's a nice idea, but it's nothing more than a transparent cash grab in the end with some clever mechanics, though outdone by Magic, Pokemon and even yu-gi-oh. If they lower the costs, then the story modes might keep you interested for a while, but as of right now, play it until you've done the free stuff, then drop it and  don't look back.

Killer is Dead - the only game of the Hack 'n' Slash/Sneak-a-peek variety on Steam.
Here, you will decapitate countless enemies with your katana, wonder what elevator you've heard the soundtrack in, brag about finishing with your ladies in under two minutes --- all while trying to figure out what in the actual hell is going on.
Killer is Dead uses an Arkham-style combat system where the higher the combo, the more blood Mondo's katana draws from his enemies. Special powers and abilities, as well as your health are powered by said blood. And there will be a lot of it.
You can also acquire new weapons and items (as well as awkward boners) during gigolo missions.
Accessing the KIDengine file and editing it to allow 60 FPS and other effects makes quite a difference. Camera controls can get frustrating if you're caught in a corner, but it hasn't often been an issue for me.

The side missions are important since they help beat the Mondo Girls missions, and beat those levels because that's how you get sub-weapons.
I beat the game on hard mode, it took about 10 hours at a leisurely pace. If you like the combat you'll get your money's worth in content.
Don't forget to edit the .ini file, that's important.

It should first be noted that this game is ten years old, but still manages to perform and satisfy excellently.
Superpower 2 allows the player to take on the role of any nation that exists in 2001 (Yes, even Vatican City/The Holy See) and guide it on its path to become a world superpower. It styles itself as a geopolitical simulator, and that is exactly what it is, although it plays more like a grand strategy game akin to Europa Universalis IV or Hearts of Iron III or a mixture of every Paradox Interactive grand strategy game ever made (although it should be noted that one cannot simply assume the role of a dynasty or a character like in Crusader Kings II). It has a very fleshed out diplomacy, military, economic and politics system, and one can even create organisations like NATO or the UN through a treaty system. It is also possible for said treaties to collapse (In one game played hours before this review was written as Britain, NATO collapsed after America withdrew). The AI is very interesting and games are random (in the aforementioned game Pakistan ended up nuking India and invading, for example).
The one problem I have with this game is that there is a constant runtime error crash as of a recent update (I believe), and I am hoping that said crash will be fixed or a workaround found. I also want to congratulate Nordic Games on getting this great game on Steam.
All-in-all, I would recommend this game to anyone who has the money - it's an excellent purchase.

Over all, I find it's a good game and the critics reviewed it properly, but had it not been for the ridiculous marketing campaign maybe people would have said nicer things about it.

Ustaka, and friends went out on an expedition to collecting amber and straw. On the way, she discovered a crevasse with dragon bones! Thinking of how rich shed be, she lead the party of eight to mine the bones. Getting attacked by rock trolls in the process, trying to get away, Ustaka lost her sister and two gatherers.
Now she wasn't good at math so she counted on her fingers 1,2,3,4,5. Five out of eight people left, not bad she thought, lets keep going! With five people in the expidition Ustaka lead the party on the long walk to the sight of amber and straw.
Then a wind storm hit; one unlike any Ustaka had seen before! People were flung, Every Which Way! But the storm did pass, eventually, and left in its wake Ustaka, a child, and only three others. She stared at the group with her strabismic eyes. The gears in her head, turning, s l o w l y. One in the party said 'I think we should leave.' but no, Ustaka got them here and she knew that the town needed these supplies.
So they worked for days, collecting all that they needed. All was good, till the goblin hoards attacked. There was no escape so they had to fight, and fight they did. All but Ustaka, the child and one other named Cestimir, came out alive once the wounded died off.
This time when Ustaka counted she, knew they needed to leave; and they did. The walk was long and tormenting, they escaped the notice of spiders, demons, and more goblins. They did manage to make it back to the town, alive.
But the storm seen earlier, returned. This time with a vengence. Moaning 'Give me my child!' the people of the town were awe struck. Who could have taken a child form a mother? Everyone looked to Ustaka, who had a sword drawn and a shield in hand, those same strabismic eyes looking the monster up and down. 'Charge!' a battle commenced and twas the first true victory received in a long wile. But Ustaka was killed in the process. RIP Ustaka #Never Forget#Remember the Alamo

Possibly my biggest complaint is that it takes so long to get research points, followed by the fact that sometimes the RNG numbers just do not work in your favor (my village ended up with two men I think and I just wasn't having any children being born). However, starting a new game on a new map with new randomly generated resources didn't feel like a negative, it felt like a chance to make new choices and get better.
This isn't a game I play every day, but it is a game I enjoy for a few hours here and there when I want something slower paced.

Initial impression was positive, before the sexism, homophobia and transphobia went off the charts in chapter 4 when you have to play as Captain Nate.
Game mechanics: Switching between characters is an exercise in patience as they walk around aimlessly for awhile before hand off. Voice acting is excellent. The character movements are cool (except when switching characters.) Despite Ivo's ridiculous scantily clad girl-elf armor, she's a pretty interesting character, and the brains of the party. Wilbur is reasonably clever too. Many secondary characters are interesting, like the little rat warrior. Storyline is highly engaging, and the puzzles, while sometimes tedious or frustrating in the usual point-and-click manner, are mostly interesting and fun.
Further into the game - chapter 4 - you're stuck being Captain Nate. Captain Nate is a jerk. He is such a jerk that I'm having a hard time progressing in the game now that I'm forced to interact through him.
Captain Nate objectifies all the women he interacts with. They're just sex objects to him, so I'm a bit bewildered by the "girl power" tag associated with this game. He cuts down everyone around him like an insecure school boy. He goes on and on about what it means to be "a man" in this archaic, tedious litany of outdated stereotypes ... I'm just so sick of the culture remnants of shaming people who don't fit some stupid cultural concept of "normal." This guy is desperate to be "normal" where normal is some kind of ignorant, chauvinstic male pig and proving it at every turn. I think it might have been intended as humor? If so, it failed. Badly.
There's a character in Captain Nate's sequence who's a pink-clad paladin with high heels on his pink banner. I'm all for flipping paladins♥♥♥♥♥♥as a timeworn gamer tradition, but this was deeply inappropriate. Liking pink doesn't make you weak. Wearing heels doesn't make you weak. Besides the obvious misogyny and sexism of demeaning femme-stereotyped gender stuff, it's also a train wreck of genderqueer shaming and pacificist shaming. I'm so done with this kind of thing in our culture. Teenagers kill themselves over "humor" like this. Leelah Alcorn didn't have a chance because of attitudes like this. Stop it. It's shaming and bullying and it's time for us to be better people. I keep trying to get through these scenes with Nate and the pink paladin, hoping that there will be some kind of redemption, but it just keeps not happening, and I'm running out of patience.

If you do not own the first Xenoverse, this is a fantastic buy for dragon ball fans. It has almost everything for fans of Dragon Ball Z, Dragon Ball GT, and Dragon Ball Super. The game provides an RPG custom character experience like no other. The game itself is very decent.
However, if you already own the first one with all its DLC, you 80% own the second one. This game is far too similar to the first. I can make a short list of the things that are different.
List:
- Worse camera angles than Xenoverse 1
- Super Saiyan 3 and a few other transformations for other races
- Dragon Ball Super PQs and characters
- New PQ style side missions in the form of orb or relavant character home time rifts
- Attacks of all varieties from Dragon Ball Super
- New City hub
- Slightly different campaign (Although very similar and most quests are reused)
- Some new Clothing
- Slightly less broken pvp experience (characters are nerfed in some catagories in general even in single player, but have a higher overall stat distribution per level)
- Nothing else
Overall, Its up to you to decide if this is enough change to justufy another $80 buy ($60 if you want half the content). If you do not already own the first copy, I'd say its worth the buy for sure. If you already own the first copy I'd say the opposite.

Fantastic - probably the best Metroidvania-revival game I've played next to Guacamelee. Control is fluid, the music remixes are great, and the power-ups varied. Sure, you got your staples like the double-jump, but you also get some interesting ones beyond that, like a knife-throw attack that can be endowed with elemental attributes. My only real gripe is that the boss battles manage the rare feat of being too easy, but also feeling very cheap - you will take damage from some apparently unavoidable attacks, but they do so little damage there's no real incentive to try to learn to avoid them. I also wish the objectives were presented a little more creatively than having your AI computer thing just tell you where to go. Finally, it's lacking some of the zaniness of the original Strider - sure its got a mecha-gorilla callback, but where's the stuff like the Politburo transforming into an armored dragon? Or a dinosaur popping out of nowhere? Or some even crazier original ideas?
If you enjoy Metroidvanias, you owe it to yourself to play this.

The unique twist about this game is that instead of having to think of what your opponent will do next, you have to predict your opponent's next FOUR moves every turn and react accordingly. You don't take turns laying down cards, instead you play basically 5 (or less) rounds, and you place all of the cards you want to use down all at once. You character then basically fights through these cards, gaining their dropped resources, and other buffs after defeating them.
You really have to plan out what you drop, and in which order to ensure that your character is coming out better each round. You basically want to have the most health, armour, and attack at the final battle, or at least a better combination of the three than your opponent.
