I would give this game a neutral rating, if there was one. I love the writing, the soundtrack is a perfect match, the skill system has great potential, and the below average graphics are offset by some cute drawings. What killed the game for me was the combat system. I find it so annoying, I just could not bring myself to continue playing despite the captivating story. As such I do not recommend it.
I don't know if it's their adaptation of this classic combat concept, or if guns and turn based doesn't work in general. It's cool on a statistical scale, but on the individual level it is random to a point where strategy feels pointless.
Hit chances are comparitively low, you can easily miss someone standing right in front of you. Crit chances are extremely high and the difference is significant. There is a cover modifier, which doesn't have much to do with reality or common sense, probably due to simple technical limitations. It turns low hit chances into a waste of ammo across a room with a chair and a plant in the way. That is a problem, because ammo is at a premium. The sniper brings five rounds. Turns being split into two huge timeslices again defy common sense, and create an interesting strategical scenario, which has nothing whatsoever to do with the physics of this universe.
The same strategy can turn out a walk in the park or utter defeat. Trying to kill the not-meant-to-be-killed Orc at the beginning a few times proved that nicely. Maybe it's intentional and part of the atmosphere, but the result feels random and artificial, and could be a lot of fun after a lobotomy.
It's too bad, because the story really is a lot of fun, except for the ridiculous zero to hero approach, which seems to become more and more popular these days. Puberty probably helps digging that.

A solid story and interesting setting that are marred by the game's execution. The actual strategy mechanics are extremely basic and slow, the UI is sluggish and glitchy, and the engine has some significant problems. Graphics and animations tend to not be important (see: Avernum) but they have the same stupifying effect that they did in Wasteland 2. It's like playing with Lego men. The UI's problems really manifest in the boring virtual reality/rigging sections, where buttons, skills, and movements frequently freeze the game and require bizarre input sequences to fix.
The combat rebalance mod takes some of frustration and monotony out of the system but a Shadowrun game shouldn't need a day 1 overhaul mod like a Bethesda game. I enjoyed the story enough that I wanted to play the fan campaigns and main story again, but trying to restart the game with the terrible beginning characters was too droll to tolerate. The skills require heavy point investment to become useful so the builds lack variety. At some point you get three instead of two action points which makes combat less tedious. The downside is that the AI never gets this bonus and the combat sequences become too simple. Instead of making smarter opponents the game just throws waves of them at you.
For the price I paid for this on sale ($1.27?) it was a good game, but the dev studio has a lot of work to do if they want to cultivate a fanbase with this new series. This is the director's update of an improved expansion to the first game, which means I have no desire to play the original reboot and am avoiding the next installment (Hong Kong). People comparing this to strategy games like X-Com or Jagged Alliance in their reviews are really overselling it.

There's a fully developed story for this game, which you are only told half of for the sake of being ambiguous. Mondo is a good main character, and wanting to see him interact with the world ends up being the main incentive to progress the story.
The side missions are important since they help beat the Mondo Girls missions, and beat those levels because that's how you get sub-weapons.
I beat the game on hard mode, it took about 10 hours at a leisurely pace. If you like the combat you'll get your money's worth in content.

Watch Dogs takes a slice of real-world issues of increasing dependence on technology and the growing distrust in privacy. with its theme of hacking and explores the idea of a world where technology can be exploited. And by hacking, I mean just pressing and holding on a button to hack stuff all so instanteously it’s almost unbelievable silly.

Watch Dogs' main protagonist is this phone-addict guy called Aiden Pearce, who loves wearing hats and thinks masking his mouth is enough to protect his identity. The story follows your atypical revenge story excuse of a videogame MC as he chases after those baddies responsible for killing his precious niece while slowly becoming troubled by his vigilante antics and consequences of it. The game tries to keep you on the vigilante route by punishing you with some kind of karma system (eg. if you kill or injure civilians similar to Assassin’s Creed), but it's hard to believe when you're too busy hacking and stealing from random people's bank accounts all the time, stealing cars  and destroying city infrastructure.
The original game will have graphics that could disappoint, if you had high expectations after watching the E3 trailer. This is no doubt my biggest complaint about the game. I just can't stand when devs mislead people with superior graphics when not CGI, Ubisoft being the biggest culprit of all.  They had to downgrade for the next-gen consoles but for PC, Ubisoft had no reason to downgrade the graphics apart from their possible idea that ''all platforms must be treated fairly''. Thankfully, a simple patch fix by TheWorse restores the game to its E3 glory and fixes all the anti-aliasing mess and ugly textures.
There’s some technical issues I guess is worth pointing out if you’re playing with keyboard + mouse. The problem is being unable to customize your keybinds without it always resetting back to default. It can be fixed by force-quitting the game but pretty jarring that Ubisoft never bothered fixing this.  I played with the Deluxe edition of the game so I don’t know if the same occurs for the original version.
There’s also the issue of some horrible mouse movements, thankfully again, possible to be fixed manually through INI files.
I can't say much of anything that bad about the gameplay mechanics in Watch Dogs. Truthfully, it's excellent how Ubisoft combines and shares the best game mechanics among their games. Watch Dogs is almost the pinnacle of that. Climbing and traversing obstacles feel just as fluid as in Assassin's Creed, while the stealth aspect borrows from Splinter stealth system and incredibly brilliant enemy AI. Speaking of which, enemies aren’t that dumb in Watch Dogs.  In fact, they’re quite darn smart, capable of flanking you and flush you out with grenades. You can flank them likewise even when spotted to take them out one-by-one, making combat quite a sweet challenge.

If you;ve been playing too much GTA, the driving in Watch Dogs will at first feel foreign to you. Notice how the people who complain about the driving have barely spent much time playing the game to write their empty reviews. At first that's how I felt as well. ''Oh, the driving is horrid, Why can't it be like GTA?''
Meanwhile if you've been playing some actual racing games like Need for Speed or others like Sleeping Dogs, you should feel right at home with the driving in this game. The stronger steering and acceleration of vehicles requires more skill and control as you drive. From chasing other vehicles to online races, the infrastructure of the city makes the frantic driving through the roads phenomenally fun once you get used to it.
Watch Dogs is based on the city of Chicago, split into several districts.
Chicago is a bustling city to explore, from the lowly slums to the high-end cities, it's like a playground of destruction for your silly hacking antics. But above all, its the pedestrians and liveliness of the people doing activities that makes the city feel so alive. There may not be so much openness and freedom like in the world of GTA but Ubisoft does a great job at making the dense WD world feel so much more believable. For instance, running around with a gun will immediately cause people to freak out and might even call the police. When it rains, people actually take out umbrellas or run to shelter (something GTA V lacked for some reason).
Furthermore, is the profiling feature, which allows you to find out important and sometimes amusing details about every single person you encounter in the game world. The extra info doesn't really have an important role in the gameplay but does give the civilians all around the city a lot more substance to individual identity, which is pretty cool.
Mission design has always been a weakness for Ubisoft games I feel and likewise, Watch Dogs falters a little with the kind of stuff you can do. There's a TON of side content to do in this game but can be overly repetitive after a while, especially Fixer missions. That’s not to say they aren’t fun. However, worse is how the main missions are really not that much better in scope, requiring you to do the same things you're already tasked with in side missions like Fixer Contracts (infiltrate, car chase, shootouts etc.). There’s also a lot of camera spying involved, and by a lot, I do mean, A LOT.
A huge lot of segments in the game are stealth-based, which is quite fun, playing out like a much easier version of Splinter Cell but there are also sufficient times when you can optionally engage in direct combat.
Apart from that are some unique minigames like QR code scanning and more and more hacking..
Funnily enough, the most enjoyable side content has to be the Digital Trips, something like arcade games where you play as Aiden Pearce getting high on drugs. There's four Digital Trips, ranging from playing as a madman driver to playing as a giant Spider Tank that wrecks havoc on the city. Each of the digital trips are so well established, they probably have the potential to become separate games.
I don't usually review multiplayer components in what's largely a single-player game but this isnt the case for Watch Dogs. THIS is where Watch Dogs sets itself apart.
The online component in this game is just so well intergrated together, it's hard to ignore. The moment you're free to roam the game, you're already connected to multiplayer.
In the same vein of showing everything is interconnected with technology, the game world itself is interconnected among players.  While playing the game, you can occasionally get invaded by other players (labelled Fixers) who will attempt to either tail you or hack you. Because the transition is absolutely seamless, there’s no obvious indication of the moment someone invades you.  No loading screen, nothing. Once they do successfully hack, it becomes a game of cat-and-mouse which can lead to all kinds of different intense scenarios of hacker vs hacker. It's here where I feel the game truly shines and brings an extra amount of serious fun to the game. There's nothing that beats the satisfaction of killing the invading players or successfully hacking other players at their game.
Despite being a tad ridiculous, I really liked the concept of easy hacking in this game. I’ve played a ton of sandbox city games but this game simply takes the cake for being one of the best…so for.
Watch Dogs is sadly, a too underrated game hampered by over expectations from its E3 graphical downgrades to just having to be released right after GTA V, a bad time for a new game setting a benchmark.
Pros:
+ Seamless online integration and game modes
+ Digital Trips
+ Enjoyable and challenging driving mechanics
+ A bustling lively world of Chicago at your hacking fingertips
+ Smooth controls and great AI
Cons
-	Graphical downgrade
-	Dull missions
Overall: 4/5

Good Stuff: Nice worldbuilding - kind of like Elder Scrolls and Witcher, this world has a pantheon of original gods, elves, orcs, humans, and demons (though demons seem to be magical monsters which are naturally occurring or created by gods, and some are benevolent).  The art is fun, though I was slightly confused that my human villagers apparently included people who looked like dwarves alongside much taller people.  I did notice two places where the text describes a demon as having yellow eyes, but in the art the eyes are not yellow - perhaps that will be a minor bug fix in a future version.
Not So Good Stuff:  This is quite a slow paced game, both for getting research points and for the time each battle takes.  The micromanagement of crafting and gathering and equipping characters is also part of the slow pace, though certainly this type of gameplay is part of the RPG and strategy game paradigm.  I lost both my first two games due to having more villagers killed of than were born or willing to join me; the second game I almost starved right at the beginning because my starting location didn't have any food but seaweed.  (This is for a game on normal difficulty and all settings default - there are some options for increasing animation speed and customizing difficulty that I haven't tried yet.)
Despite all the micromanagement during the game, you don't seem to be able to micromanage the starting set-up, like by placing your village or choosing appearances for your villagers.  You can re-name them though, that part is nice.  There might be a way within the game to build a second village or move your village, but if there is I didn't find or unlock it.  You also cannot manage save files - you can't even quit without saving if some disaster has just occurred.  I can see how this fits with the idea that each game unlocks new options in future games, but it's still frustrating to lose half your villagers, especially when pursuing one of the main quest lines, so it's not like you were doing something you weren't supposed to, and be unable to hit the undo button.
The combat also is a bit front-heavy; it doesn't add new features as you level up, so the complexity can baffle new players and at the same time players can get quite bored with combat before getting even halfway through a complete game.
Overall: This is a lovely game if you are a patient person who likes micromanagement and simulating a fantasy village, and doesn't get traumatized if your characters die unexpectedly.  I am not necessarily this kind of player, but I'm sure someone is.  I recommend new players play on easy difficulty, not normal.  If anyone is interested in modding this game, I would love to see a pack of colored versions of the villager art.

Welcome to the land of Thea, it may look familiar, but it is entirely different. The creators of the game managed to piece together a unique and engaging world through well written texts, very atmospheric music, and an integrated crafting system. When I came across the quest in reference to Monty Python’s Holy Grail, it simply killed me, they shall have my heart-felt praise forever.
The difficulty curve is brilliant, even small tweaks to the array of mechanisms could offer a whole new style of play. The True God of Thea level is nigh impossible without a good understanding of the core functions. The level of customization allowed for each of your villagers will be a blast for anyone with a taste for a good-old rpg setup, and the effects of random events and player choice could truly alter the ability of a character, making them unique and a real loss upon death, which maybe frequent. The card mini-game for fights and challenges are simple but versatile, bringing out unique customizations while maintaining overall balance. It works.
The devs even give us the ability to create custom events, which I must say is pure awesomeness. The ability to write your own lore and obscure cultural references into the world of Thea is unbelievably satisfying.

When I first bought this game I was expecting something along the lines of DEFCON. I guess I got that, with a touch of civilization (minus the turn base), and ultimate control over diplomacy/markets.
This game is interesting to say the least, and was worth the buy ON SALE. This game as stated previous, gives you a world map (or the Earth in 3D) and you are allowed to choose a nation. With this nation you can build up your military, work your political magic, and look after your monetary situation. The military tab you are allowed to build anything that walks to anything that treads water to anything that may fly in the air. You can also customize vehicles which is a brilliant perk. In this tab is also covert military actions which allow you to manipulate political structures around the planet, and there is also a nuclear launch missile control available as well. Onto the 2nd tab which is the political station, one can choose whether they want to be fascist, communist, socialist or whatever. You also get to decide internal laws such as same-sex marriage and can limit how many kids a family can have. The diverse control the game lets you take into your hands is amazing. Some would say it's better left to the computer (which you can have) and some say it's better to micro manage (which you can choose to have as well)! I like the fact you are given the chance to choose what you want. Within the third tab which is the monetary settings, you can literally choose what you want to fund down to the level. Want to enhance education? Go ahead? Want to fund the military, screw it and do it! You can build more nukes if you'd like, or heck start getting covert warfare going by hiring some spies and sending them to other countries. And yes, nuking is oddly satisfying but really can screw up your political reputation. What is another cool feature is that you can watch your units fight the opposing side in real time (double left click on the battle to see).
Another interesting feature is that anywhere in the world you can right click and do quick treaties, such as alliances, common markets, weapon trade (or even embargo), research partners (and a lot more choices - you can even annex countries).
BUT.... (DEVS PAY ATTENTION HERE)!
The only few complaints I have is that you are not able to use the keyboard to quickly select which countries are in for what treaties, and can get extremely annoying using the mouse to select EVERYTHING (especially on the menus). Another complaint is that some countries are literally impossible to select. Even if you right click and attempt to do a quick treaty, sometimes if you try clicking on Israel you'll get Palestine. Same thing with Chile and Argentina.
Overall good game. Would be even more intense if they let you control the units when you can watch them fight. I would give this game an 8 if it was something that was truly unique to it's genre. Even though it didn't hit an 8, I would recommend buying on sale and playing!

I recently purchased SuperPower 2 to play with friends, and right away I loved it. The  game seems to offer endless possibilities (especially when you're playing on a server with others), and each country you play as results in a different scenario each time.
This game gives you everything you would want in a geopolitical simulator, and more. Choose a country, build alliances (among other treaties), start wars, conquer land, control your economy, military, goverment, and of course, build nukes. While it can be slow to start off, you can even turn countries like Kenya into economical powerhouses with a stacked military. Many reviews make it seem like this is easy to do, and this can be offputting to those looking for a realistic simulator. In reality, it is only easy if you are willing to put your country in billions of dollars of debt and anger every country on Earth, and this will eventually backfire.
Despite all this, the game does have a tricky interface. It's not exactly welcoming to new users, as there is a lot of menus and options to choose from, but this is expected in such a complex game. Of course, as many people complain, this game has its share of bugs, and your screen resolution can cut out most of the battle screen, but this is abosolutely not a reason to overlook this game.
Overall, if you are going to buy this game, I reccomend that you do it with friends, because it makes things much more interesting, but singleplayer is fun as well. For the price of $10, you are easily getting a good deal.

I got this game two days ago when it was on sale for $2.49. I thought it would be one of those games you get, play once, and then never touch it again, and I though; well I’d play that for two and a half hours so I guess it was worth it. I then went in and did the tutorial and then got into the game. Automatically I chose America, like most people who choose their home country, and at an instant I realized I was dead wrong, this game is absolutely amazing.
In this game you control one of over 150 countries; you manage their politics, economy, and military while dealing with debt, invasion, terrorism, natural disasters, and nuclear annihilation. Politics allow you to create treaties, change laws, and change your government (for instance democracy to communism). In your economy you will first have to get your country out of debt, then you have to manage your budget, inflation, interest, income tax, resource production, financial aid and agreements, and trade. Finally, military; your military can be either your life saver or your demise depending on your economy and diplomatic relations. In your military you can build, buy, sell, and deploy troops and vehicles. Besides that you can design your own units and research more technology for better stats on your designed units. If you are have a problem with another country why not strike them with your entire nuclear arsenal or send covert ops into their country and wreak havoc on their product and economy.
But this game isn't perfect. The games multiplayer doesn't run unless you open unsecure ports on your router. Your military can't invade a country unless your navy is 750 km away from your enemy’s shore, but if they have even a single boat within 1500 km of your navy you can't invade and occasionally the enemies ships don’t appear and you can't make a land invasion, which is beyond frustrating. But besides that I haven't run into to many other problems.
So is this game worth your $10? Yes. Would I recommend you wait until a sale? Not necessarily, it would be better if you did but this game is worth the full price. I've played this game for roughly 14 hours and t has become one of my favorites.

Absolutely love this game. It's easily my favorite DCCG. Coming from Hearthstone and want to know what sets it apart? This is based on probably a hundred or so hours playing the game using the Bethesda launcher. Here are the major differences from Hearthstone to get you started:
1. Rewards, in general, are much more generous. This is partly because of point #3 with bigger deck sizes and can have 3 copies of many of the Legendaries. You get like 10-50 gold and a spare card (can even be Legendary or a pack!) every 3 wins instead of just 10 gold. WAY better. End of season rewards... I forget how HS works, but you get a ton of gold and soul gems and like 1-3 packs for end of season purely based on what rank you are. In addition, they release a new card every month, and you get 1-3 copies based on your rank as well! 1 copy at rank 9 or better, 2 copies at rank 5, 3 copies at rank 1. You can craft monthly cards anytime after that for ones you've missed, but you'll never find them in packs.
2. Generally less RNG than HS. The randomness that is in the game (for the most part) has some interesting control, and not totally random. The really RNG cards typically aren't competitive, but still fun to throw 1 or 2 in your deck at times.
3. Solo Arena. Basically like Versus Arena, but against enemy AI. You earn cards in a similar fashion, same type of 30-card draft, but against enemy AI with random lane and game start effects. Rewards are similar to HS as well. Guaranteed pack for playing, even if you lose all 3. Infinite time to play, THIS COUNTS FOR QUESTS. There is no timer for playing, so you can take forever or walk away to do something if you get pulled away. I think you can even log off and it will pick up right where you left off if you join back in. Same goes for Practice mode, which I'll go into later.
4. Constructed decks have 50-70 cards, with 1 Unique copy of each Legendary allowed. If it's not Unique (the Golden circle at the top of some Legendary cards), you can still have 3 copies of a Legendary card, or any other card except ones marked Unique.
5. Constructed ladder. You win, you gain a star. Lose, you lose a star. However, you can't go down in rank in a given month. You go down to a separate 2-star constellation (rank) called Serpent. Below rank 5, a Bonus Round will randomly be in a given match. In that match, the winner gains 2 stars. The loser still loses 1.
6. Now for the big ones. Lanes. There are 2 of them. Yippee... you say sarcastically. But really it changes the play a LOT more than you'd think. I've heard it helps the defender. Left lane is normal. The right lane is, by default, the Shadow Lane. Every creature played here gains Cover for one turn. This can be played around and affected. Some cards can Move, or switch lanes, as part of their lane effects. Trust me when I say: 2 lanes are better than 1. I was made a believer.
7. The other BIG one. Prophecies and Runes. Here's where things get really interesting. Each player has 5 runes to start the game, at 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 health. When your health drops below 25 for any reason, no matter whose turn it is), you draw a card. If it has the Prophecy keyword, you get to play the card IMMEDIATELY (even during your opponent's turn), for no magicka cost, if you so choose. You can also choose to put the card in your hand. This rule goes for both players with all decks in every game type. This obviously has HUGE implications. Because there aren't many cards with Prophecy, breaking Runes in and of itself is an important decision every time. The only exception to this rule and all others is, if any player ever drops below 1 health for any reason on any turn, the game is over. Prophecies can be skipped in this way, if 6 damage is done in one attack, the last rune is "skipped". Knowing what class and colors you're playing against is key to playing around potential effects during your turn. Speaking of colors and classes...
8. Card colors / classes / card synergy / creativity. There are 5 colors, Red (Strength), Green (Agility), Blue (Intelligence), Yellow (Willpower), Purple (Endurance), plus Neutral (gray). Each color has a general theme, but can play any archetype (won't be top tier, but a taste of it). This is for balance, variety, synergy, and creativity. For example, Purple cards generally are stickier with slightly higher stats. Many Green cards are reactive or mobile (can Move between lanes). The 10 classes are all combinations of 2 of the 5 colors, plus Neutral cards can be in any deck. The Summon ability will activate any time that card comes into play, even if another card summons it. This makes for MUCH more card synergy than Battlecry in HS, which only activated when the card was played from your hand.
9. You can play Practice mode to get soul gems. 5 for a win against Easy, 10 against Normal, 15 against Expert. 300 gems per day cap. A Legendary every 4 days if you max it. Not bad with very fast aggro decks like mono red. You play against a random class with standard lane effects and starting conditions.
10. Chaos Arena is very fun and helps shakes things up once a month for the weekend. Random lane conditions and special conditions even on top of that sometimes. It's the first "new" game mode they've introduced.
11. A few new keywords. Haven't played HS in a while so some of these may be dupes. Breakthrough lets you overkill a creature into their face for damage. Pilfer activates any time the creature damages the enemy hero. Regenerate brings that creatures current health back to maximum at the beginning of your turn. Drain gives your hero back the same amount of health as the attack damage it deals.
12. No Secrets (Prophecies fill that role), but Supports instead. These are either limited use or perpetual, until removed. There are a few cards that can remove Supports. They typically either buff all your creatures while in play, summon a creature per turn, or buff 1 of your creatures with limited uses.
13. A few cards trigger if you have more health than your opponent. You may have noticed that 2 lanes and Runes / Prophecy tend to favor the defender, but clearly this favors the aggressor to maintain balance. These mighty few let aggro decks maintain momentum through all those extra (and potentially free) cards.
14. Heroes can never attack. Can't equip your hero with items. No hero powers. This makes cards, card draw, and X/1's more valuable since there are fewer ways to kill them without requiring a finite resource.
15. Card costs in soul gems (shards in HS). Legendaries in TESL cost 1200. Epics cost 400. Rares cost 100. Commons cost 40 (I think).

For those that don't know anything of SupComFA, you have 4 factions: Aeon Illuminate, a faction of humans that follow The Way, teached by the Seraphim; Cybran, a faction of humans with cyborg enhancements and with an AI implemented into them, sort of a hybrid; United Earth Federation, the usual faction of humans with the technology you'd expect; and finally Seraphim, an alien race.
Each plays differently, and each has its cons and pros. The UEF's pretty good at turtling and such, their shields are huge and they are the only faction with tier 3 land turrets. Cybran is the usual all-in offensive faction, you can even upgrade your Commander to teleport and have what is called "Microwave Laser", which basically is a huge♥♥♥♥♥laser that can kill any other Commander unit in a few seconds. Then the Aeon are kind of a mix, they've got Seraphim technology, so their units look pretty "alien", and it's a bit harder to pick up. Seraphim as well, they've got some pretty nice technology no other faction has, like their tier 2 battlecruisers being able to submerge and act as submarines as well.
As for the game itself, it's on a huge scale. You'll be doing some micro, especially on economy since it's fluid, meaning that you spend resources as you build or produce stuff instead of just waiting until you have X resources to automatically build one thing like in other RTS games. But it's mostly macro stuff, you can pretty much automate everything, from buildings, to units. You can set a factory to just loop a certain unit, you can set your units to patrol a certain route, you can set your engineers to reclaim a certain place and then go help on stuff, you can set waypoints for your factories, you can save templates of starting builds and things you frequently build to just have them start on one click. That means that you'll be pretty much focusing on keeping your economy flowing and then on the massive battles, by land, air and sea. If you reach late-game, you'll probably build what's called "experimental" units. Huge massive units that can pretty much take on other armies with a bit of backup or even by themselves. Every faction has its own different experimental units with, again, its cons and pros.
If you are going for multiplayer, I'll strongly suggest checking out Forged Alliance Forever, a community-made multiplayer lobby. There are about at least 2 thousand unique players each day on it, so you'll find a game on always. And it also has quite a few nice features, like coop campaigns, different game modes and maps, live replay, and a vault of stored replays, a matching and ranking system for 1vs1 games, a IRC chat, clans, and a long list of other features I'm not going to mention to not bore you. Seriously, just try it, it's awesome, and the FAF guys make a great job at adding stuff to the game and maintaining a balanced game.

Strider 2014 is more of a Remake from the classical Strider (Originally Arcade, then ported to different Consoles later on) which also combines some Gameplay Elements from Strider 2
The Gameplay is fastpaced and plays like Metroidvania Games (Exploration/Backtracking of the Stages, Areas which are closed until you get an Upgrade for your Sword to pass, etc.)
At the Beginning you have only your Sword and nothing else. Later you get Kunai's (Throwable Daggers), Double-Jump Boots, different Plasma Upgrades (Normal/Reflective, Fire, Ice and Magnet) for your Sword (The Upgrade Names heavily implies on the same Upgrades from Metroid Prime for those who know it ;) ), Robo-Equipment (Panther, Eagle and Flying Saucer), etc.
The Stages are mostly 2 Layer based which means, that you can later switch from one side of the stage to the other.
They are based in the Kasach Region where you will explore the City, Military HQ, Research Lab, Underground Facilities, etc.
Like in the Original, you will fight against Bosses at specific Times where at the End you get rewarded with an Upgrade most of the Time which enables you to explore new Areas or track back for earlier Stages to get Upgrades which was before impossible to get without the right Equipment.
The Graphics are good and the Effects aren't overly used on the Display to avoid losing Orientation in Combat. Also good BGM during Exploration and Combat.
Here are some of my + / o / - Points:
Positive:
-Good fastpaced Remake in the Style of the Original Strider
-Character can climb on almost any Surfaces which makes for a good fastpaced Running in the Stages (especially later with Character based Upgrades)
-Many Upgrades and Extra Collectibles (Skins, Concept Arts and Enemy Infos)
-Challenging Boss Fights
-Some Boss Fights returns also from the Original aside of Grandmaster Meio (Mecha-Pon, Solo, Ouroboros and the Chinese Sisters)
-Mostly Easy Achievements for those who likes to collect them
-All of the 4 Sword Upgrades are important and balanced for different Enemies/Obstacles
-Kunai's can also be upgraded (More Range, More Kunai's in one Throw)
-Kunai's and Plasma Catapult can be upgraded like the Sword with the 4 Elements and have different Effects while changing the Plasma Type (Example: With Fire Plasma you can throw Explosive Kunai's which explodes after sticking to an Object, etc.)
-3 different Robo Equipments which can aid you in Combat
Neutral:
-BGM gets later a bit repetetive while the earlier BGM's where more remarkable in my Opinion
-Heavy Attack not so much usable (I rarely used it, since Light Attacks are faster and can deal more Damage over Time)
-The Kunai Weapon is gained as Upgrade much later in the Game, while i personally preferred it that they should be made earlier available, since they are very useful as Anti-Air Weapons
Negative:
-Not much of a Story (Kill Grandmaster Meio) or especially a short Explanation at the Beginning. You get thrown right on the 1st Stage withough knowing what's going on if you didn't read some Infos beforehand.
-Short Duration of the Game with ca. 5-7 hours depending on your Skill (It took me 5 and half an Hour for completing the Game while collecting all of the Upgrades, but not all of the Collectibles)
-Not much Variety of Enemies (Mostly you will fight against Light/Heavy Soldiers and Drones with different Weapons)
-Stages are also lacking of Variety (Mostly Military Complexes and Facilities) while Original had also Jungle/Tundra based Levels
-The Lack of a General Map to orientate makes it later difficult to navigate for collecting Upgrades/Collectibles
Fazit:
The Game is fast and the Movement is amazing. Good and fair Boss Fights.
For Fans who like Metroidvania like Games, i can recommend it.
Due to the short Duration of the Game it is up to you if you want to wait for a Sale or get it now.
I also really recommend playing it with a Gamepad since using a Keyboard gets to be troublesome in some Stages.

Game can be completed within probably 4-8 hours depending on whether or not you try to find all the hidden upgrades and collectibles (costumes (which are just recolors), enemy intel, concept art, etc.). But yes, it does get very grindy mid-game.  To level up each different job you pretty much do the same thing over and over and over again.
As for Pvp... no real tactics involved.  Shoot first, overpower your opponents with superior weapons and a higher job level.  If you're low-level there's just no chance you'll survive against bored higher-level players who are after cheap thrills.  Grief killing happens a lot.
The game in and of itself is okay, I guess.  Not horrible, but nothing too special either.   If you have nothing better to do, go ahead and try it (hey, if you get a copy for free, why not right?) --- but I would not recommend paying for it, it's not worth the money.

Think Assassins creed, think far cry, think open world. Think repetitive missions, poor copies, closed world, no climbing, poor mechanics, and nothing like any other thing that you liked about Ubisoft games.
That's Watch_Dogs. Sure, the hacking is fun, but after the starter mission, that's nearly everything you will do for the remainder of the game.
It feels like one of those mock-up game boys from back in the 90's; there was tetris on every one of them, and usually another game or two. This is exactly that, but instead of running around in real life enjoying the outdoors and forever lasting batteries, you do this in front of a computer screen with keyboard and mouse or a controller. Like some cavedwelling animal.
If you want to keep your dear memories of OK ubisoft titles, don't get this game. Every little aspect is just a little below OK. The missions feel a little less than rewarding. And the storyline is just plain awfull. Awfull how?
Alright, think of this: you're the best hacker in town and you love your niece. Criminals get involved.
You can fill in the blank yourselves. Why no spoiler alert? Because at the start of the game, it's already spoiled and you can fill in the plot by asking a 6 year old kid about what would happen next..
The idea was great, the whole hacking thing. The mapping of a real city, the running around in it. But this game is just not rewarding enough to even think of doing side quests.

I bought Watch_Dogs a couple years ago and at the time, I wasn't impressed. Then a week ago today I reinstalled it and decided to give it another go. I am happy to share with you that I have finished the game and give it a solid 7/10.
Pros: Cool hacking features; massive car crashes, nice variety of vehicles, Gang Hangouts are awesome! Better than average AI. Playing this on a GTX 1080 with all settings at Ultra is a real treat.
Cons: Meh story and the hero Aiden Pierce is as bland as oatmeal. Wardrobe could have been better. Chicago neighborhoods are not faithfully recreated and that is a bit of a bummer. Downtown is better but the outlying areas outside of Lake Shore Drive are confusing as hell to navigate - and I have lived here all my life!
Overall this is a game worth buying on sale if you enjoy other Ubisoft titles like Assassin's Creed, Tom Clancy's, etc.
My score is a solid 7/10 and will pick up Watch_Dogs 2 when it goes back on sale again.

Probably one of the most thematically difficult games to experience due to the graphic potrayal of real-world issues: conflict diamonds, arms races, disease-attrition (malaria), internally displaced persons/refugees, and ideologically-fueled factions fighting for control over scraps of impoverished landscape. Unlike it's sequel, FarCry 3, this game feels less cartoony and emotionally vapid because it keeps the player vulnerable, evenly equiped with enemies, and isolated in the vastness of the maps. This can be frustrating at times, but ultimately (I argue) makes for a more valuable experience. Your mortality is quickly equated with that of the world's other NPCs and inhabitants, and so the destruction, or implied destruction, of those lives is more profound.
While FarCry 3 represents a huge step forward in gaming technology and is a worthwhile experience in it's own right, it's emotional impact and themes fell flat for me because of how the game held your hand throughout and superpowered the player very quickly with outrageous rewards for menial tasks. I played FarCry 2 after finishing the third game, and felt a much deep connection to the aesthetics of this one. Although I think it's fair to say that the plot is almost non-existant, and certainly not a coherent narrative than a series of similaraly motif-ed scenes joined by some key characters and locals; the plot only really comes together toward the end of each "chapter" when the principle antagonists are reintroduced to the game after remaining shadowy figures, alluded to but not seen or felt.
Overall, a fastastic game with some flaws, but one that has given me more pause to consider the real world than anything else I have ever played.

DISCLAIMER: If certain things were polished I would recommend it. Read on to find out why I think this game is not worth the full price of admission.
Much as I am a fan of the series, and thus, have some love for this game and this predecessor - I cannot recommend it at this price.
Not only did they fail to polish out some of the major issues with the past game, but this one feels like a rushed, and poorly done, expansion pack for Xenoverse 1.
Some of the design decisions come off as completely lazy and unthought out. For example, in this version, you can turn Super Saiyan 3, which is an improvement from the first game. You can transform using a new slot, which is another improvement, but to keep things dynamic, you can be knocked out of your transformation mid-go. This would be fine if it was the same for enemy AI. When enemies transform, the entire field stops and anything that was previously going on ceases to exist. If you are about to KO an enemy, and say, Gotenks is his ally and decides to transform, your attack loses all power and it goes to a mini-cutscene of Gotenks transforming. When you come back, you're almost always open to damage, and your finisher never even connected. You still lose ki as if you shot it off, but no damage or effect is actually done. This also happens in Expert Missions, even when playing in multiplayer, and can also happen when a new enemy or ally arrives on the field - destorying the flow of game play and sometimes costing you the fight.
Balance issues with enemy AI leave some fighting experiences to be difficult and downright frustrating at times - which can be nice in some games when you want a fair challenge. But this games mechanics almost exclude it from being fair in the single player element. That is just one example of many small design flaws this game has. They are easy to look past in a few cases, but in most they come up during the heat of battle, and can sway things unfairly in the way for the enemy AI to start beating you down. Some of this comes down to how fast the AI can react to your button inputs, as well as how floaty the inputs can feel. Targeting is also an issue that is easy to see as soon as you get into your first difficult mission with multiple enemies.
As for the multiplayer - I haven't noticed many issues. If you really dedicate yourself and get good, you can likely compete in PVP and team multiplayer can be quite satisfying when things work right. There are some obviously lag and connection issues from time to time, but no worse than I've seen anywhere else. It's actually somewhat bearable.
Overall, I don't recommend this game at it's full price. The lack of polish and it's mechanical flaws hold it back from being the truly enjoyable experience it could have been. If this was the first of the series, I may give it a pass. But considering how little of an improvement it is to it's predecessor, I cannot. The gimmick of having a custom character is not worth the price of admission.
Get it if you're a die-hard DB fan - you will probably find some things you enjoy, despite it's major drawbacks (many of which I forgot to list such as : lack of depth in Frieza and Buu transformations, although the source material is already there, lack of real diversity in attacks, lack of character choice, etc). But I would still only recommend it if it's on sale. Maybe XV 3 will actually be the finished product XV 1 and 2 were supposed to be. This feels like a late beta phase of the the past game, and fails to justify itself as being its own release.
Update: having gone through more of the Expert Mission content, as well as experimented with other races...I more than stand by my non-recommendation. Not enough interesting transformations or ideas for any race to feel really better than the other (besides Saiyan - which was a drawback in Xenvoerse 1), and they only manage to grab a bit of gameplay change and visual nuance, with examples such as the Nimbus or Giant Namekian transformation as my proof of point.
As for the Expert Missions...you're screwed if you do it offline, and the servers are still so laggy that it is almost impossible to do some of them online. If offline, your AI teamates will only 1/10 times perform the ki super required to damage the opponent, leading you to be the main attacker, as well as try to keep your team alive, yourself alive, and stay within the 15 min time limit across 5 increasingly difficult fights, with each enemies health-bar getting substantially larger each time, and their techniques start to become more spammy and difficult to deal with.
The progression of the expert missions are also a bit stupid, with Expert Mission Extreme Malice being the third last, but extremely difficult by comparison to all the others.
All in all, it may seem like small nitpicks to update with, but with every other issue this game has, it is clear it lacks polish and is not worth the $100 price-tag.

As someone who grew up playing command and conquer, this is the best RTS ever created.
The sheer scale of supreme commander is part of its appeal - the smallest unit is as tall as a tree, your commander towers many times taller than that and the 'experimental' endgame units are many times larger than even that. The excellent physics simulation and solid unit animations make the light units feel agile, while hulking mechanical monstrosities shake the earth with each ponderous step. Maps start at five kilometres square, and end at 81x81km strategic nightmares where it feels like troop movements take forever. All areas of combat are accounted for - land, sea, air and intelligence (even space, sort of) are each a powerful tool, and a game's outcome can be decided by any one of them. Weapons range from those wielded by rank and file units to fight one another, to strategic nuclear missiles and enormous artillery pieces able to fire clean across most maps. Each and every projectile is simulated - a launching nuclear missile can impact on enemy aircraft flying overhead. Units can physically block incoming fire from vulnerable targets. A high-flying bomber can accidentally bomb an interceptor flying beneath it.
Making all this manageable is an excellently implemented strategic zoom and robust waypointing system that allows orders to be queued long in advance to make best use of your limited attention. And your attention will be limited - there is so much to keep an eye on in supreme commander that you'll always have something to be doing. Upgrading your economy, managing units, keeping ahead of the tech curve and making sure your ACU, the commander at the core of your forces is safe. The commander is an exceedingly powerful engineering unit, but is also the most powerful combat unit on the field in the early stages of the game, and as a result using him aggressively can be the best way to gain the upper hand. This creates a somewhat unique mechanic in which your lose condition must fight on the front lines in order for you to survive, creating great tension.
The Forged Alliance Forever community project has taken FA and kept it alive, offering matchmaking services as well as regular balance and bugfix patches to keep this incredible game going. By far the best RTS I have ever played, and likely ever will play thanks to its unique scale, vast amount of options and effective interface.

This review is for Hearthstone players, listing all the differences first, and my personal review is at the bottom. I've been playing this game since open beta.
So what are the differences in Legends compared to Hearthstone?
- There are far less RNG cards and elements in the game. Sure there are some, it's healthy, but those cards are almost never game winning effects and even some RNG cards CAN BE MANIPULATED (Ally cards, their summon effects only trigger if the top card's color matches with the Ally card's color, and you can affect that by putting more cards of that specific color)
- There are no real "classes", but 5 colors and you can use up to 2 colors and combine them to make a class. For example, Purple (Endurance) and Green (Agility) makes Scout, which is more or less on par with Druid in Hearthstone. All of these colors have exactly what they can and cannot do. For example, Endurance (Purple) has no hard removal whatsoever, only transform and silence effects, but it is counter balanced by the fact that the color's creatures are highly statted for their magicak cost and has one of the beefiest late game minions. Intelligence (Blue) doesn't have any silence effects nor able to transform things, but has damage based removal and burst damage, with tons of action synergy, but it's creatures aren't well known for being able to stay alive and/or cost a lot for their stats because of the powerful effects attached onto them (looking at you, Speaker Terenus).
- There are 2 lanes to play your creatures on, which adds A LOT of strategic decisions. Thanks to this, there are almost no "best plays", because there is always that "what if I played this to the other lane". It's sorta like chess and mind games. Love it.
- Prophecy system. Your 30 health is decorated by 5 runes at 25, 20, 15, 10 and 5 health. If your health gets lowered to these intervals, you draw a card. If that card has the Prophecy keyword on it, you can play the card FOR FREE during your opponent's turn! This is a way to make even aggro players question whether they should go face or not, because there is the chance that they'll get massively punished if they overextend too much. Some people hate this system, some people love it. I definitely enjoy it. Most people who hate it probably just either overextend too much or break runes in a position where they can die to Prophecy cards (such as Lightning Bolt)
- Generous rewards. In Hearthstone, you can win 3 games and get 10 gold, while in Legends, you win 3 games and get 15-50 gold and a random card which can be any rarity! This is kinda counterbalanced by the fact that there are two type of legendaries (unique and non-unique, you can put 3 copies of the latter) and there are equal amount of epics and rares, but overall it sprinkles rewards at you. Especially if you complete the story mode, which will be our next point...
- Solo content. Actually better than Hearthstone's. It has cool story, very interesting and new mechanics in each boss and added flexibility on what bosses do and how the encounter is set up thanks to having more mechanics. Both the campaign which serves as a tutorial, the latest PvE Story (The Fall of the Dark Brotherhood) and Solo Arena can bring you a lot of enjoyment.
- A few more type of cards. Instead of having only actions (spells), you have actions, items and supports too. Items are buff cards with mostly a keyword attached to them or an effect. An easy comparison would be:
Support are ongoing effects or usable effects with mostly limited charges. They are placed next to your portrait and they can only be destroyed by support removing effects, or, if it has charges, when you use it up all.
-Deck size has to be atleast 50 cards. This comes with the fact that you can put 3 copies of any card, except unique-legendary cards. It can have more cards but it is not recommended because the deck loses consistency.

I think it's a fun game, definitely worths the try. Every class and color is viable (except Neutral only decks, they are for memes). A lot of diversity and constant updates are released. Card changes are a lot quicker than in Hearthstone. And not just nerfs, buffs too. I used an OP card deck to test this before Legends came to steam. If you are F2P the games will play as normal before you achieve something, such as leveling up or completing your daily task/s. Then the games you play before you achieve something, you will lose and it will give you a losing streak of about 5-10 games. You can even test this for yourself by creating an OP card deck and playing until you are about to level up or achieve something. With my OP card deck 100% of games when I wasn't going to achieve something I won and 100% of games before I was just about to achieve something I lost.
When you play a game, before you achieve something the game makes it so you play the game normally, then before you're about to win, it tips the sides and you will not receive any important cards anymore (like guard cards and magic ability cards). Your enemy will receive all the important cards instead. I once had 30 health and my opponent had 1 (this was when I was using my OP card deck) and the game decided to tip the sides and make my opponent win. I could even see the game doing it when it didn't allow me to have any guard cards or anything important yet my opponent received all the important cards to win the game.
I've updated it a little here and there since I did the test and also the game has been updating but it should still be OP and do the job if you want to test it for yourself.
Overall, the game is rigged for F2P players and if you are not planning to spend any money on the game I wouldn't bother with it. Bethesda have put this machanic into the game to keep you playing the game and to tire you out so you eventually spend money on it. It's an old money making tactic for F2P games.

Note: I had about 100 some odd hours on this game on the Bethesda launcher and hit Legend with Arrow Tempo back when the game first hit Closed Beta.
+: More friendly to the F2P player than Hearthstone, with generally better reward systems.
+: Is pretty similar to Hearthstone in many respects (similar Mana mechanic, similar types of Keywords, etc) while still having some significant meta differences due to differences in card design.
+: Solid music.
+: The single story in the game is pretty alright (especially if you like Elder Scrolls lore) and the first Adventure (Fall of the Dark Brotherhood) is also pretty solid.
+: The UI is pretty comptently made and works great on PC.
+: The Prophecy mechanic is unique and while when you're new it'll seem to be RNG you quickly learn how to play around it and mitigate risk. (it's still less RNG than Hearthstone)
+: Minimal cards with RNG on them.
+: Adds a new card every month which you can earn free copies of through ranked on top of Expansions coming + Adventures.
-: The sound effects get repetitive especially since in classic Elder Scrolls fashion there seems to be like 4 actual VAs used for all the cards.
-: The "feel"/"crunch" of the game isn't as good as Hearthstone. Some spells do have pretty good crunch, but there's a lot of underwhelming sound / visual effects compared to Hearthstone. Trading minions doesn't feel anywhere near as good, which bites because this is still a minion trading based game.
Overall, it's a pretty good game and if you like Hearthstone but don't like mass RNG and/or enjoy Elder Scrolls you should enjoy this quite a bit.

ADDED (answers to fan-boys):
Lets start with EA, EA is when you pay a bit less money and get the game that is not finished yet, be that because you want to support developers or just because you think the game will be great and want to save money. What you expect from the EA games is: bugs, glitches, crushes, substantial participation of developers in public discussion about the game (it could be them asking which features members of community would like to see in game or just to reassure everybody that they have a clear plan for the game development), frequent updates that significantly change the game, and improvement over time. Not all EA titles go along the same path, but those are the most usual things to expect. And out of those GRAV has just the first 3. Developers resurface once every couple weeks, they ignore all critique, tech support issues or tough questions, thank fan-boys, and vanish into the void. Updates come once or twice a year. And if you tell me that there are frequent updates - those things really don’t qualify, they are patches or minor fixes, which is kind of ridiculous because Bitmonster just wastes their time on polishing the game that is unfinished. And improvement over time, well, it has actually been just going downhill. Just look at the number of active players and history of sales, almost every person who has ever played this game got disappointed. And developers know that, so they put their game on sale every time they can just to squeeze more money without doing much work and eventually they will completely abandon the game. Lets face it, GRAV will never leave EA or it will do so just formally.
And now sandbox, the favorite word of fan-boys to throw at you when they are trying to protect GRAV. First of all, GRAV is not a sandbox. GRAV is an open-world third person shooter with some elements of MMO and survival (hunger, hazardous environment, crafting, and very limited building system). Unlike many other survival games like Minecraft or Empyrion GRAV does not even have a sandbox mode. So this argument is just plainly pointless from the very beginning, but I'm in a good mood today, so lets just assume that all survival games are a bit sandboxy (which I know for a fact is not true). Now lets compare GRAV to the game that made the survival genre the way it is now, Minecraft. Minecraft was also an open-end game with no clearly set goals, but was there something to do apart from grinding mobs and resources? Yes, there were dungeons, villages, temples etc. to explore. Now what about GRAV? Nope, just the grind, craft and building, nothing else. Did Minecraft have an end-game despite being open-ended game? Hell yes. Minecraft had ultimate dungeons to explore to find ender pearls, build the End portal, and kill the ender dragon. GRAV? No dungeons, no bosses, all the same mobs everywhere. And it's not even a sandbox.
PS: Oh, and neither GRAV is an RPG, seriously, just get real or I will start calling it a strategy.
PPS: It is about as much RPG as Fallout 4, which is 0%.

I've often read about this game as an "update" or a "remake."
It's not - this game is a remix - mechanically similar to but thematically different from the original work.
The original Pac-Man was - and still is - a pretty fatalistic game.
You'll run from the ghosts forever, trapped in the maze - your only hopes of escape are either a horrible death or crashing the game and ending the universe.
But you probably won't make it that far - after all, the ghosts are just plain faster than you are.
The only times you can feel remotely safe are in the 3 situations where you move faster than they do:
1) when you eat a power pill
2) in the tunnels which warp you across the maze
3) turning corners
Pac-Man CEDX+ ditches that nihilism, takes those three (fleeting) moments of empowerment, and runs with them.
You are always faster than the ghosts, paths to warp across the map are (usually) plentiful, and best of all time slows down when the ghosts are almost on top of you, giving you a chance to reverse course, duck around a corner, or even use a limited supply of bombs to send the possibly dozens of ghosts chasing you back to their base in the center of the screen.
Yes, dozens of ghosts. You didn't think they'd let you move so fast and not give the ghosts anything either did you? Mazes are littered with sleeping ghosts which will follow your exact path after you move past them. The original ghosts you know and "love" will still be after you, following (more or less) their classic attack patterns (I feel like Pinky isn't quite as prescient as he used to be).
So now when you eat a power pellet, you can be looking at a lot more than that coveted 3000 points for a 4-ghost combo - how does up to 3600 each sound? In a chain of 10-20 (or more)?
For a 30+ year pac-veteran like myself, it sounds like catharsis.
I only have 2 complaints about the game - overpriced DLC that brings nothing new to the table, and the fact that the player must manually select to end their game from the main menu, rather than being able to just escape or cancel button out from the title screen. FaceBook users may find the passive-agressive auto-posted dialogue directly translated from the Japanese to be tedious (some other reviews harp on this a lot), but I don't have an account, so I can't really say.
The game itself comes heavily recommended - but the DLC bundles and alternate Namco game reskins are completely non-essential.
But hey, it's Steam - there will always be a sale!
If you like puzzle/arcade experiences that reward high risk behavior, or if you've been playing Pac-Man since the punk rockers at the local arcade had to find you a chair to stand on so that you could reach the joystick, then I think you'll have a lot of fun with this one.

So much has changed recently for Vindictus. I've been playing this game on and off for several years, and it feels like they are making it much more tolerable for people who like to play casually.
Vindictus always had great potential in its gameplay and singleplayer story. With raid bosses and story bosses, this game really brings the thrill of slashing down giants. The music is incredible and noticeably improves every season. Character customization is still very expensive, but it holds up being very diverse with many themes across fantasy. You can spend hours adjusting your appearance in the stores. Gathering and hunting for materials also gives this game its RPG/warcraft experience. You don't need to grind dungeons until possibly later levels. They've worked to reduce this grind too.
The huge update to streamlining the main story feels wonderful for solo play. The new Path (Paladin/Dark Knight) transformation skills and rework feels much more enjoyable compared to getting one transformation every real-time hour. Plus, all of these gears that I've saved millions for in the past are now worthless and easier to afford. I don't mind it if this is for the sake of improving accessibility to strong gear for all players. However, I will still cry a little inside from time to time.
Vindictus is showing that it is working to improve the game for more people, and that is the best feeling this event is bringing. Something I am currently trying to look into is whether people will still fill up raids as enthusiastically in the past. While solo play and working on multiple characters is much more enjoyable now, I really did like hopping into 24-man raids against those 3 dragons, polar bear, and giant spiders.
Overall, these changes were finally enough to turn my recommendation from a No to a Yes. Give this game a go. This review will be updated after playing the revolution update to a point of grinding and accessing endgame gear.

I really want to like this game, I'll continue to play but only because EA still can't compete. Almost everything wrong with last years game still exists. Phone conversations are buggy, dialogue choices in both GM and My Career are even less clear than before, and sometimes will select the opposite bianary choice. Seriously, you never have more than two choices and about a quarter of the time doesn't choose the one that you had highlighted. My Career in general seems programmed specifically to humiliate the player. As usual, you start off with the skill level of an 8th grade track star who only plays basketball to stay in shape and shares Iverson's feeling on practice. Improving is even more of a grind than before.
All balancing was done with multiplayer in mind. Too easy to get good shots in multiplayer? Solution can't make good shots, game wide. Too easy to make the kick out passes? Solution players fumble perfect passes and step out of bounds like dizzy children. Ally-oop play too powerful? Don't even think about attempting it without a badge. A badge, I might add that requires you do the thing you can't do to obtain it. You'll be a pretty bad free throw shooter early on. How do you get better? By playing a drill that only rewards you for making free throws... what a paradox. Finally slog through that to improve a little? Do it again, but you'll need two times as many points.
Worse still the game is built around tempting the purchase of VC. Anything and everything costs VC, lots of VC. It takes several thousand VC to get enough points in any particular shot before it stops punishing you for taking said shot. You have to invest several games worth of VC into a single skill to make it vaible, and then the game will still regularly deny you even that.
There is nothing more infuritating than having announcers speak incredulously about a bad miss, as if the games own programming isn't what caused that in the first place. It's such a slap in the face to have the game itself taunt you about things that are entirely it's fault. How wonderful it is to invest thousands of VC into a layup skill only to slam the ball into the rim as if you had no idea it's a physical object.
At this point you may think I'm maybe just bad at the game. No, I'm statistically doing great. Have several career triple doubles through about 25 games. Shooting around 50% despite the fact I have no 3 point shot, and barely ever take anything from midrange. Nope I only shoot when close to the rim, and only when open and still I shoot 50% overall. There is no feedback to explain this. Just need to grind for badges they apparently forgot to monetize. Seriously, they paced the badges as if you could kick a few real dollars their way to unlock them quicker only to forget to add that feature.
My Career is a step back. Gameplay still has far too many canned animations and far to often does whatever it pleases. Pressing the steal button is a total gamble for instance. You might take a swipe at the ball. More often you just take a swipe. Honestly you look like you're attempting to land a hook. But every now and again you just fly off in a random direction. I've gotten far more steals by accidentaly being in the way than actually poking the ball lose. Players don't step out of bounds on the baseline as often as they did, but they will just dart off to get a backcourt violation at double speed. A theme that continues all throughout. Fix one thing, break another. It's like the game is barely holding everything together and at least 4 or 5 times a game it just falls apart.
Again, I'd love for this game to be great. It just isn't.

As with alot of people I thought this was just a RS lore based Hearthstone clone, but after getting burnt out of the aformentioned game I decided to give it a go after I saw Chronicle was now on Steam. You soon realize the only things in common with Hearthstone is that you use cards and your collection/disenchanting works in the same manner.
The gameplay really is a breath of fresh air and quite innovative. You play as one of five legends with a deck of 30 - 35 monster (enemy) and magic (support) cards against an opponent using mainly gold (which could be alikened to mana) as a resource. You play 5 chapers where you're allowed to lay down 4 of your cards in each chapter against your opponent in a sequence on a 3D game board, at the end of the last chapter you fight your opponent in a final battle. The most refreshing aspect of all of this in my personal opinion though;
Each monster you fight gives you a reward or has some effect to influence the game, be it more attack damage, more armor, damage your oppenent etc. Generally the stronger the monster, the better the reward. There are deck archtypes that don't focus on monster killing though, some use the gold as a resource and rely on magic cards, others specialise in creating a good weapon for the final fight. Almost all the Legends play completely different from the other.
So with all this in mind, you find yourself playing an almost 'PVE game' trying to build your legend up in those first few chapters fighting your own cards for rewards with the intent to then move into a 'PVP game' in the later chapers (or straight from chapter 1, I'm looking at you aggro decks). All of this makes for very interesting, sometimes complex, but definity fun games.
You gain packs pretty quickly and the basic decks posted online are still competitive with decks that cost more to build.
Definitly recommend this game.

Reading through some of the reviews for this game, I must correct a few errors most of them seem to have (not sure if they were paid to praise this game so much, or if they honestly just don't understand). All this is based on my first ~40 hours of play time, unlike the reviews who praise the game all the way into high heavens after playing it for 2 hours.
Anyone who says that this game isn't 'Pay To Win' doesn't know or understand what that means, because your winrate will keep rising the more you pay and collecting (good) cards is extremely slow if you don't shove a considerable amount of money into it. This will probably be less of a problem if you grind it 6 months straight, but at start this is a serious problem.
Also there is very little strategy or tactics involved, the outcome of the game is based primarily on which player has paid more for their deck and secondarily by RNG. If both players have decks (and common sense*) of similar level, the outcome of the game is based on which player gets better hands for the particular deck they're playing against and if they get lucky aiming the "counters" against them.
*If you're familiar with deck building from MtG, HS or such, piling up all the few good cards you own for your deck (which ain't that hard since you won't have much) and picking the least bad fillers after that, you will notice that almost all strategy ends there. After that all that remains is the timing when to play your cards and in which order, and that really ain't as hard as some people seem to think.
After all that being said, I still think that the game is good. Or at least it would be if one would be able to grind cards faster (you stop getting the in-game currency after 10 or so wins). The gameplay is fun and games only last 5-10 minutes, which allows you to play as many games as you currently have time on your hands.
But I just can't recommend this because your winrate is dominated by the 2 devils called P2W and RNG.
EDIT 1 (~80 hours): Also worth mentioning, that 90% of the games where both decks are on a similar level are won by the player who gets to start (because that player gets to start the whole game). And if you're playing a deck that can't win by chapter 3, it's not worth playing. Since there's 5 chapters + the end fight to play, why are the decks who win in 2 or 3 chapters completely dominant?
You should check this out, it's surprisingly interesting.

As someone who (personally) couldn't get into Hearthstone, I'm actualy VERY pleased to say that I enjoy this game! Everyone has the ability to get the same cards as higher-ranked players, and even the best decks can be beaten with some very well-laid-out thought and strategy. While most card games have you facing off against your opponents' decks, you'll be facing not just your opponent, but also yourself. Every card you play can either cost you the game later on down the road, or save your skin and carry you to victory. It's a satisfying experience, and one I'm thouroughly happy with.
Pros:
-Active player-base with many knowledgable players willing to help you improve your deck and playstyle
-Fun and exciting gameplay that requires both careful thought, planning, and luck
-Five Legends (currently), each with their own unique decks and playstyles
-Includes Solo (VS AI), Casual, ranked, and Dungeoneering gamemodes
Cons:
-Earning money can be a bit of a grind for some builds
-Some builds are notoriously difficult to counter (and perhaps a tad overpowered in some aspects)
Nit-picks:
-Certain Dailies are set to be completed through PvP, Solo, or both. There is no distinguishing between the two (It's probably best to assume most, if not all, are obtainable through PvP only)
-Earning copper is a bit of a grind, especially if you run into a lot of difficult-to-counter builds
-The risk-reward for some cards are odd sometimes. That's just me, though.
-Just like most CCG's (M:TG, Hearthstone, *insert CCG name here*), there are obviously decks that will, more often than not, completely trample players of all skill levels and playstyles, to a point where it gets (admittedly) dumb and dull as hell. My advice: Learn 'em, and counter them anyway you can.
Outside of that? I love it! I'm happy to add this game to my list of favorite games. And, coming from somebody who usually loathes PvP with a passion, I believe that says something.
9/10. Great game.

The plot is pretty simple, you're a ninja sent to kill the evil mastermind Meio who has dominated the world and for that you have to infiltrate into his city fortress, making your own path by destroying his minions and getting stronger in the process.


By pressing the map button you also can access the menu:
The map can be zoomed in and out and it highlights power ups if you happen to get nearby enough. It also allows you to check maps of the areas you already explored.

Then you have an equipment tab which only purpose is to tell you the skills and power ups you unlocked so far.
And finally a suit tab, as you explore you will find different ninja suits which can used as soon as you get them. These suits have a small lore and are purely cosmetic (they're just palette swaps).

It's quite fluid. The controls are very responsive and easy to use. Hiryu moves really fast and can jump into walls and ceilings, moving between them is relatively easy and this allows to explore the map to find hidden bonuses and power ups.

Hiryu can run/jump/climb and attack with his sword at the same time giving him a lot of fluidity while attacking. You can also change the angles of your slashes. Depending on the situation, charge your attack and deal a high damage slash or deal quick slashes at the speed of your button mashing skills.

Each area is interesting in its own way, the first areas are quite basic, letting you learn the ropes and the limits of your starting abilities and each area increases the platforming difficulty taking into account the mobility skills you have acquired, forcing you to use them to its maximum potential. ex:
As you go further into the game, you unlock different types of "swords" and skills which, in a really metroid-esque style, allow you to gain access to previously inaccessible parts of the map or warp between areas. The map is indeed big so these fast travel devices really help at moving around the areas (which you will do a lot if you want to find all the hidden power up and extras which are almost always behind a door that can be unlocked with one of your newly acquired skill).

The enemy variety is quite lacking tho, it relies on upgraded version of the same enemies to up the difficulty as you keep advancing.
You have infinite lives, there are a few checkpoints in each area, if you die. You get a fision mailed screen and then spawn in one of them so you can try again.
The enemy variety is like this: mech-soldier, turret, big dudes and stationary cannons.
Outside of bosses, the game is relatively easy even on hard difficulty. The charged attack has a wide range, deals high damage which allows you to take care of many enemies in a row and just needs approx. 2sec. to charge. Your normal attacks interrupts most enemies so as long as you keep hitting them they wont retaliate. As you get more power ups and new skills, you keep getting stronger to the point where most enemies won't really pose a threat to you.
Platforming is also quite forgiving. Stepping on the acid/lava deals low damage as long as you jump out of it asap (which is pretty easy since the pools are shallow, they reach Hiryu's thighs at most) and anything that should one-shot you just does some chip damage and then returns you to the closest safe place you landed before so you can try again. So save for some exceptions, it's almost impossible to die from failed platforming,
The bosses difficulty is harder compared to the normal enemies. They follow attack patterns as you lower their hp and enter "phases". this can be learned mid-fight, so as long as you learn it, the easiest ones should be doable on the first try.
You're most feared enemies will be the popup messages by npcs which take space near the bottom of the screen, hiding enemies, traps and projectiles which you could have seen otherwise.
There really isn't any memorable soundtrack here, nor there are area specific music, so you will end up hearing around 5 different musics as you play.
There are a few extras that are unlocked by discovering them in hidden parts of the world areas.
Strider is a decent game, It takes around 10hrs to clear the game if you backtrack to get all the power ups and most extras(I got around 78% of the extras when I cleared the game) I did backtrack on my own to get them earlier as soon as I unlocked a new skill, thinking I would never go back if I hadn't... The game had me go back anyways. So knowing this, one a new run it would take me 1 hour less or so to clear the game.
The controls are nice and each new skills adds a lot to your mobility and damage but they don't really offer enough to provide the possibility of multiple playstyles until very late game. the platforming is quite challenging but also very forgiving in deadly areas via re-spawn. The difficulty is intermediate even in its highest difficulty with not much enemy variety.
I would recommend it as long as you buy it on a 50%+sale.
