I've only got 2 hours logged on Steam, but thousands of matches played before the Steam release (
).  I have played several card games in recent years, and this is easily my favorite.
To get the inevitable Hearthstone comparison out of the way, I'll go over which core mechanics are the same/similar.  You gain 1 maximum magicka (mana) each turn, up to turn 12.  Creature combat involves you choosing which creature will attack and what its target will be, using the HS system instead of "blockers" et cetera like magic/eternal.  You draw one card at the start of each turn.  Each player has 30hp.  Arena drafting works similarly to Hearthstone, offering 3 cards at a time until you have a full deck.  Now for what sets this game apart!
One of my favorite mechanics unique to TESL is the rune/prophecy system.  At each 5hp interval on your health bar (5, 10, 15...) is a rune.  When your health first reaches these thresholds, you will draw a card.  This is great for mitigating the effects of a bad early hand, since you'll gain cards if your opponent decides to immediately apply pressure.  Additionally, some cards have the keyword "prophecy", which means that if you draw them from a rune loss you can play them immediately, for 0 magicka - even on your opponent's turn!  You have to really weigh the cost of attacking your opponent, and ask yourself if you are prepared to deal with the prophecies they might have.
Another huge defining mechanic of the game is the lane system.  The playing field is divided into two lanes - the field lane on the left, and the shadow lane on the right.  Creatures in one lane cannot attack creatures in the other.  Creatures summoned in the shadow lane cannot be attacked for one turn.  The result is that trading initiative is given to the first player to get a creature in the field lane, as expected, but in the shadow lane the *second* player gets initiative.  The first player's creature can't be attacked for one turn, but that's irrelevant with nothing else in the lane.  The second player can then safely play something that gets a favorable trade.  The seemingly simple decision of which lane to play into becomes incredibly complex, and provides great depth as well as a great comeback mechanic at times.
Deckbuilding!  Arena decks are 30 cards to save you time on the draft, but constructed decks are 50-70 cards.  Cards can be one of 5 colors, neutral, or dual-color.  Your deck can contain up to two different colors.  So competitive decks will be a combination of two colors and probably a few neutral cards.  Dual-color cards count as both colors at once, not either/or, so if you have a blue/green card you can only put blue or green cards in a deck with it.  You can have up to 3 copies of a card in your deck, or 1 copy of unique cards.  Giving each class 2 colors allows them each to have a unique flavor, while still keeping a huge amount of variety in deckbuilding possibilities.
The free-to-play experience in this game is pretty good.  I hesitate to go beyond "pretty good" just because we all know the free player experience is never ideal.  Still, rewards were more generous than expected.  Rerollable daily quests give 40-70 gold, usually at least 50.  Every 3 constructed wins nets you 15-50 gold and a card (any core card, even legendaries) or a card pack.  Note legendaries/packs from this are VERY unlikely of course, but epics happen semi-regularly.  Packs are 100g, arenas 150g.  Always play arena!  Even if you lose every match, you're guaranteed a pack + some goodies.  Wins improve your rewards, up to 7 wins where you get your gold back + huge rewards like 4 packs.  Packs contain 6 cards.  You can build a competitive deck pretty quickly.  Hitting legend (highest ladder rank) in your first month is pretty hard, but a good player can definitely do it in their second month.  You can't derank from losses, only from season resets, and those don't push you down too far.
There's also a lot of PvE content.  You'll play 20 chapters of story missions to learn the game and build your collection at the start.  The most recent expansion includes 25 more unique missions.  There is solo arena, where you play against AI with unique lane rules.  There are AI practice matches that give you soul gems (card crafting material).
All of this doesn't matter without good card design, but thankfully Direwolf has made loads of interesting cards and actively works to make sure they are well-balanced.  Give the game a try!

The Elder Scrolls: Legends is a great alternative to Hearthstone, which is inevitably what people will be comparing it to. This game deserves to be judged on it's own merits, in which it excels in many aspects over many digital card games, but I'll personally be comparing it to Hearthstone because that's a base game many people here will be familiar with.
Over Hearthstone, this game has many upsides. The gameplay itself is much more deep than Hearthstone. Rather than there being heroes representing classes, there is instead colors, and they are as follows: Blue (Intelligence), Green (Agility), Yellow (Willpower), Red (Strength), and Purple (Endurance). You can combine up to two different colors to make 50 card decks with three copies of most cards allowed. The colors synergize with themselves, so you have to consider how much of one color you're putting in a deck over another, usually making one color the primary color and the other the supporting secondary one. Overall, this makes for a more enriched and in-depth deck building experience.
The board is very similar to Hearthstone, but it has some differences that add a little more depth to the gameplay. There is a lane system consisting of two different lanes, one regular lane and one lane which gives every card "stealth" played in it, which prevents minions in one lane from interacting from one lane to the other. The stealth on every minion might sound OP at first, but there's plenty of removal to deal with scary minions that could be placed over there, and they can be targetted by spells when stealthed unlike in Hearthstone.
There is a "draw as you take damage" system in this game that helps alleviate some of the problems with draw luck, and there's even a keyword called "Prophecy", which allows you to play a card if it's drawn via these means, allowing you to actively counter your opponents moves. It also incentivizes you to be cautious with how much you attack your opponent, making decision making more complex. Also, unlike in Hearthstone you can run three copies of most legendaries, except for unique legendaries, which are a subclass of legendary cards which you can only run one of. You can tell these apart by the red jewel at the top of unique legendary cards
It also has an infinitely better free to play system. You get rewarded with not just gold, but also a card for winning three games, and leveling rewards you with actual cards rather than just golden versions of cards, including epics and legendaries. Crafting prices are identical to Hearthstone, except for legendaries, which rather than costing 1600 of the card crafting currency it instead costs 1200, which helps make getting legendaries cheaper.
The game's ladder system is similar to Hearthstone's rank system, but there are some notable differences as well. Unlike in Hearthstone, where if you win more times you gain bonus stars until rank five, Elder Scrolls has a thing called bonus rounds, which I will cover more in the downsides, as I prefer Hearthstone's bonus ranked system more. There are only twelve different ranks, but rather than you having to win a couple of times to rank up like in Hearthstone, you instead have to win several times, ranging from rank to rank. If you are about do derank from losing enough times, you will fall into a special rank where you have to fight your way out of it to continue progressing. You cannot fall out of this rank, though, so deranking isn't possible.
The game also offers an arena "draft a random deck" style game mode that costs the same as it does in Hearthstone. This game also offers a single player version of it, which rewards you less since it's easier, but is still worth the cost and makes for a more new player friendly experience. It does get harder the more times you emerge victorious, and become much less new player friendly, so keep that in mind.
I do prefer this game over Hearthstone, but there are things that Hearthstone does better that can't be ignored. This game's presentation is good, but it's not as good as Hearthstone's on an objective level. Golden/animated cards aren't very collectable, as the difference is hardly notable, so I often find myself dusting them. There is alternative card art you can collect however, which is enjoyable and many of them improve over the originals. Also, the collection manager leaves a bit to be desired over Hearthstone's.
There are some gameplay elements I prefer in Hearthstone, such as the way Hearthstone rewards you for playing well with bonus stars, while Elder Scrolls: Legend's bonus system is random. Occasionally you'll come across something called a bonus round, where if you win rather than progressing once through the rank you're in you'll progress twice. It's completely random, though, so rather than rewarding your ability to win it just happens completely out of your control.
As previously mentioned, you are able to run three copies of most cards, including legendaries, and while the game lowers the prices of legendaries, they are still quite expensive. Getting to a point where you feel like your collection is robust can feel like a daunting task. I've found myself focusing one color specifically to offset this and make sure I can compete at high levels of this game, which is fine, but can also get repetitive only playing a few decks. Go about this any way you please; buy packs (the prices are fair and there's special offers for new players), grind arenas, focus only one color, etc., but I'm sure you'll notice this as a new player.
Also, while I love the ES:L community, it's quite small when compared to Hearthstone. If you're like me, you love watching Twitch streams possibly even more than playing the game. There are some great ES:L streamers out there, but compared to Hearthstone it's slim pickings. Since this game is new to Steam and communities often see growth when exposed on Steam, I believe this will become less of an issue over time, but it's still worth bringing up.
The Elder Scrolls: Legends is a great game with many mechanics to offer over Hearthstone, a game people will inevitably compare this to. It has a better f2p system, better and deeper game mechanics, and a better arena system with a single player option. There are downsides, such as the presentation, collection completion, and a small (but growing) community, but this doesn't take too much away from the game. It's definitely worth checking out, and I'm sure you'll find yourself enjoying it as much as if not more than you enjoy Hearthstone.

Trying to configure the game to personal preferences can be a real downer; the game is capped at 30 FPS so it's required to go to the .ini file and change the "30" limit to "60".
A window mode option isn't present in the options menu anywhere so I pretty much had to set the launch options to start in window mode.
The keys and buttons aren't rebindable and there isn't a way to change the look sensitivity for either controller or mouse.
The main story doesn't take very long to finish though there are some side missions (which are mostly basically just extra challenges) that sort of accomadate for that.
Art style's pretty cool though often times it can be very inconsistent with the lighting the current setting is trying to represent.
Most of the English dialogue, voice acting, and perhaps the humor even in this game feel off and I'm sure at least sounds better and/or makes more sense in Japanese. I set it to English because it's synchronized to the mouth movements during the cutscenes and I liked hearing
voice. There's not much of a story going on here especially with it being short and even shorter if the cutscenes are skipped. Despite how
the entire game is I didn't find the story very engaging so a lot of the crap shown and said didn't make sense for me until I watched all the cutscenes a second time during my last playthrough.
Checkpoints seem to be oddly placed if not just have a minimal amount. There are checkpoints where they're too far apart and there are ones that are placed before a cutscene or two. This means that if you choose to restart from a checkpoint at some point you may have to skip the perviously shown cutscene just to get back in. Also they're often placed before unskippable cutscenes. I think it's fine if checkpoints are kept to a low number but I think the least that could have been done with them is appropriately place them so as to not discourage retries and replayability.
The levels aren't anything special as they're mostly linear when it comes to getting from point A to B. Even the barely open levels aren't very big.
The camera has a habit of rotating to where you don't want it to be so enemies that were in sight around you will likely be off screen temporarily which can result in you taking damage before you could get the camera back to where you'd want it.
The fact that you sort of auto-target an enemy can be highly detremental;
Depending on the attack being thrown at you this can pose major problems. This could probably be just me using a controller but it did seem to be a persisting problem that I didn't find in other somewhat similar games like MGR: Revengeance.
There's another problem with the auto-targeting in this game; if you choose to aim with one of Mondo's ranged subweapons and you face an enemy then it will automatically target/lead the crosshair to the enemy Mondo is facing. This is highly detremental when facing against multiples that are on the same side because then there's a big chance the crosshair will automatically target a baddie you didn't want to aim at in the first place.
Some form of manually locking on to an enemy would have been nice and with the way the controls are set up with a controller they could have made the D-pad more useful as opposed to making that the "select handicap item" section which I've never used, and I think there are only two of them in the game so only the left and right d-pad are ever binded.
A big problem if either the enemy or you are strafing left and right because then it will constantly zoom in and zoom out greatly as your crosshair marks them which makes attempting accurate shots a lot more annoying & difficult than it is easier. It's a real problem because I can't seem to turn the upgrade off.
Combat can be pretty rewarding here; if you kill an enemy they tend to drop upgrade items that further boost the "Lv." of your health and "Blood" meter during the combat itself, basically like materialized EXP.
As far as I'm aware dodging has no invisibility frames and most enemies aren't difficult to dodge or block.
For some reason you can also do Just Guards (basically "perfect guard") during a dodge.
Boss fights aren't very unique and are all very simplistic when it comes to dealing with them; dodge, block or run from attacks when you see them, retaliate with either adrenaline burst or regular attacks afterwards, repeat.

is the latest title made by the iconic game creator SUDA51. In it you get to control the newest recruit of a reputable execution agency, Mondo Zappa, as he stalks and beheads a wide variety of criminals all across the world (sometimes even outside of it). As he settles into his new job, he also comes to terms with his own inner demons, balancing his talent for dispensing swift and brutal justice with his fleeting memories of a traumatic past, and peppering it all with his many sensual conquests.
Gameplay wise this is an extremely fun game. It is very simplistic and linear, yet you will have a good time slicing through large ammounts of enemies with your katana. Combat consists in lots of button smashing though, which after a while, gets repetitive, but you have a nice diversity of enemies too keep it "fresh". Combat which is in its majority through the game, insanely frenetic and challenging at times, being the boss fights the strongest attribute of it. You also have a nice selection of secondary weapons too once you unlock them through side-missions. Side-missions which are a nice way to offer some diversity to this game, since the main story missions are super linear, with a few collectables here and there, but excepting that, you will be walking around corridors most of the time. Some of these side missions are very fun, others are kinda lame after a while since they get extremely repetitive (gigolo missions), but they help giving the japanese vibe that this game possesses.
The game also as a good longetivity, I spent around 12 hours in order to complete it (side missions included).
I found the story to be very weak. It was insanely confusing and awkward with lots of bland dialog and boring cutscenes. The oscillating tone does not work well too, it varies from emotional scenes to lame humor very fast. It has some pretty cool characters though, which help this category of the game.
Graphically this game is marvellous to look at. Incredibly stylish cel-shadded graphics give life to this incredible world. Most of the levels are gorgeous and well designed. Some are kinda lame though. I remember that one of the chapters was so dark that I had many difficulties to navigate through it, even with the brightness maxed out. Also a minus the lack of graphical options in the menus, since there is only one option to choose that goes from low, medium, high, no other options whatsoever. Despite that, the menus are slick and easy to navigate, loading screens are fast, and the menus also have a nice array of music to complement them.
The music and sound effects in this game are great. I deeply enjoyed the soundtrack, and the sound effects all felt right too. Voice acting is kinda "meh", nothing special, the story and dialog surely dont help in this case.
Performance is great. I played on a considerably weak laptop and almost never dropped from the 30 fps cap on max settings. Unfortunately it is locked at the 30 fps mark but you can change that in the config files by following this guide -
. I also had to change the resolution in the config files since my native one was not available in-game, which is a big minus.

Fact of the matter is, people want to play games but they don't want to spend money on them, which is another reason why F2P games are so popular.
Now for the meat.
The game itself is entertaining, dialog is nice and funny if a little dodgy in the translations every once in a while. The season 1 story gets interesting at around level 30-40ish and i found myself losing even more hours to it as i went back to discover more and i haven't played much of the second season yet.
You level fairly quickly in the beginning and I only really noticed a big slow down at around 40-50. Which isn't bad considering you get most of your characters main skills at around 30, so you have a good idea of their capabilities and play style.
The combat itself is similar to a Dynasty Warriors game, which you use heavy movement and large attacks to damage enemies that come at you in small groups of up to i think 10 at once in some areas.
Missions consist of an instance for your party, which for normal missions is a max of 4 people. Later on, you find larger raid boss missions that can have anywhere from 6 people all the way to 20+ The big boss battles are fun and are easy once you know what their attacks are and how they will react to yours. I am also under the assumption that every mission in the game is solo-able if you are just that good, i however am not. I can play just about everything in season 1 by myself but need a decent party for the big raid bosses.
The community from what i've seen isn't as trolly and elietest as some might say, whether they used to be or not i have no idea but i've not come across very many distasteful people in the times i've played. I also play on the West server, due to my understanding of it being strictly the U.S server, while the East server is Europe's. I have at least 100 hours if not a bit more, as i don't play as often as i used to but i have two characters 60+ and others in their 40's-50's.
The anime-esc visuals are quite pretty and the game can get quite fan-servicey which is also a love or hate type of deal. I personally love being able to look good and even some of the full armor sets look very good on either gender.
Character creation is somewhat limited as you pick a pre-determined character but get to mess around with them a bit. Changing hair, height, size of various body aspects, tattoos and skin color, as well as their underwear which "can" consist of skimpy outfits but there are non skimpy options as well.
Lastly, i am not an MMO person. I don't typically like the styles they use and i don't really play the ones i like most of the time. But Vindictus is one of those games i enjoy and still come back to and it's loads better when you play and level with friends. I don't think it's the best game out there cause it's sure as hell not but it's free so it's something you don't have to devote time and money to if you don't want to. That being said, some of the money options are very helpful, and a couple of them are rather dumb but it doesn't hurt the experience much at all.
It's free, you don't need to spend any money to do what everyone else can do. Just play it for a while, get to around level 20 and then decide if it's worth your time or not.

In a nutshell: takes the classic Pac-Man formula (eat dots, avoid ghosts, score points), and puts it through a Hotline Miami filter.
In not so quite a nutshell, Pac-Man CE:DX+ is as much a puzzle game as it is a high-score competition with your Steam friends list. The most obvious change to the classic formula is that, normally, the ghosts are obstacles to be avoided, right? Wandering the stages according to a brief list of AI rules, only to be eaten when you chow down on a power pellet and briefly turn the tables? In this game, that's slightly altered: the ghosts wandering the maze will chase you (with a nice '!' sound effect) when you get too close, stacking as you pass more 'sleeping' ghosts that block the maze. Eventually this queue of ghosts either gets so long that you end up crashing into your stack and dying, or you come across a power pellet, turn around, and wipe them out. The longer the queue, the more points you receive: risk and reward.
Second change: how the game board ('maze', 'level', whatever) works. Classic Pac-Man had you eat all the dots on the stage to progress to the next level, with charming animated interludes. This time around your goal is still the same, but played against a timer: you can get strategic in order to maximise your score. Put simply: eat all the dots on one side (left or right) of the stage, and a fruit item will spawn on the
side. When you eat that fruit item, the
side of the game board will warp into a new layout.
Thus, to really rack up the points you need to manage the ghosts on your tail, and keep on top of the stage that changes around you as you play. Then there's the countdown timer until Game Over, the speed level controlling your movement and the ghosts', and of course the fantastic, pounding electronic soundtrack that gets more and more intense as the seconds tick away. This game fires all the neurons that Hotline Miami did, and I love it.
What I disliked: how the 'classic' Pac-Man skin is hidden behind in-game 'medals' that are separate from the achievement roster, and how 'sharing on Facebook' accounts for three of these medals. There's also no simple way of comparing your progress with your friends' - for a pick-up-and-play arcade game based on high score tables, I loathe having to go to a discrete 'LEADERBOARDS' option from the main menu. I would have thought that this would be front and centre, flashing at you at every possible choice. 'FRIEND has beaten your high score on TABLE in GAME MODE', etc. In short, it doesn't - from the course selection screens you can see your position in the 'global rankings', but that's it.
To summarise, if you want your hair to go grey and wear your nerves down to smoking, charred wire, buy this game and go for the 'score 1,800,000 in five minutes' medal. If you're not a fan of fast-paced, arcadey, twitch-based puzzlish gameplay, avoid.

Enjoyable storyline, interesting gameplay. I particularly like the turn-based style they designed. The graphics are original and stunning, I loved the creativity in the design of the maps and the detail given to each area. I thought the story was well developed, really up until the very end I was still interested.
Yet, there are some very -very- annoying problems throughout the game.
For one, the probability of missing is atrocious. You could fire, 3 times in a row, 75+% hits and miss all three. For a turn-based, strategy combat game, this completely takes out the strat and leaves entire battles to chance.
Two, there are some really basic failures in moving around the maps and interacting of objects, indicating that there was sloppy testing. I occasionally needed to click something 4 or 5 times to get it to intereact properly; and I would have to get my mouse right into a proper sliver to indicate I wanted to move to a square next to another character.
Three, there are some options in the game that are entirely useless. I barely used Dietrich and some of the "etiquettes" language options are never used, or used only once, in contrast to the "Street" etiquette, which I saw at least 5 times. Decking was a silly exercise, read other reviews for elaboration.
Overall, would recommend buying on sale, at least 15-20% off. Otherwise, not worth it for an unpolished game.

I've now played three installments of the Shadowrun series; the original, Hong Kong, and now Dragonfall.
The first two I devoured immediately. I played all the way through the campaign in a day or two. Dragonfall I did not.
The start of this game is incredibly aggravating. From an RNG that I swear lies (I couldn't tell you how many times I missed a 99%, it was a lot though) to several missions which seem designed to tick the player off coming at you immmediately this game is hard to break into. Not only that but I do believe that it is the longest of the three campaigns produced. My first few attempts to play this game? I stopped. I lost interest. This game is frustrating and at times very intentionally so.
With that said it does have strong redeeming qualities. Many of the characters are the best I've seen in the series and the ideas they all possess are strong and unique in their many faceted ways. Not only that but the ultimate payout of the plot is immensely satisfactory and you are given choices that you know will have a huge impact upon the world.
If you want a great story in the Shadowrun setting, this game is definitely a keeper. However if you're in it for basic gameplay and don't care as much for the story itself turn away from this game immediately.
There are no milk runs, Shadowrunner.

I'll give it thumbs up as soon as this moves out of beta. 40 great hours of gaming didn't make up for the 2 hours of raging frustration.

Phone conversations are buggy, dialogue choices in both GM and My Career are even less clear than before, and sometimes will select the opposite bianary choice. Seriously, you never have more than two choices and about a quarter of the time doesn't choose the one that you had highlighted. My Career in general seems programmed specifically to humiliate the player. As usual, you start off with the skill level of an 8th grade track star who only plays basketball to stay in shape and shares Iverson's feeling on practice. Improving is even more of a grind than before.
All balancing was done with multiplayer in mind. Too easy to get good shots in multiplayer? Solution can't make good shots, game wide. Too easy to make the kick out passes? Solution players fumble perfect passes and step out of bounds like dizzy children. Ally-oop play too powerful? Don't even think about attempting it without a badge. A badge, I might add that requires you do the thing you can't do to obtain it. You'll be a pretty bad free throw shooter early on. How do you get better? By playing a drill that only rewards you for making free throws... what a paradox. Finally slog through that to improve a little? Do it again, but you'll need two times as many points.
Worse still the game is built around tempting the purchase of VC. Anything and everything costs VC, lots of VC. It takes several thousand VC to get enough points in any particular shot before it stops punishing you for taking said shot. You have to invest several games worth of VC into a single skill to make it vaible, and then the game will still regularly deny you even that.
There is nothing more infuritating than having announcers speak incredulously about a bad miss, as if the games own programming isn't what caused that in the first place. It's such a slap in the face to have the game itself taunt you about things that are entirely it's fault. How wonderful it is to invest thousands of VC into a layup skill only to slam the ball into the rim as if you had no idea it's a physical object.
At this point you may think I'm maybe just bad at the game. No, I'm statistically doing great. Have several career triple doubles through about 25 games. Shooting around 50% despite the fact I have no 3 point shot, and barely ever take anything from midrange. Nope I only shoot when close to the rim, and only when open and still I shoot 50% overall. There is no feedback to explain this. Just need to grind for badges they apparently forgot to monetize. Seriously, they paced the badges as if you could kick a few real dollars their way to unlock them quicker only to forget to add that feature.
My Career is a step back. Gameplay still has far too many canned animations and far to often does whatever it pleases. Pressing the steal button is a total gamble for instance. You might take a swipe at the ball. More often you just take a swipe. Honestly you look like you're attempting to land a hook. But every now and again you just fly off in a random direction. I've gotten far more steals by accidentaly being in the way than actually poking the ball lose. Players don't step out of bounds on the baseline as often as they did, but they will just dart off to get a backcourt violation at double speed. A theme that continues all throughout. Fix one thing, break another. It's like the game is barely holding everything together and at least 4 or 5 times a game it just falls apart.
Again, I'd love for this game to be great. It just isn't.

I had a pretty good time with this. I didn't know what to expect, having never played a Strider game before, and I was pleasantly greeted by a fast-paced classic side-scroller. Gameplay is very hack and slash oriented, your primary weapon is a sword that can be swung incredibly fast in multiple directions, even while airborne. This gives you a wide range of flexibility when attacking enemies, which is nice. Along the way you pick up upgrades and special moves/weapons that offer some variety to your attacks. These upgrades also represent the metroidvania elements of the game, as they can be used to further explore areas of the free roaming maps that were previously inaccessible.
On the technical side the game runs smooth and fast, as expected from a game of this genre. It offers a pretty good selection of graphics tweaking options, though I assume most PCs these days will have little trouble handling the game. While it’s not a visual spectacle by any means, it manages to look pretty nice, showcasing the unique art style in great detail.
Overall, Strider is pretty fun through and through if you're looking for a game of this type. There are a few downsides; combat can get somewhat repetitive before you gain all of your abilities and a few of the bosses are pretty disappointing in terms of challenge, however, they are not too detrimental to the overall experience. You can run through the game pretty quickly (there's an achievement for beating it in under 4 hours), however fully exploring each area will undoubtedly add some extra playtime. Definitely recommended if you're a fan of this genre.

The Elder Scrolls: Legends is a great alternative to Hearthstone, which is inevitably what people will be comparing it to. This game deserves to be judged on it's own merits, in which it excels in many aspects over many digital card games, but I'll personally be comparing it to Hearthstone because that's a base game many people here will be familiar with.
Over Hearthstone, this game has many upsides. The gameplay itself is much more deep than Hearthstone. Rather than there being heroes representing classes, there is instead colors, and they are as follows: Blue (Intelligence), Green (Agility), Yellow (Willpower), Red (Strength), and Purple (Endurance). You can combine up to two different colors to make 50 card decks with three copies of most cards allowed. The colors synergize with themselves, so you have to consider how much of one color you're putting in a deck over another, usually making one color the primary color and the other the supporting secondary one. Overall, this makes for a more enriched and in-depth deck building experience.
The board is very similar to Hearthstone, but it has some differences that add a little more depth to the gameplay. There is a lane system consisting of two different lanes, one regular lane and one lane which gives every card "stealth" played in it, which prevents minions in one lane from interacting from one lane to the other. The stealth on every minion might sound OP at first, but there's plenty of removal to deal with scary minions that could be placed over there, and they can be targetted by spells when stealthed unlike in Hearthstone.
There is a "draw as you take damage" system in this game that helps alleviate some of the problems with draw luck, and there's even a keyword called "Prophecy", which allows you to play a card if it's drawn via these means, allowing you to actively counter your opponents moves. It also incentivizes you to be cautious with how much you attack your opponent, making decision making more complex. Also, unlike in Hearthstone you can run three copies of most legendaries, except for unique legendaries, which are a subclass of legendary cards which you can only run one of. You can tell these apart by the red jewel at the top of unique legendary cards
It also has an infinitely better free to play system. You get rewarded with not just gold, but also a card for winning three games, and leveling rewards you with actual cards rather than just golden versions of cards, including epics and legendaries. Crafting prices are identical to Hearthstone, except for legendaries, which rather than costing 1600 of the card crafting currency it instead costs 1200, which helps make getting legendaries cheaper.
The game's ladder system is similar to Hearthstone's rank system, but there are some notable differences as well. Unlike in Hearthstone, where if you win more times you gain bonus stars until rank five, Elder Scrolls has a thing called bonus rounds, which I will cover more in the downsides, as I prefer Hearthstone's bonus ranked system more. There are only twelve different ranks, but rather than you having to win a couple of times to rank up like in Hearthstone, you instead have to win several times, ranging from rank to rank. If you are about do derank from losing enough times, you will fall into a special rank where you have to fight your way out of it to continue progressing. You cannot fall out of this rank, though, so deranking isn't possible.
The game also offers an arena "draft a random deck" style game mode that costs the same as it does in Hearthstone. This game also offers a single player version of it, which rewards you less since it's easier, but is still worth the cost and makes for a more new player friendly experience. It does get harder the more times you emerge victorious, and become much less new player friendly, so keep that in mind.
I do prefer this game over Hearthstone, but there are things that Hearthstone does better that can't be ignored. This game's presentation is good, but it's not as good as Hearthstone's on an objective level. Golden/animated cards aren't very collectable, as the difference is hardly notable, so I often find myself dusting them. There is alternative card art you can collect however, which is enjoyable and many of them improve over the originals. Also, the collection manager leaves a bit to be desired over Hearthstone's.
There are some gameplay elements I prefer in Hearthstone, such as the way Hearthstone rewards you for playing well with bonus stars, while Elder Scrolls: Legend's bonus system is random. Occasionally you'll come across something called a bonus round, where if you win rather than progressing once through the rank you're in you'll progress twice. It's completely random, though, so rather than rewarding your ability to win it just happens completely out of your control.
As previously mentioned, you are able to run three copies of most cards, including legendaries, and while the game lowers the prices of legendaries, they are still quite expensive. Getting to a point where you feel like your collection is robust can feel like a daunting task. I've found myself focusing one color specifically to offset this and make sure I can compete at high levels of this game, which is fine, but can also get repetitive only playing a few decks. Go about this any way you please; buy packs (the prices are fair and there's special offers for new players), grind arenas, focus only one color, etc., but I'm sure you'll notice this as a new player.
Also, while I love the ES:L community, it's quite small when compared to Hearthstone. If you're like me, you love watching Twitch streams possibly even more than playing the game. There are some great ES:L streamers out there, but compared to Hearthstone it's slim pickings. Since this game is new to Steam and communities often see growth when exposed on Steam, I believe this will become less of an issue over time, but it's still worth bringing up.
The Elder Scrolls: Legends is a great game with many mechanics to offer over Hearthstone, a game people will inevitably compare this to. It has a better f2p system, better and deeper game mechanics, and a better arena system with a single player option. There are downsides, such as the presentation, collection completion, and a small (but growing) community, but this doesn't take too much away from the game. It's definitely worth checking out, and I'm sure you'll find yourself enjoying it as much as if not more than you enjoy Hearthstone.

This is a great game, I've played it quite a lot on the Bethesda launcher up to a couple month ago, even though I'm not really active on the game at the moment, I still feel compelled to write a review to support its growth.
It's a shame it has had such a small player base and has been so slow developping a competitive scene, hopefully the steam release will help with this and that.
A lot of the others' reviews already cover the details of the game better than I would, but to make it short it's very much like Hearthstone - no need to hide that fact - but it improves upon the general model over several aspects. For exemple, compared to Hearthstone, it feels like a bigger proportion of "printed" cards are within the range of playability, which is a good thing as far as deckbuilding/teching goes.
Generally speaking the game always felt really well balanced and mostly devoid of the so-called "bad RNG", it's mostly about effects which you can play around to an extent so as to mitigate their effects, typically the prophecy system which is all about pondering risk vs rewards and the potential consequences of one's action over the next couple of turns. This as well as the lane system adds a certain layer of complexity over what you'll find in most Hearthstone game, where to be honest a substantial amount of games kind of simply play themselves for a given draw.
Also, important point for people who understandably wouldn't want to spend money on a game relatively similar to HS - with incremental improvements -, this game is MUCH more free to play friendly than HS, arena rewards are extreme in comparison, 7 wins which is the maximum gives you up to 4 packs, gold for another entry, sometimes a random legendary card, while also costing 150 golds. It's also relevant to mention the ability to farm up to 300 soul gems (dust) a day vs expert AI, which potentially means crafting a legendary in 4 days.

TL&DR: Definetly worth your cash at this price and it has amazing devs.
I've been wanting to write this review for days, but everytime I put it back because "just one more turn and I'll close the game" turns into a loop that goes well past midnight. The game is amazing and they have been adding content steadily for the past year or so. The exploring gameplay is interesting and challenging. The combat encounters require thought and planning and the non-combat encounters give you this feeling of "Yeah Morgana the Witch sure is pulling her weight by protecting the party from the horrors of the Darkness.". Furthermore, the resource gathering is addictive and a constant (fun) effort to balance "Just a little bit more mithrill" and "I should probably get all of this stuff to my crafters back home."
The devs are evidently roleplayers who are in touch with their community, and the game presents plenty of oportunities to roleplay if that's the kind of thing you like. Want to play a super-racist band of human warriors? Thea's got you covered. Want to play a group of magic-tree-hugging elves? Sure, build your entire city out of elvenwood and the elves will come. Equip your dudes with armor or shields made of magic bones, and they are now magical combatants.
I do feel like the game could benefit from different starts (I'd like to start with a dwarf-only group, or maybe a Goblin-only group) pehaps attached to the different gods. And having a bigger random encounter pool could also enrich the gameplay. I also feel like the stat system could be presented somewhat more effectively, maybe color coding the stats depending on how good a character is at that specific skill, to make discerning which characters are good at what at a glance much easier. But I'm nitpicking here. At a 20$ mark this game definetly has given me way much more fun and roleplay oportunities than many AAA titles. And while there is plenty of room to grow and improve, i'm more than happy to go along for the ride!

Killer is Dead is another one of  those games that I enjoyed playing, however, it ended up feeling very hollow in the end.
=======
CONS:
- Repetitive: It's a hack and slash, obviously, so this is basically up to opinion. However, I love games like Devil May Cry, so, that's not the complete meaning behind my calling the "repetition" a negative point. What I mean is that you "accept a contract", "navigate through the level", "fight the boss", "repeat". Read my next point for the reason why this is a problem.
- Story: Why is the repetition an issue? Well, it wouldn't be if the story was well put together enough that it could drive the hack/slash gameplay to a point. But... it's confusing, vague, and not concrete. There's a lot of "You don't know this, Mondo? Well... *DEAD*". You don't get a lot of answers, and this repeated cycle of trying to further the plot, by not really furthering it, through adding mystery, but devolving said mystery due to repetition of uninteresting "You don't understand?" dialogue is not very appealing. The ending of the game is something else... you have to really think to piece it together, and even then, it takes a bit of faith to say "it makes sense, now". Because, well... there's a lot of info missing, glossed over, or that just remains obscured. Perhaps they are planning on a sequel to answer these questions..? That's the only thing I can think of, because this game doesn't really provide many answers.
- Gameplay mechanics (Jumping): I really feel like this game lost a lot of grand opportunity by restricting the player's movements and gameplay to solely being on the ground. I understand that there's no real need to jump, as you have the Musselback's gun mode, but... I'd like to be able to jump into the air to hit those enemies with my sword, sometimes, rather than just have to gather blood and shoot. I'd also like to be able to jump over boxes (though, I'd be fine with some obstacles being purposely unable to hurdle over). It feels too restricting, when compared to other games of this ilk (e.g.: DMC, again), and it would have been a fantastic addition that, sadly, would have bumped up the gameplay had it been present, but wasnt. Disappointing.
- Boss fights: They were fairly short, and not very difficult to figure out how to defeat the bosses. Maybe it's harder on Nightmare mode, but... I don't want to go through that. Want to know why? Read below...
- Replayability: There isn't any. Once you beat it, you've beaten it. My only advice is to play all the side missions and gigolo missions as you play, between missions, when available, to boost up Mondo's skills/gain new weapons, and level up your abilities. Then, once you finish, like I have, well, you'll be satisfied leaving it alone.
PROS:
+ Visuals: This game is stunning; absolutely gorgeous. The contrasting colours, the vivid details... it's brilliant. Fantastic design choice by the developers. Props to them~!
+ Gameplay mechanics (attacking): Very intuitive, especially when using a controller like I did, and very easy to get into. It's satisfying to fight through some enemies, although, when he gets disoriented and you have to wiggle the joystick.. well, that was just annoying >.< But, combat was fun, and very tight controls made it even better.
+ Voice Acting/Characters: Very likeable characters, and solid voice acting. The characters don't feel too forced (Mika can feel that way at first exposure, but that soon goes away), and Vivienne is a little too cliche, but, it doesn't hurt the game. You grow to like the characters well enough, and their voices suit them appropriately. This can't be said for a good deal of games, so, this is a valid point to consider. It keeps you in the headspace of the universe of the game, and lets you suspend reality a little better as you play. Good job, voice actors/actresses~! :)
+ Style: The entire vibe of the game is just... groovy. It's got a great aesthetic and feel to it, overall.
=======
So, do I recommend "Killer is Dead"?
Well, given that there are more negatives than positives.. yes, I do.
Here's why:
It's a game that has solid gameplay, great visuals, likeable characters, and a good atmosphere about it. Of course, it's only real detriments are the story/plot, and the lack of jumping, for me. A lot of people rag on the Gigolo missions, but really, it's not that big a deal. If you don't like it, don't play it. It's minimal, unnecessary, and people have blown it way out of proportion. There are countless numbers of games dedicated to things like this (e.g.: visual novels, dating sims, etc.), and those don't get ragged on. Why? Because they aren't always made by major companies, and only people who enjoy them, play them. You don't like it? Just let it alone, and don't entertain it, Simple.
...Regardless, getting back on track to the review...
Killer is Dead is a fun game, that deserves at least a play through, or to have you give it a go. If it's not for you, well, it's not for you. It won't be for everybody, for sure. I liked it, although there were flaws to it, but they never really made me feel like I disliked it, or wanted to stop playing. I wanted to finish it, did finish it, and I'm glad I followed through.
...Just don't pay full price for it, by far.
Wait for a Steam sale, and, well, if you can get it for less than 10$, give it the go-ahead.
You won't regret it.
Though, you won't find any replay value, here.
Uninstalled (*a single tear*)

I am a long time player of tabletop RPGs and tactical RPGs and I must say that I loved this game. I just finished the game for the first time in Hard difficulty and I plan on playing it again in the highest difficulty next. The game is the second in a serie of (currently 3) but I feel like the stories are disconnected so you probably can play them in any order.
The story is great and well set in the shadowrun universe. Characters are well written with a deeper and often darker aspect to discover. The storyline is not too complex to follow but complex enough to enjoy.
The battles in the game know how to be stressful. Many of the "fights" are very well scripted with multiple actions to take in sequence that increase pressure on you. For instance there is a battle where you need to press two switching in two rooms in the real world while your decker has to open the way for you from the matrix. The game knows how to keep you on edge.
Graphics are nothing too fancy but perfectly integrated in the style of the game. Though I played on a not so good for gaming laptop and had to set graphics setting low.
The main issues I had with this game are linked to the UI. It can be very frustrating at times. Here are a few things I found annoying in the interface. I'll detail that because I hope the developpers will read this and do what they can in future versions. I give a fairly long list but that is mostly to the developpers benefit. The game is good !
-The combat rules are somewhat kept unknown. It is not clear to me what each statistic is doing or what some of the acronym stand for. A particular instance: Some weapon have a Ar-P statistic which I guess stands for Armor Piercing. When using it some of the armor points of the enemy unit blinks but seem to come back in the same round. I guess Armor Piercing is different from Armor Striping but making it clear would be nice. In the current form Armor seems to be a typical DR (damage reduction) and it is not clear to me that there is a real difference in practice between +3 Ar-P and +3 DMG.
-the UI can be very hard to read for me. Maybe it is becuase I am color blind but the overlays in same tone can be quite hard to read. In particular, the techniques icon in the matrix often features white writing on white background and the cooldown of a not yet used technique can be hard to read.
-the HP of an enemy can be very hard to read because its health bar is essentially hovering over the units head but whatever is behind that unit can make it hard to read. Even pointing to the unit does not really help: more information appear in  box that is transparent and depending on what is behind the text might be very hard to read. It could be fixed by giving a setting for the opacity of these infobox.
-It is sometimes hard to understand what an action will do some actions might require you to move first but the "trajectory line" is small so you might not realize your character will have to move to accomplish this action. In comparison in FireEmblem, a (too) heavy line will show you the path your character will take.
-Some attacks can damage neighbooring  unit (shotguns, miniguns, glory's closecombat), it would be good if the units potentially in the line of fire could be indicated. especially the shotgun widespread shot can be fairly hard to predict.
-It can be very hard to point to some tiles in the game. Trying to move 4 characters on a 2x2 area is very difficult because you keep on pointing to one of the character.
-When healing outside of combat, I find it annoying that I can not see who has inventory and who needs healing. A simple tweak would be to display a "currentHP"/"maxHP" information next to the character's name in the "who to heal" dialog.
-In terms of gameplay, some things were annoying as well. You can not give an ally an item once the mission has started. I ended up in ridiculous situations where the leaders inventory was full but Glory's inventory was empty and when finding an item I had to send it to the stash.
-It would be good if some action (reload in particular) could span between two rounds. Often with the apex' drone shooting costs 2AP and reloading costs 2AP but the drone only has 3 AP. I'd like to be able to fire, start reloading and pay -1AP next round to complete reloading.

Strider is the name, and the game is speed. Very fast, high paced, no compromise, 360 degree platforming action. An effective cross-breed between free-running and a metroidvania style map makes this a modern day halmark for the genre and the series.
So the original strider was a platformer with some sick hack 'n' slash elements. It had cool moves and a whickedly long sword that was fast to boot. You'd make your way from one end of the level to the next while slashing everything to bits; including the Soviet parliament. Good times.
The new version is not a remake; more like an emulation and update. With the finesse of today's hardware Strider has been made more agile, and faster. Everything about him is smooth and flexible. You can attacks in eight directions, while in motion, on any surface. Ok, not while hanging from a ceiling, but it is still more than you're getting from Simon Belmont. The flexibility of Strider's movement options is so amazing you'd wish you could play other games with them.
Along with the fluid movement options you also acquire a number of powers. Like shield drones, energy panthers and power hawks, along with elemental powers and kunai. All these tools are needed to fend off the never ending tide of conscripted enemies and bosses. You can clear a room on the fly, but sometimes you need to stop and think and moderate your approach before being gunned down by a crossfire of machinegun bullets. It is awesome and fun to deal with obstacles in such a fast and agile way. It helps keep the pace up and the fun coming.
You make your way through an open world, with indicators telling you where to go. Certain abilities unlock new areas, just like in the classic Metroid games (I'm calling them classic now; I have little faith in Nintendo at this time). This sends you round the world with the option to go back for more powerups or to plow on ahead, straight for the boss' head. Three ways the game offers you a level of freedom. In movement, in combat, and in exploration.
The game takes a step back from it's Soviet roots and propells you into a Soviet controlled neo-industrialist nation that is being opressed by a powerhungry madman. Standard fare. Not much time is spent on story or expostion. Just so you can get back to that sweet high speed action all the faster.

Besides no game is perfect.

A brisk, kinetic action-adventure (or metroidvania, if you’re down with that), which puts the player in the role of invincible cyberninja Strider Hiryu. At the time of its release, this type of game wasn’t quite as abundant as it is now, but the standard formula was set in stone: explore the world (smacking baddies as you go), find new items, and use these to explore further.
is comfort gaming in that it does nothing to shake up the formula, but is pleasant to look at and play, and is over before it outstays its welcome.
I used a gamepad to play, and it worked well. Hiryu, with his flowing scarf and permanent crouching dash, is a real treat to control. He’s always fast and agile, and fans of the series will be pleased to hear that his cartwheeling jump is present and has been perfectly realised. The movement and animation is smooth, but I found that Hiryu would cling a bit too readily to walls and ceiling, and his movement when in this clinging state is significantly slowed. It’s hardly a deal breaker but I did feel it wasn’t as slickly executed as the other running and jumping. It would be remiss of me not to mention that you can’t bind movement to the d-pad, which will probably be a deal breaker for some players.
Unlike some games of it’s type, there isn’t much menu hopping in
, so you’re free to roam and fight. A creature of habit, Hiryu uses only one weapon, a kind of laser sword, and he’s so comfortable with it it's like an extension of his body. Hammering the light attack will produce a series of very quick attacks, and holding it will charge up for a big horizontal swing. This can stagger the game's weaker enemies, and - BONUS! - it makes a wicked slicey sound. You can do launcher attack as well, but I rarely used it as you can’t launch larger enemies for air-juggling, and the weaker ones go down quickly enough with basic swings. This isn’t a game where you’ll have to memorise combo attacks, which makes it more accessible but also means the combat has little depth. The iconic appearance of the sword and the sound it makes means it feels great to use, and at the start of the game I was cackling with glee as I tore through entire regiments of robot enemies, but as the large mech enemies began to appear at the end of the game, and even footsoldiers started to carry shields, I longed for a bit more variety in my means of attack. At that point your tactics basically come down hit the bad guy in his unguarded back, which works in almost every instance.
Some variety comes in the form of unlockable kunai which can be thrown to pepper weak flying enemies or hit far switches, but they don’t have any of the punch of the sword and can’t be thrown often enough to be much use in a heated fight. In addition to these, you’ll find different modes which affect the sword and kunai, for example an icy blue one which can freeze enemies solid, useful for both traversal (frozen enemies are platforms) and combat. You can switch to any state with a single button push, so can vary things up as much as you like without getting bogged down in menus. Lastly, Hiryu can collect three “Options”, powerful tools which can seriously damage bosses, but which are limited in use by an energy meter. I, ahem, always forgot to use them, but they’re there and they work fine.
My biggest complaint about
is that it’s short and fairly samey throughout, definitely a more linear kind of metroidvania. You explore one large city, Kazakh, themed around a soviet dictatorship. Although you’ll travel through a prison, an army base, and an underground lab (oh, and a sewer for some dumb reason) each area looks pretty similar to the last. I didn’t get lost much in
, but that’s not because I’ve got a great sense of direction or was able to navigate by landmarks, but simply because most areas aren’t very big and don’t allow for much in the way of diversion. If you go down the wrong track, more often than not you’ll find a “secret” pickup, usually a piece of concept art, and then you’ll have to double back and go the other way. The map is actually pretty good, but you won’t often use it.
The story, such as it is, isn’t worth mentioning. These guys are baddies, and Hiryu has to stop them, simple as that. There’s a smattering of cool bosses in here, but also some weak and forgettable ones. None of them really tested me as a player, and honestly I breezed through the game on the standard difficulty. But, I’m not complaining: I tend not to finish a lot of games these days, so it was nice to play one which gave me just what I was expecting, and didn’t throw up any big roadblocks.
With good controls and animation, okay combat, and so-so level design,
doesn’t quite do enough to really stand out from the pack, but if you’re looking for a quick, bombastic adventure, you’d be remiss not to at least give it a try.

Fantastic action-platformer with some metroidvania-style gameplay elements. It combines the best of all older Strider games, like the arcade machines, the NES game, and the later adaptations for home consoles. It throws them into a blender, and underlines the delicious mix with flawless visuals, pumping sound effects, an excellent soundtrack, fluid and responsive controls, awesome boss battles, and a gameplay that has perfectly tuned difficulty settings. Hunting down collectibles and extra challenge modes will give you plenty of extra re-play value, as well.
And yes: you will see gravity break. Just as you should in any good Strider game. The gravity-warped areas are back. So are the Four Winds, Solo, and facing off with Grandmaster Meio.
This. This is how you remake an old game series. This is the definitive Strider experience.

Overall, a very enjoyable experience. I will definitely be playing Critter Chronicles and The Book of Unwritten Tales 2.

Only downsides are that I found the latter third of the game playing with Nate drags on a little bit, and the ending is a little abrupt. Forunately there's two more games to move on to, so at this point in time I'm able to be more forgiving. There is also some issues with widescreen resolutions on the game - I had to drop the resolution down and stretch the screen to actually be able to see and complete some puzzles. Occasionally walking in to a new location would slow the game down to a crawl, and I had to exit and re-enter scenes until they came right. This didn't happen too often and didn't affect my enjoyment of the game.
Overall, a fantastic and fun adventure, one that I thoroughly enjoyed. Looking forward to playing subsequent titles!

This is, like, the prime example of why I'd want a "meh" button. The game isn't awful. Far from it. The graphics are passable, the voice acting is mostly decent, the music is alright, and the puzzles themselves make enough sense in-universe. The game's got a pretty decent length (maybe too long) and a good amount of humor.
But it's just... boring.
I will sum up the problem in one single image:
Do you see this? At the start of the fourth chapter, the current protagonist says this. And this is exactly what happens.
You cannot. Be. The. Thing. You. Are. Trying. To. Parody. It just does not work. You have failed as parody if you are doing the exact thing you are mocking.
A lot of the game devolves into tedious fetch quests. The story is nothing special. It's a basic "save the world" vaguely plot. Fantasy/RPG setting. That's fine. The point is the comedy.
And it does succeed there, in some regards. The first chapter is a bit light on it, but the second chapter is just jam-packed with humor and had me playing practically straight through. It kinda comes to a halt when the story intervenes though, but for those two or three hours I had tons of fun with the game. The mage diploma, the real-world MMO, the "magic" tricks, the lampshading of death in adventure games... it's all good comedy. It's an interesting world.
And then... chapter 3 hits. Where you go through a temple in search of the plot device. No subversions. No real comedy. It's a stretch of the game where nothing really happens except more puzzles. The plot moves forward, sure, but the game has already established at this point that the plot does not matter. Why should I care about the plot. Why should I care about these characters. Wilbur is the only character that's really interesting in any way, and is why the second chapter works so well. Ivo is boring and without any personality whatsoever. Nate is an unlikeable jerk and cements his status as such at the end of the third chapter. Sure, the game calls him out for it too, but. He can be unlikeable to other characters without making him unlikeable to the audience as well.
And the real nail in the coffin. After Nate does "the bad thing" that makes him so unlikeable... he is the primary controllable character for the rest of the game. You play as Wilbur for two short scenes and Ivo/Critter for one relatively small scene. The rest is him.
I do not want to play as the unsympathetic jerk. I actually put the game down for a week at the start of Chapter 4 because I was dreading having to play as Nate. Sure, he spends the rest of the game trying to make up for his mistake, but I don't believe it. I don't feel compelled by it. I don't like him and that's not going to change.
It doesn't help that the humor revolving around him isn't as good, nor are the characters he has to interact with. The dead lovers are kinda amusing. The paladin character and especially Nate's attitude towards him are an UTTER TRAVESTY, absolutely disgusting. The buffalo is boring. The Orc brothers are a very basic smart/stupid. The dragon is about the best character met in this chapter, but she comes in only near the end and doesn't do much, we don't see her much. Plus, her animation is pretty horrible and brings down that short section a lot.
And then... you get to replay the last section of the fourth chapter from a different perspective, hearing basically no new dialogue, visiting no new locations, and doing very few new puzzles. And then the game... ends. It doesn't even make sense how it ends, either.
SPOILER ALERT because I need to have this bit in my review.
Why did they need to bring the Earth Pixies to the tower? Why did the other three need to be there alongside Ivo? At that point, all that needed to be done was for Ivo to leave the tower. The artifact wasn't in the chest, so the villains wouldn't have it. There was an easy way for Ivo to leave the tower unnoticed and unharmed. There was no reason for the entire out-of-the-blue pixie invasion and dragon reappearance with the other, except to force that cliche fly-off-into-the-distance ending. And wasn't it established that the monstrous villain lady (who we NEVER see) is really powerful? She could slaughter those pixies - heck, probably did off-screen. And Ivo intentionally drew her attention. For what purpose? Who knows. God. Everything about the ending is completely nonsensical, even aside from the fact that it just... happens. Very abruptly. The last puzzle in the game... is shrinking an orc in a completely different location from the climax.
All-in-all... the game's a bit tedious, light on the comedy for most of the game, and overall just not a worthwhile investment of your time. It's alright, but not great. It has many, many problems. I'd say, pass.

If you're like me, you haven't played Runescape or World of Warcraft because you have better ways to spend your time. This is one of the better uses of said time.

The unique way cards are played makes this simple and fast, but interesting to wrap your head around. Mastery of the way the game is played is just as gratifying as getting new cards.
Explaining it is tricky, and I'm sure others have done better. Please, give it a shot. It's free, after all.
As a side note for those of you wondering about buying more card packs; it's a lot cheaper than Hearthstone. This game knew it had to compete with hearthstone, and made its packs bought with money cheaper than packs bought in Hearthstone. Runescape Legends earns my recomendation for knowing how to business.
If I can make one complaint, it's that that the game might be a little too fast, currently. It's designed to be fast, which is great. Hearthstone was fast in a way that discouraged slower decks for a long time until recently, and this game is fast because of the way its played instead of just the cards used. That said, just the cards being used makes this even faster. Games can end on the third, or even second round if your deck doesn't match well againt the opponents. Keep that in mind before decided to get really invested.

Ricks Review
Summary:
Gameplay: 9/10 - Simple and complex political-combat-economic action which is realistic yet playable.
Combat: 8/10 - Very basic combat mechanics which require the construction of units, from Land, Sea, Air and Infantry. Many unit types are customizable for better battle performance and outcomes for the selected state. However in battle the player can not perform direct actions in the battle screen and is mearly the observer to the battle.
Politics: 9/10 - Limited in political details compared to games like Ruler of Nations and Masters of the Universe. But the game provides very indepth fields around the countries language and religious demographics, laws and government types. Although little is made in the changing of demographics, laws and governments except from saying Yes, No or Maybe. It does allow for a detailed and easy way for you to create your nation.
Economics: 9/10 - Amazing, indepth field of economics which allows the player to experience how the economics of any nation works. Through trading, diplomacy and domestic taxes, you can influence how your economy sways. Managing the budget can be tricky and challenging in various states, it is exciting and sometimes thrilling to compare various strategies and tactics which can improve the states economy.
Audio: 9/10 - Dynamic music to the situation, losing, winning and nuclear war are the main music types.
UI: 5/10 - Beautiful UI for the game type, however can be a bit quirky in situations. Where the movement of troops can be difficult and unpredictable where the units move several miles from the intended location.
Technical Side: 7/10 - Editor fails in stability and many stability and technical issues arise in the main game. Sometimes with many players experiencing game crashing on high-spec scenarios like nuclear war, dramatic economic changes or huge wars.
Moddability: 6/10 - Various mod types are available from historical scenarios to gameplay changes/additions to some fantasy and hypothetical scenarios, you can experience a game where Hitler wins or Communism is supreme. However the poor score is detailed because of its poor modding methods and editor, with its poor technical stability on modern computers and the extent of the moddability to scenarios only, it can limit potential and the lifespan of the game.
Community: 5/10 - Although this is not directly affected by the game, there is a large community atlarge in this game. However do expect a lot of bitter members which vary.
Servers & multiplayer: 2/10 - I honestly enjoy Roleplaying servers and messing around with servers. But it is so difficult and awkward to start a server, it is not worth the trouble. And starting a public server risks potential hackers, trolls and generally unwanted visitors. Although you can enforce passwords and friends only, those threats can exist still.
Main Points:
This game was made back in 2004, making the technology behind the game pretty old compared to modern standards, but with the games potential it proves superior among many other titles. But before considering buying the game, make sure to get into contact with other players to compare specs and computer technology to make sure the game will work on your machine.
Great Gameplay for a Political Simulation game which extends to Combat, Politics and Economy which can diversify depending on the nation you play as.
Amazing dynamic audio which changes depending on the current situation of your state or the global situation.
Stability can be poor on modern computers and the modding editor will not work on Windows 8.
Servers can be hard to set up and not advisable for quick games with friends.
Improvements:
Improve upon the modding capabilities to allow for modern computers to be accepting to the capability. Meaning modern computers can use the editor or an alternative means to mod the game. And making sure the player can mod anything in the game, from scenario to UI to menus.
Improve the servers by making sure a anti-cheat/hack system is installed and allowing for every player to create their own servers with players capable of joining.

The game is interesting, I guess kind of like King of Dragon Pass crossed with a bit of a 4x game, maybe a bit of Fallen Enchantress in there stylistically, a bit of FTL sometimes mechanically, it's hard to pin down. Fundamentally it's a game where you are presented with lots of choices in random situations and various numbers influence what choices you can make and which ones will work, the bulk of the challenge, such as there is, involves being able to intuit what numbers challenges are going to require from you, and making sure you have the right numbers in your group (because the game has a lot of different numbers to keep track of and is not especially good at showing which are relevant and when, it takes a long time to gain a feel for this)
Where the game falls flat is that there is so much randomness involved that you are frequently given challenges you can't realistically beat, other than by doing back in time and swapping out your group for another one, with another set of abilities. The game requires you to build specialized groups to be successful at a particular type of challenge, but will randomly throw unavoidable challenges at that group which they cannot solve with their skillset, building a generalist group is not practical unless you have a huge number of people, so mostly your success is determined by whether or not the game wants to roll a "rocks fall everybody dies" event on your group, replacing rocks with "obscenely strong enemies which are only weak to diplomacy or a special option you don't have" or something similar. I particularly like the event that can trigger from any point after the game begins which poisons your entire party unless you beat a strength challenge, which can only be cured by travelling across the world to a specific place and beating a challenge which your party members might not be able to do, or even get to in time. Or the other event that does the same thing to your home village without even a chance to avoid it. The game has a lot of that sort of thing in it.
The game is charmingly if a little cheesily written and obvious work has been put into giving lots of different approaches to situations, but precious few of them are going to be practical for any given group, and if you're given an event that your group can't handle, you can easily lose half your accumulated strength, so much of the game depends on just whether or not the dice want to kill you that the rest of the game feels irrelevant, you can spend all your time making interesting choices for marginal gains and losses, only to have the game decide it just wants to kill half your people and end your playthrough 200 turns in. It would perhaps benefit from being a better developed strategic game, where you could see threats coming and plan an approach, but the game really likes to just trigger random events when you start a new turn, or move one square, or an enemy decides to move into your square, or due to dialogue choices, or more or less any time. Imagine Civ 5 if enemy armies just sort of teleported around your city every now and then and you had to figure out how to beat them, it doesn't work very well, or fit with the perfectly functional strategic layer.
TL;DR, game is Tomb of Horrors, Civilization of Dragon Pass edition. If that's your cup of tea, well, I hope it's less frustrating for you than it is for me, I guess?
