Killer is Dead is another one of  those games that I enjoyed playing, however, it ended up feeling very hollow in the end.
=======
CONS:
- Repetitive: It's a hack and slash, obviously, so this is basically up to opinion. However, I love games like Devil May Cry, so, that's not the complete meaning behind my calling the "repetition" a negative point. What I mean is that you "accept a contract", "navigate through the level", "fight the boss", "repeat". Read my next point for the reason why this is a problem.
- Story: Why is the repetition an issue? Well, it wouldn't be if the story was well put together enough that it could drive the hack/slash gameplay to a point. But... it's confusing, vague, and not concrete. There's a lot of "You don't know this, Mondo? Well... *DEAD*". You don't get a lot of answers, and this repeated cycle of trying to further the plot, by not really furthering it, through adding mystery, but devolving said mystery due to repetition of uninteresting "You don't understand?" dialogue is not very appealing. The ending of the game is something else... you have to really think to piece it together, and even then, it takes a bit of faith to say "it makes sense, now". Because, well... there's a lot of info missing, glossed over, or that just remains obscured. Perhaps they are planning on a sequel to answer these questions..? That's the only thing I can think of, because this game doesn't really provide many answers.
- Gameplay mechanics (Jumping): I really feel like this game lost a lot of grand opportunity by restricting the player's movements and gameplay to solely being on the ground. I understand that there's no real need to jump, as you have the Musselback's gun mode, but... I'd like to be able to jump into the air to hit those enemies with my sword, sometimes, rather than just have to gather blood and shoot. I'd also like to be able to jump over boxes (though, I'd be fine with some obstacles being purposely unable to hurdle over). It feels too restricting, when compared to other games of this ilk (e.g.: DMC, again), and it would have been a fantastic addition that, sadly, would have bumped up the gameplay had it been present, but wasnt. Disappointing.
- Boss fights: They were fairly short, and not very difficult to figure out how to defeat the bosses. Maybe it's harder on Nightmare mode, but... I don't want to go through that. Want to know why? Read below...
- Replayability: There isn't any. Once you beat it, you've beaten it. My only advice is to play all the side missions and gigolo missions as you play, between missions, when available, to boost up Mondo's skills/gain new weapons, and level up your abilities. Then, once you finish, like I have, well, you'll be satisfied leaving it alone.
PROS:
+ Visuals: This game is stunning; absolutely gorgeous. The contrasting colours, the vivid details... it's brilliant. Fantastic design choice by the developers. Props to them~!
+ Gameplay mechanics (attacking): Very intuitive, especially when using a controller like I did, and very easy to get into. It's satisfying to fight through some enemies, although, when he gets disoriented and you have to wiggle the joystick.. well, that was just annoying >.< But, combat was fun, and very tight controls made it even better.
+ Voice Acting/Characters: Very likeable characters, and solid voice acting. The characters don't feel too forced (Mika can feel that way at first exposure, but that soon goes away), and Vivienne is a little too cliche, but, it doesn't hurt the game. You grow to like the characters well enough, and their voices suit them appropriately. This can't be said for a good deal of games, so, this is a valid point to consider. It keeps you in the headspace of the universe of the game, and lets you suspend reality a little better as you play. Good job, voice actors/actresses~! :)
+ Style: The entire vibe of the game is just... groovy. It's got a great aesthetic and feel to it, overall.
=======
So, do I recommend "Killer is Dead"?
Well, given that there are more negatives than positives.. yes, I do.
Here's why:
It's a game that has solid gameplay, great visuals, likeable characters, and a good atmosphere about it. Of course, it's only real detriments are the story/plot, and the lack of jumping, for me. A lot of people rag on the Gigolo missions, but really, it's not that big a deal. If you don't like it, don't play it. It's minimal, unnecessary, and people have blown it way out of proportion. There are countless numbers of games dedicated to things like this (e.g.: visual novels, dating sims, etc.), and those don't get ragged on. Why? Because they aren't always made by major companies, and only people who enjoy them, play them. You don't like it? Just let it alone, and don't entertain it, Simple.
...Regardless, getting back on track to the review...
Killer is Dead is a fun game, that deserves at least a play through, or to have you give it a go. If it's not for you, well, it's not for you. It won't be for everybody, for sure. I liked it, although there were flaws to it, but they never really made me feel like I disliked it, or wanted to stop playing. I wanted to finish it, did finish it, and I'm glad I followed through.
...Just don't pay full price for it, by far.
Wait for a Steam sale, and, well, if you can get it for less than 10$, give it the go-ahead.
You won't regret it.
Though, you won't find any replay value, here.
Uninstalled (*a single tear*)

Supreme Commander Forged Alliance or SupCom Fa (My rough view of such game):
The game that justifies "Supremacy","Command" and "Epic Proportions". Despite being a stand alone expansion perhaps projects itself of being the best game of the series through prevailing through the years of its active release while in a way it shares positive similarities with SupCom 1 and SupCom 2 (less). It presents a redefined approach through its differences.The game displays a literally huge project of future technology battling it out within these factions that players can choose. Each with a unique playstyle. All with the same goal of supremacy.
SupCom Fa does a superb job at defining the genre of "real time strategy". Having the capabilities of generating large scale battles across complex maps. To the simple yet fluid battles that take into account miniscule details from the player.
Most of the time games span from early-mid-late game transisition like all strategy games.There is never an idle state and if that is the case expect the unexpected. From the dreaded nuclear launch, surprise experimentals,innovative strategies or just a total economy stall.
Heading into SupCom Fa's later years most people nowadays play on the Forged Alliance forever client(requies copy of game).A cosy community keeping this ancient treasure alive and updated. A testimony of how tenacious SupCom Fa is to its fans and providing the all out RTS experience. A true recommendation for fans of the RTS genre. Be weary of the somewhat steep learning curve and required dedicated time needed to play and maybe having to learn. But that is a worthy price to pay for what great potential can be mined from SupCom Fa.

Runescape is a game I have been heavily into for ages. When I heard \'Runescape was making a card game\' though, and saw the first few images of it, my first thought was, \"Hearthstone ripoff?\"
Well... I will say this: Aestically, the game has some similarities to Hearthstone. Also, the cards use a similar stat system to Heathstone. But beyond that, however, the game is completely something on it\'s own. Instead of fighting your enemy\'s monsters, you are fighting your OWN monsters, with each card you defeat having either a benifit to your characer, or a hinderance to the enemy\'s character. The goal is to basically make your character the strongest out of the two, or make your oponent lose all their HP before the end of the game.
If you are a fan of, or have played Runescape, there is tons of little nods to it, with all the cards being bosses, characters, items, and gear from both modern Runescape, and Oldschool Runescape. However, even if you have not played Runescape before, the game still is more than playable on it\'s own merit.
Is it perfect? No. There is a few minor balancing issues here and there, and the game does have a lot of \'luck-based\' moments. However, matches are pretty short, lasting only 5 rounds, gameplay is fairly easy to pick up, and the different characters you can play as all have different playstyles, adding quite a bit of variety to the game. An example? An oponent picks up a weapon card, boosting their attack to 10. The enemy has 10 hp, and deals 10 damage, but gives them some extraordinary bonus for beating it.  So... they would kill the monster in one hit if things go properly, BUT, the moment before they attack the monster, you could play a card that causes their weapon to break, causing them to not be able to kill the monster in one hit... And the monster might just kill them, or leave them severely weak afterwards.
Personally, I prefer this game over most other card games, and find myself going to it when I have some free time. Since it is free to play, you might as well try it. I wouldn\'t say everyone will like it, but considering you can get a feel for the game pretty quickly, this is a \'Why not just give it a try?\' type scenerio. I have had a lot of fun with it, and while I feel the game does need more content, I know that will likely come in time.
Hearthstone? Chronicle? Same same, but different, but still same.

First off, I  want to mention that I finished this game. Being a game that can last up to 20 hours the majority of my time was offline.
Hark back to the days of adventure, by clicking on random pixels, picking up items, and combining items in random or "logical" ways in hopes of finding your way through the adventure. This game is a throwback. A "Point and Click" adventure game. While there have been many since the days of Monkey Island, and even in recent years, this is probably one of the best since Monkey Island.
You take the role of a young gnome named Wilbur who yearns for adventure and hopes to remove himself from his menial life, the beautiful elf Ivo who just so happened to be in the right place at the right time, and a wise-cracking cocky human with a peculiar past named Nate. Nate on the run from a bounty hunter has a furry sidekick called "Critter" whom speaks nothing but nonesense (familiar?).

Spoilers:  The adventure begins with a ring...among the backdrop of a war between the Alliance (gnome, dwarf, human...) and an army of orcs.
I'll stop my spoilers there. It should sound familiar to you. This game is humurous, using obvious references to help out its humor, but it doesn't over do it. A wonderously funny game in its own right, It doesn't bash nor does it even spoof what it references. It's good natured ribbing over the typical Toklien-esque fantasy world, and certain games and films we've all come to know through the years, but again it doesn't over do it.  It brings up some good points about gaming in general though, mainly directed at the MMORPG when Wilbur asks "Why would people feel the need to leave their real-life to play a fictitious life...." That's not a direct quote, but it was along the same lines. Most likely done in jest,  to me it still brings up a good question about our hobby.
The art style is superb. Bright colors and details abound, and I caught myself wishing there was a 3D space to it, to be able to explore more deeply than you're able in the game. The dialogue is also detailed. Click on certain items on-screen, and you'll get a simple explanation of it, but enough that it may give you a nice background and history of the world. Even minor points of interest, and minor characters have some history and background to them. In summary, this is just a nice game with lots of spirit. Beautiful artwork, clever dialogue, and never a time of frustration, it deserves your attention. I've been gaming since I was a kid,  this is one of my favorites.
P.S. Soapbox time: As for Wilbur's question, we all have our reasons to "game." I've been lucky enough to travel and have real life adventures in this world. I SEEK it out. What motivated me to do all that? Playing games as a child. The fantasy and the worlds I got sucked into, it motivated me to find it in real life. Hope you all seek your adventures just the same.

Strider is a 1990s-style Metroidvania made with the technology and game design sensibilities of the 21st century. A solid and attractive platformer built around a rather nonsensical plot, the game runs the player through a variety of environments as they slowly unlock new abilities for the main character, allowing them to access more and more of the world in a fairly linear fashion.
This game takes the design of Metroidvania games and does it much better. Backtracking? There isn’t much of it here; the game is designed to take the player on a linear route through the world, and while it feels nice and convoluted, the overall amount of backtracking is very minimal. This is an excellent piece of game design that many other Metroidvanias could learn from; the only real backtracking required is a few areas which have to be unlocked by later abilities.
The core gameplay itself is pretty enjoyable. The platforming feels good, you can climb along the walls and ceilings, there aren’t too many bottomless pits, the enemies are reasonably varied, there are tons and tons of bosses (about one every half hour or so), with new enemies introduced like clockwork in the meanwhile. The game is always kept feeling fresh, and at the end, you get to put all your skills to work taking down the big bad.
The game has decent voice acting, but the plot itself is pretty much nonsense; it isn’t really clear what is going on beyond “There is a bad guy who is in charge and you need to kill him.” Who sent Strider? Who are all these people? Why is the big bad doing what he is doing? Who knows? Who cares? It doesn’t matter!
Your goal is to cut your way through his minions, and the game employs you admirably in this.
Overall, this is a pretty great game. The graphics ae solid, the game is the right length for what it is and doesn’t feel stretched at about 9 hours to 100% it, the protagonist has a reasonably diverse set of skills which can be employed in a few different ways to make your way through the levels and beat down the bad guys – if I had a complaint, it would be that the standard game difficulty might have been a touch on the easy side at times, but overall, it wasn’t really an issue. Checkpoints were pretty generous and never really felt like they set you back too far even if you did fail.
Was it perfect? No. But I had fun playing it, and the game had excellent pacing which kept me interested and kept me wanting to play after I got rolling through to the very end, even though it gave me many, many possible break points to choose from.
All in all, this is a great reboot, and the game was really quite fun and was worth the 9 hours I invested. It isn’t something with a great story, but the core gameplay was pretty much exactly what I was hoping for from a game like this.

Like swords?  Remember the Striders running, jumping, doing the usual platformer mischief?  You're in luck!  From arcade to consoles, it's been a fun ride for Strider, and in Strider HD/Strider 2014, you get a quite-faithful modernization of the classic.  Upgrades and backtracking a bit for other unlockables, aren't too out of the way, but some require navigating with precise timing against hazards.  Others need prerequisite skills to reach.  Hey, like bosses that present at least a bit of challenge?  The boss fights aren't boring, and run from signle foes, multiple bosses at once, giant whirring mechanations, dazzling explosions, lasers, and mysticism which isn't terribly predictable, and will give you a feeling of accomplishment, in their death throes.  You'll be looking at your map to track down some unlockables, but despite the game having clearly defined locations to reach, you'll find yourself diverting to a far corner, to see if there's a bit of exploring to be had.  Controls at later levels, with skill unlocks, becomes very wide-open, and you'll be slashing through rows of baddies!
Now, regarding the bad.  This game is known to be unstable on integrated/discrete video chips, but seems quite reliable with dedicated video cards.  Then, there's input; you may need a DirectX-XInput wrapper, like x360ce or others, so the game can "see" your gamepad.  After this quick bit is tended to, you'll be enjoying the variety of enemies and tactics!  I generally think of reboots as trash, but this is one that is worthy of a few sessions on the couch.

This is practically as generic as a 2D hack-n-slash game can get. You just mash against the enemies until they die for years. I pursued the campaign in hopes that the enemies become more challenging and creative. They don't become anymore than punching (or, rather, slashing) bags until very far into the game. And even then, it barely takes much effort at all to shove them aside and continue towards the objective point.
The world aspect itself is in the style of Metroid or Iga-related Castelvania games. Much simpler than the likes of those games, though. Finding extras doesn't take much effort, you either find them by going through unexplored areas, or simply go back to it later when you have an ability to overcome the 'obstacle. (read: Funny-looking Door)' Everything felt like the beginning of Super Metroid, where they're easy to attain. And it just seemed to stay that way for this title.
Bosses are not challenging in the slightest. There isn't anything more to them, for the most part, besides avoiding their attacks. Once they're not attacking, mash against them like your life depends on it.
I really don't understand why there's much praise for this game. Just like when this team took a crack at Silent Hill, it feels unimaginative and bland. Almost soulless. But I will give credit where it's due, Strider himself controls excellently, it makes it an even bigger shame that they put a character that functions as well as this in a game that has almost nothing new or exciting to offer.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

Strider is a great 2D action side scroller.  It's fast paced, requires a fair bit of finger dexterity, and is roughly a 12-hour game if you take your time to complete ~85% of the game on Normal.  The graphics and sound a fantastic as well.
I can't remember any crashes or hangs, so it's quite stable as well.
Like other 2D side scrollers of this sort, you get what you put in.  If you run through the game and skip most bad guys, and skipping out on the exploring and grabbing upgrades then it would grow old fast.  However, if you do generally the opposite then the game offers quite a bit of challenge and diversity to keep you interested.

Quick summary: Strider is a side scrolling hack/slash platformer game, like playing Mega Man with a sword. The game uses modern particle graphics and is overall a fun (but challenging) way to spend about 9 hours.
You play Strider Hiryuu, a kind of futuristic ninja fighting against the forces of Grandmaster Meio, who rules the city with an iron fist (+ magic powers). Your fellow striders have fallen in battle, and you can find their remains occasionally as you wander the areas of the game. Finding a fallen strider gives you a new skin (just a different color suit). Grandmaster Meio isn’t your only problem though, he has an army of henchmen, cyber troops, and bosses for you to battle before you even see him.
As mentioned before, the game is a two dimensional side scroller and you will spend most of your time double jumping, climbing walls, and boosting around with your plasma catapult (a kind of air dash). Since there is no money or exp to pick up, you can actually run or jump past most of the enemies in the game. That’s why the game has an achievement for completion in under 4 hours. I took 10 hours my first run through since I tried to grab all the upgrades around the game world. Strider has a world map similar to Super Metroid, where you can see most of the upgrades on the map as soon as you get close enough, and you’ll constantly be encountering doors that you can’t open until later in the game with the appropriate weapon. Almost all of the fighting is done with your trusty sword “cypher” that can be upgraded with special effects like fire, ice, and bullet reflection later in the game. You also have special attacks like throwing kunai, and “summoning” support, but your sword will deal with 95% of your enemies.
Pros:
+The game is challenging (especially some bosses) but there’s no penalty for dying so you can try out a bunch of different ways to tackle enemies. Be aware though, that some bosses have an unskippable dialogue scenes so if you keep dying and restarting boss fights you’ll get annoyed with their long-windedness.
+You can cling to almost any surface and with double jump + plasma catapult there’s all sorts of nooks and crannies to explore in the city. A lot of upgrades can be found this way.
Cons:
-Not much of a story, but the game is pretty casual (not the difficulty) so it’s not that big a deal. You’re probably playing for the ninja action anyway.
-Some of the gameplay elements aren’t explained very well.  I didn’t understand until about halfway through the game how the energy system worked or what the “combo meter” did. Neither of these things are critical to winning (at first), but a short tutorial would have been helpful.
Overall, Strider is fun and just challenging enough that you’ll find yourself respawning a few times at the bosses.  If the regular enemies become too repetitive, you can just run and jump past them. You should probably play this game with a controller though I used keyboard (no mouse input). The reason I used the keyboard is that you mash on the attack button a lot, which I don’t like to do on my controller.

I did not know what to expect coming into Strider.  I only had a passing awareness of what the game was from AGDQ and Hiryu's likeness from other games.  So, no expectations.
I have to say, though, that Strider is really good at what it is.  I went straight to the hardest difficulty and didn't have much trouble except for a few bosses, so it's not a difficult game, but it is a good game.  The level design is definitely that classic Metroidvania-style and the sheer number of collectables and power-ups provides plenty of reason to backtrack to get it all.
There's not much enemy diversity and most of them can be felled by actually just mashing the attack button, but the game still rewards planning and awareness, especially through a few key sections that are basically bullet hells.  Some of the segments are basically puzzle-platformers, others are straight-on combat, and the variance is nice.  The game is paced well.
My one major gripe with the game is a gravity mechanic that comes into play a few times (including the final boss fight).  The controls while in gravity fields are not intuitive, so I had to fight my instincts in order to get fluid movement.  This mechanic is only used three times in the entire game, so it's not game-wrecking, just an occasional annoyance.
A good game.  I intend to 100% it soon.

Let's be clear up front. In it's current state, this game is rough. VERY rough. So why have I given it a positive review? Because I have some faith in this could be gem, and considering it is free, I am willing to continue to give it more of my time so long as improvments progressivly debut. I'll give a short summary of the game, and my experience with it so far.
Clash of Monsters is a classic 2D plane fighting game featuring in horror themed characters from both popular film and literature works.  As of current, the game has 8 characters, with only 7 seemingly playable These include in no specific order, The Living Dead (Classic Zombie), Nosferatru (The O.G Vampire), The Headless Horseman (Pumpkin Lord). Ichabod Crane (Sleepy Hollow Protagonist), The Bride of Dracula (Traditional Vampire), The Invisible Man (Basically a Phantom), and Bones (A Skeleton). The 8th character is supposably "The Phantom of the Opera" but I am unable to pick him myself for whatever reason.
Each character currently has two punches, two kicks, and a throw. There is currently no block button, and this is something I think is certainly needed as it is otherwise too easy to get pummeled (tho maybe I just need more practice.)  When testing around with each character, it is apparent they each have unique abilities such as The Bride of Dracula sprouting wings and leaping across the stage, or the Living Dead latching onto an opponent to munch on their torso, which is great and adds unique flavors to each character. Speaking of stages, there is currently only one, known as Sleepy Hollow, and it is pretty basic featuring a stone walkway, some fog, and twisted trees and water in the background. Nothing too exciting, yet.
While the game has controller support, it definetly needs some work. Navigating the menu can be a struggle with the cursor flying all over the place, and fights in general are very clunky. It feels like some of my moves are delayed, and that is a big no no in fighting games. The game has a special moves list for each character, but this can only be accessed in battle and frankly was sometimes tough to open. I have not attempted to use the keyboard often because I don't find them suitable for my fighting game needs.
The graphics are maybe comparable to that of the early Ps3/Xbox360 era. They could no doubt use some work, but the inspiration is clearly there, it just needs to be put into further motion with more detail being desired by myself. The games audio is average. It needs more music as there is currently only one mind numbing song which gets repetative quick due to its distinct "epic" theme. And the sound effects in general are for the most part seemingly shared among characters with a few small exceptions.
In it's current state, I would have to give this game a 5 out of 10, maybe a 6 if I was feeling generous. The inspiration is there, but this game is far too rough in its current stage to be what I would consider a Beta. However, in an era where couch co-op is rapidly fading, and games like thisoffer more of those chances,  I am willing to put my hopes in the future of this game so long as the Dev's take note in what the public desires in order to mold and shape a quality fighting game worthy of anyone's steam library.

TL;DR: Shadowrun: Dragonfall is a brilliant narrative-driven RPG, which, despite several questionable decisions in design, is absolutely worth your time.
• Fantastic setting, fusing cyberpunk and high fantasy in a futuristic Berlin
• Compelling plot with interesting writing, moral questions and multiple endings
• A range of role-playing opportunities, both in character customization and within dialogue
• Often several approaches to completing missions
• Generally intriguing support characters
• XCOM esque tactical combat is somewhat simplistic
• Plot occasionally delivered through info-dumps
• Clumsy and inefficient menus
• Turn based movement can remain active even when enemy pods are inactive
• Limited exploration
• Some bugs

There are a number of things that this game has going for it. The main thing, of course, is that the game design is good. It implements the turn based system well, there are opportunities for different character builds that play differently, and depending on which teammates you choose the missions play out differently. Also of significance, it's true to the source material. Shadowrun is a very rich universe, and this game captures it well. I really like that it's set in Germany. Too many games are based in the country of origin (American games in the US, Japanese games in Japan), but this game took the Germany sourcebook and really ran with it. It was great to see what was happening in Europe in the Shadowrun universe.  The side quests with the different teammates are excellent. There are a couple of quibbles that I have. I'm not sure I like the Matrix/Decking... one of the troubles with it in the Shadowrun tabletop is that if you have a decker you end up with essentially a 1 on 1 between the decker and the storyteller, while the rest of the players sit there. This implementation of the system, when you switch in and out during the turn is undoubtedly the best that I've seen, but the underlying problem of sending one party member into a parallel combat/adventure from everyone else is still a bit awkward. Second, the story is a classic RPG set piece, many parts are on rails, and no matter what you do you're going the same place. Of course, the open world games that became common after this game was released have spoiled us all, but the fact remains that this game is telling a particular story. Fortunately for this game, the story is a good one, and I was glad to play through it. There are some significant choices at the end of the game that affect the ending you receive, which is pretty great. Overall, this game is worth playing, probably twice or three times at least to try out different character builds.

To me, this is still the definite real time strategy game. It may be a bit graphically dated, as well as demanding significant single-threaded performance, but its strengths in UI, scope, unit and strategy diversity still shine as much as they did when it was released. The automatition and construction planning options are likewise second to none in the genre, allowing to truly focus on the big picture, long term plans and multiple assaults at once.
Thanks to the rate-based energy and mass economy, sacrificing an army or two as a diversion or loosing a fleet or even base to a clever ploy is no big deal, so you can both experiment and take risks. Most maps are big enough to comfortably house a bunch of backup facilities anyhow. Not to forget the endgame units are both a great way to dramatically resolve too balanced battle situations and just tons of fun to see unleash their might amongst smaller foes.
The storyline missions are nice enough. Sure the dialog is a little ridiculous at times, but it has a bit of B-Movie charme and gives each faction a nice coloration, motivating to go through all of them. They also don't hold your hand much. While this is a standalone expansion to the original, you're expected to know your way around enough to dive right into it once you decide to tackle the campaign. This also means less filler missions though. But the real meat is in the multiplayer, which, especially with mods, offers almost endless replayability. There are some great balance tweaks, the all-important sorian AI improvements and the fun commander updates and new endgame units of Black Ops, for example, but many mods and a very much alive fan-made multiplayer project still exist (though as the steam version added matchmaking services, it's not even needed to enjoy it).

Interesting game, a very non-traditional 4x game, that has given me back the "Just One More Turn" feel that we all like to have.  You have a settlement, you collect food and wood, you have an expedition that sets about exploring the vast country side.  You make decisions on where you want to research, what you build and craft.  This game is a micro management game as you do need to produce and craft in order to drive research.  While you do get research from fighting, better to keep your crafters busy.  In order to keep your crafter busy you have to gather, either during battles with booty, or setting up a camp with your expedition and bring more exotic materials in.
Combat is simple, with a card like game play reminiscent of MoG.  It is a bit confusing at first, but after a few battles it really is not that hard.  There are plenty of events, monsters places to explore to help you gain experience and loot.  your Settlement has to be looked after, so while you may want to send your warrior party out as an expedition, you may want to ensure your crafters and gatherers have weapons and skills.
There are battles other than just fighiting, all similar but you can have social, hex, tactical battles so you need  a good rounded party.  This game has a lot going on, and so far it is a lot of fun.

I can't reccomend this game.
The way the difficulty is in this game is VERY poor game design, basically it scales. However, if you get behind(And in the higher difficulties you always are, through the BS events that you have no control over and usually end up losing about 4 people due to poor RNG, nothing you can do about it.)and/or have less than 20 people by turn 100 in the higher difficulty(And you basically can't get 20 people that early, because again, events are BS, and even if they aren't you usually only get about 3~ people by that time.)
Not only that, but the combat is pretty shoddy.
And, here is the kicker, if you thought vanilla civ 5 was bad in where it placed your first city, imagine you are FORCED to settle where ever it places you, even in flatland desert without any hills or anything in miles. You can't move cities in this game, where you start is where you are. That's it. I have had starts where I had a single resource of food, that's it. Nothing else, no string, no wood, no nothing. Because reasons. You can NEVER make new cities, you can only set up camps, which, again if you have less than 20 people in that camp, you will be killed. In a game where getting people past 15 is nigh impossible, even with insane attraction rating in villages.
As I said, everything is scaled. Everything. When you have more people, you get less coming in from the world and less children grow up(Did I mention RNG?), but the less you have the more you get. But that's by no means any sort of realistic expectation when your party is killed by 4 skulls at turn 80(Imagine in WoW if you had a fel reaver drop kick you are level 10. That's what this is comparable to.)You probably won't get anyone new, because again, RNG.
So with all these complaints, I can't say this game is worth it. It's an indie game, I should expect it, but these flaws are painful. When they actually fix some of these issues, adding in growth maybe or something, I will change this review.

A lovely adventure game somewhat betrayed by its simplicity.
Throughout the course of the game you gain control of 3 characters (you can maybe count it as 4 even), playing some sections exclusively as one character, or sometimes getting the option of switching to another. All three are fun to play and have their own distinct personalities which also translate into their observations of the world, which you can directly see by inspecting the same items with different characters. Although the last one you are introduced to does take a little while to like, since at the beginning he's quite obnoxious.
The story is one of the most important parts in an adventure game, and here it certainly does not disappoint. It is a lighthearted save the world plot spanning through a diverse set of areas with a real feeling of adventure. However the ending did feel rushed, and compared to the rest of the game the're just the feeling that not as much thought went into designing it.
The biggest problem the game has is that there is only one usable button, you do absolutely everything with only the left mouse click. This means that even if you get stuck somewhere, it is not too difficult to brute force your way through, because there is a much more limited number of possibilities than in traditional adventure games.
But perhaps there is some sort of an upshot to this as well. The game flow is rarely interrupted and you're not going to get frustrated over some random puzzle, although there is one particularly annoying area in a mine which for some reason uses a top down camera instead of the traditional sidescrolling one.
The Book of Unwritten Tales is certainly lengthy enough without the need for convoluted puzzles, it took me 13 hours to finish it, but I didn't spend much of that time trying to figure out what to do next.
7 / 10

I wasn't sure about this at first, as it's a little uneven in the early going, but the longer I played it, the more I enjoyed it. It's a fairly standard fantasy point-and-click adventure, where there's a big bad guy trying to get a powerful magic item, but it has a number of features that make it more entertaining than what you'd expect from such a generic situation.
One of the best innovations I've seen in a while is that hotspots will disappear after you've done everything possible with them. That really helps eliminate wasteful backtracking and double-checking of red herrings. You also switch around between three characters, all with totally different personalities and abilities. It's a bit reminiscent of older LucasArts games like Maniac Mansion and Zak McKracken. These two features help keep the game moving.
The other thing that sets this game apart is its excellent sense of humor. The game walks a fine line between meta-humor and camp while playing with genre tropes and expectations from RPGs and graphical adventure games. Fantasy geeks will appreciate all the jokes referencing other games, books, and movies. The voice acting is also very good, which helps with the delivery of a lot of the humorous lines.
The 3D graphics are mostly good, although there is some clipping and other weirdness here and there, and the cutscenes are only fair. Scenes are shown from widely varying angles to allow access to everything you need, which is appreciated.
It took me twelve hours to complete, and I feel like I went at a fairly steady pace, so I'd expect 10-15 hours for almost anyone to finish it. Overall, any experienced adventurers will enjoy the game quite a bit, and it's easy to recommend for such folks.

I came across a review of this game on RPS by Alice O'Connor on August 10th, 2015. To quote:
"Far Cry 2 is a game about plans and contingency plans, then desperate makeshift plans when those both go wrong, then finally, after a crucial grenade rolls back down a hill towards you, hoping that your buddy will come pull you out the fire – and that you can cover them. [...] The problems some complain about – malaria, jamming weapons, NPC outposts respawning with silly frequency, and so on – are what make Far Cry 2 so much fun, creating more opportunities for unexpected cockups for you to triumphantly recover from. That’s where Far Cry 2 shines."
That's exactly right. All of those things which I have seen people complain about with this game are actually part of what makes Far Cry 2 so good. The game is simply not out to make you feel like you are in control — it does EVERYTHING in its power to boost the sensation of hostility in the game world. You cleared out an enemy camp? It makes no difference, the camp will be restored by the time you come back to it. The frequent enemy respawns ensure that you never take the same route going back; it is a game about constantly improvising and measuring the stakes.
This is barely a game. It is more like an eternal struggle, a perfect fantasy for a Nietzschean male mind. That's what they wanted it to be.

Far Cry 2: Fun gameplay lightly sprinkled amongst long portions of tedious travelling.

(sigh) I finally decided to reccomend this game. For its mediocraty it provided me with a fun experience, and is by no means a poor purchace decision at all.
Let me get the "big problem" out of the way. My biggest problem by far was the fact that during travel between missions, it was impossible to get around enemies, whom always respawned in the loaded area every time. This resulted in a confrontation every two minutes, and because stealth is impossible in this game (honestly, I tried, again and again, you can't do it) it results in a frustrating repetative routine:
Steal vehicle, drive, see enemy vehicle, crawl into gunners seat, shoot, repair vehicle, drive, see enemy vehicle, crawl into gunners seat... over and over and over and ov....
...For 30 hours. If there is one thing that could have made the game near-perfect (and replayable)... it would have been a better fast-travel system, or at least a way to perminantly clear an area larger than a shack on a hill.
There are other things that I could nitpick. But with the big problem out of the way, I can now praise the game for everything it did right. In no particular order:
1) Soundtrack and environment work well together to give you the proper 'feeling' in the game.
2) The survival elements of gun damage and malaria added a nice touch to the game, and I am sad that few other games do this.
3) The use of other selectable characters in the game as NPCs creates a sense of a larger world.
4) AI is intellegent and challenging.
5) Gunplay is epic. Yes, that describes it well.
6) The villan is not stereotypically easy to hate.
It could certaintly be FAR better, and I would replay it if it was not for the "big problem". Nonetheless, I cannot say that this is an unbuyable or bad game... and so it gets a reccomendation.

There is a decent chance that if you came across this though Steam your first though was "Runescape is still a thing?". Yes, Runescape is still around and it's doing well. Well, decent. I still play it.
Runescape:Chronicle is Jagex's latest game. Honestly, their last few tries have been....less than stellar (Ace of Spades is struggling on Steam), so when I heard they were making a new game, I was cautiosly optimistic.
When it was annonced as a trading card game, alot of people instantly claimed Hearthstone rip off, which it is defenitly not, but people have been claiming Runescape is a World of Warcraft rip off for years now (Even thou Runescape came out 3 years before WoW, but ok....).
So is it good? Yes, I think so.
Chronicle is just as much board game as card game with constant references to Runescape in its content. Half the cards you can pretty easily understand without context (Armoured Zombie, Skeleton, Green Dragon, pretty standard fantasy stuff), others are more RS exclusive (Saradomin brew, Corporeal Beast, even Party hat). Knowing the context for them is enjoyable, although if you don't know you're not missing out on much and the names dont matter in terms of gameplay.
The gameplay is solid. Original concept, each character has a distinct strategy, good variety of cards, graphics hold up well and has an overall nice feel to it. There really isn't too much to complain about for mechanics or gameplay.
I have a few niggles although. Characters have a tendency to over-react (Vanescula acts like she just walked straight out of Sims 2), which is kind of distracting. There's no chat function, but there is a friends system, which is weird because if you can't talk to people in game there's no point in adding people you meet, just your friends from Steam or Runescape. The currency you pay for with real life currency is labeled as "Platinum tokens", while the free currencey you earn are "Copper coins", which make you feel something like second class scum (This complaint is really nit picky I know). Also, when Jagex first announced Chronicle they said they were aiming for a game you could play at the same time as you played Runescape, which is a bit awkward for the amount of attention Chronicle requires. However, none of these issues are deal breakers, and it's defenitley worth it for the total price of $0.00
Chronicle is sold as a free game that you can pay to get extra booster packs of random cards (Imagine how when you were a kid and saved up your allowance for Yu-Gi-Oh cards). Most Free to play games with micro transactions usually knee-cap you if you try get trhough without paying, but in Chronicle you can do perfectly fine without paying for anything in real life. Booster packs are given as rewards for playing the game,  or you can buy with the currency you earn in game easily enough, and really, once you've got a decent few cards spending a ton on Platinum tokens won't help much anyway.
But it's a really good enjoyable trading card game. You get decent mileage out of playing it fo free and the gameplay has clearly had good work and effort put into it. Besides a chat function, not much is missing. I'm looking forward to more characters and cards, which from the positive reviews so far it should be on the way. Hopefully it brings more attention back to Runescape too, which is still chugging along happily as an MMO when most other seem to be struggling, but you can easily play one without the other if you like.
TL;DR Good game, can play for free, RS is still a thing, not a Hearthstone rip-off

When I first saw a game made by Jagex, I didn't know what to think: I liked oldschool Runescape and I told myself I wouldn't look back when I stopped playing their games...
...Based on what i'd heard upon its release: It's similar to Hearthstone and is not only cheaper (as in, you don't have to pay at all, if you don't want to) but it can take longer to acquire bronze coins/money to purchase booster packs and card backs from the Store. I haven't played Hearthstone before, so I can't really compare them, but what I do know based on my current gameplay is that Runescape Legends is sort of it's own unique game. Sure, there are similar aspects that I have seen in Hearthstone, but you don't get bored of playing this game because of it's selection of heroes and how they completiment the unlockable cards, which can be used to your benefit when confronting other players (and are all completely free, technically).
Sure, it can be a little rough at unlocking good cards and levelling up, but when you get used to the gameplay and how each Legend works, then you have up to three different game modes to play: Practice (Basically a combination of the Tutorial and Campaign, the AI is pretty good!), Casual/Ranked (Casual is good for practicing the stratergies in your deck, but can effect your rank and help you earn extra EXP), Dungeoneering (When your total level reaches 15, you can go in a dungeoneering game using randomly selected cards and test your true skills for some extra loot!)
The game and deck choices seem to be pretty fair on both players and all of the 5 possible Legends. Whether you treat this game like marmalade or not, it's definitely worth a few hours just to try it out! 90/100!

SuperPower 2 has to be the best Geo-Political Grand Strategy-esque game I have ever played. This game is almost a genre of its own. My first game I thought I would start off playing as the Congo (Not to be confused with the Democratic Republic of the Congo, our big neighbor to the east) to give myself a bit of an extra challenge. It turns out that I accidentally picked the easiest country to play as in Sub-Saharan Africa. Compared to the DRotK's whopping GDP per Capita of 52$/year, the Congo seemed cozy at ~14k/capita/year. You don't need to know all of the terminology and the geography involved with Geo-Politics (although it does help) because the game has a tooltip function that is both concise and descriptive enough to be a very useful tool. One of my favorite aspects of the game has to be designing my own military units. Although the number of parts of designing the look of your unit is limited, modifying the stats is where the fun comes in. You can make your unit a cheap, low quality overall or high quality specific, or an expensive, all-around excellent machine. The detailed political system in the game models International organizations like the EU, NATO, WHO, and many, many, MANY others. And if that isn't enough, you can start your own! Finished developing your nation in Africa yet? Go ahead and start the African Union and limit membership to African nations only, and help your struggling brethren climb out of the hole that you yourself just emerged from. Then, form an alliance with your fellow African nations to form a strong military coalition that can threaten even NATO. Or, you can take advantage of the struggling nature of your fellow African nations and use your advantageous position and conquer them all and have all of Africa for yourself, you evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ;). Don't worry about the age of the game, the game, unlike others its age, has stayed compatible through the ages, and will work up to Windows 8 x64 (what I have), so do not fret. This game will run at maximum performance on your common everyday laptop (also what I have XD), so there is really no reason to not get it unless you are simply uninterested in the topic of the game. And hey! If you are a heathen 'Merican pig like me, this game will help you learn about foreign politics and also the good it could do for the US and the rest of the world if we trimmed our military budget down to a reasonable size, and began investing in healthcare and more foreign aid. :D 10/10 would play Turkey and get annexed by Iran, then launch my ICBM's from my last province and kill 90% of their population in a last-minute "♥♥♥♥ you too, buddy!" again.

Clash of the Monsters intrigued me when I first saw it because of its concept; classic movie monsters battling it out, so it was promptly added to my wishlist.
Here we are, the game is out, and just over an hour into it, I cannot recommend it. At all.
The developer says the game is in beta, but from attempting to play it, it feels more like a very unpolished early access title. In fact, if this were released in early access, I’d be more forgiving toward it. But alas.
The game has controller support, but I don’t know why; controller usage is horrendous. Even a slight move of the stick causes the cursor to move rapidly. Tilting it to the right to select a character sends the selection flying. This occurs with both my Xbox One wireless, and Steam controllers.
Character selection is okay, but slightly odd. I question why Ichabod Crane is a character, when he wasn’t a monster. Or why there’s a monster called “living dead”, ie: zombie. There’s no creature in horror movie history called “living dead”. Developer’s claim of it being from Night of the Living Dead is dubious, at best. As for levels, there’s only one, and it’s very generic.
Hovering the mouse over a character doesn’t do anything, but clicking instantly chooses that character for you. Why? Why can’t I click once to see the character, and again to confirm? Once you’ve gotten to the screen to select the level, you can’t go back; if you want to change characters, you’ll need to start the match, exit, and redo everything. Not sure why a “back” button is so difficult, but I digress.
Graphically, the game is quite ugly. The models are very basic, the only available level (as of this review) is basic. Sound effects and music may as well be absent; I’d prefer silence over the bad effects in this.
Controls while fighting are questionable. Escape does nothing, but spacebar is the pause button. When I tried to quit a match by going to “back to menu”, it looked like a box popped up asking if I was sure, but immediately disappeared, leaving me to let the timer run out. There’s also no mouse cursor in the pause menu, so you have to use the keyboard, which wouldn’t be a bad thing if the menu actually responded to what you wanted. The only way to actually get the three options to work is to use the mouse to click them, as the keyboard controls just pop up and then disappear. But since the mouse doesn’t actually have a cursor and you have to guess where it’s hovering, this is ridiculous. And once you do click “Yes” to exiting to the main menu, you have to press space to close the pause screen before it loads the main menu. This is not the 90s, things like this should not happen.
As for multiplayer, you’re basically back in the early nineties where you need the IP address of the person in order to connect. Yeah. I had no problem doing that when I played Doom back in 1993, but it’s 2016.
Lastly, it’s free to play. Not necessarily a bad thing, but there are no advertisements and nothing to purchase so far, so I question where the revenue comes from. Perhaps the developer will release additional character packs over time. Hopefully those packs will come after the game has been put into a playable state.
It may be free to play, but it’s best to avoid this until (if) it gets some major fixes. Controls are horrible, graphics are horrible, gameplay is horrible, and it’s just, overall, a pretty terrible game at the moment, and I really don’t know this is not in early access. The current state is definitely more alpha than beta.
I wish the developer the best of luck, and will gladly change this review and even purchase items if the core of the game gets fixed. Until then, find your fighting need elsewhere.

Rating: 7/10 - A fun platform game, with light Metroidvania elements. Completion time: 7:30.
= THE GOOD =
- It's a very fun game to play; you slay eniemies, upon enemies, upon enemies
- Very stylish graphics
- Very responsive controls
- The weapons, and their upgrades, are quite interesting, and make sense (although at the end, you'll use only plasma type 3 and 4)
- The enemies are relatively varied
- The bosses are quite fun
- The maps are relatively large
= THE SO-SO =
- Although the graphics are beautiful, it lacks the variety and creativity of the first Strider, which is a big big shame
- This could be somewhat classified as Metroidvania, although it's quite linear - in reality, you're only going to do a big backtrack at the end to pick up the missing powerups
- The NPE/Bosses don't move their mouths while talking; this makes them a bit weird looking.
= THE BAD =
- You can't customize the keys. Arcade stick is not supported
- You need 11 keys (ELEVEN!!) plus the 4 directions when playing, plus another 6/7 other ones used exclusively in map mode. This is very irritating; they could have made a more economic and intelligent choice.
- Shielded enemies of type 2 can only be killed with Plasma 2, not 3/4. This has no real strategic implications; it will only force the player to switch the plasma, klll the enemy, and switch back again, which is nothing else than annoying
- Many bosses will need to be killed several times over the game. It's quite boring to meet a past boss again.
- You can't skip the bosses' blabbering, which is cheesy and banal, and ultimately irritating
- The controls in "floating" gravity are a terrible mess, especially in the last boss
- There is no ending. DAFUQ!?!

Highly recommended to any fans of the genre or ninja themes.

I bought this game when I was made aware of the added co-op free DLC that was made for it. It does something I've always loved and is rarely done in city-management style games, even in RTS; allow you to have two players co-op through the main campaign.
The game has a lot of rogue like elements, and rewards replaying with out-of-game advancement in the form of levelling up the gods that represent the player. You start with two gods unlocked, and unlock more as you level up gods. In co-op, both players share the same god and level up that god's progress. Progress is saved on a per-host basis, meaning that both players can have a saved game, or if you have a consistent partner you can just both use the same one to maximize avancement.
The gameplay itself resembles something along the lines of King of Dragon Pass. You busy yourself with building up your home town while sending out expeditions to gather resources and adventure across the landscape. Random events occur in a mostly-positive ratio to mix up the gameplay. Unlike King of Dragon Pass, however, your individual villagers are much more important, and you're dealing with very small numbers of people typically. You start with 10, and build up from there, and have to split them up to make expeditions. There is a story through the game, involving finding out why the world ended, why the world started recovering, and working to make that recovery permanent(or not?). It has a nice blend of fantasy elements, and like KoDP its emphasis on magic is both subtle and highly impactful. You don't really cast spell, per se, but magical skills can make huge differences on how events play out.
A few tips I would give to anyone looking to play it, I highly encourage you play a game or two single player to get a feel for it before playing co-op, and THEN look at some guides to see what you were doing wrong. It's a complex game and actually ends up having something of a build order to it. Once you have that done, co-op will go much more smoothly. You wouldn't want to fail someone who's relying on you afterall!
tl;dr: Thea is a somewhat complex but inventive co-op adventuring city management game. It's roleplaying elements go down to individual villagers and their equipment, and the story is well written and imaginative. The interface could use a little work, but it's very functional and intuitive. The music is good, and the artwork that represents the game elements is pretty great.

GREAT game! This is the ultimate "one more turn" turn-based 4X game, with a variety of refreshing elements. First of all, there is a FASCINATING card-layer to how events and combat are worked out... I was really impressed with this. Every person has their own skills and stats in your settlement, so while all your fighters might fight well, and crafters craft well, and gatherers gather well... the REAL fun comes from needing to think about a variety of skills to have in your group to handle obstacles in your choice of ways, or certain challenges that require magical, technical, or obscure knowledge to tackle. The Card-Combat game is the same no matter if it's a regular battle or disarming a deadly machine or unravelling a hex, but the stats for each character's cards are different based on their skills and the challenges at hand. So maybe you can kit your party out so that everyone is decent in a straight up fight, but all of a sudden in a social or stealth challenge your front line fighters are taking a huge back seat to a couple of clever or specialized folks in your group. It's LOTS of fun and there is a lot of depth to it. You might have characters that do a GREAT job supporting front liners just like you have front liners that are GREAT if supported but meh otherwise. The card game is split between "Frontline" and "Tactics" piles of character cards... so you have to decide if you want to bring in tactics people "tapped" and get stuck in, or have the tactics guys buff your guys, nerf the enemy, change turn sequence... so much stuff. A guy with a bow and strategy skills can buff damage for a person on the front line, confuse an enemy, or allow your guy to hit first... all sorts of choices going on, which sometimes turns into "I have two people who have the lore or technical skill to unravel this challenge, how else can I set up the other guys to buy them time to do that?" The card layer is REALLY nice. Unlike many 4X games where you build lots of towns, you only have one town which you improve with better technology and materials you gather in the world. Crafting equipment for your people is also LOTS of fun... your adventuring party brings back all sorts of wood, food, metal, stone, gems... a wide variety of all sorts of commodities to play with. Then your crafter can go to town finding interesting combinations of the materials for weapons, armor, jewelry, shields. It's not just about what makes a sword sharper or an armor hardest though -- with the right elements and skill you can get armor to boost attractiveness for social challenges, add magic skill so even regular brute fighters have a better shot at helping against supernatural or magical threats, and a variety of other skills and abilities that have an influence in combat and challenges (like "leech" healing when you do damage, or "feint" or "Sturdiness" or "Stealth" -- all of which have different impacts in tactical challenges, regular fights, magical combat (hexing), etc. The world and story behind it are engrossing enough, and there is a sufficient beastiary and fun loot and lots of events that give you choices and risks to take, as well as all the dialogue being decently voice acted. There are multiple endings and really a lot of depth, as well as a pantheon of gods which give your followers more and special bonuses the more you "Level them up" by succeeding in the game. Few 4Xs have me startng a new game right after I finish the old one... but sometimes when I play this game I'm just psyched to unlock another god, or play again with the new powers my leveled up current god now has from my last game. This game was a TREAT. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.

Instead of just having the four ghosts, now every stage is filled with them (sleeping, you have to move next to them to activate them) and because each half of the stage transforms as you eat pellets and items, they'll continue to spawn in, doggedly chasing you in a massive conga line. Then, when you eat a power pellet it's really satisfying to get that big ghost combo and drive that high score up. You'll still have the four main ghosts though and they still serve as the biggest obstacle, as the four regulars have erratic AI as they always have. Several different levels and several activities per level keep things interesting enough, though for me I just enjoy putting it on for a few quick games now and then. I'm also a pretty big fan of the music, it sets the mood and adds energy to the game that it just didn't have before, emphasizing the frantic nature of things.
Unfortunately, they added (after the game was out for a few months (at least on the PS3 version)) social media buttons into it and yes, it's just as disgusting as it is in every other game. No, I don't want to share my pointless steam achievement to facebook, Namco. No decent person thinks that kind of thing is worth telling their social media friends about. Every time you finish a stage, facebook buttons. Hell, even on the main menu they push that trash in your face. It's irritating and detracts a little from the fun of the game, however I would still recommend PAC-MAN CE DX despite it. There's sheer gaming joy to be had here so I'll keep playing it.
Now, there's a mistake you can make regarding buying this game that I feel compelled to warn you of. ONLY buy the DX/DX+ version. There is an earlier version simply called Championship Edition that's on the playstation store (PSP, PS Vita, PS3) that has very little of what I've described here. There's one quiet song, no ghost chaining (just the original four), one level and the speed mechanic is not very noticeable. I found it boring, especially coming from this and looking for a portable version. If that sounds more like your kind of thing than the DX version, don't let my warning stop you. It's pretty much just a slightly more interesting version of Pac-Man. I just want to give context, that's all.
In a nutshell: Pac-Man dumbed down for the modern gamer. Everyone gets to feel like a rock star superstar stud so...no one does. Wheeeee...

Unwritten Tales sits somewhere between the two. It's not perfect, but it is good enough to enjoy. The voice acting is good, the scenes look good and the puzzles are fairly logical. There's good features like double clicking an exit to skip the walking to it - so there is not much time spent waiting for characters to traverse scenes (and generally there's not absurdly long routes in any particular scene or area unlike Deponia). Instead of attacking your opponent directly and clearing their minions in order to survive, you're trying to build a hero that will beat their hero. You're basically sending them on a journey; supporting them with supplies and giving them creatures to fight, so they'll grow stronger. At the end, the grand battle happens and the last man standing wins! Of course there's spells you can use to try to kill your opponent's hero earlier than that, but without those that's the basic flow of the game. Wow, this game is fantastic, hands-down THE best RTS I've played. My friend says that he'd play it over DEFCON, and with good reason. It's an RTS that has a great combination of economic, political, and military control for any nation of your choosing (The game takes place in the year 2001 though, so some nations may not have up-to-date flags, territory control, etc.).
Pros:
-Play as ANY nation. Some nations are harder to develop than others, but if you'd like to make Nepal or Sierra Leone a world superpower, then you can do it.
-Game makes you feel like you're actually running a country. Multiple layers of depth are found under economy, politics, and military tabs. You can control things as intricate as raising taxes of vegetables and fruit for your nation.
-The battle system is pretty well designed, with multiple types of vehicles with different uses and statistics. You can even design your own mechanical weapons.
-If you manage to find a multiplayer roleplay server, the experience is great
Cons:
-The game doesn't come in full screen. It's not a huge issue to me, but devs said they're working on it for those who do mind.
-The AI can act a little funky sometimes. Nations will sometimes declare war on nations 2 continents away for no reason.
-I didn't find the game to be easily moddable, such as when I tried to install a "modern-day setting" mod that crashed the game upon startup. Maybe I did it wrong.
-The multiplayer server lobby is glitched, with servers not being taken off the list despite them being shut down. I recommend going to the game's discussion site to find multiplayer servers.
The game is well worth the $10, and devs are currently working on fixing some bugs it has, so I'm looking forward to playing more.

This game really scratches a particular itch, and does so well.
The event-driven map-based exploration is spot on, and the deck/turn-based combat system is light yet nuanced enough to stay interesting for the several playthroughs I've done so far. Moreover, the story branches, giving some nice replayability. The wide array of options for characters is huge, and the wide array of gear you can find and craft is nearly as impressive.
If you want a turn-based resource management/exploration/story-driven game, this is probably your jam. I know it was mine.
Worth the full price; if this is ever on sale, do not hesitate.

I thought Shadowrun: Returns was an impressive game, but Dragonfall makes it look like a mere proof of concept.
Combining an outstanding plot, a remarkable amount of content (much of which is easily missed), multiple ways to solve quests (particularly non-violent solutions, given that combat awards neither experience nor loot), memorable characters, distinct differences in character builds and solid mechanics, this is one of the best RPGs I've played,
It's not flawless - loading times are slow, some mechanics are poorly explained and there are lingering bugs, but every great RPG has a few rough edges.
This is a game well worth experiencing.

Shadowrun: Dragonfall is a great game. It really is. I bet that you'll play through it at least twice.
Dragonfall made a huge step forward from its predecessor: the classes became more diverse, the story got more refined, the dialogues feel much more fluent and more natural than in the original Shadowrun. While the first game was enjoyable but felt like a sample of a game that it could have been (you know, with all those corridor levels and little choice for the character), Dragonfall lets you decide on literally everything and play in a way you want.
Nowadays I meet less and less games that can leave you totally satisfied, the games that you can't complain about. Well, Shadowrun: Dragonfall is one of these games. I highly recommend buying it.

I was a player on West server that has now quit the game entirely. I have experienced the game from 1-80, and currently have a level 80 character, as long as 60-70 for most other characters. So all of what I have to say is from experience.
Pros
Combat is engaging and skillbased.
Engine can be funny at times.
Cons
Nexon is a terrible company.
The community is full of trolls and elitists.
Economy fluctuates rapidly without rhyme or reason.
Pay2Win
Unbalanced classes.
Early-Endgame is intimidating and unrewarding.
Progression becomes incredibly difficult.
Vindictus by definition is a Korean-made Hack 'n' Slash action game, with a choice of 8 current character classes (one upcoming) that each mostly fill a niche in the game as it stands. Storywise? The game is lacking. It's apparent that the voice acting in cutscenes are terribly synced, with zero enthusiasm whatsoever. Not to mention, it barely makes sense, it's tough to relate to any of the characters, and questing/story has devolved into a way to level up faster. As far as mechanics go, the game is amazing. Early on, the game guides you along in combat, but hits a wall in skill requirement once you begin to transition into endgame (Level 60-80). This leads to a challenging, engaging experience, as you require quite a bit of skill, and knowledge of both your character and the boss in order to succeed. Example being the solo videos out there on YouTube, which are quite impressive. Vindictus currently runs on source engine, the physics can be wonky at some times, however. With such things as clipping, or bulging polygons extending throughout the map, or a monster getting launched into space for no reason whatsoever. These can lead to much hilarity. The problems in Vindictus however, are too large for me to be able to enjoy this game anymore.
First off, let's talk about your experience from beginning to end. So you start up Vindictus. 8 characters to choose from, how exciting! Can you change their genders? Though this is something that is common in most MMOs, no. Can I change my appearance? Your options in the beginning are very limited, if you want to change up the look of your character, expect to pay $20 or more on just that. Now let's discuss the balancing of the characters, and the roles they play in Vindictus. Though this topic is very short-lived. The balancing of the game is handled very haphazardly. Currently, Hurk and Kai hold the position of godtier within the game. Where everyone else is disregarded. So if you're looking for stats, choose those two. So you've chosen your character! Time to get into the game! But wait, why don't I have any money? Well, that's because Nexon decided it would be a great idea to gut the early game by preventing gold gains from 1-25. Why? To combat botters. This is concerning however, because the earliest parts of a game are usually the most important to ensure people stay around. Surely the game will pick up right? Correct, the game does end up picking up once you are able to make some money, and have gained a general bit of knowledge about your character. Sadly, this is also when Vindictus transitions into a grindfest. Your experience at this point will consist of rushing through the "storyline", leveling up with barely any money, until you finally hit a brick-wall -- endgame. Endgame in Vindictus is atrocious. If you're not willing to expend any real currency within the level 60-80 range, don't expect to be progressing at all, unless you're incredibly lucky with drops. This is where players frequently quit, if they haven't already in the beginning. As the game becomes frustrating and unrewarding as it attempts to milk you of your money. Upgrades are incredibly hard to come by, and risks can leave you with absolutely nothing. Only the longterm players have stuck around at this point, when the game becomes a social hub for them.
The community itself is terrible. New players on the nexon forums are frequently driven away when attempting to ask questions. Which in itself is filled with trolls, and sarcastic elitists. Don't even get me started on the ingame community. Where if you don't meet the standards of the host, you can be kicked out without hesitation. So yes, the game itself is also filled with elitist jerks. Though it's to be expected out of any game, I have not seen any community similar to Vindictus in this aspect.
Now, let's talk about Nexon. Nexon is notorious for treating its players terribly. Send in a ticket? We'll answer with an automated message then get back to you after a few months. Concern about bugs and patches? There's a chance we'll even consider reading about your concerns, and if we do, it's likely we'll do nothing about it. However, here's a poorly designed event to hopefully make you forget about all of these problems. Updates? Maybe we'll release a bit of content after half a year, of course we won't tell you anything about it. Over my time with Nexon products, I'm ashamed I've stuck around with their games for so long. If Vindictus were to be handed over to another corporation, I'd gladly come back, but the way that Nexon is handling Vindictus is slowly killing the game.
TL;DR Vindictus is slowly dying. Fun for a while, but then you hit a brick wall.

Supreme Commander: FA is a RTS game that merges a plethora of unique or, at least, unusual mechanics with a classic base building strategy core to create something truly exceptional.
Some strategy games allow you to build a 'wonder' to win; here you instead build experimental units that roll over the map rather than trigger a boring win counter.
Reckless rushing and failed attacks are punished - wrecks of destroyed units can be salvaged, so a failed attack can go into the opponent's pocket, providing unique comeback potential if the attacker can't maintain constant pressure.
Resources are spent gradually over the time of building/unit construction instead of in bursts.
Now, for the downsides.
The official multiplayer is dead, however the community managed to establish a new server (google Forged Alliance Forever).
For some this is a plus, but there's only 1 real win/lose condition: respectively, destroy all the enemy Armoured Command Units (ACU) to win or have your own ACU destroyed to lose. This can lead to frustrating sniping, as each player starts with only 1 ACU and there's no way to acquire extra ones.
Single player experience is underwhelming. Relies on attacks from inaccessible areas of the map for difficulty, which is very, very cheap.

This is a fun game for the time in which it was created. The game finds its most charm in multiplayer where you can freely send nukes over the globe and bomb the hell out of your friends. However, there are a lot of problems that plague having full enjoyment of it otherwise. A lot of things need to be addressed for when SuperPower 3 comes out and I will address some of them here in my review.
First and foremost, there needs to be a much better interface. There are a terms the game wants you to handle in this game that go on unexplained in the National Budget. Things such as inflation, global tax mod, telecommunications, education. Inflation in particular you're told is very bad and you want to keep it around 2%, but you're never told why and there is no visible effects of anything going bad in your economy even if you keep it around 10% for 50 years. Additionally the only way you're given to control it is the interest rate for your economy, which has a negative effect on it. So why would you ever mess with a good thing? The entire interface just needs an improvement altogether. I'd like to know how each bar directly effects the economy.
Secondly, there needs to be popups for important events and a system that allows you to make certain events in the game popups and ignore the rest altogether. For example...I was hanging out as Israel and doing my thing. I had just reannexed the Gaza Strip and everything was going well. And then suddenly, the United States and China had declared war and nukes were flying over the globe. I would have loved to have a popup that would have paused the game in this instance so I could switch to slow-mode and watch the nukes fly and decide for myself after the damage whom to support and who to try to take land from. But as the game sits right now someone can declare war on you and invade your entire nation and you have no notification whatsoever. That's a thing that needs to be improved.
Treaties need to be improved upon. There's not really a way for you to improve the relationships you have with other nations. Eventually if you wait long enough and no great wars are started, the positive effects of the EU and other treaties already in place at the start of the game will bring you to positive relations and will result in world peace. But I should be able to give money to any nation I want to bring relations up. And currently, there's no way to do that. Nations you have bad relations with will always have bad relations with you because they'll carry out hostile actions against you. The only way to fix it is to take em over and annex them, which pisses off the world and makes them do the same thing.
Fourthly, there needs to be a great wikipedia and a company web forum for this game to help with misunderstandings. This has the capacity to be a pretty complex game and people love them and would love to enjoy them. But even now there are things I don't understand like how to do naval bombardments and marine invasions. The game doesn't explain it to me in any way. I'd love to ask on web forums, except none exist. I'd love to check a wikipedia, but the one existing is sorely lacking on almost all subjects. So that needs to be improved.
All in all, SuperPower 2 is not a great Geopolitical Simulator. It's a game that finds its most charm in nuking your friends online as a Wargame. So if you're into that, you'll find a lot of fun in this tame. Go for it!
