A fantastic 4X game that really challenges you. You start off by selecting a god who is then tasked with making sure his people survive and grow.
You have builders, gatherers, warriors, hunters, mages, demons, and all kinds of other creatures that can join your village. You gather resources, send out parties to gather supplies or fight enemies. You build and craft new buildings, items, weapons and armor that you can then equip to your people to make them stronger. Your villagers level up over time increasing their stats.
There's a ton of quests all voiced which will have you choose different outcomes based on the skills of your party members. Want to sneak into a camp instead of a direct assault, or talk you way through the enemy? You can in some cases. Some paths lead to little rewards, while other paths lead to better rewards. There are plenty of choices that lead you to wonder what the other choice would have given you or done to your party member.
Combat is sort of a card game where you have a few starting characters, and other characters that can use different abilities, or enter the battlefield themselves. Equipping shields mitigates damage, and other characters can provide protection at the expense of entering the battle.
Lots of combat choices, and it takes a little while to master. It's fun to watch but I find myself skipping the early battles and really playing the combat in the later battles with 2-3 skull enemies and above.
Villagers can be killed permanently from their wounds in battle and you are always struggling to gather enough food and wood to stay alive (not really that hard once you get the hang of it).
I haven't done much of the story, but it's a very intriguing world, one which I hope to enjoy for many hours to come!

Where to begin! Well... I’ve probably put in over 1000 hours of play into this glorious gem over the years. Incredibly detailed slider control over just about every relevant aspect of a country. You can micro-manage just about everything.  Such as, determining exactly which natural resources to exploit, how much money goes into building infrastructure, and which religion you want to convert your population too. Not a big fan of micromanagement? No problem! let the AI handle the areas you don’t want to bother with. Every decision matters and can have huge consequences. Take control over military research, including nuclear arsenals, naval, and land. Battles on land and sea have neat little animation scenes.
Nuclear conflicts are VERY satisfying. Reminds me fondly of the War Games movie in the 90s.
The game is a bit dated now, but still looks and feels nice on a new PC. Unfortunately does not support high resolutions but, once you get past this, it’s worth every penny and every minute in playtime.
There is really something quite satisfying about turning Gaza Strip and the West Bank into a global superpower! Or perhaps you would like to nuke Canada? Then this is for you.

I went through a phase where I just really wanted to live in an apocalyptic wasteland. Seeing as I couldn't, I bought a bunch of crappy games.
We were all kids once.

BUT
Why do I start with the word 'but'? Because I don't know how to write butts? No, I know how to write that.
The reason why is because this game has some pro's, and a lot of cons. I recommend, BUT.
The gameplay is refreshing, ammo-management makes the game more interesting, mostly in the campaign mode. Infantry feels nice and marching over the field with 20-30 men feels like you have a huge army, while in most games you would laugh when you see 30 grunts run towards your base.
However, there are a lot of annoyances, first off the vehicles. The vehicles are extremely fast, of course they are based from cars, but it just feels unnantural driving with 100 km/h through war-raging wastelands. It also means that your vehicles have already engaged and 3 minutes later your infantry finally arrives unless you completely micromanage the movement.
Another annoyance if your soldiers picking up all kinds of weapons, I start an assault with 10 rifleman, and suddenly 6 of my men turned into mortars and when I give an order to attack an enemy soldier, they either do nothing at all or attack the enemy with knives. While it's nice that you can pick up weapons, it should not do it by itself, or at least keep it in reserve.
Skirmish mode is decent fun, the AI isn't the stupidest ever (though they do tend to attack with 3 soldiers half the time rather than a full force). But after the first few minutes, you often start piling up on ammo. Negating the idea of limited ammo. Once you capture another outpost or a resource building, the stockpile of ammo goes through the roof. And when you attack an enemy, often you kill so many enemies you can just pick up their ammo and continue.
The game is fun for 5-10 hours. After a couple of hours you some things will start to bug you a bit, and I expect the longer you play it, the more they will annoy you.
I do not recommend buying this game for 14 euro's.
But for 5-8 euro's you can get some good hours out of it.

I actually kind of like it. The story and characters are actually pretty decent, even Aiden has started to kinda rub off on me. The voice acting and motion capture are top notch, my favorites are Noam Jenkins (Aiden Pearce) and Aaron Douglas (Jordi Chin), they did a fantastic job. The atmosphere for the game is also really well done, its always fun to whip out your phone and start listening on people's phone calls or text messages, its easy to see that the writers had a lot of fun working on those.
What KILLS IT however is how it works mechanically, and I'm not talking about the "Q to hack" thing, that's fine. The entire game just feels unpolished, sound assets sound off, the way civilians react, it doesn't feel right, you can drive somewhat near a sidewalk and people will start freaking out.
But that's not the biggest problem, the BIGGEST PROBLEM I have with the game is the DRIVING, DEAR GOD THE DRIVING. First off, all the cars and roads feel much smaller then they should be, excluding the bikes there's just some weird issue I have with it. But the driving, its atrocious, it moves like friction doesn't even exist, its impossible to control, and is just clunky, the bikes are a bit better but its still there. Number one problem with the driving is that you CAN'T SHOOT A GUN WHILE DRIVING. You'd think in a game like this where there are missions in which you have to take someone down who's in a car that they'd let you fire at them while driving, buuut nope. I had a multiplayer game where this guy would get ahead of me, shoot the car's engine to shut it down, then get back in and keep driving, because I COULDN'T SHOOT HIM WHILE IN A CAR.
Car rant over. Other then that the shooting is very jerky and I had problems aiming properly, the UI, most notably the phone menu, is a little wonky but its not too bad.
TL;DR: The best thing I can say about Watch_Dogs is that, while the story and characters are interesting and well acted, mechanically the game suffers. With really weird controls and handling you're gonna get frustrated easily. I still do reccomend it but pick it up on sale if you can.

Most people know this game was unplayable for most people in the start when released with troubles like bad performance, bugs and so forth. The game has changed since then both in playability but also price. The game in my personal opinion is fun and entertaining to play and I really enjoyed my time playing. It is true that the game is not one of the best titles from Ubisoft but I personally think they have a solid model when creating these open world games. Older examples like Far cry or Assassins Creed show that they are capable of creating great games of course with some bad ones here and there but still enjoyable to play. I got the game when first released and had some problems myself, nothing game breaking or frustrating in any way but I did have to wait a little until I could get the full experience.
The biggest flaw in my opinion is the story and the characters because Ubisoft are very capable of creating amazing characters to keep you engaged and interested in the story and what is to happen with them. You are able to get emotionally attached to these characters and keep being engaged of what is to happen next and what the consequences of your actions might be. This title didn't live up to my hopes in that matter but it definitely didn't let me down completely. I did find the characters interesting most of the times as well as the story appealing. So it was not a terrible story in any way, it is just not as great when comparing it to other titles of the same genre. But i did enjoy the story nonetheless and found the game fun and interesting since i haven't tried a hacking game before and even though they could have done somethings differently were i satisfied with the mechanics and gameplay overall.
The biggest letdown when it came to the hacking aspect was probably that it was too simplistic. I didn't expect to write lines of code or hack into the pentagon but some of the parts of the hacking aspect seemed to straight forward. All you had to do to get anywhere was a single button and then you’re good to go. The reasoning of this is because this game is an action game and needs to keep you engaged as much as possible. The menu, mobile, and weapons functions did get a bit frustrating at times and they went with some new ideas and ways to do things, which I find good so you don't get the same way of doing things over and over but they should maybe have stuck to some of the ways that they know work from previous experience. However, even though I have a feeling I want to hate some of the bad parts of the game I don't when I think about it a little more. It had its flaws what nobody’s perfect and I like the game.
Overall, I enjoyed my time playing this game and it is worth every penny when on sale. And learn from my don't buy every game on release maybe let it settle down a little and see where it leads.

I’m unsure how
landed in my inventory but as a fan of hidden object games I knew I would play it at some point. I enjoy games that dip into history for inspiration, this one plays with the tale of Elizabeth Bathory who was accused and found guilty of torturing and murdering many young women. You would think with such a spooky theme this would be a slam dunk but it was not. The game is short, the story is rather boring and the gameplay mechanics aren’t fun; the one thing in its favor is very lovely artwork. However, good visuals can’t save a game if the story and gameplay fall short in my opinion.
Your sister has summoned you to Slovakia to aid her in her work as an archaeologist, however, once you arrive you sense something is amiss. Her mail hasn’t been checked in days and her house is empty. After some snooping you realize that your sister Rose has been kidnapped. As you look into the matter you learn other girls have also met the same fate and that the disappearances are linked to the legend of Elizabeth Bathory. The game offers a slightly alternate version of history for the countess, mixing in magic and ghosts. The story tries to paint Bathory in a better light and doesn’t do the best job of it, failing to fully capitalize on the historic horror story. Most of the supporting characters are rather useless and have no personality and the main character is never even given a name. There was one plot twist in the story and even that wasn’t enough to keep me fully entertained, for a story about a bloody countess things were overall very tame.
A weak story I can tolerate but bad gameplay is hard to look past. This is a hidden object adventure game. As you walk around you’ll be met with hidden object scenes where you’re given a list of items to find in a jumbled mess. First issue, there aren’t enough scenes. Second, a personal peeve of mine, the list only shows four items at a time not all at once. Third, you’ll be playing the few amount of scenes repeatedly to find important items but also to collect gold. Why gold? To buy hints of course! Or to instantly charge your skip button during a mini game. While I find these veiled microtransactions annoying they’re not game breaking, what is though is the merchant shop. In the game there is a nice merchant you have to talk to during the story, later on he starts selling goods you can buy with gold. You can’t avoid this, you
to buy his items to progress in the story meaning you have to grind hidden object scenes over and over again to collect gold to do so. This gets boring but thankfully, and unfortunately, the scenes are rudimentary as are the very few puzzles in the game. The game offers no map, though you’re only given a small area to move around in anyway, though the arrows don’t make this very easy. A quick note, any object in the hidden item scenes that is hidden, like behind a curtain, isn’t pointed out so you won’t know that it is behind an extra step unless you click aimlessly.
The one area the game does excel in are visuals, the artwork is beautiful. The game boasts hand-drawn artwork, a lovely thing to see in the digital age. The colors are bright when need be but the game still manages to look unsettling as well. The characters are well-drawn and while the animation is limited it doesn’t hurt the game, I was actually relieved that there wasn’t much animation when characters spoke because it often makes them look lifeless. However, I found that certain items in the hidden object scenes weren’t always easy to find due to their colors blending in too well with the background. While rare, it was annoying nonetheless. There is no voice acting in the game at all and while there is music, it’s basic and uninspired.
Having read previous reviews I knew not to get my hopes up for
, but what I ended up playing was worse than expected. I beat the game in under two hours and there is no bonus content at all. The game has good ideas but they’re not implemented well. Collecting gold could have been done in a fun way instead of being repetitive in nature, items bought with gold could have been bonuses in the game or even bonus content but this didn’t happen either. There aren’t many puzzles and they’re very easy so there is little to help break up the monotony of this title. While this title has Steam trading cards there are no achievements and overall what you get is a promising idea that falls short of what it could have been. Grab on sale or avoid, this is too easy for veterans of the genre, nor something I’d recommend to new players.

A bright gem in the world of FPS shooters, Far Cry 2 takes us to a place we all know, or at least the members of our family from generations past knew - the world of struggle, strife and corruption. It comes alive in spectacular style and is one of the most realistic of all the fictional locales used in today´s PC games. The guns, the glory, the greed all merge and create an authentic and powerful story. Driven by an excellent gameplay engine, Far Cry 2 enables you to fight in a variety of ways, from employing stealth to outright firefighting. You can kill you enemies silently from afar, using the vegetation as your cover, or engage in gun battles in a variety of ways. The hillsides offer excellent fallback positions and allow you to plan your next  move. Whether you want to pick everyone out in an area using your sniper rifle, or burrow  your way through their compounds and outposts, Far Cry 2 will offer you ample chances to do both.
This installment offers a wide diversity of of weapons,  manual loading, semi automatic  and fully automatic. Explosive weapons are also available. Some come with their own scopes, allowing you to sniper bomb enemy cars before, or after the driver and his fellow soldiers get in.  The grass and trees can be set on fire, allowing you to create a shield of fire to drive the enemies while you reposition yourself and shoot them before they can regain their bearings.
A serious game for a veteran player, Far Cry 2 is a haven for the creative killer, the adventurer and the explorer. Get it, if you really want to see the wild side of Africa in all its glory.

This is a game about inventory management, random events and clicking end turn until crafting and resource gathering timers are done.
When I started the game up I had high hopes.  The world seemed interesting and it looked and sounded nice.  However I was immediately overwhelmed by an abundance of stats, resources and strange encounters.  The game isn't overly difficult as it turns out, but the hopeless tutorial and poor user interface make for a very steep learning curve.
The heart of the game is crafting.  Send your villagers out to gather lots of resources, then bring them home and craft items to make them more powerful, allowing you to research better items and repeat the whole process.  Each recipe has many possible results depending on what resources you use.  This means there is a nice variety of items to make, but unfortunately you need to gather every possible resource and then combine them manually, one by one, until you find the best option.
While your are going about your business you will be given quests and be afflicted by various random encounters and wandering monster attacks.  This is where the abundance of stats come into play.  Each encounter can be resolved by various means according to what your expedition is good at.  Sadly (and obviously) you cannot plan for the random encounters and even if you could, trying to balance the numerous stats of 6+ different characters would be a nightmare due to the lack of any sort of expedition overview.
The actual resolution is achieved through a card-based mini-game.  These all work the same way, but the names of abilities and stats are different depending on the encounter.  While tactical play is possible, the mini-game is moderately interesting at best and slow and tedious at worst, when it needed to be amazing.  You can auto-resolve, but this just makes it even more of a dice roll.
Inventory and equipment management was a huge let-down and a major part of why I cannot recommend this game.  The interface is as you would expect in an RPG with a single character, but here you are managing 15+ characters and sending out expeditions of 6+.  As a result, the vast majority of my time was spent in the equipment screen, trying to make everyone effective without exceeding their weight limit.  In the end, too much work and not enough play.

I'm generally a fan of free-roam first-person shooters, but Far Cry 2 was a big disappointment. If you're a hardcore shooter fan that likes a challenge, solid gunplay, diverse gameplay, and refreshing mechanics, this isn't the shooter for you.
Nearly every quest boils down to "drive to the other side of the map and kill some people / blow something up". There is no variety in enemies - you face thugs with low health and bad AI toting rifles, or thugs with low health and bad AI toting shotguns, or thugs driving trucks with mounted machine guns on the back. There is very little recoil to any of the automatic weapons, which really hurts the gunplay. As a result, none of the traditional firearms are fun or interesting - if you are in it for the grenade launchers, double-barrel shotguns, and flamethrowers, you might have more fun than I did.
The game is pathetically easy even with the difficulty maxed - I had to install a mod that further increases the difficulty and weapon recoil just to feel like I wasn't playing a kids' game. The only moments when the game is difficult are when the AI is cheating - bullets can penetrate sheet metal and thin wood, which is cool, but the enemies can see through anything they can shoot through. Taking cover in a shack or some brush is signing your own death warrant, because your enemies will continue shooting you accurately even though you can't see them. This isn't some intelligent "he went into that shack so I'll shoot at the shack" AI - they can just see through walls, and they'll do it whether or not anyone saw you enter.
The game certainly has its moments - the first time I was rescued by a buddy was one of the most memorable experiences I've had in gaming (but the buddy-rescue system quickly gets stale and sometimes becomes a nuisance when you have to babysit your buddy for 20 ****ing minutes so they don't get killed). The large and diverse landscape is a refreshing change from the scenery in most shooters - you certainly feel like you're in Africa. I found the unique realism elements - the map you physically hold in front of you in the game (accurately simulates crashing while looking down at the map!) repairing vehicles, weapons that degrade in quality, and fire propagation, very interesting.
There isn't much of a story to the game - you can take random copy-and paste quests all over the map (I am not joking about copy-and-paste) or take story quests from either of the two factions in the central town. Neither faction represents the "good" side, so I felt no connection with the events in place beyond getting paid diamonds to complete missions. I guess that's how a mercenary would look at things, but it doesn't make for an engaging game in my case.
Far Cry 2 has some good ideas, but overall the game doesn't quite click for me. On the other hand, there are a lot of positive reviews for it, so your milage may vary.

Short: It's great and a unique blend of 4X, RPG, crafting and card game and quite some survival aspects. Plus it has pretty good quest writing to my mind and some of the nicest devs around.

You are on the road with your group/expedition all the time as you complete quests and chase rare materials. There is an abundance of events. My game says I participated 15% of all events... and I paricipated in A LOT OF EVENTS already. They are wonderfully written and the speaker is pretty good.
In my favorite quest a dwarf smith wants to date a somewhat evil forest spirit. This one then wants you to help "rescue" children from evil orcs, plot twist the orcs are nice and you can convince them to leave the children with you. Thea features a unique mix of gameplay elements from fantasy RPGs and 4X games. Its core conflict resolution mechanic is a deceptively simple card game, which is easy to learn but hard to master.
In a nutshell, your villagers gather resources to craft better gear which they use to overcome various challenges like bandits, ancient tombs, giants, werewolves, dragons, and witches who are trying to steal your children.
You send expeditions (parties made up of your villagers) into the wilderness to find rare materials and deal with problems or quests head on. If all goes to plan your party won't be cursed, poisoned, robbed, severy wounded or worse.
The game features evocative art and a nice soundtrack. Quests are excellently narrated. The game doesn't take it self too seriously and there is plenty of humor. It is highly replayable due to the randomized nature of the encountered events / resolutions. It has the same strong "one more turn" drive that Civilization has (incidentally, a game of Thea also takes about as long as a game of Civilization).
Highly recommended.

I tried to like this game, and it has a lot going for it -- a hex-map turn-based survival game! -- but an uninformative interface and some irritating gameplay features made me put it down.
You start out as a god in control of a single village which serves as your home base, populated by a starting band of villagers of varying skillsets.  These villagers trek out into the world under your control to gather resources, defeat enemies, and solve mysteries.
The basic problem is that, as you play, the world slowly gets more threatening.  To stay ahead of the curve, you need to continuously level up your villagers.  Unfortunately, once you're well into the game, these initial villagers become irreplaceable because you can't level up replacements fast enough to keep up with the world; if your main party takes a beating, you will likely be in a losing battle against the world and consigned to a grinding loss.
Also, the game's interface doesn't provide enough information to deal with the massive number of encounter types.  The game displays the absolute difficulty of an encounter (1-5 skulls) but doesn't provide any information on your own party's abilities or even what skills are relevant.  Determining your party's suitability to engage in a tactical vs hunting vs intellect  vs sneak challenge is extremely tedious at best, and can't be done at all once you're presented with an encounter option.  Combat can also be quite frustrating because of the near total lack of information about an enemy.  I easily dealt with several two-skull challenges in one game only to be demolished by a two-skull encounter with a radically different enemy composition--details about an enemy party are presented only when it's too late to decide and even then are incredibly vague.  And no, you can't scout them out beforehand.
I liked the crafting/resource gathering aspect, and the combat/encounter system was interesting but had started to wear out its welcome when I gave up.  The designers also clearly put a lot of effort into the story and writing, but it wasn't enough to keep me engaged.

I would liken this to King of Dragon Pass, or other sort of RPG and exploration type of game. The obvious similarity, as pointed out by many others, is to the exploration phase of Civilization, when much of the world was still shrouded in the fog.
Here the concept: You start with a village in the aftermath of a world destroyed by darkness. Now, your aim is to survive, thrive and eventually defeat the big bad. There is a village simulator, in the sense of producing resources, crafting, and keeping the village alive and healthy. You lead expeditions or parties of characters out to explore the world, find treasures, search ruins and destroy evil. You have to balance the 2, as well as many other luxuries - but you won't have the resources or time to obtain them all in a desolate and unforgiving world.
Pros: Good world-build and narrativising. The lore really sets a sense of dread and devastation at every turn.
Solid mechanics, from combat to research to building the village.
Some complexity, but aided by clear and extensive tutorials (and even video tutorials). Combat is quite different from most other games, but the tutorial clears the confusion after a battle or two.
Varied encounters, enough that it doesn't devolve into a nonsensical choice merely between 'search for goodies' and 'leave'. Has any gamer ever picked the 'leave' option??
Cons: This has been likened to a rogue-like, in that you will lose often. However, what is good for me is the meta-ability to power up your villagers after every game, based on how well you have done. I am sure there's a mode/mod for the full rogue-like experience of having no advantages if you prefer that too.
For me, the innovative gameplay and emphasis on narrative makes this interesting and fun enough from other games out there.

I personally had never heard of this little gem until I watched Jesse Cox's Fan Fr-aturday where he played The Book of Unwritten Tales 2,
.  During that gameplay, I found that the game's quirky comments, characters, music, and look was really entertaining.  Of course, it was clear that there was some story involved, and having never heard of the series, I decided to play it from the beginning.
The game itself is a point-&-click puzzle rpg.  Meaning, movement, interactions, even crafting, all just simply requires your mouse.  It is set in a medieval fantasy-esque world where there are mages, dragons, gnomes, elves, bounty hunters... The world is very colorful indeed.
:  This game was released in 2009, and the graphics are pretty evident of that.  It is by no means an ugly game, it is very colorful and the characters all are very unique.  The animated scenes are nothing to boast about, but it could be worse.  Overall, compared to games that are out today, the visuals are in short, dated, and the characters look quite... odd.  Especially the wood elf, Ivo.  That being said, I still enjoyed the look of the game keeping it's age in mind.
:  The music is lovely, though, there isn't a huge variety of tracks.  Still, the music fits the various scenes you are in, and, doesn't get annoying after listening to it over and over, especially if you get stuck in an area.  The character voices are charming, and fit each of the characters.  Sounds of the various items in the world and creatures, all good.  No complains on sound at all.
:  As I said, this is a point and click game.  So, you can pretty much toss your keyboard to the side and just sit back with a cup of tea in one hand, mouse in the other and have at it.  There are some areas where the positioning of the various items you interact with are close to your "items" toolbar, which sometimes calls for maneuvering of the character's positioning, if possible.  The item's tool bar goes into auto hide until you hover your mouse down over the area, then it pops right up like toast from a toaster.  The cursor often changes to a orangey-red color when you are hovering over an item you can interact with, so if you get stuck, scanning around for intractable items is a good way to try to figure out how to move forward.  Overall, I had no issues with the controls.
:  The story was... well, broken up into four chapters.  Each chapter taking you into a different area.  There is no epic background story of the world and various characters like you would find in some rpgs.  In fact, there's a war going on between an evil witch queen and her creatures verses the arch mage and the humans, dwarves, and so on.  The mission is to prevent the evil queen from obtaining something that can shift the balance of the war, yet, it really felt the war was just a simple backdrop and most of the game was the characters bumbling about.  The interactions between the characters are preciously adorable at times, and over all, it is entertaining.
:  For the most part, the puzzles were not too difficult.  Some, easier than others.  My problem was that I would already have figured out how to solve the puzzle, but, would be ten steps ahead of what the game itself has lined up.  So instead of doing steps 1-5 in consecutive order, I would do step one, and see already how to complete step 5.  Of course, that would leave me running around trying to figure out where the hell do I go for steps 2-4.  The game is pretty forgiving, dialog options allow you to redo them if you selected the incorrect choice, and most puzzles just reset if you made a mistake.
:  The ending did feel a bit abrupt, and, while I felt that great sensation of completing a game, I felt that the ending was a bit rushed.
The Book of Unwritten Tales is a fun and witty puzzle rpg, of the point-&-click kind.  The puzzles vary in difficulty, but to the perceptive and detailed oriented player, they should be no problem.  Story is a bit short and unengaging, but it doesn't really matter for the game play.  Characters are fun and unique enough, providing entertaining dialogues.  Over all I'd recommend this game to anyone who is interested in the genre and isn't picky about the dated look.

PROS
1. The graphics- for a small adventure game I thought the graphics were outstanding especailly the backgrounds, there are also certain characters who look great, such as the minotaur in chapter 4.
2. the voice acting- the va work in the game is for the most part amazing espcially wilbur, for the most part all the voice actors get into their roles and you can tell are having a blast playing these zany characters.
3. Length- I was actually shocked this game was so long my play time says 15 hrs but is actually longer bc I played the demo first to see if I liked the game. So when I purchased the full game I sped through the demo parts that I had already beaten.
4 Dialogue- the Dialogue is pretty great, I would say a good 80 percent of the jokes land, and there were more than a few times I laughed out loud.
5. Difficulty- as adventure games go this one is good for beginners, there a few brain teasers but for the most part the game is pretty easy, especially if you use the spacebar (the spacebar highlights all interactive hotspots on the screen). Your sister invites you to her current excavations, however, she's nowhere to find and it seems that she was kidnapped. Could it be in relation with the castle nearby, owned by the legendary Bathory, a cruel countess?
The story is interesting in itself. However, the course of actions is perhaps very disturbing. I mean, I can't see why some actions have to be done. I mean, why would I need milk instead of steam to show an hidden message. You've understood: the translation isn't quite a success, hence the confusion that can reign if you're not playing in English.
However, the major failure of the game is the gameplay: while it's the standard one (find items, use them, clear hidden objects scenes, solve puzzles), I was mainly thrown into a game where I only managed to understand that the town place can be moved on the side after a long time (when you're stuck and searching for a mechant... that's when I accidentally discovered the trick). Sometimes, you have also arrows on the side. And if you want to go back? Well, you have a return arrow next to your inventory (functionning also for the puzzles or hidden objects scenes). As I've already said for Ghost Encounters: Deadwood, it's not possible to have that kind of gameplay now as people are used to see arrows on the middle of their screens. And it was also a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to make the inventory appears. But like I've said, the actions to take are sometimes hard to guess. As I was already♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with the gameplay, I was finishing a scene and clicked on a pen that was near the arrow for backing out. Guess what? I'm not sure my pen was counted or not, but I got a message saying that if I go back, I'll loose the progress in the scene. Do I want to get out? Nope but I was still booted out. I don't know if it's because I assume that Yes = exit and No = stay and that I've misread the question or if it's a translation problem but it was really frustrating.
And the frustration was already at a high level as I was stuck, realized that the translation was badly done and that clicking on the right object wasn't always counting (I remember the glasses on the sister's desk: I was clicking on them but it has only counted when I clicked on the left glass - not even the right was working).
And that ammount of frustration couldn't be lowered with the nice idea of buying hints or objects at the famous mechant with money you can find by completing hidden objects scenes with a gold coin on them. It is a nice idea. But I prefer to hunt for hints that play hidden objects scenes and get frustrated by the clicking, the translation and the arrow back.
I loved the graphics, in a cartoon style. I really liked the mystery behind, the flashy colors when needed and the soundtrack was ok.
But Bathory: The Bloody Countess is a bloody mess. Even Deadwood was less frustrating but there... I'm under the impression that the game was made for just having a Bathory tale, without any consideration for the player. Bad gameplay killed the game. It could have been an ok one but there.... Avoid it (unless you're into trading cards but in that case, buy it at a low price or in a bundle).

TL;DR Play it for the exploration and platforming.
Strider is a metroidvania style game. For the uninitiated, this means it's a platformer with vast explorable levels and tons of little nooks and crannies to find unlockables and hidden items. It's also got an emphasis on combat and by the end of the game you'll find you have a lot of tools at your disposal to be able to take care of the various enemies that get thrown your way. That said, I'm going to break this review down into the various components that are considered essential in the execution of a good metroidvania and see how
measures up.
Strider is an excellent protagonist. He's extremely capable and exists as an extention of your fingertips. From the moment you start the game, you'll notice how fluidly and accurate the control scheme is and this allows you to truly take ownership of the game. For the most part, if you get hit, it's because you failed to react in time and not because the controls failed you.
Strider sticks to any wall or ceiling and is able to climb every surface from the start. Sword attacks are directional and instantaneous so you're easily able to parkour your way through the levels, slicing and dicing as you go. This feeling is unique to the game, and I think what makes it a lot of fun.
Combat is somewhat lacking. The majority of your experience will have you mashing the attack button repeatedly to take down enemies, and the only true variation on your regular attack is the charged form. Shielded enemies provide incentive to use your charged slash, but end up feeling like more of a nuisance that breaks up the button-mashing than a variable challenge. Additionally, you have special abilities you unlock as the game goes on, all of which better enable you to steamroll your way through the game. But you will likely rely on your sword slash for the majority of the game as it retains its strength throughout.
Not only is the typical combat somewhat repetitive, but there is absolutely no incentive to kill anything. I realized this about a half-hour into my playthrough and just started skipping all nonessential enemies. There is no kill score to rack up, no experience points or customizable character additions to get. You kill red shirts for being annoying and that's about it. So yes, it's still fun, but I think it's a huge missed opportunity not to reward a player for killscore. Add to that that it largely lacks challenge, and you find it fall short here.
I have mixed feelings on this. At some points the level design is brilliant and rewarding, and at others it's equally dull and infuriating. Games in this style commonly emplace artificial barriers to progress. Think of The Legend of Zelda, where you need to get that next gadget (such as the boomerang) before you're able to reach certain areas of the game. The way strider uses this mechanic, however, can be infuriating. You'll find yourself skipping so much content because it's behind a door that you can't unlock yet or you haven't gotten the kunai. It's not fun. By the time I was able to access everything, I no longer cared to backtrack through the entire game to find the stuff. Compare this to a game like Shadow Complex, where part of the game actually has you backtracking through previous areas for actual progression after you've unlocked all the gadgets and you'll see that Strider falls short here.
Where the game shines, however, is the platforming. This is something that I can confidently say the game did well. The game gives you a lot of tools to navigate its levels and you'll find yourself using all of them simultaneously before you even realize it. This ninja-feel is something the game achieves well, and is extremely rewarding.
One of the things I'd read about going into the game is that the boss fights were repetitive and recycled. I actually couldn't disagree more. Even though you see some bosses more than once, they are not at all the same fights in most of those cases. Now, one of my qualms is that they are sometimes unfair in that some attacks are impossible to react to on your first attempt. Unfortunately this is typically the only challenge to overcome as they generally are very easy to best. Overall, boss fights are fun if not a little frustrating at times.
I have mixed feelings for the game overall. Up front, I'll say that I played it on Normal difficulty and don't intend to play it again. It lacked challenge for the most part, and I saw a lot of missed opportunity in a somewhat decent game. My biggest problem with it is the abysmal level design. Still, it was a fun game to play once and I think a lot of players will have found enough reason to go back for all the extras once they've unlocked all the gadgets. I do recommend waiting until the game is on sale, but it's definitely worth your time to play once you own it.

Well, this was an unexpected pleasure. I'm struggling to think of a single complaint... It's not an earth-shatteringly innovative game, but that's ok. Strider is a exceptionally well crafted metroidvania-style game, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. Didn't take itself too seriously, which is always appreciated. Extremely fast, fluid and reponsive character movement and combat. Backtracking never felt like much of a chore, it's fun just running around. Combat is reasonably challenging (and there's always Hard mode for the masochists out there). The addition of new abilities was well paced, and mixed things up just enough to keep it fresh. You really owe it to yourself to check Strider out, if you're at all a fan of the genre.

I don't know exactly why this game is so fun, but it is.  It's fairly text-heavy, the graphics are pretty basic, some of the areas start to look the same, the world has limited interactivity beyond objects immediately relevant to the plot, there are a number of little glitches--and yet, in spite of these drawbacks I've logged about 100 hours in cyberpunk dystopian Berlin.
The variety of character classes is one of the biggest draws for me, plus the fact that you can actually play a couple of truly viable hybrid classes. I played a Shaman on my first playthrough (steep learning curve, there) and a Decker/Rigger on my second.  The different skill trees and 'etiquette' functions are incorporated nicely into the dialogue and story options, so that based on your character's configuration, you will have to come up with different problem-solving techniques for various hurdles.
Monika is written as a bit of a MarySue, but the other party members have wit and interesting back stories.  Several of them experience dynamic shifts in their relationship with you as the game progresses, which is cool.  It also seems like there are several different endings, based on a series of decisions you make in the last two missions, which gives the game a better replay value, imo.

King's Bounty: Warriors of the North tells the story from a young Viking who started his journey to help his own homeland, but due to twist and turns ends up in a conquest that threathens the whole world! The game cleverly uses the old games in their story by references and characters that you may remember. Personally for me this is a big plus: it makes the world more alive, it feels like actual changed has happened and that the story is not just another seperate world threathning event going on in the world.
The story is quite well made, everything exist out of dialogues though, quite some long ones at times. So be prepared to read a lot if you want to follow the story and side quests! The game rarely forces you to follow the main story and gives you plenty of freedom to do your side quests.
The combat I personally found more difficult yet better balanced than the previous games. For newcomers: the combat is a turn based battle in which one group of units moves at a time. During your turn you also got the ability to use spells to power up your own units or weaken / damage the opponent. Every unit kind has it's weaknesses and strenghths. For example: Undead get bonusses fighting on a graveyard while Demons get a bonus fighting in Fiery areas. You also have to consider how your troops react to eachother. Another example: Humans morale will drop if you also have undead troops in your army. Not to mention your skills and items can improve certain groups or improve the morale. All in all, it 's realy a strategic game in which you need to take a lot of factors in consideration and not just barge in with the strongest units you can find.
Just like the previous King's Bounty games, the game does an excellent job at making each gameplay unique by randomizing where you get certain units and the exact composition of enemy armies, this really improves the replay value of the game and can make it quite unpredictable at times.
The only real negative point I can say about this game are the unavoidable crashes. Once again this is one of those games you need to be sure to

King’s Bounty: Warriors of the North is highly underrated game which in my opinion deserves more time in the spotlight. Even though the game is a bit older at this point it still has a lot to offer for people who enjoy tactical RPGs like The Heroes of Might and Magic when that series used to be good.
When compared to the earlier entries to the King’s Bounty series, it doesn’t offer that much more new content. The gameplay is pretty much the same, graphics are a bit enhanced but it doesn’t look that much different and it overall follows suit. But nevertheless, it is worth the playthrough. It offers a lengthy campaign that is similar to the earlier entries but still throws a few twists and turns here and there. The score is fitting to the game and overall very well made.
However, the game has its flaws. The occasional boss fights are really annoying and they force you to a specific setup in order to get through them, there is a lack of voice acting which is really required in game these days and the need to kite mobs can get tedious in the long run.
All in all, I can recommend the game in good conscience to people who are looking for a tactical RPG and who can look past the clunkiness brought by the years.

This game is fantastic.
I've heard people say that it's just one of these typical early access strategy games, but I disagree with that opinion.
Thea is an turn-based strategy game in a pre-industrial, mystic attached world. You play as one of 8 unlockable gods from which each one has special bonuses. In the begin you get two of them randomly unlocked. You start with a little village which you can devide in different groups to explore the land, gather materials and food or fight enemies. Combat happens through card games whereat the villagers in your group are your cards, but you can also choose to skip the games if you are not into this style of fighting. I suggest to at least try this out once because it is really enjoyable.
Beasts attack more often at night - unfortunately the "nights" are longer than just one round (it's the human's fault, but shh... spoiler!).
The game has an amazing, unique combat system which allows you to fight with many different options. You can fight directly in willingness to take chances and maybe let some of your villagers die or you can try to find a solution in challenges that are social, sickness, hunting, magic, physical or logical. Because of that each of your villagers is important in it's own way and has it's own skills. Villagers can level up and gain new skills or improve old ones - randomly generated so that no villager has the same skills as another.
There are many different classes of villagers, so many that I didn't get all of them in my 19h playtime. You beginn with 3 classes: warrior, gatherer and craftsman. Later on you get healers, hunters, witches, wise mans, inventors, animals, bandits, ghosts, demons, dwarves, elves, orcs, mystics and more. Some of them you get through quests, some of them settle down and some are childs that are coming of age. For childs you can choose which class they will become - in the begin there are just few options, but the more buildings you explore and build, the more choices you have.
You can explore recipes by gathering exploration points which you get by doing quests or going through experiences. There are 3 kinds of recipes: One for better items you can gather, one for things you can craft with your craftsmen and one for the buildings.
There are 3 different ways to win the game (yes, the number 3 has a deep meaning in Thea xD). One is by pure domination - that means, you have explored a lot and a well build village with a big population -, one is by solving the worlds tree quest and one is by solving the giant quest (which I think is the most difficult way). There are a lot more quests than these, one for example deals with the god/godess itself, but you don't need to solve them to win.
Thea has an interesting point of view - villagers matter, each one of them is important. You have a different perspective than in games like Anno, because although you are a god you don't look down on the people - you play them. I sympathized with the villagers a lot more than with the ones in other games, also because of the character design through which each of my people becomes unique (different cards with different names, designed fitting to the different classes).
I could tell a lot more about Thea, but I think these were the most important things to say.
All in all it's a really fascinating game with a thrilling story and a dark, mystic atmosphere. If you love to explore, I certainly suggest you to try it out. Also if you love to play with cards, read interesting quests, make your own choices (yes, choices are important!) and improve your villagers.
Big kudos to the developers.
I will now continue playing Thea.

This game is refreshing, innovative and set in the universe of a game that's deeply rooted into my childhood. It's nothing like Hearthstone or Magic, it offers a whole new set of rules that you can explore and master.
As mentioned above, this game is
like Hearthstone or Magic, as far as I'm aware, there aren't other games that use this style. Each game consists of 5 Chapters, and each Chapter you can play up to 4 cards.
As with all card games, you start with a hand drawn from your deck. You do not play cards directly against your opponent. Rather, you play cards against
. Let me go into a bit more detail on this.
All Legends start off with 2 base attack, 30 health and 0 gold. Gold is used to 'pay' for weapons, armour and other effects. You gain gold either by slaying creatures, or other support cards. Certain cards can be used to directly strike your opponent, which will help you  in the final battle. It is possible, and often very worth it, to raise your base attack, as all weapons in the game can only be used a certain amount of time before breaking. The final battle is an event that occurs when you reach the 5th area of the 5th Chapter. As the name implies, you and your foe beat each other senseless until one stops moving and explodes.
As with Hearthstone, there are several game modes that you can take part in. Sadly, while the names vary from Hearthstone, the effect is the same.
Solo lets you test new decks against each of the classes in the game, and give a few Steam Achievments for completing them.
Casual lets you play against other players with nothing but your pride on the line.
Ranked lets you play against players of similar skill and lets you climb the ladder.
Dungeoneering is like the Arena in Hearthstone; You get to choose from a few random cards to build a new deck to face off against other players that built new decks on the spot.
Sadly, getting booster packs on this game is pretty hard unless you pay for them, and some of the high tier cards are pretty crazy. Some daily quests give you 40 coins, while some give you 200. Epic Quests tend to double or triple that.
The problem is, buying a booster will cost you 1000 coins.
There are some level up rewards, but in my opinion it doesn't justify the insane cost of cards.
That being said, there are no quest-ecxlusive cards that give an unfair edge like Naxx in Hearthstone, and Jagex still have to make money out of this. So honestly speaking, if you like the game, feel free to spend a bit of money on it. If you don't, you'll still be able to have fun as you play!
Now, I'm not sure of this next one is the game's fault or mine, but the resolution seems a bit fuzzy, even at its highest settings. Though I only have a GTX 650 for a graphics card, so this might be a problem on my end. Either way, it's not nearly enough to deter me from this gem of a game.
Well done, Jagex, keep it up!

Shadowrun: Dragonfall is an outstanding improvement upon Shadowrun Returns and an excellent example as a presentation of a cyberpunk universe and as a roleplaying game, that you most certainly would like to see in your library of roleplaying game collection. It is also a different approach to the linear, minimalistic design of Shadowrun Returns, all thanks to the development behind the magic which clearly listened to its community. By this, in my book, Herebrained Schemes has proved themselves as one of the open and progressive development teams in the industry. - Which, undisputably, rocks.
Shadowrun: Dragonfall, starts with a simple enough campaign introduction which includes a small group of Shadowrunners doing their everyday job. As they, along with our protagonist, proceed deep into this twisted, mysterious job, they face a plot twist that shakes the foundation of their own perspective of the world and history. - Therefore, the Dragonfall Campaign starts as our heroes fight against a great set of conspiracies and problems regarding their community, as well as their personal nightmares that were haunting each and every one of their pasts. Needless to say, our heroes are scarred but resistant team of excellent runners from different backgrounds.
Remember, Side Quests and enviromental details that are being presented within optional storylines are the ones that makes a roleplaying game; a live, breathing world.
If you aren't familiar with the Shadowrun brand itself and/or would like to try out a turn-based roleplaying game like this, I strongly recommend you to start from Shadowrun Returns and proceed to Dragonfall campaign. Only then, you will agree with my opinion that this franchise and this development is worth following and supporting.
Would you like to know something that also rocks? - It runs on GNU/Linux. Which, again in my book, is a huge thumbs up for any product.

I must say that I came through a few bugs during gameplay. Once I was at the end of a battle that lasted quite a while and I was really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that that occured. For example the enemy turn would just not continue or you can not do any action even though you still have Action Points. If any of these 'freezes' occur, I found that opening the menu and closing it (maybe twice or going into Karma menu) it goes away. With this finding my experience improved. Nonetheless, I find it odd that such a fundamental bug is still in the game.
Gameplay
* I loved seeing a tree for attributes and skills with free reign of how you want to build your character
* Load/Save can be abused for putting points in skills that affect dialogue because you can see the prerequisites in the dialogue option.
* Hard mode was only hard in the beggining while I adjusted to the game. Understanding of cover mechanics, skill points optimization, tazer guns (that thing is too OP) made the game a bit of a chore of repeating strategy to advance without any harm.

All in all I would definitely recommend this game. Big thumbs up!

It is common for developers to tout their "dark and emotionally complex" character arcs, and it's usually just an excuse for grimdark angsty plots that do not engender emotional investment in the characters.  No matter how sad a character's fate is, its emotional impact is limited by how much the game can make you care about the character in the first place.
Dragonfall genuinely made me care about its characters (with the possible exception of, uh, what's his face, the rigger, he felt like an afterthought).  The gameplay is more polished than in Shadowrun Returns, but the story is just on an entirely different level.  The dialogue trees are engaging and full of surprises that play with genre conventions, the main storyline is intriguing, the loyalty mission chains are fascinating and occasionally heartwrenching, and basically I recommend the hell out of this game.

Shadowrun: Dragonfall is effectively a giant DLC, the size of another game, for Shadowrun: Returns.  Because of this, most praise and criticism in
of Shadowrun: Returns applies to this game as well.  This review will primarily focus on the changes.
Some aspects of the design were improved.
Shadowrun: Dragonfall is less linear than Shadowrun: Returns, and most important decisions you make will affect the ending.
Several new weapons and spells have been added.
You can now save at will, outside combat and conversations.
Other aspects of the design are disappointing.
I was hoping for more new weapons, spells, and armor, and perhaps other positive changes in the combat system (more statuses, called shots, a matrix that feels different from meatspace, etc.).
Most music is reused from Shadowrun: Returns.  Yes, it was good.  Yes, some new tracks were added.  Yes, they are of similar quality.  It still feels disappointing.
The Bloodlines quest has an infuriating stealth segment.  Guards literally seem to have eyes in the back of their head, such that you will be spotted even if they are facing away from you, unless there is a wall in-between.  The guards patrol very quickly, making it hard to get past them in time, even when you know what needs to be done.  Worst of all, your train of companions cannot be directly controlled and will frequently get spotted.  This should have either been turn-based, with proper vision cones, or removed.
The developers have clearly favored a small number of possible builds for the main character and party.  Players without clairvoyance will be punished for deviating from the favored builds mid to late game.  Having to start over, after investing so much time, is likely to prevent many people from enjoying the game.
Since you now have a large number of companions, you will want to play a build that is not redundant.  The only main character builds that are not redundant are adepts (still somewhat redundant due to Glory) and mages (recommended).
You better buy and keep any tasers you find, and any other action point damaging weapons or spells.  Be sure that most if not all party members (not just your main character) have a way to cause AP damage.  It will be almost impossible to win the final battle otherwise.

I've played the previous King's Bounty Games and liked them so why not continue in the series?
Well there are good parts about this game and there are ugly parts.
Some of the good parts include being able to rank up your units for further stronger units, high level and leadership playthroughs, and more units! Of course there are several others but these are just some of the highlights a returning player can look forward to.
But what about the ugly parts? Crashes, many of them during mid battle and usually around the same amount of turns taken. There are small fixes to these such as doing other actions or changing your settings but these are all just annoying to do especially if you have to do them every few battles.
While the game is longer, it is just TOOOOO long, and if you own the dlc which adds a whole new area and more units to the game... yea that's about 10 to 20 hours longer. You may think it's well worth it but it's just so unnecessary. The battles get progressively easier, almost to the point where all you'll do is start off with a spell or two and just kill everything from a ranged distance. It's dull, the other games at least challenged you with bigger armies, with variety, to deal with, but this game puts mundane battles at you and puts many at you. It is just too much and isn't fun. You have to play the game for yourself to know what I mean.
Lastly, the second half of the game's bosses are a huge disappointment. They are not only weak but do so little damage that you'd be questioning: "wtf is this, why is the last boss so easy?". The second half is a huge let down and for that I suggest you skip this game.
There's just so much unnecessary stuff that was added to the game and it felt like you get no reward for it. The quests are a big problem, there's too many of them. Most of them just reward a paltry amount of exp and gold so there's no such thing as kite and explore for free levels anymore, which is what you could've done in the previous King's Bounty games. For better or worse, even if you didn't use the kite and explore trick the quests feel disappointing to do because again, they give paltry rewards. Here's an example: Defeat this villain that is at your level and has a Very Hard rating almost equal to your leadership to get 51 exp and 451 gold. Mind you that right now at this point in the game, each non-hero battle gives you at the very least 3k exp and 5000 gold and you need about 25000 exp to level. So yeah... what the hell is up with that crappy reward?
If you have to play the game mainly because it's in the series and you're a fan or just like the game, make sure you have patience. Units being able to rank up only adds to the unnecessary time wasting this game provides. If you have to 100% the game, it could take as much as 100 hours to do that.
I'd honestly skip this game for now. Go play the other titles first, which means play Dark Side first. Come back to this one when you feel REALLY bored. Because this game will bore you with endless pointless battles.

This one is really difficult. It's cheap. It offers a lot of play time. But at the same time the time actually spent with the game is rather boring and it's worse than the 2 predecessors, so "meh".
Anyone who has played King's Bounty and Armored Princess will feel right at home after starting up the game. And this is exactly wherein the problem lies. It's just more of the same. I pretty much completed all of the side quests I encountered and battled all the enemies I could find, and in the end I clocked in about 50 hours, which is WAY too much for what the game offers: moronic side quests and the same fights over and over again. Heck, there is pretty much nothing new in this game. All the mechanics are the same, the troops are the same (the only new troops are the Vikings I think...and a few "icy" reskins of existing troops). Instead of a demon box or a baby dragon you now get help from heavenly valkyries (which you unlock throughout the game), but the abilites aren't really all that interesting or new. Oh, your warriors now level up after a while...up to level 10. The bonuses they get are quite substantial later on (10% more HP for example and several points in attack, defense, crit, heal, etc.), which is on the one hand pretty cool and on the other pointless, since you will need to exchange your troops eventually. Viking troops will not readily be available for a long time for example. Same happens to human troops later on. This is quite irritating of course.
The quests have you running from one end of the world to the next way too often. I think half the time of the campaign I spent backtracking and retracing my steps. At least you can still put notes on the map. It's really not so bad in the beginning, when you can sail to individual islands, but once you get to the mainland...and then Demonis...oh my, ♥♥♥♥ you Demonis and your stupid elevators. You might wonder why we're back in Demonis...well, that's the whole mainland and Demonis are reskinned as well. I didn't even know this was taking place on the same world. It's all a bit confusing, but basically this is King's Bounty the Legend with a few additions. Armored Princess/Crossworlds was better by far. Even some of the bosses have been rehashed.
Then there are the bugs and constant crashes and no auto-save feature. Do yourself a favour and press F5 every few seconds. The game pretty much crashed once every hour on average. Only get this if you really want more King's Bounty...and devs? Please, for the love of God, if you don't speak English well, hire someone who does. The dialogue is terribly written, the quests are mostly boring stuff and spelling and grammar are atrocious. Not to mention that somehow you've managed to write the names of characters in 2 or 3 different ways in ONE dialogue window! How? That's a really unpolished product in that regard.
The best of the series. Not perfect or smooth as legends or crossworlds but better than those.

The Book Of Unwritten Tales is a very nice and fun adventure to play! The story is about the classic fantasy cliche about an ancient and powerful artifact, and the mission to recover it and save the world. You'll guide 4 main characters, sometimes together, sometimes alone.
The puzzles, all mainly based around collected objects, are not difficult at all, and the ending is a bit rushed out, but all the rest represents a great tribute to classic adventure games of the past, from Monkey Island to Legend of Kyrandia, from Day of the Tentacle to King's Quest.
Graphics and art are really beautiful, locations come to life and are very well characterized. There's a subtle but well played soundtrack and voice recording just nailed perfectly each character. Humor comes out from every single line of text, there are also a lot of fun quotes from mainstream games and movies, like The Lord of The Rings and Mission Impossible.
It's thanks to small but passionate developers like King Art, but I also think to Daedalic and Wadjet Eye, that we're still able to play adventure games like this one nowadays. Playing TBoUT was like returning back to mid '90s, and I surely hope to see more adventure developers to take the risk and the challenge to reinvent and innovate the genre, keeping the good from the past.
In the meantime, I'm looking forward to try this game's prequel, The Critter Chronicles, but even more its true sequel, the just released second chapter, which from what I read is going to be even more good!

TLDR: Buy this game, 10/10, it's awesome. A dash of 4X, a dash of RPG, some lovely art, voice-acting and a nice system as a whole come together for one of the more novel, engaging and enjoyable experiences I have had in a while.
I have played through a few rounds of thea now, having to restart due to a patch during my most recent advanced game; that didn't bug me in the slightest. My god's level advanced a bit and I got to play things slightly differently... and it was fun!
I play a lot of games, make the odd game and think (and occasionally write) about games, the people who play them and what it says about our culture. Of late, this has been depressing. Thea is the exception. The game has familiar elements, but it is fresh, combines things in novel ways and has an excellent narrative; it feels like it has created a new gaming experience. It's also an enjoyable gaming experience, and it's well worth the sticker price (but we all like steam sales).
Think an early civ game for exploring and resources, but you can't build more cities, and your troops are unique and varied. The choices and combat immediately show the departure from a purely civ-esque game. Along with the narrative--nearly all excerpts are pleasantly voiced by our storytelling narrator--the combination of events and their subsequent choices, and the combat engine give a very strong role-playing feel.
Unlike most RPGs, you do not have a character, you have a population. However, your people are all very individual. They have classes which give them tendencies towards subsets of the large number of skills. Your people all level up at once, and there is no choice in progression, but the type of people in your population tend to skill up based on what they are. Your witch might improve in magic, but is not likely to make gains in crafting. You can thus level-up your population as a whole, taking fine-grained control of how it develops by carefully tending your village.
The technology aspect lets you shape your city in terms of buildings, which affect who flocks to your city, and how people are raised there, as well as buffing for certain skills. You can also use technology to expand resource availability, a key element of the game. Lastly, you can advance technology to allow you to craft different varieties of things, from food, to weapons, armor and utility items.
I enjoy how Thea combines its variety of resources with its crafting, building and support systems. You unlock a type of thing to craft, but what you can craft and its properties are dependent on which resources you use, allowing a great deal of creation and customization. Even the buildings can pick up useful ancillary effects when you make use of novel construction materials. I am eagerly awaiting goblins after redoing several buildings with obsidian. Thea allows for variety in food production, and encourages its use by giving bonuses based on the variety of food. Your people eat food every turn, so your village and expeditions need to carry a varied supply if you want all the bonuses.
All challenges, be they combat or diplomacy, unfold using the same "card-based" combat system, different skills serving different purposes, depending on challenge-type. I find it easier to think about the combat system without inheriting any hang-ups from false associations with other card systems. The key thing is that what you can do is dependant on the skills of each unit involved. Your units are split into one of two groups, a combat group that gets to attack in two combat rounds, or a tactical group which can use its skills to augment various things or enter into the fray for the second combat round (soaking up damage in both rounds). Some skills are rare, so an approach that works well in a fighting challenge can be pretty useless in other types of challenge. Events give you some choice, depending on skill levels and group composition, as to what types of challenge you can use to resolve the various events, and the rewards (and failure penalties) can vary based on this. I find this mixes it up well enough that combat remains interesting.
Science itself, like experience, is doled out through the various events. While challenges gives you lots of experience, allowing your population to go up levels, technology comes in smaller amounts. The majority of technology comes from the crafting system. Rarer/bigger/better things, both buildings and equipment, give you more technology. Each level of technology takes more points, but if you don't deviate to expand resource availability, or the items/buildings, you end up building things you do not need, just to get tech points (a costly distraction). It leads to choices, but they feel like choices that affect the approach you want to move forward with, not the ability to move forward. I have tried a few different approaches, and aside from adjusting which skill challenges and some of my tactics, there was no issue, so it does not feel like you can easily make untenable tech choices. This really improved replayability for me, and encourages players to pay attention to the lay of the land early on.
One of the things that I felt were maybe less polished was the ease of remembering outcomes of choices in events. There are events all the time, and they keep things interesting, and are part of what makes the game great. While it does seem that there is some variety in outcomes, I felt that it was a bit thin.  When you find the herbs, you proceed to fight the spider-queen. It's never anything else and it always plays out the same (enemy numbers are the same). I have not looked at the event scripting system (which appears available directly, good for the devs for doing this!), but many events seems light, and easily gamed.
If you do not know that you can speed up the challenges rate of doing combat rounds, you are going to be irritated. Watch it play out slower a few times to get a feel, then speed that up or you will drive yourself nuts and waste lots of time, distracting you from an otherwise lovely game.
Making sure you are crafting a variety of foods is a nuisance. I recommend putting it in its own tab, then iterating on ways to make it more useable. The variety of foods and recipes is very good, it just needs a better interface.
The spear-based combat is broken. There are not enough fatty-filled combats to make the more direct-damage alternatives (even with what appears to be epic bonus potential) worthwhile. So far, this remains true on hard-mode as well. You can get 2-3 rounds of combat instead of 1-2, effectively. This needs further balance, particularly with high-strength characters.
Swarms of units generally win. It would be nice if there were size limits on expeditions, or more limits on cards-in-play during challenges.
That said, the positives massively outweigh the areas that need improvement. Buy this!

TL;DR: If you love challenging crafting/strategy/rpg-type games with a decent amount of RNG, this is phenomenal.  As a barometer, the other video games that I have spent a lot of time on in the past few years are: X-Com, Darkest Dungeon, Life is Strange, This War of Mine, and Hearthstone.
Thea: The Awakening is a wonderful game.  Before I continue extoling its virtues, let me pause and say that it is also a flawed game that clearly does not have the limitless resources of a blockbuster company.  It is hard to make an argument for certain gathering certain resources and trying certain playstyles (I’m looking at you, nimblewood, and you, bows, and you, all types of stone that weigh too much and prevent me from walking back to my village!) especially as you play on the harder difficulty settings.  If you play through a long game (my first game that I won was by turtling – to give a sense of that, it took me almost 2,000 turns to survive and build up.  There were a lot of mistakes made and ill-timed adventures that led to clicking my way to a bigger population) you will see the same quest many times over.  It is also a punishing, challenging game, especially if you are the type of gamer who likes to start their games on “difficult” (*raises hand*) – but to me, that is a positive.  I list it up here just because this will not be a game to play if your frustration threshold is low.
Now that I have talked through the game’s major challenges, let me talk through its high points.  The developers have really hit the nail on the head with their “leveling system” over multiple playthroughs.  Even after losing a game after a hundred turns in, I can watch the experience bar on my god shoot up, giving me a new trinket or additional buff on my next playthrough.  The gods themselves are wonderful – anyone who is a fan of mythology will appreciate the pantheon presented in the game.  The story is interesting– a lot of text, but even skimming through it will give you a few chuckles.  The best part is that after every playthrough I want to immediately start a new game.  Will there be an ever-elusive source of silver near my village?  Will this be the game I finally manage to recruit an elf to my side?  Will I survive on Godlike difficulty?  What are the resources like?  Each time I boot up a new game it gives me that sense of being about to take the edge of a quarter to a scratch-off ticket.
Let me conclude this review by saying that this is a game that makes me want to see more from its developers.  This is the first time a game has made me think I am doing a disservice by not writing a review (indeed, my first steam review) and it is also the first game that I’ve donated money to the devs to afterwards in the hope that they can continue producing lovely content.  If you’re still waffling at this point – just give it a try.
